Forward

The Bowdle Centennial Committee has endeavored to prepare a complete
history of the City of Bowdle and the surrounding area. Many long hours
have gone into research, going through the newspaper files and consulting
and visiting with longtime residents of the city and their descendants.

We are thankful for the good memories of many of the people who began life
in this community. Without them there could have been no book. We greatly
appreciate the cooperation of all who submitted histories, shared pictures
and who in any way prepared this information for publication.

That we have made mistakes there can be no question, but we did endeavor
not to make them. Some of the data was relayed by memory and memory fades
and sometimes differs according to the individuals consulted.

We gratefully acknowledge our advertisers who have helped defray the
expenses of publishing this book.

Most of all we wish to thank our forefathers for enduring the hardships, so
we the next generation, could enjoy a better life.

THE HISTORICAL COMMITTEE

Dedication

We respectfully dedicate this book to those hardy people who came to this
area when there were few trees or other comforts of life, and through their
hard work and devotion, brought this city into being and made possible the
progress of the community; many of whom are no longer with us, but are
appreciated and kindly remembered.

All men are like grass,
And all their glory is like the flowers of the field;
The grass withers and the flowers fall,
But the word of the Lord stands forever.

I Peter 1:24, 25

Toast To Bowdle

Bowdle, you've lived a century,
Center of this community,
Where we enjoyed a peaceful life--
Free from discord and racial strife.

Starting from tents, you quickly grew,
When tracks were laid and trains went through;
Pioneers made their homes of sod,
And building churches, worshipped God.

People who lived in this small town,
Greet us with smiles and seldom frown;
They work together; celebrate too--
Bowdle, our town, we're proud of you!

May coming years be kind to you,
Prosperity reign; and problems, few;
Your people well provided for,
May Bowdle thrive forevermore!

Esther L. Voller
[June 5, 1983]

                THE WHITE HOUSE
                  WASHINGTON
               February 21, 1985

To the Citizens of Bowdle:

I am pleased to send warm greetings to all those gathered to celebrate the
centennial of Bowdle.

The spirit which has built and sustained your community reflects the
energy which has forged America into a land of wonder. As a community held
by fellowship and goodwill, Bowdle has become "home" to many who love it
dearly. Further, it stands as an example of the blessings of liberty and
freedom to those around the world.

My hearty congratulations on this proud, historic occasion and my best
wishes in the years to come.

Ronald Reagan

                        Executive Proclamation
                         State of South Dakota
                        Office of the Governor

WHEREAS, Bowdle, South Dakota, was founded May 20, 1886, on Section 21,
Township 123, Range 73 in Edmunds County, as was named by the Milwaukee
Railroad in honor of the land buyer, Alex M. Bowdle; and,

WHEREAS, From its original platting, Bowdle remained the terminus of the
Milwaukee Railroad until 1900; and,

WHEREAS, Dr. William Edwards opened his medical practice and the only
hospital in the county with the assistance of Rose Holzman, R.N., in 1886,
and he served the community's medical needs until his death; and,

WHEREAS, The Bowdle Pioneer moved to Bowdle, began publication on March 23,
1886, and is still serving the community today; and,

WHEREAS, The Bowdle Flour Mill is one of the oldest businesses in town and
in 1904, it won silver and gold medals at the World's Fair; and,

WHEREAS, In 1924, for the first time in the history of South Dakota, a
carload of South Dakota butter was shipped directly to the European market
from the Bowdle Creamery, which, in 1928, held the distinction of being the
only creamery between Aberdeen, South Dakota, and Miles City, Montana; and,

WHEREAS, In 1909, Bowdle gained the nickname the Windmill and Garden City
because of the 96 windmills in the community; and,

WHEREAS, Today, Bowdle is a thriving community of people who are proudly
celebrating Bowdle's first one hundred years with memorable festivities and
commemorations:

NOW, THEREFORE, I, WILLIAM J. JANKLOW, Governor of the State of South
Dakota, do hereby proclaim June 27-29, 1986, as

                BOWDLE CENTENNIAL CELEBRATION DAYS

in South Dakota.

IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand and caused to be affixed
the Great Seal of the State of South Dakota, in Pierre, the Capital City,
this Seventh Day of November, in the Year of Our Lord, Nineteen Hundred and
Eighty-Five

William J. Janklow, Governor

ATTEST:

Alice Kundert, Secretary of State

A SALUTE TO BOWDLE - - -

as the community gathers to celebrate the Centennial of its founding.

It is a great pleasure to extend my congratulations and best wishes to all
of you as Bowdle attains this significant milestone in its history, and to
thank you for making it the fine community it is in which to live.

I am sure the pioneer railroad builders would be proud of the way you have
progressed through the years and how well you have served the agricultural
community of north central South Dakota.

Your public spiritedness, your outlook and optimism through good years and
bad, has been responsible for this progress.  Above all, you have been good
neighbors in the finest sense.

May your progress and prosperity continue for another century.

With best regards to all of you, I am

Sincerely,
JAMES ABDNOR
United States Senator


Dear Friends:

The residents of Bowdle and the surrounding rural community certainly have
a great deal to celebrate on this wonderful occasion of Bowdle's centennial
anniversary.

Day by day, South Dakota pushes into the future, leaving an
ever-lengthening story of development and achievement. Yours is a proud
heritage.  The courageous pioneers who settled Dakota Territory when it was
a vast, isolated stretch of land had a strong sense of duty to family,
church and community.  The history of South Dakota was shaped in towns like
Bowdle and today we should reflect upon the principles and the ideals that
are America's true strength.

I congratulate you on this 100th birthday celebration and extend my very
best wishes to all.

Sincerely,
Larry Pressler
United States Senator

                United States of America 1886

EVENTS

January 19: The Presidential Succession Act is adopted. It stipulates that
if both the President and Vice President die, resign, or otherwise are
unable to function, the presidential succession shall pass to the members
of the Cabinet in the order in which their offices were established.

March 1: President Cleveland informs the Senate that despite the Tenure of
Office Act the President is authorized by the Constitution to suspend or
remove officers without the consent of the Senate.

March 1 - May 3: Railroad workers belonging to the Knights of Labor wage an
unsuccessful general strike against the railroad system controlled by Jay
Gould.

April 8: A bill calling for the free coinage of silver, sponsored by Rep.
Richard P. Bland, is narrowly defeated in the House of Representatives.

May 4: At a mass meeting in Haymarket Square, Chicago, called to protest
the shooting of striking workers on May 3, a bomb is thrown, killing seven
policemen and injuring many others.

May 10: In Santa Clara County v. Southern Pacific Railroad, the Supreme
Court rules that the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment
protects the rights of corporations as legal persons. ' '

June 19 - August 20: Eight alleged anarchists accused of conspiracy in the
Haymarket bombing are convicted in a trial in Chicago. Seven of them are
sentenced to death and one to prison. Two of the death sentences are
commuted to life imprisonment, and one man commits suicide; the other
four men are hanged Nov. 11, 1887. The three survivors are pardoned in 1893
by Governor John Peter Altgeld, who severely criticizes the trial.

August 3: An act of Congress authorizes the construction of additional
ships for the United States Navy, which is brought up to date by Secretary
of the Navy William C. Whitney.

September 4: The Apache chief Geronimo and his band are captured by Gen.
Nelson A. Miles, ending a struggle in Arizona, New Mexico and Mexico that
has lasted since 1876.

October 28: The Statue of Liberty, given to the United States by the people
of France, is dedicated by President Cleveland on Redloe's (Liberty)
Island, New York Harbor.

December 8: The American Federation of Labor evolves from the annual
convention of the Federation of Organized Trades and Labor Unions. Samuel
Gompers is its first president.

SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY

1. Bell develops wax disks for use with a modified version of Edison's
phonograph.

2. Westinghouse establishes the Westinghouse Electric Company and builds
America's first commercially successful alternating current power plant in
Buffalo, New York.

3. James E. Keeler, Illinois astronomer, discovers that Saturn's rings are
made up of tiny pieces of meteors. His telescope was built by Alvan Clark,
Massachusetts astronomer.

4. Ives developed a halftone photoengraving process.

5. Thomson patents an electric resistance welding process.

6. The U.S. Forest Service is established as the Division of Forestry, U.S.
Department of Agriculture.

South Dakota, known as the Sunshine State, is the state to the town of
Bowdle. The state's history originated in 1803 when the State of South
Dakota was acquired by the United States through the Louisiana Purchase.

In 1861 President James Buchanan signed the Organic Act creating the Dakota
Territory. Twenty-eight years later in 1889, the Omnibus Bill or Enabling
Act was adopted by Congress which provided for the dividing of the Dakota
Territory into the states of North and South Dakota and enabled the two
Dakotas, Montana and Washington to formulate constitutions.

The South Dakota Constitution was adopted in 1889. The first constitutional
convention seeking South Dakota statehood was held in 1883. This was the
first time the people of Dakota Territory petitioned Congress for admission
to the Union. A second convention was held two years later.

In 1889 the third convention drafted the final constitutional provisions
and Nov. 2, 1889 President Benjamin Harrison signed the document that made
South Dakota the 39th or 40th state.

North Dakota was admitted to the Union on the same day, and the President
intentionally shuffled the two proclamations so it is not known which was
signed first.

The South Dakota Constitution provides that the governmental powers of the
state are "divided into three distinct departments: the legislative,
executive and judicial; and the powers and duties of each are prescribed by
this Constitution."

                        EDMUNDS COUNTY

County Seat--Ipswich         Population--5,548         Square Miles--1,158

Edmunds County was created in 1873 and organized July 26, 1883. It was
named for Newton Edmunds, a New Yorker who was second Territorial Governor
of South Dakota. He was appointed by President Lincoln in 1863 and served
until 1866.

The first settlement was by Ezra Drew and Ira Dribble and families on
October 16, 1882.

The Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul Railroad built into the county from
Aberdeen. In the center of a triangle formed by the towns of Freeport,
Edmunds, and Georgetown the town of Ipswich was plotted on October 2 1883.
It was named for the hometown of Charles Prior, Superintendent of the
railroad. This line still serves our county.

The first county seat was located at Edmunds July 26, 1883. On October 2,
1883, Ipswich become county seat, as it is today. Willard Brown was the
first white child born in the county.

The first public school building was in Ipswich in 1886. The first classes
had been held in store buildings and homes until the school was built.

Early churches were held in homes and store buildings. In 1883 the
Methodist Church and Powell Township Presbyterian churches organized. The
Baptist Church organized in 1884. The first Catholic mass was held in
Ipswich in 1884. The Catholics built their first church in 1887.

One of the first post offices was in Powell Township and opened May 16,
1883. Morris Jones was postmaster. This was a Welsh settlement called
Powell Colony. On August 7, 1883, Jones was appointed Official Postmaster by
the Government. In 1884 a postal building was erected. Powell is 10 miles
south of Ipswich and still maintains a Presbyterian Church and town hall.

Ipswich is known as the "Home of the Yellowstone Trail" and "Arch City".
Mr. J. W. Parmley was father of the Yellowstone Trail, now Highway 12, and
it started from Ipswich in 1886. It goes from Puget Sound, Washington to
Plymouth, Massachusetts.

The Memorial Arch was built after World War I, when the people of Ipswich
were welcoming home the servicemen. The first Arch was wooden and built
across Main Street. When traffic required it be moved it was placed over
Highway 12 where the "traffic of the continent would pass under it". After
several years it was destroyed by a tornado. The people rebuilt it this
time of stone. A sealed metal box containing the history of Edmunds County
and the Louisiana Purchase are buried in the south pillar along with Indian
artifacts. Bronze plaques commemorate the dead of World War I and J. W.
Parmley. The stones of the Arch come from all over the world. In 1974 it
became necessary once more to move the Arch. It now is in Ipswich Park.

Also at Ipswich is a Pioneer Village and Schoolhouse and Prayer Rock Museum
and Library.

Lake Parmley at Mina has a state park and recreation area.

Hosmer is located in the northwest corner of Edmunds County. The name was
given by Captain Arnold who had married a lady whose maiden name was
Hosmer. The town was established in April of 1887. The first post office
was established the same year. On January 3, 1888 a petition for
organization of a school district was presented at a regular Commissioners
meeting held in Ipswich, South Dakota. Roscoe was started in July 1883. It
wad named after Roscoe Conklin, a New York statesman.

Charles P. Morgan and J. W. Parmley were the first settlers in April, 1883.

Henry Huck from Chicago started a newspaper business and published the
"Roscoe Herald". Mr. Huck proved to be a great community leader.

The first white child was born to Mrs. Elmer Lewis. The baby was named
Roscoe.

A couple years after Roscoe was founded, the railroad come through, went on
west and branches also went to Orient, South Dakota and Linton, North Dakota
from Roscoe, making the town a railroad center.

There were several bad fires in Roscoe in the 1890's that threatened to
destroy the whole town.

The town purchased its first electric light and power plant in 1916.

In 1933 Roscoe lost a bitter fight for the County Courthouse.

Bowdle which was platted in 1886 was named after the townsite agent Alex M.
Bowdle. The first issue of the "Bowdle Pioneer' was dated May 10, 1886. Mr.
Fred J. Bowman was the editor of the paper.

There is a possibility that a salon may have been the first business in the
new town.

The C. M. & St. Paul Railroad was completed to Bowdle on September 9, 1896.
Bowdle become a booming railroad town upon the completion of the railroad.

Bowdle has a museum and library under construction, and an airport today.

The town of Loyalton, once a busy little community, has lost all its
business places. In the early 1970's it lost its post office.

Beebe, a ghost town, was located eight miles west of Ipswich, and was started
in 1910. During its lifetime, Beebe had many businesses. All buildings
disappeared from the townsite in the early 1960's.

Towns in Edmunds County are Bowdle, Hosmer, Ipswich, Mina, and Roscoe.

Some of the towns that have come and gone are Beebe, Cravan, Gretna,
Loyalton, Powell Settlement, and Vermont City.

There are three Hutterite Colonies in Edmunds County. They are PlainView in
Rosette Township, Deerfield in Belle Township, and Pembrook in Harmony
Township.

Before Bowdle Was A Town

It seems that there were three quite separate groups of settlers who came
to the Dakota Territory. First came the French trappers who stayed quite
close to the water areas. Then came a wave of Americans from the eastern
United States, plus several from western European countries.

This second group settled primarily during the years 1875 to 1890. The lure
of "free land" brought most of them, and when they found that hard work and
deprivation were included with the land, they went back East.

The third group, starting in the early 90's were the Germans, and the
Swedes, and the German-Russians, and they came to stay.

George Nies's grandparents, George and Mary Ryan, came with the second
group in 1883 and stayed on. Their grandparents/great-grandparents had come
from Ireland in 1710. George and Mary had three surviving children: Mable,
who married Robert Wagy; Ethel, who married Peter Nies and Helen, who
married Joe Szarka.

The following letter tells us how it was.

                [By George W. Ryan]

Horace Greeley, that eminent journalist, at one time said: "Go West, young
man, and grow up with the country."

So a number of us followed his advice and went west from Chicago over the
Chicago & Northwestern Railway, landing at Ordway, the terminal at that
time. It was the first time we had seen a prairie country. There was very
little that attracted our attention at Ordway except a huge heap of trunks
piled up on the ground sky-high, many of them smashed and their contents
scattered by the four winds of Dakota. So we drifted down to Aberdeen, the
only Hub of the universe west of Boston.

It was April 1883. A real land boom was on. It was land, land, land! The
only patch left and yet obtainable was in the neighborhood of Swan Lake,
and that was going rapidly.

This garden spot was on the proposed railway from Aberdeen to LeBeau. And
what about LeBeau? Why, LeBeau was the geographical center of Dakota
Territory. It was located on the great Missouri River and destined to
become the Capital City of the third state in size in the Union.

There were four young men in our party. We listened attentively to the talk
of the smart men of the west; were credulous enough to believe everything
they said and having heard, that "fortune knocks at every man's door once
in a lifetime,'' felt that we were at the very threshold of the wealth
which every young person hopes for. We procured a small pamphlet and map
and read it, and caught the same fever with which those around us were
afflicted. Our fever ran high, our pulse beat quick and fast. No wonder,
this pamphlet and map described and pictured Swan Lake and Swan River, a
beautiful body of water and a beautiful river emptying into the lake at one
end and running out of the lake at the other end and flowing on towards the
west until it formed a junction with the Big Muddy right where the great
city and beautiful capital of the wonderland state was sure to be located.

Imagine our anticipation! A strip of timber from one to two miles wide was
said to extend the whole length of Swan River and all around Swan Lake. And
game! O, my! Of every kind except maybe elephants and tigers and a few more
like that. And the fish! Just lots and lots of them. And wild fruit too.
How hungry we got right away for the feasts we would have when we got there.

On this map were pictured yellow sulfur springs, black sulfur springs,
beaver dams, mill sites and dam sites. So we bought an ox team, a wagon, a
plow, a tent, a stove, some blankets, a quantity of provisions, a sack of
ground feed, a bale of hay, a muzzle loader shotgun, a supply of ammunition
and everything else the Aberdeen dealers told us we should have, hitched
up, drove in front of the Aberdeen bank, called out the cashier to look at
our outfit, told him we wanted to go west.

He asked us where? But we couldn't tell him for we didn't know. But we told
him that if he would loan us $100 he could take a mortgage on all we had.
But he should do business quick as we were in a hurry. We got the money and
he got the mortgage and this was the first chattel mortgage I ever signed,
but it was by no means the last one.

So we started west. One of our party was an oxdriver. He had had experience
in using the gad. He was proud to show what he could do. The rest of us
didn't know beans about driving oxen. He had all the "cuss" words of the
English vocabulary at his tongue's end and the way he could swing the whip
and fling those expletives was a caution.

Our oxdriver took the lead. We arrived at Snake Creek a little before
sunset. The water was deep and murky. Before we plunged in we thought it
best to investigate. One of the party with a lath in hand walked out on a
plank, reached into the water and mud beneath to try the bottom, lost his
balance and pitched forward, head first into four feet of icy water. Our
driver piloted the oxen across and soon we were on the west side of Snake
Creek. We pitched our tent and camped for the night.

The next day we pushed on until we got near Freeport (now Ipswich.) The day
was warm and our oxen were tired. When night came we pitched our tent and,
at my suggestion, we tied the oxen to the yoke, thinking that they were too
tired to move before morning. About midnight a fierce cold wind from the
northwest struck us. Before daylight one of the boys looked out of the tent
and reported that our oxen were gone. After hunting in every direction with
a lantern for two hours we discovered that our oxen had started back on the
road towards Aberdeen dragging the yoke with them.

Well, the boy who had fallen into Snake Creek the night before and myself
walked back nine miles, got the oxen and returned to the tent before
breakfast. A tramp on foot of over 20 miles before break- fast! Just
imagine.

Breakfast over, we started on. A little after noon we arrived at Roscoe
(advertised as a second Chicago.) Here Harry Morgan was running a hotel in
a big white tent. Here we ate dinner. A day or two before R.L. Walker had
shot a buffalo near Swan River, so Hotel Morgan had buffalo beef for
dinner. The boys guessed it was the old buffalo that Noah had in the ark.
And judging from the dark color of the meat and the toughness of fibre,
their conjecture, apparently might have been correct.

After dinner we continued our journey toward the setting sun. Two more
nights passed and the following day we reached old Theodore--a board shack,
three tents and a sod stable. The whole prairie was barren of vegetation as
a floor, not a tree in sight. Where was the beautiful river? Where was the
beautiful lake? Where was the belt of timber? How about the fish, the game,
the mill site, the sulfur springs and the dam sites? Well, our oxdriver
said the whole blamed country was a damn sight.

We were now located in the glorious West. Our sack of ground feed and our
bale of hay were eaten up. The prairie grass had been burned off slick and
clean for hundreds of miles in every direction. Our oxen were tired out and
footsore and the boy who had fallen in the water was sick and no doctor
nearer than Aberdeen. Yes, we were located. We couldn't go ahead and we
couldn't go back. Two days passed and Jim said, "As there is nothing doing
around Swan Lake I will go back to Aberdeen." And he went.

Our oxdriver expressed no intention of giving up. To keep our oxen from
starving we hauled up from the lake old grass, that apparently had been too
wet to burn when the fire went through.

A few more days went by and we were coming from the lake to the tent, a
distance of four miles, in a storm. It was a mixture of snow and gale. For
some little time our driver had not said a word, something very unusual for
him. But when we got to the tent he jumped off the wagon and his pent-up
forces broke loose. It was a veritable explosion. What he said about Dakota
wasn't the least bit nice. Said he, "I wouldn't be dead in a place like
this. Tomorrow morning I start for Aberdeen. If you ever get a chance to
send my trunk to Aberdeen I wish you would. If not, let it go to _ _ ll. I
am going back to Pennsylvania and I am going to stay there." And he did.

Myself and the sick boy stayed. It was the only thing we could do. Just
about the time our edibles were exhausted blackbirds, plovers and ducks
appeared. And, at the same time, Sam Lovet, a little Englishman, was
located near us in a good 8 by 10 shack with an oil stove and a few cooking
utensils. He was placed there to guard the rights of the soldiers colony.
We made his acquaintance and found him to be a good, pleasant and obliging
young man. Birds were plentiful now. And by the use of the shotgun and with
Sam to prepare the meals we all lived on the fat of the land.

Yellowstone Trail

JUNE 5, 1913
  Work was begun on the Twin City-Yellowstone Trail where it passed through
Bowdle. Contractor Sampson began work on the 3-mile stretch from Bowdle to
the Walworth County line. His outfit consists of an elevator grader pulled
by a gasoline engine. The grading on this stretch is being done at a cost
of $50 per mile to the contractor. The state will build one mile of the
road through the state lands east of Bowdle, thus leaving 8 miles in the
Bowdle division under the supervision of Mayor Kelles and H.C. Gross.

JUNE 4, 1914
  Every telephone pole on the south side of the Trail from Bowdle to the
Walworth County line three miles west wears a yellow band a foot wide since
"Trail Day" May 22. The markings were made equally well for nine miles east
by the evening of that day and we understand have since been connected with
the markings of Roscoe, making them continuous to Ipswich.

JULY 24, 1924
  A number of crews are at work at various points on the Yellowstone Trail
through Walworth and Edmunds counties to the Brown County line. From there
east the Trail is graveled. After next year it will then be possible to
drive a motor car from the Missouri River wagon bridge at Mobridge to the
Atlantic Ocean on a graveled or paved Yellowstone Trail every foot of the
way.

JULY 24, 1924
  A.W. Tyler of Sioux Falls and Theo. Basler of Frankfort are setting up
the markings on the Yellowstone Trail. This road is No. 16. All the signs
are made of wood painted white with black letters and are of various
shapes. A square board designates warning of schools, side roads, narrow
or cross roads; a diamond shape means hill, curves, sharp turn or winding
road and round signs for railroad crossings.
  A board about 10 by 16 inches is put up at every cross road or section
line. A movement is underway to standardize the markings of trails and 11
states have accepted the markings used by South Dakota.
  The markings were completed to the county line west of town, at least,
Wednesday of last week.

SEPTEMBER 22, 1938
  The Summit Construction Company oiled U.S. Highway 12 through this city,
completing their job of blacktopping. The oil mat extends over a length of
about 40 miles, running from Ipswich to six miles west of Bowdle.

How Bowdle Got Its Name

        Written by Mrs. Alex M. Bowdle in
        June 18, 1936 Bowdle Pioneer

        Alex Milton Bowdle      Amanda Bowdle

Alex M. Bowdle of Mitchell was employed by the Chicago & Milwaukee Railroad
to secure townsites. During one of his trips to Milwaukee he told his
family that the company had asked him to name a new town for them. Various
names were considered and the matter forgotten. A few weeks later, to his
surprise, he was notified that the town had been named "Bowdle" for him.

Alex M. Bowdle was born in Van Wert County, Ohio May 31, 1849. He lost his
father when he was six months old and at the age of 15 years began to
support himself. In the year 1856 he moved to Tama County, Iowa and after
attending the Agriculture College at Ames and Mt. Vernon College, both in
Iowa, he graduated from the Bryant & Stratton Mercantile College at
Davenport, IA. Then he became Deputy County Auditor for two years.

At the age of 21 Mr. Bowdle located in Eldora, Iowa where his active
business life began. Here Mr. J.D. Newcomer and he formed their partnership
which broadened into the Iowa and Dakota Land Co., in which J.Q. Adams of
Spencer, Iowa became a member. Mr. Bowdle was president of this firm.

Nov. 7, 1872 Mr. Bowdle was united in marriage with Miss Amanda M.
Reynolds, daughter of Rev. and Mrs. C.P. Reynolds, at Brighton, Iowa. They
had one son, Ralph Raymond Bowdle, June 25, 1876.

In the Spring of 1882 the family moved to Mitchell where he became manager
of one of the banks of which Mr. J.D. Lawler was president. He was employed
by Chicago & Milwaukee Railroad to secure town sites and it was on one of
these trips that he was asked to name the town which was later named
BOWDLE. The town received its name in the early spring 1887, but Mrs.
Bowdle was not sure of the exact date.

Alex M. Bowdle had an ambitious life, according to his accomplishments
during his short life. He was in legislature at the time of the division of
the territory and formation of the two states. He was Mayor of Mitchell and
instrumental in locating the University of Mitchell, now called Dakota
Wesleyan University.

At the time of his death he was president of his own bank. Death occurred
June 9, 1893 at the age of 44, in the Emergency Hospital at Chicago. He died
from surgery for a disease he had suffered from for two years.

His funeral was held at four o'clock in his home at Mitchell. Later a large
procession, headed by a band, followed by a commendery of 31 men and a line
of 150 carriages made the solemn trip to the gravesite. It was known to be
the largest procession in the history of the town of Mitchell.

To show the popularity of Alex M. Bowdle the Mitchell paper, The Sunday
Republican, June 18, 1893 dedicated the entire paper in his honor. Many
articles were written by people who remembered him, including his complete
funeral service.

In 1893 the other surviving relatives were his stepfather, Orrin Burright,
living at Toledo, IA, age 84; the mother, age 75; a brother, J.A. Bowdle of
Hebron, NE and a half brother, D.W. Burright of Mitchell. (Mrs. Bowdle
stated in her report that Alex's final resting place is in the beautiful
cemetery in Toledo, Ohio.)

JUNE 20, 1985
  Two couples from Texas, Lowell & Edra Bowdle and Harvey & Wava Bowdle,
visited the town that has their surname of Bowdle. None of them are sure of
any relationship to Alex M. Bowdle, the person who supplied the city its
name.

City Dads and City Government

        Compiled by Alma Leno and Adeline Miller, assisted by Joyce Giedt

Bowdle was named for Alex M. Bowdle, a land buyer for the Chicago,
Milwaukee Railroad in the late 1800's. He never saw the townsite named in
his honor for services rendered as a purchaser of the "right of way." A
nephew visited the city about 1940 when Albert Senn was the publisher of The
Bowdle Pioneer, but Mr. Bowdle never saw the town. He made his home at
Mitchell in Dakota Territory. However, he did own some lots in the city.

Cedric Marion Lindholm was the first white child to be born in Bowdle,
arriving April 12, 1882. He later moved to Hennepin County, Minneapolis, MN
where he held the office of Chicago Probation Officer for that county.

Bowdle was governed by a board of trustees elected by the populace,
beginning in 1886 and the only trustees on record are A.G. Bickert, H.G.
Slyder and Pete Geib with H.E. Yaukey (the druggist) as clerk.

        Alex M. Bowdle

DEC. 21, 1911
  The new Corporate Seal of the City of Bowdle was received last week. In
the center is an old Dutch windmill, signifying our city of windmills and
abundance of good water, surrounded by the wording, "City of Bowdle, S.D.
Corporate Seal."

                1911 - 1912
Bowdle was incorporated as a third class city on August 21, 1911. The
population of the town was 900 persons and the first mayor elected was Dr.
Wm. Edwards. Dr. Edwards served from 1911 thru 1912 and was succeeded by
Rev. Keller of the Lutheran Church.

                1914 - 1916
Ole Larson, owner of the jewelry store, was elected to the office of mayor,
serving until 1916 when Jacob Kurle, the village blacksmith, was elected.

There had been many opportunities to improve the city during these first
five years the mayors served, but unfortunately there is no record of their
accomplishments. There was a city light plant by that time, which kept the
town well lighted until midnight when everything went dark. This plant was
located at the flour mill at one time and later moved to a lot on the S.E.
Corner of 5th Avenue and Main Street.

Jacob J. Kurle  John C. Gross
 1916 - 1920     1920 - 1922
 1946 - 1948

                1918 - 1920
J.K. Kurle was elected mayor again in 1918 and John Rhodes, a realtor, was
city auditor. Contracts were let to lay cement sidewalks to replace the old
wooden walks. A building permit was issued for the St. Augustine's Roman
Catholic Church. A five acre dump ground was established on land owned by
Fred Pietzke.

                1920 - 1922
John C. Gross, Mayor; Martin C. Gross, Auditor. The city voted to have
Gedney and Murphy install water and sewer lines. Fire protection was
provided with the purchase of 1200 feet of hose, 4 nozzles and 2 hose carts
for $1,550 from Eureka Fire Co. The city purchased land from John Meakins
for the city ball park west of town (present site of Larry Haar's
Trucking.) Limits for the fire department service were extended to cover the
entire platted city in 1921.

Dumont Street (now 3rd Avenue) was extended to cross the Milwaukee Railroad
tracks to the north. The Bowdle Produce Creamery was issued a permit to
build on Main Street, the present site. Final settlement on the water and
sewer system totaled $157,805.

                1922 - 1923
C.W. Young, Mayor; later replaced with Lou Merkel as mayor and Karl J.
Kundert, Auditor. The city made a donation of $125 to the Yellowstone Trail
Association.

JUNE 13, 1907
  For the first time in its history the town of Bowdle has been sued for
$100 for damages caused by a broken sidewalk. Mrs. Maggie Fix and child
were thrown a few weeks ago and the Board refusing to pay damages as asked,
a suit was filed.

                1924 - 1926
John Erbe, Mayor; R.A. Ellwein, Auditor. Pay for judges and clerks were
raised to $3.50 for an election and councilmen to $15 a year. The painting
of the water tower and tank cost $85. A proposal was made from the Mobridge
Light and Power Co. to purchase the light plant, lines and equipment for
$5,000. Other conditions included 24-hour service at 16 cents KW; power at
10 cents KW and a 20-year franchise. This light plant proposal received 132
yes to 58 no votes.

                1926 - 1928
K. Kundert, Mayor; A.C. Merkel, Auditor. Five thousand dollars from the
sale of the light plant was used to pay the water bond. In 1927 the city
purchased a building (red building) over the septic tank for $233.

                1928 - 1930
John Erbe, Mayor; F.G. Grosz, Auditor. The city's new well was constructed
at a cost of $646 and the building for the well cost $445. Repair and
painting of the water tank cost $115. A permit was given to the Evangelical
United Brethren Church to move a church building to Bowdle.

JUNE 11, 1914
  Current will be supplied every Wednesday forenoon from 8 to 11 o'clock
for the use of those possessing electric irons. A petition from the
housewives was presented to the council at the last meeting asking that the
plant be run these hours. Over 30 irons are in use in Bowdle at that time.
The irons can be procured at the power house for the small sum of $3 and
they are guaranteed for 5 years but will last indefinitely. Cost of current
is cheap, about 3 cents per hour.

AUG. 16, 1906 ... "This & That"
   By C.T. Smithers, editor
If you want a prosperous town where people can come who are disposed to
make homes, then do away with and bury from sight all jealousy and spite,
work, move for common propriety and mutual benefit. Wake up, rub your eyes,
roll up your sleeves and go to work. Do not work with fear and trembling,
but take it for granted that blood will tell. Leave results to themselves,
borrow no trouble, but all unite to make it the biggest kind of a town. Go
to work!

     Dr. F.A. Miller        Albert Berg

Robert Beadle, Mayor; Joyce Giedt, Finance Officer. The city approved the

The lease was extended to 40 years. Accomplishments are short, due to the
fact Mayor Beadle is just serving his term at this writing in 1985.

Water was of prime concern before and during Mayor Beadle's term. City
Council members faced three (two in 1983, one in 1985) referendums against
their actions regarding the hooking up with the WEB Water Pipeline which
runs along U.S. Highway 12. All three elections went against hooking up to
the water pipeline.

Action by the council members was based on the scientific findings of
contamination of the shallow water wells and scarcity of quality well water.

FROM JUNE 10, 1920 BOWDLE PIONEER
  Gedney & Murphy of St. Cloud, MN gave the lowest bid. They will complete
the sewer and water works for $147,120.13. This includes labor and material.

FROM SEPTEMBER 2, 1920 BOWDLE PIONEER
  Water pipes are along the streets of the city and have hung red signal
lanterns at all points of danger on our work but some are vandalizing by
rolling the pipes in the street and carrying off the red lanterns.

FROM NOVEMBER 25, 1920 BOWDLE PIONEER
  The contractors for the water works have secured one good well on the
lots purchased by J. Mueller. This well is 90 feet deep and has 55 feet of
water in it. Also drilling a well back of the present power house.

FROM MARCH 3, 1921 BOWDLE PIONEER
  Work on the supply tank for the water works system is progressing nicely.
The tower which is 150 feet high, is up and part of the tank has been put
into place.

FROM DECEMBER 8, 1921 BOWDLE PIONEER
  An examination of the elevated tank did not disclose any severe defects.
It appears to be a standard 50,000 gallon Pittsburgh-DeMoines Steel Tank. The
concrete cap stones carrying the tower legs appear to be poor in quality
and workmanship.

FROM AUGUST 10, 1922 BOWDLE PIONEER
  The drinking fountain, donated by the Bowdle Hardware Co., was installed
by the city Friday. Now all who are thirsty can drink of the city water.

FROM JUNE 10, 1937 BOWDLE PIONEER
  The tower was repaired and repainted in aluminum. The word BOWDLE was
painted in great big letters in dark green on both sides of the tank.

FROM BOWDLE DIAMOND JUBILEE BOOK
  March 10, 1920 a special election was held for the purpose of voting on
water and sewer system bonds. This election carried. The water and sewer
system was completed in 1921 at $157,804.94.
  There was a lot of dissatisfaction with the construction work as quite a
number of leaks appeared in the water mains upon testing, so final payment
was withheld. The bill was finally paid off. The city water bond was in the
amount of $40,000 and the sewer bond was in the amount of $23,000. The
balance was to be raised by the sale of water and sewer rights for all
property lots, some of which were never paid. Except for some errors in the
survey for depth of sewer, we have one of the finest systems in South
Dakota.
  We have the distinction of having the highest water tower in South
Dakota. Since that time we have added new wells, reservoir and disposal
plant. The last $3,000 of the city water and sewer bond
was paid off August 1, 1949.
  In 1985, as an interesting note...talking with some citizens of Bowdle
they recall, "The water tower was brought to this city by mistake. It was to
be transported to another town. Due to the expense of moving it, Bowdle
decided to keep it."

APRIL 21, 1921
  C.H. Gross has the honor of being the first in town to use city water.

Firsts of Bowdle

   Researched and compiled by Connie Goetz

C.T. Smithers, Editor of The Bowdle Pioneer, wrote this article in a
special edition of December 1906.

Bowdle grew from an empty prairie land in the spring of 1886, into a
thriving, hustling, little city. The town is situated two miles from the
west line of Edmunds County in Section 21, Township 123, Range 73 West 5th
P.M. and 1,995 feet above sea level in Edmunds County. It lies directly
east of a range of hills and is well drained with a gentle slope toward the
west.

The townsite of Bowdle was First in the process of being platted in the
early part of April 1886, but was not officially completely platted until a
Saturday night, May 20, 1886.

The town was platted at the time the C.M. & St. Paul Railroad was extended
west from Ipswich and was the terminus of the line until 1900 when the
railroad again extended west to the Missouri River which is 35 miles from
here.

Whether it was by chance or not that the town was platted in this certain
spot depended entirely upon the decision of the railroad officials and the
surveyors as to where in 1886 the railroad would have its terminus. It
certainly was a spot well-chosen especially for its water facilities. Very
few towns located in South Dakota had the water facilities that Bowdle
enjoyed. Water was found at a depth of 15-75 feet. It was the purity of the
water that made it ideal for drinking and irrigation. The railroad
authorities considered it to be the best water to be used in the boilers.

The town of Bowdle was First incorporated Aug. 5, 1895 and the First
officers were as follows Clark Hudson (trustee, 1st ward); J.U. Miner
(trustee, 2nd ward); H.D. Baillett (Trustee, 3rd ward); C.H. Musser (clerk)
Wm. Edwards (treasurer); H.C. Ward (Marshal); James H. McKoane (Justice of
the Peace); Jacob Strobel (Assessor); Albert Lawein (Street Commissioner.)

The First paper issued was The Pioneer, by Fred J. Bowman, May 10, 1886,
who removed the plant from Scranton in Walworth County. It was then called
the Scranton Pioneer.

The First saloon built in town was by Tom O'Malley in August 1886.

The First effort to light the city by electricity was in 1896 when Wm.
McGlenn ran the flour mill. The plant was next run by the creamery for one
year and about 10 days by Myron Sayers with his large, bucking gasoline
engine. This machine would run fairly well in the daytime, but at night
would stop short and the lights were not a very big success. In 1897 Ring
Bros. (Simon C.A. Ring and Eugene E. Ring) ran the plant in connection with
their feed mill, making it successful. They remodeled, rewired and put in
electric meters and rewired the houses, making it the best.

The First child born was a daughter to M.T. Dewwody and wife Tuesday, Oct.
12, 1886. The First doctor was Wm. Edwards who built the First hospital.

The First wedding to take place was Rev. H.H. Parkhurst and Miss Carrie J.
Ham of Theodore at the residence of J.G. Davies by Rev. Wm. McCready of the
Congregational Church Nov. 24, 1886.

The lot for the First school was donated by Messrs. Bowdle and Newcomer.
The deed is dated Sept. 20, 1887. The First school board elected in 1886
and consisted of the following members: H.G. Tuller, chairman; J.N. Paul,
treasurer and G.C. Aurand, clerk. The First school in Bowdle was held
during 1886-1887 upstairs in G.C. Aurand's store building, for the use of
which a rental of $10 a month was paid. The First teacher was Mrs. E.P.
Price. She received a salary of $40 per month. A.F. LeClaire & Co. secured
the contract to build the First school in 1887. G.J. Schellenger was hired
as the First principal. Aug. 3, 1898 an addition was added to the school.
During the year 1905-1906 the total enrollment reached was 153. First grade
had 43 pupils.

Rev. Bernard Hens, pastor of Ipswich, in passing through Bowdle on his way
to Hoven, baptized the First child of Catholic offspring and said the First
Mass in Bowdle in a hall over Cox's Store. He performed the First marriage
ceremony of Stephen Gross and Mary Schumacher. The First funeral was the
death of Joseph Kessler. Rev. Hens was in charge until March 1888 when
Joseph A. Stephen became his successor at Ipswich. Mr. Stephen held
services at Bowdle in the houses of the various Catholic settlers. In 1893
the First meeting was held in the McCaul Elevator to organize a congregation
and erect a church building. The First church building was begun in April
1894. It was a modest frame structure 24 by 40 feet on a stone foundation
and cost $500. With 35 families, an additional structure was added to
enlarge the church. Rev. Father Sock held the First service in the fall of
1894.

A group of settlers met Sept. 5, 1886 at Mr. J.G. Daws to form a
Congregational Church. Rev. Wm. McCready was the First pastor. The First
church building was erected in 1887. Before that services were held in the
dining room of the Dumont Hotel.

The First Methodist services held in Bowdle were by Rev. S.F. Brown of
Bangor in 1886. The First services were held in the Dumont Hotel. In the
winter of 1886, they organized the First Sabbath school, with Mrs. Susan
Matteson as superintendent holding their sessions over the store of Aurand
& Amerpohl. Services were held at the store and at the hotel. In 1893 the
First church building was erected, complete with furnishings and a bell for
$1,600.

The First German Lutheran services held in Bowdle were as early as 1888 by
Rev. Geo. Lehme, who at that time was pastor of Watertown. The First
Congregation was organized in 1891 by Rev. Volkert who was the First
presiding minister and during his stay the First parsonage was built. In
1897 the First church was erected with Rev. R. Fehlau as pastor. In 1905 a
spendid bell was hung in the tower of the church. The First child baptized
was Josie Ketterling. The First couple married was Peter Schaak and
Elizabeth Baer.

The First lawsuit was held Nov. 13, 1886 before Justice Vantine, the
plaintiff being John Bell and Thom Johnson, defendant, for stealing a buffalo
robe. Verdict, not guilty.

The railroad was First extended west in 1900 and is being extended to
Seattle on the Pacific Coast in 1906. The Bowdle railroad station is noted
for its water. It has the largest supply and is considered the best for the
engines.

The First man to handle Uncle Sam's mail was A.L. Henderson.

The First car of wheat shipped from Bowdle was Oct. 6, 1886 by A.F.
LeClaire.

The First entertainment was given Jan. 14, 1887 by Miss E.M. Vath of
Aberdeen, an elocutionist, in Gamble's Hall.

The First load of wheat was hauled to Bowdle September 22, 1886 and was
stored in the barn of John Hill.

The First building to be erected in town was the Bowdle Bank building by
Bowdle and Newcomer. The First draft issued was to N. Dysinger, second was
to H.J. Richmond and the third one to F.J. Bowman. The second building was
the home for The Pioneer, erected by Fred J. Bowman.

The First hotel built was the hotel known as Hotel Boyle and changed to
Hotel Dumont in honor of H.D. Dumont, a capitalist of New York and a
brother of the vice-president of the C.M. & St. P. Railroad.

The First Pioneer Meat Market was erected by David Gamble June 21, 1886 and
has changed hands often since.

The First horseshoeing ever done in Bowdle was by MacEachran and Wright
July 26, 1886 for S.D. Peterson.

The First train to reach Bowdle was a construction train Thursday, Sept. 9,
1886 and the First regular train arrived Sunday, September 12, 1886. The
trainmen were John Cheeseman, conductor; S. Cook, engineer; E. Trussel,
fireman; Joe Murphy, baggageman; Wm. O'Brian, brakeman. The First snow
blockade was January 12, 1887 and lasted a week.

MAY 16, 1895
  Bowdle is preparing to incorporate. Geo. Merriman went out there Monday
to survey the plot to be incorporated. Mr. Merriman is a practical surveyor.
(Edmunds County Democrat)

MAY 18, 1905
  The first cement sidewalk to be laid in Bowdle was done so Monday, on
Main Street, In front of the Central House by a firm from Faulkton.

MAY 29, 1902
  The new method of placing incandescent lights on every corner in town
will be a great improvement in the lighting of our town next winter.

FEB 6, 1913
  All meters in the city were set back to naught on Saturday, it being the
first day of February and the beginning of the municipal light service.

JUNE 21, 1900
  A two-weeks session of teachers institute at Bowdle. The enrollment
reached 112 being the largest held in the county for some years past.
Professor Wheeler conducted the sessions.

MAY 9, 1918
  Architect J.W. Henry of Aberdeen for Bowdle's new school. Ground building
will be 58 ft. by 99 ft. with a high basement and two stories. Gymnasium is
a big room 34 ft. by 51 ft. in size with no pillars.

AUG. 28, 1919
  There are 12 residences now under course of construction in Bowdle.
Including these there are 172 dwelling houses in the city each one occupied
by a family. Figuring five to the family, this would indicate a population
of 860.

AUG. 14, 1919
  Philip Merkel returned home Friday from overseas military duty. He was
one of the very first to enlist and among the last to return. He took an
active part on the front and was a member of the Army of Occupation in
Germany.

JULY 4, 1929
  Plans are being made to form an Izaak Walton League for the preservation
of wildlife and development of Spring Lake.

AUG. 19, 1943
  Miss Violet Thurn is Bowdle's first woman pilot in the service.
  Editor C.T. Smithers tells how it was in 1886 and then in 1906.

THE CENTRAL HOTEL

The Central Hotel was First built in the fall of 1886 by Mr. Christianson
who sold the next spring to Robinson Bros. In 1888 Mr. James O' Reilly
purchased it.

G.C. AURAND STORE

G.C. Aurand in 1906 was known as the oldest businessman of Bowdle. He
First came to Bowdle in 1886 with his partner L.E. Amerpohl. Together they
built the First store. For 20 years they were acknowledged as one of the
leading firms in this state.

GENERAL STORE

Baer Bros. was composed of Herman C. Baer & Henry B. Baer. Henry
conducted the business. Herman conducted the machinery and grain business.

Henry came to Bowdle in 1889 and later bought the Andy Gerup business. In
1906 he built the First cement block building 28 by 86, two stories high. It
was built on the foundation of the original store of Andy Gerup. This store
sold groceries, hardware, shoes, stoves, furniture and caskets. Henry also
specialized as a tin worker.

GROSS BROS.

This business is the pioneer implement business of Bowdle. The First
proprietor in 1886 was Dan Mason. A few years later Mr. Mason sold to
Sparling & Son who again sold to Sparling, Gross & Co. (John Sparling,
Jacob Gross and John Gross.) In 1899 Jacob Gross died and then the company
continued as Sparling & Gross. In 1903 Sparling sold his interest to the
Gross Bros. In 1906 this firm consisted of Henry, Chris and John Gross. They
also had branches in Selby and Java, but later sold them. The line of
machinery they handled were McCormick haying and harvesting machines, J.I.
Case threshing outfits, Deere and Weber line of buggies, wagons and plows.
Gross Bros. had the reputation for being the largest dealers in the state
for J.I. Case threshers and Deere-Weber goods. They also had a large
windmill business and sold the famous Mound City paints. In 1903 they bought
the Hans Furuset Elevator on the west side of main street.

GENTS FURNISHING STORE

Harry A. Campbell came to Bowdle in 1904 from Iowa. He made tailor-made
clothing. His store was located on the north side of main street right
opposite the Bank of Bowdle.

BLACKSMITH

One of the First well-known blacksmiths in Bowdle was Fred P. Merkel. He
came to Bowdle in 1890 and purchased the Pioneer Blacksmith Shop which was
operated by MacEachran & Wright. In October 1903 a fire destroyed his shop
so he bought the Engle Bros. shop. Fred owned the best Blacksmith and wagon
shop in the area. His entire outfit of machinery, even including his
bellows, were run by power. He had a trip-hammer, shearing machine,
punching machine, circular saw, planing machine, polisher and the largest
turning lathe in this part of the state. Fred had the experience of being a
horseshoer for 20 years. His shop was located one block south of main
street.

REAL ESTATE

Arthur G. Bickert from Nebraska was the realtor in 1906. His business was
First started by Jackson & Bickert, but Jackson was killed in a train acci-
dent. Bickert continued to raise his fine blooded horses.

Another realtor was C.E. Lennan who was the pioneer real estate man of
Bowdle beginning when the town First started in 1886. He did a large
business in South Dakota and North Dakota.

FLOUR MILL

The Bowdle Roller Mill dates back to 1892 started First by Wm. McGlenn
and John Klein. In 1897 it burned down and a new company was formed by John
Klein, Fred Merkel, J. Kurle and P. Jeli. The mill was First incorporated
at this time. In 1899 the mill was sold to the Robb Bros. In 1900 the Ring
Bros. (Simon C.A. Ring and Eugene E. Ring) bought one-half interest. In 1903
Robb retired and a new firm was started. John Koch got possession of
one-third. This mill was the best in the state. In 1906 the records showed
that they shipped 53 cars of flour, 32 cars of other mill products and 83
cars of wheat or 100.000 bushels.

THE WATSON HOTEL

R.A. Watson from Vermont came to Bowdle in 1904 and started a stud
stable, while working at this business, he took in a few room boarders. This
became known as the Allen House. In June 1905 Mr. Watson purchased the
First hotel in Bowdle, the Dumont Hotel. He remodeled it and operated it
until 1906 when he sold it to F.J. Ham.

CENTRAL LUMBER CO.

In October 1886 E. Bach moved from Ipswich and established this lumber
company. Matt Cowley was the First manager. This business continued until
1901 when M.A. Robinson became the manager. March 26, 1903 the yard and
coal sheds were destroyed by fire, only saving the office. The old office
was removed and they built a new one. The manager in 1906 was N.A. Brown.
They sold lumber and coal. Matt Holzman worked here known as the pioneer
lumberman of Bowdle. They also sold the famous Pittsburgh Perfect Fence,
made of steel wires which were electrically welded. This building was
located near the depot.

BARBER SHOP

W.E. Johnson came to Bowdle in 1903. He and J. Rositch purchased the
business from J.A. Henderson and in 1905 purchased the share owned by J.
Rositch. This shop was First used as a barber shop since the starting of
the town.

THE BANK OF BOWDLE

It was First organized in 1886 and incorporated in 1891 with a capital
stock of $6,000. This was the First bank organized in Bowdle and the
building in which it is located was the First building constructed in the
town. In 1906 the bank had a deposit of $135,000.

GENERAL MERCHANDISE

A.W. Lewis from Ohio purchased the general mercantile business known as
the Bowdle Cash Store. He sold groceries, dry goods and hardware.

POOL & BILLIARD PARLOR

John H. Richmond from Pennsylvania came to Dakota in 1884, being one of
the First men to settle at King's Ranch, west of Bowdle.  When Bowdle
started he built himself a store and for years sold cigars and tobacco.
Later he purchased the Merritt building adjoining Yaukey's Drug Store on
the east and remodeled it for a pool and billiard parlor. He put in three
pool tables and a billiard table. He made plans to add a bowling alley.

HARNESS MAKER

C.H. Musser came to Bowdle in 1888 from Minnesota and started a business
with his father, C.V. Musser. He was known to be a good mechanic and made
the best harnesses ever. For the city of Bowdle he was the assessor for a
number of years. In sports Clayton was a good baseball player. He played
with the First team ever organized in Bowdle.

RESTAURANT & STORE

L.J. Muenz came from Ohio in 1886 and in 1904 operated a store selling
fruits, candy, groceries, nuts and other goods.

CITY MEAT MARKET

Ludwig Merkel came to America in 1893 from South Russia. He worked as a
butcher when he came to Bowdle and in 1904 started his own business. He
built the butcher shop which had an elaborate icebox and machinery. He also
rented the Pioneer Meat Market and now has full control over all the meat
business.

KENNEDY'S CASH STORE

W.D. Kennedy was a pioneer of Bowdle, building up his business on his
own. His motto was "Sell more goods on a smaller profit than any other store
in Bowdle or Edmunds County."

DRUG STORES

There were two drug stores, one owned by Henry C. Maas who came to Bowdle
in 1892 to work in the drug store for Dr. Edwards. In 1900 his building
burned so he rebuilt.

The other druggist was known as H.E. Yaukey who came to Bowdle and formed
a partnership with Robert T. Hill, later owning it himself. Both stores
carried drugs, paints, wallpaper and gifts.

CONTRACTORS & BUILDERS

J.P. Hunt & Son came in 1905. They had large work crews working for them
and were busy.

DRAY LINE

George Danser came in 1884 and for years worked for Clark Hudson the
First dray man of Bowdle and since 1900 has owned the line himself. He was
the distributing agent for the Heileman Brewing Co., they having a large
storehouse here for beer. He distributed the beer as far as Evarts and to
all other points near here. George was also the distributing agent for the
Standard Oil Company furnishing oil for Selby, Java, Bangor, Hosmer, Hoven
and Roscoe.

George had some of the finest mules for this work that could be found.
The man who handled the lines was an old pioneer, Ed Stroup. Later Mr.
Danser went into partnership with John J. Hoffman in manufacturing cement
blocks.

HOLLANDSWORTH-HART LUMBER CO.

These yards were the First to be established in Bowdle. They were started
in 1886 before the trains reached here. The First owners were Miner &
Willard. In 1906 W.W. O'Malley operated the business. They handled soft and
hard coal, lime, plaster, cement, barbed wire and fencing called the
American Fence.

REAL ESTATE & LOANS

John Rhodes had his office on the north side of main street. In 1906 he
had 500 quarter sections of land for sale.

BOWDLE CREAMERY

B.A. Oestreich came from Watertown, WI in 1903. He came to Bowdle and
opened up the creamery which had been closed for two years. Instead of
handling the milk at the creamery he only handled cream. Mr. Oestreich
educated the farmer that the hand separator was the right thing to own. The
plant was First built in 1896 by a stock company and proved a failure until
Mr. Oestreich took over. In 1906 he operated branch creameries at Roscoe
and Strasburg, ND and had cream stations at Hoven, Hosmer, Java and Bangor.

THE JEWELER

O. Larson came from Norway to Bowdle in 1888. He built his own store on
the corner west of Mason's Store. He was the official watch inspector for
the C.M. & St. Paul Railway and was considered to be the best jeweler in
this area.

MASON STORE

H.A. Mason came from New York in 1887 and started a hardware business.
His entire business was destroyed in 1900 so he rebuilt with a brick
building. It was three stories high, heated with steam and had an elevator
to carry freight. He sold hardware, shoes, dry goods and the third floor had
furniture and caskets. Mr. Mason was also an undertaker.

POST OFFICE

The First postmaster Henderson started at Kelley, two miles southwest of
Bowdle. Later the Post Office was moved to Bowdle where Henderson continued
to officiate and then W.W. Vantine took the position. When Harrison became
President of the United States F.J. Bowman, editor of The Pioneer, received
the appointment. After four years George Bickert became the postmaster. In
1906 E.J. Edwards became postmaster, who rebuilt the Post Office after it
burned in 1900. He was the brother of Dr. Edwards.

MILLINERY STORE

Mrs. E. Flashman came from England to Bowdle in 1884. She started the
First millinery store and had the latest styles of hats.

BAER & WAGNER IMPLEMENT

This business was First started by Jacob Gross and Herman Baer in 1897.
In 1899 Colman Wagner of Selby bought out Mr. Gross's interest and now is
known as Baer & Wagner. Mr. Baer manages the business in Bowdle and Mr.
Wagner in Selby.

In July 1905 they purchased the Miner & Willard Elevator. They handled
the Massilion threshers and Blue Ribbon buggies. The Mandt wagon was
popular with the farmers.

BUILDERS & CONTRACTORS

W.J. Hill came to Bowdle in 1896 and worked with V.E. Peckham. Together
they built the largest and best buildings in Bowdle. He was in partnership
with M.A. Robinson and later with Henry Schenk.

TAKEN FROM 1921 BOWDLE BUSINESS DIRECTORY

Bowdle is a progressive little city of nearly one thousand inhabitants,
located midway between Aberdeen and Mobridge on the main line of the
Milwaukee railway and the "Yellowstone Trail."

It is a city of fine homes, many churches and excellent schools.

Bowdle has municipal electric light and power service, sewerage and water
systems, and is the trading center of a large general farming,
stock-growing and dairy district.

The business institutions of the city are many and varied and include two
banks with deposits aggregating nearly a million dollars, a large butter
factory and a first-class flouring mill of 150-barrel capacity.

Land in this district is yet low in price, ranging from $40 an acre up,
according to location and improvements. Good water is plentiful and easily
obtained in shallow wells.

TAKEN FROM DECEMBER 16, 1926 BOWDLE PIONEER


L.E. Amerpohl, former merchant, remembers when he lived in Bowdle 23
years ago and "I often think of the pleasures and hardships we went through
from 1886 to the crop year of 1892. I think those years were the worst South
Dakota ever had. In fact they were so poor that I had to go on the road
selling shoes while my partner, Geo. Aurand, stayed at the wheel until the
relief came. I think it was the winter of 1886-1887 that we run out of
everything except oil, those days we had to use lamps, flour, coffee and
sugar. No kerosene to light our way. Often we would be without mail for 10
days. No town is alive without a band. We had a band in Bowdle from 1886
until I left in 1906. Those were the good old days.

TAKEN FROM JANUARY 13,1927 BOWDLE PIONEER

"Bowdle is a city of 1000 inhabitants located on the main line of the
Milwaukee railroad and the Yellowstone Trail, a national highway from coast
to coast, in the midst of the best farming, dairying and stock growing."

"The city has 24-hour electric light and power service, graveled streets,
sewer and water systems, an accredited 12-grade public school housed in a
modern $50,000 building, 6 churches, community hospital, 2 physicians and
surgeons, dentist, large flouring mill, fine creamery, 2 banks with
combined deposits of nearly a million dollars, 4 general merchandise
stores, 2 hardware stores, 2 farm implement stores, 2 harness shops, 2
blacksmith shops, 3 garages, jewelry store, photograph studio, undertaker
and embalmer, 5 filling stations, 2 cafes, 3 rooming houses, 2 pool halls,
newspaper, 2 lumber yards, 3 grain elevators, 2 real estate offices, 4
cream stations, drug store and 2 barber shops."

Business History ... Old and New
        Compiled by Connie Goetz, Alma Leno, Adeline Miller.


                THE BOWDLE PIONEER
                By: R.W. [Bob] Holsworth

No one is alive who saw the opening act of the Bowdle Centennial ...
perhaps the opening acts of the centennial celebration, but not that
frenzied flurry of activity 100 years ago which indicated that history just
a few days prior to May 20, 1886.

No television crew was in attendance to record the birth of Bowdle; no
historian was present to switch on his word processor to purposely or
specifically set down a record of the founding of the town. Legal documents
may be scrounged up to show the exact locations, the exact dates, but the
color and excitement cannot be found to exist--other than a few yellow
tatters of cheap pulp paper upon which remain some ink stains impressed
upon it by the descent of the platen of a hand press, with the power behind
the squeeze being exerted by the muscles of one Fred J. Bowman, pioneer
printer, frontier publisher and dreamer of dreams.

Volume 1, Number 1 of The Bowdle Pioneer was dated May 10, 1886 at Bowdle,
Edmunds County, Dakota Territory. Issue Number 2 bore the date of May 24,
which would indicate that the logical sequence of a weekly publication was
disrupted by some circumstance.

The May 24 issue proclaimed to the world that "the town was platted
Saturday night, May 20, 1886." It also indicated that in addition to The
Pioneer five other businesses existed, all saloons. News and booze
apparently were deemed necessities, but religion and education were of a
lesser priority, inasmuch as no churches nor schools were mentioned in this
early edition.

Fred and Emma Bowman were married in 1876 at Prairie du Chien, WI where
they published The Union. They moved on to found one of the early townsite
papers (Gary Interstate) in Dakota, just west of the Minnesota border. They
later moved on deeper into the territory to establish The Pioneer, first in
the river cowtown of LeBeau and then shifted it to the short-lived
settlement of Scranton before again moving it to its permanent location in
Bowdle, where it remained on the site which is now the Aldinger property on
the corner of Main Street and 2nd Avenue.

Shortly after Bowman's reign, the editorial duties were assumed by a J.L.
Owens, of which little is known at this late date, and whose activities and
accomplishments have faded into the dark recesses of the past.

Others may have, and probably did, wield the pen and swing the composing
stick before the name of Fred Zimmer appeared in the masthead about the
turn of the century. Zimmer was assisted by Miss Caroline Hupp of Ipswich,
who eventually became his wife. Mrs. Zimmer relinquished the editor's chair
in 1918 to W.Z. Todd, who accepted the chair, but not the title.

W.Z. installed a Linotype and along with it a personality that left a
pronounced mark on South Dakota journalism. He never used the title of
"Editor," but rather listed himself in the masthead as "Architect"--One who
"built" his paper each week.

Todd left Bowdle in 1928, purchasing the paper at Veblen and when hard
times pinched he moved on to Oregon where he lived out the rest of his life.
His son John was postmaster at Bowdle at one time, serving until well into
the Thirties.

Following Todd was Patsy McNeely. This Will o' the Wisp of South Dakota
newspapering came to Bowdle from Mobridge in 1928, remained until 1932,
then took over The News in Dupree. The record for "stretchin' the misery"
at The Bowdle Pioneer to date goes to Albert and Julia Senn. They operated
the paper from 1932 to 1958.

Albert was the son of Edward L. Senn, the so-called "Final Proof King" of
Dakota. Research has turned up a list of Edward Senn-originated papers
numbering 51. He was appointed the state prohibition administrator for the
state of South Dakota in 1925 and filled the position until the 18th
Amendment was repealed in 1933.

It was from this rich newspapering background created by his father's
endeavors that Albert Senn came, and with his wife Julia, spent more than a
quarter century guiding The Pioneer through an interesting period,
including the end of the Great Depression and two wars.

Principles and projects that The Pioneer backed and promoted during this
quarter century include: black topped streets, refurbishing the old
hospital, remodeling the school to enlarge the gym, building of the
American Legion Hall, development of the City Park and Meakins Playground,
among many others. Albert died in 1961, three years after selling The
Pioneer because of ill health.

Dale and Nancy Lewis followed the Senns in the ownership of The Pioneer in
1968. Dale was the son of R.F. Lewis, long-time publisher of the Pennington
County Courant in Wall, who at one time, was the "professor" at Roscoe
School. Dale and Nancy caused The Pioneer to grow and prosper for about
five years, until they made a sales agreement with a Texan by the name of
Russell Wadleigh.

Wadleigh operated the paper until 1967, when Lewis took back the ownership.
During this period the plant was moved from the location it had always
occupied just north of the Chevrolet Garage to the former Braufman Store on
Main Street. Wadleigh went to Chicago and several years later was shot and
killed.

When Dale Lewis repossessed ownership in 1967 he found it physically
impossible to run two papers (Wall and Bowdle) with such a distance
separating them and he offered The Pioneer for sale through a classified ad
in a Minneapolis Sunday paper and it was seen by R.W. (Bob) Holsworth, who
was working on a paper in Clarkfield, MN but had a desire to return to
South Dakota.

Negotiations were rapidly carried out and by the middle of June 1967 the
Holsworths took up the reins at The Pioneer. Bob had "deviled" at the
Carlton (MN) County Vidette beginning his freshman year of high school in
1935. By the time the family arrived in Bowdle he had worked on three
weeklies in Minnesota, a daily in Illinois and three papers in South
Dakota, one of which they had owned. Arlene had been news editor and press
operator on a paper they had managed in northern Minnesota and had learned to
operate the Linotype when they owned the Hamlin County News in Bryant in
the late fifties.

A crisis came in the fall of 1969 when Bob suffered a severe heart attack.
Arlene worked the news and ads alone and set as much of the news as she had
time for up to Wednesday noons, then loaded the type and remaining copy in
the car and printed The Pioneer in Gettysburg. She hauled the papers back
to Bowdle and mailed them. This went on for nine weeks until Bob returned to
the shop. They asked their son Dan to leave college and join them at The
Pioneer.

In January 1971 Bob suffered another coronary and the Holsworths offered
the paper for sale. W.H. Jahraus and his wife Lee were the purchasers and
took over the summer of 1971.

Bill, or Bud as he was also known, Jahraus began his publishing career in
Mound City. He also owned the Prairie Picayune in Herreid. In 1969 he sold
out and purchased the paper at Rockwell City, IA. When he sold that paper
he moved back to South Dakota and took a position on the daily at Huron.
Six years after buying The Pioneer, the newspaper was converted from
letterpress to offset May 26, 1977.

In June 1980 Bill and Lee Jahraus went into retirement with the sale of The
Pioneer to Larry and Mary Lou Gauer. They became the first publishers of
the paper to be "non-hot type printers" ... they had not worn their
fingerprints off by hand spiking type nor did they bear the bum scars of
"squirts" of type metal from the Linotype--the first of a new generation of
country printers.

        From Letterpress and Linotype ...

        ... To Offset and Computers.

Mary Lou worked for Bill Jahraus for about 2-1/2 years as the Compugraphic
operator--the person who operates the typewriter-like keyboard of the
computer which composes type in a variety of sizes and faces far beyond the
capability of the Linotype, and much faster and cleaner. She also learned the
fine points of paste up, ad layout and the like that are so necessary to
"building" a paper, as W.Z. Todd was wont to proclaim. Her husband Larry was
principal and coach at Bowdle High School during this time. When they
purchased the paper he shifted academic gears to the journalism range.

They carry on the tradition of 100 years of newspapering in Bowdle in a
firm, positive way that upholds the standards set for them by the procession
of publishers who preceded them, but perhaps not with the vitriolic fervor
that personified the publishers of a century ago.

Despite the fires and other drawbacks, we trust this brief history is a
factual as we can make it at this period of time. We are thankful that The
Pioneer arose from ashes like the Phoenix of old and still carries forward
the true tradition of Gutenberg, the Fourth Estate and those pioneer
printers who had the foresight and intestinal fortitude to bring to the
frontier the institution of the weekly newspaper which has been the
backbone of small towns across the vast expanse of the Dakota prairie.

DEC. 25, 1930
  Mrs. Koch mentioned that the printing office at the time was located
where the Fred Grosz residence now stands. The Kochs have taken the Pioneer
continually since the first issue was published by Fred Bowman in 1886.

NOV. 7, 1963
  The Bowdle Pioneer was put in its new home (Braufman's Store) in October
after 77 years in the same building. The old Pioneer building took a
journey to Hoven to be the new home for the Hoven Review.

ADOLPH BRAUFMAN'S STORE

Aug. 29, 1963 Bowdle Pioneer: "The closing of Adolph Braufman's Store after
being in operation for 49 years will be history. The building was sold to
The Bowdle Pioneer.

After arriving from Romania in 1905, Adolph worked for his brother Jake
selling piece goods from a horse-drawn wagon between Bowdle and Eureka for
two years. Then he went to the Twin Cities area and engaged in door-to-door
selling. After six years he returned to Bowdle to work for his brother in
the store that was located in the now vacant lot just east of the Post
Office. Shortly after this building burned Adolph rented the building next
to the present City Liquor Store in 1914. After arrangements were made to
open the store he left for New York where he married. He returned with his
bride Sarah in the fall 1914.

The closing of Braufman's marks the end of the general-type store in
Bowdle."

        Photo taken in 1916 of Adolph and Sarah Braufman behind the counter
        in their original building.

ALMOST 60 YEARS OF SERVICE
        [By Julia Senn]

Adolph Braufman lived almost 60 years of his life serving this community as
a merchant. In tribute to this man, who in his quiet, unassuming way,
contributed much to the community, the Centennial Committee took a
sentimental journey through our memories.

Mrs. August Schick: "We used to bring in a 12 dozen case of eggs to
Braufman's Store. The eggs paid for the groceries and he packed them into
the crate and we took the cream check home for savings. He used to total up
the grocery bill in his head as he made the selections and he would say 'If
I am wrong, you get the groceries free.' He was never wrong.

Martha Weiss: "Mrs. Braufman was such a nice lady. She used to spend a lot
of time at the store."

Julia Senn: "Braufmans were our good neighbors for 20 years. When the city
was staging some special event and the merchants were asked to help sponsor
it, it was Albert who went to collect from Mr. Braufman. When he came in,
Mr. Braufman would always say, 'How much do you want this time?' I was
going home early one morning from the printing office, just after a Jewish
Holy Day and heard such beautiful singing -- it was Mr. Braufman going to
work singing some of the music of the liturgy. He had a beautiful voice and
I was sorry when the singing ceased. "

Bertha Schuh: "My daughter worked there and enjoyed the job. Thus we learned
that he paid more taxes than most of the businesses on the street."

Patty Dewald: "I remember the big sacks of candy we got for a nickel when I
was a kid."

Adeline Miller: "My mother used to buy a lot of yard goods there but I only
bought groceries there when I was a teenager."

Gertie Olson: "My mother liked to trade there and on Saturday evenings she
would visit there with people she would not get to see otherwise."

Milton Hagele: "When I think of Braufman's Store I can hear again, him and
his wife talking so fast in Yiddish as I came in. It may not have been so
fast, but I felt that way because I could not understand them."

Mrs. Joe Herman Jr.: "My mother liked to shop there and especially enjoyed
buying the dress material from Mrs. Braufman. She liked her very much."

Mrs. Mary Wiepking: "Fourth of July used to bring many people to town and I
recall Mr. Braufman coming out of the store with dresses over his arm. He
would call out, Dresses! Dresses! They sold for only a dollar or two and
he had good sales on the Fourth."

Mrs. Edward Huber: "There were those who looked down on Mr. Braufman
because he was a Jew, but they didn't know what a kind person he was. When
a poor person charged groceries, Mr. Braufman would often tear up the bill.
He helped a lot of people that way. I worked at their house two years for
$4 a week and thought I was getting rich. I also worked at the store
Wednesday and Saturday nights. After Ed and I were married and I would go
there for groceries, he would not let me pay for them. They were his gift
to us."

Mrs. Darlene Walz: "Their store was open 6-1/2 days a week, but Sunday
afternoons they enjoyed a bit of leisure and I recall how nice and mint-new
their Buick always looked when he would drive it out of their garage for
their weekly ride. They really enjoyed this bit of relaxation."

There must be many who join Mrs. Connie Goetz in remembering items that
were available only at Braufman's -- the smoked herring, Greek olives
(black and salty,) the lutefisk he stocked at Christmas time and would put
in a small barrel outside the door and the Halavah candy -- so different
from the usual sweets.

The Christmas treat she enjoyed most was the St. John's Bread which her
father would heat in the oven to soften so it could be eaten. It made one
think of a thin, dark, ripe banana and had a sweet flavor. Curiosity about
the fruit drove her to the encyclopedia where she found: "Carob is a dark
evergreen tree which grows wild in the Mediterranean area. It grows a
brown, leathery bean-like pod 4-10 inches long. The pod contains a sticky
pulp that is fed to horses and cattle and it was reported to have been
sustenance to John The Baptist when he lived in the wilderness, from whence
it gets its name. The carob tree is occasionally found in the southern
United States. Bread made from the meal of the carob is known as Locust
Bread."

        Braufman Store approximately 1937. Adolph Braufman and clerk Arthur
        Huft.

He has been gone these 20 years, but in memory Adolph and Sarah are still
with us. He began his business here in 1906 and after he had established
his general merchandise store at 3039 Main Street in 1914, he was ready for
the most important step of his life -- he went to New York City and
returned with his bride Sarah (nee Silverman) on his arm. His 59 years of
service is not forgotten by the community. He was a member of the Hiddenwood
Lodge A.F. & A.M. of Bowdle and the Bnai Isaac Synagogue in Aberdeen.

Through the 1929 stock market crash we learned of his concern for others when
he canceled outstanding accounts which had been long overdue. He trusted
his fellow man to be honest with him. When he realized he was stuck with
two customers whose "charge it" had really mounted up, he finally marked
the bills paid and sent them to the debtors. One of those debtors
unabashedly came in the next day, after being forgiven $800 worth of food
and clothing and asked for the privilege of charging his needs again.

In 1964 Sarah's health failed and she was taken to Minneapolis for care.
Life did not mean much to him without her and the following year he also
needed medical care. He died in Minneapolis in January 1966.
