        building, now the Bowdle Youth Center.

BOWDLE YOUTH CENTER

The Bowdle Youth Center is located at 3026 Main Street in what's called the
old bank building. The building was donated to the Church of God for the
expressed purpose of using it as a Youth Center by Vincent Hoven in July
1981.

The main level was remodeled, which included a new lowered ceiling,
electrical work, painting and carpeting. Materials, labor and money were
donated by business leaders, individuals and the Church of God.

The Youth Center was furnished with an Atari, pinball and video games, a
ping-pong table, fooseball table and selection of table games. Pop, candy,
potato chips and pizza are sold at the Center. It is open to the community
each Saturday 7 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.

This building has served the Bowdle community since around 1913. It has
twice been a bank (Bank of Bowdle and Security Bank), a bakery and a post
office. It was originally built by the Bank of Bowdle. The bank vault, with
the exception of one door, remains intact and is used for storage of games
and equipment. The exterior of the building remains essentially the same as
when it was built. Plans are underway to continue the remodeling of the
building and it has been designated a Historical Building by the South
Dakota Historical Society.

        Bank of Bowdle about 1908.

THE BANK OF BOWDLE

The Bank of Bowdle was established in 1886 and was incorporated as a State
Bank in 1891. Originally the Bank was located at 445 Main in a small
woodframed building and it was enlarged and remodeled in 1904. C.F. Drewry
was president of the Bank of Bowdle. Cashier was O.J. Coons and assistant
cashier was G. Smithberger.

The present site of the Bank of Bowdle was in 1898 a General Store which in
all probability was partially destroyed by the fire in 1900 that destroyed
almost the entire north side of Main Street. G.L. William and W.G. Mathieu
purchased the lot and structure from "a single woman" named S. McCartey in
1902 for the Bank of Bowdle.

In 1908 construction began on the Bank of Bowdle building. The Bowdle
Pioneer reported, "work has been commenced on the New Bank building and the
same will be rushed to completion as soon as possible." The Nov. 19, 1908
edition of the Pioneer reported "The new bank building is nearly enclosed,
the contractors are certainly pushing the completion as fast as possible.
It will be the prettiest building in the northwest part of the state." The
next week's paper reported that "The Bowdle Artificial Stone Company laid
the cement walk in front of the new bank building last Friday and Saturday.
How's that for Dakota? Nov. 20th and 21st laying cement walks and it is one
of the best cured walks in town. Henry Leidholt being the artist who did
the work."

The Christmas Eve edition of the 1908 Pioneer reported that "The decorating
and finishing touches are being done on the new bank building. The interior
finish is one of beauty and we doubt if its equal can be found in the State
of South Dakota." The Bank of Bowdle opened their new building for business
on Monday, Feb. 8, 1909. According to the Pioneer, "They have certainly a
fine place to do business in and the best location in town."

The advertisements the Bank of Bowdle placed in the newspaper reveal some
hints as to why the Bank relocated and their choice of materials. The ad in
the Feb. 11, 1909 edition of the Pioneer stated, "Bigger, Better, and
Stronger than ever." The ad listed these features: "Fire Proof Vault,
Burglar Proof Safe, Safety Deposit Boxes For Rent." The safe was purchased
from the Victor Safe Company, the finest and securest safe made.

Perhaps because of the many fires that had plagued Bowdle, the owners of
the Bank of Bowdle were determined to build a building which would stand
secure. But it is also rather obvious that they wanted the building to be
distinct in its architecture. The cement Greek columns set off the brick
used to construct the building. The interior included beautifully finished
woodwork, ornate gas lights and a majestic impressed tin ceiling.

After the bank closed the building became the home of the U.S. Post Office
for over 20 years. Following the relocation of the Post Office in a new
building across the street, the building was used for a variety of things
including a bakery. Currently it houses the Bowdle Youth Center. The
building was donated to Bowdle Church of God by Mr. and Mrs. Vincent Hoven
to be used as a youth center. The Hoven family can be credited with the
building being in such excellent condition today because they owned and
maintained it for nearly half of its life.

The Rev. Sam Saylor of Bowdle Church of God made application to have the
Bank of Bowdle building listed as a National Historic Landmark in November
1984. In March 1985 he received a letter that stated, "The South Dakota
Board of Cultural Preservation is proud to inform you that the National
Park Service of the U.S. Department of Interior has listed the following
property on the National Register of Historic Places: Bank of Bowdle, 3026
Main Street, Bowdle, South Dakota."

        First State Bank in the 1920's

FIRST STATE BANK

The First State Bank moved into its new quarters in November 1919 to the
east room of the Gross Store building. The bank had previously occupied the
building housing Don's Barber Shop at present.

The 25th anniversary of First State Bank of Bowdle was observed Jan. 9,
1932. The anniversary called to mind the panic year of 1907 when the
institution was born; the dry years 1910-1912 when souls were severely
tried; the boom years of the war when money literally grew on bushes; the
post war deflation period 1920-1924 when dark clouds hung over the
financial horizon of banks and individuals and the depression of 1930-1931.

On its opening day First State Bank had a capital stock of $10,000 fully
paid up. Original board of directors were John C. Gross, H.C. Gross, C.C.
Gross, Jacob Gundert and John B. Gundert. John C. Gross was elected
president at a salary of $75 per month. A few years later Jacob Gundert
became president. In May (same year) John C. Gross was promoted to
president. H.C. Gross retained his post as vice-president 25 years.

Ludwig Merkel was the first citizen to make a deposit ... he deposited $5.
The first day's deposits were $3,992. Local jeweler O. Larsen was the oldest
depositor on the books of the bank.

During the Banking Crash of 1932 First State Bank was closed Nov. 14, for
the Banker's Holiday and was unable to reopen.

Dec. 31, 1932 a new bank, Bowdle State Bank, was started. J.K. Kurle served
as president 1932-1947. Henry Gross was made president of the bank in 1947
and held that title until Dec. 31, 1961.

At one time there was only one employee and all checks were hand posted.

MAY 6, 1920
  The First State Bank received 150 steel deposit boxes that had been
ordered last September. The boxes were put into place and the bank is now
able to take care of all comers for safety deposit boxes.

BOWDLE STATE BANK

The Bowdle State Bank began when the newly elected board of directors;
namely, J.K. Kurle, J.C. Baer, Henry Bauder, M.C. Gross and H.L. Woodworth
of Ipswich, selected bank officers and adopted the corporate charter and
bylaws the evening of December 23, 1932. Elected to the presidency was J.K.
Kurle. Vice-presidents were F.G. Grosz and John C. Gross. The first cashier
of the financial institution was H.C. Gross.

Since its conception in 1932 the bank has been owned and controlled by
members of the Gross family. Its first president, J.K. Kurle, was married
to Rose Gross, a sister of John C. Gross, H.C. Gross, M.C. Gross and C.C.
Gross. J.K. Kurle served as president 1932-1947. Henry C. Gross assumed the
presidency in 1947 and remained until his retirement in 1961.

Gardner and Robert Gross, sons of John C. Gross, gained controlling
interest in the bank in 1961. Gardner assumed the role of president in 1961
and held that position until his death in 1971. Following Gardner's death,
Robert Gross became the fourth president of the bank, as well as, chairman
of the Board of Directors and currently serves in that position.

In 1935 the bank became a member of the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation, insuring each depositor's account up to $10,000. Present day
accounts are now insured up to $100,000.

The first Bowdle State Bank occupied the building now housing Erv's
Furniture. Due to an increased volume of business, the directors decided to
build a larger building, safer from fire and burglars. The Bowdle State
Bank moved to its new and present quarters in 1965.

The present bank is a thoroughly modern facility with an after-hour
depository, built-in alarm system and private offices. It has piped-in
music with the capacity of playing over 600 selections before repeating
itself. Above the teller windows are four clocks indicating the different
time zones in the United States.

The Bowdle State Bank has had an insurance agency within its confines since
1932. The firm is known as Gross Insurance Agency. There have been only two
managers during its history. Fred Grosz managed the firm until 1961 when
Mahlon Gross took over the agency.

Brian Nelson of Langford began as a trainee in the insurance department in
October 1984. Mahlon Gross went into semi-retirement in January 1985.

With a beginning capital assets of $15,000 in 1932, the bank has grown
steadily and now has assets of over $10 million. The present bank has
modern computer equipment to handle the volume of transactions daily.

Employees of the bank are Robert Gross, president; Mahlon Gross,
vice-president and manager of Gross Insurance Agency. Cheryl McCarlson was
assistant cashier and assumed the duties of Mac Mashek who died Nov. 8,
1984 after an illness. Mrs. Mashek was cashier, supervisor of operations
and a director at the time of her death. Computer operators, tellers and
bookkeepers are Bonnie Siebrecht and Darlene Bollinger. Tellers and
bookkeepers are Doris Schlepp and Joann Bieber.

Board of directors are Robert Gross, chairman; Mahlon Gross, vice-chairman
and secretary; Helen Gross, Susan Geyerman and Arelene Gross, members.

DEC. 16, 1965
  The first deposit made in the new Bowdle State Bank was by Gary Walz.

NOV. 24, 1983
  Bowdle State Bank went "on-line" with its new computer system.

FARMER'S LAND BANK ASSOCIATION

Feb. 25, 1965 Bowdle Pioneer: "A small office on the corner of Main and
Newcomer Street was the loaning agency owned by farmers and ranchers.

Federal Land Bank was organized in 1917 to offer long-term loans to relieve
the financial distress of farmers and ranchers. The Bowdle Office was set
up in 1924 at the Security State Bank of Bowdle with Karl J. Kundert as
secretary-treasurer.

In 1932 the office was moved to the old Atlas Co. lumber yard at the corner
of Railroad and Newcomer Streets. In January 1933 A.C. Merkel was elected
secretary-treasurer and in 1936 he purchased the Larson Jewelry Store
building (1985 Dental Office) and moved the office to its present location.
Mr. Merkel is now in his 31st year of service to the bank as manager.

The Federal Land Bank Association makes farm and ranch type loans for a
period of up to 30 years, which may be paid in full anytime without penalty.
The farmer member leaves in 5% of the loan in capital stock. Interest
rates charged by Federal Land Bank have been as low as 3-1/2% and for a
time were 6%. Present interest rate (1965) is 5-1/2%.

TALE OF A TREE

   I write of a beautiful cottonwood tree,
   That in spite of drouths had grown to be.
   Immense and branched symmetrically;
   Rough bark formed a protective sheath,
   Guarding the flowing sap beneath.
   Close to a walk, the great tree stood;
   Now its remains are lifeless wood!
   A chain-saw roared in savage glee,
   While it destroyed that stately tree.
   I viewed the scene while passing by,
   And asked myself, "Why must it die?"
   For countless years, it offered shade,
   But some just saw the mess it made,
   When downy seeds came floating down,
   To drift like snow around the town.

   Last fall, when other trees were bare,
   And leaves were swirling everywhere,
   That tree, adorned in gold array,
   Was granting us a last display;
   Defying winds and autumn's chill,
   To make that doomed tree's final will.
   To me, it left a gorgeous view,
   Of artwork only God can do;
   From its branches, hanging high,
   Leaves of gold, against blue sky.

                Esther L. Voller
                [April 25, 1979]

        Opera House cornerstone laid May 31, 1898.

June 12, 1924 Bowdle Pioneer: "In tearing out part of the Opera House,
Christ Schlaht found a copy of The Bowdle Pioneer dated May 6, 1898 (editor
A.L. Owens.) Bowdle Town Hall cornerstone laid May 31, A.D. 1898. This hall
was built by a stock company. One of the needs of Bowdle so far has been a
town hall. Nothing is more conducive to the upbuilding of a city or speaks
better of a town than a large, roomy hall. When strangers come into a town,
if they go the Opera House and see a firstclass entertainment, they feel
good and are disposed to feel kindly upon the town and its institutions,
and as a result they invest and locate at once while they might not under a
different state of affairs. Size of 40 by 80, which will give Bowdle by far
the largest hall in this section. The location will be on the corner lots
across the street from Robinson's livery barn. The lots have been bought and
paid for. The hall will front on Dumont Avenue. It will have a good
substantial foundation and will be painted, plastered, fitted and furnished
in good style throughout.

Pertaining to the incorporaters of the stock company board of directors,
W.L. Boyd is the only resident of Bowdle.

Robinson's livery barn mentioned in the Pioneer's article as being opposite
the town hall has long since been removed from the site, which is now a
part of the Dr. Edwards Park.

The site of this building was where the present (1985) Dave's Repair is
located.

Many classes were held in this building in the late 1918's because the
school building was not completed until Christmas Time.

BOYD HALL

Boyd Hall was built in 1907 by W.L. Boyd. It was designed for roller
skating, dancing and public gatherings. The building was located where the
present American Legion Hall is now located, west of the Bowdle Creamery.

Boyd Hall was the scene of many public dances on Saturday nights and was
the main attraction for roller skating enthusiasts during the week. The
hardwood floor was laid in a circular pattern to make it easier for dancing
or roller skating.

The building was leased from Boyd by J.B. Houlihan Jan. 1, 1931. Houlihan
announced his plans to renovate the building into a "talking picture"
theater. The machinery and a complete new Vitaphone sound equipment were
installed. Houlihan later purchased the building from Mr. Boyd with half
interest belonging to Vincent Hoven later that spring. The first talking
picture in Bowdle of any record was "The Kohens & Kellys in Africa" and was
shown April 24, 1931 at the H & H Theatre, as the business became known.

John and Vincent Hoven purchased Houlihan's half interest in the business
May 7, 1931, thus becoming the sole owners of H & H Theatre. The Hovens
installed new equipment, including cushioned seats while hiring Samuel
Ludwig as the manager of the theater. The building was sold to the American
Legion in 1946. Shows were held there until the building burned.

MAY 3, 1934
  Albert Huber will assume management of H & H Theatre.

BOWDLE THEATRE

Vincent Hoven, along with his father John Hoven, owned Boyd Hall, then
known as H & H Theatre, until it was sold to the American Legion in 1946.
He continued to hold shows there until the building burned.

In 1948 a new theater, designed by U.L. Freed of Aberdeen, was built on the
north side of Main Street. The proprietor Vincent Hoven named the theater
the New Bowdle. He was assisted by his father in much of the construction
work.

        Boyd Hall burns. Bowdle Theatre built in 1948.

It was built as a very modern building with a lobby finished with red and
white tile, recessed lighting and red molding and trim. Seat lighting along
the aisles, modernistic chrome sidelights in the auditorium, chairs
upholstered in red with auto type cushions and a lounge and restrooms in the
basement made it a great theater. There was also a cry room for mothers
with restless children.

The building, constructed of cement blocks, also has two small business
places on each side, Ray Bachman Insurance Agency and Montana-Dakota
Utilities Co. At one time there was a lunchroom in the basement and two
apartments on the second story.

In October 1958 Ruben Goehring purchased the theater from Vincent Hoven.
After one year, along with a business transaction, Henry Boschee purchased
the theater.

Richard Meyer of Selby leased the theater for two years and Myron Schock
leased it about four.

In 1970 Ray and Lila Bachman purchased the theater from Mrs. Henry Boschee.
Bachman's daughter Vicki Knecht manages the business. Movies are shown
seasonally on weekends as Bowdle's main entertainment

OCT. 21, 1954
  Cinemascope was put into the Theater. The first picture to be shown on
this wide screen will be "The Robe."

DUMONT HOTEL

This hotel was first known as Hotel Boyle and later changed to Hotel Dumont
in honor of H.D. Dumont, a capitalist of New York and a brother of the
vice-president of the C.M. & ST. P. Railroad.

The first proprietors of the Dumont were Boyle and Hewitt. Later this hotel
was named Watson Hotel after its owner.

SEPT. 19, 1912
  Tom O'Malley is preparing to start a restaurant and lunch counter in his
building recently used by H.E. Yaukey for a drug store. He moved in tables,
a stove and lunch counter yesterday and will soon be ready for business.

SAM'S CAFE
  The history of Sam's Cafe steps back to almost a century. It originally
was a drug store owned by Henry Maas. In 1900 the Maas building burned in
the big fire, so he rebuilt. On the first floor he operated a drug store,
while on the second floor (known then as Maas Hall) had Masonic Lodge
meetings. It was known that six secret societies had their meetings here.
Mr. Maas operated this business for 25 years.

Then Morris Jones, a brother of Dr. T.D. Jones, took over the possession of
the City Drug Store. It was well-known as Jones Drug. After being in
business here in Bowdle several years he moved to Aberdeen and began his
business on 6th Avenue known as Jones Drug.

About the 1940's the drug store was reconstructed into a cafe known as
Mertz Cafe. The upstairs was changed into living quarters for most of the
families who operated the cafe in time.

In 1951 Emil and Barbara Hoff of Eureka purchased the Mertz Cafe. After
operating it several years they leased it to Alex Riester, but after a few
months the Hoffs returned and operated it again.

        Sallie Hoff and her mother Barbara were the cooks.

        Emil Hoff [right] with a customer in Hoff's Cafe.

In 1955 Henry and Margaret Boschee purchased the cafe from Emil Hoff. In
1957 Henry Boschee and Ruben Goehring had a trade in business exchange, so
Mr. Goehring became the proprietor. John and Elizabeth Artz leased the
business from Ruben Goehring until Elmer Boschee and Morris Hettich (as
partners) leased it. Then later Gust and Katie Dumdei leased the cafe about
4-1/2 years. After Ruben Goehring's death, his sister Edna Teska continued
to manage the cafe a short time. The last to lease at this period of time
were Herman and Molly Person.

The cafe was then converted into a shoe shop operated by Jake Rieger and
known as Rieger Shoe Shop. Jake was known to fix shoes and repair
canvasses. He moved to Eureka.

Once again with the memory of this establishment being a cafe Athneal and
Bernice Buechler converted it back to a cafe. They continued to operate the
cafe business serving meals and adding the catering service. They were the
last family to live upstairs.

Jan. 1, 1984 they sold their business to Richard and Sherma Maier who did
extensive remodeling before opening. As before, it continues to be a
popular place for that special afternoon coffee break. They continue to
serve full-course meals, plus the catering service.

THE APARTMENTS

The history of this building had its beginning in 1929 when it was a
restaurant known as Carlson's Cafe. Mr. and Mrs. Carlson were operating a
cafe at this site in 1925 when they overhauled this old Muentz building,
then known as the Bowdle Cafe. They remodeled it and opened it as Carlson
Cafe. It was a successful business until one night in 1929 when the entire
building was destroyed by fire.

Without apprehension the Carlsons rebuilt their cafe in August 1929. Not
only was it a cafe, but their living quarters were in the rear. As time
progressed the Carlsons added improvements to their cafe. March 12, 1931
they announced the opening of a bakery along with their cafe.

Another change was announced June 15, 1933 when E.G. Carlson was busy
making plans to add a second story to the building. The upper story was
divided into 12 rooms and were used for a hotel. There was hot and cold
water in every room. The hotel was ready for guests Aug. 14, 1933.

Finding the hotel business to be a success, Mr. Carlson discontinued the
cafe section. The dining room was partitioned off, one room serving as a
lobby and the other part was converted into two bedrooms. Now the
institution was known as Carlson's Hotel and it served the community for
another 10 years with the same proprietor E.G. Carlson until Feb. 28, 1946
when he sold it to Emil Brockel of Selby.

Since then there have been several owners. As time continued it again
changed from a hotel to an apartment house. The previous owners, Wilmer
Schaible and Floyd Miller, as partners, sold their shares to Doctors Alfred
and Mary Klein in 1983. At present it serves as an apartment house and the
front portion of the first floor houses Sieck's Veterinary Service.

MARCH 10, 1932

45 cents.

BOWDLE HI-WAY CAFE

In 1964 the Hi-Way Cafe was built south of Highway 12 as part of Bowdle
Livestock Sales Co. The first managers of this eating establishment were
Leo and Ann Stern, who operated it several years.

Since the Sterns many managers have taken charge of the cafe. This last
year, in 1985, Joe Stappler succeeded Norman Gross as present manager.

The cafe's main business is sale day which is Tuesdays. However it is open
seven days a week, serving meals and offering a private room for parties or
meetings.

CORNER COTTAGE DRIVE INN

The Corner Cottage Drive Inn was built by Lila and Ray Bachman and son Paul
in June 1971 on the corner of U.S. Highway 12 and 4th Street. It has been
managed by Lila and Ray as a fast food and soft ice cream service. The
Bachman's daughter and son-in-law, Deb and Scott Parkhurst, managed the
business the summer of 1984.

GOLD NUGGET LOUNGE - STEAKHOUSE - MOTEL

Driving from Bowdle west on Highway 12 a "golden rock" comes into view. At
this site the Gold Nugget is found south of the highway. This place is
well-known for dining and dancing.   This establishment began in July 1976
when Gary and Dorothy Oster became owners and managers. They purchased this
dining club from Pete and Irene Hoffman, on whose property it was built.

The Gold Nugget had a grand opening with 500 people attending. Gene Allen
and the Roadmasters provided the dancing music for that special night.

In November 1978 the Osters added a dining room. This addition is used
primarily for dinner meetings, weddings and overflow. Motel units were also
added with indoor entrances.

After Gary Oster's death, Larry and Ellie Heintzman of Aberdeen assumed
ownership of the local steakhouse, lounge and motel in August 1980. Two
years later they added living quarters onto the motel unit.

The Gold Nugget continues to provide dinner beginning at 4 p.m. Tuesday
through Sunday and live music every Saturday night.

        John M. Buechler and his daughter Edna ready to serve a treat of
        ice cream or maybe a good piece of candy in their confectionery.

MAIN STOP

Believe it or not, the Main Stop, as we know it now, was once a Harness
Shop. It was later purchased by John Huber who had a dress shop there.

Beer started flowing from the taps in 1942 when Nels Waltman and his wife
purchased the building and the name of their business was Waltman's
Confectionery. A bottle of beer cost 10 cents and a bottle of pop was 5
cents. For a good 20 years they sold beer, pop, ice cream and popcorn.
There was also a barber shop inside the building run by Emery Jankert.

Harvey and Karen Bonen bought the business in August 1962. Harvey can
remember selling a glass of beer for 10 cents, a bottle of beer for 25
cents and a bottle of pop for 10 cents. For tobacco users Copenhagen was 20
cents a can and cigarettes were 30 cents a package. In the early 1970's
Harvey modernized the business and added onto the building to where pool
players then and now reside. After 20 years of hard work and doing a great
job Harvey and Karen decided to let someone else try their hand at it and
sold Harvey's Place to Bob and Kathy Leidholdt in June 1982. The business
was then known as Bob's Place.

Rick and Julie Boschee bought the business in September 1982 and the name
was changed to the Main Stop.

After 42 years you can still walk in the same door to consume a cold beer.
One big difference is that one thin dime will no longer buy a bottle of
beer, but merely a piece of candy.

BOWDLE MUNICIPAL LIQUOR STORE

Saloons were part of Bowdle's history in 1886, as stated in the May 10,
1886 Bowdle Pioneer. "Bowdle has five saloons and whiskey is prohibitive in
Edmunds County." It is assumed that some of the first business places in
Bowdle were saloons with some located in tents. Saloon business continued
until prohibition law took affect. Individuals still got their liquor by
illegal means -- bootlegging or making their own beer or wine.

According to records the city ventured into the liquor control plan by an
election held April 20, 1937 with 94 voting against and 122 in favor. The
same year package sale went into effect July 1.

Paul Goettling sold packaged liquor from a small building on north main (an
old barber shop in the east side of the present Sam's Cafe.) Later, about
1946 or 1947, on-sale liquor was added.

The Hoffman Pool Hall, which burned, was reconstructed (south side of Main
Street, presently the Senior Center.) Managers of this establishment were
Edwin (Beadle) Buechler, George Mashek, Herbert Bieber, Walter Blondo and
Art Hintz. This ended the era of the south side liquor store.

In 1976 a new liquor store building was constructed on the north side of
Main Street in the middle of the block. This new building was on the site
where Coyer's Hardware Store and the old pool hall were located.

This new establishment continues to serve its patrons on-sale and packaged
liquor. A special quarters in the back portion may be used as a private
meeting or party room.

The first manager in this new business was Edward McDowell of
Hendersonville, NC. Other who followed were Wilmer Boschee and Richard
Maier.

Since 1982 Gustav Ottenbacher of Aberdeen has leased the business from the
city and it is known as Gus's Bar & Bottle Shop. Gus and Vi Ottenbacher
continue to provide a place for people to socialize.

        Gus's Bar & Bottle Shop

DON'S BARBER SHOP

Don, with scissor and razor in hand, has trimmed many a head of hair among
the younger and older generation of men. Don remembers the price of his
first haircuts being 50 cents and a shave 35 cents.

This building originated first in the little town of LeBeau and then was
moved to its present site in Bowdle. Here it became a real estate office
with John Rhodes, proprietor. A few years later Henry Baer purchased the
building converting it to a hardware store. Then it became the First State
Bank of Bowdle owned by the Gross Bros.

After 1919 Mr. Todd operated the Post Office in this building until it was
moved to the site of present Youth Center (Bank of Bowdle in 1886.) Henry
Bonen converted the building into a barber shop and operated it until 1946.
Upon his retirement Don Hoven purchased the building and at the present
time is barbering.

VANITY BEAUTY SHOP

The Vanity Beauty Shop was started in 1948 by Lila (Buechler) Oster above
the Bowdle State Bank, now known as Erv's Furniture.

In 1951 the shop was moved to 2057 Main Street where it was in the basement
of the Oster home. At that time the business expanded to a three-chair shop
where many students took their apprenticeship training.

In 1977 an addition was built on the home which presently occupies the
beauty shop where one can still find Lila behind her hydraulic chair
greeting the customers with her favorite saying, "Howdy and any special way
you would like your hair done?"

JULY 18, 1929
  Mrs. Jacobina Weisz has opened a beauty parlor in the building next to

THERESA'S BEAUTY SHOP

Theresa Beitelspacher became a hair stylist after graduating from Stewart's
School of Hairstyling in Aberdeen. She began her career working at The
Classic in Aberdeen, but after a short time came to Bowdle to work at Alma
Leno's Beauty Shop.

After working with Mrs. Leno nine months, Theresa purchased the business in
1968. This shop was located above the Bowdle Theatre until December 1969
when the business was discontinued. Theresa moved to Hoven, continuing her
hair styling until December 1973.

Theresa then returned to Bowdle and opened a shop in the basement of her
home. Today she is still operating as a hair stylist giving hair cuts, perms
and other beauty needs.

        This picture, taken in 1940, shows Martha Weiss in her beauty shop.
        Note the equipment with all the rods and strings at the left. That
        is the way permanents were given in the 1930's and 1940's. The
        whole shop is a contrast to today's beauty equipment.

MARTHA'S BEAUTY SHOP

Bowdle's longtime beautician, Martha Weiss, was born at Watertown May 25,
1902 to Joe and Amelia (Kunert) Weiss. Shortly thereafter her parents
brought their family to a farm near Bowdle and later moved southwest of
town where they lived out their lives.

Martha completed a beautician's course in 1929 and after five years in the
business came to Bowdle in 1934 to establish her own shop, the first
location being in rooms at Mashek Cafe on Main Street.

She moved to several other locations and in 1940 when the Northwestern Bell
Telephone System went dial, she acquired the front rooms of the telephone
building on a shared arrangement so as to keep the equipment housed in a
warm building.

Martha has been in the beauty business 55 years, 50 of which were spent in
Bowdle. She recalls giving permanents for $1.95 back in the 1930's and
haircuts for two bits or a half dollar. She made her own setting solution
out of flax seed.

Not given to idle hands, her hobbies have been knitting, crocheting and
sewing and tending plants. She has also put in five years as a Green Thumb
worker and is a volunteer at the Senior Citizens Nutrition Site.

Although Martha has reached retirement age, she still pursues beauty work
and her hobbies and is extra happy to have acquired the building which
houses her Beauty Shop and doubles as a homesite
on east Main Street.

KLIP 'N KURL

Since August 1974 Mary Zimmer is the owner and hair stylist of Klip 'N Kurl
Beauty Shop, located in the front portion of her home.

This location allows Mary to be with her family and continue her business.
Today Mary continues to operate her shop giving perms and cutting hair for
men and women.

MILLER FUNERAL HOME

Bert deMalignon came to Bowdle from Selby in 1926 to start a Funeral Home
there and owned and operated deMalignon Funeral Home in Bowdle about 30
years, serving Bowdle and several surrounding communities.

In 1954 Ray Schriver purchased the Funeral Home from Emily deMalignon after
Bert's death and the Schriver family lived in Bowdle and operated the
business until 1961 when it was sold to Floyd Miller.

The Miller family resided in Bowdle, operating the Funeral Home 12 years.
During that time the facility was remodeled twice, adding considerable
space the second time and a Visitation Chapel was built in Selby.

The Millers purchased Huebl Funeral Chapel in Aberdeen in 1973 and moved to
Aberdeen. They have continued to own the facilities at Bowdle and Selby and
since that time have had two resident managers, Del Freimark and Edward
Ackerson.

The Ackerson family came to Bowdle in 1974 to manage the present business
under the name of Miller Funeral Home and the Miller Visitation Chapel in
Selby. From these facilities six surrounding communities and their rural
areas are served. The business is affiliated with Miller-Huebl Funeral Home
in Aberdeen and Floyd Miller continues a very active involvement.

REINIE J. HERMAN AGENCY ... NORTH CENTRAL SERVICE AGENCY

        Mary Wiepking going to work in March 1966.

In 1958 Reinhold J. Herman was licensed as a stockbroker for Commerce 
Brokerage Co. as the Herman Agency.  As his insurance business grew he
purchased the Ruben Schumacher building and hired Mary Wiepking for
part-time help. The business continued to expand and the office was
remodeled while Mrs. Wiepking became a full-time employee. She worked 17
years for Reinie Herman. In 1976 Marilora Nipp was hired and worked three
years as an Income Tax Consultant.

In 1962 Mr. Herman received his real estate license and Reinie J. Herman
Agency was a successful and growing business. It not only provided all
kinds of insurance and real estate needs, but provided income tax
consulting and sold hunting and fishing licenses.

Jan. 1, 1980 Milbert Schick and John Thurn of Eureka purchased Reinie J.
Herman Agency. Mr. Thurn conducted the business in Bowdle where the firm
continued to offer all types of insurance and tax service to the area, as
well as bookkeeping and investment services. It was known as North Central
Service Agency.

Nov. 1, 1983 Milbert Schick purchased the business from John Thurn and
hired Peggy Birchem as office manager with Shonda Rau as office secretary.
The firm continues to offer insurance, bookkeeping, tax and real estate
services.

RAY BACHMAN INSURANCE AGENCY

During the 1970's Harold Ehresman of Hosmer opened a branch of Farmers
Union Insurance in Bowdle. Mr. Ehresman was forced to retire due to health
reasons during the 1980's.

In May 1982 Ray Bachman incorporated the Farmers Union Insurance Agency,
now known as Ray Bachman Insurance Agency.

The agency, owned and operated by Ray and Lila Bachman, offers a full line
of insurance to the public underwritten by various companies. Lila acts as
office manager and secretary while Ray is the sales and service manager.

The office is located in the Bowdle Theatre building, previously occupied
by Montana-Dakota Utilities Co.

VETCH'S FLOWER SHOP

"The love of flowers is what started me in this business," stated Milda
Vetch. Milda received the art of arranging flowers and making corsages when
she was employed at Knecht Flower Shop.

After the business was sold Milda, along with her family's support, decided
to begin a flower shop in the basement of her home. Here she creates flower
arrangements for weddings, funerals and special occasions.

In 1985 Milda expanded the flower business setting up a greenhouse from
Beadle Floral of Aberdeen. It was the center of attraction for gardeners in
the area who purchased plants and flowers for their yards.

Milda anxiously awaited the spring season of 1986 to help beautify the town
for the Centennial.

MERTZ GREENHOUSE AND FLORAL

Ever since Ernest and Dorothy Mertz were married in 1943, Dorothy had a
huge garden. During the earlier years no one would think of going to a
greenhouse and purchasing plants. Dorothy started her own ... first on
windowsills and then in a hotbed. The source of heat in a hotbed is
well-rotted horse manure placed in layers about a foot high at the bottom
of the bed and covered with about 8-10 inches of soil. This would give off
a lot of heat and would have to be watched carefully so the plants wouldn't
burn.

After years of this, the first and very flimsy greenhouse was built. It was
placed on the south side of the garage and was a very flimsy plastic
structure. The minute the wind was strong, the plastic would rip. Dorothy
spent many a night out there patching plastic and watching so the plants
wouldn't freeze.

The next thing Ernest and Dorothy did was to move the old Greger house to
the farm and with the help of donations of many old storm windows, they
transformed this into a very serviceable green-house. A year later this
house was completely demolished by a tornado. Pieces of glass were found as
far away as 3-4 miles from the original site.

Ernest said he was tired of putting up temporary structures so they ordered
fiberglass from a greenhouse supply company in Texas and a 20 by 30 ft.
building was put up west of the house. There was also a starting house on
the south side of the family room where Dorothy started the plants before
moving them to the big house. Ernest and Dorothy put in many hours in both
houses.

During the time the greenhouse was flourishing Dorothy had a garden and of
course, many flowers. She tried to arrange them for many occasions, mostly
church. In 1964 she enrolled in a correspondence course from Floral Arts
Center in Phoenix to learn the basics and the course also supplied her with
limited amounts of supplies she had never used before.

The next spring she made a few corsages for Mother's Day. By the next year
word-of-mouth had spread the news Dorothy was in business at Mother's Day.
Many a time men were standing on the basement steps waiting for their
corsages for the wife at home.

In 1971 Ernest and Dorothy took a long deserved vacation to visit their
daughter Ruth and family in Europe. When Dorothy returned in July she drove
to Brookings to take a short course in floral design from Dr. and Mrs.
David Adams. Dorothy's father Henry Giedt died Aug. 21, 1971 and her mother
asked Dorothy to do the flowers for the funeral. The funeral director Floyd
Miller asked her if she would consider doing all the funeral work flowers
for him and Dorothy agreed.

The flower shop grew by leaps and bounds, as did the greenhouse. During the
spring season at least four other ladies were employed on a part-time
basis. A small egg cooler had been purchased from Mrs. Otto Bollinger. This
was not large enough so a large cooler from a cafe in Aberdeen was set up in
the northwest corner of the family room and they were in business. This was
often too small and the basement floor had to help out many a time.

In 1976 Ernest and Dorothy built a home in Bowdle, which also accommodated
the flower shop. This was more accessible to local trade. The shop put out
an average of 100 weddings a year.

By 1979 Dorothy could see her feet could not take the strain any longer. In
August she sold the flower shop to Mr. and Mrs. Duane Knecht of Bowdle.
This small shop had a very meager beginning, however, by the time Dorothy
sold it, it was covering a 100-mile radius.

MONTANA-DAKOTA UTILITIES CO.

In October 1945 after an extended period of negotiations, Montana-Dakota
Utilities Co. purchased the Dakota Public properties which included power
plants, transmission lines and distribution systems in 92 towns in North
and South Dakota including Bismarck, Dickinson, Mandan, Mobridge, Ellendale
and Bowdle. Five steam heat systems were also acquired. This business
transaction was financed by the sale of common stock and first mortgage
bonds. It added approximately 20,000 electric customers in the
Montana-Dakota Utilities system.

In January 1959 the 41.6 KV substation north of Bowdle was upgraded to
accommodate a new 115 KV transmission line which provided the area with
additional electrical capacity. The first mercury vapor street lights were
installed in the Bowdle business district in 1963. Mercury vapor street
lights were then installed in the residential section in 1966. Bowdle
sports fans were among the first to enjoy a lighted football field, which
was also installed in 1966. In 1979 a new city distribution substation was
installed on the east edge of town to serve the city of Bowdle.

In 1983 lights were installed in the Meakins Park softball field.
Approximately a half million dollar project improvement on the 41.6 KV
portion of the MDU substation 1/2 mile north of Bowdle was completed in
1984.

Raymond J. Moser was the first representative in Bowdle for Montana-Dakota
Utilities Co. Other past representatives included Ernest Schanzanbach, Max
Huger, Otto Schaefer and Victor Baker. Present employees are Del Huber,
cashier and Duane Steiger, district representative for the Bowdle and
Hosmer area.

U.S. POST OFFICE--BOWDLE, S.D.

The Post Office at Bowdle was first established as Kellie in Dakota
Territory May 16, 1884. The location of the office was 1-1/2 miles
southwest of the current location of Bowdle. July 24, 1886 the Post Office
was moved into what is now the city of Bowdle and was renamed Bowdle.

The first location was on the south side of Main Street. It was moved at a
later date to the north side. It was at three locations, the last being at
the corner of Main Street and 3rd Avenue. Dec. 31, 1960 the Post Office was
moved across the street to its present location.

The first postmaster in Kellie, Dakota Territory was Albert P. Henderson.
He served from May 16, 1884 to July 23, 1886. The first postmaster of
Bowdle was William Vantine and he took office July 24, 1886. Postmasters
serving after him were: Fred J. Bowman, April 1889; Mrs. Emma Bowman,
October 1892; Geo Bickert, September 1895; Evan J. Edwards, September 1897;
Hiram A. Mason, March 1911; Henry B. Baer, June 1913; John R. Todd,
February 1922; Amelia L. Rositch, August 1934; Emma Erbe, July 1945 and
Melvin R. Bollinger, February 1958.

OCT. 7, 1893
  G. Bickert, a former Ipswichian, has been appointed Postmaster of Bowdle.
Mr. Bickert will make an efficient officer and is especially qualified to
decipher the chirography on letters passing the Bowdle Office.

NOV. 20, 1911
  A post saving bank department has been established in the Post Office at
Bowdle.

JAN. 7, 1926
  The local Post office reports the most prosperous year in the history of
Bowdle. The sale of postage stocks amounted to over $5,000. Other business
Institutions of the city also report having done very satisfactory business
in 1925.

RAILROAD DEPOT

Aug. 16, 1962 Bowdle Pioneer: "Bowdle's old gray two-story railroad depot
has been replaced by a smaller structure and the old building moved to a
new location. A.G. Reuer purchased the old building.

Mr. Hartzell has no records of the year in which the old building was
constructed. It was here in 1906. According to history the C.M. & St. Paul
Railroad was completed to Bowdle in 1886. The first regular train came to
Bowdle Sept. 12, 1886.

Mr. Hartzell came to Bowdle in 1944 as the station agent. At that time
people of this area were still dependent on the railroad for transportation,
mail delivery and freight. It was during World War II rationing of tires
and gasoline had reduced the use of the automobiles.

The trains were also used for moving troops, as well as for civilian
transportation and freight. His wife brought meals to him at the station.
At one time he was so busy for two weeks he couldn't leave to go downtown
for a haircut.

The old steamers were still in use. They pulled 50-75 cars, where the
modern engines can pull a string of 250. There would be a train on every
siding between Bowdle and Aberdeen and one on the main track between.

It was the job of the agent to keep track of all those trains, copy train
orders and relay them to the engineers so they would know when and where to
meet trains traveling in opposite directions.

After the war, railroading changed greatly to what Mr. Hartzell refers as a
'push button' operation. Automatic signals were installed, eliminating much
of the agent's work.

These signals are operated from a central office in Aberdeen. The movement
of all trains is followed there and the trains are guided by pushing a
button to change the signal lights along the track from red to green when
the track is clear."

LARRY HAAR TRUCKING

Larry Haar has been trucking for 34 years. He began at age 13 when he drove
for his father Ray Haar, who operated a cattle truck and grain trailer.
Often Larry and his brother Lester would drive double for their father
while he worked part-time as a blacksmith.

The first truck was a K-B 7 International with a 32 ft. cattle trailer.
Later they purchased a 1952 Ford F-800 with a 38 ft. trailer.

Larry remembers many incidents of narrowly escaping an accident. One
experience he shares was when he was returning from Sioux City, Iowa late at
night and accidentally fell asleep while driving. Suddenly he was awakened
just a few feet away from crashing into a bridge.

When he returned home his father asked, "Larry did you have an accident?"
Larry kept denying that any accident happened. After repeated questioning,
Ray finally expressed to his son that he had a dream that night of the
whole incident. Larry finally confessed and knew that God had a hand in
this matter.

His brother Lester moved to Minneapolis and Larry continued trucking
full-time with his father. He purchased his own truck, a C-1000 Ford and
hauled livestock and grain in the neighboring areas to the Twin Cities.

In 1973 he was involved in an accident that totaled his truck and caused
leg injury. After being hospitalized two months and recuperating at home,
he didn't drive again until 1975. A few years later Larry's father died in
February 1979. Now being the sole manager Larry purchased a 1971 Peterbilt
tractor and four trailers.

Larry resides west of Bowdle and with the help of his sons Myron and
Timothy, they continue to operate two tractors and four trailers.

BEITELSPACHER TRUCKING

Leon Beitelspacher has a business of hauling livestock and grain. Leon
moved to Bowdle in September 1973 from Hoven.

The experience of trucking began in 1946 when Leon was trucking with his

from Lowry.

Many trucking hours are spent on the highway hauling the farmer's livestock
and grain.

BOWDLE LIVESTOCK SALES COMMISSION

The Bowdle Livestock Sales Commission Company was formed in 1939 by E.B.
Moser. Its facilities was located beside the tracks of the Chicago
Milwaukee Railroad. Mr. Moser built the wooden portion of the present
building on the site of the old lumber yard, with all the pens outside. In
the 1940's he added the metal portion to cover part of the pens.

In April 1954 Milton Hagele purchased the company and Kermit Ulmer started
crying at Hagele's second sale.

Mr. Hagele continued to operate the business until it was purchased by
Simon and Ulmer in 1961. They continued to conduct sales in this barn until
1964. Finding this building inadequate, Simon and Ulmer built a new sales
barn south of Bowdle on Highway 12.

BOWDLE LIVESTOCK SALES CO. INC.

Milton Hagele bought the Bowdle Livestock market from E.B. Moser in 1954.
It was then located just west of Farmers Equity Elevator. He operated the
business until 1961, when he sold the barn to Norbert Simon and Kermit
Ulmer.

In 1964 the two men built a new facility south of Bowdle on Highway 12 and
operated the barn until 1969. Clifford Goebel then took over the business
and has operated it since.

The main building is pretty much the same as it was originally, but the
surrounding land has been expanded considerably to accommodate the growing
numbers of livestock in the area.

This is a very good cattle and hog area, in so much as, most farmers and
ranchers in the Bowdle area have some livestock along with their grain
operations.

Cliff and his wife Ellorine moved to Bowdle in 1969 with their two children
Roxanne (now Mrs. Donald Gill of Eureka) and Michael of Rocky Ford, CO.
Steven, born in 1977, is still at home.

Cliff manages the business and Ellorine is the office manager. They have
approximately 27 employees and two full-time yardmen. Ruben Sandmeier has
been with them since 1969 and has done a fine job.

A new veterinary facility has been added in the last few years and also
many holding pens. The Bowdle Livestock Sales Co. Inc. is a home-owned
business here to serve the people of Bowdle. They are large enough to serve
your needs and small enough to appreciate your business.

SIECK VETERINARY SERVICE AND SUPPLY

The Sieck Veterinary Service and Supply was established in April 1964. At
that time the office was located at 3031 Main Street, the storage building
now owned by Erv's Furniture, until the summer 1968.

The office was then moved to the basement of the Theatre building until the
summer 1982 when Jacob Sieck moved into his present location at 2013 Main
Street (former Schaible Apartments, now Kleins Apartments.) Doctor Sieck
also lives there, but before he roomed as a boarder at the Gottlieb
Weisenberger home.

Lloyd Voller has been Sieck's assistant for several years. Mrs. Gerhard
Walz worked as his secretary in the office most of his veterinary years.
Since he moved to his present location he has handled the work alone.

Although most of Jacob Sieck's time is occupied with veterinary medicine,
he likes to participate in his favorite sports of hunting and fishing.

Jacob Sieck was born in Selby Feb. 8, 1935 to Arthur and Martha Sieck.
After graduating from school he received his doctorate of veterinary
medicine.

SUPER PRODUCTS INC.

Buddy and Patti Williams were the founders of this plant. Wilmer Boschee
and Alvin Bauer became stockholders of the Super Products Inc. plant. Later
they became owners and managers. Wilmer Boschee was president, Alvin Bauer
vice-president and Arelene Gross, secretary-treasurer.

This plant was located in the Bowdle Legion Hall. It began Nov. 13, 1980
with 19 employees. They manufactured a tow rope known as "Super Rope." Also
the plant in Bowdle was the distribution point for the Super Rope in an
11-state area.

This business continued in Bowdle until 1982 when it was sold to Frontier
Caps at Ipswich. Now the manufacturing plant is known as Frontier Rope,
still producing the Super Rope.

ALDINGER HIDE & FUR INC.

The Aldinger Hide & Fur Co. was started in 1954 by Ruben Aldinger and his
son Donald. Their business began with one small building. They were kept
busy in the summer traveling to different towns to buy iron and metals
which they brought home to cut and clean for resale.

By the same token their job in the winter was to go to various towns in the
area to buy fur. The furs they would get would be fox, mink, coyote, bobcat,
beaver and muskrat.

Don left for the Army in 1956 and Ruben hired Larry Bonen to help with all
the work. As time went by and Don returned from the service to work with
his father, business was increasing, so they added an additional building
to the present shop which includes seven rooms.

Ruben retired in 1979, but in the winter he would come to the shop to help
with the furs. In 1983 Ruben Aldinger died and now the business is owned by
Aldinger Hide & Fur Inc.

Those working with the company are Don Aldinger, Jack Aldinger, Dave Bonen,
Larry Bonen, Doug Bonen, Marvin Mittleider and Bobby Aldinger. Velma Bonen
is the bookkeeper.

        Original building of Aldinger Hide & Fur.

        Ruben Aldinger and son Donald.

KURLE AND KURLE BLACKSMITH SHOP

Jacob J. Kurle came to Bowdle in 1905 at age 18 and worked for his uncle in
the Blacksmith Shop until 1912 when he bought half interest of the
business. Later he bought the remaining interest, which he sold in 1919. He
was in the oil and gas business until 1921 and then bought the Bowdle
Implement Company.

In 1946 the business name was changed to J. Kurle & Sons by making his
three sons Ray, Alvin and Morris partners. The firm that Jacob started had
a complete lumber yard, millwork plant, modern machine and repair shop,
along with International Harvester tractors and farm equipment. After his
death in 1951, the firm continued to operate under the present name.

In 1981 Ray retired and the present owners Morris and Alvin ended their
association with International Harvester after more than 69 years. They are
now in the lumber and hardware business.

shop which they will use to store their stock of farm machinery and buggies.

Sandmeier who took possession the first of the week.

REUER GARAGE & IMPLEMENT

Alvin Reuer purchased the Reuer Garage & Implement in 1943 from John
Hennecke. In this establishment Reuer sold a line of cars from the Chrysler
Corporation including Chrysler, Plymouth, DeSoto and later the Rambler.
Alvin also sold a well-known line of machinery such as Minneapolis-Moline,
Farmhand, New Holland and Melroe.

Alvin believed in the motto "service what you sell" and proved it as he
overhauled cars, did body work and serviced machinery. At one time he had
15 employees.

Now in 1985 he is still selling some machinery, mostly parts and doing some
mechanical work. The car sales has been discontinued.

This Reuer Garage has a wealth of history since its roots reach back to
1886. The building was then known as the Dumont Hotel. The front part of the
building is still the original. Later the building was known as the Watson
Hotel.

In the past, when John J. Eisenbeiss purchased this building, he converted
part of it into a garage and sold cars. The front part of the building still
served as the hotel, then known as the Anderson Hotel.

OCT. 17, 1907
  Gross Bros. sold out their farm machinery business to Fred Mackaben who
hails from Illinois. Gross Bros. are interested in the First State Bank and
this business takes up too much of their time, therefore sold out the
machinery business.

JAKE'S BLACKSMITH

Jake's Blacksmith Shop was located east of the Highway 47 and Main Street
intersection. The business was begun by Jacob Voller shortly after he
retired from farming in 1950. He had learned the rudiments of blacksmith
work early in life from his father John Voller on the farm. While serving
in the Army during World War I, he shoed horses and mules.

While farming he did most of the necessary repair work on machinery and a
forge with red-hot coals was a common sight, as he shaped red-hot steel on
the anvil. Much of the work done in his shop was for farmers. He had an
inventive mind and made some of the equipment he used in his shop. One was
a saw used to cut metal. With an electric motor, it made fast work of
cutting thick steel.

As a boy, he had wanted a toy steam engine. In his later years, he built
some that other steam engine enthusiasts from out-of-state bought, when he
quit working about 1972.

        Jacob Voller ... Farmer and Blacksmith

                THE BLACKSMITH

        A doctor, surgeon and dentist is he,
        Yet he dares to practice without a degree;
        He is never seen in hospital-white,
        And his doctor's suite is an awful sight,
        With shavings and grease-rags on the floor,
        While sooty smudges adorn each door.

        When he gets ready to operate,
        He gathers tools of strength and weight.
        His patients' wounds are seldom sponged,
        But sometimes into water plunged.
        Especially, when treated with cherry-red heat,
        And a sledge or hammer is used to beat.

        He diagnoses mechanical ills
        Of countless machines; and in hay-time drills,
        In the teeth of an ailing, old buckrake,
        That suffers from a split-tooth ache;
        If a tooth is bad, he extracts the old,
        Replacing with one the lumber yard sold.
        His powerful hands, so calloused from toil,
        Keep farm machinery tilling the soil.

                                Esther L. Voller

("The Blacksmith" was published in the June 1959 issue of "Pasque Petals."
The blacksmith, Jacob Voller, was the author's husband.)

HABERER'S IMPLEMENT INC.

The present site of Haberer's Implement Inc. was constructed in 1974 by the
Star Steel Building Company. The present site consists of 113,200 square
feet. The main building contains three offices, show room and parts and
sales area, two restrooms and a display area.

The shop consists of four stalls and is fully insulated with four 14 foot
overhead doors with electric door lifts. Parts storage is on the second
level.

The building was built in 1974 by owner Orval Haberer. In 1976 a
corporation was formed with Orval Haberer, DeWayne Weisz Keller of
Mobridge. In 1978 Orval Haberer sold the business in Bowdle and Mobridge to
DeWayne Weiszhaar of Bowdle and Richard Keller of Mobridge. They are
presently the owners and managers of Haberer's Implement Inc. in Bowdle and
Mobridge.

The major lines of machinery are CASE IH and Versatile farm equipment. Many
other short lines are carried by the owners. The business supplies
machinery, parts and shop work for a wide area of many counties surrounding
the area.

FORD MOTOR COMPANY

The first Ford dealership in Bowdle was managed by Erbe and Davidson in
1915. In 1917 they sold their dealership to J.J. Eisenbeisz, who sold the
first Model "T" Ford in Bowdle. He later changed the name from J.J.
Eisenbeisz Ford to J.J. Eisenbeisz & Sons.

Jan. 3, 1919 Eisenbeisz sold the dealership to H.W. Bartels, Walt Isaak and
E.H. Kundert. During this period Runabout cars were sold for $500, touring
cars for $545, coupes for $650, sedans for $775 and one ton trucks for
$550. In conjunction with the Ford dealership they also started the Bowdle
Oil Company March 18, 1920. Later in 1920 the dealership changed hands.
E.H. Kundert took Christ Schlaht as a partner, dissolving partnership with
Isaak and Bartels.

Christ Schlaht continued running the Ford Garage and selling Fords until
1939. From 1940 to Jan. 19, 1956 Bowdle was left without a Ford dealership
and the Ford dealer in Hosmer serviced the people of Bowdle with Adolph
Treichel as salesman. He had his office at the J.K. Kurle business.

Jan. 19, 1956 Reinhold Pfeifle of Eureka obtained the Ford dealership for
Bowdle and sold cars through the Dumdie Garage. In 1957 Albert Berg
purchased the business from Gust and Edgar Dumdie. For seven years Albert
Berg ran the Ford business where the City Library is today. A new building
was erected south of Bowdle in 1963 by Berg. In 1976 he sold the Ford
dealership to Robert and Judie Beadle, the present owners.

Robert Beadle decided to expand the service department. A new addition was
added in 1979. The land across the street to the west was leased for the
truck display, Today, in 1985, there are a total of 11 employees at the
garage.

DAVE'S REPAIR

Among the latest new businesses in Bowdle is Dave's Repair, owned and
managed by Dave McCarlson. He opened his shop in January 1985 after he
purchased it from Larry and Gloria Leidholt, known then as Leidholt
Chevrolet Inc.

Leidholt Chevrolet Inc. began operation in April 1978, when Larry Leidholt
purchased the business from Wilmer Schaible. The business dealt with sales
of Chevrolet cars and trucks, service and repair.

Martin and Wilmer Schaible had owned the Schaible Chevrolet Garage many
years. March 22, 1956 Schaible's was completely destroyed by fire. That was
the end of the era of the Opera House, which had been converted into a
garage. Mr. Schaible rebuilt the present structure of Dave's Repair.

Dave McCarlson continues to operate a mechanical shop working on cars,
trucks and machinery and plans to incorporate new areas.

SCHILLING SERVICE [Haberer's Gamble - Skogmo]

More than 50 years ago in the 1920's, Al Englehard owned a large framed
building on 4th Avenue south of Bowdle Hardware, from which he conducted a
cream, egg and poultry business and in a small addition, a gas and oil
business known as the WNAX Station.

In 1933 Wm. Schilling announced he had purchased the WNAX Station and Fred
Schumacher would be the manager. He served in this capacity a couple of
years. Bill moved the station to a small building between Englehard's and
the hardware. In 1935 a fire, ignited by the starting of a car, destroyed
the station and the bulk truck.

October 1936 saw the WNAX Station in a new building which Bill purchased and
moved from Roscoe to lots west of Bowdle Hardware. The building, formerly
used as a garage, was partially stuccoed. The filling station and a room
for car washing took up the front half of the building. The back part was
partitioned off for living quarters for Bill and Hilda and their family.
Work of changing the tanks and pumps and building an approach from Main
Street to the station was completed Nov. 24, 1936.

March 31, 1938 Bill Schilling severed his connections with WNAX and
operated the White Eagle bulk and gas station. July 28, 1938 he installed
the hydraulic hoist and hired Eugene Aldinger and Elmer Barth to help with
the work.

Oct. 21, 1943 the Bowdle Pioneer reported, "A crew of men are busy
completing the frame work of the addition to the Schilling Garage which will
double the building in size and take care of his expanding business."

Oct. 8, 1945 the Pioneer reports, "The Schilling Service will have a nice
display room as soon as the remodeling and redecorating is completed. Mr.
Schilling has closed the car entrance at the front of the building and
installed large plate glass windows to give plenty of light. The display
room is the entire width of the building with a small office in the
southwest corner."

Bill Schilling and Bill Miller had been granted a franchise for the Ford
dealership. This was the era of the Kaiser car.

        Hilbert Jurief, Julius and Bill Schilling, Fred Schumacher, Elmer
        Barth

        Bill and Hilda Schilling, a salesman, Eugene Aldinger, Fred
        Schumacher

The year 1946 brought tragedy. A fire erupted when the gas tank of a car in
for repairs was punctured. The loss was estimated at $20,000. Richard
Schumacher, Elmer Barth and George Krumm were the mechanics. The gas poured
onto the floor. Richard Schumacher and Jake Lassle had been working on the
car on the hoist and were lowering it to the floor. Schumacher ran to get
something to catch the gas, but it spread onto the floor and reached the
furnace.

Schumacher screamed a warning to the others and ran for the back door.
Krumm and Barth followed, but the high pressure from the fire forced the
door closed, catching Barth's leg. Lassle stumbled and fell over some tires
on the floor, burning his hand and ears.

The first explosion followed, breaking out the windows and the other men
Jake Lassle, Ed Huber and Raymond Haar, who were in the garage on business,
were then able to get out the small door.

The second blast caught Krumm, who was scorched and his hair singed. The
entire building was on fire from the explosion. The back roof collapsed and
the Bowdle volunteer firemen fought the blaze 1-1/2 hours before they could
control the blaze.

Fifty gallon drums of gasoline and alcohol added to the hazard of the fire.
The firemen sprayed water on the men and barrels until they could be rolled
out of danger. The men (Schumacher and a helper) became like walking
icicles in the bitterly cold December weather. Some tires and small
equipment were saved.

The loss of the 60 by 80 ft. structure was estimated at $20,000 with $2,000
worth of tractor tires and a greater amount of tools, accessories and farm
implements. Three cars, belonging to George Sebert, Joe Voller and John
Barth, were destroyed in the fire.

Bill Schilling continued in business by closing off the back part of the
building until it was rebuilt in 1947 and then a fireproof structure was
erected. Bill said he had not realized how hazardous it had been to operate
in a building that was not fireproof. Mr. Schilling sold out in 1958 and
moved to Aberdeen where he was employed by South Dakota Wheat Growers.

In 1963 Mr. and Mrs. Merle D. Haberer opened a Gamble-Skogmo Store in the
Schilling building. They carried a large stock of clothing, hardware, tools,
sporting goods and auto supplies. Later they just sold dairy supplies.

Again the building is vacant as Haberer took his dairy business to Aberdeen.

FARMERS UNION OIL COMPANY ... BOWDLE, & TOLSTOY CENEX

The Farmers Union Oil Company of Bowdle was incorporated Jan. 29, 1946
after many months of soliciting all interested area farmers. Stock was sold
for $25 a share. The first directors were John Bieber, Ray Nelson, Fred
Buechler, Jacob Heilman, Fred Eisenbeisz and James Kane, who was
secretary-treasurer. The first location was in the building adjacent to the
Commet Cream Station.

Shortly after incorporation Edwin Bieber was hired as the first manager. At
this time his father, John Bieber resigned from the board and was replaced
by Ernest Schumacher, who became the first chairman of the board of
directors. Elsie Reede Miller was the first bookkeeper.

The initial annual meeting was held the first Wednesday of the following
March at which time there were 86 stockholders with a paid capital of
$12,900 and the number of patrons was 110.

The first audit report was from April 1 to Dec. 31, 1946 and it didn't show
a very bright picture. The business owed $1.30 for every dollar of current
assets. The next audit was Jan. 1, 1947 to July 10, 1947 and showed 102
stockholders and 160 patrons.

Due to ever increasing patronage and an increase in stockholders it started
on the upgrade. After 25 years of operation there were 392 common
stockholders, 241 preferred stockholders and 434 patrons.

The total savings for the first year of operation was $8,000 plus compared
to 1970 amounting to $46,652 and in 25 years of operation there were total
savings of $603,167.

The Co-op passed a milestone at the end of 1981 when gross sales reached
over $1,000,000 after 36 years of operation.

Today services have increased to fertilizer, propane and chemical spraying.
In 1982 Stotz Oil Co. was purchased from Gordon Stotz and he then joined
the staff of employees.

Present directors (1985) are Jimmy Jackson, LeRoy Beitelspacher, Maurice
Hoffman, Harlan Hettich and Richard Mitzel. Walter Wiskow is the manager
and employees are Gordon Stotz, Dennis Schock and Sylvia Fiedler as
bookkeeper.

Past Directors are Fred B. Buechler, Ernest Schumacher, Fred Eisenbeisz,
Ray Nelson, John Bieber, James Kane, Jacob Heilman, Mike Mitzel, Clarence
Schumacher, Ted Leidholt, Ray Hoerner, Marvin Miller, Ernest Mertz, Otto
Bieber, Don Thomas, Walter Johnson, Ruben Bollinger, Ray Rieger, Erhard
Beitelspacher, Allen Strouckel, Norman Gross and Edmund Dewald.

Past employees include Helmuth Eisenbeisz, Dale Murray, Roy Kraft, Ervin
Kamlitz, James Goldade, Emil Bollinger, Wilbur Klein, Melvin Maier, Richard
Maier, Leo Buechler, Maurice Hoffman, Albert Berg, George Seurer, Edward
Dewald, Chester Schmierer, Roger Huber, Roger Jacobs, Victor Stotz, Victor
Schlepp, Mark Bollinger and Evon Job.

Past Bookkeepers were Elsie Reede Miller, Dorothy Sebert Berreth, Clara
Fischer, Delores Bachman and Connie Heinrich.

Past managers include Edwin Bieber, Eugene Vilhauer, Walter Fischer, Jay
Ausland and Garlan Bigge.

STANDARD OIL BULK AGENCY

Standard Oil products have been in the community of Bowdle for many years.
Mr. Jacob Bitz moved to this area from Eureka in March 1926 and became a
bulk agent for Standard Oil. He purchased the truck which was owned by the
bank. The truck was operated by Christ Weiszhaar.

Oct. 10, 1929 the first advertisement for Standard Oil Products appeared in
The Bowdle Pioneer. ISO-Vis Motor Oil and Palorine Motor Oil, products of
Standard Oil of Indiana, were introduced 20 years prior to 1929. Oil was
selling for 30 cents a quart in 1929. Mr. Bitz operated the truck until
1930 when he sold it to Ray Moser who operated the truck along with a
station.

In 1934 C. Weisgram became the bulk agent. He operated the bulk truck one
year and in 1935 turned the business over to Joe Kelsch, who ran this
thriving business six years. In October 1941 he sold out to Martin Schaible.

Mr. Schaible operated as the bulk agent 10 years and increased the business
even more. In 1951 he sold to Albert Berg. The business thrived as more
farmers went to Standard Oil products. Mr. Berg ran the truck until 1957
when he sold the agency to Gordon Stotz.

In 1960 the price of stove fuel was 16.9 cents per gallon. From the time
Standard Oil of Indiana products came to Bowdle the tanks and pumps were
owned by the company and the agents owned their own trucks. Jan. 30, 1976
Standard Oil changed to the Jobber System which forced agents to buy all
the pumps, storage tanks and assume their own accounts receivable. This new
system put the bulk agent on his own.

Gordon Stotz was the first and only jobber Standard Oil (now known as
Amoco) had in this area. He operated this business 25 years and in November
1982 he sold it to Cenex of Bowdle. Standard Oil Bulk Agency has been
absent from the community since then.

        Gordon Stotz, Standard Oil Bulk Agent 1957-1982.

PHILLIPS "66" STATION

Oscar Metzger purchased the Phillips "66" Station, bulk fuel and gasoline,
from Jake Keszler in January 1947, but along with farming, did not operate
the station until Nov. 1, 1947. The station was located east of the Oscar
Metzger home along old Highway 12.

Oscar operated this station each day of the week, only closing for one
holiday, Memorial Day and otherwise taking turns with help during the other
holidays.

Only one hired man helped him until 1952 and then with an increase of
labor, two men were hired and a warehouse was built near the station to the
southeast.

When the new highway was built south of town, most of the traffic went
around town so Oscar decided to build a new station along the new Highway
12. J. Kurle & Sons of Bowdle constructed the new station. After completion
in October 1958 a grand opening was held for the public with each customer
receiving a 5 pound bag of sugar.

When Oscar retired in 1976 Duane Knecht purchased the station (now known as
D & D Oil Co.) in 1980 Duane also purchased the bulk fuel and gasoline.
Although Oscar is retired, he still helps work at the station.

Oscar can remember, "My first gas delivery was to the city council building
and my last delivery was to Oscar Huber and Wilbert Blumhardt.

NOV. 6, 1980
  Oscar Metzger ends a 33-year history of providing service to the
community as Metzger Oil Co. began Nov. 1, 1947 and ended Nov. 1, 1980.

D & D OIL COMPANY

Duane Knecht purchased the Phillips "66" Station from Oscar Metzger in
1976. The business became known as Duane's 66. He hired Lawrence Vetch who
retired in 1984 due to health reasons.

Duane did general car repair and major body work while Oscar Metzger and
Lawrence Vetch pumped gas, changed tires and helped customers.

Art Hintz was employed from 1978 to 1982 and still works on a part-time
basis.

In 1980 Duane Knecht purchased the bulk plant from Oscar Metzger. Duane's
son Dave became a full-time employee after he graduated from high school
and worked in the bulk plant operation with his father and Oscar.

In 1982 Joe Pesicka Jr. was hired as a mechanic and is still employed
there. The business is known as D & D "66" Service or D & D Oil Company.

Duane, Dave and Joe do all types of general car repair, major car body
repair, gas, oil and tire sales. Duane, Dave and Oscar handle the bulk home
heating needs, farm fuel and oil purchases.

The building itself was constructed by them and with the help of Ferdinand

BOWDLE CREAMERY

The Bowdle Creamery was established in 1903. It was a block north of its
present location. Not only did they manufacture butter, but ice cream as
well. They were also dealers in eggs and poultry, which was how it got the
name Bowdle Creamery & Produce Co. The proprietor was B.A. Oestreich. He
was a pioneer in raising potatoes and was known as the Father of Potato
Raising in the vicinity. Oestreich later sold out to C.W. Young.

Nov. 7, 1921 a building permit was issued for the construction of the
present Bowdle Creamery. Gross Land and Loan Company sold it to Minnesota
Creamery Company of St. Paul Nov. 7, 1930, who in turn sold it Dec. 18,
1939 to Crescent Creamery Co. also of St. Paul.

April 1, 1946 Crescent Creamery Co. sold to Leo C. Parrish and Phillip
Brickner of Scranton, PA. Brickner soon died, leaving Parrish sole owner.
Upon Parrish's death in 1969, he had willed 51% of the Creamery to Edwin J.
Blumhardt, who had been manager of the Bowdle Creamery since 1926. Prior to
his management A.J. Englehart was manager.

The other 49% of the Creamery was willed to a nephew Leo Parrish. In order
to settle the estate the Creamery was sold Aug. 26, 1970 to Frank Thomas of
Greenwood, WI and Jerome Hageman of Hoven. In December 1974 Thomas sold his
share to Robert Streeter of Pollock. Present owners of the Bowdle Creamery
are Jerome Hageman of Hoven and Robert Streeter of Pollock.

Edwin J. Blumhardt retired in 1970 and Edna Erlenbusch became the manager,
a title she still holds. Edna started her work at the Creamery June
30, 1947 as secretary and bookkeeper. She still does
all the bookkeeping, along with being manager.

The Creamery has seen many ups and downs. During years of drought there
were many times when it seemed it would be the end of the plant, as many
farmers were forced to sell their cows due to feed shortages. The cows had
to survive on Russian thistles, wild onion, pepper grass and other weeds.
The flavor from these weeds was very strong in the cream, which made the
butter flavor strong and it was almost impossible to find a market for the
butter. It had to take a big discount on the price when it was sold.

Cream was received from cream stations in nearby towns. Some was shipped by
rail and some was brought in by team and wagon, along with local producers.
For a short time they had a farm milk route, skimmed the milk at the plant,
used cream for the butter, then hauled the skim milk back to the farm. This
did not prove to be too successful. The horse and wagon transportation was
too slow and the skimmed milk got very sour and housewives complained of
washing out the sour smelling cans to get them ready for use the next
morning.

        E. Rieba, Alvin Blumhardt, Conrad Fix

In the 1960's and 1970's the Creamery manufactured from 1-1/4 to 1-1/2
million pounds of butter a year. This meant many long hours and hard work
since all the cream was brought to the plant in cream cans from the many
stations throughout the area, including several in North Dakota, as well as
South Dakota. People shipped cream to the plant by rail and truck from many
points in the Dakotas, as well as Montana and local patrons dropped their
cream off at the plant.

During the summer Sunday was always the biggest churning day. All the cream
came in on Saturday nights and had to be churned as quickly as possible
during hot weather. At one time the first crew would start at 11 p.m.
Saturday or as soon as enough cream was in the plant to start. This crew
would work all night. The next crew came at 6 a.m. and worked all day
Sunday until all the butter was made, usually about 5 p.m. Sunday.

Trucks had to wait in line to unload their cream until there was enough
cans emptied to make room on the floor in the plant to set the full ones.
Buttermilk was put into a cistern and farmers would line up to buy this for
one cent a gallon to feed their hogs from spring to fall.

Things changed quickly when cheese factories came into existence and
farmers sold their milk, rather than separating it and selling the cream.
This has dropped the volume of butter manufacturing to less than 1/2
million pounds per year. Along with this change came the switch of cream
being delivered in bulk trucks from the cheese factories. The cream is
pumped directly into the vats, no more heavy cans to wrestle, only the very
few that are still delivered by farmers still separating. Butter- milk is
now cooled thoroughly, put in an insulated tank and picked up for drying
purposes for animal consumption.

Except for what butter is sold locally from the plant and some surrounding
area stores, all the butter is shipped to a firm in New Ulm, MN. Some is
packaged in bulk of 68 pounds to the box. Most is put up in one pound
prints. The print butter is wrapped in whatever label the purchaser desires,
who furnishes the wrap. All butter sold locally is wrapped in the Bowdle
Butter label.

Butter that was sold in one pound prints used to be hand cut and wrapped
until 1971 when a butter printing machine was purchased. Before the
printing machine was installed, there were only enough prints made up for
local sales and stores in the area. None was shipped outside of South
Dakota. The price received for print butter is better than bulk pack
butter, which was the main reason for purchasing the printing machine.

Presently employed at Bowdle Creamery are Edna Erlenbusch, manager; Victor
Fischer, buttermaker and David Wurtz, assistant buttermaker.

OCT. 12, 1950
  The Bowdle Creamery & Produce Co. was awarded third for the manufacturing
of quality butter in a contest sponsored by National Butter Co. of St. Paul.

FARMERS CREAM STATION [Written by Albert Eisenbeisz]

The Farmers Cream Station of Bowdle ... just the mention of the name brings
to mind a kaleidoscope of activities and "local color" what with the German
language being spoken and German traditions and customs being observed by
many townspeople and farmers in the Thirties (my growing up years) farmers
who found it necessary to spend some time in the cream station on business
and some of the townspeople, retired farmers, who found it a place to
while away the hours in pleasant conversation; gumitlichkeit.

My dad, David H. Eisenbeisz, having been trained to operate the business,
became sole owner of it in 1920 and from then until around 1980. He bought
cream and bought until there was no more cream to buy ... literally, as
cheese processing plants became more numerous and farmers changed to
selling whole milk. He continued to buy eggs for a few years after that,
but gradually closed the station more and more hours each week until
January 1983 when a broken hip immobilized him and soon thereafter the
cream station building was sold to next-door business neighbors.

As is not unusual for some small town businessmen, so too my dad had to
engage in several businesses to make a living. Some activities at various
times included: buying hides and furs, wool and poultry and selling baby
chicks in the spring to farmers who also bought various chick feeds and
block salt.

At one time in the 1930's drought my dad managed the sale of hay to the
farmers which was shipped in from Minnesota. He sold Watkins products in
the cream station. He also developed an ability to repair sewing machines,
shoes and tarpaulins.

One of the most interesting activities was the buying of turkeys, ducks and
geese in autumn for shipment to the markets in Chicago and Milwaukee after
they were dressed and cooled. The geese and duck feathers were then sold to
a furniture manufacturing company in Minneapolis.

Because of the boiler system to create steam for cleaning cream cans, my
dad was also able to help a farmer or city dweller with the butchering of a
hog occasionally, as the steam and hot water aided in the removal of the
hair on the hog's skin.

And so over a period of about 60 years, there was a wide variety of
business activities in "THE" Farmers Cream Station.

APRIL 14, 1932
  The Farmers Cream Association, under David H. Eisenbeisz, has been one of
the leading stations of Bowdle. Mr. Eisenbeisz worked 5 years for Turner
Cream and Produce Co. in Mitchell before coming to Bowdle.
