                BOWDLE FLOUR MILL

        Photo in 1904 of Bowdle Roller Mill Co.

The Mill, originally a corporation formed by local people, began operation
in 1892, utilizing the wheat grown on the fertile prairies made into good
flour and shipped all over the world. Early brands were Diamond and Kaiser.
The latter was dropped during World war I. The last batch of Bowdle flour
was milled about 1967.

The peak years were 1931-1933. Farmers came as far away as 150 miles to
exchange their wheat for flour ... no cash transaction.

The mill was steam powered until the early 1920's and also produced
electrical power for the city. When the power company bought the power
rights, the mill converted to electric motors to drive the machinery. In
1968 it became a feed mill.

        Photo in 1909 of Bowdle Roller Mills

Wm. McGlenn, original owner of the Flour Mill, an uncle of Charles, Edna,
Wm. and Dwight Commet. The little building behind the Flour Mill was the
Electric Light Plant.

McFLEEG INC.

The McFleeg feed mill building in Bowdle has a history dating back to 1887
when E.E. Ring and his brother Simon incorporated and began construction on
Bowdle Roller Milling Company to produce flour. The mill was operated by
John Erbe, John Cock and G.L. Baumgardner.

In 1910 the Farmers Coop Milling Company purchased the mill. The large
engines used to run the mill had power to sell, so as an additional source
of income the mill began supplying power to Municipal Light and Power. In
1927 the mill ceased operation as a flour mill. John Cock leased the mill
and operated it as a grain elevator until 1931 when it was acquired by
Gross Land & Loan Company.

John Leno purchased the mill in 1931. He installed additional sifting
machinery and began to produce flour for the local trade. His two sons
Helmer and Reinhold continued the business after his death in 1946. Helmer
purchased his brother's shares in 1949.

During 1946-1948 the company saw broad expansion, around the clock
production and movement into the export market. In 1948 production for
foreign trade ceased due to competition from large flour mills. From
1949-1959 Helmer specialized in private label flour production for Super
Valu and Nash Finch. The product was distributed primarily in North Dakota,
Minnesota and South Dakota.

In 1971 the mill was purchased by Litehiser Grain and Feed which was owned
by Darwyn Boysen and manufactured and sold feed in addition to operating a
grain business. After a few years of operation, the mill was closed.

Boyd Fleeger, president of McFleeg Inc., purchased the mill in November
1980. After a year of expensive renovation the mill was reopened.

McFleeg was incorporated in October 1976. The business manufactures and
markets feed in North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota and Iowa from Bowdle,
Willow Lake and Watertown. A new 11,000 square foot headquarters retail
store was completed in Watertown in 1985.

A native of Willow Lake, Fleeger said his roots in South Dakota's history
go back to about the same time the mill was built. His grandfather was a
doctor from 1900-1952 in Willow Lake and his wife's grandfather homesteaded
by Willow Lake in 1878.

Boyd Fleeger's brothers Don and Vern joined the company in 1979. It has
grown dramatically and Boyd Fleeger expects continued growth because of the
quality reputation they have established and because of the excellent
people that have joined them.

"People build companies," he stated. "And we feel that our employees are
head and shoulders above the competition and that includes secretaries to
management."

AUG. 4, 1930
  Fire from sparks of a passing Milwaukee train completely destroyed John
Geib's elevator which was located just north of the depot in Bowdle.

SEPT. 12, 1940
  Grain elevator men of the city report for the first time since 1932 all
storage bins in their elevators are filled.

J.W. GEIB ELEVATOR

The J.W. Geib Elevator had its beginning in 1919 when John W. Geib moved
from Minnesota to form a partnership with Pete Geib, a cousin. The
partnership was dissolved soon after.

The original elevator, which stood on the same site, was set on fire by a
steam locomotive and burned to the ground Aug. 4, 1930. Estimated loss was
$22,000 including building, equipment and stored grain.

The elevator was rebuilt and opened for business in 1931. It cost John Geib
$12,000 and held 20,000 bushels. The Oct. 2, 1930 Bowdle Pioneer printed:
"The new building will be all in one piece with no annex. The storage
capacity will be about 22,000 bushels. A fine improvement over the old
system is that he will not have to shovel a single bushel of grain into a
car or out of the elevator. This new building is being built a bit farther
above the ground and will be so arranged that the grain will run out
without assistance."

The business served the community as a center for grain trade, feed
grinding and feed sales. In 1946 the elevator was sold to Joseph Stappler,
whereupon the Geib family moved back to Minnesota. The elevator was later
purchased by the Farmers Elevator of Bowdle and still stands today.

JULY 19, 1906
  The Victoria Elevator Company has a new wagon dump and a gasoline engine
installed to take the place of the oldtime horse power. The horse running
the business was blind.

JULY 6, 1911
  The Victoria Elevator Co. has torn down its elevator at this point and is
rebuilding it. This elevator is one of the first in Bowdle and the years of
service and decay have made it unsafe.

BOWDLE EQUITY EXCHANGE

A charter of incorporation was issued to William Haupt, Christ Miller,
Gottlob Goettling and others July 6, 1914 which started the corporation of
the Bowdle Farmers Union Equity Exchange in Bowdle. The first elevator was
a ballon-type building with about 18,000 bushel capacity.

The names of managers and their years served follow: Herman C. Baer,
1914-1915; Henry Bauder, 1915-1917; George Sautner, 1917-1918; W.A.
Rademacher, 1918-1922; Fred Pietzke, 1922-1925; Elevator closed in 1926;
Henry Theilen, 1927-1928; Fred Stotz, 1928-1971; Ignatius Nickolas,
1971-1978; Hudd Siebrecht started in 1978 and is the present manager.

In 1935 the old elevator was razed and a new 20,000 bushel cribbed house
was erected on the same location which was enlarged in 1954 with a 60,000
bushel cribbed annex.

In 1959 a steel building with a capacity of 90,000 bushel was erected. In
1969 the Joe Stappler elevator, known as Gretna Grain, was purchased. In
1979-1980 the driveway was raised and the elevator rewired.

MASON STORE

The Mason Store was completely destroyed in the big fire Feb. 22, 1900.
That same year it was rebuilt as a large brick building on the same site by
the same proprietor, H.A. Mason.

(A reprint from The Bowdle Pioneer Feb. 1, 1906 by C.T. Smithers editor,
well describes the store and Mr. Mason.)

"Mason's Store is a fine, large two-story brick building with basement,
occupying a whole block and built and designed by Mr. Mason himself, he
owning every stick in it.

Mr. Mason has been located in this section 38 years, knows everyone we
might say and every dollar he has is an honest one. Mr. Mason is not only
one of the foremost businessmen of the state, but he is also a practical
tinner, a licensed embalmer and he has every detail of the business at his
fingers end.

The offices are large and handsome. There are several vaults built right in
the walls and the woodwork and everything else is the best. The floor space
measures 18,000 feet and it is literally crammed with a stock of general
merchandise, furniture, etc.

Mr. Mason began in a small way but his energy, foresight, integrity and
business judgment soon told his emphatic success. As often was stated,
Misrepresentation, substituting or overcharging is unknown here and you
always receive to the full limit of value when you deal with Mr. Mason."

        Office of H.A. Mason about 1900. South Dakota State Historical
        Society Photo.

OZZIE'S SUPER VALU AND ERV'S FURNITURE

The largest building on Main Street was built in 1900 by Henry A. Mason. He
operated a general store.

In 1908 Gross Bros. (Henry, John, Christ, Martin) purchased the building
and continued to operate the general store. Christ Gross managed the men
and dry goods department. Martin managed the grocery and furniture
department. Martin died in 1939 and Christ continued to operate the store
until 1946.

Christ's son Don managed the store from 1946 to 1951. He moved to Eureka
and Erv Gross then managed the store from 1951 to 1965. In 1955 the
department store was remodeled into a supermarket. In June 1966 Ozzie and
Vonnie Schlepp purchased the supermarket and Erv Gross purchased the
furniture store.

At one time the upper half of the furniture store had two apartments where
families lived and later was made into a beauty salon, where Lila Oster had
her first shop and the Edmunds County Draft Board had their office.

SEPT. 2, 1909
  Mr. Mason gave the keys to his store to the Gross Bros. He will retire in
Bowdle.

  Gross Bros. opened a new variety department in a large floor space in the
front of the basement of their large store building. They will have a style
show.

G & O ELECTRICAL AND PLUMBING

In 1886 G.C. Aurand and Louis Amerpohl came to Bowdle and started a store
east of the Central Hotel (present site east of Joe Pesicka home.) The
building they erected was 20 ft. by 40 ft. and had a lean-to built on the
back. All the lumber in this building was carted from Ipswich with an oxen
team.

The building was a 1-3/4 story. Two rooms upstairs in front were finished
as sleeping rooms for Aurand and Amerpohl. The rest of the upper story was
used as a school room, for Sunday School and on Saturday afternoons as a
courtroom. This area remained the only school room in Bowdle until a school
house was built.

Mr. Aurand brought his family to Bowdle in 1887 and they occupied the front
rooms of this building as a dwelling until they built a home. They sold
goods at this location for six years.

In 1892 they moved the store to its present location. They jacked up the
building, put rollers under it and in 11 days had it to the new location.
Business continued every day as usual en route to its new site. Mr. Aurand
moved because Wallace & Smith and others were getting most of the trade.
Farmers from Walworth and Campbell Counties would stop with loads of grain
at Gerup's feed barn, sell their grain and do their trading at the nearest
store.

At this new location they added to the size of the building until it was 46
ft. by 80 ft. Aurand and Amerpohl continued as partners in business for 20
years until 1906.

G.C. Aurand operated the business by himself until 1919 when he sold his
general merchandise store to Chas. L. Gross of Gross Weinstein Co. in
Minneapolis, who had a chain of 16 stores. There were stores located in
Selby, Mound City, Mobridge and more. Benjamin Kritch and Nathan Gross as
manager operated the business for many years, known in the community as
Bowdle Mercantile Co. They sold general merchandise, as well as clothing
and groceries.

During 1939 remodeling took place. The large glass windows were installed
on the front. In 1946 the business became a Red Owl Store when John Haller
of Eureka became owner and manager. Fourteen years later, in 1960, Greg
Kramer purchased the Red Owl Store from John Haller. In 1978 Roger and
Margie Huber became the new owners of Kramer's Red Owl and renamed the
store R & M Red Owl.

In May 1981 Berkeley (Rocky) Gisi and Ward Oster leased the building from
Mr. Kramer. Since then Kramer gave the building a new look, sheeting it
completely with metal.

Rocky and Ward continue to operate with a variety of services including
plumbing, electrical work, heating, septic tank pumping, trenching and
selling appliances.

DEC. 1, 1932
  Hennecke Electric will open soon in the old building occupied by Chaffee
Studio.

OSTER'S ELECTRIC SHOP [Plumbing and Heating]

This business originated with John Oster as proprietor. He built an
electric shop next to Commet Produce in 1948 (the present bank parking lot.)

When that shop was destroyed by fire in 1950, he built Oster's Electric
Shop on south main where John specialized in wiring, plumbing and heating.
He sold appliances, Pittsburgh Paints and Zenith televisions and radios.
John Oster also serviced appliances, televisions and radios.

In 1965 Robert purchased the building and business from his father. He
continued to operate the business in the same manner. In 1976 the business
was moved to the present Adajar Clinic. In May 1977 the building on Main
Street was rented to Schnaible's Department Store with Dick and Agnes
Schnaible of Selby as owners.

Meanwhile Robert added an addition to his home on east main where he still
operates his business, Oster Electric Plumbing and Heating. The original
building on Main Street was rented to Our Closet in June 1984. This
clothing store was owned jointly by Milo and Sandy Opp of Eureka. Hilda
Schilling was manager and Carla Knecht and Eileen Job were sales clerks.
The business was discontinued in May 1985.

BOWDLE MEAT MARKET [Also known as Waltman's Meat Market]

According to Mrs. Nels Waltman, Nels made his own sausage in his home.
People would come and buy sausage. A friend of Nels, George Blondo, told
him he should try to sell the good sausage he was making. This is how
Waltman's Meat Market was started with Nel's righthand man Milbert Preszler
(Preszy to everyone.)

Waltman Meat Market was constructed in 1962 by Schumacher Steel Co. Richard
Schumacher was the contractor and Henry Leidholdt, carpenter and cement
worker.

Slaughtering was done on the Ernie Merkel farm and brought to the shop to
be cut and packaged. Helpers at the time were Mary Brown and Elizabeth
Schick.

Mrs. Regina Waltman used all her recipes for the various types of sausage
which the family had used for many years. The meat had to be cut by hand as
there was no electrical equipment, grinding and mixing was all done by hand
to make the sausage. Curing was done by a hand pump and the meat was placed
in a wooden barrel to cure.

When Ernie Merkel died in 1964 Everet Lemke did the slaughtering and helped
with other duties. Helpers at this time were Eugene Larson, Frieda Dewald,
Anita Bachman and Angie Lemke.

As time went by the work became easier due to the modern equipment, using
electric saws to cut the meat and the electric grinders.

Robert Huber went to work with Everet Lemke in 1967, doing the slaughtering
and Everet did the meat cutting. In 1968 Everet purchased the shop and
changed the name to Bowdle Meat Market, doing the same type of work with
the help of Frieda Dewald, Anita Bachman, Angie Lemke and his two righthand
men Robert Huber and Preszy.

In March 1978 Robert and Marilyn Huber purchased the shop with all the
modernized equipment for cutting meat and are in commercial meat
processing. The crew at the shop has included Kathy Huber, Frieda Dewald,
Eileen Job, Harvey Leidholt, Rodney Schlecht and Preszy, who is the
handyman.

A & B SHOP

The A & B Shop originated Oct. 13, 1948 when Bill and Adeline Miller
purchased from Les Olson, the druggist in Bowdle, his merchandise and some
fixtures. Since there was no doctor or hospital operating here, Olson
decided it was time to sell.

The store was named A & B Shop (Adeline and Bill) and there were many
changes through the years. The first two years the store was located in the
Bowdle Theatre where Les Olson operated his business, now where MDU is
located. After two years they wanted to expand, so in 1950 on a lot across
the street, a new brick and tile building was erected. In August the
building was ready for a new soda fountain. This service was short-lived as
REA began to supply the rural areas with electricity. Most homes had deep
freezers and the people bought ice cream from the stores.

During the years many name tagged items were sold and eliminated as times
changed. Some of these are even collectibles. Gifts, greeting cards, Black
Hills Gold and Silver, chocolates and nuts were specialties, as well as a
complete veterinary supply. The latter discontinued when a veterinarian was
needed in the surrounding area.

Adeline Miller says, "We tried to supply the needs of the community and
during this time we made many acquaintances through the 34 years in
business and appreciated their patronage. As the years went by and our
health began to fail, we had to cut down and we started looking for a buyer
or discontinue our business."

After Bill Miller's death in January 1981 Adeline continued operating the
business until it was sold to Lloyd Jones in February 1982. He was a son of
one of Bowdle's former pharmacists, Morris Jones.

Lloyd and Sally Jones sold the Bowdle business April 1, 1985 to Doug and
Mary Turner of Aberdeen and the business is now known as Turner Drug. Doug
and Mary have established permanent residency in Bowdle.

        Bill & Adeline Miller in 1973 25th Anniversary of A & B Shop

BOWDLE HARDWARE

The Bowdle Hardware goes back many years. It all started when Henry B. Baer
built the two-story, cement block building in 1906 and his brother Herman
C. Baer became his partner. The land was bought from Andrew Gerup and his
wife Lena. They specialized in heating, plumbing and hardware.

In 1917 Jacob G. Eisenbeisz and John M. Buechler began operating the
Hardware Store.

Jacob Moser and Otto Helmer took formal possession of the business April
15, 1923 and carried on the same line of service. Installing furnaces in
the home was a hot item in those days.

In the spring of 1948 Bernard and Margaret Carlson and Harold and Frances
Bauer of Napoleon, ND purchased the Hardware Store, continuing on with
hardware, plumbing, heating, wiring and appliances.

The partnership did not last long, as Harold was anxious to try another
venture, and he and Frances started a restaurant called the Dew Drop Inn,
east of the brick building where Erv's Furniture is now located.

Bernard Carlson became the sole proprietor of the Hardware Store in July
1949. He and Margaret lived in an apartment above the store with two
children: Bernard, age 3 and John, age 1.

The Bauers purchased a home for themselves and their children Billy,
Rodney, Tommy and Sheila on 8th Avenue from William Hoffman, which later
was the Gordon Stotz residence. In the spring of 1951 the Bauers sold the
Dew Drop Inn to Mr. and Mrs. Ervin Kamlitz and moved to Bismarck, ND.

Harold died Nov. 9, 1979 in Aberdeen where they had made their home for
many years. Frances still lives there and one sees her at Pred's where she
is a part-time clerk.

In 1954 the Carlson family moved into their new home at the corner of 2nd
Street and 5th Avenue when the family had increased to four. Susan and
Richard had been added. Later Timothy, Stephen and Dennis arrived.

Bernard continued in the hardware, adding many new things, including
trenching and excavating. In August 1984, after 36 years in the business,
Bernard retired. They continue to make their home in Bowdle.

MARCH 31, 1932
  The Bowdle Hardware, under the ownership of J.K. Moser and O.W. Helmer,
established their business April 15, 1923.

Hobos [Written by Julia Senn]

Old soldiers just face away. So did the hobos of the early years of our
country. Hobos were men who, for the most part, were either looking for work
or excitement, sometimes on the way to a good strike--some who did not want
to work and some who wanted to see the country and found this a cheap way
to travel. Mostly they rode the railroad boxcars, or freight train's
undercarriage. This was termed "Riding the Rods." It was a cat and mouse
game between the bos and the railroad cops if they got to ride the rails.
Sometimes their pullman was a boxcar that might get locked before the train
left the station and they arrived at a destination not on their schedule.
Occasionally the box car proved to be their casket, as they were dead when
a non-stop train pulled into its distant city -- no water, no food on their
journey.

Annie Hoven told of her brothers walking from their farm near Seneca to
North Dakota before the turn of the century, and no doubt, those who shared
food with them on their journey felt they had fed tramps, as they were
usually called. But they did return in the fall with funds to tide them over
winter.

Gertrude Goettling Olson spoke of Bos coming in on freight trains and
asking for food. One asked for a gift of overalls. Usually they were
willing to work and would chop wood or perform other chores around the home
or farm in return for the meal. In Aberdeen, she recalled, there would be
groups of these men sitting along the railroad tracks. About the time of
World War I they became known as Weary Willies or the IWW's, "I Won't Work."

Paul Goettling tells of the hobo jungle in the area by the Bowdle Flour
Mill where a spur to the mill allowed the railroad to shunt in a car to
deliver or pick up grain or flour for shipment. This was taken out in the
early 1930's. He also told of the hobos having a sign language for marking
homes where they had been given a meal. He said the mark was made on the
telephone poles. Others thought it was done with stones laid in a certain
pattern and another opinion was that they always looked for a big house,
thinking the occupant might be rich and generous.

Bertha Nickisch Goettling had a rich memory of them as she told of her
mother baking bread every day because her father insisted no one be turned
away hungry. It was hard in those days without freezers or refrigerators to
have food on hand to feed unexpected guests, but they often fed as many as
23 men daily. They had come in from the freight trains. The tracks were
just a few rods from their home. At night they slept in the barn loft and
other out buildings. Finally the work sapped her mother's strength and her
father, A.G. Nickisch, consented to relief from this charitable duty.

While in her early teens Bertha sometimes was left alone on the farm beside
the Milwaukee Railroad, only 1/2 mile northwest of town. One day, alone and
getting water from the well, she saw three men approaching and warned them
not to come into the yard because she had a big dog. One insisted there was
no dog he could not make friends with and continued to advance. Again she
warned, "Do not come beyond that rock or I will let the dog loose." He came
on and she loosed Prince's chain with instructions to, "Get him." Prince
did. The man's pants were torn so badly he had to get a replacement and
left mouthing dire threats and foul words.

When Bertha was about 17 years old Bowdle experienced an influx of IWW's.
They congregated in the business district, sitting on the edge of the
sidewalk. They refused to work because the farmer could not pay what they
wanted, slept in boxcars and the section house, begged at the homes for food
and refused to move on when ordered.

The young men of the area knew what to do. They organized. Carl and Richard
Lemke, George, Charles and Dan Nickisch, John and Bill Brandt, Bill, Oscar
and Paul Goettling and Edward Ketterling armed themselves with clubs and
guns and were joined by some of the townsmen and the City Cop who told the
Bos to get out of town. They were laughed at for their trouble. Then the
Bowdle posse gave the Weary Willies a deadline of midnight or look for
trouble. The next morning all was peaceful and no vagrants.

Before the First World War Bertha used to help out at the Aurand and
Amerpohl Mercantile Store. In cold weather the storekeepers would serve
coffee and cookies to their customers. Seeing a vagrant standing watching
others enjoy their treat, she invited him in. At first he refused, but then
came in. That evening he came back to the store to thank her and said he
was leaving on a train that was coming in. Tramps or hobos usually managed
to come to a home at meal time and usually remarked, "The food smells so
good."

Editor Senn often fed tramps by giving them a note to take to the local
cafe for a meal. He said that way he knew the man got food instead of
drinking his meal. This writer's last tramp experiences was in 1961 on a
spring Sunday as I crossed the street to my home from the Methodist Church.
I met an aging man, tall and gaunt, whose skin was tightly drawn from the
weathering of many years. He carried a grain sack of belongings on his
shoulder and asked for food. Church was at 9 a.m. I could see he was hungry
and was glad I had food that could be served quickly though it was not the
hot meal he should have had. I often wondered if he got to his destination
or if his strength failed along the way.

THE HOMESTEAD HOME ON THE PRAIRIE

The European prairie settlers were very brave
  Those poor, weary people knew how to save.
The U.S. government gave them free land to own
  A century ago there was no F.H.A. loan.
Most of these people were homesick and poor,
  So many a hardship they had to endure.
A house was usually their foremost need,
  Besides money for food, clothing and seed.
After one had obtained title for one quarter of land
  Relatives and friends lend their helping hand.
To build that sod house on that new claim.
  It took a know-how to build a building by aim,
The home was constructed of rock and sod;
  Involved was much hard work and faith in God.
The sod was cut with an oxen-pulled hand plow
  Up went a home for man, chicken and cow.
The sod was cut square by spade, layered like brick,
  On top of each other with walls two feet thick.
With clay and rock a fireplace was built within,
  Which was used to heat, cook and bake bread therein.
Wood was used on roofs, windows and doors;
  Dirt and sand or rough boards were for floors.
Very few rooms, no closets were inside,
  Togetherness they hade to take in stride.
The walls were smeared with mud and straw by hand
  Even inside they used their new found land.
In their whitewashed walls they took pride,
  While blizzards raged, the family was cozy inside.
This structure was no beautiful sight,
  But to a lost traveler it was a delight.
There were also those creatures, such as the mouse
  Who so often would tunnel her way in that house.
Our ancestors in their "soddies" led a humble life,
  By hard work and God's grace they did survive.

Gertrude Buechler [Author born and raised in a sod house]

BUFFALO HUNT

[Information obtained from Walworth County Record; Copy "The Blue Blanket,"
a paper published in 1884 at Brown's Corner in Walworth County and from the
Edmunds County Democrat.]

John Erbe, who lived in Walworth County, killed one of the largest and last
buffalo seen in these parts a few days ago. He saw it while breaking, and
having his Winchester with him, got within shooting distance of the huge
animal without being observed and landed a bullet behind his left shoulder.

The buffalo started off without any ceremony and received four more shots
before he was brought to the ground. He brought the meat to Ipswich where
he found a market for it for 12-1/2 cents a pound, estimated weight was
1800 pounds.

From the tip of the nose to the center of the head he measured two feet.
The horns at the base had a circumference of 12 inches. The head was the
finest we ever saw, the hair in front being eight inches in length and very
curly.

AGRICULTURE IN 1886, FROM JULY 23, 1914 BOWDLE PIONEER

Memories by W.F. Davis, an old pioneer

The crop of 1885 was a good one. A field of oats at Kelley yielded 60
bushels per acre. The crop of 1886 was a failure. Potatoes, for size, were
like robin eggs. Potatoes were shipped in from Minnesota and sold for $2
per bushel.

This territory in Bowdle had a fearful hailstorm Aug. 15. Rabbits and
prairie hens were killed in the path of the storm and a pet deer belonging
to Mr. Trace.

The crops of 1887 and 1888 I know but little. In 1889 they were fair to
middling. From 1890 to 1893 they were good. The crop of 1892 beat all crops
ever raised in this part of South Dakota.

From 1890 to 1895 prices were low enough to suit you. In the southern part
of this state corn and oats sold for 8 cents per bushel; not quite so cheap
here--28 cents for imported corn. I bought wheat bran at McGlenn's Mill for
$5 per ton. I sold a fat cow to the butcher for $17. Such a cow today (1914)
is worth $75. Geo. Merriman (register of deeds at the time) bought three
head of cattle for $40. The butcher (his conscience as tough as his meat)
sold beef from 4 to 10 cents per pound. Some falls I sold beef by the
quarter for $3.50 and $4 per hundred.

THE OXEN

The oxen played an important role in the lives of the early Bowdle
pioneers. For many it was a mode of transportation to bring them to this
new section of land. This strong beast became the vital instrument in
breaking the sod. Slowly the oxen turned the prairie into plowed fields
ready to be seeded.

One of the early pioneers remembers his oxen. John Meakins paid a sum of
$185 for a team of oxen. They broke many acres of sod for Mr. Meakins. He
remembers, "The 25-mile trip with a load of wheat to Bowdle took three days
as I had to make the trip with oxen. The oxen were nice to work with even
though slow."

HOMESTEAD ACT

The Dakota Territory was a vast undeveloped area which the U.S. Government
hoped to settle with people from our eastern states and immigrants from
overseas.

Congress passed a measure in 1862 to give settlers 160 acres of the public
domain to govern the disposal of land.

After filing a claim with a $10 fee, the farmer would immediately
thereafter have to reside upon or cultivate the land for five years, after
which time he secured final title.

An amendment to the Homestead Act was the Timber Culture Act of 1873. It
allowed thousands of homesteaders to expand their holdings to a workable
size. An additional 160 acres was granted a farmer if he planted at least
one-fourth to trees in four years.

These urged farmers to migrate to the land of plenty. All that was needed
was diligent labor and economy for an early reward.

June 11, 1886 Rustler: "A Dakota man being asked what the homestead law was
replied: It's a game where the government bets you 160 acres of land that
you can't go on it and live five years, and gives you seven years to do it
in, and nine times out of ten, the government wins."

APRIL 9 1908
  We have 15,000 acres that you can select tracts from 160 acres for 510-12
per acre and we will file you a homestead right free.

FROM APRIL 16, 1914 BOWDLE PIONEER

Memories by W.F. Davis, an old pioneer

I think it was in 1891 when a lying whelp started the report that the
Indians on the reservation west of the river were on the war path, had
crossed the Missouri in great numbers, were killing the settlers and
burning their homes.

The report spread like wildfire. I think it was safe to say that in 24
hours nine-tenths of the people of Walworth County were in Bowdle. If there
was one house in town that was not full of people, I don't know where it
was.

My house was full. Among the numbers was a family by the name of Jeneson
who moved with us from Minnesota. They lived west of Bangor. They left home
about 2 o'clock in the morning in a lumber wagon. Some hay and quilts were
put in the wagon on which Mrs. Jeneson and three children laid down. When
day began to dawn, Mrs. Jeneson raised up and looking over the wagon box
saw the tops of two stacks "Hurry up, Joe!" she said, "They are after us--I
see'em." And then the dirt flew.

THE INDIAN SCARE OF 1890 [Taken from Walworth Centennial Book]

The Record once published a very interesting account by Miss Tillie Hilde
of the Indian scare in Walworth and other River counties in 1890. I was
living in Bowdle at the time and remember the event quite well. I had also
been out along the river and seen evidence of the pow-wowing and ghost
dancing of the Indians, and do not wonder at the terror that took
possession of large numbers of people in Campbell, Walworth and Potter
counties and possibly further south where news of their purported crossing
at LaGrace reached the ears of the pioneer settlers and they came fleeing
into Bangor, Mound City, Bowdle and other nearby towns to seek protection.
It was feared that a second outbreak, similar to that at Mankato and New
Ulm, MN in 1862 was about to occur. Sheriff Sayer of Mound City wired the
governor for guns in order that the people might arm and protect themselves.
T.G. Orr raised a company of men at Bangor and C.O. Peterson another
company at Smalley. The governor answered the appeal by sending a stand of
100 guns and promised to send more if needed; these were distributed to
various persons throughout this section.

The report of the Indians crossing to this side and killing people was soon
found to be a fake and most of those who left returned to their homes, yet
many half doubted it, and often long, weary night watches were kept up by
the vigilant and fearful. So great was the rush and influx of fleeing
settlers to Bowdle that the hotels were overcrowded and in this emergency,
the empty store building, vacated by Wallace and Smith at the foot of Main
Street was thrown open and beds made upon the floor for tired stragglers as
they came in; sometimes in groups and families, sometimes alone or with a
single companion. I can recall seeing Judge Burns and Willis G. Brown
coming in from Bangor for ammunition. The latter was carrying a rifle and
told me he came by way of the south road--below Spring Lake--and was out
doing a little scouting on his own hook. While the citizens of the more
inland towns did not feel at all afraid--being further away and in greater
numbers--the people of the outlying settlements were very much alarmed--as
well they might be.

"How would you like it, Green? ' I remember Charles Ottman saying, "If you
were away out here almost alone and unprotected on the open prairie?" The
Ottmans, by the way, had come from Minnesota and not far if I recall aright
from the terrible massacre there in 1862. "You wouldn't like it
yourself--now would you?" and on reflecting over the matter--I came to the
same conclusion, and told him so. While the affair soon died down in and
west of Bangor there were other points south and southeast where it refused
to die down and for weeks afterward people still kept coming to Bowdle. I
remember several families near Hoven deserted their homes and went back to
Minnesota and Wisconsin for a year or so but came back afterwards and have
since made a success in life.

A number of very comical and ludicrous incidents connected with the scare.
One family I believe in their haste to get away forgot a sleeping baby in
its crib and had to go back to get it. James Brown, a former director of
mine in East Cora Township, Sully County also tells one of a certain barber
by the name of Godden who was somewhat smitten by the charms of the two
good looking Traversie girls and was busy shaving Mr. Brown's father-in-law,
Joseph Wilding. He had gotten one side of Mr. Wilding's face shaved and was
about to commence on the other when a courier hastily entered and informed
them of the "uprising" and that "the Indians were coming." Dropping brush
and razor the brave young gallant exclaimed, "I must go and protect the
girls," and hurried off leaving his customer with a half-shaven face. There
were other occurrences not so comical: some even bordering on the pathetic;
sick, infirmed and bed-ridden old folks carried out on sick beds and carted
off in farm wagons and driven at a rapid rate over stony roads, receiving
nervous shocks from which they perhaps never fully recovered.

Well, it was nothing but a scare after all, thank God; but what if it had
not been a scare? I tremble when I think of the awful results that might
have happened to the sparsely settled neighborhood for hundreds of miles up
and down the Missouri; the old river telegraph gone; Fort Sully dismantled
and a thing of the past; no post or soldiers stationed nearer than Ft.
Yates, 80 miles up the river, settlers without arms and Sitting Bull and
his band just across the river.

True, there was the Indian police, but they were a mere handful, when
compared with the Indians and would have been utterly powerless by
themselves to cope with the large and well armed following which Sitting
Bull and other leading chiefs had. It might even have equaled or surpassed
Mankato and New Ulm in fatalities and you and I, pioneers, might have been
among the killed. About a score of years ago I recall the state sent out a
party to collect and return the guns furnished on this occasion. One of the
last ones gotten, according to Geo. H. Parker, Mound City, old stage driver
who accompanied this man in search of the guns, was found in the possession
of Jesse Paine who formerly lived south of Bowdle but later moved to Emmons
County. I believe most of the guns were eventually found and returned to
the state. -- Perhaps written by E.B. Green.

EARLY FARM LIFE

Adequate housing was a most pressing need. Caves were often dug in the side
of a hill until the rough dwelling known as sod houses were built. Frame
buildings replaced these as soon as possible. A few years in a sod house
convinced many a pioneer that the Great Plains was no place for them.

The search for water was just as difficult. If they lived near a stream the
precious fluid was hauled to his home in barrels. The only alternative was a
hand-dug well.

Fuel was as hard to come by as water. Wood along streams was used so long
as the supply lasted. Many depended on dried buffalo chips which were
gathered for winter use. Twisted hay and corncobs were also used for heat.
A rag burning in tallow was used for light.

Grasshoppers was another plague that threatened the plainsmen. An invasion
came without warning flying north in clouds nearly blotting out the sun.
Hoppers ate everything--cornstalks, grain, vegetables, leaves and bark from
trees, sweaty wood from pitchforks, lumber on buildings, fence
posts--leaving nothing but the mortgage.

Prairie fires often ranged across miles of countryside of tinder-dry grass.
When autumn gave way to winter the storms swept across the open grasslands.
Property loss and discomforts were common hardships the early pioneers
endured. Certainly these early settlers had to live in a world of dreams.
They concentrated on their immediate problems and needs.

FOOD AND CLOTHING

Procurement of food and clothing was a big project for the pioneer family.
The women and children milked the cow and tended the garden. Potatoes,
carrots, sweet corn, cucumbers, cabbage and onions were raised because they
could all be kept through the winter.

Potatoes and carrots were buried in the root cellar, often the original
dug-out, and the onions were hung from the rafters. Sweet corn was dried in
the sun or in the oven. Cabbage was made into sauerkraut and cucumbers into
various pickles.

The oldest boy, as soon as he could carry both the shotgun and a stick to
rest it on for shooting, went hunting for the small game that thrived on the
prairie.

Pork and beef was put down in brine or dried. Game was treated the same way.

Milk was set to allow the cream to rise to make butter. The skim milk was
not allowed to go to waste. What the children didn't drink was made into
cottage cheese or harder cheeses that would keep during the winter. The
whey from cheese making was fed to the pigs or chickens.

FARMING: TURN OF THE CENTURY

What was farm life like at the turn of the century? The farming operation
of Richard Lemke (1879-1943) is a typical farm of that time. It was more
self-sufficient than our modern day farm. Mr. Lemke depended entirely on
horse power and manual labor. The horses were fed home-grown hay and oats
and in return furnished power, colts for power replacements and manure to
replenish the soil nutrients. The animal, feed, manure cycle met his
standards for soil improvement.

Lemke's diversified operation included cattle, horses, sheep, poultry,
oats, corn, wheat and alfalfa. The land was improved by spreading manure
and the never-ending job of picking rock to which the huge rock piles
attest to this day.

The fields were prepared by using a one-bottom 3 horse sulky plow or a
two-bottom 5 horse gang plow. The gang plow even had a seat. The fields
were harrowed and then seeded with a 4 horse grain drill. Weeds were
controlled in corn with a single or double row cultivator with two or three
cultivations a season.

For harvesting wheat and oats Mr. Lemke used a header and later a binder.
The grain later was put through a threshing machine to separate the grain
from the straw and chaff. A one-row corn binder cut the corn and tied it
into bundles, which were later hauled home and used for winter livestock
feed.

Other horse-powered farm implements used by Mr. Lemke were wagons,
stone-boat, manure spreader, grain elevator, mower and hayracks. He managed
a horse-powered threshing rig before 1910. Mr. Lemke farmed until 1943 when
he died of cancer.

        Gerhard Blumhardt, with his tractor, was hired in 1923 to shred

FIRST THRESHING CREW

Sept. 7, 1906 Bowdle Pioneer: "Charley Nelson started his first threshing
rig on his place Monday afternoon and threshed some wheat and oats. The
wheat went about 17 bushels to the acre and sold to the Mill Co. at 72
cents per bushel. The oats was rusty and only yielded 40 bushels per acre.

This piece of wheat was considered the poorest that Charley had, so the
yield will average far better than 17 bushels, but he has only 550 acres of
wheat of his own.

Charley Nelson is perhaps the busiest man this section of the state. He is
starting out three steam rigs and has a large crew of men to look after.

        The Commet and McGlenn threshing outfit as taken in 1890. This was
        one of the first threshing machines in Walworth County.

        CHRISTOPH SCHUMACHER THRESHING RIG This was taken at the John
        Bieber Sr. farm the fall of 1906. John Bieber Sr. and sons are on
        the wagon. Matt McGovern was the oiler. Christoph (owner) standing
        back at large wheel and Sam Rathke was the straw-feeder. This
        Northwest Steamer engine was fed by straw and coal, operated with
        Buffolo Pitts grain separator. The engineer on top wheel watched
        gauges and fuel of steam engine while oiler serviced threshing
        machine working between two grain stacks. The men pitched the grain
        into the feeder. The engineer stayed with the steam engine around
        the clock keeping up the steam. Help only paid for "belt time"
        meaning only when machine was in operation. Cook car in the rear
        was run by the two cooks; Standing are Mary (Rathke) Heerwald and
        Rose Jedderberg. There was no discrimination with women rising
        early to cook, bake bread and pies for a crew of 10 or 12 hungry
        men. Lena (wife of Christoph) in buggy holding Clarence their
        firstborn. The buggy with her horse Flory was Lena's means of
        transportation.

APRIL 10, 1913
  A.G. Bickert had a Spaulding Deep Tilling Machine shipped in. It can run
10-20 inches deep and turns the soil up in fine shape. It consists of two
large discs, one running in front of the other. The front disc takes the
surface soil and throws it to the bottom of the deep furrow where it will
not weather out but gives up its plant food while the rear disc cuts up the
subsoil and brings it to the surface. Five horses are required to operate
it at the greater depths, about 2-1/2 acres can be plowed in a day as it
cuts a furrow about 14 inches wide. This machine is used extensively in the
dry farming states and will eventually be used in this section.

JULY 24, 1902
  For Sale: One good secondhand 14 hp threshing machine, 36-inch cylinder
and wagon. Price $125 cash--B.F. Zimmerman, Roscoe, SD.

MAY 23, 1929
  Reduces Plowing Costs, by Herman Buechler. We got a 15-27 tractor about a
year ago. We are using it mostly for plowing. We are farming 275 acres. The
cost an acre is about 45 cents for fuel. With two gang plows and horses we
could plow 10 acres in one full day. With the tractor we plow 12-15 acres.
That shows we save one man and a team and get more work done in a day. We
also use the tractor for sawing wood for fuel and for grinding feed. A
tractor is a great help to farmers. It would be hard to do without one now
that we are used to it.

raise these new crops.

        BOWDLE ROLLER MILL

TAKEN FROM FEB. 25, 1965 BOWDLE PIONEER

Area farmers as far as Minnesota during the 1920's and 1930's would line up
as many as 100 wagons at a time to have their wheat converted to flour.

For 16 months the mill was manufacturing flour at the rate of 3,000 pounds
daily, 7 days a week. Three or four companies packaged the flour under
their own brand names.

The flour was shipped to England, Greece, Portugal, Ecuador, Spain and
Columbia. Foreign trade ceased in 1948 due to competition from the larger
flour milling. Afterwards Mr. Leno specialized in private label flour
shipped to North Dakota, Minnesota and South Dakota contracted with Super
Valu and Nash Finch.

The mill became a dealer for Nutrena Feed Supply in 1961. In 1962 a Daffin
Moblie Feed Mill was purchased with a capacity to mix and blend 10 tons of
feed an hour.

THE DIRTY THIRTIES

        A Typical "Dust Bowl" Farm -- 1958 Yearbook of Ag.

There seems to be a shortage of recorded agriculture history of what is
known as the "Great Depression" or the "Dirty Thirties." It was a time that
many had hoped was but a dream. In this "dust bowl" duststorms darkened the
skies every day. Children returning home from school were forced to follow
fence lines to keep from getting lost. The dry soil was blown into drifts
often completely covering fence lines.

With no pasture feed or hay to feed the livestock farmers had to dispose of
the livestock. But how? The markets wouldn't buy the livestock so the U.S.
Government came to the rescue.

After the animals were condemned the farmers were paid about $8-11 per cow
and less for the smaller ones. Then the animals were driven into the large
pits where they were shot and buried. According to some of our older
citizens some were buried 1/2 mile south of town, some 3-1/2 miles south of
what today is known as the Gross gravel pit. Another pit was made at the
present dumpground east of Bowdle and another burial site supposedly was
northeast of Bowdle on the Geo. Robinson farm, now owned by Albinus Thomas.

Many farmers abandoned their farms and moved elsewhere. The remaining
hardly provided for their families by working on WPA projects. On these
Work Project Administration jobs they were paid about $30 a month to help
build roads or dams. It provided for the necessities of life, but few of
their wants.

        WPA RELIEF LABOR In July 1936 75 men were put to work on three
        different projects, 25 men being assigned to each project. One
        project was grading and graveling the streets of Bowdle. Men of the
        town, as well as farmers, have been assigned to this job. In the
        photo Ruben Aldinger is the fifth person in the back row.

building. The 150-foot lumber shed of Central Lumber Co. was blown down,
telephone poles between Selby and here were blown down. The Bowdle
Mercantile Co. had the upper windows in the glass front blown in. Barns and
out buildings were damaged. Hay was scattered. Winds were clocked at 45-50
miles per hour.

WINDMILLS By Mrs. Esther L. Voller

I have been told that Bowdle had many windmills before the city had a water
tower. In Bowdle's 1961 Diamond Jubilee book, one resident is pictured with
a high windmill in action. Farmers needed windmills and those in town were
most likely sold to farmers. I remember seeing a windmill at the John A.
Gross home in 1934. It was pumping water for a large vegetable garden.

There were different types of windmills. Some had wheels made of wood and
towers also of wood. These were not very high and could be used in pastures
where there were no buildings or trees to interfere with wind.

Windmills made of galvanized steel and angle iron were used in farmyards.
They were manufactured and sold, but had to be assembled where they were to
stand. The windmills at the Jacob Voller farm were about 40 feet high; but
many will remember the tallest of all that stood in a farmyard north of the
highway between Bowdle and Selby. It was said to be 80 feet high.

Setting a windmill tower in the right spot must have been difficult for the
pumprod had to be exactly above the pump's pumprod. At the base of the
tower, the distance from comer to corner, was about nine feet. The corner
angle irons were set in concrete and here again, the construction required
careful attention so that the height of each corner was the same. After the
concrete was dry the rest of the tower was added in sections and bolted
together. There were three sections and to brace the tower, there were
X-shaped braces made of heavy twisted wire that was fastened to the corner
angle iron legs with bolts. The corner tapered and at the top of the
highest sections was a wood platform where men stood while working on the
wheel, vane, gears and pumprod.

To reach the platform some windmill towers had a steel ladder fastened to
the framework; and others had iron steps attached to a corner leg. The
pumprod was made of hardwood, about two inches thick, with a metal end that
connected with the pumprod by putting a steel bolt through matching holes in
the rods. If one had to pump by hand, this pin was removed.

Turning the windmill was done by releasing a hardwood handle that rested
flat against a corner leg and was kept tightly in place by a wire band. To
shut off, the handle was returned to the corner leg and the band slipped
over it.

The wheel was put together in sections with bolts and when done was about
eight feet in diameter. The vane that kept the wheel turned toward the wind
carried the name of the brand. Dempster was a well-known brand. Windmills
were strong, but tornadoes crumpled them into masses of twisted steel.
Whenever storm clouds appeared, someone shut off the windmill.

        All wooden windmill of Albert Wiepking.

ELECTRICITY MODERNIZED RURAL LIVING

The tallow lamp gave light to our early settlers which gave way to the
kerosene lamps. Later electricity was put into use. Windpower was used to
generate 6-volt or 32-volt electric power. Usually a set of large batteries
to store the power was found in the basement of the home. Engine-driven
generators also came into use.

In 1935 the federal government passed legislation giving low-interest loans
to consumer/member REA Cooperatives to build electric transmission lines to
the farm area. In 1943 the ground work was started for the present day FEM
Cooperative.

Electricity on the farm! Will it ever happen? many farmers asked
themselves. Can we afford it? A $5 membership and $5 per month was a sum not
to be taken lightly. The volunteer sign up teams found it better to have
the farmer's wife present when they talked about the benefits of
electricity. Lights. washing, cooking, refrigeration and running water were
some of the benefits of REA.

Community meetings in Faulk, Edmunds and McPherson counties were held to
explain what this REA program could do for the local farmers. Easements
were obtained for the power line poles with construction begun shortly
thereafter. By Christmas Eve 1948 electric service was available to slightly
over 200 members. FEM currently serves about 2,159 people in seven counties.

        First 6 or 8-volt windcharger on Fred Rieger house. Lower part of
        house made of mud.

MATT BACHMAN: PIONEER AWARD

Matt Bachman of Bowdle, an original incorporator of FEM Electric
Association Inc., was the recipient of the Pioneer Award by FEM Electric for
his longtime service to the rural electrification program. Pioneer Awards
are presented throughout the nation to a few selected individuals as part of
the commemoration of rural electrification's 50th Anniversary.

The award was presented to Matt Bachman June 12, 1985. It signifies his
lasting and valuable contribution to the development of rural
electrification. His work helped not only consumer/members, but also the
entire community.

Matt Bachman was a director of FEM Electric from December 1945 until he
retired in 1979. Rural electric systems are owned and operated by the
people they serve. Board directors are elected at the cooperative's annual
meeting.

RURAL FIRST LADY

About forty-five years ago, when I was a farmer's wife, it was customary
for strangers who drove into the yard, to honk the horn and wait for
someone to come out. That may not seem proper, but when a large, barking
dog, with neck hair bristling, glares at the driver, we can excuse a seeming
lack of courtesy.

One afternoon, a well-dressed gentleman drove in and honked. When I came
out, he explained that he was trying to find a certain farmer and mentioned
his name. I had never heard of him and said so. The man seemed puzzled. He
spread out a map of several counties over the steering wheel, and indicated
where he thought he was. I pointed to the location of our farm on the map
and he said incredulously, "But that's in Edmunds County, and I'm in
Walworth County!"

"Well," I replied, "I ought to know where I live! We have been here 22
years! Our place is on the SW 1/4 of the SW 1/4 of Section 16, Range
124-73, in Modena Township, right there, on the map! We are two miles from
Walworth County and three miles from McPherson County!"

The man seemed lost and I had tried to tell him exactly where he was. He
thanked me and added, "You are the first woman I ever met, who knows where
she lives!"

Even a farmer's wife can be a First Lady. The First Lady returned to her
household tasks with a smile, recalling a familiar quotation: "Let me live
in a house by the side of the road, and be a friend to man!"

                                        ESTHER L. VOLLER
        (This anecdote was awarded second place at the 1984 South
         Dakota State Fair.)

        WILBERT A. BLUMHARDT, 1985 EMINENT FARMER

The Eminent Farmer Award honors two farmers each year for their outstanding
contribution to the quality of rural life in South Dakota. Selected by the
South Dakota State University Cooperative Extension Service--College of
Agriculture with the approval of the Board of Regents, these individuals
are chosen for their community service, willingness to help others and
their accomplishments in the field of agriculture.

Portraits of these honored Eminent Farmers hang in the Hall of Fame in the
Agriculture Building on the campus of SDSU in Brookings.

Wilbert A. Blumhardt has made many contributions to this community, county,
state and nation. He played a vital role in establishing the Edmunds County
Conservation District in 1956 and was instrumental in the establishment of
the South Dakota No-Till Association in 1984.

Wilbert has been a leader in the community bringing new technology and
ideas to this area which benefit South Dakota agriculture. He has lent a
helping hand whenever possible. The people of this community, county and
state share in his accomplishments, as he shares his accomplishments with
them.

Edmunds County has had only one other Eminent Farmer. In 1944 John Davies
from Kent Township was honored. Mrs. Mathew Evans of Ipswich was honored as
Eminent Homemaker in 1962.

NO-TILL FARMING

        Walter Johnson seeding winter wheat into standing stubble using a
        no-till drill.


The newest farming technique is the no-till farming method. No-till is a
procedure where a crop is planted directly into a seedbed not tilled since
harvest of the previous crop. No tillage is done during the growing and
maturing season.

Drills and planters are specially designed to plant into standing stubble.
In no-till farming, herbicides take the place of tillage for weed control,
before and after planting.

Some objectives of no-till farming are to save soil, save moisture, save
fuel, cut operating costs and increase yields.

ODE TO A GOPHER

Bright-eyed, agile, bushy-tailed gopher,
Busy digging, you're no loafer!
Always looking neat and cute,
In your tan all-season suit;
Dining well on sprouts and corn,
At noon. at night, and early morn.
You dig up soil from underground
And leave a large and grassless mound.

Frisky little prairie dweller.
You hibernate in nested cellar,
Awaiting Nature's signaling,
That snow is gone. and it is spring;
Time to raise another brood,
To be on guard, lest guests intrude.
When badgers prowl about at night,
Gophers flee in hasty flight,
Through holes without a single mound,
Routes of escape, so quickly found!

On you, by night, the badger preys;
By day, a man with rifle, lays
In wait for you, with steady aim,
For every tail, two cents to claim.
You are trespassing on his land--
You're really classed as contraband!

He wants an end of gopher burrows,
Craves land that's flat, in level furrows.
He says it's he who pays the tax!
So if you hear loud rifle cracks,
Rush underground, and there relax!
Those rifle shooters think they're wise,
But can they grow fur coats, their size?
You raise your young without a penny;
And as for loans, you don't need any!
The Internal Revenue ignores you,
And bill collectors shun you too.
Oh, to live like you, carefree,
And with my lot, contented be!

                ESTHER L. VOLLER
                September 20, 1984

SUMMER STORM

Indoors, the summer heat was stifling,
Midday so dark, we ate by artificial light;
No breezes stirred to ease the sweltering heat.
The lightning flashed--a blinding, bluish white,
And the silence of the sultry gloom
Was broken by a shattering thunder crash
That reverberated, shuddering windows in the room.

Fearfully, we scanned the stormy sky,
Where restless clouds churned constantly around;
Far southward, a sinister arm of twisting cloud,
Reached down to wreak destruction on the ground.

A transient breeze rippled the dotted curtain
At the open window; a roaring, rushing sound
Came from above, and suddenly there fell
Crystal stones of bouncing ice that drowned
All other sound as they beat upon the roof.
The rain that followed, washed the farmyard clean;
Rubbish-laden, foamy rivulets eddied
And tumbled on, in quest of a low ravine.

Gradually, the incessant drumming ceased;
Once more, the air was calm, yet fresh and cool.
The murky darkness speedily decreased--
Clear, blue sky appeared in the west,
The sun peeked out, a rainbow spanned the sky.

With joyous shouts, in scanty clothing dressed,
The barefoot children splashed and searched the pools
For melting bits of hailstone treasure--
Grateful to the summer storm for having given
This unanticipated hour of childhood pleasure.

                ESTHER L. VOLLER

("Summer Storm" was published in the July 1952 issue of "Pasque Petals."
After its publication, it was read on an Aberdeen radio program by Helen
Holgate of Aberdeen. It was written after a storm when the Voller family
lived on their farm.)

Blizzards ...

DAKOTA BLIZZARDS BY E.C. SLOCUM [January 13, 1927 Bowdle Pioneer]

Each year, Jan. 12, 1888, we remember that tragic blizzard. With a cold
that is intense and below zero, a terrific northwest gale drives the finely
powered snow in a swirling veil so thick as to obscure objects only a few
feet away; in fact, one's eyes are so quickly filled with snow that vision
is impossible; and the danger of these great storms is in their sudden
onset giving people no chance to reach shelter.

In 1888 many people lost their lives in the southern part of the state, as
it began after people had gone to do their daily duties. In this part it
began so early in the morning that few were stirring.

The dates of the great blizzards were Feb. 18-19, 1884; Jan. 12-13, 1888;
Nov. 26-27, 1896 and March 15-16, 1903. They all struck at night or early
in the morning, few lives were lost.

        Blizzard in March 1942.

DECEMBER 22, 1927: There were more sleds in town than there were
automobiles. There were at least 50 sleds on the streets.

        Snowbanks as high as buildings in 1950 Blizzards.

JANUARY 3, 1949: A severe 3-day blizzard when a snowstorm covered an almost
bare ground. In the afternoon a high wind began piling the snow into depts,
which by night halted the traffic.

Although all the roads were blocked, the Milwaukee Road had done an
incredible job of keeping its trains operating and with only a few delays,
the train ran nearly on schedule.

JANUARY 5, 1950: On the anniversary of the terrible blizzard of 1949, the
weatherman had another blizzard on Jan. 3, of this year. An electric power
failure left many without a means of providing warmth. Some families
depended on their old coal furnace and many took to their basements where
laundry and oil stoves kept them warm.

        August Schick Farm in March Blizzard in 1966.

FEBRUARY 2, 1950: Many cars stalled on the roads. Garage men were busy
towing in cars. It was estimated that 40 stalled cars were brought into
town.

        To milk his cows in March 1966, August Schick entered the barn
        through the hayloft.

FEBRUARY 2, 1950: During the lull between blizzards which have been
happening the past six weeks of winter, Adolph Treichel and Arlyn Erbe made
flights over the area, aiding the snowbound people. Mail delivery was made
by airplane to many of the stranded farmers by Art Hoffmann and pilot Arlyn
Erbe. Mr. Hoffman said, "It was the first time he had ever made a mail
delivery in this fashion." As the planes flew over the various farm homes
the farmer and his family came out to wave. Many of the homes didn't have
mail for three weeks and some of them had no telephones. Their only contact
with the outside world had been the news on their radios.

FEBRUARY 9, 1950: A weasel was brought in from the Red Cross Unit to aid
people during the blizzards. During the week the weasel was here 42 calls
were made including sick calls, calls for food and fuel and expectant
mothers. Whenever possible the G.I.'s and their machine visited many
farmers. Adolph Treichel, Bob Senn and Kenneth Mayer assisted as guides
into the country. The drifts in the country covered the trees in the farm
yards and buried tractors, low houses and sheds.

        Snow piled high during March 1966 Blizzard.

MARCH 2, 1950: Forty inches of snow is the amount estimated to have fallen
in this vicinity since Dec. 15. Snow on the level is knee high with drifts
10-12 feet high. Mike Hoerner reported to have cut steps into a 12 foot
snowbank to get down into his house and also in one at the windmill. A
bulldozer went toward Tolstoy to open roads, but had to plow themselves out
on the return trip as it had drifted shut behind them.

        Snow removal on Main Street after 1966 Blizzard.

MARCH 30, 1950: Another snowstorm hit for three days. Northwestern Bell
Telephone reported 1,000 wire breaks and 69 poles down due to the storm.
The worst damage around Bowdle, south through Gettysburg.

        Mertz Roadside Park during Blizzard of 1966.

MARCH 27, 1952: Ervin Gross helped some of the farmers to bring two trailer
loads of cream and eggs to the highway where Erv met them with a panel
truck and brought them to town. In return the farmers traded groceries and
returned home with tractors and trailers.

Arlyn Erbe was busy flying the teachers to their respective schools. Bob
Jarvis was flown into town so Doc. Miller could care for a toothache.

Eggs were a problem at Fred F. Buechler's where 3,000 eggs had accumulated.

        Main Street during Blizzard of 1966.

MARCH 10, 1966: This blizzard is a memory of many living citizens of Bowdle
today. Like other blizzards the wind increased, causing blinding visibility
and halting all traffic in Bowdle. The farmers were staying at home.

As the storm increased in velocity the electricity came to a halt in all
homes in town, as well as farm homes. Their only means of communication were
their transistor radios for the news of the storm.

All business in Bowdle except the hotel and Buechler's Cafe were closed. It
was the first time in the history of Bowdle that the Post Office was closed
due to weather.

Many homes didn't have heat, so many people moved in with neighbors who had
heat. Others wrapped up and stayed in their cold homes.

On the fourth day the sun was a welcome sight by the citizens. Bowdlelites
were busy checking on their neighbors and making openings for entrances.
The Blizzard of '66 was over. It was known that many suffered great
financial loss, like several hundred of cattle, but not a single loss of
life or serious accident took place.

MARCH 7, 1985: The most severe snowstorm in recent years began early
Saturday morning and continued into Monday. The storm, which covered
practically the entire state, dumped varying amounts of snow on the area
averaging between 12-30 inches (including an estimated 20 inches in the
Bowdle area.) Streets were completely closed.

WINTER STORM By Mrs. Joe [Marie] Herman

The following is one of the many experiences we had living near the
Yellowstone Trail, now known as Highway 12.

It was about fifty years ago and winter had been with us for several weeks
-- deep snow covered the fields. It was Saturday, the day farm wives went to
town to do their weekly shopping, sometimes accompanied by their husbands
and children. Clouds were building up in the west. We decided to make a
quick trip to Bowdle. We drove the Chevrolet touring car with side-curtains
to the house and loaded the 10-gallon cream can and eggcase and were on our
way. Our son Victor, about four, was with us.

The road was in very poor condition which interfered with the driving.
Entering Bowdle we drove to the cream station and then delivered the
eggcase to Gross Bros. Department Store.

I put in my grocery order and then went through the store picking up what I
needed and buying a little gift for Victor, making him very happy. After
visiting with other ladies for a short time we were ready to start home.

Driving out on the highway all went well until about three miles from home
when we ran into heavy snowfall and a strong northwest wind. Visibility was
zero. What made it possible to know we were near home was the dim view of
the two red gate posts of our gateway to the farm yard.

Driving up to the house we immediately went to check the livestock. We
returned to the house and Victor took a nap while we sat down to relax.
Suddenly, there was a knock at the door. Opening it we found three men
standing on the steps asking if they could come in from the storm. At that
time we were using only two rooms of the house, the kitchen and bedroom,
and kept the other rooms closed to conserve fuel.

Knocking continued until there were 17 men and one boy about 10 in the
kitchen. The boy and his father lived in Minneapolis. An hour later, again
there was a loud knocking. Four men stood in the doorway saying they were
badly in need of help. They said two women were in a stalled car about a
quarter of a mile from our home. One lady was very ill. Several men went to
the barn and hitched a team to a small sled, one carrying a quilt that I
gave him.

Before coming to our house the latest visitors had hung a red sweater on
the woven wire fence near the women's stalled car as a marker. The sled was
driven through a field along the fence to the marker. Two men climbed over
the fence and wrapped the sick woman in the quilt. They carried her to the
fence and lifted her into the arms of two men who laid her in the sled.
They helped the other lady over the fence and she rode in the sled to our
home.

When the sick lady was brought in, her companion and I removed her outer
clothing and laid her on our bed. We did all we could to make her
comfortable and hours later she fell asleep. The other lady laid down
beside her to rest.

It was a long night. Some men sat on the floor, some stood and some took
turns sitting on the four kitchen chairs. I had a large pot of coffee on
the coal and wood burning stove and on the table I placed homebaked bread,
butter and jam, sliced ham and canned sausage I had heated. They all helped
themselves.

What a surprise when morning came! The wind had diminished and just a few
snowflakes were falling.

Some of the men went to dig out their cars and some went to the barn to
help milk and feed cattle. When the boy, who had slept on the bedroom floor
wrapped in a quilt, heard about milking he asked to go to the barn because
he had never seen a cow milked. Later when the milk was separated in the
kitchen, he just could not believe what he saw -- cream going into a
utensil from one spout and skim milk from another spout going into a pail
on the floor!

Later one of the men shoveled a path to the chicken house. The boy did not
know where eggs came from and learned when he put his hand under a hen on a
nest, he found eggs.

After the men left to dig out their cars I made breakfast for our family,
the two ladies and the little boy. The sick lady had improved. Neighbors and
people from town came with shovels to help, and with two of our teams the
cars were pulled out. The stalled cars had come from both directions and men
worked most of the day to get all of the cars out of the deep snow. I had
food and coffee on hand all day for the snowbound travelers.

What a story the little boy must have had to tell his family and friends
when he arrived home!

The help and shelter we gave our unexpected guests was greatly appreciated
by them and our hearts were warmed by their expressions of gratitude and
our opportunity to help so many. There was a feeling of emptiness in the
house after all had departed.

Fires ...

PRAIRIE FIRE [Written by Esther L. Voller]

A lifetime resident of the Bowdle area related to this writer her awful
experience while teaching at a rural school in Odessa Township in 1922. At
the time she was known as Gertrude Goettling and lived with her parents.
Later she married Oscar Olson.

Among her pupils were the children of Mr. and Mrs. William Thurn and a
Doerr family. One of the Thurn girls was absent in the forenoon and Mrs.
Thurn brought her at the noon hour. The children were ready to enjoy lunch
when a dark, fast-moving cloud of smoke appeared southwest of the school.
Gertrude ordered the children to leave their lunches and run as fast as
they could to a plowed field a short distance east of the school. She
picked up the Thurn child and ran to the plowed field, expecting to see the
schoolhouse go up in flames.

The children were frightened and crying and she tried to calm them. The
fire reached the school grounds, but the playground was bare and flames did
not touch the school. When it was safe to leave the field, she took all of
the children to the Goettling home, where they feasted on peanut butter
sandwiches. They were not sent home because she supposed that their parents
were gone fighting fire.

The fire had started between Hoven and Bowdle and there were several badly
burned victims and deaths.

MARCH 14, 1891: Intelligence is received, just as we go to press, that the
large grain elevator of the J.W. Hoyt Company at Bowdle was consumed by
fire about noon today, along with 5,000 bushels of flax and 3,000 bushels
of wheat and other contents. (Edmunds County Democrat)

FEBRUARY 22, 1900: The explosion of a lamp in the basement of T.G. Ward's
general store caused a conflagation at Bowdle last Thursday. The wind
blowing from the northwest, the fire wiped out the entire block before it
could be checked. The total losses and insurance upon the property
destroyed were as follows:

H.A. Mason, hardware and furniture, stock and building, $55,000; insurance,
$25,000.

T.G. Ward, general store, building, $3,500; stock and fixtures, $12,000;
insurance on stock, $8,000; building, $1,000.

Post Office building, $1,000; insurance, $500.

People's Bank, building, $1,000; insurance, $500.

O. Larsen Jewelry, building, $1,000; stock, $400; insurance, $700.

Olson & Christianson, general store, stock, $5,000; building, $1,000;
insurance on stock, $2,500; no insurance on building.

C.T. Slate, drug store, stock, $2,800; building, $1,500; total insurance,
$2,000.

C.T. Slate, general merchandise, building, $1,800: stock. $8,000: total
insurance, $8,300.

Besides the losses noted above, many persons sustained more or less not
enumerated, caused by the removal of goods from their homes to the streets,
some of which were ruined or stolen. (Edmunds County Democrat)

JANUARY 1906: The fire was located at Rudolph Dusel's, better known as the
Harry Gidley machine sheds and office on the west end of Main Street. The
building burned completely, including most of the machinery.

OCTOBER 21, 1909: The start of a prairie fire was from the railroad track
east of Bowdle and two other places further east all caused by sparks from
an engine. The wind blowing and dry vegetation didn't help. These three
fires came together and hundreds of stacks burned, grain stacks, granaries,
barns and some houses.

It continued southward for two days and loss of over $100,000 was
estimated. Farmers are practically out of business, their stock must be
sold, impossible to get feed. The engine set at least a dozen fires from
here to the River that day.

SEPTEMBER 9, 1910: The little town of LeBeau was nearly entirely wiped out
by fire. Only eight businesses remain. Total loss is $150,000.

        Fire fighters try to control blaze of May 1911.

MAY 18, 1911: This morning nearly a whole block of Bowdle business places
lay in ashes. The fire originated in the rear of Gottlieb Sippert's pool
room and took with it Yackey's Drug Store, the building occupied by John
Keen as a butcher shop but now vacant, Western Land Co. office, Medinnus
Millinery Store, Dr. Merriman's office and the photography gallery owned
by A.L. Artz. The Central Telephone Office stands amass of charred ruin; it
was at this point the fire fighters got control of the fire with their
chemical engines and stopped the blaze.

        A block of business places lay in ashes in 1911.

OCTOBER 5, 1922: Raging flames claim two citizens Oct. 3, 1922. Driven by a
40 mile wind from the southwest a prairie fire originating about 3 miles
north of the town of Hoven swept a strip of country two miles wide to the
city limits of Bowdle, leaving a trail of death and destruction in its wake.

Killed were Robert Gundert, age 14, son of Wm. Gundert of Tolstoy and Jacob
Bollinger Sr., age 65, retired farmer. Jacob Huber, about 65, was badly
burned and so was Arlo Stroup. Others with burn injuries were Theodore
Artz, Ed Shama, George McClellen and John Artz Jr.

Automobiles loaded with men and boys strung out along the roads and started
to guard against the spread of flames. Men with the chemical engines of the
city helped too. Trying to save the Houck farm the wind whipped around and
a sea of flames enveloped buildings, cars and men. This is where Mr.
Bollinger and the Gundert lad were killed and many injured. Many escaped by
cars.

The barns, granaries, all buildings, except the dwelling house, grain and
hay and about 60 head of hogs were destroyed. The John Artz place was also
destroyed. Many of the men again were surrounded by fire and forced to
flee, some sustaining severe burns. Everything was destroyed on this farm.

Every available man in town was at the fire, leaving only three or four to
look after affairs in town and the men from the farm adjacent were all
present. The heroic work of all combined being all that saved the city from
destruction.

Nick Frost lost several buildings and animals. S.J. Commet lost 150 acres
of wheat and tons of hay. John Hoven lost several tons of hay.

Shortly had these flames subsided when a fire broke out north of town about
five miles, burning the barn, some stock and hay on the farm of Christ
Heilman, a shed of Alex Nehl, part of the threshing rig of Fred M.
Eisenbeisz and the Nehl School House.

JANUARY 3, 1924: The general merchandise store of Samuel Jacobs & Co.
burned to the ground about 3 o'clock in the morning. The building and
contents were entirely burned. The fire fighters saved the adjoining
buildings, the meat market and city cafe. It was 20 degrees below zero.
Henry Eisenbeiss was overcome by smoke. Jacobs bought the building from
George Sautner.

JUNE 7, 1928: The John Ketterling building between Baer's Hardware Store
and the Post Office on the north side of Main Street suffered a 75% damage
by fire at midnight. The stock, furniture and fixtures of John
Stickelmeier, who occupied the building as a pool hall, were completely
destroyed.

MAY 16, 1929: Wednesday morning about 2:30 fire was discovered in the rear
of the Steele Cafe which spread to two other buildings and left them all
ashes. Estimated damage was $20,000. The Steele family escaped. Nothing was
saved from this building.

From the Steele Cafe the fire jumped to the building to the east owned by
Mrs. Ida Edwards and Mary Searle, where they have always made their home.
Mrs. Searle, a daughter of Mrs. Edwards and her husband were on their
honeymoon at the time. This building was built in 1889, used first for a
hospital, later as a sort of hotel and for the past years has housed the
Edwards family.

The heat was so strong that the fire soon moved on to the old Bank of
Bowdle building, which was owned by the State Banking Department and housed
the dental offices of Dr. Olson, living quarters of E.G. Carlson and the
rooms of Dr. Bell.

Dr. Olson saved most of his tools and dentist chair. The high winds helped
spur the fire on to greater damage. Pieces of lumber and coals were found
at distances of more than 3-1/2 blocks from the fire.

DECEMBER 11, 1941: Hoffman Pool Hall was destroyed by fire. Joel Mueller,
Alex Kiesz and Reinie Leno suffered severe injuries when they were caught
by a falling brick wall.

        The start of the fire at Boyd Hall in 1947.

        Boyd Hall burning in 1947.

FEBRUARY 6, 1947: American Legion Hall, formerly known as H. & H. Theatre
(Boyd Hall), burned to the ground in a fire which consumed the building in
about 40 minutes. A high northwest wind about 50 miles per hour and 20
below zero hampered the fire fighters. Mrs. Oscar Olson turned in the
alarm. The cinders were reported carried by the wind as far as the Kesslers
Service Station. Dr. F.A. Miller was the commander of the American Legion.
They purchased it from Mr. Hoven about a year ago. It was still used to show
movies.

        Nothing remained after Boyd Hall burned in 1947.

JULY 20, 1950: Fire badly damaged the Kundert Shoe Shop. This building was
built during 1890. It was used as a garage and implement shop, electric
shop, office of Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. and freight house for truck
lines.

MARCH 22, 1956: Fire of undetermined origin wiped out the Schaible
Chevrolet Garage, badly damaged the Pioneer and caused some damage to the
Fred Thommen house. Wilmer Schaible family barely escaped. All household
goods and garage equipment were destroyed.

The building served the community as a theater, dance hall and apartment
building in early times. Mr. Schaible set up an office in the Dew Drop Inn
building.

OCTOBER 26, 1978: A large prairie fire about six miles west of Bowdle near
the Murray farm covered an area one-half mile wide and two miles long and
destroyed 17 haystacks belonging to Bob Stangl and John Stefanich. The fire
was started by a passing train.
