Protection ...

BOWDLE VOLUNTEER FIRE DEPARTMENT

        Back: Ozzie Schlepp, Roger Jacobs, Ron Brown, Glenn Blumhardt, Doug
        Larson, Oscar Metzger, Bob Drake, Dave McCarlson, Dewayne Syhre,
        Walter Fischer. Front: Mike Nehls, Aaron Aldinger, Ruben Brown, Ted
        Knudsen, Curt Bollinger, Bob Beadle, Gordon Stotz, David Karst. Some
        firemen were not present for the picture.
        
It was April 17, 1901 that the Bowdle Volunteer Fire Department was
organized. C.L. Wood was elected fire chief, L.E. Amerpohl, assistant chief;
J.L. Owens, secretary and R.T. Hill, treasurer. The fire company consisted
of 36 men.

Equipment of the first company consisted of two chemical wagons and a hook
and ladder cart. After the city water system was installed two hose carts
were purchased. One of the original chemical wagons and a hose cart remain
in the possession of the present fire department.

Bowdle's first fire alarm system was a large bell mounted on a tower. This
bell, today, maintains a prominent place in Meakins Park.

The first electric fire alarm was erected in April 1929. Today's alarm
system was furnished by the State Civil Defense organization. It can be
activated by a telephone answering system located in the homes of the fire
chief, assistant chief and department secretary. This unit is also used to
warn the city residents of impending severe weather conditions or tornadoes.

The first fire truck was purchased by the city of Bowdle in 1948. The
farmers of the community organized in 1956 and purchased a fire truck which
serves the rural area. This truck is manned by the Bowdle firemen.

        Fire extinguisher used at the Bowdle Flour Mill in the early
        1900's.         

        The Bowdle Volunteer Fire Department sponsored an Open House and
        Pancake & Sausage Supper in 1985 with proceeds given to the
        Centennial Fund.

A new fire station, adjacent to the City Shop, was constructed by the city
in 1973. This provides housing for all the fire vehicles and equipment. At a
later date, an office and meeting room were added to the fire station. This
was financed by the Fire Department.

The Bowdle Fire Department is equipped with two fire trucks, a 2,000 gallon
tanker, a pickup with a high pressure pump and hoses to fight prairie fires
and a van for transporting fire fighters. A modern radio system provides
communication between the fire station, fire chief, ail vehicles, Edmunds
County Sheriff Department and Bowdle Hospital.

BOWDLE CITY LAW ENFORCEMENT

Sept. 1, 1982 the Bowdle community entered into a contract law agreement
with Edmunds County for law enforcement services. The agreement was signed
by Dennis (Mike) Olson, Edmunds County Sheriff: Raymond Forkel, Chairman of
Edmunds County Commissioners and DeWayne Weiszhaar, Mayor of Bowdle City.

The Edmunds County Sheriff Department is contracted to provide 25 hours of
law enforcement service each week. At the present time Bowdle and Roscoe
are contracting for law enforcement services.

In September 1982 Phil Toft was hired by the Edmunds County Sheriff
Department as a Deputy Sheriff and resided in Bowdle. In November 1983
Deputy Toft moved to Aberdeen and continued his career in law enforcement
with the Brown County Sheriff Department and Deputy Mike Nehls moved to
Bowdle from Ipswich where he had resided one year. The current resident
Deputy Sheriff in the City of Bowdle is Bryan Locke, who joined the Edmunds
County Sheriff Department in August 1985.

The Edmunds County Sheriff is Dennis (Mike) Olson. Deputies are Mike
Nehls, resident of Ipswich and Bryan Locke, resident of Bowdle. Dispatchers
are Stacy Lacher, Carol Schaffner and Maddie Schumacher.

The 26-member department has been provided with the latest in fire
fighter's wearing apparel and apparatus. Plans are being made for the
purchase of a new truck in 1986.

Health Care ...

Compiled by Julia Senn and Alma Binder, assisted by Ruth Miller and David
Green.

People living to be 90 or more years of age is not unusual in these 1980
days, but a century ago the life expectancy was in the 40's and the longer
life span can be attributed to increased knowledge in diets, foods
available and medical care.

Privation and hard work characterized the life of the first immigrants to
Dakota Territory. Their homes were of sod, as there were few trees on the
prairies to make lumber. The ventilation was sometimes too good and
sometimes not good enough. There was an abundance of wildlife to help them
live off the land and, in some instances, the settlers could bring
medicines with them and could learn to use what nature had caused to grow
on the prairie. For the most part, this knowledge had to come from the
Indian tribes.

Contagious diseases and infections were catastrophic to settlers and early
day travelers. Historical records show that during wars more soldiers died
of infected wounds than of bullets. When kindly neighbors came to help at a
settler's home, usually the first question was about the need of a draught,
such as castor oil which no doubt killed many an appendix sufferer.

Poultices of mustard and flour or bread and milk were often used for
infectious bites and camphor for a headache was a common remedy. Hard work
characterized all labor, whether it was farming or housework and many a
farmer was injured when the horses ran away and there was no help to put his
broken bones together. Hot toddies were also used as a medicine for colds
or "flu."

The bearing of many children and hard work of keeping a home shortened
women's lives and it was not uncommon for a homesteader to have buried
several wives. Quarantining of families in their homes was the only means
of preventing epidemics of measles, small pox, scarlet fever, typhoid and
diphtheria. It was not uncommon in those days to see a neighbor bring food
or necessities to a home, set it down and go away before the door was
opened.

Neighbor helped neighbor when sickness occurred and some of these angels of
mercy remembered today are Mrs. Katie Schlepp, whose daughters Tillie Oster
and Maggie Gross and some grandchildren are Bowdle residents. Mrs. John
(Katie) Hagele and Mrs. Philip (Christina) Hoffman also had healing hands.

Anna Hoven told of Mrs. Schlepp's helping at the birth of her youngest
daughter and how she had taken dinner plates, warmed them and put them on
her chest during a bout with pneumonia, restoring her to health.

Tillie Oster said she is sure her mother brought several hundred babies
into the world.

THE DOCTORS

The first settlers came to this area of Dakota Territory in 1883, as nearly
as can be ascertained and those with health problems struggled as best they
could with help of neighbors until 1886 when Dr. William Edwards and his
wife Ida came to make their home in the Baer District or Theodore, about 12
miles southwest of Bowdle.

Dr. William Edwards

He was born in Madison, Wisconsin and graduated from the University there
and in 1877 opened his first office in Taopi, Minnesota where he met his
future bride, Ida M. Wells. They were married in 1879 and their first home
was at Dodgeville, Wisconsin. They later moved to Madison (South) Dakota
Territory before moving to Theodore. In 1886 with the arrival of the train
to Bowdle Dr. and Mrs. Edwards brought their family here to live.

They had two children, a son Frank who was a civil engineer by profession
and who was employed during his lifetime as city engineer by Oklahoma City,
OK and a daughter Mary whose musical talent was enjoyed by many. She became
the wife of Attorney Alex Searle.

In 1892 Dr. Edwards was elected State Senator from this district and served
the city as its first mayor from 1911 to 1912 after its incorporation. He
also served as President of the State Board of Health under Governor Andy
Lee and held all official positions on the State Medical Association. Dr.
Edwards also established the first drug store in the city and the first
hospital.

He was active in the civic life of the community, contributing in many ways
to the development of town and country. He owned several farms in this area
and was the first to grow alfalfa in Edmunds County and a great believer in
sweet clover.

His thirty-four years of compassionate service to the people of this area
ended in 1920 with his death, but their love for him is often recalled at
this time.

Dr. Murdy opened a practice here in 1894, but soon moved to Aberdeen and in
1898 Dr. George Nickisch and family arrived from the southern part of the
state and purchased land from Dr. Edwards. Doctors Adolph Krause and A.J.
Button also served the community, but there is very little record of their
activities.

From 1910 to 1923 Dr. Grant S. Carpenter and Doctor Edwards were partners.
Then Dr. Carpenter took his family to North Dakota where he was later
appointed Superintendent of the State Hospital in Jamestown. He held this
position until 1952, when he retired.

Dr. T.D. Jones of Aberdeen often assisted Dr. Edwards at Bowdle and it was
on such an occasion that he brought Baby Buechler, daughter of Mr. and Mrs.
Fred Buechler, into the world. She was named Irma, her birthdate is Oct.
15, 1918 and she is the wife of Ted Leidholt.

Dr. Thomas D. Jones, a graduate of Northwestern College in Chicago, opened
a practice here in 1920. He brought the first X-ray machine to Bowdle,
using it in his office. He earned the love and respect of the community
during his 18 years or more of medical ministrations and worked with Dr.
Anton Hyden as a co-worker until the late 20's when Dr. Hyden moved to
Sioux Falls. In 1932 Dr. and Mrs. Jones spent time in Europe where Dr.
Jones continued his medical studies and Dr. Hogeboom took care of the
medical needs of the community until about 1935 when he left for Billings,
Montana. Dr. Jones returned to resume his practice and after spending a
year in Aberdeen returned to Bowdle in 1934. In 1940 he moved to
Chamberlain where he lived seven years, returning to Aberdeen in 1947
because of illness. He died in 1950.

Then Doctors Neukamp and Steiner of Hosmer helped by keeping office hours
at the Bowdle Hospital several days a week. There has been a lot of
cooperation on the part of Bowdle residents and officials to obtain
professional aid here. Often a doctor would come and be in need: sometimes
of furnishings for their home, sometimes the need was for citizenship
papers and sometimes they just needed everything.

        Dr. Thomas D. Jones     Dr. Rainis Berzins

After World War II many "displaced persons" came from war torn Europe to
the U.S.A. Among them were Dr. Rainis Berzins and family. A medical student
at Krakow University in Latvia, he had been pressed into the surgical unit
of the military hospital by the conquering German Nazis. He continued his
medical studies in Germany and he and his family were residents of Sioux
Falls until he completed requirements to practice in this state.

Dr. Zveniks also of Latvia came to Hosmer in 1953 and the two men
cooperated in the Bowdle Hospital. Dr. Berzins arrived in Bowdle in 1953 and
remained until about 1970 when his family moved to Aberdeen. Dr. Kitzler of
Gettysburg and Ipswich spent a few years here, then went to Yankton where
he was in charge of the medical unit of the State Hospital where he
suffered a heart attack and died. Of him, Mrs. Fred Miller recalls how he
would say, "If only I could give these old people new organs, they want to
live and cannot."

Doctor Alejandro Adajar of the Philippines, who had practiced in Chicago,
was Bowdle's doctor ten years until 1983 when he and Mrs. Adajar spent a
year in West Virginia, returning to Bowdle in May 1984.

        Dr. Walter Kitzler     Dr. Alejandro Adajar

Dr. John Ottenbacher was on staff in 1982 and 1983 and left to head the
medical staff at South Dakota State University in Brookings. He is the son
of Mr. and Mrs. Gus Ottenbacher of Bowdle.

        Dr. John Ottenbacher

Dr. Mary Klein and Dr. Gordon Philips were welcomed to Bowdle in 1983 and
1984 and were a team to maintain clinics in Bowdle, Hosmer and Selby, as
well as working at the hospital.

The new Bowdle Clinic, located between the nursing home and hospital,
opened for business in August 1985 and had its grand opening Sept. 8. The
clinic is a modern facility and is staffed by two medical doctors, Dr.
Stephen Grant and Dr. David Wolff. They are assisted by Claire Jo Knecht,
LPN and Mary Turner, receptionist.

        Dr. Stephen Grant       Dr. David Wolff

FLORENCE NIGHTINGALE SISTERHOOD

The time is the turn of the century. The scene is Doctor Wm. Edwards
Hospital at the end of a busy day. The doctor has gone on a country call and
travels by means of horse and buggy with the owner of the town's livery
stable doing the driving so as to give him time to relax and read.

Rose Holtman, RN is left with the care of the hospitalized patients.
Everyone knows that if anyone can bring the pneumonia patient through the
crisis it will be Rose. She treats him with mustard plasters, being careful
to lubricate the skin with olive oil to keep it from blistering. Though she
has been on duty all day, she continues with his care with only the aid of
the housekeeper and cook. The feeble light from the kerosene lamp shows his
breathing is becoming shallow and she prays silently as she applies all the
skill she knows to keep him alive for the sake of his family. She speaks
words of encouragement as she moves to the other patients, hoping that the
doctor will soon be back.

There is no electricity, no indoor plumbing, the food has to be carried in
and out, and the patients' beds are only knee high so that giving temperate
baths takes a very strong back to keep it from aching. There is no
back-rest on the beds and patients have to be elevated on pillows for
meals. To raise a patient the nurse offers her arm with the hand bent to
her body, and the patient takes hold and is raised upright.

Then in 1918 the new building was ready, and what a help. Beds with
back-rests that were adjustable, modern and the main floor served three
patients and a ward along with the doctor's office.

When the hospital addition was built in 1927 13 patients could be cared
for, as there was a four-bed ward, a two-bed ward and three private rooms
with one added later by closing off the west end of the hall and additional
patient rooms in the basement.

        Ottilia Hennecke, Druggist Morrio Jones, Wallie Merkel

Lurene Walters (Merkel) RN and Ottilia Hennecke RN joined the staff.
Ottilia was Superintendent of Nurses until her marriage to John Weibel in
1934. Mrs. Agnes Wagner RN worked until her triplets were born. Tena
Stevens became the Superintendent.

Through the years it was Wally Merkel and Mrs. Ruth (Fred) Miller RN whose
response to the call for help kept the hospital going, whether it was
surgery or a heavy patient load that caused them to leave their homes and
assist. These two nurses were relied on in times of sickness, injury or
death when the town was without a doctor. They were the people's first aid.

Nurses were busy every minute of their shift, taking care of patients,
sterilizing equipment so it was ready for the next surgery, night duty
nurses put in any free time making dressings and the day nurses also
cleaned the hospital. Thermometers had to be sterilized and ready for the
next use. Mrs. Miller recalls doing a regular duty shift and then spending
the night on a cot in the room of a critical patient to be available for
care.

Others who kept the institution going were Althea Blumhardt Moser, RN;
Vivian Hoven Snethen, RN. Mrs. Tena (Walter) Stevens took over the
management and held the first Nurse's Aide classes with Erna (Mrs.
Reinhold) Huber and Alice (Mrs. Albert) Huber as students. The hospital
closed from 1961 to 1954 until Dr. Berzins became the town's physician and
Mrs. McMann RN was in the top position. Eloise (Lickfelt) Eisenbeisz RN and
Clara Feickert were also on staff.

Erna tells of a nine months duty period when she and Alice worked their
shift for nine months without a day off, and recalls that with 13 patients
to care for if an obstetrics case came in, they had to go to the delivery
room and help, care for the baby, then clean the rooms, take the laundry to
the basement and put it to soak and still take care of patients.

An X-ray was part of the equipment and Ruth Miller also recalls how the
nurses carried patients down the steps when they required this service.
There was always work to be done and when Elsie Blumhardt was the cook she
not only prepared the meals, but also carried trays, did the laundry and
sometimes checked in on the patients in the basement.

Installation of the bed pan sterilizer in 1956 was a boon to nurses. At
that time only the critically ill were given intravenous feedings and then
the doctor had to administer it. At present registered nurses administer
and monitor intravenous medication and are qualified for many skilled
services, thus their responsibility is greatly increased.

When the move to the present hospital building was made in 1962 the
addition to the staff included two lab technicians, one administrator and
accounting department, but the change that lifted a load for nurses was the
cleaning and laundry personnel.

PHARMACY

A century ago a physician not only treated the patient, but also prepared
the medications he prescribed to cure the ailment. The United States
Pharmacopoeia was adopted as standard for the country in the Food and Drugs
Act of June 30, 1906 and is revised every ten years by a convention of
physicians and pharmacists.

Unfortunately there is not much of a record of the men at the turn of the
Century who "kept the store open" so that there was service for those who
were ill. The first pharmacist or druggist in Bowdle is listed as J.E.
Sparling, who came at the invitation of Dr. Wm. Edwards. The seventy-fifth
history lists a Hooper Drug Store in 1886. Sparling was followed by Charles
F. Slate, who came in 1888 and C.C. Merriman.

Mr. Maas came to Bowdle from Hoven in 1892 to clerk in the drugstore owned
by the late Dr. Edwards, receiving his board and $2 per week for his
services. He worked for Dr. Edwards six and one-half years.

In 1898 Dr. Edwards sold his drug store to Charles F. Slate who worked
there about one and one-half years with Mr. Maas. Fire destroyed the
building. Then Mr. Maas decided to start his own business, rented the
building known as the Old City Hall (1925 known as the Frank Werner Shoe
Shop) and ordered a modest supply of drugs and medicines and he was in
business. The same year he began the erection of the building in which the
store is now located and in July 1900 moved into the building. He built up
property to the estimated value of $25,000 or $30,000, proving "where there
is a will, there is a way."

In 1925 Henry Maas sold to Morris Jones, brother of Dr. T.D. Jones. Mr.
Maas moved to Aberdeen.

        Winter of 1914-1915 H.C. Maas City Drug Store

H.V. Yaukey had established a pharmacy on the northeast corner of what is
now Main and 3rd Avenue. In 1930 he moved his store to Mobridge
consolidating it with a store he owned there.

        Morris Jones

This left Bowdle with only the City Drug Store, owned by Morris Jones.
During World War II when Bowdle was without a doctor, the people turned to
him for aid with their ailments until they could get out of town to a
doctor. Twenty-one years after coming to town, on May 1, 1946, Mr. Jones
moved his family to Aberdeen where he had purchased a drug store on Main
Street, later moving it to 6th Avenue. Morris had sold his store here to Les
Olson, who remained only a couple of years and then moved his family to
Three Forks, Montana. Mr. Jones continued in the pharmacy business and his
son Lloyd joined him in 1954. Morris died in 1968 in Aberdeen.

        Lloyd Jones     Doug Turner

Bowdle was without a pharmacy until 1982 when Lloyd Jones opened the Jones
Drug Store, succeeding the A & B Shop. During the years Bowdle had no
pharmacy Wm. (Bill) and Adeline Miller helped the community by opening the
A & B Shop, making available over-the-counter medications. April 1, 1985
Mr. Jones sold the pharmacy to Doug Turner of Aberdeen, a registered
pharmacist.

DENTISTRY

Dentistry 100 years ago -- it is difficult to conjure in your mind what it
must have been like. Many pioneers must have found the only relief from an
aching tooth was to have it taken out -- and for a child it meant, for the
most part, tying a string around the tooth -- then tying the other end to a
door knob -- positioning the child just right and then slamming the door
and thereby the tooth was extracted.

The first dentist to serve the area was Doctor Goodman, and later Dr.
Merriman, both of whom are reported to have arrived in 1883. A museum is
about the only place where the dental tools of the trade in the 19th
Century can be seen.

Dr. Oscar P. Olson came in the early part of the 20th Century and was the
only dentist here for the entire area until he was succeeded by his son
Alfred in 1935. Alfred moved on to Rapid City in 1939.

Dr. F.A. Miller came to Bowdle in 1937 and has the record for the longest
term of service, practicing his profession until 1977 when he retired. He
served in the U.S. Army Medical Corp during WWII from 1942 to 1945. Dr.
Miller opened his first office here in the old Security State Bank building
(now the Youth Center) in May 1937. He moved to the Rositch building on 3rd
Avenue in May 1937. In the summer of 1941 he fixed up the building that had
been occupied by the Blumhardt Implement where he continued to serve the
public until his retirement.

        Dr. Fred A. Miller      Dr. Curtis G. Baltz

In 1979 Dr. Cutler of Aberdeen opened an office here, coming out a day or
two each week to care for dental patients, after men of the city donated
funds and labor to remodel the Art Merkel building (on the corner of 4th
Avenue and Main.) He was succeeded by Dr. Jackson of Hoven, who in June
1984 announced the sale of his clinics in Bowdle and Hoven to Dr. C.G.
Baltz. Dr. Baltz is a graduate in Dentistry at Marquette University, Class
of 1970 and a native of Wisconsin.

HOSPITAL

Bowdle's first hospital was built by Dr. Wm. Edwards shortly after his
arrival in 1886 and Rose Holtman's services as his nurse were always
recalled whenever the hospital or Dr. Edwards were spoken of, even in later
years. The hospital was a two-story frame structure, the second building
east from the southeast corner of Main and 3rd Avenue. Mrs. Fred (Theo)
Grosz told of coming to Bowdle in her teens for an appendectomy in the
Edwards Hospital as at that time Ipswich did not have a hospital.

A disastrous fire wiped out the hospital and several other buildings in
that block in May 1929. This building was built in 1889, used first for a
hospital, later as a sort of hotel and for the past years had been the home
of Mrs. Ida Edwards and her daughter.

Fortunately Dr. Edwards had felt the need to expand his hospital and had
built a concrete block building on 3rd Avenue South for a hospital in 1918.
It housed a reception room, two patient rooms, a lab and examining room and
an operating room. This building was still used in 1985 as the Bowdle
Clinic and has also been used as Dr. Oscar and Dr. Alfred Olson's Dental
Office.

Dr. Edwards died in 1920 and Dr. T.D. Jones began his practice here. Soon
his patient load became greater than the little hospital could accommodate
and through the formation of the Bowdle Community Hospital Association, in
which shares were sold for $100 each, more space was added in 1927. The
addition included a large operating room, five patient rooms, one of which
was later taken for the autoclave and lab work. The Association operated
the hospital with hiring the staff and supervising all activities until Dr.
T.D. Jones rented the facilities. Shares in the association were also sold
in the 1940's.

Dr. and Mrs. Jones went to Europe in 1932 where the doctor spent a year
studying and he returned to his practice here in 1934 operating the
hospital with the aid of Otillia Hennecke, RN and Tena Stevens, RN until
1940 when he went to Chamberlain.

After World War II donated funds of $17,000 were used to renovate and
improve the building. Later it became apparent that the association could
no longer carry the financial load, and on Sept. 6, 1949 the association
deeded the property to the city of Bowdle. The officials effected a
compromise settlement of the $2,500 mortgage which the association had
outstanding and set up a governing board of three City Council members and
two citizens appointed by the mayor. One of these men was Fred C. Grosz.

Vivian Hoven, daughter of the late John Hoven, had earned her registered
nursing degree in Minneapolis and with a friend kept the hospital open for a
year or two. Doctors Neukamp and Steiner of Hosmer took care of the medical
needs and Mrs. Lottie McCall, LPN, kept the hospital open beginning in 1942
for a few years. May 7, 1961 the hospital was closed because of lack of a
doctor and staff and due also to the financial deficit.

In 1954 Dr. Rainis Berzins, a native of Latvia, opened a practice here and
the hospital was reopened with Tena Stevens, RN as Director of Nursing. She
conducted the first classes in Nurse's Aide work and among her pupils were
Erna (Mrs. Reinhold) Huber and Alice (Mrs. Albert) Huber.

Tena and her husband, Lee Stevens, moved to Aberdeen and she was succeeded
by Mrs. McMann as Superintendent. She moved to Wallace, Idaho. Mrs. Alice
Gerberding succeeded her in 1958 as Director of Nurses. Funds to purchase
an X-ray machine were raised and the machine was installed in the basement
of the hospital.

During the time that Joseph V. Stappler served as mayor (1952-1960) the
need of hospitals nationwide received a lot of attention and brought about
the Hill-Burton Act in Congress for funding of hospital construction in
1959. Edward Schmidtgall donated the land for a new hospital and also later
made available the land for the nursing home.

The community voted to bond itself and with funds raised by public
enterprise and the work of the Hospital Auxiliary and many donations,
including aid from the State Board of Health, the present $350,000 hospital
was built and dedicated June 3, 1962 by Mayor Helmer Leno. Gardner C. Gross
was Chairman of the Building Committee and Mrs. Gerberding, Director of
Nurses and Mr. Pinkerton as Administrator.

The community was justly proud of the new 20-bed facility which included a
surgery, labor room, delivery room, examining room, emergency room,
laboratory room, X-ray room, nurse's lounge, modern kitchen, laundry,
doctor's lounge, administrative offices, 10-bed nursery with three
incubators and conference room.

MAY 20, 1926
  Hospital to be enlarged ... the ground will be broken for the addition to
the Community Hospital building. The structure is to be of hollow tile and
will be 68 ft. by 31 ft. in dimensions and will be divided into 12 or 14
rooms.

JANUARY 4, 1935
  Bowdle's triplets (Robert, Ray and Roger Wagner) have passed their first
birthday.

JULY 26, 1962
  The Infant daughter (Karen) of Mr. and Mrs. Vernon Oban of Loyalton, born
July 17, was the first baby to be born in the new Bowdle Hospital.

JUNE 7, 1962
  About 1,700 people attended the dedication of Bowdle's new hospital. Lt.
Governor Joe Bottum was the speaker.

        1962 Anesthetic Machine at Bowdle Hospital

        Sheila Hoffman with new anesthetic machine purchased in March 1985.

Every effort is made to keep the hospital abreast of new equipment for the
greatest service to patients. The Hospital Auxiliary has led the community
in fundraising for the purchase of the most modern equipment.

During the last few years the following have been added to the Bowdle
Hospital equipment:

Fetal Heart Monitor: Monitors the unborn baby's heartbeat during labor; is
able to detect and alert to possible complications.

Gemini Chemistry Analyzer: Analyzes blood chemistries thus aiding in more
accurate diagnoses and is capable of doing 21 tests.

Holter Monitor: Monitors and records patient's heartbeat for specified time
periods while going about normal activities.

Blood Gas Machine/Cardiac Monitor: Equipment to more accurately diagnose
patient's condition.

Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: Hospital personnel now required to learn CPR.

Miscellaneous: Patient lights, electronic thermometers, gas gastroscopy and
several pieces of nursery equipment.

Complete X-ray: Through Mrs. Lloyd (Christine) Koch's donation of $40,000
in 1977 the complete X-ray was purchased, including the darkroom and
developer.

        Lab Technician June Merkel working in the lab at Bowdle Hospital in
        1985.

Unfortunately it is impossible to publish a complete list of those who have
served as Director of Nursing during the past 20 years: Helen Fleming
succeeded Mrs. Gerberding and Alma Binder 1972-1975, Sheila Hoffman to
1978, Char Schlepp to Jan. 1981, Alma Binder 1981 to April 1982, Colleen
Harner to 1983 and Sheila Hoffman 1983 to the present time.

SEPTEMBER 10, 1964
  Triplets were born to Mr. and Mrs. Harley Ulmer of Hosmer, delivered by
Dr. Berzins. This was the first multiple birth at the 3-year-old hospital.

The following have held the responsible position of Administrator of the
hospital: 1962 Wm. Pinkerton, 1964 Ramon Richardson, 1965 Robert Joens,
1967 Mrs. Patricia Lee (temporary), 1968 Helen Fleming, 1972 Leonard
Meysenbourg, 1973 David Gilbert, 1974 Alma Binder, 1975 James Hanson, 1975
Ronald Bender, 1977 Mildred Aldinger, 1979 Rodney Kosters (Dakota Midland
Hospital management agreement), 1980 John Daly, 1981 Alma Binder, 1981 Tony
Plantier and Dave Green (Adventist Health System management agreement),
1983 Leased to AHS and Dave Green continued as Administrator.

Financial problems continued to cause concern about the operation of the
hospital and early in September 1984, Administrator David Green stated that
the department heads of the hospital came up with two ways to add revenue
to the ever-shrinking hospital income: one dealt with the newly instituted
Swing Bed Program. At that time four beds in the hospital were used for
that purpose: the care of patients waiting to be admitted to the nursing
home, which was already at capacity load. The idea was to expand the
program to increase beds to 14, and in the event that medical patients
needed the beds, the patients would be placed elsewhere until the crisis
passed. The second recommendation was to remodel the hospital to
accommodate a medical clinic. The Swing Bed System was adopted in October
1984 under the guidance of Dave Green, Administrator.

Mayor Beadle appointed a task force of councilmen and other persons of the
community to investigate the problem of lack of in-patients at the hospital
and to recommend ways to keep the facility open.

Another change in the management of the Bowdle Hospital occurred when
notice of termination of lease of the Hospital and Bowdle Nursing Home was
given to the City Council by the Adventist Health System, Sept. 24, 1984.
Leonard Marsch, Vice-president of AHS-EMA, cited operational losses and
complications with the local medical staff as reasons for terminating the
lease contract. Final date of termination was Nov. 30.

David Green who had been administrator of the facility since 1981, left
early in November having been transferred to Marshfield, WI to a similar
position. Rob Montague, who was also affiliated with AHS took over this
position until Dec. 31, 1984. The Task Force's suggestion of considering
the Westworld Community Healthcare Inc. of Forest Lake, CA was discussed by
the City Council and then presented to the public at a meeting. Westworld
Inc. operates 22 hospitals and nursing homes, including a hospital at
Custer, SD which now offers alcohol abuse treatment and where Westworld
Inc. has built a wing onto the structure, and the hospital at Estelline, SD
where they have added nursing home service.

Westworld Inc. leased the two institutions for a term of 30 years and
considerations are a fee of $1 per year for the hospital and $2,000 a month
for the nursing home until the bonded indebtedness is paid off in 1990.
Thereafter the nursing home will be leased to Westworld Community
Healthcare Inc. for $1 per year until 2015. The papers were approved and
signed by the City Council and Mayor Beadle Nov. 19, 1984 and by WHC
Vice-president Jeffery Smith. This action saved jobs for 60 or more persons
in Bowdle.

In return the company takes over all financial obligations for the two
facilities including maintenance, capital improvements and equipment
purchases. A board made up of citizens from the community will help govern
the actions taken by Westworld Community Healthcare Inc.

        Barb Nehls, Sheila Hoffman and Ed Leake are pictured with the
        Bowdle Hospital Courtesy Van, a service added by Westworld Community
        Healthcare Inc. in 1985.

A finalizing step in the transfer of the management of the Bowdle Hospital
and Nursing Home to the Westworld Community Healthcare Inc. of Forest Lake,
CA was completed Jan. 25, 1985 when Ed Leake began his duties as Bowdle
Health Care Administrator.

Mr. Leake came to Bowdle from Bismarck, ND, where he was the Administrator
for a 60-doctor medical clinic and before that, had been one of the
administrators for an 1100-bed hospital at Northwest Memorial Center in
Chicago and has also served as Administrator of the University of Chicago
Hospital and Clinic. Mr. Leake was an English instructor in Chicago ten
years.

Mr. Leake believes in a healthy working relationship between the
communities to provide quality care. He stated, "In order for Westworld to
be successful, the corporation has to move fast with the setting up of
satellite clinics and in order to meet this goal of satellite clinics in
the surrounding cities, additional medical doctors are imperative."

To start the satellite clinic concept Westworld Community Healthcare Inc.
has employed Orval Haberer as an assistant administrator. He is in charge
of setting up clinics in the surrounding areas and began work Feb. 1, 1985.

THE NURSING HOME

The year was 1964, the foresight belonged to the Bowdle Commercial Club
which sent a delegation of its members including Dr. R. Berzins, Dr. F.A.
Miller, Duane Steiger, Oscar Olson, Gardner Gross, Wm. Miller, Greg Kramer
and Morris Kurle to the City Council meeting of July 20, to request the
building of a nursing home to care for the elderly who could no longer care
for themselves. After deliberation Mayor Leno and the Council acceded and
Gardner Gross was asked to contact the Small Business Administration to see
if it was possible to secure financial aid for this purpose. Apparently
their reply was negative as the City Fathers decided to go the bond issue
route.

        The dining room is a favorite meeting place for the residents.

Nov. 19, 1964 The Bowdle Pioneer published a "Notice of Public Meeting" to
be held at the Legion Hall on Nov. 20, to discuss and explain the proposed
nursing home. Present to answer questions were the City Council members,
the City Attorney and members of the Commercial Club. Members of the
Council were Aldermen Dwight Commet, Albert Perman, Christ Voegele, Christ
Bollinger, Gust Dumdei, Auditor Otto Huber and Mayor Helmer Leno.

The first architect's drawing of the proposed home showed a T-shaped
building, the east and west wings for patients and the north and
southcentral portion for administrative, culinary and utilitary purposes.
Three hundred eight voters turned out for the election on Monday, Nov. 23,
1964 with only 38 opposing votes cast. This opened the way for letting bids
for sale of the $175,000 bonds at 6% interest.

The Pioneer reported, "A site for the Home for the Aged has not been chosen
but it is expected that it will be near the hospital." Nance Engineering of
Mobridge estimated cost of construction and furnishing to be between $3,000
and $4,000 per bed. Pioneer editor Wadleigh stated that taking the high
figure would be sufficient funds to build a 40 bed hospital with $15,000
left for unexpected expenses.

The City Council met Dec. 7, 1964 and on motion by Bollinger, seconded by
Dumdei, retained the Nance Engineering of Mobridge to perform the
architectural and engineering services in connection of the approval of the
nursing home contract. The contract was to be examined by the City Attorney
and upon acceptance Mayor Leno and Auditor Huber were authorized to execute
the contract on behalf of the city of Bowdle.

A new statute of the South Dakota Code Laws regarding the issuing of city
bonds, necessitated the authorization for the city to issue them in
sufficient amount to pay for the construction and furnishing of the home
and guarantee the first two years interest and operating capital. This was
also reported in the April 5th minutes of the Council.

Notice had been given to the public of a special election (published April
8, 1965) to vote on the issuance of $50,000 additional revenue bonds for
the purpose of acquiring the site and to furnish and equip the nursing home
and assure its initial operation. April 22, the Pioneer published a "Notice
of Bond Issue Election" and April 29, the returns showed 9 out of 10 voted
in favor of issuing the additional $50,000 bonds, 274 voted yes and only 28
opposed. Mayor Leno and Treasurer Christ Bollinger signed the Nursing Home
Bond July 1.

The architectural drawing accompanying the above news item depicted a
Y-shaped structure, much larger than the original T-shaped structure
considered. Edward Schmidtgall made additional land available for the
nursing home on land adjoining the hospital.

July 22nd President of the Bowdle State Bank, Gardner Gross accepted a
deposit of $225,958.61 from City Treasurer Christ Bollinger, City Auditor
Otto Huber and Mayor Leno. The check was drawn on the account of Kalman and
Co., Minneapolis Investment Brokers, from the proceeds of the sale of the
bonds and the accrued interest from June 1 to the date of the sale.

March 24, 1966 The Pioneer reported 12 patients admitted to the nursing
home. Mrs. Veronica Kapperman (a sister of Joseph Stappler) who transferred
from the Selby Nursing Home and Caroline Jeschke who transferred from a
home in Strasburg, ND were the first to register on March 15, one day after
the city officials accepted the building from the Holzworth Construction
Co. Eight of the twelve resident patients were transferred from other
nursing homes. Thirty names were on the waiting list.

Nursing Home Administrator, Robert Joens said the opening went as well as
expected, considering that the severe blizzard of March 4, 5 and 6 blew
snow into the attic causing need for new ceilings in some rooms and the
fact that there was some additional work to be done. The home was fully
staffed and ready to handle 40 residents. Mr. Joens plans also include a
"Sunshine Ladies" group for the home so members can contribute time to make
the Bowdle Nursing Home more pleasant. All the women from Bowdle and
surrounding towns were urged to join.

Home Administrators since its opening have been Mr. Joens in 1967; Patricia
Lee, Alma Binder and Helen Fleming in 1971. The facility was leased to
Dakota Care Center (Joan Kempf) in 1971, whose license was lifted by the
State Board of Health in 1983, and the Adventist Health System leased the
Home.

        Ruth Aman measuring ingredients for baking.

Improvements made since 1983 include: On January 1983 when the Adventist
Health System began leasing the Bowdle Nursing Home there were 76
deficiencies. Deficiencies have since been reduced to six. The Medical
Review Team from Huron rated the Bowdle Nursing Home VERY GOOD. Cleaning
staff has been doubled, substantially increased food purchases, new
furniture in dining room, TV room and lobby, new curtains in all resident
rooms and hallways, every resident room and lobby completely repainted, new
lighting, new flooring in some resident rooms.

        4-H Clubs entertain the residents at the nursing home.

January 1, 1985 Westworld Community Healthcare Inc. leased the Nursing Home
and began operating it with Ed Leake as Administrator.

A skilled nursing home is in the making for Bowdle Nursing Home. The
skilled facility will provide better healthcare to the residents with the
addition of a physical therapist and 24-hour monitoring by registered
nurses and/or licensed practical nurses.

BOWDLE AMBULANCE SERVICE

Ambulance services throughout the state were furnished for many years by
the funeral homes, as they were the owners of vehicles that could be used
for such purposes. Floyd Miller of the Miller Funeral Home in Bowdle had
the only ambulance service here, and at one time, served not only Bowdle,
but also the towns of Hoven, Akaska, Selby and Ipswich. They operated the
only ambulance between Aberdeen and Mobridge for years, and Bowdle had one
of the two ambulances in the state that was equipped and certified approved
by the State of South Dakota.

JANUARY 30, 1964
  Floyd Miller received a Cadillac combination funeral care/ambulance.

When Medicare became part of the Federal Health System, the Miller
Ambulance Service found they were becoming more and more entangled in red
tape and technicalities, such as when having to transport a patient to
Aberdeen for medical care not available in smaller hospitals, Medicare
demanded that the ambulance deliver the patient to the Ipswich Hospital --
it being the one passed en route. When informed that there was no doctor
there they required that a statement be obtained from the doctor that he
was not there before proceeding to Aberdeen. Medicare imposed more and
more regulations and problems, and frustration set in, until all the
funeral homes wanted out of the business.

Mr. Miller stated that at the time he terminated his business his charge to
make a trip to Aberdeen from Bowdle was $25 and there was no subsidy for
gas or maintenance. He reported making 140 ambulance runs a year at that
time. There are only two funeral homes in the state now supplying ambulance
services.

In the July 1, 1971 issue of The Bowdle Pioneer announcement was made as
follows: "The City of Bowdle has taken over the Area Ambulance Service and
will begin operation of the same July 1, 1971. However help is needed to
operate this service and volunteers are now being solicited. Those wishing
to serve the community and fellowmen in this manner are asked to contact
the City Auditor at once. Those needing the ambulance service are to call
the hospital."

Those who responded were members of the Bowdle Volunteer Fire Department:
John G. Gross, Glenn E. Dippert, Fred Schlecht, Gordon Stotz, Ruben Brown,
Alvin Kurle, George Mashek, Morris Kurle, Duane Steiger, Wilmer Schaible,
Bernard Carlson, Floyd Miller. Mrs. Albert (Alice) Huber took a 22-hour
ambulance emergency course when Dr. Kitzler was the local physician and
1974 saw her again improving her efficiency in emergency technique when
she, with her son Jack and Milton Gross took the 60-hour course at Mobridge.

Dr. F.A. Miller, Mayor, presided at the Bowdle City Council meeting Feb. 7,
1972 when a motion was made by Alderman Schaible, seconded by Steiger, that
a resolution be sent to the North Eastern Comprehensive Health Planning
Council recognizing the city to represent the area. On roll call vote, the
motion carried.

On motion by Kurle, seconded by Carlson that the city of Bowdle accept the
resolution agreement of the Edmunds County Commissioners, dated Dec. 29,
1971, regarding the purchase of the ambulance. Thus the city acquired the
1966 Chevrolet (station wagon) ambulance from the Miller Funeral Home with
the necessary equipment already installed for the sum of $3,000. Title to be
recorded in the name of the city of Bowdle.

Financial problems necessitated the introduction of the following on Feb.
7, 1972:

                RESOLUTION
WHEREAS there is a deficit of $1,081.65 in the operation of the Ambulance
Service between July 1, 1971 and Dec. 31, 1971, and that the city of Bowdle
present the Edmunds County Commission a voucher for the amount to reimburse
the city for that amount.

Motion for the adoption of this resolution was seconded by Alderman
Schaible and on roll call vote was adopted.

A shuffling of city funds helped. On motion by Alderman Kurle, seconded by
Aldinger to borrow from the Old Hospital Maintenance and Operation Fund the
sum of $1,500 and deposit that amount in the Ambulance Fund for the purpose
of paying $1,000 as part-payment on ambulance to the Miller Funeral Home;
$318 to R.J. Herman Agency for liability insurance and other expenses. On
roll call vote the motion was carried.

Moved by Kurle, seconded by Aldinger the city of Bowdle pay the Miller
Funeral Home $125 for the month of January 1972 being rent for the use of
the ambulance for the city of Bowdle for the period pursuant to the county
agreement with the city of Bowdle, dated Dec. 29, 1971 from funds received
from the county and carried.

March 6th at the regular City Council meeting payment of $1,000 on the
ambulance and $125 rent and payment of $2,000 on the ambulance and
equipment is reported. March 7, Edmunds County Commission proceedings show
a payment of $2,000 on the ambulance and $200 to the city of Bowdle on
operating and maintenance expenses on the ambulance. May 6, 1974 the City
Council changed the name of the Bowdle Hospital Ambulance Service to Bowdle
Ambulance Service.

Federal regulations in 1975 brought another change: Station wagons could no
longer be used for ambulance purposes and that vehicles for such use must
be fully equipped as per government standards. This also changed auto
dealers business as only ambulance companies could sell ambulances, as per
regulations. Edmunds County financed the purchase of the new ambulance for
Bowdle and for Ipswich through Revenue Sharing Funds.

Dec. 11, 1975 the city of Bowdle published "Notice for Bids" for one Type
II Ambulance. The vehicle and equipment must meet design criteria and
specifications for ambulance emergency care vehicle and notice stated that
the bids would be accepted until Jan. 5, 1976. Specifications were
available at the City Finance office. Nine bids were received, some from as
far away as Tennessee and Florida.

Jan. 8, 1976 at a special City Council meeting with Mayor Miller presiding
and County Commissioner Ray Bachman present, motion was made by Steiger and
seconded by Kurle to purchase: "1975 Wayne Chevrolet Vanguard 60" at a bid
price of $16,525 from the North American Ambulance Sales Co., 1960 Cliff
Road, Burnsville, Minnesota." On roll call vote the motion carried.

The March 4, 1976 issue of The Bowdle Pioneer announced, "Pictured above is
the new Bowdle City Ambulance acquired last weekend. This is the latest in
ambulances and has a price tag of $17,000. Funds for the machine were
furnished one-half by the State of South Dakota and one-half by Edmunds
County. Cost to the city was about $1,000." Pictured with it was Fred
Schlecht, driver of the vehicle.

        Bowdle Ambulance in 1985

The ambulance is inspected annually by the South Dakota Department of
Health, thus it is kept up to standard.

Sherma Maier, Candice Huft and Kathy Huber took the ambulance attendants
course in Aberdeen in 1976. Police Officer Glenn Dippert, who for several
years was on call for ambulance duty, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week,
terminated this service in 1982.

In 1982 they responded to 48 calls and in 1983 to 64 calls. This was
written in 1984 so the year's figures are not available.

Mrs. Ruth Miller RN and Erna Huber and other nurses have also accompanied
the patients when their condition necessitated transfer to larger hospitals
for care.

The ambulance service was also included in the leasing of the Bowdle
Hospital and the Bowdle Nursing Home when the Westworld Community
Healthcare Inc. leased the two structures for 30 years in November 1984.

Bowdle American Legion Post #264 ...

Compiled by W.H. Jahraus and Walter Fischer

        Left to right: Ted Sandmeier, Helmuth Sandmeier, Leonard Erbe,
        Bernard Carlson, Willard Erbe, Gerald Hilbers, Art Hintz, Walter
        Fischer, Arnold Doerr and Robert Doerr.

The Bowdle American Legion Post was organized following World War II
December 21, 1945 with the following World War I veterans forming the
nucleus: Oscar Olson, Fred Gross, Albert Senn, John F. Bieber, John Oster,
George Knapp, Christ Bollinger and Oscar Goettling. Fred A. Miller was
elected commander; Ruben Schumacher, First Vice-Commander; Edwin Buechler,
Second Vice-Commander; Robert Gross, Adjutant and Finance Officer.

The first Legion home was the old H & H Theatre building. This building
burned to the ground Feb. 3, 1947. Members of the Post then decided to
construct the present Legion Hall.

From the time of its inception the Bowdle Post has always conducted the
following programs: Memorial Day Services, Military Funeral Rites for all
deceased veterans, Boys State, Baseball, Advice and Aid to all veterans
seeking medical and hospital benefits and place grave markers for all
deceased veterans. The Post has always made available to the public use of
the Legion Hall for all types of functions.

During the past several years this Post has participated in the Venison for
Veterans in Hospitals and Homes Program. Many of the members, plus others
in the community, contribute venison for this cause and in 1985 the local
post won the State "Big Buck" Award (plaque) for contributing the most meat
in this statewide "contest."

The Post raises most of its funds through its annual Pow Wow which is a
popular public event staged every third Thursday in November. The only
other way the Legion has of raising money is through hall rentals, which
include dances and public meetings.

Adjutant is one of the most important and time consuming positions in the
Post. Walter C. Fischer has served in that capacity for 14 years, followed
by M. M. Hartzell with 10 years. Mahlon Gross has served as Finance
Officer for many years.

Another important position is that of Sergeant of the Firing Squad. This
position has been filled by Leonard Erbe for many years and, more recently,
by Aaron Aldinger. The squad is used for all Memorial Day Services and all
Military Funerals.

The Bowdle American Legion Post has just two World War I veterans left on
its membership role. They are Oscar Olson and Emil Spiry.

        Oscar Olson     Emil Spiry

MAY 6, 1943
  Sgt. Richard Schumacher was awarded the "Purple Heart" by the U.S.
Military authorities for bravery and heroism at Guadacanal.

MAY 31, 1913--FIRST MEMORIAL SERVICE
  This was the first Memorial Service ever held in Bowdle. They closed all
the businesses and attended the services at the Opera House. It was filled
to its capacity. There were present four aged veterans from the 50th
anniversary of Gettysburg. The four honored old soldiers were George Brown,
G.C. Aurand, W.F. Davis and M. Hart. From the Opera House all marched
following the band to the cemetery honoring the dead with flowers. They
found four old soldiers resting there: Geo. Kreash, A.F. Sayer, C.V. Musser
and Comrade Cooley.

JUNE 3, 1943
  Jones Drug is displaying the first service flag in a Bowdle business
place, the badge of honor having been hung up Friday. The three stars on
the flag are for Staff Sgt. Oscar Olson, now a prisoner of the Germans;
Pvt. Harold Baer, who is stationed in the Hawaiian Islands and Pvt. Reinie
Eisenbeisz in Atlantic City, NJ. All were former clerks in the store.

1984 BOYS STATE LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR

When Don Gross was selected the 1984 Bowdle American Legion Post Boys State
representative, he began making plans to win the coveted position of Boys
State Governor. In his words ... " Might as well go for it." He almost made
it.

The 1984 session forced Don to alter his goal somewhat. His party's caucus
leaders convinced him to run for Lieutenant Governor to balance the ticket.
"The debate on Thursday morning decided the election," Don said. "It was
the longest three hours of my life."

Don was elected 1984 Boys State Lieutenant Governor, the highest office
ever attained by a Bowdle Boys State representative.

Bowdle American Legion Auxiliary ...

Compiled by Esther Voller

        SOME AMERICAN LEGION AUXILIARY MEMBERS AT A 1985 MEETING Back row:
        Esther Aldinger, Mildred Sandmeier, Alma Leno, Lee Jahraus, Alvina
        Berg. Front row: Alice Holweger, Clara Fischer, Julia Senn, Maggie
        Buechler, Martha Weiss.

In reviewing the records of the Bowdle American Legion Auxiliary #264,
since its organization Jan. 30, 1946, one realizes that service to
community, state and nation has been its aim. Patriotism, Americanism and
charity have been stressed throughout the years; and the welfare of Veterans
and their families, handicapped or able-bodied. For God and country,
Auxiliary members have served.

When the Bowdle Unit was organized, there were 25 charter members. Of the
original group, three are still members: Martha Weiss, Edna Gross
Bebermeyer and LaVaughn Gross Schlepp. Charter members are: Katherine
Hoffmann, Irene Buechler, Irene Thommen, Ruth Miller, Vangie Olson, Patty
Senn, Vivian Gross, Cecelia Krause, Lenora Kurle, LaVaughn Gross, LaVerne
Thommen, Cecelia Bieber, Mildred Aldinger, Rosina Kiesz, Helen Glatt, Viola
Olson, Sylvia Schumacher, Thelma Schumacher, Betty Helmer, Theo Grosz, Elsie
Buechler, Martha Weiss, Edna Bebermeyer, Catherine Thommen and Alice
Heckenlaible.

Two years later membership had increased to 93, including 12 junior
members. Membership gradually declined and from 1955 to 1961 the average
annual membership was 50. By 1984 membership dwindled to 34. In spite of a
reduction of members, the organization has fulfilled all the obligations
required by the Department of South Dakota Progress Chart and managed to do
its work as capably as in past years.

The following ladies have served as president (several two or more terms):
Ruth Miller, Katherine Hoffmann, Gertrude Olson, Mary Huber, Cecelia
Krause, Marcella Grosz, Alma Leno, Irma Erbe, LaVerne Gross, LaVaughn
Schlepp, Esther Voller, Katie Burrer, Marion Knudson, Clara Fischer,
Virginia Voller, Rose Hintz and Mildred Sandmeier.

Cecelia Krause was elected President of District 14 and later became
Department President. She was also a member of the American Legion.

        Cecelia Krause

Americanism has always been stressed in American Legion Auxiliary work.
Each year, flags have been presented to first graders who have learned the
Pledge of Allegiance. Cash prizes are offered to students annually for
Americanism essays and poetry relating to our country. Sherri Steiger's
essay won first place in District 14.

For several years Auxiliary members sold U.S. Savings Stamps weekly at the
school. Demonstrations on flag-folding were held and flag etiquette was
studied. In 1984 the Auxiliary presented a large flag to Meakins Park.
Members have reminded Bowdle citizens that flags should be displayed at
polling places according to regulations and on streets and at homes on
National holidays.

Sponsored by the Auxiliary, Girls State delegates have gone to Mitchell
each year. The 1971 delegate, Corrine Hoven, received a $200 Scholarship
Award at Girls State. Beginning in 1947 the delegates are listed:

BUDDIES WEAR POPPIES

Veterans' poppies, made by handicapped veterans at Hot Springs, from
materials provided by the Auxiliary, are ordered annually. Orders are
generally 1500 or 2000 and in addition, large poppies are ordered for table
or stage decorations. Poppies are sold by members and school children
during Poppy Week. Poppy corsages are also sold and bouquets are placed on
Veterans' graves. In May a window display on Main Street is made, in
remembrance of those who died in the service of our country. After the cost
of poppies has been deducted, 25% of the Poppy sales income is returned to
the Veterans who made them.

Poppy poster contests are sponsored annually for elementary and high school
students with cash prizes awarded. In 1974 Sherri Steiger's poster won
District 14 and Department of South Dakota awards. In an Auxiliary contest
Esther Voller won District and Department awards for a Poppy poem.

As a community project the Auxiliary began sponsoring Snow Queen and Talent
Contests in 1946. In later years the Bowdle Jaycees became the sponsors and
at present the Bowdle Community Club and Bowdle Service Club are
co-sponsors.

Each year in August groups of Auxiliary members entertain residents of the
Bowdle Nursing Home bringing lunch, a birthday cake and providing a form of
entertainment.

        Mrs. Theo Grosz pins a flower on Mrs. Joseph Krumm at a Mother's
        Day Tea in May 1958.

The Legion Auxiliary sponsored the Senior Citizens organization in 1973 and
1974. When funds were being raised for Bowdle's Bicentennial Celebration
the Auxiliary's kitchen and equipment was used for a community
Pancake-Sausage-Egg dinner and members assisted other organizations for the
meal.

In 1946-1947 two baby cribs were donated to the Bowdle Hospital. Needy
families have been given financial help and baskets of groceries at
Christmas. Children with speech problems were taken to Aberdeen during
summer months to receive speech therapy. Members attending Northern State
College provided transportation. A severely handicapped child's medical
expenses were lessened by a donation. A rummage sale at the Legion Hall
raised funds and provided clothing for a family who lost everything in a
fire. A cash donation was made to another family, after a fire.

At the rummage sale, members of the family who had lost everything,
selected what they could use. Unsold articles were stored until warmer
weather and another sale was held. The income was deposited as an Emergency
Fund, to be used in future emergencies.

A Chest X-ray Clinic was sponsored in 1958-1959 at the Legion Hall. Members
have assisted with immunization clinics. A public card party was held for
the Hospital Fund during the 1959-1960 year and there was a Hospital Benefit
dance. The Hospital Auxiliary was permitted to use the Auxiliary's kitchen
for meetings and fundraising events.

Two wheel chairs have been available for people in the community. A
little-used new wheel chair was bought in recent years and a fee of 50
cents per day is charged. The Auxiliary has collected funds for Polio and
Cancer Drives. For the March of Dimes, a card party was held.

For many years Halloween parties were held for school children and
pre-schoolers at the Legion Hall and there were times when the Auxiliary
paid the cost of a movie for a Halloween treat. In recent years members
have assisted the Bowdle Mothers' Club at Halloween parties held at the
school.

JULY 24, 1941
  The housewife is asked to search through her kitchen cupboards for
aluminum pans. A pen has been erected in two business places to be used as
an aluminum dump. The aluminum will go to Pierre for sale. The proceeds
will be given to the U.S. Government.

        Dumdei          Feiock

For many years public Mother's Day Teas and programs were held at the Hall.
They were elegant affairs and flowers were pinned on all guests. Gold Star
Mothers were honored with corsages. Our original list of Gold Star Mothers
included Mrs. Joseph Krumm, Mrs. Earl Erbe, Mrs. John Dumdei, Mrs. Jake
Leidholt, Mrs. Regina Dangel and Mrs. Christ Feiock. Mrs. Art Merkel and
Mrs. Matthew Bachman were added when their sons were killed in the service
of our country. The last Gold Star Mother, Mrs. Dumdei, died July 13, 1981.

        Leidholt        Krumm

Veterans at the Veterans' Hospital in Hot Springs are faithfully
remembered. Wrapped Christmas gifts are sent annually to the Gift Shop and
cash gifts, playing cards, hospital gowns and bibs. Good used men's
clothing is sent and members have made slippers of yarn. The Department
President's Project, an annual addition to make life more convenient or
pleasant for patients, has always been sent a donation. Rug material is
collected for the Hobby Shop. Rugs and other articles from the Hobby Shop
are sold by the Bowdle Unit. One Department President's Project was the
beautifying of the National Cemetery at Sturgis. We have supported
legislation that is beneficial to Veterans and to have Memorial Day and
Veteran's Day observed on their original dates. The Auxiliary assists the
Legion in planning Memorial Day Programs.

        Erbe            Bachman

When floods at Rapid City left some homeless, the Bowdle Unit sent $50 to
provide food and clothing to the Flood Fund. Funds have been raised in many
ways: serving large banquets, reception lunches, public card parties,
serving lunches for Pow Wows, auction sales and dances, rental fees from
kitchen and equipment, rummage sales and sponsoring pillow cleaning days.
Pillow cleaning is done by professional cleaners who pay a percentage of
the income to the Auxiliary. Auxiliary volunteers assist with the record
keeping.

        Maggie Buechler         Alma Leno

Alma Leno and Maggie Buechler have been chosen District 14 "Legionette of
the Year" and Esther Voller was the District 14 "Ambassador of the Year."
She also won in the District, Department and Northwestern Division (seven
states, including South Dakota) essay contest, "An Imaginary Trip to
Korea." It was one of five essays that went into National competition.
Korea was studied in the Foreign Relations Program. In connection with
Foreign Relations, donations to CARE are made.

        Esther Voller

Members over eighty have been adopted as secret-grandmothers by junior
members, who remember their grandmothers with cards and gifts on holidays
and birthdays. Our junior members will carry on the American Legion
Auxiliary's work in future years and their help at Poppy time and
entertainment is greatly appreciated.

THE METHODIST CHURCH 1886 - 1968

The history of the Methodist Church is linked very closely with the early
events in the town of Bowdle. It began meeting in the store buildings
around the year 1886 and earlier held services and class meetings in the
homes of settlers. Early meetings seem to have been held in the Tom Ward
General Store building where an upper room supplied adequate space for
meetings. Sunday School classes were held in the upstairs of the Aurand and
Amerpohl Store building, which at that time was located across the street
from the City Fire Station and pump house (east.)

After the building of the first Hotel (Dumont House--now Reuer Garage)
worship services were held in the Hotel dining room every two weeks. The
Rev. Samuel Franklin Brown of Bangor was the pastor. Bangor was a small
town southeast of Selby, no longer on the map. In the summer 1887 Rev.
Brown organized the Methodist Society of Bowdle. The schoolhouse was
completed in 1887 and Rev. Harrington became the first resident pastor.
Services were held in the upstairs of the school. Through funds raised by
the Ladies Aid Society an organ was purchased to help with music.

Rev. E. O. Bullock became pastor and he recorded the first memberships,
that of Mr. and Mrs. G.C. Aurand Dec. 19, 1888. July 31, 1892 Rev. Ward
received as members Mr. and Mrs. Charles Dorwin and Mrs. Mary Baker. The
devotion of these people as workers in the Sunday School and in the church
ran for 30 years. Early pastors eked out a living by working part-time. One
of these, Rev. L. McCullock, worked at the Aurand and Amerpohl Store and in
his spare time built a home in the community.

In 1895, a big year for the church, a building was erected. This was
possible by the hard work of the Ladies Aid Society and a grant from the
Methodist Extension Society along with donations from the community. Due to
the large German-Russian influx into the community most of the other
churches used the German language. The Methodist Church became the home for
those who spoke or preferred English in the worship services. In 1923 Mr.
Aurand died and left a bequest to the church that financed the basement. In
1945 the church was redecorated and remodeled with some new carpets. This
was financed in part by the sale of the parsonage and funds from the sale
of the Mound City Methodist Church and money raised by the Ladies Aid
Society. Oscar Olson was prominent in this remodeling.

In 1968 the Methodist and the Evangelical United Brethren merged nationwide
to form the United Methodist Church. In 1969 this merger became known
locally as the Evangel United Methodist Church of Bowdle. After this merger
worship was continued in the EUB building and the Methodist building was
sold to the Gospel Tabernacle.

        Earl Erbe took this photo in 1949 at a Methodist Ladies Aid supper.
        Back: Adeline Voller, Theo Grosz, Gertrude Olson, Julia Senn.
        Front: Wally Merkel, Ruth Goldade, Kathryn Thurn, Rosie Mashek.

Pastors serving this church to the time of merger were: 1886 Samuel
Franklin Brown; 1887 Harrington; 1888 E.O. Bullock; 1892 A.M. Ward; 1895
J.B. Dibble; 1897 Frank Grossman; 1898 Lyman McCullock; 1911 J.E. McKinney;

L. Lane; 1923 A.E. Folley; 1929 C.L. Glenn; 1930 J.W. Terry, died in office
in 1932; 1933 Dr. M.A. Chase; 1934 L.L. Goodwin; 1935 Ernest Currier; 1942
