Ervin Brink; 1964 John Iszler, served to Dec. 31, 1972.

JUNE 22, 1916
  Bowdle had quite an honor this week in entertaining the S.D. Conference
of the Congregation Church. Fifteen ministers and 40 delegates, besides
many visitors, were here. The local pastor is Rev. Brakemeyer.

BOWDLE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH

According to the records this church was chartered Dec. 31, 1886 in Bowdle.
Evidently families were served throughout the area as they gathered in the
homes or other buildings. In 1901 churches were organized among the rural
settlers of the area. However in 1911 the church in Bowdle began attracting
members from the rural area. Under the leadership of Jacob Gross and
Christian Gross the rural people came to town.

March 17, 1912 the name "Friedensthal Evangelical Congregational Church"
was chosen. Fairly accurate records were kept from the year 1911.

The following pastors ministered in the community: 1911-1914 E.B.
Kaitchuck; 1914-1921 G.L. Brakemeyer; 1922-1923 Carl Schatz, 1924-1929
Jacob Rath; 1930-1937 Jacob Kessler; 1937-1941 Dan G. Schurr; 1943-1946
Julius Houn; 1948-1952 Bernhard Moos; 1953-1958 John A. Baris; 1958-1961
W.E. Janetzki; 1961-1972 John Iszler.

The Congregational Church being short of pastors was served by the
Evangelical United Brethren pastors starting in about 1958. Then came John
Iszler who served them along with the EUB Church and under his leadership
the EUB and the Methodists merged to form the Evangel United Methodist
Church in 1969. About 10 years later the Congregational Church voted to
close and some of the members united with the Evangel United Methodists.
Records show transfers of members in the years 1978 and 1979.

SEPT. 25, 1902
  The Ladies Aid of the Congregational Church will give their annual
Thanksgiving dinner and Bazaar this season in the basement of the church.

EVANGELICAL UNITED BRETHREN CHURCH

At the Annual Conference in Casselton, ND a new mission was established
known as the Frontier Mission, which included Bowdle with Eureka as the
center. Seven pioneer pastors took turns coming here to preach in the homes
of the early settlers. By the turn of the century there were 18 appointments
that these men of God visited to preach the Gospel. In 1905 the Rev.
Melzian, residing in Eureka, began a regular ministry in Bowdle Prairie.
This church was 10 miles south of Bowdle and constructed in 1912.

        Evangelical United Brethren Church

In 1928 the church building in Bowdle was sold and the Bowdle Prairie
building was moved to town along with many of the parishioners and it was
settled on the present site in the year 1929 and dedicated to the glory of
God in 1930. They developed a Sunday School, a Women's Society and a fine
group of laymen. This church was part of a merge in 1968 with the
Methodists.

Pastors serving, ministering from Eureka, were Melzian 1905; G. Heuer
1910-1911; William Butchet 1911-1914; A. Ermel 1914-1918, E. Melzian
1918-1920; S. Finkbeiner 1920-1923.

In 1923 just south of the church a building was bought. S. Finkbeiner
became a resident pastor until 1928. Pastors following were O.N. Helberg
1928-1931; J.C. Sipple 1931-1934; George Raile 1934-1935; O.W. Ferk
1935-1939; G.H. Kowalke 1939-1943; H.C. Docktor 1943-1945; O.W. Ferk
1945-1946; R.H. Miller 1946-1949; E.E. Boegler 1949-1953; W.E. Janetzki
1953-1961; John Iszler 1961-1968.

John Iszler continued as pastor after the merger until 1972.

EVANGEL UNITED METHODIST CHURCH

In the year 1968 the Evangelical United Brethren Church and Methodist
Church merged to form the United Methodist Church throughout the United
States. Only a very few churches voted to remain outside this merger, some
of them being Brethren churches in Montana, linked themselves with some in
Canada. These churches had similar polity handed down from John Wesley.

In the year following this merger the Evangelical Church (EUB) and the
Methodist officially became the Evangel United Methodist Church of Bowdle.
This change was effective under the leadership of John Iszler who had
pastored the EUB Church since 1961. The Congregational Church of Bowdle was
also being served by Pastor Iszler. The Congregational Church, though
cooperating many years, joined the Evangel United Methodist in 1978 and
1979 (shown by the transfers of members.)

        Evangel United Methodist Church

It was under the leadership of John Iszler that plans were developed for a
new parsonage and this was built late in 1972 and ready for the new pastor
Stanley Caine, who came in 1973. The old parsonage was sold to Frank
Gabriel.

The Evangel United Methodist Church began worshipping in the former EUB
building and sold the former Methodist building and the former
Congregational building. The Methodist building was sold to the Gospel
Tabernacle and the Congregational building was sold to Herman Person.

The women were organized into a unit called the United Methodist Women.
They have worked faithfully at many projects. In 1983 they put new cushions
on the pews and purchased a dehumidifer for the parsonage basement where
the office is kept. A faithful group of men work together taking on various
projects. The sign was redone in 1984. New storm windows are about to be
put on the windows to assist in making the building a bit more weatherproof.

Pastors serving the Evangel United Methodist Church of Bowdle include 1969
John Iszler; 1973 Stanley Caine; 1978 James Cissell; August 1979 to 1982
Paul Budd; 1982-1983 Johthaya Samuel; 1983 Roger J. Thomas.

JUNE 15, 1922
  Trinity Lutheran Church, 12 miles southwest of Bowdle, dedicated June 18,
1922. Rev. S. Baer will preach. It will be remembered that the "Baer"
Church, which had been a landmark for many years, was destroyed by fire in
September. The new structure was built largely by the members themselves at
a cost of $3,000. The old church was 25 years old.

TRINITY LUTHERAN CHURCH [BAER CHURCH]

In 1888 Pastor Lahme, a resident of Redfield, served the Lutherans in a
territory from Mound City to Clark. During his pastoral trips he arrived in
Bowdle and with a number of families gathered at the Wm. Haupt home for the
first Lutheran service in the community.

In 1889 Pastor Volkert served the small congregation, soon followed by
Pastor C.F. Malchow. In 1892 Pastor Julius Engel served as pastor. Late in
1893 Pastor R. Fehlau served the parish until 1900. The congregation was
organized Jan. 12, 1894. The charter members were Bernhardt Baer, Johannes
Baer, Johannes Mueller, Michael Trikowski, Peter Schaack, Christian Baer,
Wilhelm Heerwald, Jakob Baer and Andreas Reide.

This Lutheran Church, located 12 miles southwest of Bowdle, was dedicated
in 1898. It was built near the former townsite of Theodore. The parish was
served by the following pastors: Pastor J.C.A. Gehm (1900-1904;) Pastor
Otto Keller (1904-1916;) Pastor Carl Schweppe (1917-1920;) Pastor F. Traub
(1920-1927) and Pastor Paul Albrecht (1927-.)

During Pastor Traub's term in September 1921 the church was struck by
lightning and burned to the ground. Shortly thereafter a new church was
constructed and dedicated June 18, 1922. The new structure was mainly built
by members themselves at a cost of $3,000.

The church celebrated its 50th Jubilee Aug. 28, 1938.

In November 1945 the church was sold to First Lutheran Church of Faulkton.
The proceeds went to the building fund of St. John's Evangelical Lutheran
Church in Bowdle. The bell was removed and hung in the tower of the new
enlarged St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church in Bowdle to symbolize the
union between Trinity of Theodore and St. John's Evangelical Lutheran of
Bowdle.

        Trinity Lutheran [Baer] Church

THE NEUGLUECKSTAHL CHURCH [THE BUECHLER CHURCH]

The congregation was organized in May 1891 with Rev. Volkert as pastor. At
the beginning during the 1890's the sermons were held at the Michael
Buechler Sr. home and later in the Buechler School House. In 1901 the
Neuglueckstahl Church was built with approximately 35 families.

The charter members were as follows: Frank Doherr, William Haupt, William
F. Soerweid, John Rosin, Michael Nusz, William Schick, Jacob Buechler, John
Buechler, Jacob Kurle, Christian Himmerick, Michael Buechler Sr., Michael
Buechler Jr., August Fitzlaff, John Brandt and Gottfried Fitzlaff.

The only recorded pastors serving the church were Pastor A. Ottersburg from
Hosmer, serving the church in 1897 and Rev. Kirchdorfer from Java, who
served from 1902-1918.

Other pastors serving the congregation were Rev. Hanselmann (1919-1928-)
Rev. Leo Seeman (1928-1932;) Rev. Henry Nagel (1932-1934;) Rev. Bernhard
Nagel, son of Rev. H. Nagel (1934-1935;) Rev. E.H. Vetter (1935-1943;) Rev.
Theo. H. Judt (1943-1946.)

In 1946 the congregation disbanded and several members joined St. Paul
Lutheran Church in Java. Others joined St. Paul Lutheran Church in Bowdle.
The church was moved to Mound City.

The site of the Neuglueckstahl Cemetery is on a hill in Harold Nies's
pasture.

ST. JOHN'S EVANGELICAL LUTHERAN

St. John's had its start in 1888 when Pastor Lahme, who resided at
Redfield, came to the Germans living in the area. Coming to Bowdle, he
gathered a number of families in the William Haupt home to conduct the
first Lutheran services in the area.

The Minnesota Synod, which later through merger had become the Minnesota
District of the Evangelical Lutheran Joint Synod of Wisconsin and Other
States, sent Pastor Volkert as St. John's first resident pastor in 1889.
Pastor Volkert also served the Theodore Township church southwest of
Bowdle. The first part of the parsonage was also built at this time.

Until now the congregation had not been organized. Pastor C.F. Malchow came
to St. John's and May 10, 1891 the congregation was organized. The 15 men
who signed the constitution were Frank Doherr, William Haupt, William F.
Soerweid, John Rosin, Michael Nusz, William Schick, Jacob Buechler, John
Buechler, Jacob Kurle, Christian Himmerick, Michael Buechler Sr., Michael
Buechler Jr., August Fitzlaff, John Brandt and Gottfried Fitzlaff.

Pastor Julius Engel served St. John's for a few months in 1892. In January
1893 Pastor R. Fehlau came to serve the congregation. It was not until Oct.
10, 1898 that St. John's dedicated its own church. Public school rooms had
been used until now.

        St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church

OCT. 26, 1905
  The Lutheran Church has purchased a fine large bell weighing 1,100
pounds. The bell will be placed in position as soon as possible.

Pastor J.C.A. Gehm took over the pastorate in 1901. Pastor O. Keller
accepted the call in 1904 and served the congregation until the time of his
death in December 1916. During his pastorate the parsonage was enlarged, a
bell was purchased by the Ladies Aid in 1905 and a schoolhouse of cement
block was built in 1908. In 1906 St. John's was accepted into the Minnesota
District. The schoolhouse built in 1908 was razed in order to make room for
the present parsonage in 1928. A basement was added to the church at this
time to provide a place for schooling the congregation's children.

Pastor Carl Schweppe succeeded O. Keller. In 1920 Pastor Schweppe took over
the presidency of our Synod's Dr. Martin Luther College in New Ulm,
Minnesota. Pastor F. Traub then served St. John's until he accepted a call
to our Synod's Academy in Mobridge. In 1927 the vacancy was filled when
Pastor Paul Albrecht accepted the call extended to him. Nov. 21, 1943 a
building fund was started for improvement of the church. At its annual
meeting Nov. 11, 1945 a decision was made to enlarge the church. In the
fall 1947 the new and beautiful structure was dedicated.

St. John's observed its golden anniversary Aug. 29, 1936. Former pastors
J.C.A. Gehm and Professor C.L. Schweppe and two sons of the congregation
Pastors Samuel and Alvin Baer, served as festival speakers.

Trinity Lutheran Church of the Theodore Township, which together with St.
John's had formed a parish from the beginning, now decided to disband. The
horse and buggy days were over as improved roads and automobiles prompted
its members to join St. John's in 1945. The Theodore Church was sold to
First Lutheran Church of Faulkton. The bell, however, was removed and hung
in the bell tower of the new enlarged St. John's Church where it still
serves to call members to worship.

Hearts were disturbed in 1959 when the congregation was split resulting in
the formation of the Church of the Lutheran Confession.

Professor K.G. Sievert of our Academy in Mobridge served as interim pastor
until November 1962 when W.F. Sprengler of Cedar Rapids, Iowa was
installed. He retired from the preaching ministry in May 1970. Loyal
Schroeder accepted the call and served St. John's spiritual needs until
February 1978. Pastor Mark Johnston was assigned as a graduate from the
seminary in Mequon, Wisconsin. He was ordained and installed in July 1978.
Six years later Pastor Johnston accepted a call to the home mission field
in Florida. By God's grace another graduate from our seminary, namely Paul
Marggraf, was assigned to St. John's. He was ordained and installed July
15, 1984 and presently serves St. John's.

Throughout the years the Ladies Aid has been active with willing hands in
church improvements here at St. John's, as well as helping the work of the
Lord for various educational, mission and charitable agencies of the church.

The mixed choir has served the church during past years until the present
time. It certainly has helped to edify the church services.

The young people of our congregation have an organization of their own
known as Youth Fellowship. Bible study, discussion of timely topics and a
chance for the young communicants to keep in touch with one another fulfill
the purpose of this organization.

St. John s Evangelical Lutheran Church presently has 123 communicant
members and 166 baptized members.

        St. John's Lutheran Church School built in 1908.

Christian education in the knowledge of the Word has been faithfully
carried out at St. John's. Confirmation instruction with the benefit of
Sunday School taught the children "in the way they should go." The
congregation enjoyed the blessings of a parochial school during 1931-1939.
The congregation built an educational annex in 1959. The knowledge of the
truth is also taught by means of summer school and Bible class. The present
Sunday School has 21 children.

ST. JOHN'S EVANGELICAL LUTHERAN LADIES AID

St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Ladies Aid has been an organization
throughout the years of the congregation's existence. The goal of this
society is to render assistance in the work of the church, locally and
through affiliation of the Lutheran Women's Missionary Society and the
Medical Mission in Africa.

We are not in a position to list the names of the Charter Members, because
no such list appears to be available. Mrs. Esther Blumhardt has been a
member of the Ladies Aid since 1924. At the present time she has been a
member of the Aid the longest.

The Ladies Aid plans the social functions and cleaning of the church,
enlisting the help of all the ladies of the congregation.

ST. PAUL AMERICAN LUTHERAN CHURCH

In 1918 seven men met to organize a Lutheran church in Bowdle under the
guidance of Rev. George Kirchdoerfer of Java. Rev. Kirchdoerfer was at this
time serving the Neuglueckstahl Lutheran Church northwest of Bowdle. The
organizing group established itself as the Evangelical Lutheran St. Paul
Congregation Jan. 24, 1918. It used the guidelines of the Iowa Synod as the
basis for its regulations.

One of the first orders of business of the newly organized church was to
move the old Catholic church building. Built in 1894, this was now moved to
the church site. This feat was accomplished with the aid of a man from
Selby who had moving equipment and two tractors.

Rev. George F. Hanselmann was officially asked to serve the congregation
Sept. 15, 1919. He was serving a Lutheran church in Lowry at the time of
his call.

The first parsonage was a rented home approximately one block west of the
church. When the time came to move the new pastor and his family from Lowry
to Bowdle members of the Bowdle parish hitched their horses to hayracks and
wagons and proceeded to transport the household goods to Bowdle.

Nov. 19, 1919 the Neuglueckstahl Church, the St. John Church located north
of Bowdle and the St. Paul Congregation of Bowdle received their charter
from the State of South Dakota which united them into a three church parish
corporation. This three church congregation remained in effect until 1946
when the Neuglueckstahl church yielded to the pressure of the times and
disbanded. Its members transferred to either St. Paul Lutheran Church in
Java or Bowdle. In 1947 the St. John Congregation closed and made St. Paul
in Bowdle its church home.

The construction of the first parsonage was begun in 1920. This was to be
the home of the pastors and their families until 1972 when a new parsonage
was built on 9th Avenue. The former parsonage was retained by the
congregation and used as the parish educational center.

The church property was again expanded in 1921 with the purchase of the
land to be used as a cemetery. In 1926 a schoolhouse was purchased and
moved to a location behind the church. This building was used as an
educational unit until the construction of the basement beneath the church.

Through the years many improvements and changes came about in the church
and its properties. Ever-growing needs for expansion became a cause for
many meetings, investigations and searching. A building committee was
organized and in the fall 1976 construction was begun on the present church
home. The dedication service for the new church was held May 1, 1977.

Pastors who have served St. Paul congregation since its beginning are: Rev.
George Kirchdoerfer in 1918, Rev. George F. Hanselmann (1918-1928;) Rev.
Leo Seaman (1928-1932;) Rev. Henry Nagel (1832-1934;) Rev. Bernard Nagel
(1934-1935;) Rev. E.H. Vetter (1935-1943--the first English services were
held during this time;) Rev. Theo H. Judt (1943-1947;) Rev. G.T. Kern
(1949-1955;) Rev. A.A. Krause (1955-1957;) Rev. George Landgrebe
(1958-1959;) Rev. Rueben Schnaidt (1959-1962;) Rev. Archie Lovaas
(1962-1970;) Rev. Gerald Lorenz (1971-1973;) Rev. Spencer Brien
(1974-1978;) Rev. Mark Smith (1978-1982) and the present pastor Rev. Eugene
W. Roesler who came to serve the St. Paul congregation in July 1982.

        Interior of St. Paul American Lutheran Church

St. Paul's, with its existing membership of 210 confirmed members, has an
active women's group known as the American Lutheran Church Women (ALCW.)
They pledge themselves to participate in Bible Study and other learning
opportunities and to respond to God's love in their home, in the church, in
the community and in the world. They are leaders in their Bible Study, sew
quilts, make layettes, support help to the needy for Lutheran World Relief
(LWR) and in their community. They sponsor an annual fund raiser called a
German Smorgasbord which is held Memorial Day. This is a public event.

        This photo was taken in May 1983 while the ladies were busy making
        cheese buttons for the German Smorgasbord. Left to right: Virginia
        Voller, Anna Weiszhaar, Millie Bieber, Mardella Bieber, Clara
        Fischer, Karen Bonen and Lila Oster.    

The young teenagers of the American Lutheran Church belong to an
organization called The Luther League and they meet for fellowship and Bible
Study and sponsor events in fellowship with other religious organizations.

The younger group of children attend Sunday School on Sundays and a Bible
Study held in the summer. They all become confirmed members after three
years of Bible Study under the study of the presiding pastor. These studies
begin in the seventh grade age group.

St. Paul's of Bowdle is looking forward to the new merger of three Lutheran
bodies. This will become a reality Jan. 1, 1988, when the American Lutheran
Church with its 2-1/2 million members, the Lutheran Church of American with
its 3 million members and the Association of Evangelical Lutheran Churches
with its 110 thousand members unite to become a 5-1/2 million Lutheran
body. The Commission for a New Lutheran Church (CNLC) task force was
authorized Sept. 8, 1982.

After governing assemblies of the three Lutheran Church bodies voted to
unite to form a new, more inclusive body. The commission, which includes 70
representatives of the uniting churches met seven times in 1982. The
constituting convention of the new church will be held within the period of
April 28 to May 3, 1987 in Columbus, Ohio.

The members of St. Paul American Lutheran Church of Bowdle look forward to
working, serving and praying together and to taking a significant place in
Bowdle and its community.

ST. AUGUSTINE CATHOLIC PARISH

Early Catholic settlers in the Bowdle area were Jacob Strobel, Patrick
Hughes, Charles LeMare, James Guhin, Conrad Bickert and Thomas O'Malley.
These men and their families, as well as the many Catholics who followed
them, sought to celebrate their Catholic faith in this area.

In the fall 1886 Rev. Bernard Heus, pastor in Ipswich, said the first Mass
in Bowdle in a hall over Cox's Store on Main Street. During his visit he
baptized the first Catholic child born in Bowdle performed the first
Catholic marriage ceremony of Stephen Gross and Mary Schumacher and
officiated the first Catholic funeral for Joseph Kessler.

Besides Father Heus (1886-1988) other priests served the growing Catholic
community: Fr. Joseph Stephen (1888-1890 from Ipswich,) Father Wolf
(1890-1891 from Hoven) and Father Victor (18921893 from Hoven.)

Construction began in April 1894 on a 24 by 40 foot frame structure on a
stone foundation at the cost of $588.80 on the sight of the present church.
The Ladies Aid Society raised $356.48 for the new church through bake
sales, needlework projects and dinners. Father Sack held the first services
in the new church in the fall 1894. The Church Board of Trustees consisted
of Jacob Strobel, chairman; James McKoane, secretary and Conrad Bickert,
treasurer.

Father John Lumisch was pastor in Ipswich and served the Bowdle Church
1894-1896. During his term the number of families increased to 35 and in
1896 an extension of 22 feet was added to the church building. Other
pastors were Fr. J.J. Dahlmanns (1896-1897 from Ipswich;) Fr. Joseph Cuenn
(1897-1899 from Ipswich;) Fr. A. Smith (1899) and Father J. Hansen
(1899-1902 from Ipswich.) July 1, 1902 Fr. Stephen Duren was appointed
pastor at Ipswich with Bowdle as a mission church. He served the parish
until 1906. Bishop Thomas O'Gorman of Sioux Falls made his first official
visit to St. Augustine's Church in Bowdle in 1908 and confirmed 96 children
and adults.

FEB. 15, 1906
  A resident pastor has been appointed for the Bowdle Catholic Church. Rev.
J.A. Krebs of Brooklyn, New York arrived. This 18 the first time Bowdle has
had a Catholic pastor residence within its limits.

Father John Krebs (1906-1912) became the first resident pastor of the
parish. He rented a room at the Watson House until a house was purchased
June 11, 1906 for $1,000. In June 1909 the Louis Amerpohl residence was
purchased as the parish house and the old house was auctioned. In 1908 the
Bowdle Cemetery Association deeded the Catholic parish about three acres to
establish a Catholic Cemetery. Aug. 21, 1908 solemn ceremonies were
celebrated for the opening of the new cemetery and a 25 foot wooden cross
was erected in the center of the cemetery. March 17, 1909 Miss Madelyn Wenz
was the first to be buried in this cemetery.

OCT. 8, 1908
  In the cemetery there is a life-size image of Christ crucified will be
erected. This figure is a handsome specimen of the Guiliani Co., an Italian
firm of St. Paul. This monument will represent an outlay of almost $100 when
In position. We are pleased to do something special in the "City of the 
Dead."

Father William Krause came in 1912 and served the parish until 1916.
Because there were now over 70 families the need was seen for building a
bigger church. Father John Kettler arrived May 13, 1916 (also serving as
priest for the churches in Selby, Mobridge and Roscoe.) With the unanimous
support of the parish, excavation for a new church began April 25, 1918.
The L.W. Jonason Company of Aberdeen was the general contractor with George
Issenhuth, architect. The first services were conducted in the new church
Holy Thursday, April 17, 1919. The cost of this brick church was $35,000.

AUG. 6, 1918
  Aug. 6, the ceremony of the laying of the cornerstone for the beautiful
new Catholic Church. The ceremony was performed by Rev. Father Dermody of
Aberdeen. It will be a monument that will stand for generations to come.

        Monsignor Joseph Hensbach

Father Kettler served from 1916-1932, Father William Schmitt from
1932-1936, Father Joseph Hensbach from 1936-1955 and Father Gaudentius
Althoff, OP from 1955-1983. During the time Father Althoff was pastor, the
interior of the church was redecorated (1957) and a new brick-faced rectory
was built on the south side of the church. In 1982 Father Althoff
established the first Parish Council with Bernard Carlson, August Thomas,
Matt Bachman, Esther Voller and Edmund Dewald as appointed members.

Father Owen Klapperich was appointed pastor in 1983 when Father Althoff
retired to Aberdeen. A Team Ministery was formed July 2, 1984. This
includes the Catholic parishes in Bowdle, Roscoe, Hosmer, Eureka, Selby and
Herreid. These parishes are now served by co-pastors Father Owen Klapperich
at Hosmer, Father Donald Marohn at Herreid and two Presentation Sisters,
Sister Karen LaFollette and Sister Darlene Gutenkauf at Bowdle. This Team
Ministry ushers in a new aspect of religious service to these communities.

        St. Augustine's Pastoral Team: Sister Darlene Gutenkauf, Sister
        Karen LaFollette, Father Donald Marohn and Father Owen Klapperich.

The Catholic Church in Bowdle has been a very active community through the
past 100 years. The women of the parish have held annual bazaars, dinners,
bake sales and other fundraising events. The parish members have decorated
and cleaned the church, taken care of the grounds, educated the children in
the truths of the Catholic Church and provided music for the liturgies
celebrated in the church.

Over the years a number of men and women from St. Augustine Parish have
decided to dedicate their lives in full-time ministry to the church. They
are Monsignor Henry Hoerner RIP (son of Baldaser Hoerner), Rev. Paul
Bachman (Joseph Bachman), Rev. Joseph Mardian (Anton Mardian), Rev. Pius
Mardian (Anton Mardian), Sister Appolonia, SSND (Leonard Bachman), Sister
Assumpta, SSND (Joseph Bachman), Sister Mechtild, SSND (Michael Dewald),
Sister Bernice, OSB (Adam Thomas Sr.), Sister Vera, OSB (Adam Heintz),
Sister Vita, OSB (Peter Heilman), Sister Mary, PBVM (Adam Thomas), Sister
Julia (Joe Heintz), Sister Barbara, SSND (Anton Mardian), Sister Christine,
SSND (Anton Mardian) and Sister Margaret, SSND (Anton Mardian.)

        St. Augustine's Catholic Church won the Purple Rosette Sweepstakes
        award in the Bowdle 1961 Diamond Jubilee parade. It also won the

        The float was designed by Mrs. Jacob Voller and the small church was

        Althoff, all of the Priests grew up at Bowdle.

SEVENTH-DAY ADVENTIST CHURCH

The Bowdle Seventh-day Adventist Church had its beginning in 1889 in a
rural area located south of Bowdle. At that time a small group of believers
met in the home of Philip Dollinger for their Sabbath services.

The following year May 4, 1890 the company was organized into a church by
pastors Valentine Lehr and Conrad Reiswig. The 15 newly baptized members
from the Bowdle area were joined by another 15 members from the Sutley
Church near Java to form this new congregation. Among the first elected
church officials were Adam Hagele Sr., who acted as local elder; Adam
Eisenman, church clerk and Ferdinand Knecht, deacon.

In 1894 the church members decided to construct a sanctuary about 71/2
miles south of Bowdle. This site was more central for all those members who
had to travel many miles with horse and buggy or wagon than in the town
itself.

By 1906 the church had outgrown its facilities and it was decided to move
the church building to a site four miles north of Tolstoy for the members
living in that area and to erect a larger sanctuary on the site vacated by
the original church. The original Bowdle Church building then became the
property of the Tolstoy Seventh-day Adventist Church.

The new structure served the Bowdle congregation from 1906-1945. At that
time the congregation voted to remodel the building and wire it for the
electrical facilities which would soon be available to the rural areas. It
was also decided to turn the building to an east-west position onto a
basement with the entrance towards the east. From May to December the
laymen worked many long hours in the construction of the basement,
foundation and foyer. When the building received its finishing touches in
December a whisp of smoke was noticed coming through the roof of the church
which signaled the beginning of a fire. With no water immediately available
to put out the blaze, the workers could only try to salvage their belongings
and most of the church's furniture. No immediate cause for the fire was
given except that the combustion occurred in the attic. The remaining
out-buildings were sold on a later date. The Seventh-day Adventist cemetery
is still located on that site.

From December 1945 through 1946 the congregation rented and used the Bowdle
Methodist Church for Sabbath services. In January 1946 the decision was
made to build a church in Bowdle. Several lots were purchased in the
western part of town along old Highway 12. This is where the church is
presently located. Again many hours of toil were put into the structure by
the laymen to get it finished.

Sabbath, May 24, 1947 the new building was dedicated to the Lord. Special
services began on Friday night, May 23. Sabbath afternoon the dedicatory
service was presented by the vice-president of the General Conference Elder
W.B. Ochs, basing his remarks on Genesis 28:17,19. The dedicatory prayer
was offered by Elder Rostad of the South Dakota Conference. Albert Eisenman
of Mobridge sang "Bless This House." Elder C.A. Renschler gave a brief
history of the church since its organization. Others attending were Elders
Paul Kemper and H.B. Davis.

The 60th anniversary of the church was held Nov. 2 and 3, 1951. The Friday
night speaker was Elder McKinley. Elder Jere Smith of the Northern Union
presented the Sabbath morning sermon. Afternoon speaker was Professor
Hartman of Union College in Lincoln, Nebraska.

Since then the church has been remodeled with the installation of
wall-to-wall carpeting, upholstered pews and a complete kitchen in the
basement. In the basement a sliding door has been installed which makes it
possible to convert the fellowship room into two separate classrooms. This
was accomplished in 1985.

Twenty-two ministers have served the Bowdle Church: Valentine Lehr, Elders
Goede, Wentland, Wall, E. Oswald, Schwindt, J. Hein, Carl Beck, Sam Reile,
C.A. Renschler, Adam Rudy, Harley Sahander, C.H. Turner, Kenneth Allen, W.
Kurth, Henry Preston, Peter Samograd, J.T. Robinson, F.C. Petty, Arthur
Mitchell, Jerry Moon and J. Clarkson. Pastor Clarkson left in 1984.

The membership includes Bowdle territory with members coming in from the
Java, Eureka, Tolstoy and Roscoe areas. Its "Welcome" mat is out for anyone
wishing to worship with them. A Christian education can be obtained in the
Dakota Academy in Bismarck, ND; Maplewood Academy in Minnesota and Union
College in Lincoln, NE which is just a listing of those close by.

CHURCH OF GOD

The Bowdle Church of God was organized in April 1981, under the leadership
of Rev. Wayne Masser. An old church building (St. Paul American Lutheran
Church) was purchased from Erv's Furniture. The building had been used for
furniture storage several years. The congregation remodeled the interior,
including new carpeting throughout the sanctuary. The ceiling was lowered
and new lighting installed. Upon completion new pews, pulpit furniture,
public address system, piano and organ were installed. The church was
dedicated June 21, 1981.

The Bowdle Church of God has been served by Rev. Wayne Masser, his wife
Joan and sons Bryan and Andy; Rev. Rick Dorr, his wife Jean and Adam and
Nicki and the Rev. Sam Saylor, his wife Penny and sons Brian and Barry.

The church purchased three lots in November 1981 just behind the church
with the intention of building a parsonage. However, in February 1983 a
house was purchased at 3084 8th Avenue to be used as a parsonage.

The Bowdle Church of God is a member of the Church of God with
international headquarters in Cleveland, TN. The Church of God shares the
year 1886 with the city of Bowdle as its beginning, for Aug. 19, 1886, what
is now called the Church of God, was organized as a small group calling
themselves the Christian Union.

Richard G. Spurling, a Baptist minister, spoke on the need for a Christian
Union to be formed that would reassert the intrinsic doctrines of the Bible
and whose ultimate objective would be "to restore primitive Christianity
and bring about the union of all denominations." He was to die a little
over a month later and the leadership of the fledgling church fell on his
son Richard G. Spurling Jr.

Ten years later at Camp Creek, NC in a revival conducted by a layman W.F.
Bryant something happened to change the source of the small church. "The
people earnestly sought God and the interest increased until unexpectedly,
like a cloud from a clear sky, the Holy Ghost began to fall on the honest,
humble, sincere seekers after God, while the meetings were in progress, one
after another fell under the power of God and soon quite a number were
speaking in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance."

The name Church of God was adopted in the General Assembly of 1903. The
Church of God is America's oldest Pentecostal Church and now has churches
in 105 countries with membership well over 1-1/2 million.

APRIL 21, 1927
  The Bowdle Cemetery Association has dug holes preparatory to setting out
about 100 Black Hills spruce trees around the grounds.

REDEEMER LUTHERAN CHURCH

Redeemer Lutheran Church, an affiliate member of the Church of the Lutheran
Confession, was organized in 1962. Following the adoption of the
constitution March 28, the church was formally incorporated with Henry
Giedt, Wilbert Blumhardt, Albert Berg, Norwin Walz, Morris Kurle, John F.
Bieber, Fred M. Eisenbeisz, Robert Kilber and Rayfeld Rieger serving as
members of the first church council. The Reverend Paul G. Albrecht was
called as the first pastor.

Initial services were held in the Bowdle Theater. The first service in the
newly constructed edifice was conducted June 17, 1962. The church structure
included educational facilities and the adjoining parsonage was completed
before the end of the year. Building committee members were Alvin Kurle,
Art Hoffmann, Henry Weisz, Arnold Kiesz, Gordon Kilber, Ferdinand Walz,
Merle Haberer, Fred M. Eisenbeisz, Fred Rieger, Jacob B. Mertz, John F.
Bieber, Melvin Maier, Lester Giedt, Rayfeld Rieger and Wilbert Blumhardt.
Pastor Albrecht served as architect.

        Rev. Paul G. Albrecht   Rev. David Lau

        Rev. Wayne Mielke       Rev. Terrel Kesterson

Redeemer Lutheran Ladies Aid actively assists in the work of the church.
Sunday School and Confirmation Class help provide Christian education
for the church's youth. Educational services include an annual Vacation
Bible School for children, as well as an adult Bible Study Class.

In September 1963 Redeemer Lutheran Church established a cemetery
approximately one mile north of Bowdle on the west side of Highway 47. More
than 20 graves are located there.

In August 1966 Pastor Albrecht requested he be released from his call so he
might retire from full-time pastoral service. Pastor David Lau was called
in September. In 1972 the tenth anniversary of the church was observed.
Reverend Wayne Mielke was called that year. He served this congregation
until 1981. The Reverend Terrel Kesterson is currently the called pastor.

Throughout its quarter century of existence, Redeemer Lutheran Church has
undergone many renovations, repairs, improvements and additions. The most
recent dedicatory offering is the installation of stained glass windows on
the east side of the church proper. This was made possible by efforts of
students from Immanuel Lutheran College and Seminary at Eau Claire,
Wisconsin.

        Stained glass windows adorn Redeemer Lutheran Church

BOWDLE GOSPEL TABERNACLE CHURCH

The Bowdle Gospel Tabernacle was incorporated as an interfaith,
interdenominational church in the state of South Dakota March 4, 1964. The
founder of the church was Raymond Haar. He served as president of the Board
of Directors, Sunday School Superintendent and filled in for services when a
pastor was not available. He served in this capacity until his death in
1979.

Those who helped fill the pastoral position of the Gospel Tabernacle have
been Rev. Sexton, Rev. Loren Sundberg and Rev. Wayne J. Buechler.

The Gospel Tabernacle Church began as a basement church. It was located on
7th Avenue and presently serves as the basement for Andy Grismer's house.
In 1970 the old Methodist Church on 3rd Avenue was purchased by the Gospel
Tabernacle as the new church sanctuary and it remains in that location to
this day.

During 1976 Pastor Wayne J. Buechler and Raymond Haar decided it was
important to reach individuals in other parts of the country and world in
an evangelistical fashion. Therefore, the Wayne J. Buechler Evangelistic
Association was formed as an outreach of the Gospel Tabernacle Church.

        Founder of Gospel Tabernacle Raymond Haar and his wife Helen

        Pastor Wayne J. Buechler, his wife Anita and their son Adam Wayne

Pastor Buechler, his wife Anita and sister Colleen traveled many miles each
year spreading the Gospel of Jesus Christ, conducting Bible Teach
Institutes and establishing interdenominational churches. Twice a year
during May and December the members of the Gospel Tabernacle hosted a
campmeeting which was a special three-day meeting when people from the
various Bible Studies, churches and groups reached through the evangelistic
outreaches of the church were invited to come and fellowship together.

Presently Wayne J. Buechler is helping to start an interdenominational
church in Aberdeen and is helping to supervise the activities of the Gospel
Tabernacle.

JULY 16, 1931--HOW TO KILL YOUR CHURCH
  1. Absent yourself from the Sunday services. The minister will note your
     absence and feel it.
  2. Stay at home whenever it rains on Sunday, or it is too hot or cold.
  3. Never let the minister know he has done you any good.
  4. Take a class in Sunday School and be in your place about three out of
     five times or late the other two.
  5. Attend no church meeting if you have the opportunity of going elsewhere.
  6. If a stranger is near you never hand him a hymn book and let him leave
     the church without handshake.
  7. If you are sick, do not send word to your pastor, but let him find out
     himself. He will probably call about the time you are able to go out and
     spend the day. Then complain about his carelessness in pastoral work.
  8. If times are hard, money scarce, business dull, inform your minister
     that you must give up your subscriptions. You cannot afford to do 
anything
     for the church this year. By the time you have paid for all your
     luxuries you really haven't anything left for the needs of the church.

MARCH 13, 1902
  One quarter section of school land in Bowdle Township was bid up to 
24-1/2 cents on a five-year lease, or nearly $40 a year. Good hay land is
getting valuable it seems.

AUG. 28, 1902
  The No. 4 schoolhouse in Modena Township was struck by lightning last
Tuesday during the electric storm and was badly smashed. The School Board
was thoughtful enough to carry insurance so the loss will be covered.

Country schools were being added to the landscape as the population
increased on the prairies. So by the 1930's they had become a way of life
for the rural family. This carried over into the 1940's but by the late
1950's and 1960's there were fewer and fewer. Today they are a rarity. The
white Country School on east Main Street of Bowdle testifies to that. It
has been restored and the benefactors, Bowdle Historical Society, hope it
will remain a landmark. It was last known as the Leidholt School located
southwest of Bowdle. It is owned and maintained by Bowdle Township and is
used as the township's business meeting and polling place.

        Interior of Country School now Restored.

There were three other schools in this township. The Southeast was also
known as the Blondo School, the Northeast as the Thomas School and the
Northwest as the Lemke-Haupt School. Erma Maier taught in three of those
schools. Marie Schumacher was one of the last teachers in the Southwest white
Country School. These schools educated as many as 80 students per term in
District 9-1/2.

        THOMAS SCHOOL IN 1936. Oakland belonged to Richard Lemke.

Each country school board hired its teachers. The one teacher in each
school was supervised by and responsible to the County Superintendent of
Schools. This official was responsible for the coordination of the more
than 100 schools in the county with the state office of Public Instruction.
The classroom climate was set by the teacher. Many a stalwart citizen today
still remembers his rural school days and the influence of his teachers.

The school ground was an unfenced patch of prairie. Often there was a barn
to house the transportation and always there was a "boy's" and a "girl's."
No time was lost there during Dakota winters, but their use was much
increased when the weather cooperated. The flag pole was the center of
interest on the grounds. Children gave their Pledge of Allegiance as the
first order of the day. The ash heap was always there. Not all schools
provided swings, merry-go-rounds or play equipment but children and
teachers were ingenious and through the Young Citizens League (YCL) and
teacher's endeavors of pie and box socials, carnivals and such, would
provide some of these "fun" things.

        THOMAS SCHOOL STUDENTS IN 1934 Back row: August Thomas, Joe
        Heilman, Teacher Erma Lemke. Middle: Walter Thomas, Magdelina
        Heilman, Cecelia Heintz, Pius Heilman. Front: Lenora Barth, Esther
        Barth, Virginia Heilman, Nickolas Heintz.

Steps would lead to a landing that opened into the entryway. One side of
the entry was the coal bin. The pass-through hall could only be used in
good weather to hang wraps or set lunch pails. Upon entering the school
room the most important piece of equipment was the stove. Often this was a
large jacketed affair in a central location. It took a special knowhow to
get favorable service. Often a considerable part of the day was spent with
students wearing coats and overshoes, sitting near the stove. If the same
clothing was used for barnyard chores, a difficult climate was endured. What
an improvement when the Heatrola replaced the stove! Later fuel burners
became common. Fires could not only be banked, but set for weekends.
Across the back of the room would be a shelf with coat hooks underneath.
Girls wraps were hung on one side, boys on the other.

APRIL 18, 1929
  The Roosevelt Y.C.L. at Bowdle N.W. rural school elected the following
officers for the last six-weeks period of the school year: Edwin Rieger,
pres.; Harold Haupt, vice-pres.; Vina Rieger, sec.; Edna Hoffman reporter;
Otto Buechler, treas.

NOV. 13, 1930
  There will be a program and box social at the Buechler School three miles
west and three miles north of Bowdle Nov. 25. Miss Lucille Hildebrandt,
teacher.

Furniture consisted of desks of various sizes. When the enrollment was in
the 20's there was very little extra space. Some of the desks were designed
for two students. There was a teacher's desk and chair. Often a few shelves
underneath the chimney held all the supplies like chalk, paper, sweeping
compound, etc. Sometimes there was a "library" (book shelves) to hold
storybooks. Some schools might have a piano or organ, sandbox, reading
table or little red chairs. There was always a recitation bench. Sometimes
it had no backrest. It was placed in front of the teacher's desk and
children would be called for class recitations.

A common waterpail and dipper, with a wash basin, was placed on a bench or
table at the rear. Children would bring their own water supply or it was
fetched from the nearest neighbor. Hot fall days were long without a drink.

A lot of activity went on in the one-room school. Often there were eight
grades with one to five students in each. After the flag salute there would
be opening exercises with singing and children giving "newsy" items. The
basic subjects of reading and arithmetic were covered before lunch with
possibly spelling and penmanship. Everyone looked forward to recess breaks
and their dinner pail lunch at noon. Often lunches were consumed in a hurry
so that the fun games could be continued. A congenial teacher was a part of
all activity and fostered the school "family" feeling.

JULY 25, 1918
  President Johnson of Northern Normal at Aberdeen has announced that Miss
Agnes Schlachter of Bowdle, 1st prize winner of $50 offered by M. Plin
Beebe for the high school senior receiving the highest marks for the year.

In the afternoon history and geography were taught as separate subjects
until social studies replaced them. There was also language which
encompassed composition, poetry, diagramming and English. Science, health
and safety were taught and 7th and 8th graders completed art plates as a
graduation requirement. All 8th graders wrote the state exams at some
designated location in order to graduate.

The YCL meeting was a once-a-week "fun" thing. Here children were guided as
they planned their extra-curricular activities, parties and fund raisers,
conducted meetings, levied self-assessments and dealt with the many
problems in developing leadership, initiative and goal setting.

Children and teachers usually walked or rode horseback to and from school.
This could be up to 10 miles for teachers and up to five miles for
children. There was enough necessary activity in their lives that no
physical education was ever talked about!

MARCH 2, 1950
  The Bowdle Township School, Blondo School, burned to the ground. Children
from the school, which was taught by Gideon Schuh, will complete their
school year in the Bowdle City School.

        SPRING LAKE SCHOOL ABOUT 1900

COUNTRY TEACHERS

There was a little elderly lady, Hortense Insley, who taught north of town.
She would get her classes so organized that when the rural mail carrier made
his run past the school Friday afternoon, she was waiting to "catch" a ride
down to Highway 12 (six miles) and proceed to hitchhike on into
Aberdeen-sometimes carrying a dozen eggs because they were cheaper from the
farmer.

In the spring we would take hikes and when it was an unusually warm
afternoon, we'd end up wading in the country ponds. When the overgrown boys
would beg to go over the hill to the bachelor's farm and spend the
afternoon using his boxing gloves, that excursion ended in the classroom
with the bad boy standing by his desk (two hours) until dismissal.

I accepted a position in a rural school over eight miles from the nearest
town out on the lonely prairie. Walking distance housing was too crowded to
accommodate me. Snows came early that year and another teacher's borrowed
car couldn't navigate passage anymore. The farmer/landlord rented the use
of his horse, providing no saddle was used, because it would be "too hard
on the horse." This resulted in the teacher moving into the one-room
school. Snow piled up with storm after storm. Often the students couldn't
get there. One night, when horses sought shelter beside the school, the
teacher was in a real scare, until one of the horses whinnied. As spring
came on, children still were not able to attend regularly. There were long
weekends of solitude. More white stuff piled up as Easter came on. The
teacher packed a small case and set out for the town of Roscoe to spend
Easter at home. After walking the 8-1/2 miles she arrived just in time to
"catch" the train to Bowdle. It had been delayed about 12 hours due to the
unusually high drifts.

At one of the rural schools on a busy road with a very capable teacher,
Ruth Eder in charge, a knock was heard at the door soon after school was
called. The trucker standing there wanted to know how he could be of
assistance because the upside down flag waving out there on the pole was a
distress signal. The puzzled teacher glanced about and the mystery was soon
solved as two of the older children redfaced and sheepishly got up and
moved out to right things. They had been in such a hurry for a few moments
of play before school they hadn't noticed the flag. This incident shows the
concern of all for the welfare of children and teacher in the country
school.

Another serious young man, Henry Wederhoft, who carried on a full-time
farming operation, walked 8 miles to get to his school, using a lantern in
the darkness. High snowdrifts prevented his horse and buggy passage. His
wife substituted for him during his busy season. "Teaching school" so
impressed the elder daughter, now Mrs. Rayfeld Rieger, that in 1948 she was
employed as a teacher in her local district after 12 weeks training in
summer school. Teachers of this era were known as six-weeks wonders. They
were issued permits to teach in rural schools to alleviate the teacher
shortage at that time. They were, however, required to pass strict
competency tests in each subject they would teach. These were administered
by the State Department of Instruction.

Public School . . .

Compiled by Beulah Schumacher and Elaine Geier.

Bowdle School history is linked closely with that of the city, both
beginning in 1886. The old stagecoach trail hit Bowdle before its existence
about where the present schoolhouse stands. The first term of school was
held in the second story of the first business place constructed. This
multi-purpose room was also used for Sunday School and court reflecting the
early settlers' respect for education, religion and justice.

Increased enrollment necessitated the construction of a two-story frame
building on the present site in 1888. A southeast wing was added in 1908.
No school activities could be held at night because of inadequate lighting.
A windmill provided water and there were outdoor privies. Ruth Boyd and
Grace Baker were the first graduates from the accredited four-year high
school in 1912.

Crowded conditions and the danger of fire in the old building caused public
support for a new brick building on the same location. School bonds for
$40,000 were issued and construction completed in 1919. During construction
school was held in the Opera House and Masonic Hall. This same year the
Kellie Common School District deeded Block 29, the location of the school
building, plus four rural schools to the Bowdle Independent School District
No. 9. A rural-city controversy led to a lawsuit which was appealed to the
South Dakota Supreme Court. Following legal action the district was divided
into Common School District 9-1/2 and the Independent District of the city
of Bowdle in 1932.

An addition for a gymnasium was voted on the second time and approved in
1936. Bonds were issued for $9,000 which, added to federal funds, helped
provide local jobs on this project completed in 1938.

In 1959 the Bowdle School District went through reorganization, absorbing
neighboring districts and adding buses. Although two buses were operated in
1920-1921, bad roads caused this service to be discontinued.  In 1985 six 
buses were available.

A new grade school, vocational agriculture shop, bus housing and land for
an athletic field were secured through a $260,000 bond issue in 1960. The
concrete block building, housing the grades, joined the 1919 school on the
south, while the shop was built on the north.

        Bowdle School built in 1919 and demolished in 1977.

        1985 Bowdle Elementary

        1985 Bowdle High School

        1985 Bowdle Gymnasium

Due to the deterioration of the east wall of the high school, a $750,000
bond issue was passed in 1976 to construct a new high school, joining the
grade school on the east. This modern facility includes classrooms,
offices, library, stage and spacious gym seating 1200.

DEC. 7, 1933
  Hilda Jarvis was elected to the honor of the first "Queen of the
Cossacks." It was held before the game between Glenham and Bowdle. Din and
Joey Muller, co-captains, crowned the queen. Attendants of the queen were
Violet Thurn, Cora Haring, Pearl Gruenhagen, Martha Blumhardt, Emma Sippert
and Goldie Helmer.

DEC. 13, 1951
  With court procedure the Bowdle High School discarded its old nickname
for its athletic club and took on the name "Bobcats." After some 30 or more
years, the student body decided to discard the name "Cossacks," for
something with more of clean fight than the name of the Russian soldier. A
vote of 82-6.

Long-term school board members include: J.K. Kurle (15 years), F.G. Grosz
(17 years), A.C. Merkel (20 years), Alvin Bauer (18 years) and Mike Mitzel
(18 years). Wilmer Schaible served 26 years as clerk. Emil Bonen retired
after serving 17 years as custodian.

High school enrollment varied from 32 with three teachers in 1919-1920 to a
peak at 141 in 1940-1941 with five on the faculty. The largest class
consisting of 34 students graduated in 1943. The 1985 enrollment was 56
with 11 teachers.

Changing with the times curriculum offerings included home economics,
industrial arts, agriculture, foreign languages and computers.

Athletics, music, publications, plays and other extra-curricular activities
continue to challenge BHS students.

Bowdle defeated Roscoe 16-14 to win the first District Basketball
Championship in 1929. In 1973 the Bobcats defeated Eureka 66-61 in a
thrilling Regional triumph advancing to place fifth in the State "B"
Tourney.

Eleven-man football was introduced by Ken Greeno as coach with the first
home game in November 1933. Bowdle and Java had cooperative football for
two seasons, 1983 and 1984.

Top track records are prominently displayed in the gymnasium lobby. Girls
athletics received a boost with track being introduced in 1971 and
out-of-town basketball games. The first Yellowstone Trail Conference
Tournament was won by the girls in 1975.

School papers have been published with Bowdlette becoming Bobcat Pride. The
Cossack annual, first published by the class of 1936, is now the Bobcat.

Vocal and instrumental music have continued to be offered. Theo Grosz, who
played for the school dedication in 1919, provided gratis accompaniment.
Crowded trophy cases in the gym lobby attest to special honors in
athletics, music and other areas.

Education and the world show rapid change from early days when there were
no TV's, ballpoint pens, hot lunches and computers. Skip day and the prom
have been replaced with a flight to Washington, D.C. -- the objective of
providing students with basic skills and knowledge remains.

During the 73 years (1912-1985) that the four-year high school has been in
existence, the following superintendents served:

AUG. 25, 1893
  Seventy-eight applications have been made for
the position of teacher in the primary department of
the Bowdle Public School.

APRIL 21, 1904
  Professor J.E. Johnson just elected principal of the Bowdle School at a
salary of $75 per month.

SEPT. 11, 1893
  The Bowdle Public Schools opens Sept. 11, with G.A. O'Reilly, present
Deputy Register of Deeds, as principal.

AUG. 10, 1905
  E.J. Edward resigned the position as treasurer of School Board and John
Rhodes was appointed in his place.

MARCH 1, 1906
  Bowdle School will hold its first Declamatory Contest. An engraved solid
silver medal will be given to the winner. (Alice Robinson was the winner.)

FEB. 8, 1906
  Bowdle Public School report ending Feb. 2, 1906 total enrollment was 138.

JAN. 7, 1971
  School will begin Kindergarten with Venoy Kurle as instructor. The St.
John's Lutheran Church educational wing will be used for the classroom.

THE WAY IT WAS . . .

Fire Drill, Fire Drill, the Bell is Ringing! Remember two giant open slides
extending from the second story of the brick high school? Four boys eagerly
volunteer as "catchers" and slide down first. Look from the open door! It's
a long way down and the slide is shining silver. Shrieks of fear, but no
hesitation and no exceptions. Down you shoot hoping the boys stop your
slide for life. If they miss, it's skin and bruises. Thrills and spills!
Descending modestly was difficult in the days of the dresses. Later, just
to show off, you could climb up on the outside and go scooting down again.
Did the teachers escape? No by using the slides. Much too hazardous. Later
an enclosed circular slide, like a giant caterpillar, shot down the
students landing often on their backs. How ho-hum to simply march out today!

                        Beulah [Erbe] Schumacher

Bowdle High in the thirties had only a closet-like library, no windows, no
table, no chairs -- but a few shelves of books and a large ladder leading
to a closed skylight. Ruth Feiock, Cora Haring and Violet Thurn were in the
library one day during study period. Cora and Violet were curious to see
what the roof of the school looked like. If they climbed up the ladder and
raised the trapdoor, they would find out. Ruth consented to guard the door,
holding the knob firmly. The harder she pulled on the door on the inside,
the harder was the pull on the outside. Finally the door was forced open,
overpowering Ruth's strength. There stood Principal Jerry Moriarity who
asked, "Ruth, what are you doing?" She replied, "I'm holding the door shut,"
just as Cora and Violet came scrambling down the ladder. Staying after
school was the punishment. Outside was a stormy blizzard and Christ Feiock
had come from the farm to pick up his kids. Ruth got to go home. When were
Cora and Violet dismissed? Ruth doesn't remember. Do they?

                        Ruth [Feiock] Eder

Note passing was forbidden. If intercepted, the note was read before the
class unless it was hurriedly swallowed. Yuck! Paper airplanes with pins
attached became deadly darts. Look before sitting to avoid a possible tack.
Discipline was swift and harsh under these circumstances. In grade four
Adeline Schumacher and Irene Kraft were caught whispering -- banished to
the cloak room to receive a few swats with the rubber hose -- humiliated and
fearful they remembered the rules. Eventually the hose was found cut to
pieces and not replaced. An upper grade teacher laid a cow's tail across
his desk with a sobering effect. Spitballs were another popular pastime.

Peanut showers, as well as, orange and apple rolls were a welcome break in
the strict routine. Planned to surprise the teacher, peanuts came flying in
all directions -- then a scramble to gather most for a quick lunch. One
memorable day walnuts were added to the barrage, causing the teacher to
rush crying from the room. The superintendent lectured and that was the end
of peanut showers.

                        Adeline [Schumacher] Miller

Sixty-five years ago some original thinker created this bit of nonsense
based on the names of four teachers. "If Miss IKE (domestic science)
squeezed a LEMON, would she HOLLER and TALLET?"

                        Arlo Stroup

I remember Halloween night kids put a horsedrawn wagon on the schoolhouse
roof. They also stuffed a pair of men's long underwear and flew it from the
flagpole.

                        Fern Bieber

The football trip to Faulkton in 1940! The football players crowded into
Edward (Eddie) Bentz's 1931 Chevy, which often produced a cloud of smoke
due to excess use of oil. As they cruised down the road some of the players
decided to smoke -- breaking the rule. That day in the locker room Coach
Stahl remarked, "Bentz, your car is really using a lot of oil. Why the
smoke even rolls out of the windows."

                        Edward [Eddie] Bentz

"Be willing to stand alone for frequently the crowd is wrong.

                        Advice on 1932 Report Card

Every student who ever attended Bowdle Grade School should remember the
beautiful willow tree at the north side of the playground. It was really
seven trees. It was a sad day when the willow had to die for the sake of a
new building. It was the best playground equipment this school has ever had.

                        Marjorie Buechler

In the early days townspeople gathered at popular Spring Lake to mark the
closing of the school year with a picnic. That came to an end when people
gathered in cliques and wouldn't share the food. Some enterprising
youngsters started early to walk around the lake. At day's end they came
dragging back finding the hike longer and more exhausting than anticipated.
The high point was the special treat furnished by First State Bank with
Henry Gross dipping free ice cream cones.

During the thirties finances were lacking due to drouth and depression with
wheat down to 25 cents a bushel. Farms were sold for taxes. In 1934-1935
lowest paid teacher received $62.50 a month, the superintendent $104 and
the janitor $75.

People had fund raisers for playground equipment. A child was hurt and the
superintendent decreed the equipment removed. One little first grader was
asked, "What do you do at recess and noon when there's nothing to play
with?" -- the teeter-totters, hand-walker and swings were all gone. Her
reply was, "The boys chase the girls until they are tired ... then the
girls chase the boys."

There was some good superintendents -- such as Oscar Olson, who had worked
so hard to get his education, he could not understand the children's lack
of appreciation for their opportunities. Lloyd Lane, who held the position
eight years stated that he saw the number of graduates going to college
increase tremendously during that time. Eric and Lorraine Holscher inspired
the students to greater scholastic achievements as well as increasing the
appreciation of music. Many students won honors at the music contests.

Severe winter weather during pre-bus days meant opening the homes in town
to farm students overnight. No school, but the excitement of a winter
blizzard was too great to stay indoors. Great fun! High school boys helped
rescue livestock when they strayed during the storm. During World War II
they helped with the harvest when farm laborers were few.

                        Julia Senn

On a warm spring day the driver's education class of sophomores Mark
Bieber, Roger Wolff, Dean Schumacher and Donald Kurle with instructor Dale
Ziegler drove northwest of Bowdle. They decided to take a section line with
Don Kurle driving. It had started to thaw. We knew we were in trouble when
the car went fishtailing down a muddy road. Halfway down at 30 mph they
were losing power. Kurle said, "I'll put the hammer down." Mr. Ziegler
said, "I Don't think so." Climbing the next hill the fishtailing became
worse. Just as they approached the crest a tractor and loader appeared in
the center of the road. Kurle hit the brakes and cried, "I can't hold her
Mr. Ziegler." He urged, "Well, do something like corrective steering." But
it was no use. The car lurched over on its side into the ditch. Steam
rolled out and panic set in. As the steam cleared, Mark's form became
visible suspended from a safety belt. Mr. Ziegler was EXCITED! Mark pressed
the belt release and fell, crushing Roger Wolff. Then reason was restored
and we crawled out topside.

The farmer asked if we were okay. We answered we were, although we were
plenty shook up. The farmer got a chain, righted the car and pulled us half
a mile to the gravel road. "Let's finish the drive so we can all have our
turn," we said. Mr. Ziegler replied, "No way!" and chauffeured us back to
the last half of Mr. Wooledge's biology class.

                        Dean N. Schumacher, Class of 1968

Water, Water Everywhere!!! Was this the year the elementary building had a
leaky roof??? The water poured in a stream through a crack right above the
classroom door. Emil Bonen nailed a large piece of plastic sheeting over
the door so we could at least walk in and out without an umbrella.

Of course watching the construction of the new building was exciting since
it occurred right next to the fourth grade room. I felt right in the middle
of the action from caterpillars to finishing work. Elodie Schmierer and I
were the best sidewalk engineers checking progress nightly.

Winter of '77 ... Would we have school or not?? Keeping the children in
overnight ... which amounted to two nights of arrangements of who is
staying where ... quite a memorable experience!

                        Janice Schock

In 1976-1977 we had evacuation drills for the students and teachers when
the east wall of the old school was being supported by beams. There were
times when we could see the wall shake. These drills were held in case the
wall ever gave out during school.

                        Mrs. Tim Dewald

The trend is "Back to the Basics" now keeping the best of the past. No
attempt has been made to list achievements of individuals, but their lives
following BHS testify to the success of their training. More than half of
the graduates have gone on to college, while others are a credit to their
home community. May the future of Bowdle High School be as bright as the
past has been productive.

                        Beulah [Erbe] Schumacher

SPRING LAKE PICNICS

[Taken from May 20, 1926 Bowdle Pioneer]

SCHOOL PICNIC HUGE SUCCESS -- The picnic was at Spring Lake by the Bowdle
Commercial Club for the Bowdle Schools, over 500 being in attendance. Had a
baseball game and other races with prizes given. A table 48 feet long and
3 feet wide was spread with food, 30 gallons of ice cream, 1500 ice cream

For a period of time these picnics were held annually at Spring Lake.)

BOWDLE P.T.A.

In the early fifties the Band Parents Club was formed with the main thrust
being to purchase band uniforms. Their purpose was to also assist in
lending moral support for band, to assist in fundraising activities and to
cooperate with the school officials in creating a successful instrumental
program. In 1954 their dreams of obtaining uniforms came true and Bowdle
School Band marched off in style.

In 1958 the Band Parents Club evolved into the Parent Teachers Association
as members felt the need for a broader involvement with the school. One of
the primary objectives was to bring into closer relation the home and the
school, that parents and teachers might cooperate intelligently in the
training of the child.

The organization remained active during the sixties promoting such
activities as: eye, ear and speech clinics, get-acquainted suppers, speakers
and films on education and children, the senior tea, immunization clinics
and fun nights to raise money.

One of the outstanding fundraising nights brought the Aberdeen Elks Chorus
to perform for a sell-out crowd. The organization also purchased books for
the library, playground equipment, donations to improve the teacher's
lounge, Harvey Dunn prints for study hall and the Christmas trees for grade
and high school.

In 1968 the organization began awarding a $75 scholarship to a deserving
senior. Later this was changed to two $50 scholarships, one to a student
attending a vocational school and one to a student attending a four-year
college.

Due to waning interest the group decided in the spring 1968 to change to
the Parent Teachers Organization, ending state affiliation. Finally in 1972
the organization gave up the fight and disbanded completely.

FUTURE FARMERS OF AMERICA

The Bowdle Future Farmers of America (FFA) and Vocational Agriculture found
its beginning during the 1936-1937 school year with Earl E. Julson as
advisor. Bowdle was the first school to offer such a course in Edmunds
County. Areas taught were Animal Husbandry, Crops and Soils.

Judging livestock was an integral part of early FFA as several farmers were
visited in the first year for judging contests. Many worthwhile activities
were undertaken by the 38 members of the new organization.

The first officers were president, Milton Buechler; vice-president, Emil
Bieber; treasurer, Robert Gross; secretary, Ervin Bader and reporter, Gordon
Loebs.

The second year Farm Management was added to the Vocational Agriculture
curriculum.

1938-1941: The FFA and Vocational Agriculture came under the guidance of
Vivian M. Chitwood the fall of 1938. He remained until the spring of 1941.

Delegates attending the South Dakota State FFA Convention in 1940 were Ted
Schick, Herbert Buechler, Edward Dewald, Vincent Bachman, Emil Bollinger
and Rayfeld Rieger. Several returned with awards for judging livestock and
seeds. The first Father-Son Party (a forerunner of the present
Parent-Member Banquet) was held in 1940.

Some activities for 1940-1941 included candy sales at athletic events,
Father-Son Party, State and District Contests, Chapter Basketball Team and
raffling a turkey and a duck.

1941-1942: In the fall Lawrence Kehrwald took the helm. The close of the
year brought the end of the program in Bowdle for 37 years, due to the war
effort and a shortage of vocational agriculture instructors.

1979-1980: In May 1979 the Bowdle School District 22-1 hired Gary Bachman
as Vocational Agriculture instructor and once again offered Vo-Ag and FFA.
The charter officers of the new chapter were president, Rod Moser;
vice-president, David Stephan; secretary, Lowell Perman; treasurer, Wade
Eisenbeisz; sentinel, Todd Bachman and reporter, Paul Knecht.

During the year the chapter celebrated FFA Week with a tractorcade and the
first local Businessman's Breakfast. At the State FFA Convention the
chapter was granted its charter and also placed in the top 15 (Bronze
rating) in the following areas: National Chapter Award, Chapter Safety
Award, Building Our American Communities and Triple Crown Award.

1980-1981: The first Bowdle Judging School and Contest was held in the fall.
Lowell Perman placed fifth in South Dakota in Ag Salesmanship and Paul
Knecht was elected District VI Reporter. The FFA purchased a Radio Shack
TRS-80 Model III Computer. At the State Convention Lauren Oster placed 11th
in Crops while Tim Stotz placed 16th out of 212 individuals. Stotz, Oster
and Mike Weiszhaar placed 7th of 72 in Crops Team competition.

1981-1982: The Bowdle FFA placed first at the South Dakota State Fair in
Chapter Booth competition. The display, depicting South Dakota Agricultural
Products, was shown at the National FFA Convention in Kansas City,
Missouri. At the Leadership Contest Ron Doerr was elected District VI
Reporter and Paul Knecht won the Extemporaneous Speaking Contest. Knecht
later placed 3rd in the state.

The Bowdle FFA built two sets of bleachers to be used at the football field
and Meakins Park ball park. The group built a 12 ft. by 8 ft. solar panel
which was available for public use as a demonstration on solar heat. In
cooperation with the Bowdle Mothers' Club the FFA built an elevated
playhouse at Meakins Park.

At the State Convention in Brookings the local chapter was awarded Silver
ratings in the Building Our American Communities, National Chapter Safety
and National Chapter Award areas. Paul Knecht was elected State Treasurer.
During the summer the chapter held an exchange with the Coon Rapids, Iowa
chapter. The event was later featured in the National Future Farmer
Magazine.

1982-1983: The Bowdle FFA started the school year with a bang, winning the
team title at the Northeast Area Range Judging Contest. Mike Geier took
first overall, Lauren Oster 4th, Jami Rohrbach 10th and Tim Heilman 12th.
These four students and advisor Gary Bachman attended the National Range
Judging Contest in May at Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. In December an Adult
Welding Course was implemented with 11 members.

The State Convention again brought honor to the Bowdle FFA. It placed 12th
in Building Our American Communities (Silver, ) 13th in National Chapter
Award Program /Bronze,) 9th in National Chapter Safety Program (Silver) and
2nd in Chapter Scrapbook competition. Tim Heilman took first place in the
Home and Farmstead Improvement Efficiency Award area.

Gary Bachman resigned effective at the end of the school term

1983-1984: Miss Julie Leier became the Vocational Agriculture instructor.
Tim Heilman was awarded a Bronze award at the Regional level for his Home
and Farmstead Improvement projects. The FFA sold fruit for the first time.

At the State Convention the chapter placed first in the Scrapbook Contest.
Paul Knecht became involved in the FFA's Work Experience Abroad Program and
spent three months in a farming community in Japan.

1984-1985: John Rist was hired as Vocational Agriculture instructor and FFA
Advisor. Under his direction the FFA constructed a dugout at the softball
field in Meakins Park with funds donated by the Joe Mueller family and a
long jump runway on the school grounds. Geri Knecht placed second in the
District VI FFA Job Interview Contest and later took second in the State
Contest.

Special Recognition: Over the years the Bowdle FFA has had several highly
honored members and friends. They include: State Farmer Degree recipients
Paul Knecht and Wade Eisenbeisz in 1982, Ron Doerr 1983 and Tim Heilman
1984.

Honorary Chapter Farmers named were Calvin Sandmeier 1980, David Karst
1981, Jay Ausland 1982, Larry Gauer 1983, Blake Eisenbeisz 1984 and Gary
Bachman and Stan Zimmer 1985.

Outstanding Business Supporters include J. Kurle & Sons 1983 and Bowdle
Livestock Sales Company Inc. 1984.

An Outstanding Alumni Member Award was started in 1984 and presented to
David Karst.

FUTURE HOMEMAKERS OF AMERICA

As early as 1920 high school home economics students belonged to home
economics clubs. The clubs were sponsored by adult groups who were
interested in home economics education.

In May 1945 four representatives from South Dakota attended the regional
meeting of the National Organization of High School Home Economics Clubs
held at the University of Minnesota. In December 1946 South Dakota received
its state association charter from the national organization.

In 1983 the Bowdle High School implemented a vocational home economics
program after over a twenty-year void of offering home economics. In 1984
eight home economics students chose to affiliate with the national
organization, Future Homemakers of America (FHA.)

A pizza party was held after a girls basketball game to encourage
membership with National FHA Officer Trudy Rausch of Hoven as a guest.

Students attended the regional meeting in Hoven at which three students
gave presentations called Action Activity events. FHA members helped the
FFA members with the spook house at the Halloween Party sponsored by the
Bowdle Mothers' Club.

National Family Week was celebrated by making posters for downtown
businesses and holding a family potluck.

The excitement of the Christmas season was enhanced by Secret Santas who
did special favors and gave little gifts to a number of surprised faculty
and students.

The FHA served supper to the FFA members and after each group held their
business meetings, they joined together in a game of volleyball.

Vocational Education Week was celebrated with Singing Valentines. Valentine
wishes were sent by phone and sung by FHA members and every student in the
school received a valentine from the chapter.

St. Patrick's Day students visited people in the Prairie View Housing Inc.
units and residents at the Bowdle Nursing Home. FHA members and residents
joined together in song.

Attending the state meeting at Sioux Falls was a year end highlight for
many of the students. The dynamic speakers and excitement of being with
over 1100 other FHA members was contagious and an exuberant group returned
to Bowdle to share with other members the ideas they had learned from other
chapters across the state.
