        Chris Anderson, Doris Heilman. Home Economics instructor and FHA
        Advisor was Kay Wolff.

HAPPINESS? IT'S AT BOWDLE First Time To The State B

The 1973 Bowdle Basketball Team will forever live in the memories and
hearts of the Bowdle Community when this group of young men upset the
Eureka Trojans at regional play in Aberdeen March 1-3, capturing honors and
representing Region 2 at the State "B" Basketball Tournament in Sioux Falls
the following week.

        COACH TERRY JORDRE

Coach Terry Jordre was confident of his Bobcats as he told them, "Do not
consider yourself weaker than Eureka (Eureka was ranked fourth and Bowdle
l9th in the final AP poll) so don't slow down and do anything special. Play
your game as you always do."

This advice was taken by the team who had been coached by this coach during
their basketball career at Bowdle High. Coach Jordre depended heavily on
Ron Stotz, a 5-11 senior, for his average 20 points per game, his quickness
and sharp shooting; but pointed out that the contribution of his other
players was also vital to the victory.

Kevin Schlepp, a 6-0 junior guard, averaged 16 points per game. Mike
Heilman, a 6-4 junior and leading rebounder, averaged 9 points. Senior Lyle
Perman, a 5-11 forward, averaged 10 points and senior guard Steven Giedt,
5-8, averaged 8 points. Senior reserves were Owen Schumacher, Ken Schuh and
Kim Jahraus.

In 1972 the Bobcats compiled a 20-5 record and in 1973 a 24- 2 season
record had the Bobcats losing to Bristol by one point and the second loss
was to Java by three in first round play of the Yellowstone Trail
Conference Tournament.

The excitement and anticipation of the coming victory with the minutes and
seconds ticking away was evident as the Bobcats stole the ball, scored and
fouled the Eureka Trojans to upset them and lose their concentration. The
Bowdle booster fans chanted, "We're No. 1," as the opposing banner,
claiming they were No. 1, was removed and the Bobcats proved that they
indeed were No. 1.

Experience and balance were the key to Bowdle's success along with teamwork
and perseverance. The running Bobcat team won Districts in 1971 and 1972,
but each year was eliminated by Eureka, definitely the toughest team to
beat.

The town of Bowdle was buzzing over the victory and plans were underway for
the trip to Sioux Falls. Superintendent Carl Ochsner and Principal Jim
Anderson were at the school early to make plans for the distribution of
tickets. Mr. Ochsner stated, "It is a pleasant job!"

Cheerleaders Kay Jahraus, Linda Rieger, Bobbi Nies, Cindy Lemke and Margie
Mittleider led their cheering clan and spent a busy week planning for the
event, making posters, practicing cheers and brushing up on new routines.

Playing on the large arena floor, plus the excitement and getting into
foul trouble all added to their first defeat against Parker 64-44, when the
Bobcats played their first game of the tournament. However the Bobcats were
not about to give up and came back with victories over Woonsocket 62 - 60
and upsetting Bennett County 68-60. Coach Terry Jordre, with his assistant
Jim Larson, along with his weary, but happy team, accepted the trophy and
medals proudly.

A welcoming committee met the players and coaches for a homecoming
celebration at the school gym. The players received congratulations from
their hometown fans, former athletes and alumni.

The year 1973 was indeed a good basketball season for Bowdle, but our
Bobcats came back the next year (minus the seniors) and again had the taste
of victory so close when they met Leola in regional play, but had to take
second place when the Leola Pirates claimed the victory. Some ... day, some
... day the Bobcats will rally again and make this trip to the State
Basketball Tournament.

        RON STOTZ

Ron Stotz, a regular player for the Bobcats for four years, was placed on
the All-State Tournament Class "B" Team, the only player to hold this honor
at Bowdle High. Ron averaged 20.3 points a game. During his senior year he
clipped along at 49% (248-507) from the field and 72% (92-128) from the
line. During his career he scored 1, 767 points, grabbed 919 rebounds, 291
his senior year and 296 his junior year.

Ron also holds the school's scoring record of 43 points when Bowdle
defeated Cresbard in 1973. Previous record holder was David Karst, who
scored 40 points Jan. 25, 1966 against the Roscoe Hornets.

        BERT LEIDHOLT

One of the few Bowdle athletes who gained national notoriety was Bert
Leidholt. He held the national record for most tackles per game in six-man
football in 1954. Leidholt also set school records in the high hurdles
:15.2 and the high jump 5 ft. 9 in. He set the two records at the state
track meet while placing second in both events. Leidholt went to Northern
State Teachers College where he was a starter for the Wolves football team
and is the 1985 Minot (ND) State College football coach.

throw while placing third in the event.

SCHOOL BUS DRIVERS ARE SPECIAL LOT By Dorreen Rosevold

There is a special place in heaven for school bus drivers. It is a place
where no one under 18 years of age may enter. It is a place where kicking
the back of someone else's chair can bring about the death penalty. There
will be no shouting allowed in the school bus driver's heaven and giggling
will be permitted only between the hours of 11 a.m. and noon.

The smell of wet mittens and snowboots will be canned in an aerosol form so
that, under the rare circumstances that a former school bus driver should
become lonesome for it, it can be released under his authority only. The
heaven-resident bus driver will also be blasted with warm wind at every
5-minute interval to balance the cold air he withstood every time he opened
the school bus door as a mortal.

In school bus driver's heaven, not one of the buildings, nor anything
contained within them, will be painted any shade of yellow. Even the sun
itself will be pink so as to let the residents relax at leisure.

The furniture will be upholstered in natural fabrics throughout school bus
driver's heaven. Vinyl -- especially drab brown with a little cotton
batting sticking out of a cracked surface -- will bring about the wrath of
God.

The roads in their heaven will be maintained to perfection. There will be
no potholes in which a wide-bodied aircraft could fall into. There will be
none of that mud that makes ruts deep enough to change the surface of
relief maps. The kind of ruts that tickle the underbelly of the school bus,
but don't "tickle" the driver very much will be nonexistent.

There will be no ice in school bus driver's heaven. Not on the roads
anyway. Perhaps there will be some in the refrigerator for drinks when the
school bus drivers get together to talk about the first time one of their
passengers got bus sick or about the time of the great blizzard and they
were stranded with 40 children and only one Hershey bar.

There will not be any activity scheduled before 10 a.m. or after 6 p.m. in
school bus driver's heaven. School bus drivers will never have to go out in
the dark, never have to stop at railroad crossings, never have to scrape
bubble gum off any surface, never be compelled to decipher the dirty words
written on the ceiling of the bus before they wash them off.

There just has to be a special place in heaven for school bus drivers.
Those special people who can break up a fight in the back of the bus just
by glaring into the rear view mirror. Those chosen few who can tolerate the
blare of the two-way radios, the tape players and the high-pitched squeals
of junior high school boys whose voices are changing, behind them for at
least three hours a day without losing control and pulling open the
emergency exit door.

Those special school bus drivers that see a little bit of everything
deserve a peaceful everlasting. Especially after seeing nearly every mother
in the school district waving them on when the kids aren't riding --
wearing only her flannel nightgown and her husband's cowboy boots. Seeing
sleepy-eyed first graders at 7:15 a.m. trying to crawl up the bus steps
without opening their eyes, while wearing big boots, a snowmobile suit and
holding a piece of toast. Seeing the house lights come on when the bus
turns into the driveway and then having to watch the commotion through the
living room window as mothers brush hair, wash faces, clean teeth and tie
up the lunch money all with the same washcloth.

Yes, I am sure God looks down at 7:00 every school day morning, sees the
school bus drivers crawl into the buses and head out in caravans and He
says, "It is good. I shall go to prepare a place for them."

        Arthur Hoffmann, Dr. Berzins and Fred Rieger exchanging "fishy
        stories" in 1955.

Sports and Recreation . . .

Compiled by Victor Schlepp and Alvin Bauer

JUNE 16, 1887 BOWDLE PIONEER By Fred Bowman

Our baseball club is winning honors thick and fast. They have the scalps of
a number of clubs dangling from their bats, and on the lookout for more
victims. They have sent challenges far and near in the territory, and don't
meet with many to accept. The Groton and Frederick clubs were to meet them,
but got scared out.

The Aberdeen club has been considering the propriety of meeting them for
sometime and finally agreed.

Great interest is manifest over this game here, as the Aberdeen club is
said to be of good stuff.

Last Saturday the Bowdle club played the Theodore nine defeating them by a
score of 46-16. The reason of the large score received by the Theodore boys
was owing to the absence of pitcher Green, who is above the ordinary in his
line. Our boys used them well, provided supper for them at the Dumont and
sent them home as happy as they could be under their defeat.

Members were: A. LeClaire, captain; E.G. Green, pitcher; L.E. Amerpohl,
catcher; Charles Dahl, 1st base, H.D. Baillet, 2nd base; W.W. Vantine, 3rd
base; A.F. LeClaire, shortstop; C.R. DeWoody, left field; H.E. Austin,
right field; Thomas Blair, center field; E.F. Hewit, president and umpire
and W.W. Vantine, secretary.

APRIL 28, 1904
  The first ball game of the season was played Sunday afternoon between the
kid nines of Selby and Bowdle on the diamond here. The score stood 20-8 in
favor of Bowdle. A return game will be played at Selby Sunday.

The Boston Belles, in bloomer bright, will bat the ball clear out of sight

BASEBALL TOURNAMENT IN BOWDLE

JUNE 16, 1904 BOWDLE PIONEER

Bowdle had made arrangements with Ipswich and Gettysburg baseball teams to
have a two-day tournament with the local team of Bowdle.

This baseball tournament was a great event for the town. A grandstand was
erected to accommodate the fans, seating about 500. The Bowdle Band played
sweet music for the on-lookers. On the first evening a grand dance was held
at the Opera House.

The first game, between Bowdle 2nd Nine and Java, was won by the Bowdle
boys. They won the purse of $20 with a score of 12-7.

The second game was between Gettysburg and Ipswich. Pitcher Engler struck
out 15 men and allowed but few safe hits. The game took 65 minutes and
Gettysburg won with one point in the whole game. After the game a horse
race was held with four horses in a 3 minute race.

The next day the champions, Bowdle and Gettysburg, played at 10:30 in the
morning. Gettysburg won 6-4. Gettysburg then played Ipswich. With a batting
streak Ipswich won with a score of 11 points, thus winning the $100 purse.
The umpire for all the games was F.K. Haw of Aberdeen.

Other events to conclude the day was another horse race in the afternoon.
In the evening a dance was held at the Opera House which was well attended.

BASEBALL

Webster's Dictionary defines baseball as a game played with a ball and a
bat by two opposing teams, properly of nine players each on a field with
four bases forming a diamond. Baseball apparently grew with the city of
Bowdle, as early newspaper reports show a time in the year 1887 when
players traveled as far as to Aberdeen to play this exciting game.

The first baseball field in Bowdle was reported as being north of the
railroad tracks. Some of the first players at the time (early 1920's) were
school teachers including Frank Tinker, George Partoon and Mike Close.
Other local players were Stormy and Chester Cook, O. Smith, J. Johnle and C.
Marlatee. Not all names of players were listed.

Traveling to games was done mostly by railroad in the 1800's. Since Bowdle
had at least five trains traveling through Bowdle, it was no problem for
players to hop on a train to the neighboring towns. No matter what kind of
celebrating event took place, there was always a baseball game.

Rules for this game have changed over the years. In the 1920's players were
being paid to play. Pitchers and catchers were the most sought out players
being paid.

The weather never seemed to hamper the love of the baseball player or the
fans. The greatest fans were wives and children of the players. Children
were packed along with the lunch and braved the 90-100 degree temperatures
for an afternoon of fun. Blankets were spread under shady trees if there
were any.

Around the 1920's the baseball field was moved west of Bowdle (now owned by
Larry Haar Trucking) where it remained until moved to the park area. It was
always a dream of the players and fans to have a lighted baseball diamond,
but the reality of this dream never came.

Players in the early 1920's (some salaried) were J. Manydeeas, Joe Day, C.
Wildung, A. Schlepp and Al Englehardt. Manager was Rich Lemke. In the
latter part of the 1920's a new manager Ed Shame joined the team along with
players J. Loebs, G. Loebs, B. Hardt, B. Johnle, Ernest Merkel, Andrew
Bauer, Walt, Rudy and Ted Goettling. Early 1930 players were Paul Goettling
(who managed the team for some time) along with Ed Merkel, Walter
Shoenfelder, Hank Edinger, Wm. Miller, Joe Kelsch, Alvin Blumhardt and
Conrad Fix. Later players were the Mueller twins Joe and Joel, George
Mashek, Leo Reede, Jake Schick and Ed Eisenbeisz.

As the years went by farmers formed their own baseball teams and some of
these well-known teams were the Haars, Aldingers, Buechlers, Biebers,
Walzes, Schlepps, Bauers and Millers.

        FATHER & SON BASEBALL PLAYERS Roman Walz, Adam Schlepp, Vic Schlepp
        Seated: Christ Walz

Bowdle's first State Baseball Tournament team was in 1942 in Aberdeen.
Bowdle played Renner and lost 2-0. Players on this team were Joe Mueller,
Marvin Gross, Ervin and Roman Walz, Bill Bauer, Wes Franks, E. Sonnenfeld,
Alvin Knottle and Marvin Miller. Dr. Fred Miller was the manager. The only
other Bowdle baseball team in state tourney play was in 1g46 at Watertown.
Manager Fred Miller added Ed Bachman, Victor Schlepp, Ozzie Schlepp, Alvin
and Edwin Bauer, Stu Holdhusen, Tom Morgan, Jack Buechler, Ruben Schumacher
and Edward Dewald to his list of players.

JULY 6, 1905
  B.A. Oestreich, the creamery man, furnished our boys with new white suits
for the baseball game and they looked swell.

        Ozzie Schlepp

In the late fifties amateur baseball began to fade in the Bowdle area. In
1961 the Edmunds County League was formed, but did not include Bowdle until
1965-1966.

Bowdle formed a Junior Legion team which was sponsored by the Bowdle
American Legion, but after several years it was turned over to the city as
the cost was too much for the Legionnaires. Coaching this team most of
those years were Oswald Schlepp and Dr. F.A. Miller. Some of the players
were Brad Schlepp, Jim Schlepp, Curt Eisenbeisz, Dennis Stotz, Curt
Houghtaling, Rusty Person, Terry Miller, Ricky Bollinger, Mark Bollinger,
Carney Haberer, Stacy Haberer, Wayne Buechler, Rodney Schlecht and James
Schlecht.

In the spring of 1970 the official baseball diamond was moved, in an
exchange of land with Raymond Haar. The diamond, at its present spot on the
northwest corner of 10th Avenue and Main, is no longer an official baseball
diamond, but is used for Little League baseball and softball.

In 1983 lights were installed at the present diamond. A new fence and two
dugouts were added, along with a wooden outfield fence donated by business
places.

Baseball teams are organized in the Bowdle area for the boys with Little
League Midgets and PeeWees, along with the girls softball teams. These
teams are sponsored as a recreational program with funds from business
places, Community Club, City Council, Fire Department and American Legion.

With the game of baseball fading in the small communities, teams have been
organized with several towns combining to make one team. Players in the
1960's and 1970's who played their last years as the Bowdle Merchants
Baseball Team were D. Schnaible, Kenny Stephan, Jim Geier, Bruce Huber, Mel
Olsen, K. Bodkins, Verton Schlepp, Don Pfaff, Doug Larson, David Karst and
Larry Bauer, who was the manager.

Baseball players forced to join neighboring towns so they could continue to
play this much loved sport were Ron and Todd Stotz, Ron Brown, Neil and
Kevin Schlepp, Steve Giedt, Jerry Sandmeier, Jeff Buechler, Curt
Eisenbeisz, Rod Moser, Mike Weiszhaar, Don Gross, Darren Stephan, Vince
Gauer and Curt Weiszhaar.

The last Teener Baseball team was-organized in 1975 with Ron Stotz as
coach. This team was sponsored under the recreational program, along with
the PeeWee team. Teener players were Denis Bachman, Steve Dewald, Tim,
Dennis and Steve Carlson, Stuart Carlson, Bryan Haberer, Scott Weiszhaar,
David Knecht, David Stephan, Shannon Jordre, Lowell Perman and David Stotz.

As long as Bowdle continues to have a recreational program for their young
boys and girls people will continue to gather at the diamond whenever they
hear or see a game in progress. Let's hope the day will never come when the
call of the umpire's voice booms, "Strike 3 you're out!" "You're safe!" or
"Ball 4, take your base!" will be silenced because of the lack of players
on a baseball or softball diamond.

  A young girls Kittenball Club was organized consisting of 11 members.

SOFTBALL

Softball ... a ball, is a ball, is a ball ... not so in softball. This
sport, which has replaced many baseball teams that were dominant in Bowdle
and the surrounding area towns, is played as slow pitch or fast pitch,
using balls of 12, 14 and 16 inches. The 12 inch slow pitch game is the
most popular in this area.

This game attracts fans of every age group and is well attended. It is a
very popular sport and is played in spite of high temperatures or rainy
weather.

Former baseball players switched to softball and the team became known as
Bowdle Merchants. This team played for several years. With the determined
efforts of Kenny Stephan and Mel Olsen the softball team, known as Leidholt
Chevrolet, was organized with the help of Dick Ulrich and Jerry Elshire.

Starting the new game of softball took a great deal of time and effort, but
after years of playing, winning became a great joy to these teams. Trophies
came in abundance and smiles were on all the faces of the players, along
with the fans.

In 1981 the Bowdle Merchants folded. Larry Gauer, Bruce Huber and Blake
Eisenbeisz were instrumental in keeping the Leidholt Chevrolet team going.
The name has been changed to Stephan Ranch and is still playing the game
today.

        Kenny Stephan, Wayne Schmidt and Larry Gauer.

NOVEMBER 10, 1904 BOWDLE PIONEER

One of the First Basketball Games

Those who attended the basketball game were somewhat surprised to see the
kind of ball played by Bowdle High School.

The Bowdle boys were all new beginners at the game. except Prof. Johnson.
With their inexperience going against a strong team like Aberdeen Normal it
looked like a sure defeat.

During the first half of the game the score was 12-2 in favor of Bowdle. At
the end of the game Bowdle was victorious with a score of 17-13.

This was Bowdle's second game of the season and they won both. The team
from Aberdeen were the champions of the state in 1903 and all were in
training since the football season. When they saw the small fellows from
Bowdle to play they were confident of an easy victory.

AMATEUR BASKETBALL

Amateur basketball has been a prominent part of the sports life in the
Bowdle community beginning with the Legion Team of 1947. Those members
included Ozzie Schlepp, Gordon Stotz, Morris Kurle Alvin Kurle, Don Gross,
Leonard Aldinger, Bob Senn, Leonard Lickfelt, Lefty Engelbritzen and
manager Dr. Fred Miller. The team had a second place finish at the State
Amateur Tournament in Brookings with Brookings winning the championship.
The team also placed second at the State Legion Basketball Tournament in
Webster against Oldham.

Under the management of Elmer Boschee, Ken Stephan and Bruce Huber, amateur
teams continued to compete in league play.

Beginning in 1963 the team, under sponsorship of Erv's Furniture and
management of Delmar Schock, competed in the Missouri Valley Indee League
and regional play. The team won the league championship 10 consecutive
years beginning in 1972. From 1962-1982 the record was 431 wins and 42
losses.

In 1977 Erv's Furniture competed in the State Amateur Basketball Tournament
at Mobridge with a 4th place finish. Sioux Falls won the title. The Bowdle
team also competed in the State Tournament in 1978 at Madison and in 1980
at Mobridge.

BOWDLE GOLF CLUB

The Bowdle Golf Course has a long history, dating back to the early 1920's,
according to information supplied by Erv Gross, who served as a caddy on
the original course.

The first course in Bowdle was located in Lu Merkel's pasture, which is
today known as the Lawrence Vetch farm. The course of the 1920's grazed
cattle, contained much cow manure and rock piles. The greens or sands were
small and fenced in with a double strand of barbed wire to keep the cattle
out. Many breeches were ripped as the golfer crawled through the wire to
putt the golf ball.

Today golfers play with colored balls, as well as white ones, but in those
days they also had colored balls ... they rolled in the cow manure. No
problem. The golfers fished the ball out of the "pile", wiped it off and
drove it. Many times as the golfer drove the ball, it would ricochet off
some rock pile. Regardless of the heat, rocks, grasshoppers and cow manure,
these determined golfers kept the course in operation.

In the early 1930's the course was moved north of Bowdle, where it is
presently located. The course at this time was made up of 40 acres. In the
early 1940's it was cut in half to the size it is today, with seven holes.
Two holes were played twice to make it a regulation course. In the late
1940's two more holes were added.

An old cook shanty was used to serve refreshments to the golfers during
tournaments. One day a strong South Dakota wind came along and blew the
shanty away. The golfers had to use a tent for a number of years. In 1970
an old farmhouse was purchased, moved and set on a foundation which served
the needs of the golfers for many years. These early golfers are to be
commended for their determination and hard work in keeping the golf course
alive in Bowdle.

APRIL 15, 1926
  Alex Searle and a force of men were busy the past week or more getting
the grounds in shape for the opening of the Bowdle Golf Club and Sunday
will be the opening day. The grounds are situated in the L. Merkel pasture
east of town. The course will consist of nine holes.

        WOMEN GOLFERS Adeline Schumacher, Edna Gross, Elvera Kundert,
        Frieda Jost, Christine Miller and Freida Jeskey.

        Clubhouse at Bowdle Golf Course in 1985

Today, in 1985, Bowdle still has a golf club with golfers possessing the
same determination to keep the course going for future generations, just as
their fathers had done.

The golf club today has a modern clubhouse with 90 members to its credit.
The club's dream is to encourage more and more people of Bowdle to join and
make it a family game of inexpensive fun--a game you can play, way past
the age of 80.

BOWDLE SPORTSMEN'S CLUB

The Bowdle Sportsmen's Club was started in 1955 with the Articles of
Incorporation dated Dec. 7. William Miller, Michael Mitzel, Gordon Stotz,
Donald Hoven and Walter C. Fischer were listed as the five directors of the
new club.

Throughout the years the members have strived to uphold the motto: "Help
protect and conserve our country's soil, water and other natural resources;
without these there would not be any wildlife or fish. Help protect and
conserve our wildlife and fish."

Aside from the many trapshoot events held at the Bowdle Trapshoot grounds,
the club has sponsored some other unique fundraising events.

In 1970 one members was chosen by lottery to go elk hunting at Custer State
Park. A large bull elk, shot by Orval Haberer, was brought back to Bowdle
where it was prepared and served by the Sportsmen's Club at an Elk Feed at
the American Legion Hall. All proceeds from the feed went to the club.
About 35 participated in the lottery.

The club also sponsored a Fishing Derby with valuable fishing equipment
given to the fishermen catching the biggest northern, walleye or white
bass. The last derby was held in 1983.

The club donated $250 to help pass the controversial Dove Hunting Bill in
1980. Efforts of the various clubs in the state paid off, as dove hunting
is now allowed in South Dakota.

The boat ramp at Thomas Bay on Lake Oahe was built in 1982. The Club
donated $200 towards the project. Local conservation efforts included the
purchasing and planting of trees near Bowdle.

Officers of the club in 1986 are Mark Bieber, president; Arnold Kiesz,
vice-president and Dr. Jacob Sieck, secretary-treasurer.

JANUARY 14, 1932
  150 hunters are to meet at the pool hall where they then will leave for
the S.J. Commet farm southwest of Bowdle. There will be a number of sleighs
at the farm with which to haul the hunters about the land. The object of
the hunt is to secure as many rabbits as possible, then secure a market for
the hides and use the revenue to buy feed for the pheasants. The Department
of Game and Fish is furnishing feeders which can be set up in any sheltered
place and used to great advantage in feeding the birds.

        WHOOPING CRANES [Earl Erbe Photo]

Whooping cranes were so numerous in this country in 1906, that they made a
nuisance of themselves in the cornfields and were considered fair prey of
farmers and Indians.

The pair of whooping cranes in the photo were killed in the Spring Lake
area. These birds were about 5 feet tall.

Today these birds, which were the only ones on this continent said to be as
tall as a man, are on their way to extinction.

Hagart of Minnesota, Trevis Burns of Texas, Gary Langdon of Texas, Otto
Bieber and Vic Schlepp of Bowdle.

BOWDLE BASS BUSTERS

The Bowdle Bass Busters is one of 1,300 affiliated chapters of the national
bass fishing organization headquartered in Montgomery, Alabama, which has a
membership of over 400,000. In the state of South Dakota there are only
five clubs.

Bowdle organized as a bass club in 1982 with six charter members: Dave
Wurtz, Dewayne Syhre, Evan Haar, Dave McCarlson, Al and Randy Sandquist.

In 1985 there are 13 members in the club. Dewayne Syhre is president and
Victor Fischer, secretary-treasurer. Local members include Dave Wurtz,
Orval Haberer, Evan Haar, Steve and Jason Heintzman. Sportsmen from other
towns complete the list of 13 members in the club.

The Bowdle Club has four tournaments each year. The top six people catching
the fish with most pounds are eligible to go to the annual State Bass
Tournament. The club fishing in the local lakes in the area seek the bass
with the most pounds. A trophy is given in the tournament to the one who
catches the "big bass." A requirement is that the bass must be 12 inches
long.

Every year an annual picnic is held at Lake Molstad.

ROLLER SKATING

Alvin and Edna Erlenbusch provided the sport of roller skating for young
and old from January 1951 through 1967. Alvin taught many of the youngsters
how to master the sport.

Many of them have moved away several years ago, but when they return they
always tell him that they still remember him from roller skating. There
were a lot of hard falls at times before they knew how to stay on their
feet instead of their seat.

        LaRita Merkel is getting her skates put on by her dad Albert while
        her mother watches.

        Verna Kiesz was the ticket seller. The Carlson boys were skate boys.

Alvin was an excellent skater. Edna never did any skating. She took care of
supplying the skaters with their proper size skates and the refreshments.
Verna Kiesz sold tickets. Often times there was a long line of youngsters
waiting to buy their tickets and she kept them in order until starting time.

The skates needed weekly check ups and repair work so it kept Alvin and
Edna very busy with the business, but it was worth it all to see so many
enjoy themselves at roller skating.

Roller skate pins were presented to skaters who attended every week. Many
received these pins for perfect attendance.

OCTOBER 17, 1907
  Boyd Hall, 80 ft. by 50 ft., will be ready for skaters. It has a hard
maple floor costing about $800. The building will be lighted with electric
lights and heated by steam. It will be used for skating and athletic
purposes.

YELLOWSTONE TRAIL POOL LEAGUE

For many years playing pool has been a favorite sport among young and old
in Bowdle. In 1983 Bowdle organized several pool leagues. At present there
are three leagues in Bowdle. Rick Boschee is captain for the Main Stop,
Dennis Schock for Gus's Bar & Bottle Shop and Steve Heintzman for Gold
Nugget.

The teams meet weekly to play, rotating every-other-week to another town,
either Java, Selby or Akaska. The five-man teams play for 20 weeks. During
these sessions trophies and awards are presented at different intervals to
the local teams.

At the end of the season a tournament is held to determine the grand
champions. This allows the winners to continue to advance to the state
tournament and may eventually receive the honor of attending the State
Valley 8-Ball League in Las Vegas, Nevada.

CHAUTAUQUA ENTERTAINMENT AT BOWDLE [By Esther L. Voller]

At the time when the Rev. Father Krebs was pastor of St. Augustine's
Catholic Church, his sister Anna came from the eastern part of the country
to assist him. She had a deep interest in music and good entertainment
provided by professional entertainers, as well as liturgical music. She no
doubt was influential in getting a Chautauqua group to come to Bowdle. The
church, used today, had not yet been built and the tent for Chautauqua was
erected on the church grounds.

I don't know how long the Chautauqua lasted in Bowdle, but was able to
attend some afternoon and evening performances at Ipswich about 1917. There
was a raised stage with a piano. Entertainment included many forms. There
was vocal and instrumental music, lectures, performing magicians,
monologues, etc. and all in good taste, far better than the majority of
today's television shows. On warm days ladies brought their fans and sat
fanning themselves during performances. Tickets were sold for the entire
week and were punched when one entered the tent.

Residents who knew Anna Krebs remember her work with school girls, training
them to perform and sing. They say that the girls gave a program in
connection with the Chautauqua Company.

FEBRUARY 15, 1906
  "Caught in the Web" was practically murdered upon the stage here last
Saturday evening. The acting was perfectly rotten. All who went feel that
they were caught in the web.

JANUARY 21, 1910
  A Ladies Orchestra of Bowdle had its last dance at the Opera House. It is
mostly composed of Bowdle young people.

TAKEN FROM JUNE 15, 1916 BOWDLE PIONEER

  The Chautauqua will be July 1-4. The school grounds were selected as
being the best location for the tent, it being far enough from the railroad
so the noise of trains would not interfere with the programs. A booster
club was sent out to help provide money to help pay for this program.

Single admission ticket would cost 35-50 cents each or nearly $5 for the 10
big entertainments. If you buy a season ticket it will be $2 now.

BATON TWIRLERS

Miss Janice Leidholt was crowned Miss Majorette of South Dakota in 1954
when she won the state title in Huron. Janice was 12 years old. She is the
daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Leidholt.

Wilmer Huber, Bowdle's baton artist, was honored to be awarded a citation
Activity Medal in 1951 for his contribution to the art of baton twirling.
The citation and medal were awarded by the South Dakota Department of
Veterans of Foreign Wars. Wilmer is the son of Mr. and Mrs. John Huber of
Bowdle.

Wilmer was one of the few from South Dakota listed in the 1952 edition of
"Who's Who in Baton Twirling." He was drum major with the Edmunds County
4-H Band, the Northern State Teachers College and American Legion Drum and
Bugle Corps in Aberdeen.

FUN AND MUSIC [Esther L. Voller]

In pioneer days there were no televisions, radios, movies, football games
or Snow Queen contests; so what did they do to make life interesting
besides working, visiting or playing cards? They danced to good music
whenever musicians and floor space was available. The Christ Walz family of
Bowdle, assisted by Fred Walz and William Miller, could provide the music
if a hall or barn were available.

At nine Gary (Gerhard) Walz was already playing with the family group which
also included his brothers Ervin and Roman, sister Metha, father Christ,
uncle Fred Walz and William Miller. Christ Walz was a left-handed
violinist. Miller played drums and Metha was pianist. Other instruments
played by the group were saxophone, banjo and accordion.

When a barn was built the owner was allowed to have one dance in it without
obtaining a license. Barn dances were held at the John Bieber farm, where
Mark Bieber now lives and at the Pete Arbach farm near Hoven. When John
Hoven's barn was made he had a dance to celebrate the event. The group's
renditions of fast European waltzes and polkas drew enthusiastic fans to
dance halls such as Matt Gaden's in Hoven, Roscoe and Bowdle Halls.
Hometown people are still enjoying music by Gary and Fred Walz occasionally.

Guests at private wedding dances wore ribbons to indicate they were
invited. At public dances ribbons were given when admission was paid, which
averaged 25 cents.

When asked how a piano could be lifted to a hayloft, Gary replied, "oh,
that wasn't hard; all you had to do was get some guys to lift!"

Kerosene lanterns provided light in the barns.

Another Bowdle man, Jacob Diedtrich, also played violin and accordion for
dances and parties at Bowdle and nearby.

FEBRUARY 25, 1909
  A new band was organized with Harry F. Smith as the leader.

JUNE 14, 1934
  George L. Campbell, hired as band director for the coming year, will
direct the City Band.

BOWDLE'S FIRST BAND

Members of Bowdle's first band were Ed Green, Fred Bowman, Ed Warner, L.E.
Amerphol, Prof. Jester, Dan Barnett, Walter Brant, Frank Bowman, A.C.
LeClaire and manager Dave Gamble.

There was a band called "Silver Cornet Brass." Their uniforms were black
plub hats and Prince Albert coats. One member Walter Brandt, the station
agent, had a white fuzzy plug hat. Frank Bowman was a little boy in knee
pants and a dinky hat who played an alto horn as big as himself. The band
played all over the territory, being the only organized of the kind in the
northern party of this state.

        Baer and Christ Baer. Seated: Henry Baer, Fred Johnle, Fred Baer
        and Herman Baer.

        Baer, Gary Walz and Fred Walz. Seated: Quentin Walz.

FIRST FOURTH OF JULY CELEBRATION
JULY 7, 1887 BOWDLE PIONEER
Written by Fred J. Bowman

At 4 o'clock in the morning national salutes were fired arousing the
citizens of Bowdle from their slumber.

At 9 o'clock the Bowdle Cornet Band took station in the square at the
Dumont Hotel. People from Bowdle, as well as from surrounding towns, formed
a long procession, headed by the band, with the stars and stripes floating
in the breeze.

Behind them marched the Bowdle and Pembrook Baseball Clubs, together with
their uniformed small Boy's Baseball Club. Following these clubs were
carriages, with the Calthumpian Brigade bringing up the rear. The
procession took up four blocks. Upon arrival at the pavilion grounds, it
was learned that the train was 40 minutes late. This train brought the
orator of the day, Hon. L.A. Burke.

The program at the pavilion began with S.F. Brown of Bangor giving the
prayer, followed by J.G. Davis reading the Declaration of Independence. The
president of the day, H.H. Potter, introduced the speaker, Hon. L.A. Burke,
who was an early pioneer and the receiver of the U.S. Land Office at
Aberdeen. At the close of the oration, five-minute speeches were given by
prominent men of the neighboring communities. At the end of the program the
Bowdle Choir sang and the band played.

The crowd of about 1000 people dispersed to witness the baseball game
between the Pembrook and Bowdle Clubs. Bowdle won 29-4.

After the game there were many races: horse races, mule races, slow races,
foot races, bicycle races, wheelbarrow races and greased pig races. Cash
prizes were given for all the games and races.

After a fireworks display, two dances were held, one at the Merchants Hotel
and one at the big tent on the grounds.

The celebration was a complete success. Everything went off harmoniously
and quietly. Not one among that 1000 people disgraced himself by getting
drunk. The people were all in good spirits and doubtlessly will long
remember Bowdle's first celebration with feelings of pleasure.

        BAND STAND The band played here every Saturday night during the
        summer months for an hour.

EARLY CHRISTMAS

In the early days of Bowdle the Christmas season was special. Most of the
presents which were given to family and friends were homemade. Perhaps
grandma knitted mittens, Aunt Bess gave a basket of Christmas cookies
shaped like animals and stars covered with delicious colored sugar. Uncle
Tom gave a watch.

Most gifts were useful in the old days, including a reefer overcoat and a
new pair of shoes. As for boughten presents, they were limited to books like
the New Testament, a sled, a pair of skates and that most wonderful of all
oldtime toys, a tin monkey that climbed a string.

Christmas dinners of those days were superior. The most special event
included was the Christmas Eve Service at the church, riding in a cutter
over the deep snow

DECEMBER 18, 1930
  Dear Santa Claus: I don't want very much this year. I want a 5-pound sack
of lead B.B. shot, a little engine for my erector set. I want a Gee-Whip
Horse Race and a bow and arrow with a target. I want a knife, too. Your
friend, Orville Stangl.

DECEMBER 22, 1932
  Dear Santa: I thought I would drop you a line to let you know what I want
for Xmas. I am in the third grade but yet I want a teddy bear, baby doll
and lots of candy for that sweet tooth of mine 19 always ready for candy
you know. I am a good little girl, 8 years old. Yours truly, Eloise Bauder.

JANUARY 29, 1932
  During this season of the year business is a bit slack in most places and
people are taking advantage of opportunities to "chat" and "play cribbage"
and "whist" at a few of the local business houses. A crowd of 15-20 can be
found most any afternoon at Schlaht's Garage where whist is the most common
pastime; at Schlecht's Barber Shop, cribbage is the principal pastime.

Clubs and Organizations . . .

Compiled by Darlene Walz and Joanne Bieber

ORDER OF EASTERN STAR

Social life of the community changed greatly when families needed two
incomes to keep afloat and then in the 50's television added its attraction
and societies began to break up from lack of attendance.

Such was the case with the Rebecca and Odd Fellows Lodges and the Order of
the Eastern Star and Hiddenwood Lodge A.F. & A.M. in Bowdle.

The Bowdle Chapter of the Order of the Eastern Star was organized in 1897
on the petition of Mrs. Ida Edwards (wife of Bowdle's first doctor) and
other Bowdle ladies. The charter was signed by Mrs. Jeanette E. Herreid,
wife of South Dakota's Governor, as Worthy Grand Matron.

To list the officers who served the Chapter during its 50 years of service
is prohibitive due to lack of space. Mrs. Mary (Sam) Boyd served the
Chapter as secretary for 29 years and the Chapter was honored to have five
of its members appointed Grand (or state) Officers. They were Mrs. Aurand,
Mrs. Dorothy (Dr. Thomas) Jones Fuller, Mrs. Theodosia Grosz, Mrs. Julia
Senn and Mrs. Catherine Jones.

May 7, 1957 the Bowdle Chapter affiliated with the Selby Chapter of OES,
which had been a child of the Bowdle Chapter. Fire damaged the Chapter room
when the Jones Drug Store was damaged and this contributed largely to the
loss of the Bowdle Chapter, despite the faithful service to the last of Mr.
and Mrs. Ernest Merkel, Mr. and Mrs. Fred Grosz, Mr. and Mrs. Art C.
Merkel, Mr. and Mrs. Julius Schilling, Mrs. Julia Senn, Mrs. Marian Commet,
Mrs. Lenora Murray, Mrs. Ella Stangl, Mrs. Gertrude Olson, Mrs. Lois Stangl
Wolf, Janice, Joyce and Shirley Murray. Many OES Chapters have met a
similar fate. The Java and Eureka Chapters have also affiliated with the
Selby Chapter.

Mrs. Stangl and Mrs. Wolf remained faithful members going from their home
in Java to attend meetings regularly. Both hold offices and serve as
pianists. Mrs. Olson and Mrs. Senn are the only members of the OES living
in Bowdle.

FLYING CLUB

In March 1951 Arlyn Erbe was in charge of the group known as Flying
Farmers. Pilots enlisted were Ted Sandmeier, Orville and Norwin Walz,
Herbert Bieber, Arlyn Erbe and Albert Berg. All the men except Berg owned
their own planes.

According to the Bowdle Pioneer in March 1952, the Henry Leidholt farm was
to be the location of the new airport. It was located only 1l/2 miles from
town and about a mile off U.S. 12. Most folks know it better as the old
Artz farm. Henry Leidholt was to take care of the landing strip.

20TH CENTURY CLUB

In the spring of 1938 the following ladies met with Mrs. Julia Senn to
organize the 20th Century Club, whose motive was the study of American
writers and composers: Almeda Riba, Dorothy Jones, Catherine Jones, Wally
Merkel, Emily deMalignon, Mary Hoven, Genevieve Smart, Theo Grosz, Esther
Blumhardt, Mary Searle and Vivian Beck.

Each member contributed a book review during the year's program and the
lives of composers and their works were also enjoyed. Social events
included a four-course dinner for the members twice a year. Mrs. Ruth
Goldade and Mrs. Lola Merkel became members when two others moved away.

Through the gifts of various types of books from the citizens in town, the
club promoted the beginnings of a public library, which was located at the
back of Bowdle Mercantile, now G & O Electrical & Plumbing. Edna Baer Weron
was one of the young ladies who served as librarian, through the NYA, a
government funded make-work project for young people. With the coming of
World War II, the NYA project was discontinued, the books were stored on
the second floor of the Bowdle Hardware and the library was no more. The
war also disrupted the lives of the club members and it faded away.

BOY SCOUTS TROOP

The Boy Scouts organized in the spring of 1957. Loren (Red) Baker was
scoutmaster until 1960 when he was transferred to Ipswich. Gardner Gross was
instrumental in the organization of the Boy Scouts and served on the Scout
Council along with Bernard A. Carlson, Dwight Commet and Kenneth Eisenbeisz.

The troop held its weekly meetings in the Reuben Schumacher building where
he operated the Mobil Oil Agency. R.J. Herman Agency occupied this building
and at present North Central Service Agency is located there.

Fund raisers included a yearly paper drive. Papers were taken to Miller and
made into insulation. The troop's community project was to keep firewood at
the Roadside (Mertz) Tourist Park west of Bowdle.

The scouts had many nature and outdoor ventures, as every summer the troop
went to Lake Sakaweja near Wilmot for a week of camping twice a year. They
spent a week at Lake Hiddenwood and in the winter time a "Camp Out" was
held at Lake Richmond using the 4-H Building.

The Scout-A-Rama was held annually in Mobridge where their work was
displayed. Troop members fathers composed the adult Troop Committee for the
most part.

MAY 25, 1950
  The county tree planter planted 300 trees in Meakins Park. The job was

BOWDLE MOTHERS' CLUB

The Bowdle Mothers' Club was organized in September 1948 with 12 charter
members: Lenora Berg, Margaret Carlson, Peggy Gross, Alice Heckenlaible,
Lorraine Kurle, Irma Leidholt, Mac Mashek, Adeline Miller, Irma Moser,
Eileen Paetznick, Cylvia Schumacher and Marie Schumacher.

The theme of the club was the study of preschool and school-age children.
The purpose of the club was to start a park for the children. The city had
a gift of lots for this purpose for 13 years, donated by John Meakins, to
be used only for park purposes--beautifying these lots instead of having to
look at the eye sore of a weed patch as had been done year after year.

Voters of Bowdle defeated the first levy for park maintenance, but in 1951
it was passed and we were on our way. We had many financial and local
donations. County agent O.E. Prestegard of Ipswich gave us many helpful
suggestions on planting and arranging and commended the Mothers' Club on
their undertaking. The county tree planter was loaned and trees were
donated by Herman Erbe. The job was completed by hand by club members when
it was found that the soil was too hard on the north side for the planter
to do the work.

During the summer months, Tuesday night was park night to bring your hoe
and lawn mower to help. Husbands and members labored to make picnic tables,
outhouses and brick grills with donations coming from the community for the
projects.

Every year the club engaged in various fundraising projects such as food
sales, paper drives, galloping and silver teas and flower shows, style
shows, pie and ice cream socials, pancake suppers Stanley parties,
anniversaries, Tupperware party, tasting tea's rummage sales, Pillsbury
Cake sale and cake walks, plays and quilt raffles to raise funds toward the
purchase of additional land and equipment, landscaping and general upkeep
of the park. The archway was built in 1956 at Meakins Park and each year
more equipment was added, such as swings, slides, sandboxes, tennis court
and teeter-totters. All installation work was done by volunteer labor. The
club did many other things such as Christmas gifts for Abbot House, puppets
for the hospital, Kenny drive and sponsored an orphan.

The members of the Mothers' Club entertained their children at an annual
Christmas party with Santa to delight the children. An Easter egg hunt was
an annual spring event at the park for the children of the community.
Annual family picnics were enjoyed during the summer months. A number of
valentine card parties were held for club members and their husbands. A
Mother's Day Tea was held with each guest presented a nose-gay of white
carnations and rosebud center.

The club purchased a silver tea set and Santa Claus suit to be used by the
club for rental purposes.

It was heartening to know people would rather come to Bowdle for picnics
rather than drive 25 miles or more to Hiddenwood, Mina or Aberdeen.

The present club continues many of the original goals and activities of the
charter group. Improvements at Meakins Park remain the major project. In
the past 10 years equipment added has been swings, covered slide, zoom
slide, barrel, teetertotters, benches, tables, picnic shelters, bike rack,
flag pole and wooden fort.

The bell was donated by Bowdle School District when the old school building
was demolished. Flags have been donated by the American Legion. The
original flag was purchased by Mothers' Club. One of the newest and biggest
projects has been the removal of the dead and diseased trees on the south
side of the park. Members spent many hours removing and replanting 15-foot
green ash trees. The old flowerbed has been replaced with shrubs.

Some of the larger items for the park have been purchased through the
cooperation of AAL and Federal grants.

Fund raising has been accomplished through the bi-annual Christmas Craft &
Bake Sales, along with plant, food and pie and ice cream sales.

Some community events held are baby-sitting clinic, CPR, mental health
speakers, Halloween party and Easter egg hunt.

An enduring feature of Mothers' Club is the activities that include the
families--annual Christmas party, Valentine's party and picnics.

Meetings are held the first Monday of each month except July and August.
Programs are given on a variety of topics to the 20 members of the Bowdle
School District. Collecting and publishing favorite recipes in a Bowdle
Centennial Cookbook was the club's major Centennial project.

BOWDLE HISTORICAL SOCIETY

The organizational meeting for the Bowdle Historical Society was held Aug.
19, 1977 at the Country School (white school on the east end of Main
Street.) Charter members are Gertrude and Oscar Olson, Maggie and Dave
Buechler, Reinie and Laura Herman, Esther Voller, Wilma Lemke, Gretchen
Sprenger, Katherine Hoffmann, Rev. John Schmierer, Marie Schumacher
(deceased 1984) and Erma Maier.

Officers elected at the first meeting were president Erma Maier;
vice-president Gretchen Sprenger; secretary Esther Voller and treasurer
Gertude Olson. At present Erma Maier is still president, Gretchen Sprenger
is secretary and Katherine Hoffmann treasurer.

The purpose of the Historical Society is to pre serve and restore the
Country School building and to encourage any other restorations of
historical value.

The first major project was accomplished through a grant from Job Service,
a Public Service Program and volunteer work from club members. Adolph
Sandmeier and Virginia Voller were employed as handy man and project
director. They restored the white school built in the 1920's known as the
Leidholt School and moved into Bowdle about 1940. It is located on the
comer of East Main and 1st Avenue. Most of the work was completed in 1978.

        Soldering iron with gas-fired blow torch used often to open water
        pipes leading from well to tank and a crescent wrench.

Projects are backed by the Bowdle Area Senior Citizens, Bowdle City
Council, Bowdle School Personnel, Bowdle Township Board and Bowdle Library
Board, as well as many interested individuals. The Bowdle Township assumes
the upkeep of the school and grounds. Electric heat has
been added.

        China spittoon at top, Grar granite spittoon and kerosene table
        lamp with wick.

Much work was also done at the local museum after the school project was
completed. Objects were identified, cleaning and more economical and
pleasing arrangements of displays have been finished.

The second major project was locating, moving and restoring the red
schoolhouse. This building is over 100 years old, built for a business
place and then moved to the school site in a lonely pasture setting. It was
donated by the Jordith family of Lebanon. It was moved by Leo Kraft in 1979
to the cement pad behind the museum for $300. Restoration work was done by
Leo with the help of Mark Kindelspire and donated labor by Melvin and Emma
Maier, Gretchen Sprenger, Angie Lemke and others. Original plastering was
not feasible so other materials were used. The school opened for public
viewing Oct. 10, 1980.

        Before little red school was moved from the pasture at Lebanon.

Funds were generated through quilt raffles with members donating many hours
of work to complete. Other events to raise funds for the Fall Fun Fest
included a dinner at the Legion Hall, white elephant sale, silent auctions,
food and craft sales. All material and labor bills have been met. A
connecting entry way between the museum and red school has been slated for
the next project. The quilts realized the greatest return with Lucy Dippert
in charge of sales.

A Fund Fest was held in October 1981 to provide funds for the entry way. It
was also in 1981 that negotiations were carried on with the City Council to
get the much needed roof repairs for the museum and library. After repairs
were completed members urged friends to help clean and replace the displays.

The group is proud of the buildings and items preserved. Many of the
antiques in the museum were donated by Rev. Martin Bieber. The books,
before 1930 in the Little Red Schoolhouse and after 1920-1930 in the White
Country School, have been donated by interested citizens.

MARTIN BIEBER PUBLIC LIBRARY

April 18, 1971 marked the grand opening of the Martin Bieber Public Library
in Bowdle. It was three years before, in 1968, that Rev. Bieber gave not
only the building, but also his book collection to the city. The first
workers who started constructing bookcases and sorting books were members
of the City Council and their wives, Duane Steiger, June Gross and Helen
Miller. However the job was so overwhelming that work stopped.

It wasn't until Beulah Schumacher, Joanne Bieber, Irma Erbe and Helen
Miller started a drive to open the library that work began in earnest in the
fall of 1970 with many other people helping. Many clubs, organizations and
Bowdle businesses donated money for books and furnishings. The City of
Bowdle finances the library. They appointed a Library Board composed of
Joanne Bieber, chairman; Beulah Schumacher, secretary; Floyd and Helen
Miller and Irma Erbe.

Present Library Board members are Joanne Bieber, Beulah Schumacher, Elodie
Schmierer, Alice Heckenlaible, Karen Karst, Pam Drake and Mary Rieger.

The library collection includes not only a children's fiction and
nonfiction section and adult fiction section, but also a large reference
section, a well-stocked philosophy and psychology section, an unusually good
group of current biographies and an impressive religious collection. The
books are catalogued for easy access.

Many activities have taken place in the library such as plant exchanges,
pattern and paperback swaps and art and hobby displays by Bowdle residents.
Each year the Library Board hosts the Bowdle School teachers to acquaint
them with what the library has to offer them and their students.

The summer reading program has grown through the years. Over 40 youngsters
often crowd the facilities while enjoying a story and craft session for
nine weeks each summer. Bonnie Schuh, Ruth Eder, Mona Kennedy, Marcella
Walz, Lenora Berg and Pam Drake have led the youngsters in these activities.

The first librarians were Helen Nies and Pansy Stephan. Pansy remained for
12 years as a faithful worker. Others serving as librarians were Bonnie
Schuh, Margie Mittleider and at present, Mona Kennedy.

Library hours are Thursdays and Saturdays from 2:30 to 5 p.m. It is open on
Saturday afternoons only in the winter months of December through March.

AUTHORS OF BOWDLE

May Phillips-Tatro was a well-known poet/writer. One of her most remembered
poems was In Hayin' Time. Another well-known American author Walt Whitman
tells how he loved to read May's poetry.

Mrs. Tatro was the wife of an early Bowdle depot agent. She came to Bowdle
with her husband G.W. Tatro in 1886 and died at age 37 in 1902.

Flosie McCafferty Briley, an early day school teacher of this vicinity and
daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Van McCafferty, authored two books for children
which have been published: Three Grandmothers Flew South and Over the
Cuckoo's Nest.

Lorena Hickok. Her father was a buttermaker in the creamery here about
1900. Lorena began her literary career as a reporter for the Minneapolis
Journal, later a free lance writer. During Franklin D. Roosevelt's campaign
in 1932 she was the political reporter. After she was in the White House,
she was associated with Mrs. Roosevelt as her reporter and was President
Roosevelt's representative on tours of the depressed areas in the United
States.

Martha Ostenso was a novelist. Her father was a buttermaker at the creamery
but it is not known at what period. She is best known for her book Wild
Geese.

Mr. Steffler came from Bowdle and was known for writing a grade school
arithmetic book. It is not known if it was adopted to be used in the South
Dakota schools.

Elvera Ziebart Reuer wrote the novel The Last Bridge. It tells of the 2,500
mile trek of her mother Eva, beginning in the Province of Glueckstahl,
South Russia to Bessarabia and then during World War II to Poland and
Germany.

In December of 1949 Elvera came to South Dakota with her mother Eva,
brother Albert and sister Gertrude. They came to live with her mother's
sister Katherine and son Bill Haeder, southwest of Bowdle. She married
Ervin Reuer and now lives in Aberdeen.

BOWDLE HOSPITAL AUXILIARY

The Bowdle Hospital Auxiliary was organized Oct. 22, 1946. The meeting was
held at the school with 37 ladies joining the organization.

Mrs. Art Merkel was elected president, Esther Blumhardt vice-president,
Alice Heckenlaible secretary and Ruth Miller treasurer. Monthly meetings
were held at various church basements. Later these meetings were held in
private homes. Dues were $1 per member and lunch was served at each meeting
at a cost of 15 cents per person. Short programs were provided consisting
of solos, recitations, papers given by the doctors and singing by school
children. Often ladies were asked to bring a dish towel or a needed kitchen
tool to the meetings.

Early fund raisers included auctions, rummage, candy and food sales, pie
socials, square dances, galloping teas, sponsoring the Elks Chorus, having
a huge food stand at the Diamond Jubilee, card parties and tag days.
Recently having a soup kitchen during basketball tournaments, pancake
suppers and raffles have been added to the list.

An open house was held May 12, 1947 for the reopening of the old hospital.
Much painting and cleaning was done in readiness. A complete set of heavy
dinnerware was purchased for $57.85, a complete line of cookware for
$28.77, an electric iron and ironing board for $11 and a washing machine
for $75, furniture for the nurse's room, drapery, bedding and other kitchen
equipment have been purchased.

In 1961 the Auxiliary sponsored a float for Bowdle's Diamond Jubilee
depicting a hospital room and sewing room scene. The ladies did a great
deal of mending and made many gowns then and still do so today.

June 3, 1962 an open house was held again, but this time for a new
hospital. This lovely facility is used today. Cookies, bars and coffee were
served and guided tours given. Drapery, lobby and dining room furniture
were purchased for the grand opening. A layette was also given to the first
baby born in the new hospital.

The ladies also gave a scholarship to a senior nursing student if she or he
would come to work in the Bowdle Hospital for one year following graduation
.

Today the women are busy having fund raisers and making holiday tray favors
for patients. Sunshine ladies go to the hospital daily in an attempt to
brighten a patient's day.

One project used to earn money was the apron game. Small half (doll size)
aprons were made, each containing a pocket. Friends and relatives were
given or sent these and asked to donate a penny per inch of their waistline
while hoping their far away friends had added to the middle since they last
saw them.

During National Hospital Week tags were sold in the Bowdle and Hosmer area.
Everyone wore a bright tag letting people know they had donated to the
Bowdle Hospital Auxiliary for a worthwhile cause.

A gift cabinet has recently been purchased and gift items for sale are
displayed. Lights for the patient's rooms have been replaced, a nursery
isolette and scale, calendars for the rooms and educational material have
been purchased. There is always a long list of needs for the hospital.

With concern for the nursing home residents the ladies had a pancake supper
in 1984 with proceeds going towards new drapery at the nursing home.

Presidents who have led this organization of dedicated women are Mrs. Art
Merkel, Mrs. Wm. Miller, Mrs. Reinie Leno, Mrs. Leonard Erbe, Mrs. Oscar
Olson, Mrs. Edwin Blumhardt, Mrs. Joe Stappler, Mrs. Fred Grosz, Mrs.
Mahlon Gross, Mrs. Clarence Schumacher, Mrs. Helmer Leno, Mrs. Kenneth
Eisenbeisz, Mrs. Oscar Metzger,

Mrs. Ray Kurle, Mrs. Ray Bachman, Mrs. Joe Thomas, Mrs. DeWayne Weiszhaar,
Mrs. Clemens Heinrich and Mrs. Dave Karst.

At the present time the Bowdle Hospital Auxiliary has about 80 members.

BOWDLE AREA SENIOR CENTER

Longer life span brought with it complications that the government Social
Services sought a solution for--something to keep life interesting for
citizens no longer able to do productive work and March 1, 1973, through
the sponsorship of the Edmunds County Commissioners, the Bowdle Area Senior
Citizens Center organized. Twenty-nine persons assembled at the Legion Hall
with Rev. John Schmierer as chairman and Alma Leno secretary. The business
meeting elected Gertrude Olson as the first president, a position she held
three years. Other officers were Emma Hoffman, vice-president; Mary
Schmierer, secretary and Otto Huber, treasurer. Emma Haberer was kitchen
director.

Raymond Bachman reported on the help the Commercial Club and City Council
would give. Dues were set and bylaws and a constitution drawn up and
committees appointed. The Senior Citizens met at the Legion Hall for three
years and then through a federal grant and money they had raised from bake
sales, potlucks and other fund raisers, They were able to purchase from the
city in 1976, a building on the south side of Main Street, which had been
replaced with a new liquor store building across the street. All the
members worked hard to clean up the old liquor store building and a kitchen
was built by Oscar Olson, Jake Diedtrich and Fred Rieger.

The Center observed the Nation's Bi-Centennial serving lunch to over the
80's, an antique display, Oscar Olson and Anna Hoven represented Uncle Sam
and Martha Washington in the city's parade riding in a 1916 Dodge car owned
by Arlyn Erbe. A flag and banner were purchased for the Center.

Transportation to Aberdeen has been provided by the Center by its members
twice a month and one meal weekly has been served to the members with lady
members volunteering to prepare it. The Arts and Crafts Committee made many
quilts which have increased the treasury. It has taken the cooperation of
all members to enjoy successful programs. The Bowdle Center has joined all
other senior centers of the state to distribute cheese and other
commodities when requested.

An addition to the south of the building made possible a pool table room
for members to enjoy, along with bingo games and card games.

At the January 1984 meeting the members voted to take part in the Nutrition
Meals program. All persons 56 years of age or older are eligible for all
privileges of membership.

Presidents who have served the organization are Gertrude Olson, Emma
Hoffman, Erma Maier, Rev. John Schmierer Frieda Rieger, Julia Senn and
Walter Fischer.

THREE-COUPLE COOKIE CLUB

In the year 1971 Virginia and Harold Voller were visiting Wilma and Wilmer
Boschee at their farm home. The ladies came up with the idea of baking
fancy cookies for the holidays. Each would make her own cookie dough, then
get together to do the baking. They did this for five years on the farm.
The Vollers moved to their new home in Bowdle in 1976. At this time Anne
and Oscar Metzger joined the group and they named their organization the
Three Couples Cookie Club.

The couples meet once a year, each one brings their own cookie dough,
colors, flavors, decorations and colored sugar. The last three years they
have a new recipe for filled spritz cookies, which is very time consuming,
but ever so good. The couples meet at a different home each year. The
evening begins with a supper so they are not tempted to taste the cookies.

In the beginning each of the women got an electric Super Shooter for
Christmas from their husbands.

Each one has a job. Wilma is the baker. Virginia fills the cookie press.
Wilmer and Oscar put the cookies on the sheets. Harold stacks the cookies
and washes the cookie sheets when needed and Anne does the decorations.

At midnight they have their tasting tea of cookies and whatever the hostess
cares to serve. The cookies are divided for each one to take home. This has
been a fun thing to do each year.

        December 1981: Oscar finishes a sheet of cookies. Anne decorates
        while Virginia gives instructions.

COOPERATIVE EXTENSION SERVICE

Extension Service began its first service to Edmunds County in April 1918
when R.R. Buchanan was installed as an emergency agent. During the spring
of 1919 he was called to Roberts County and was followed by W.C. Boardman as
emergency agent. Following him came Dean Davis who continued his work here
until 1921. J. Carl Laney succeeded Davis from 1921-1923 as the last agent
to be employed up until the drought emergency period of 1933. During the
fall of 1933 Fred A. Beers was appointed emergency agent.

Boys and Girls Club work, now known as 4-H, had its first beginning in
1920. Club work then consisted of one main project such as livestock, corn,
gardening, canning, sewing, etc. The first 4-H club in the Bowdle area was
the Singing Needles led by Mrs. Gertrude Olson and Mrs. Alice Eisenbeisz in
1938.

Extension Homemakers was a new program for the women of Edmunds County in
1934. The first homemaker club in the Bowdle area was the Golden Rod Club
whose chairman in 1938 was Mrs. Robert deMalignon.

Extension work was rejuvenated in 1935 when the County Commissioners
appointed a County Extension Board. Members of the board were Wm. Stafford,
George Weishar, John J. Biegler, Richard F. Huber and J.A. Theis. They
proceeded to organize and hired Mr. A.D. Lienemann as the first County
Agricultural Agent Dec. 15, 1935. The first 4-H Achievement Days was held
during the summer of 1935, a joint effort with the women's program. The
first Corn Show was also held that fall.

H.C. Baer and M.A. Hoerner, both of Bowdle, were elected president and
director of the County Crop Improvement Association which was organized in
1939. Other charter members from Bowdle were Matt Bachman, John C. Gross,
F.G. Gross and A.E. Mardian.

The 4-H Achievement Days grounds were expanded in 1962 with the addition of
a livestock barn and again in 1972 with the construction of a large
all-purpose building.

The present Extension Agents are Carole Sweeter, Extension Home Economist
who assumed her duties in 1976 and Dale C. Curtis, County Agricultural
Agent who began in 1979. Their duties include serving as advisors to the
132 members in 12 4-H clubs. Other organizations they work with include
Extension Homemakers, Crop Improvement Association, Livestock Improvement
Association and County Weed Board, as well as numerous individuals on a
day-to-day basis.

The roots of the Extension Service have remained with the people of the
county due to the service of many dedicated extension board members over
the years. At present members of the board are Marvin Uhrich, Vernon
(Johnny) Oban, Virginia Spiry, Jan Heinz, Larry Olson and Sharon Sandmeier.

WALCO EXTENSION CLUB

Walco Club, a Walworth County Extension Club, was organized in 1950 with
Mrs. Jake Rabenberg of Selby assisting. Charter members still active
include Mrs. Art Bieber and Mrs. Norman Schumacher.

Ever extending education is the goal of Extension using the sociability of
a club's atmosphere to benefit both in subject matter and leadership skills.
Community service involvement through volunteerism benefits young and old.

Officers and project leaders rotate so all may experience leadership.
Members learn about nutrition, clothing, home management, citizenship, child
development, home furnishings, health, safety, international, recreation,
consumer education, money management, leisure activities and others. The
program is flexible, responding to new interests and needs.

The Christmas Kit has been laid aside. Joanne Bieber, Plunge to Pierre
chairperson, coordinates this opportunity for members to see their state
government in action and become better informed citizens.

Action booths and interest to the Christmas Fair began in 1960 with
visitors participating in crafts and skills. A Spring Tea is held on
alternate years featuring speakers and entertainment. Club booths feature
breads, aprons, table-setting, cookie capers, nature's leftovers, Norway,
dough art, gift wrapping and fantastic foam. Recipes were contributed to a
county book from favorites in the kitchen.

Children are counted as the most important of crops. Walco has served and
assisted 4-Hers on Achievement Days, sponsored the Spring Lake Lads &
Lassies 4-H Club, awarded shears to the 4-H Junior Dress Review winner. A
"Fun" activity such as a fish pond has been sponsored at the Bowdle
Mothers! Club Halloween Party for community children. Entertainment and
treats are provided twice annually for Bowdle Nursing Home residents. Less
fortunate such as persons at the Redfield State School are remembered with
cards and gifts. Contributions are made to the Memorial Art Center,
Crippled Children's Hospital, Agricultural Heritage Museum and other worthy
projects.

Highway safety was promoted with a float during the Bowdle 75th Jubilee and
the club helped serve during the Walworth County Centennial. Walco donates
books to the Martin Bieber Library.

Social meetings include hosting a Christmas dinner party, entertaining
husbands at a Valentine party or theatre and family picnics in July.
Educational tours have included Sieche Hollow, Dakotah Factory in Webster
and places of interest in Aberdeen such as the School for the Visually
Handicapped. Members attend state and national conventions including
Brookings in 1967 and Laramie, Wyoming in 1983. The list of benefits to
community, state and family through project participation is immeasurable.

Present members who continue to learn and serve are Millie Bieber, Beulah
Schumacher, Caroline Lee, Dorothy Mertz, Mardella Bieber, Carol Fiedler,
Joanne Bieber, Darlene Walz and Wanda Moser.

        Back row: Beulah Schumacher, Caroline Lee, Carol Fiedler, Millie
        Bieber, Dorothy Mertz. Front: Mardella Bieber, Joanne Bieber, Wanda
        Moser Darlene Walz.

ABC EXTENSION CLUB

The ABC Extension Club organized Oct. 5, 1950 at the Ernest Mertz home by
Mrs. Jake Rabenberg, county chairman. Throughout the years meetings were
held once a month. Some interesting demonstrations were given at each
meeting by one or two ladies.

Community service included helping the 4-H Clubs, donating to the Mothers'
Club and things to the Bowdle Hospital. The biggest project undertaken was
helping the school get new band uniforms. Fund raisers held were rummage
sales once or twice a week for several months, selling lunches, having cake
walks and a quilt was raffled in 1964.

Charter members are Dorothy Mertz, Florence Gramm and Anna Weiszhaar, Marie
Schumacher now deceased. At present the club has 10 members and one
honorary member.

SPRING LAKE LADS & LASSIES 4-H CLUB

In 1948 Mrs. Albert Stangl and Orville Stangl had an idea to help the youth
in their area ... to start 4-H clubs. Mrs. Stangl was successful in forming
the Spring Lake Lassies for girls with Beulah Schumacher and Ella Stangl as
leaders. It wasn't until 1949 that Orville succeeded in getting the Spring
Lake Gophers started. Because of overlapping membership, the two clubs
became one the next year and the Spring Lake Lads & Lassies came into
existence.

As the years evolved members were acquired from the surrounding areas of
Bowdle and Java. Other leaders were Mary Stangl, Elaine Stangl, Tom Stangl,
Willis and Joanne Bieber, Ernest Mertz Sr. and Henry Mueller.

4-Hers pledge their heads to clearer thinking and over the years the club
took part in many activities which developed the members' ability to
organize their thoughts and present them before an audience. The club won a
purple ribbon in the county parliamentary procedure contest. County and
state judging schools were hosted at the Stangl farm. Many 4-Hers won trips
to the State Fair in judging or demonstrations with topics as varied as
Ernie Mertz's ''Knots" or Valynn Perman's "Grandma's Kuchen." Share the Fun
gave the members a chance to get together to prepare such numbers as "Does
Your Chewing Gum Lose It's Flavor on the Bedpost Overnight?"

While pledging their hands to larger service the 4-Hers challenged
themselves to learn to make new or more difficult projects which included
beef, sheep, crops, gardening, safety, handicraft, clothing, foods and
others. Many were the times they gathered at the Willis Bieber home to make
handicraft or clothing articles or yeast breads. They enjoyed treating
their parents to a special meal that featured German cookery with the help
of Bertha Schuh and Delores Walz. An appreciative audience of mothers and
grandmothers enjoyed style shows. Many of the girls like Candice Bieber,
Valynn Perman and Cloris Schumacher represented Walworth County at the
State Fair Dress Revue.

Pledging their health to better living took many forms from safety and
health demonstrations like Scott and Gregg Bieber's "First Aid"
demonstration. It also included outdoor fun things like the trail ride at
Dwayne Lee's, 4-H Club Camp at Lake Richmond, Christmas caroling rural
people in the area, picnics and Christmas parties with Dean or Lance
Schumacher in charge of getting the "Twas the Night Before Christmas" acted
out.

While pledging their hearts to greater loyalty the 4-Hers learned how state
government works while visiting the South Dakota Legislature. Trips to the
School for the Visually Handicapped, K.O. Lee Company, TV studio and many
others broadened their horizons.

Eighty-four 4-Hers from 34 families were members of the Spring Lake Lads &
Lassies from 1949-1976. These young people learned to pledge their heads,
hearts, hands and health to their club, their community and their country.

BUSY BOWDLE STARS 4-H CLUB

The Busy Bowdle Stars 4-H Club had its roots with an extension club known
as the Friends and Neighbors Extension Club. Another forerunner of this
club was the Lucky Clover 4-H Club.

This club, Busy Bowdle Stars, actually began functioning in 1954 with Erma
Maier as the leader. She was assisted by Arlene Blumhardt who worked with
the girls and Maynard Lickfelt worked with the boys.

The first Christmas party was held in the Adam Thomas home. The county
agents were Oscar Prestegard and Elenore Gruebele. First members, according
to records, were Vivian Thomas, Carol Herman, Dolorita Thomas, Ellen
Hoffman, Chloe Blumhardt, Jacki Leno, Paul Blumhardt, Delbert Bachman,
Fulton Lickfelt, Richard, Sharon and Shirley Beitelspacher, Richard Maier,
Darrell Huft, Ronald Lickfelt, Donald and Joe Thomas.

The boys and girls had separate meetings to pursue their interests, but
regular monthly meetings were combined and held in the homes. Later the
white country schoolhouse became the meeting place. The girls called
themselves Busy Bowdle Bees and the boys used the present name Busy Bowdle
Stars.

Membership was often over 20 with the club working on fun projects such as
Valentine and Christmas parties, a banquet prepared by the girls for all
members, a cookout for the entire families and picnic. The club made it an
annual event to host parents at a sit-down cafe meal.

Erma Maier served as main leader until 1965 when she served as assistant
leader several years. During that time the club earned many trophies at the
county level for highest number of points and highest average per person.
The trophies are housed in a case the club provided in the 4-H building at
Ipswich.

Allene Eisenbeisz became the main leader in 1965. She has had several
assistant leaders throughout the years.

        Erma Maier      Allene Eisenbeisz

In recent years the Busy Bowdle Stars have been very active in citizenship
and community services with the hospital, nursing home and involved with
the general public. Some of the main projects remembered are planting
flowers near the hospital in the shape of a flag in 1976, painting the
city's fire hydrants, annual showing of animals (Mini Fair) at the nursing
home. Members are active in judging, showing exhibits and demonstrations.

Five members from the Busy Bowdle Stars have received the honor of being
chosen South Dakota delegates to attend the National 4-H Congress in
Chicago. This trip is the highest 4-H honor received for leadership in the
4-H program.

        Ellen Hoffman           Sheila Metzger          Hope Eisenbeisz

        Photography             General Achievement

Some of the members of the club have been chosen Edmunds County 4-H King or
Queen, namely Sheila Metzger in 1969, Blake Eisenbeisz in 1971; Marcie
Metzger in 1973 and Heidi Eisenbeisz in 1985.
