GEORGE and MAGGIE [WALTER] BIEBER

George immigrated to the U.S. from Drulingen, Alsace Lorraine, Germany in
1909. His wife, Maggie Walter, came with her parents from Crimea, South
Russia in 1913. They met and married in Gregory County in 1917 and came to
Walworth County in 1919 with their children, Alex and Elsie.

They first lived on a small farm one mile south of U.S. Highway 12, where
it turned north after coming west from Bowdle. Here Viola, Renata, George
Jr., Nettie and Delores were born and young Alex died in 1924. He is buried
in the Perman Cemetery.

In 1930 the Bieber family moved to the George Jergenson farm, 1-1/2 miles
farther southwest. The children were attending Erbe School and then
attended Perman School. The mailing address for both farms was Java, but
the family attended St. Paul's Evang. Lutheran Church in Bowdle.

Viola and Renata entered Bowdle High School in 1925, living in light
housekeeping rooms in homes of Anton Weishaar, Betty Baer and Albert Senn
during those four years, graduating in 1939. George Jr. also attended
Bowdle High School that last year freshman.

        Back: Nettie, Elsie, Viola, George Jr., Reny, Delores Front: George
        and Maggie Bieber.

The family suffered with the community through the "Dirty Thirties" with
the extra loss by fire, one bitter cold night in January 1939, when the big
barn burned. It housed not only the horses and cattle, but also pigs,
turkeys and the family car. Neighbors and friends were very supportive,
however, George's health had not been good and this loss hit him hard. The
following January the family held an auction and moved to a small house in
Mobridge. Renata was already attending business college in Omaha, NE; Viola
joined her there. George Jr., Nettie and Delores began school in Mobridge
immediately.

In August 1940 George died and is buried in Mobridge Cemetery. Maggie and
the three younger children managed to cope. Young George dropped out of
school and returned to the Java area to work on a farm. Nettie graduated
from The Lutheran Academy and Delores from Mobridge High School. Maggie
married Fred Ritter in 1943. Their marriage of 30 years ended with Fred's
death in 1973. Maggie continued to live in Mobridge. She visited her many
friends in Bowdle, Java and Selby whenever she had the opportunity. Her
last winters were spent with her children, always returning to South Dakota
in the spring. Having reached age 85, she died in January 1983.

Elsie married Bill Edmonds in Mobridge. Both are deceased, survived by
their six children and eight grandchildren.

Viola Kersting, widowed, lives in Powell, WY, as do her two sons. She has
seven grandchildren.

Renata (Renny) married Charles (Bud) Spitzner. They live in Green Cove
Springs, FL and have two sons and one daughter.

George Jr., his wife, Frances deceased, lives in Rapid City. He has one
son, two daughters and three grandchildren.

Nettie and husband Tom Shook live in Littleton, CO. Her son and daughter
live in the Denver area with their families. She has seven grandchildren.

Delores married Vern McNeely in Mobridge. They now live in Deaver, WY. They
have three sons, one daughter and seven grandchildren.

HENRY C. and FRIEDA [BENDER] BIEBER

Henry Christian Bieber was born Jan. 17, 1902 to John and Elizabeth
(Schumacher) Bieber in Java. July 28, 1946 he married Frieda Bender,
daughter of Martin and Barbara (Prezler) Bender of Eureka. She was born
July 29, 1918. They made their home on a farm two miles east of Bowdle and
were members of the American Lutheran Church. Henry was elected chairman of
the school board in 1934.

        Back: Noel, Perry, LaMae. Front: Frieda and Henry C. Bieber.

They have three children: Novell Frieda, born July 9, 1948. She graduated
from the Dallas, OR schools and April 26, 1977 married George Dewald of
Bowdle. They have two children: Jennifer Novell, born Feb. 10, 1976 and
Paul John, born Aug. 16, 1977. They live in Auburn, WA where Novell works
as a certified dietary supervisor at a nursing home in West Seattle and
George is employed at the Tyee Lumber Co. of Seattle.

Perry Henry Bieber was born Jan. 3, 1952 and graduated from the Dallas, OR
schools. He married Wanda Smith of Maple Valley, WA May 30, 1979. They have
a child from a previous marriage: April Sue Bieber, born June 16, 1973.
Auburn is their home and Perry works as maintenance supervisor for the Tyee
Lumber Co. and Wanda is employed as receptionist and secretary of the
Coastly Trailer Repair.

LaMae Barbara Bieber, born March 27, 1958, graduated from Bowdle and June
3, 1978 married Lenny Uhrich of Roscoe. Their children are Maia LaMae, born
Oct. 28, 1978 and Genevieve Frieda born July 17, 1980. They live on a dairy
farm seven miles south of Roscoe, operated by Lenny, his brother James and
their father Marvin Uhrich.

In February 1962 Henry and Frieda sold their farm and moved to Dallas, OR
where they farmed 150 acres until 1974 when they again sold and returned to
Bowdle to live on Third Avenue for five years. In December 1979, ill health
again caused them to take up their roots and move, this time to Auburn, WA
where they now reside.

Their four children from a previous marriage are: Edna (Bieber) Jacobs and
Alvin Bieber, Phoenix, AZ; Marvin Bieber of Los Angeles, CA and Harold
Bieber of Sumner, WA.

JACOB P. and ADELINE [LEIDHOLT] BIEBER

Jacob P. Bieber was born Feb. 4, 1893 in Russia and entered the United
States with his parents, Peter and Catherine Bieber, when seven years old.
They settled in the Tolstoy area. Peter Bieber was born Oct. 26, 1870 and
died Jan. 27, 1936. Catherine Marz Bieber was also born in Russia and died
in 1932.

Jacob P. Bieber married Adeline Leidholt Sept. 14, 1924. Adeline was born
Sept. 15, 1904 at Roscoe, where she attended the public school. She was the
daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Jacob Leidholt and had seven brothers and five
sisters. Her father was born April 1, 1877 and died July 27, 1941. Her
mother was born in Russia April 20, 1878 and died Nov. 3, 1951. Jacob and
Adeline had one child, a daughter Angeline, who came to brighten their
home. She was born at Mobridge.

        Adeline, Angeline, Jacob Bieber

They raised livestock, milked cows and used horses to farm the land,
headering, binding and then threshing the grain. They "lived off the land,"
butchering and preserving their own meat, raised a garden and canned the
surplus. "We experienced the joys and troubles through the years -- some
were good and some were otherwise," Adeline reminisces.

After they moved to town, Adeline worked at cleaning jobs at churches and
the Livestock Sales Pavilion to tide them over the rough spots. The years
have been busy ones, she states, but they enjoyed picnics, family
get-togethers and social entertainment. They joined the Redeemer Lutheran
Church. Jacob died April 30, 1966.

Adeline is now in the retirement years, but keeps busy with sewing,
gardening and canning and freezing foods and baking. She always loved hard
work and appreciates that life has brought her a host of relatives and
friends. She is happy to have her daughter and family living close by.

Angeline married Everet Lemke Sept. 21, 1952 and they have two daughters,
Candice and Cindy. Candice is now Mrs. Ron Williamson and lives in Edmond,
OK. They have two children, Jennifer and Anthony. Cindy Lemke (Chip) Lowens
is a resident of Pueblo, CO.

JOHANN and ELIZABETH BIEBER

Johann Bieber was born in Glueckstahl, Russia Nov. 4, 1869. He married
Elizabeth Schumacher at Eureka Dec. 2, 1890. She was born Dec. 30, 1872 at
Neuglueckstahl, Russia. They homesteaded 16 miles southwest of Bowdle.

        Johann and Elizabeth Bieber

Eleven children were born to them. After many years on the farm they
prospered, especially during the World War I years when grain prices were
high. They retired to live in Bowdle in 1919. Elizabeth died June 30, 1930
and Johann died Aug. 6, 1932. Of their children: Christine married Emanuel
Rieger and died July 1912; Elizabeth, born Sept. 27, 1892, married Jacob
Mertz and died Feb. 23, 1985; John F. Bieber, born Nov. 27, 1894, died
Sept. 27, 1972; Rosina, born March 10, 1899, married Alex Kiesz; Henry C.
Bieber was born Jan. 17, 1902; Rev. Martin Bieber was born Sept. 24, 1904;
Marie Bieber Schmierer, born Dec. 29, 1907, died Jan. 24, 1985; Arthur
Bieber, born June 3, 1910; Fred C. Bieber, born Jan. 20, 1914 and Bertha
Martha Bieber died in infancy.

JOHN F. and CECELIA [MILLER] BIEBER

John F. Bieber was born to Johann and Elizabeth Bieber Nov. 27, 1894 at
Eureka. While still a child his family moved to a farm 16 miles southwest
of Bowdle. John was one of 11 children. He attended rural school and
Eureka College. He helped his father on the farm until 1917 when he entered
the Armed Forces and served in France.

John married Cecelia Miller June 22, 1919 at Java. The daughter of Christ
and Karoline Miller, Cecelia was born May 3, 1901 at Java. She lived with
her family on a farm 13 miles southwest of Bowdle. Cecelia attended a
country school and helped with the housework until her marriage.

        Cecelia and John Bieber

John and Cecelia established their home on a farm 14 miles southwest of
Bowdle. Five children blessed this union. Edwin (born March 7, 1920)
married Margaret Johlfs and has four children. Ed is retired and lives in
Brainard, MN. Their winter home is in Green Valley, AZ. Viola (born Feb. 6,
1922) married Vernon O'Connor. She has four children and lives in Stockton,
CA. Otto (born Sept. 30, 1923) lives in Bowdle. Wilmer (born March 9, 1927)
married Doris Oster, lives in Grand Island, NE and has two children. Vivian
(born Aug. 22, 1928) married Sam Bass, has three children and lives in
Charleston, SC.

Like their neighbors John and Cecelia struggled during the "Dirty
Thirties." No crops grew. There was no grass and no money. The family held
barn dances in their hayloft to supplement the needed income. The Walzes
were often the musicians. There was absolutely no grass or feed in this
area in early 1934. In May John, along with his brothers Jake and Art and
their uncle Fred decided to chase their cattle to the West River ranges
where the pastures were said to be better. The animals had to swim across
the Missouri River on a day when temperatures were 109 degrees. Unseasonable
heat and drought dried up the ranges in that area also. Again the cattle
had to be moved. They were driven to Lowry, loaded on a train and
transported to the southern part of the state. Times were tough in those
days!

In 1942 John and Cecelia retired from farming and moved into Bowdle. Otto
took over the farming and John sold Farmers Union Insurance in the area.

The Biebers celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary in June 1969 and
enjoyed the visits of many relatives and friends who joined them on their
special day. Cecelia died Feb. 18, 1970 and John died Sept. 27, 1972.

MARK J. and JOANN [MAHLUM] BIEBER

Mark was born Oct. 21, 1950 at Mitchell. He is the son of Otto and Fernetta
Bieber. After Mark graduated from Bowdle in 1968, he attended one year of
college in Aberdeen and transferred to National College in Rapid City. He
graduated with a bachelor of science degree in agricultural business in
1973.

Mark and his wife Joann were blessed with their firstborn, a daughter
Jennifer, in April 1973. They spent the next two years in Rapid City where
Joann worked at First National Bank of the Black Hills and Mark worked at
Bear Country U.S.A., a drive-thru wildlife park in the Black Hills. Mark
spent some tense moments with the bears, mountain lions, wolves and
tourists. Breaking up a family picnic in the middle of the bear pen will
stay in their memory a long time.

        Back: Joann and Mark. Front: Erick and Jennifer

With Jennifer two years old and their son Erick (born May 1975) on the way,
they decided moving back to the family farm would be the best they could do
for their young family. They moved back in March 1975 in a blizzard and
spent eight of the next ten days in the house because of the weather.

The last 11 years have been spent investing time and energy into the family
and farm. Summers and falls are busy with farm work and custom work Mark is
involved in. Joann has been working at Bowdle State Bank since 1981. When
they have time off they spend a lot of it hunting and fishing as a family.

OTTO and FERNETTA [BLUMHARDT] BIEBER

Otto Bieber, born Sept. 30, 1923 to John and Cecelia Bieber, was their
third child. Otto grew up on a farm 13 miles southwest of Bowdle. He
attended rural school in the area and graduated from Bowdle High School.
His father retired in 1942 and Otto took over the family farm.

Fernetta (Blumhardt) Bieber was born Jan. 9, 1924 to Edwin and Esther
Blumhardt. She attended Bowdle grade and high school. In 1942 she attended
Northern State College and taught in a country school in the Eureka area
for two years. She then returned to Northern State College and received her
state certificate and later, her bachelor of science degree in elementary
education.

Otto and Fernetta were married Aug. 10, 1945. They lived on the home farm
where Otto raised grain, corn and fed many cattle. He also did custom
combining and aerial spraying. Fernetta became a homemaker.

The couple has two children: Mark and Candice; also a daughter-in-law
(Joann Mahlum) and a son in-law (Perry Hoffman) and four grandchildren.

        Back: Candice and Mark. Front: Fernetta and Otto

In 1976 Otto and Fernetta built a home and moved to Bowdle. Mark and his
family took over the family farm. Otto helps Mark and Perry during the
summer, often times being the go-pher... go for this and go for that. He
also has an aerial spraying business. He and Gary Forrette have been in
business 29 years. Otto loves to hunt, so in the fall he's busy hunting.
Fernetta returned to teaching and has been teaching first grade in Bowdle 19
years. She says, "I love it!"

Otto and Fernetta were reminiscing as to what it was like growing up in
this area: Otto remembers going to school on the farm, hitching up the horse
to the buggy in nice weather or sled in the winter. Knowing that every
Saturday night his family went to town, he recalls his mom bought groceries
and visited, his dad played cards and the kids ran and played with friends.
The stores were open late. They always had a five cent ice cream cone from
Jones Drug.

Fernetta remembers, "I could go to the creamery and get two cents from dad
to buy a piece of Bakers sweet chocolate at Braufman's Store. What a
thrill to buy my first summer coat. I even got a hat to match. This was
special because I had just graduated from the eighth grade. My grandmother
and mom always made my clothes.

"Knowing everyone in the area, greeting everyone you meet during the day
and stopping to chat or giving them a smile, yes, we've decided it's nice
living in a small town, isn't it?"

WILLIS and JOANNE [MASTELLER] BIEBER

Willis Arthur Bieber was born Nov. 14, 1932 to proud parents Art and Millie
Bieber at their rural home. He went to rural school and graduated from
Bowdle High School in 1950. He attended one year of college at SDSU and
served in the U.S. Occupation Army in Korea. Before entering the service, he
met Joanne Masteller at a conference basketball tournament dance in Bowdle.
Romance blossomed and after his stint in the service and her graduation
from SDSU, they were married June 16, 1957.

Willis and Joanne made their home on the "Commet" place eight miles
southwest of Bowdle. Two sons were born to them: Scott Brian in 1958 and
Gregg Alan in 1961. The boys attended and graduated from the Bowdle
Schools. Scott graduated from USD in 1980 and is a Certified Public
Accountant. He married Lynelle Haak of Dell Rapids May 5, 1984. Gregg
graduated from USD in 1985 with a degree in psychology.

        Scott, Gregg, Joanne, Willis Bieber

One of the things the family will always remember is the blizzard of 1966.
The electricity was off for three days. Dining and living with candlelight
was really fun, according to the boys. Mom fixed a stand so soup and other
food could be heated above a candle. The cattle wandered over the snow
covered fences, pushed by the storm. Willis had Orville Walz fly him around
to find them. The poor cattle had snow crusted faces and some had frozen
feet.

The whole family was active in 4-H Club work with Joanne (20 years) and
Willis (5 years) as leaders of the Spring Lake Lads & Lassies. Often times
10-23 young people would gather at our home for crafts and workshops. One
bread workshop had girls and some boys around the long dining room table.
One 4-Her's dough just stuck to her hands like an accordion no matter what
she did. A little extra help from Joanne got it to the "kneading" stage.
The mothers came in the afternoon to taste and declared it was all
delicious! It's a good thing they didn't see it at one particular stage!

The Biebers raise feed grains for their cow-calf operation and they buy
feeder calves when there is surplus feed. Willis loves to talk about, ride
and train horses. Joanne enjoys being involved in community activities such
as Bowdle City Public Library, ALCW, 4-H and Extension work.

ALMA BINDER

Alma Binder, a registered nurse who spent 17 years in Ethiopia, Africa,
watches that nation with concern, understanding and sympathy for the
hardships the natives there are suffering.

Alma, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Christ Binder, grew up on a farm south of
Bowdle, took her nurse's training at Chamberlain and the University of
Minnesota, attended Pacific College at Angwin, CA, graduating with a
bachelor of science degree in nursing.

The mission fields were calling for help and in 1948 the General Conference
of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, held in the World Headquarters in
Washington, DC, again called for her services in the foreign field. Alma
responded, but it took seven months to obtain a visa to Ethiopia after
World War II. In March 1949 she left by boat for Ethiopia, via Egypt.

Eighteen months later, at the request of the Mission doctors, Alma and Lois
Bowen, RN, were organizing a School of Nursing in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia,
with Alma serving as Administrator of the School and Director of Nursing.

She met His Highness, the Emperor Haile Selassie, when he came to visit
patients in the hospital. The Emperor proudly traced his ancestry back to
David, King of the Hebrew nation. She said he was a quiet, gentle person
and it was not unusual for his subjects to request money gifts from him,
which he would grant. He was anxious to improve the standard of living for
the natives and desired that schools and hospitals be established in his
country.

When the Empress became seriously ill, Alma was called to the palace to
care for her and spent as much time as possible with her for the next three
months, until her death, which was signaled by a 21 gun salute.

Alma found it difficult to enjoy the Ethiopian food, but some of the
foreign nurses really relished it. American foods were too expensive for
people there due to having it to be shipped in. A goodly supply and variety
of vegetables provided adequate nourishment, all grown in that country.

Miss Binder found it a wonderful place to meet people from other countries,
especially when staff members of foreign embassies needed medical care. A
new and very well-equipped 110-bed hospital was built by the Seventh-day
Adventist Mission in 1969.

After her return in 1966, Miss Binder served as Administrator of Bowdle
Nursing Home and then went to Walla Walla, WA where she was director of
nursing several years until her parents illness brought her home again.
From 1970 to 1972 she worked in Hinsdale, IL and when her mother suffered a
heart attack, returned to Bowdle where she has continued to make her home.
She contributed much to her hometown through her services as administrator
and director of nursing in the Bowdle Hospital.

CHRIST and ROSE [NIES] BINDER

The Michael Binder family moved from the Menno-Scotland area in South
Dakota in the late 1870's, settling on land 13 miles west of Leola. His
wife was the former Magdalena Rueb. They had seven sons and two daughters.
Christ was one of the younger boys and he was allotted the job of herding
cattle.

One time while Christ and his brother, Dan were with the cattle and
entertaining themselves with a .22 rifle which they had acquired, a
ricocheting bullet hit Christ in the leg and passed on through. Tragedy
struck the family in 1904 when Magdalena was burned in the explosion of a
kerosene stove which took her life.

Michael later married a Mrs. Zumbaum and while they were visiting in the
Scotland area, in 1905 Michael contracted typhoid fever and died. After his
father's death, Christ came to stay and work for his brother Fred in
Tolstoy.

Being in the Dollinger-Nies community, he met Rose Nies and Feb. 14, 1910
they were married in her parents' home. During that day a severe snowstorm
developed and all the wedding party had to stay overnight. The night was
spent visiting and eating peanuts. Christ and Rose started farming a mile
east of his brother Fred's farm. Here three children were born to them:
Alma, Albert and Melvin. The 1918 flu tragedy struck Rose's parents' home
when John, Katherine and Carl were victims of the epidemic.

        Back: Melvin, Alma, Albert, Betty. Front: Rose and Christ Binder

Christ and Rose and their children moved to the Jacob Nies family farm
where they lived until they retired to live in Bowdle in 1946. In 1925 a
sweet little sister arrived and was called Betty Jean. She was the idol of
her Uncle John who lived with the family.

Alma took nurse's training in Chamberlain and went as a missionary to
Ethiopia, serving there 17 years. On her return she worked in various places
and then came to be with her parents and cared for them until their deaths.
She now lives in the Christ Binder home and held different positions at the
Bowdle Hospital until the fall 1983. Nebraska

Melvin Binder started to teach in a Nebraska high school. He had married
Frieda Womask. To this union one son, Jerry and one daughter, Bonnie were
born. Melvin taught at Plainview Academy in Redfield. Later he worked in
the business office of the New England Sanitarium and Hospital in
Massachusetts. Dissatisfied with teaching, Melvin went to the University of
Nebraska and took up dentistry. He worked for Dr. Bowman in College Place,
WA and later settled in Colfax, WA where he practiced his profession until
he retired in 1983.

Albert and his father operated the farm until Christ retired to live in
town. He is still farming on the home place. In 1936 he married Lillian
Eisenman and to this union two sons were born, Dennis and Curtis. They were
divorced in 1956. Albert married Olga Ferguson of Leola in 1983.

Betty graduated from the Academy and attended Union College and taught
school for several years. During this time she was married to Ken Brenneise
for a short time. She took a business course and worked in an insurance
office in Portland, OR. Here she met and married Eugene Dennis. They lived
at White Salmon, WA until the time of her husband's death in September 1982.
They had two sons Peter and Dale.

EMMA BINDER

A precious gift of a handkerchief, embroidered by someone in India,
intrigued Emma Binder, who has yet to use the article, but three calls for
help took her to India in 1932 where she served in hospitals 20 years.

Emma taught school in South Dakota five years before she left for Los
Angeles, CA to attend the Seventh-day Adventist School of Nursing. During
that time she earned her way through the school years as students were paid
25 cents an hour for floor duty, but that had to be used to pay for meals
and other necessities, so there were no trips home to be with her family.

After receiving her registered nursing degree she spent three months at
Berkeley University to study administration and then did practical work at
Oakland County Hospital. During this time she had been called to do
missionary nursing in India and the Philippines, but felt she was not ready
for the responsibility.

In October 1931 she received a call from a doctor, with whom she had
worked, to serve in India and returned to her family near Bowdle to
consider her answer. March 5, 1932, after a two-week visit with her
parents, Mr. and Mrs. Frederick Binder, she boarded the eastbound flyer out
of Bowdle for Chicago, then to New York where she boarded the German liner,
"The Potsdam" for South Hampton, England. A terrible storm, which whipped
up the waves over the ship, made for a rough trip and Emma found the best
solution for sea sickness was to stay flat in her bed.

From South Hampton, she went to London by train to the Mission, staying in
a hotel. Humorously she recalled going out the first morning to see the
city and failed to check her address and soon found she was confused. An
English Bobby, noting her concern, inquired where she wished to go and
directed her back.

She crossed the English Channel and went by train to Marseille, France,
boarded the S S Rampura to cross the Mediterranean to Egypt, crossed the
Red Sea and finally landed in Bombay, India.

Her first encounter with the rural natives was to see a woman sitting
against a tree, spitting red fluid from her mouth. Emma's reaction was "how
much tuberculosis there must be here, that she sits spitting out blood and
contaminating everything!" The native was chewing betel nuts, which stain
the teeth and have a narcotic effect. Arriving at the headquarters of the
Seventh-day Mission, she found she was to go by train to Poona, a large
city southeast of Bombay. She found the Nuzvid hospital a busy place,
consisting of two buildings, one for men patients and the other for women.
She had hardly more than arrived when she was called to help with emergency
surgery. What was then a 50-bed hospital is now a 150-bed hospital. The
Lutheran Mission had a 50-bed hospital and school of nursing, but it was 50
miles away, but they were in the same language area and were very helpful.

There were no graduate nurses at the hospital. Emma had to supervise the
aides and give all medication. Six months after her arrival the medical
doctor said they must start a school for nurses because the aides did not
have the skill needed. By the time Emma had been at the hospital eight
months they had established a school of nursing with Emma as administrator
of the hospital and director of nursing.

After twenty years of service Emma was called to Pakistan where she again
helped to start a school of nursing. Despite every effort, it took five
years to obtain a permit to open the school. In 1956 Emma was called to
Burma, again to start a nursing school, but in 1961 all foreigners were
declared personna non-grata and the government took over the hospital.

Emma returned to the States in 1961 and accepted the position of director
of nursing at the Seventh-day Adventist Sanitarium in Portland, OR. Not
long afterwards, the needs of a very ill patient at the 300-bed facility
called her back to the hospital at 5 a.m., after having gone off duty at 11
p.m. While making rounds with a tray of medicine that early morning, she
tripped, severely injuring her knee. Eight months later she returned to
work, but this time she responded to a call to Zambia, South Africa.

There the hospital was a hut in the jungle. She was responsible not only
for the patients, but also for 300 in little huts in the leper colony. It
was her first experience with leprosy.

Emma Binder returned home in 1970 from Africa and until 1978 did volunteer
relief work in Africa and twice in Pakistan. She says that life has been
wonderful and as she did not have a home to keep up, she was able to visit
Europe, spent six weeks in China and walked the China Wall and visited
other interesting places. During her many travels she was routed through
Beirut, Lebanon and says at that time it was a beautiful city. She is sorry
to see its destruction today.

If she could, Emma said she would do the same thing all over again, only
better. In 1983 the director of the school of nursing prepared a history of
the school and the Giffard Memorial Hospital, which was dedicated to "our
beloved Miss Emma Binder, whose dedicated service has been a source of
enlightenment to us." Her lovingly care for each student and their progress
was her happiness. The aim of the Class of 1972 was, "To lead suffering
souls to the Might Healer" and their motto "To comfort the afflicted."

FREDRICK and CHRISTINA BINDER

Fredrick Binder, eldest son of Michael and Magdalena (Rueb) Binder, was
born in 1876 in Glueckstahl, Russia. Fredrick came to the United States
with his parents when he was nine years old. His education was home-taught,
learning as he helped his parents build up and manage the farm. He repaired
the family's shoes, making and repairing harness for the oxen and horses.

Fredrick married Christina Dollinger Jan. 1, 1900, whose parents Philip and
Barbara Dollinger lived about 7-1/2 miles south of Bowdle. Fredrick had
homesteaded on land in the Leola area and in 1905 sold his homestead to his
father and bought a small farm in Madison Township. He planted many trees
including an orchard, but the cold harsh winter winds, drought and
hailstorms took their toll. With his youthful ardor, courage and trust in
Divine Power he managed to prosper through the years.

        Christina and Fredrick Binder

Fredrick and Christina had seven children. Emma and Dena were born in
Leola. The other children were Magdalena, Samuel, Helen, John and Leon.

Christina died in June 1937 and Fredrick died in 1943 at his home in Bowdle.

Because she was the firstborn March 1, 1901, Emma felt responsible for the
welfare of the other members of the family and helped at home all she
could. When a teenager her father hitched up a 3-horse team to plow and
sent her to a field. When he came later he was dismayed because her furrows
were not straight. He took the reins and Emma cried all the way home
because she had not done as expected.

She attended college and taught in the home school and received $80 a month
salary. Later she got $120 a month to teach three grades in the Tolstoy
School and was on "cloud nine" over the increase of $40 a month. Because of
the times most of her income went home to help with family finances and
taxes. It was at Tolstoy that the school board told her, "you take care of
the discipline problems, we don't want them." A student whose pleasure was
to tease liked to hit the younger children. He was changed in his
deportment when Emma suggested that he protect the smaller pupils. The
lower grade children thought he was something special because he rode a
bicycle to school and carried a crutch due to the effects of polio. Another
pupil insisted on talking out of turn, creating a disturbance. Suddenly he
found a hand over his mouth. His parents (like all parents of that day)
when told of the incident said, "He is in trouble in school, but in twice
as much at home because of his behavior." No more disturbance.

Emma later taught in the Plainview Academy at Redfield and then became a
registered nurse and served as a missionary in the Far East.

Dena, born Dec. 8, 1902, was a grade school teacher for 38 years and is the
wife of Fred Holweger. Their children are Quentin, DDS, who married Beverly
Gackenheimer and has three children. Gayle Holweger married Sharon Ennis
and is a farmer and carpenter. They have four children. Ronald Holweger
married Karla McTaggert. He served as a Major in the U.S. Army, majoring in
Opthamology. They have two children.

Magdalena Binder, born July 4, 1904, married Julius Voegele. She has been a
teacher and has two children. Twila, a teacher and wife of Mr. Bauer, has
two children. Wayne married Darlena Stanford, is a teacher and regional
director of nursing homes. They have three children.

Samuel Binder, born April 6, 1906, was a farmer and teacher of mathematics
in Rapid City High School 16 years.

Helen Binder, born Jan. 2, 1910, married Elmer Holweger. She was a teacher
by profession and died in 1972.

John Binder, born May 28, 1912, married Malida Voegele. He was an auto
mechanic and farmer. He had one daughter.

Leon W. Binder was born Oct. 1, 1918, served as a Lieutenant in the U.S.
Army and is now in business. He married Emma Wolf. They have two children.

        Back: Magdalena, Helen, Sam, Emma. Front: John, Leon, Dena.

MICHAEL and MAGDALENA [RUEB] BINDER

Michael Binder and his wife Magdalena (Rueb) Binder left Glueckstahl,
Russia via the seaport of Odessa in 1884 to come to America bringing their
children Frederick, born in 1876; Mike, born in 1877; Jacob, born in 1879
and John, born in 1881 with them. On their arrival at Ellis Island, NY they
had to clear customs and quarantine and then proceeded by train to Tyndall
where their uncle, Michael Binder met them. Other relatives welcomed them
in the late fall of 1884 anxious to hear news of friends and relatives left
in the old country. While living at Uncle Michael's, the fifth child, a
daughter Emma, was born to Michael and Magdalena.

They were disappointed to find there was no more land available for
homesteading in the Tyndall area, but free land was available to the north.
They got together a few of the most needed items, such as a pair of oxen,
double-box wagon, some tools, a single plow, lantern and other necessities.
One pair of shoes had to do for two of the boys during the first year of
their great adventure. By springtime they were in Ipswich and found
homestead land available in McPherson County. It was a long, slow journey
moving at oxen's pace and often the meals were "on wheels" on a not so much
traveled road. They arrived at Leola and the Dakota Territory government
officials directed them to land 13l/2 miles west of Leola. A record in
McPherson County Courthouse states Michael Binder homesteaded in 1885 and
seven years later paid in full for the land to the General Office, U.S.A.
Dakota Territory. Later his children also filed on land in this area. The
land was marked with flat meadows, grass covered hills and mounds with
ponds and lakes.

Michael and Magdalena Binder chose to make their home on a grass covered
mound west of Leola. The first weeks they were sheltered in a dugout under
the up-turned wagon box. Fuel was hard to come by but bleached animal bones
littered the prairie and these were picked up for fuel and sometimes sold
to buy necessities. The pioneers broke the sod and made bricks for building
their home and later, as more rooms were needed, they were built on.

Four more children were born to Michael and Magdalena. Daniel arrived in
1887, Christoph in 1889, Martha in 1892 and Benjamin in 1894.

The children born in the United States had a better opportunity to get an
education than those born in Russia. The older ones were needed to help
with the farm work. Magdalena Binder died in 1905 when a fire engulfed the
whole house and she could not find her way out. The family suffered the sad,
grim, sudden loss of a loving mother's care. Five years later, in 1908
Michael Binder took a trip to Tyndall where he contracted typhoid fever and
died on his return. Both were buried in their garden plot surrounded by the
trees he had planted.

JACOB G. and EMELIA [SCHICK] BITZ

Jacob G. Bitz was born Jan. 25, 1901 in Russia to Gustave and Elizabeth
(Becker) Bitz. He came to the United States in 1909 with his parents and
they settled in the Eureka area. He married Emelia Schick Jan. 22, 1922.
They have five children: Mildred Aldinger, Bowdle; Pearl Murnane, Decatur,
IL; Raymond, Rapid City; Marvin, Aberdeen and Keith, Tomah, WI.

They moved to Bowdle from Eureka in March 1926 when Jacob purchased the
Standard Oil Agency. During World War II he worked in the Kaiser Shipyards
at Vancouver, WA. He returned to Bowdle in 1945 where he owned and operated
J.G. Bitz Plumbing & Heating until his retirement.

Mr. Bitz continues to live in his home in Bowdle.

CLINTON and ARLISS [SCHLEPP] BLUMHARDT

at the Bowdle Hospital. She attended eight years of grade school at O'Neil
School District southwest of Bowdle and graduated from Bowdle High School in

After graduation she attended a session at NSC and taught at a farm school
for two years. She married Clinton Blumhardt, son of Hugo and Jacobina
Blumhardt July 14, 1953 at St. Paul American Lutheran Church in Bowdle.

After completing his Army term the family moved back to the farm east of

Cafe at Leola and are operating this business today.


        Back: Miles, Arliss, Florinda, Craig, Clinton, Wayde Front: Deb and
        Beth.

EDWIN and ESTHER [STEVENS] BLUMHARDT

Edwin was born March 9, 1902 to John and Katherine Blumhardt. His first
home was a sod house. He lived with his parents on a farm northeast of
Bowdle until 1913. He attended rural school near there. His father's ill
health forced them to leave the farm and move to Bowdle. His father died
six months later, so his mother got a job cooking at a Bowdle restaurant
owned by the Elmer Jacksons. Edwin often told how good this family was to
his widowed mother and her three children, of which Edwin was the oldest.

He went to school in Bowdle and after school, went down to the cafe to wash
dishes and wait on tables. As he became older he did lots of painting,
especially school houses, working with Art Stuart. He remembered the
swallowed tail coat, which was his school coat, which was given to him.
(Edwin did not like it, but it was all he had to wear.) He attended Mankato
Commercial College and returned to manage the Farmers Cream Association. He
then became manager of the Bowdle Creamery and remained there for 44 years,
until his retirement in 1970.

Edwin was the Mayor of Bowdle when the city celebrated its Golden Jubilee.
He was a member of the volunteer fire department and was on the hospital
board the year it was built. He belonged to the Sportsmen's Club and was an
avid fisherman and hunter.

Edwin married Esther Stevens in 1923 at St. John's Lutheran Church in
Bowdle. He died May 7, 1976.

Esther was born April 9, 1906 to Mark and Mary Stevens. Her mother died
when she was 4 years old so she and three other children were raised by
their father. She attended a rural school northeast of Bowdle which was
near their farm home.

        Esther and Edwin Blumhardt

As a little girl the highlight of the year was going to town with her dad
in a top buggy pulled by a single horse. It was an 18 mile trip. Aurand's
owned the general store and Esther longed for a new summer hat she saw in
it. Her dad couldn't afford the one she just loved, so she chose another,
which she wore to town for the Fourth of July Celebration. On the way home
a shower came up and her lovely hat got wet, the flowers and beautiful
ribbons faded, the colors ran and fell apart. The hat disintegrated!

When Esther was 13 her father and she moved to Bowdle where she attended
school.

She states that walking the railroad tracks (the many trains going through
Bowdle was exciting) and making and pulling taffy was often the young
people's Sunday entertainment.

Quilting bees were fun, too. The ladies would hurriedly got their housework
finished in the morning and then go quilting in the afternoon, then rush
home for supper and back to quilting in the evening. The hostess served
lunch both afternoon and evening! Often times the ladies would quilt for a
week at someone's house, then the next week go to another home to quilt.
These were enjoyable times.

Esther still lives in Bowdle and is known for her beautiful flowers and
yard. She also makes many lovely afghans. She is a charter member of the
Bowdle Hospital Auxiliary; has belonged to the Bettes Bowdle Club (Now ABC
Extension Club) for many years; belonged to St. John's Lutheran Ladies Aid
for 61 years and still is an active member. Esther was named Senior Woman
of the Year in 1968. She is a member of the Bowdle Senior Citizens.

Edwin and Esther had two children: Fernetta (Blumhardt) Bieber, who resides
in Bowdle and Howard Blumhardt who resides in Houston, TX.

FRANK and KAROLINE [WALTH] BLUMHARDT

GERHARD and EVA [DOERRl BLUMHARDT

Gerhard Blumhardt was born March 31, 1902 on a farm in Cottonwood Lake
Township where his parents had homesteaded. He is the son of Karl and
Rosina (Nuss) Blumhardt.

He was confirmed at Hosmer Lutheran Church in 1916 by Pastor Richard
Toubert. While attending country school some of his teachers were Emily
Green, Hazel Cook, Lucy Lutz and Ina Adams. He graduated from eighth grade
in 1915, passing an examination sent from Pierre. He is the seventh of ten
children.

Nov. 25, 1923 he was united in marriage to Eva Doerr of Bowdle. She was
born Jan. 26, 1902 in Walworth County to Jacob and Katherina (Bauder)
Doerr. She is the fifth of nine children: Jake, George, Gottlieb, Lisa
(Merkel), Eva, Christine (Koch), Rosina, Albert and Caroline (Babberl.)

Her family came to Walworth County in 1894 where they homesteaded seven
miles southwest of Bowdle. Eva was baptized in June 1902 by Pastor George
Kirchdoerfer in Java. She attended South Spring Lake School for six years.
Two teachers were Frank Tinker and Teresa Cain. In 1915 she was confirmed
at the ALC Church in Java in a class of 21, a combined class from seven
congregations.

World War I began and farm laborers were in short supply so Eva remained at
home and farmed and ranched with her father and brother. She and her
sisters did much of the field work and the milking.

Gerhard and Eva farmed with Karl and Hugo Blumhardt for three years. They
lived on farms south of Bowdle until 1937 when they purchased the Joseph
Krumm farm 4 miles northeast of Bowdle.

Establishing their own farm was very hard work. However, cooking is Eva's
natural talent and homecooked meals and home-baked bread have been the
daily menu in their home for over 60 years. Gerhard's hobby is carpentry
and every building had to be remodeled. They had "electricity" from a 110
volt generator, driven by gas engine for five years. He was township clerk
for 20 years and on the County Extension Board six years. In 1950 REA
electricity carne and 1952 they built their new home. They retired on the
farm and are still living there today.

        Arlene, Eva, Wilbert, Gerhard, Paul Blumhardt

They have three children: Wilbert born 1925, Arlene 1932 and Paul 1941.

Paul has an identifying feature, red hair. He attended grade school in
Bowdle and graduated from Northwestern Lutheran Academy in Mobridge in
1959. He attended NSC in Aberdeen two years and was then employed by USDA
Soil Conservation Service at Kennebec. Later he was District Forester in
Aberdeen seven years and City Forester four years. He has been City
Forester of Bismarck, ND since 1978. In 1964 he married Jody Rigney of
Kennebec. They have two children: Douglas, a sophomore at BJC and Kristi, a
high school junior.

Arlene also graduated from NLA in Mobridge in 1950. She attended DMLC in
New Ulm, MN for two years and taught country school around Bowdle for
several years. She married Walter Antolak in 1961 in St. Paul, MN. They
have one daughter Anita. In 1962 they moved to Denver, CO where they still
reside. Walter was self-employed for a number of years as a wood finisher.
He died in 1982. Arlene has been employed for many years as a marketing
associate in life insurance business. She is currently with the Empire
General Life Insurance Co. of Denver. Anita also lives in Denver, employed
at Big A Auto Parts.

Their son. Wilbert, has a separate history in this book

GLENN and CATHERINE [FISCHER] BLUMHARDT

Catherine Ann Blumhardt was born Oct. 27, 1953 to Walter and Clara Fischer

in May 1971. Catherine has one brother Robert, who resides in Rapid City.

Glenn Allan Blumhardt was born to Wilbert and Hertha Blumhardt Oct. 22,
1963. Glenn was raised on the family farm east of Bowdle and attended both
grade and high school at Bowdle. Glenn has one sister Wynn Sudtelgte of
Laramie, WY.

Glenn and Catherine attended college. Catherine began her college career at
USD and later transferred to SDSU in Brookings. Glenn also attended SDSU.

Aug. 9, 1974 the childhood classmates and high school sweethearts were wed
at St. Paul American Lutheran Church in Bowdle. The couple returned to SDSU
for their remaining year of college. Glenn earned his B.S. degree in soil
science and Catherine earned her B.S. degree in home economics in May 1975.

The couple moved back to Bowdle after graduation and Glenn began farming
with his father. Catherine went to work at the Bowdle State Bank.

In 1976 Glenn and Catherine purchased the former St. Paul's ALC parsonage
and have been at home there since. In July 1977 the Board of Education at
Bowdle School hired Catherine as the school district business manager.

Glenn has been active in church office, commercial club, fire department
and city council.

HOWARD J. And JOAN [TISDALL] BLUMHARDT

Howard J. Blumhardt was born to Edwin J. and Esther (Stevens) Blumhardt
Nov. 29, 1928. He attended Bowdle School, graduating in 1946. Howard was
very active in band and basketball. He was voted all-conference and
all-district for three years as a member of the Bowdle Cossacks basketball
team. He attended the University of South Dakota, graduating in 1950 with a
bachelor of arts degree. While at the University he was football
all-conference team member in 1947, 1948 and 1949 and Little All-American
in 1947.

Howard married Joan Tisdall of Mobridge in May 1950. They had five sons:
Jon Howard in 1951, Thomas Michael in 1954, William Jerome in 1957, James
Richard in 1959 and Robert Morris in 1960.

        Howard and Joan Blumhardt

Howard entered the U.S. Army in 1950 as a 2nd lieutenant and went to Korea
in August 1950 where he served with the 7th Infantry Division until he was
severely wounded Dec. 3, 1950. He returned to the U.S. for hospitalization
in Denver and Colorado Springs CO. While Howard served in the Korean War
his wife Joan taught 2nd and 3rd grades in Bowdle. From 1951 to 1967 he
served at military installations in Fort Benning, GA; Trieste, Italy;
Livorno, Italy; Linz, Austria; Munich, Germany; Fort Riley, KS; Boonsville,
MO; Fort Leavenworth, KS and South Vietnam.

In 1968 he was assigned to the Pacific Command in Honolulu, HI where he
remained five years, though much of this time was spent flying to Vietnam,
Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Australia, New Zealand, England, Japan, Taiwan
and the Philippines. Howard and his family were back in the states in 1973,
located at Boston, MA where they lived until 1976 when he retired with the
rank of full Colonel. Howard saw 26 years of service in the military.

They returned to live in Aberdeen, but did not like retirement and the cold
winters so when he was offered a position as a Senior Scheduling Engineer
for Strategic Oil Reserve Program in New Orleans, LA he accepted. In 1980
he was promoted to Strategic Site Manager in Lake Charles, LA. The project
was completed in 1981 and he was transferred to Houston, TX to be project
manager for Geo Pressure/Geo Thermal Energy Research and Development.

Howard and Joan currently reside in an all-adult golf community in Houston.
He adds, "We are most proud to be grandparents to five beautiful children."

HUGO and JACOBINA [WEISZ] BLUMHARDT

Hugo Blumhardt was born March 20, 1904 in Edmunds County, north of Bowdle,
to Karl and Rosina Nuss Blumhardt. He attended rural school in Edmunds
County and later farmed with his father on the family homestead.

Jacobina Ruth Weisz was born at Lowry Oct. 2, l909 to Gustave and Katherine

        Hugo and Jacobina Blumhardt

until their retirement in 1956. They moved to Bowdle and Hugo worked for a

Creamery.

Hugo died at the age of 94 at St. Mary's Hospital Sept. 11, 1978 in
Rochester, MN. Jacobina died Oct. 1, 1980 at Swedish Hospital in Englewood,
CO. At the time of her death she was staying with her daughter Chloe and
was receiving medical treatment in Colorado.

The Blumhardt couple was blessed with three children: Clinton, Rodney and
Chloe. Clinton married Arliss Schlepp (daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Adam

have three children: Troy of Arvada; Tricia, a junior at Arvada High School
and Traci, a sophomore at Arvada High School.

JOHN and KATHERINE [WALTH] BLUMHARDT

John Blumhardt was born in 1873 in Gallant, Crimea to Karl and Mary
Blumhardt Sr. His formal education was limited to three grades. In 1893 he
came to the United States with his family. They settled in the Bowdle area
where his brother Karl had migrated three years earlier. Upon their arrival
in the Bowdle area the family lived in a sod house and John labored at
whatever work was available. He broke sod with oxen and a hand plow. He was
also a carpenter.

Katherine Walth, the oldest of 10 children, was born Dec. 18, 1880 to Jacob
and Katherine Walth in Glueckstahl, South Russia. Katherine attended school
for three years in Glueckstahl. In 1889 she migrated to the U.S. with her
parents. She often recalled the crowded conditions on the boat. The Walth
family homesteaded northeast of Hosmer. Katherine was employed by other
homesteaders as the "hired girl" doing housework and outside chores. She
was always a stylish lady and remembers how she hid her corset in the
haystack so her father wouldn't know she had one. Then when she "went out"
she'd get her corset from the haystack and put it on. Katherine weighed 90
pounds!

Jan. 15, 1901 John and Katherine were married in Bowdle by Pastor G.C.
Gehm. They homesteaded 10 miles northeast of Bowdle. Their first home was
of sod. They later built a wooden house. In 1913 John's health failed,
forcing him to quit farming. He and his family moved into Bowdle. He died
April 18, 1915, leaving three children: Edwin 13, Edgar 9, Althea 5 and his
widow.

Katherine then worked in Jackson's Cafe, taking Althea to work with her
each day. She often told how good the Jacksons were to her and her family.
The two boys came to the cafe after school to help also. She raised
chickens and a big garden each summer. These foods were preserved and
stored for winter's use. She took in sewing and sewed many dresses for 25
cents each. Customers didn't always have a pattern. At times Katherine's
only guide was a picture cut out of the Sears Roebuck catalogue.

Katherine was very thrifty and a hard worker. She was happy to see all of
her children educated. Edwin graduated from Mankato Business College, Edgar
attended barber's school and Althea became a registered nurse after
receiving her training at Red Wing, MN. Katherine maintained that "where
there is a strong will, there is a way!"

        Katherine Blumhardt

All was not hard work though. Katherine was an initial member of St. John's
Lutheran Ladies Aid. She loved to quilt and attended many quilting bees
throughout the city. She enjoyed running and would run races with her
grandchildren. She was a jogger" of her day.

Katherine lived in her own home until 1964 when she went to live in the
Eureka nursing home. She died Oct. 13, 1966.

KARL JR. and ROSINA [NUSS] BLUMHARDT

Karl Jr. was born March 21, 1866 in Russia to Karl and Marie (Kilber)
Blumhardt. He married Rosina Nuss at Odessa, South Russia March 25, 1888.
She was born Dec. 26, 1866 in Russia.

Karl and Rosina came to the United States in 1890 and lived at Freeman
until 1892 when they homesteaded near Bowdle in Cottonwood Lake Township.
After 32 years of farming they retired and moved into Bowdle.

Rosina died at age 91 in October 1957. Karl died at age 99 in June 1965.

They were the parents of 10 children: Mary, Barney, Josephine (Pressler),
Emanuel, Reinhold, Richard, Gerhard, Hugo, Lydia (Baer) and Eugene. All are
deceased except Gerhard, who resides on a farm near Bowdle.

Glenn Blumhardt, a great-grandson, now farms the homesteaded land.

PHILIP and CHRISTINA [WALTH] BLUMHARDT

Philip Blumhardt came to Dakota Territory with his parents in 1893 at the
age of eight years. They homesteaded nine miles northeast of Bowdle. In
1906 Phil married Christian Walth and they made their home on a farm two
miles from his parents.

In 1919 they moved to Bowdle where they purchased a house built by a Mr.
Record and the same year entered into a John Deere Farm Implement
partnership with his nephew Emanuel Blumhardt. This business was located on
Main Street between Second and Third Avenues in the building later occupied
by the Fred Miller Dentist Office. They dissolved partnership in 1934,
during the depression years.

        Philip and Christina Blumhardt

Seven children blessed their home: Elsie Loebs, Erna Ehlers, Martha Mueller
and Gertrude Bieber, all residing in Lodi, CA; Evelyn Sippert, Mankato, MN;
Alvin Blumhardt, Clear Lake, CA; Geraldine Young, Washington, UT and
Christina Blumhardt died in 1948 and Philip in 1961.

WILBERT and HERTHA [KOM] BLUMHARDT

Wilbert A. Blumhardt was born Mar. 7, 1925 to Gerhard and Eva (Doerr)
Blumhardt in Edmunds County. He attended country school for two years and
parochial school at Bowdle St. John's Lutheran for six years. In 1943 he
graduated from Northwestern Lutheran Academy at Mobridge. For the next
several years he farmed with his father and was a self-employed trucker. He
served in the U.S. Army in Korea for two years, 1950-1952.

Nov. 30, 1952 he married Hertha Kom of Mobridge. She was born July 25, 1932
in Grant County, ND and moved to Mobridge in 1945. Her parents are Clarence
(deceased) and Emilia (Albrecht) Kom. She has four sisters and five
brothers. Hertha graduated from Northwestern Lutheran Academy at Mobridge
in 1950 and attended Presentation School of Nursing for two years. After
their marriage in 1952 Wilbert continued to farm with his father,
increasing the cultivated acreage. Several years later he purchased the
Jake Maier and John Blumhardt farms.

In 1955 Wilbert and Arnold Peterson of Ipswich were the charter members of
the Edmunds County Soil Conservation District and he is still an active
member. In 1962 he was appointed by Governor A. Gubberud to the State
Conservation Commission on which he served for 19 years -- chairman of the
board for six years.

In 1981 he was appointed to the State Board of Minerals and Environment,
where he currently serves. He has held offices in his church, also the
Bowdle Commercial Club, Bowdle Rural Fire Protection, Edmunds County
Republicans, past director of Farmers Elevator and in the interest of
conserving soil and water ventured into no-till farming in 1981.

Hertha was very active in a small dairy operation for 20 years. She has been
sub clerk at the Bowdle Post Office for the past 18 years, also Sunday
School teacher and Ladies Aid member for many years. They are members of
Redeemer Lutheran Church in Bowdle.

        Wilbert, Hertha, Wynn, Glenn Blumhardt

They are parents of two children. Glenn was born Oct. 22, 1953 at Aberdeen.
He graduated from Bowdle High School in 1971 and attended SDSU in
Brookings, graduating in 1975 as a soil scientist. He decided to farm and
ranch with his dad. He married Catherine Fischer of Bowdle Aug. 9, 1974.
She also was a graduate of SDSU.

Wynn Ann was born June 16, 1955 at Bowdle. She graduated from Bowdle High
School in 1973 and attended SDSU in Brookings, graduating in 1977 with
degrees in biology and microbiology. She is currently employed as a chemist
by the state of Wyoming at the University of Wyoming in Laramie. She
married Jerome Sudtelgte of Elkton at Bowdle in 1978. He manages an
apartment complex at Laramie. They have two sons Justin, born Jan. 29, 1982
and John Wilbert, born Dec. 15, 1984.

EMIL E. and EMMA [HABERER] BONEN

Emil Bonen was born on a farm near Bowdle Nov. 4, 1905 to Herman and Amelia
(Gill) Bonen. He grew up on the farm and attended country school. Oct. 25,
1927 he married Emma Haberer, daughter of Christian and Barbara (Sefried)
Haberer. Emma was born May 18, 1908 on a farm near Tolstoy.

They lived for a year on a farm just north of Bowdle, where their first
child, a daughter, was born. They then moved to a farm near Hoven and lived
there the next 15 years. These were bad times for the family--it was the
30's. They remember the duststorms and grasshoppers. Emil had to sell all
his milk cows for $4 each, keeping only one for milk for the family.

        Emil and Emma Bonen

In 1943 they moved to a farm four miles west of Bowdle. In 1953 they
purchased the Buechler property on the east side of Bowdle. There they
raised chickens and some livestock and Emil worked for the Stapler
Elevator. Later he became custodian of the Bowdle School, working with his
father Herman for two years before taking over the job for the next 17
years.

Emma was not ready to retire when she moved to town. After two years at
home she worked at the Bowdle Creamery for 9-1/2 years and helped Emil with
the custodial work at the school and was assistant cook. During this time
they started Bonens Trailer Court, which they have operated for 20 years.
Emma died May 2, 1984.

The family was blessed with five children: Alyce married Clifton Seidel,
lives in Wyoming, IA and has six children. Lawrence married Velma Sauer
lives in Bowdle and has three sons. Harvey married Karen Aman, lives in
Bowdle and has four children. Judith married Elmer Boschee, lives in
Woonsocket and has four children. Richard married Gurine Goetz, lives in
Watertown and has three children.

HARVEY and KAREN [AMAN] BONEN

WILMER and WILMA [FISCHER] BOSCHEE

        Back: Sandra, Rick, Dennis. Front: Wilma and Wilmer Boschee.

REV. DR. G.L. and HULDA [HELMCHEN] BRAKEMEYER

Rev. Dr. Brakemeyer was ordained in Chicago, July 3, 1885. The Doctor's
degree was conferred on him July 3, 1935. He served the Bowdle
Congregational Church from 1914 to 1921. In 1886 he married Hulda Helmchen.
They were blessed with six children.

His son Moritz was a school teacher and became president of Northern Idaho
State University. He died in California in 1980. Agnes taught in the Bowdle
School from 1915 to 1917 and was married to Adolph Thurn in Bowdle Nov. 27,
1917. Adolph's parents had a farm near Bowdle. He worked at Aurand and
Amerphol's Store and at the Bowdle Hotel. Agnes died in 1953. Mr. Thurn,
who is now 96 years of age, lives in Sturgis.

Edna taught in the Roscoe School and married Attorney Harry Woodworth of
Ipswich Aug. 1, 1917. Harry held the position of States Attorney for
Edmunds County 50 years. Harry and Agnes died in 1965.

Alma, the only child still living, graduated from Bowdle High School in
1915 and from Northern in Aberdeen in 1917. She was married in Bowdle to
Rev. J.J. Raugust Sept. 5, 1917. Rev. Raugust was ordained in Bowdle in
1916 and served the Emanuel Congregational Church in Sioux Falls. He died in
Fresno, CA in 1975. Alma continues to make her home in Fresno.

Hugo attended Bowdle High, but graduated from the Selby High School. He
served in the U.S. Army during World War I, and though totally disabled,
graduated from the University of Iowa, Class of 1921, and became a
pharmacist. In 1924 he married Dorothy Maas, daughter of Henry Maas, one of
Bowdle's early day druggists. Hugo died in Fresno, CA in 1943. His widow
has remarried and lives in the "Golden State."

The Brakemeyers lost one child at an early age. Walter was five when he
died in Chicago in 1895.

JULES and MADALYN [GOTTLIEB] BRAUFMAN

Adolph Braufman, who was an early day merchant in Bowdle, was born in 1888
in Roumania where he received an elementary school education. He married
Sara Silverman, who was born in Roumania in 1890. She received a high school
education. Adolph died in Minneapolis, MN in January 1967. Mrs. Braufman
spent several years in the Jewish Nursing Home in Minneapolis before her
death Nov. 24, 1978.

Mr. Braufman immigrated to the United States and came to Bowdle in 1905 and
operated a small store for a brother several years. When he left, he went
to the Bronx of New York, where he had met and married Sara Silverman,
bringing his wife to her new home in this small town in South Dakota in the
fall of 1914. He opened a general merchandise store in the building now
occupied by The Bowdle Pioneer, serving the public for more than 50 years.
When Mr. Braufman became ill in 1965, the store was closed, never to open
again.

Adolph and Sara Braufman had one son Jules, who graduated from the
University of Minnesota and married Madalyn Gottlieb, whose parents had
been merchants in Hosmer, but left to live in Minnesota in 1936. Jules was
employed as a Certified Public Accountant in Minneapolis until 1980, when
he and Maddy retired to live in Delray Beach, FL.

        Janie, Randi, Maddy, Jules Braufman

They have two daughters. Randi is married to Tom Newman of St. Paul, MN, a
computer engineer. They make their home in Highland Park, IL and have two
sons Brian and Mark. Randi graduated from the University of Illinois with a
B.A. in social work. She teaches in a religious school and tutors in Hebrew
language.

Janie Braufman attended the University of Minnesota and is in the field of
selling, her specialty ranging from new cars and foods, to her present
specialty, the presentation of beverages for the Eagle Wine Co. of St.
Paul.

ALBERT and HELEN [KOSEL] BUECHLER

Albert states they greatly enjoy having their children live near them, and
that though their health isn't the best because of arthritis, they just
keep going and haven't much time for retirement. "People have told me when
you don't feel retired that is what keeps you young, but sometimes I wonder.

ARTHUR C. and EDNA A. [WALTH] BUECHLER Arthur Christian Buechler was the
first born of Jacob B. and Mary (Bossert) Buechler. He was born June 7,
1911 in Modena Township of Edmunds County. Arthur had one living brother,
Albert Jacob, who was two years younger. Though the old German ways were
not quite as strict anymore, Art and Albert were raised by the old
traditions. They spoke German. Elders were respected. Honesty was expected
and Sunday was a day of worship and rest.

        Jacob B. Buechler Family Mary, Arthur, Jacob, Albert

When they were still very young Art and Albert were expected to help with
the work. At first it was just light chores which gradually increased to
include the hard physical labor that farming, at that time, required. But
even as they worked they had time for fun. There was always time for a
prank or two that they loved to play on each other or someone else. They
were quite a bit alike. They were taller than average, strong, hardworking
young men. People would often mistake one for the other.

In all sorts of weather the boys walked to school. They attended the
Northeast Lake Public School, located 1-1/2 miles east of their home. They
could have gone on to high school if either had wished to become a
minister. Although a good student, Art had no desire to become a preacher,
so the eighth grade is as far as he went. His education also included
Confirmation instructions (which meant learning to read and write German
because the German Bible and Catechism were used,) piano lessons (so he
could play for church) and later on a short course in a mechanical school.

Art was a young man when the depression came. The Buechlers had just bought
another farm. Convinced by his father that things would work better if one
of the boys was married and lived on the other place, he equipped himself
with a new Model "A" Ford and went courting. (His brother always did say
the reason Edna first went with Art was because she was impressed with the
new car.)

Whatever the reason, Edna A. Walth (daughter of Martin and Josephine Walth
of Hosmer) said yes and they were married Oct. 22, 1935. After a big
wedding at St. John Lutheran Church in Hosmer and a dinner reception at the
Buechler's, Art and Edna made their first home on a farm one-half mile
north of the Buechler homeplace. There they weathered the rest of the
depression together. A son Norman Arthur was born Jan. 4, 1938.

To make a little money during those years when nothing grew, Art did some
road grading for the county. Edna did the chores and took care of the baby
as best she could. Some days the dust from the ever blowing wind was so
bad, she would take the baby into the back bedroom and hang wet towels and
cloths over the door and windows in an effort to keep the dust out. By
evening the dust on the floor was so thick you couldn't see the design in
the linoleum.

In 1940 Art and Edna moved on the homeplace with his parents and Albert and
his wife, Helen Kosel, lived on the farm one-half mile north. The worst of
the depression and drought was now over and things started to look up. The
crops were better, as were the prices. There was a little money to paint
the buildings again. By 1941 Art's folks felt they could afford to retire
and moved to Bowdle.

The year 1942 was even better. There was a lot of rain. There were bumper
crops. And to add to their joy, there was the birth of their daughter,
Mardella Edna Oct. 9. Life was getting a little easier but there were still
the hardships that World War II was creating. There was not only rationing
of foods and petroleum, there was a shortage of man power and the awful
ache of loved ones lost in the war. Edna's brother Harold gave his life
serving in the Army Air Corps.

After the war the farm scene saw great changes. The first thing Art changed
was eliminating the sheep. They did continue to have a few range cattle,
raise hogs, chickens and other poultry as well as milk a few cows. These
chores were mostly the responsibility of Edna and the children as they
became old enough to help.

The big changes came in the field work. Partly because of the continued
shortage of farm labor, partly because of the bigger crops and partly
because of the industrial revolution, there were bigger and better machines
with which to work. The horses gave way to the tractors which eventually
gave way to bigger and better tractors. The grain was now harvested with
combines instead of threshing machines.

The lifestyle of the farm changed as well. Art and Edna added running water
in the house. The basement was repaired and enlarged. An addition to the
house, consisting of a well-equipped kitchen, was made. The pantry became a
bathroom. REA replaced the charger and batteries. RTA replaced the fence
phones. Now the house was so comfortable even in summer that there was no
need for the old summer kitchen.

It had taken a great deal of energy and strength to accomplish all these
things especially so soon after the struggle for survival through the
depression. Hired help was not always available. Happily, Edna had the good
fortune of having Frieda Stuckel to help her before the birth of their
second son Allan Harold July 23, 1946. The years, however, had taken their
toll and Edna became ill after the baby's birth and was sick for several
years. Frieda stayed on and helped for three years. She was like a member
of the family and has remained a lifelong friend.

The farm kept improving in appearance. A shelter belt of trees to the north
and west added beauty as well as protection from the wind. And the purchase
of a lawn mower powered by a Briggs and Straton mower was a great help in
keeping the yard neat.

As the children grew up they attended the same school Art had as a boy.
When school programs were given everyone in the neighborhood came and had a
great time. Another enjoyable event was the school picnic. The youngsters
always looked forward to playing softball against their fathers. The last
few years before the school was closed because of reorganization of school
districts there was even a hot lunch program. The mothers took turns
cooking government commodities and bringing them to school at noon.

Norman and Mardella attended high school in Bowdle. There was no bus
service so in the winter months they often stayed with their grandparents.
By the time Allan was old enough for high school the districts had been
organized and he attended Hosmer High.

Church always played a large role in the family. After the country church
located several miles north of the farm closed they joined St. Paul American
Lutheran Church in Bowdle. All the children were confirmed there. Art's
ability to speak before a group of people was a real asset to him when he
served on the church council and as Sunday School Superintendent (an office
he held for many years.) Art's strong bass voice and Edna's pleasant alto
were parts of many choirs. Edna was a faithful worker in Ladies Aide and
taught Junior Lutherans.

When Norman graduated from High School in 1956 he enlisted in the Airforce.
He married Arlene Schnabel Oct. 11, 1959. After his term in the service was
over he took a job with General Electric as an electronics engineer and
they moved to Phoenix, AZ. Over the years his job has taken them to various
places in California and back to Phoenix. They have two children: Dale
Norman born May 11, 1962 and Jodi Ann, born June 22, 1966.

        Arthur C. Buechler Family Back: Arthur, Norman, Edna. Front: Allan,
        Mardella

Mardella graduated from Concordia College, Moorhead, MN in 1964. After
working as a social worker in Aberdeen for a year she married Dale Bieber.
They farm in the Bowdle area.

Allan attended one semester each at Concordia College and Northern State
before enlisting in the Armed Forces in 1965. He left in September.

Since it looked like none of the children would be taking over the farm,
Art and Edna began to think about cutting back on work.

It was Dec. 18, 1965 when tragedy struck. A severe ice storm that brought
down telephone and electrical lines for miles around had left a thick sheet
of ice on everything. Art with the help of one of the neighbor boys was
getting a load of grain from the granary to grind for the calves when he
slipped and fell into the power take-off of the tractor and was killed.

With Norman's help Edna got ready for a farm auction the next spring. The
farm was rented for several years and eventually sold to Jim Huntsinger of
rural Hosmer.

Edna moved to Aberdeen where she worked as domestic help and later as a
nurse's aide. In 1968 she moved to Phoenix, AZ where Norman and his family
lived. There she worked as a nurse's assistant at John C. Lincoln for over
14 years. When she retired (because her aching feet could no longer take
the routine) she received an Honorary Plaque commending her on her faithful
service.

Allan joined his mother in Phoenix when he returned from the Air Force
after serving in Taiwan during the Vietnam War. He graduated from Arizona
State University and married Becky Osborne in 1972. They have two sons:
David Allan, born Nov. 25, 1976 and Robert Jonathan, born June 26, 1979.
Allan is a computer programmer for ITT.

Edna continues to live in Phoenix as do Norman and family. Allan and family
live in Mesa, AZ. Every summer Edna spends several weeks with Mardella, the
only member of the family who still lives in the Bowdle area.

ATHNEAL and BERNICE [VETCH] BUECHLER

Athneal Buechler was born June 3, 1928 at Bowdle. His parents are David and
Maggie Buechler. Athneal graduated from Bowdle High School and Sept. 17,
1950 married Bernice Vetch, daughter of John and Elizabeth (Biernbaum) Vetch. 
Bernice was born April 17, 1931 at Roscoe. John Vetch died in 1977 and 
Elizabeth in 1970. Bernice attended Northern State College one year and
taught school seven years.

After completing his education Athneal assisted his father with farming,
then spent two years in the U.S. Army and on his discharge worked at the
Bowdle Creamery from 1954 to 1961, when he bought the farm from his father.
Athneal and Bernice purchased Buechler's Cafe from his parents in April
1973, which they operated until December 1983 when it was sold to Richard
and Sherma Maier. Athneal then returned to full-time farming.

The couple had four sons. Gary L. was born Feb. 20 1952 at Fort Eustis, VA;
Gene L. was born April 15 1954, Glen L. Dec. 8, 1958 and Greg L. April 19,
1960.

        Back: Gene and Gary. Front: Greg, Bernice, Athneal, Glen Buechler.

Farming has been an adventure the Buechlers say, as there have been times
of drought and then a time of flooding when they had 9-1/2 inches of rain,
the Armyworms, hail, six years of ten and just plain dust and wind.

Accidents with the boys were prevalent, but fortunately nothing serious.
Also fun things are remembered like "making worms" by jumping on the grease
gun and letting it paste onto the front of the shop (the spots can still be
seen on dusty days) and the time a dead duckling was found and questioning
brought the answer, "Me just loved 'em and loved too hard!"

DANIEL and ROSINA [OPP] BUECHLER

Daniel Buechler was born to John and Magdalena (Kirschman) Buechler March
14, 1894 on the family farm six miles northwest of Bowdle.

Rosina Opp was born in Russia April 22, 1893. Her parents died while their
family was still very young. Rosina was only five years old when her mother

brothers: John, Christ and Peter, who made their home in Canada after

Rosina Opp came to this country from Russia at age 15 and made her home

        Rosina and Daniel Buechler

Elmer and his wife Irene live on the family farm. They have two children

DAVID and MAGGIE [AIPPERSPACH] BUECHLER

David Buechler was born March 23, 1904 in Walworth County. His parents,
Frederick and Elizabeth (Stotz) Buechler, farmed northwest of Bowdle. When
he was 6 years old they moved to a farm southeast of town. They had the
assistance of nine sons and six daughters in their farm work.

David married Maggie Aipperspach in 1926 and they built up a farm 1/2 mile
north of his parents home. Here they lived 35 years.

Maggie was born March 10, 1908 at Zeeland, ND to Fred and Magdalena
(Meidinger) Aipperspach. She was their seventh child and the first born in
the new frame house. The others had been born in the sod house. She had 10
sisters and 2 brothers. The year 1916 saw the family in a new farmhouse one
mile south of the North/South Dakota state line.

Maggie was a very busy girl during her teens. She had many hobbies
including raising poultry, sewing and gardening. She also learned the art of
cake decorating and pursued this 40 years, baking cakes for weddings,
anniversaries and other special occasions.

David and Maggie managed through the "Dirty Thirties" living off the land,
as a garden, eggs and cream had to provide the gas for the car, clothes,
machinery repairs, groceries, in fact, everything they had to buy.

They retired from the farm in 1961 and moved to town, turning the farm over
to their son Athneal. While on the farm David served 16 years on the
district school board and 17 years on the township board. He was also a
member of the Bowdle Sportsmen's Club and the church board. In town David
worked with George Seurer, doing carpenter work and also for the Sales
Barn. In 1965 they bought the South Side Cafe from Norbert Simon and
operated it for 8-1/2 years.

It was while they were serving the public in the cafe that the blizzard of
1966 left them with vivid memories. Maggie recalls it came in so suddenly
there was no time for preparation. Cars on main street were snowed under,
nothing could move and the Buechlers stayed in the cafe three days and two
nights. The first 24 hours they had electricity and managed with the
cooking. At night, using coats, they made beds on the booths for
themselves, their grandson Gary and Melvin Maier. The next morning ... no
electricity! A propane grill was the only cooking appliance and a
Heatrola in the back room laundromat furnished some heat.

Travelers who had been stranded stayed at the Ray Nelson hotel and came to
the cafe for meals. Jerry Hilbers and Dave managed to go two blocks to
Jerry's place and brought back batteries so they could have lights to play
cards. Kerosene lamps and candles were used the second night.

The cold drove all those who had now crowded into the cafe to the
laundromat, where they tried to sleep sitting in chairs or lying on the
washing machines and tables. During the day people kept coming and every
time the door opened, snow blew in so the floor became a puddle of water.

Jake Sieck drained the water heater at his home and that was used sparingly
for washing dishes. He also brought in blankets for the night. Feeding all
these people was Maggie's worry, but she managed with toast, bread,
pancakes, sausages and cured meats. All survived the storm.

        Maggie and David Buechler

Dave and Maggie have three children and 20 grandchildren. Verna, the
firstborn, attended Northern State in Aberdeen after graduating from high
school and taught in the Ipswich and Loyalton areas. She married Vernon
Oban. They farm south of Roscoe and have five children.

Athneal graduated from Bowdle and attended Northern State College in
Aberdeen. He married Bernice Vetch of Roscoe and served in the U.S.
Armed Forces. After his discharge he worked at Bowdle Creamery and has
since engaged in farming. They have four sons.

Delores graduated from Bowdle and then worked at Montgomery Wards in
Aberdeen four years. She married Leo Jung while he was in the U.S. Army.
They had 12 children. Delores died at age 43. The Buechlers were grateful
their son-in-law found a wonderful woman to mother the children, especially
when less than 5 years later, he also died.

Maggie is still busy quilting at home, church and the Senior Center. She is
also a member of the American Lutheran Church Women, American Legion
Auxiliary, Senior Citizens Center and Historical Society.

EDGAR and MATHILDA [GUTHMILLER] BUECHLER

Edgar (Butch) Buechler, one of the 18 children of Mr. and Mrs. Fred
Buechler, was born Feb. 5, 1916 on a farm nine miles southeast of Bowdle.
The farm was known as the Drury Ranch in Cloyd Valley Township. He attended
the nearby rural school and completed his education of eight years. He
remained at home and worked on the farm.

In 1942 Edgar married Mathilda Guthmiller who was born July 3, 1919 in
Roscoe. In 1939 Mathilda got a position teaching in one of the three
schools in Cloyd Valley Township where she met Edgar. She taught in the
district for five years.

The couple had three children: Janice Mae born May 21, 1943, Jerome Donald
born July 3, 1947 and Jerae Lou born Sept. 2, 1958. The Buechlers lived on
the farm until 1960, when they moved into Bowdle, but Edgar still farmed
until his death March 15, 1967. He had a massive heart attack while doing
chores at the farm.

        Back: Jerome, Jerae, Janice. Front: Mathilda and Edgar Buechler.

Mathilda still lives in Bowdle. She was appointed as an Avon Representative
Feb. 28, 1962 and is still selling. She became a member of the President's
Club in September the same year. At that time to become a member you had to
sell $1,000 worth of Avon in six months. She has been a member ever since,
but now you have to sell $8,000 a year. She was a team leader for 11 years
and a group leader for one. She has had five managers in her Avon career.

Janice married Ronald Feickert Oct. 22, 1961. They had two children: Ronda
Jo born Oct. 11, 1962 and Jonathan Rae born Aug. 26, 1964. Janice has been

Ronald is Director of the Physical Plant at Presentation. Ronda graduated in

and Jonathan is an engineering student attending North Dakota State
University.

Jerome lives at 5727 High Park Drive in Minnetonka, MN. He married Mary
Farnsworth of Edina, MN July 16, 1976. They have three children: Daniel
Jerome born March 6, 1979, Sarah Elise born March 2, 1981 and Melissa Mary
born May 30, 1985. Jerome graduated from Northern State College and is
Vice-president of Finance for Towle Real Estate in Minneapolis. Mary

instructor for Lonna Studio.

Jerae is still single. He graduated from Northern State College in 1980. He
is employed at Burroughs. Recently he entered the sales field for the
company in the Minneapolis area. His address is 1014 Westbrooke Way,
Hopkins, MN. Jerae is the last offspring of the Fred Buechler family.
