ELMER and IRENE [HAAR] BUECHLER

EMIL D. and FREIDA [WEISZHAAR] BUECHLER

Emil was born to Daniel and Rosina (Opp) Buechler near Bowdle March 13,
1918. He grew to adulthood on the farm and later became a barber.

Freida was born to Christ and Lydia (Walter) Weiszhaar near Selby Aug. 26,
1918. The Weiszhaar family later moved closer to Bowdle to the Buechler
Territory, allowing the families to get acquainted.

Emil and Freida were married Dec. 3, 1939. They made their first home in
Newell, where Emil was a barber and Freida had a job as bedbug exterminator
in their honeymoon cottage, which they had rented for a home. They had to
sleep in the car a whole month until Freida had the bugs killed.

A year later they moved to Mound City where Emil had a new barbering job.
During that time their son Ronald arrived Sept. 24, 1942. In 1944 they
moved back to Bowdle to Emil's parents farm home. Their daughter Karen was
born Nov. 22, 1947.

In 1950 the family moved to the Herman Buechler farm where they farmed
until 1961. During their farming years Emil and Freida experienced many
winters with deep snow, making it difficult to do the chores. With all the
moisture the crops were prosperous for them.

        Back: Karen and Ronald. Front: Freida and Emil D. Buechler

In 1961 they had a farm auction and moved to Mobridge where they built a
new home. Emil still continues to barber, while Freida enjoys her home and
grandchildren.

Their son Ronald lives in Mobridge. He married Roxann Mulloy and they have
two daughters, Rhonda and Renee.

Karen married Roger Anderson. They live in Huron and have one son, Eric.

EMIL H. and ARVA [CRIM] BUECHLER

Emil H. Buechler was born in Walworth County Jan. 20, 1917 to Fred B. and
Katherine (Hieb) Buechler. Emil married Darlene Johnson, Mar. 4, 1944 in
Nebraska. She was the daughter of Clark and Laura Johnson of Wisner, NE.
Emil and Darlene had no children. Darlene died Dec. 11, 1969.

Emil married Arva Crim Dec. 2, 1970. She has two daughters who live in
California and one son who lives in Moab, Utah. The families consist of
five grandchildren and one great-granddaughter.

Emil remembers many memories he would like to share about his life in
Bowdle. He states, "There are some who say never look back! To those, I say
nonsense, when looking ahead never forget where you came from! And in a
flip way you can say, you've come a long ways, baby!''

Today we have interstate highways, colored television, jets, outer space
explorations, microwaves, convenience foods. Yes, we have come a long way
since the days of the "Black-only Model T's." Those cars traveled down a
washboard road or "stuck in the mud" country roads.

The economic times of the late 20's and early 30's were tough, but no one
on the farms went hungry. The farmer provided food with simple machinery,
mostly horse-drawn. The horse power-drawn machinery was slowly being
replaced with the 15-30 McCormic-Deering tractor, then the "Poppin
Johnnies" (two cylinder John Deeres too.) Remember the horse-drawn grain
binders or headers, the threshing machines and the "Stone-boats."

When I finished my education in the country school, my Father saw to it
that I attended high school in Bowdle. My way of getting to school was
riding horseback 14 miles a day, round trip. And I might add that I was
never tardy. I was aware of that as one of the "city slickers" who lived
across the street from school was tardy every morning.

During my sophomore year I drove a Model "T" Ford, without as much as a top
or side curtain, to school. I suffered more from the cold in the car than I
did riding horseback. During my last two years in school, with two other
family members, we drove a glass-enclosed Model "A" Ford. During our school
hours we kept the car in Christ Bollinger's garage so we could ride home in
a warm car.

I'm sure no one has forgotten the "Dust-Bowl" years of 1934-1936. There was
a constant wind-drifting sand-tumbling Russian thistles, grasshoppers, the
need to dispose of the herds of cattle due to the lack of feed, low grain
prices. All of this added together was enough to discourage most anyone.
Many families migrated to the West Coast to find better opportunities. None
ever returned to stay.

I remember those "Prohibition Days." It didn't keep us from having our beer
during the summer and wine during the winter. None of us abused this rare
thing and that's perhaps the reason we stayed so healthy, and most of us
lived to a ripe old age. Making and bottling the beer was an event in
itself, as was the "squeezing" of the grapes.

And of course our family make its own sauerkraut, and lots of it. It was
really quite an honor to be chosen to be the one to thoroughly scrub one's
feet and then trample down the freshly shredded cabbage that went into
those big barrels or 20 gallon earthen crocks. My, how that salt did burn
if one happened to have a cut on his foot by going "barefooted" all summer.

Butchering, usually one beef and several fattened hogs, was another event.
It happened twice a year, first usually in December and again in the Spring
before the farmers planted the fields. We made several kinds of sausage,
cured our own bacon and hams, plus canned endless quarts of beef. And there
was lots of grease which was used for lard and to make soap.

        Emil H. Buechler

Other varied memories was going to town with a horse-drawn wagon loaded
with three 55 gallon barrels to get buttermilk at the creamery for the
hogs. Or the trips to town on Saturdays to get instructions in the Lutheran
religious order and mostly in the German language. Sundays, except for the
necessary daily chores, were trips to Sunday school and church. Another
event was going to August Schick's farm home to get a hair cut. Traveling
away from home was unheard, the farthest I traveled was my senior year in
school when I traveled to Mobridge for "Skip Day."

Since those ol' days, I lived in Aberdeen from 1936 to 1943. There I was a
bookkeeper for the Candy Service Co. and later was on recruiting duty for
the U.S. Navy. After living one year in Omaha, NE I was sent 14 months
overseas. I returned in Oct. 1945 and attended the University of Omaha and
then started in the hotel business in Yankton. After living several places
in Iowa, I settled in Oskaloosa, IA where I own and operate a Best Western
Travel Motel.

I have traveled extensively, covering most of the U.S. and have been in 31
countries. In my travels, I did spend a brief time in Russia and all I can
say is that I'm happy that my forefathers had the good sense to get out of
this land and come to America in the 1880's to homestead in South Dakota.
As I look about Russia, at those solemn people, I could only think that I
could have been one of them.

FRED B. and KATHERINA [HIEB] BUECHLER

Jacob and Katherina (Rott) Buechler migrated from the German settlement of
Glueckstahl in South Russia near the Black Sea early in 1890 to the United
States. They homesteaded in Spring Lake Township in Walworth County.

Their son Fred B. Buechler was born here Dec. 13, 1890. Fred grew up on
this farm seven miles northwest of Bowdle. He attended grammar school and
was confirmed in the Lutheran Church at Java March 27, 1903. He married
Katherina Hieb of Hosmer Jan. 16, 1914 in the Neuglueckstahl Lutheran
Church near Bowdle.

They established their home on a farm nine miles southwest of Bowdle for
five years before returning to the homestead in 1919. Seven sons and five
daughters were born to this couple. Three sons died in infancy.

The living children include: Emil, married to Darlene Johnson (deceased)
and remarried Arva Crim, currently living in Oskaloosa, IA. Irma married
Ted Leidholt and lives in Bowdle; Milton married Virginia Bosman and lives
in Lennox; Eleanora married Roy Brewton and lives in Pensacola, FL; Rueben
never married and lives in Rapid City; LeRoy married Esther Roesch and
lives in DeSmet; Renata Swanson lives in St. Charles, MO; Irene married
Alfred Rader and lives in Morgan Hill, CA and Delores married Alton
Schaible and lives in St. Charles, MO.

Katherina Buechler died Jan. 5, 1940. Fred continued to farm until he
retired in 1950. Although he made his home in Bowdle Fred assisted his son
LeRoy until 1955. Fred married Christine Preszler Schaible of Hosmer Oct.
27, 1954. They moved to Lodi, CA where they make their home at 530 York
Street.

        Fred B. Buechler Family Back: Eleonora, Milton, Irma, Ruben, LeRoy.
        Delores, Fred, Renata, Emil, Irene, Katherina.

The American Lutheran Church was an important part of their lives. Fred
served on the building committee of the church parsonage. He was a member
of the Spring Lake School Board, treasurer of the telephone company 30
years, a member of the Triple A Program and a member of the Extension Board
of Walworth County. He served as a member of the FmHA Board in Edmunds
County three years. A member of the initial board of directors of the then
newly organized Farmers Union Oil Company of Bowdle, Fred continued in this
capacity 10 years.

The children of Katherina Buechler recall her many efforts to care for the
family. She was kept busy. She washed the family's clothing on a
scrubboard, baked bread, raised and canned vegetables and canned beef, pork
and chicken. She sewed much of the clothing. The depression years of the
"Dirty Thirties" made it necessary to involve the children in the farming.
Milking cows was the most important work. The drought made finding feed for
the cattle difficult. Thistles were harvested for forage. Grasshoppers and
the infamous duststorms destroyed the grains and gardens. These storms
darkened the heavens at mid-day!

Many pleasant memories also remain. Irma vividly recalls the gathering of
foods for the winter supply. Barrels, crocks and bins were prepared by
sterilizing and sweetened with boiling water and sunshine. Watermelons were
harvested first. The smaller ones were used for eingemachte, erbussen (sour
watermelon.) Larger fruit was stored in the granary and covered with wheat
or barley. This allowed them to ripen slowly. Next came the cabbage. It was
cut and sliced with a huffel (cabbage slicer) and placed in layers in a
barrel or a 20 gallon crock and salt was added. Irma and Emil had to scrub
their feet thoroughly and stomp the cabbage until liquid stood on top. At
this point, a clean white cloth was spread on top and this was weighted
down with a rock. After several weeks of aging it was ready to eat.

Cucumbers were also placed in crocks, salted well and weighted down with
dill, a plate and a rock. The result was delicious dill pickles. Fresh
cabbage was stored in a cellar to be used for kraut saulade. Carrots were
also stored there. Burying them in sand kept them fresh all winter. Potatoes
were stored too. Tomato vines were pulled and hung. The family sometimes
had fresh tomatoes until Thanksgiving. Although eggs were plentiful in the
summer, the harsh winters caused the hens not to lay well. Therefore eggs
were also stored in oats. Father would go to town in the wagon and bring
home 12 100-pound sacks of flour and two of sugar. This was stored upstairs
in the house. Canned goods were stored in the cellar.

Irma feels Butchering Week was that part of her German heritage that made
the strongest impression on her. This was a cheerful period of time during
which friends and neighbors got together to prepare the winter's meat
supply. Cold days were chosen to butcher a beef and several hogs for each
family. Cutting and sawing the meat on large tables was tedious, laborious
and extremely messy. Of course there was not hot running water to make
clean up of the project and themselves easier. Crocks would be filled with
fried pork steaks and sausage. Melted, rendered lard kept this meat sweet
all winter. Shoulders, ribs and pork bellies were often salted down in
crocks. Smoke houses held sausages and hams hanging from rafters.

Sausage was made of ground beef and pork stuffed into natural casings.
These casings were the turned, scraped, cleaned and salted intestines of
the butchered animals. Liver sausage and head cheese were made and stuffed
into the largest casings. The children enjoyed pricking the air bubbles
from the casings and releasing the air. After the lard had all been
rendered the last of the pork rind and suet were used to make old-fashioned
soap. They were boiled in a large, open kettle with lye until the suet and
rind were dissolved and the soap was of the right consistency.

Most of these techniques are immersed in history. Only the tantalizing
memories remain. We cherish and revere the heritage left us by our
hard-working ancestors.

FRED F. and LENA [REEDE] BUECHLER

Fred F. Buechler was born near Bowdle in Walworth County Dec. 12, 1894, the
son of Fred F. and Magdalena (Oster) Buechler. His wife Lena Reede was born
in Freeman to John and Carolina (Haar) Reede March 1, 1895. They were
married in Bowdle March 19. 1919 and settled on a farm southeast of Bowdle.

They were the parents of six children. Their first three died in infancy.
Fred and Lena used to tell of how their twin daughters were buried in a
homemade casket which was not unusual because people did not have money for
manufactured caskets in those days, but Lena took her wedding gown and
lined the casket and used her bridal veil to make a bow on top of the
casket.

        Fred F. Buechler Family Gerold, Lena, Geroldine, Fred, Lila

In 1961 they retired from the farm, which they sold to their son Gerold and
moved to Bowdle. They built a home where the John Koch house had been in
1960. This house was a landmark in the town, having been moved here from
LaBeau. Mrs. Koch told of it having been a saloon building there. It was
sawed into two buildings to bring one to Bowdle. When Buechlers tore it
down they said there was enough lumber to build two houses as it was double
boarded for warmth. It was a very high ceilinged house.

The infirmities of old age forced them to give up living alone and in March
1978 they went to live in the Bowdle Nursing Home. Fred died Feb. 10, 1979
and Lena has continued as a resident of the nursing home.

Their surviving children are Mrs. Robert (Lila) Oster and Gerold Buechler,
both of Bowdle and Mrs. Marvin (Geroldine) Fischer of Wisconsin. They also
have seven grandchildren and four great-grandchildren.

FREDRICH and ELIZABETH [STOTZ] BUECHLER

Fredrich Buechler was born Feb. 11, 1869 in Neuglueckstahl, South Russia to
Michael and Katherine (Strobel) Buechler. In 1890 Fredrich came to the
United States and settled in South Dakota with his parents. He arrived with
his three brothers, Michael Jr., Jacob, John and two sisters, Katherine
(Himmerich) and Rosina (Merkel) including their families. All of them were
married except Fredrich and Rosina. They, with their families, homesteaded
northwest of Bowdle.

March 9, 1894 Fredrich married Magdalena (Oster.) They established their
home on the same farm with his parents.

Jan. 21, 1900 Mrs. Buechler died leaving behind four small children.
Fredrich Jr. of Bowdle, died in 1979 at the age of 85; Rosina (Mrs. Jacob
Eisenbeisz) of McLaughlin, died in 1976 at the age of 80; Michael of
McLaughlin, died in 1967 at the age of 69 and Carl died at the age of two.

Dec. 4, 1900 Fredrich married Elizabeth Stotz. This union was blessed with
14 children. They were Katherine (Mrs. Oscar Winkler) of Roscoe, died Jan.
21, 1985; Elizabeth died in infancy; David lives in Bowdle; Philip of
Roscoe, died in 1942 at the age of 37; Emma (Mrs. Theophil Winkler) of
Roscoe; Julius of Hermiston, OR; Eva (Mrs. Lyle Fletcher) of Coos Bay, OR;
Edward of Bowdle; Hilda (Mrs. Willard Walstead) of Portland, OR; Elizabeth
(Mrs. William Winkler) of Longview, WA; Edgar of Bowdle, died in 1967 at
the age of 51; Edwin of Ipswich died at the age of 53; Jack of Lodi, CA and
Otillia died in 1922 at the age of two.

Fredrich and Elizabeth lived on the farm northwest of Bowdle until 1910 and
then moved to a farm 10 miles southeast of Bowdle in Cloyd Valley Township.
Here they lived with their family until they retired in the fall 1939,
moving into Bowdle.

Fredrich died in 1941 at the age of 72 and Elizabeth died in 1959 at the
age of 82. Both were buried in the St. Paul Lutheran Cemetery south of
Bowdle.

After Henry Buechler's death in 1951 Margaret was forced to provide a

elected County Treasurer and later reelected Register of Deeds and held
this office until 1975. She retired in 1975 and died June 16, 1976.

HERBERT and MARJORIE [BAUER] BUECHLER

Herbert John Buechler, son of John B. and Mary (Eisenbeisz) Buechler of
Bowdle and Marjorie Louise Bauer, daughter of John and Lydia (Fiechtner)
Bauer of Java, were united in marriage at the St. Paul Lutheran Church of
Java July 3, 1949. In October of 1949 the couple moved to a farm 6l/2 miles
north and one mile west of Bowdle in Modena Township.

Farming was a struggle. The cream and egg checks provided groceries and
household supplies. Water was carried from the well at the bottom of a
steep hill. There were no phones or electricity. Lighting was provided by
kerosene lamps, later gas lamps. A windcharger provided electrical power to
storage batteries and light from bulbs until the day R.E.A. beautified the
countryside.

Gradually the milk herd increased to 19 cows. In order to get feed to the
cattle a team of horses was a necessity, pulling the bobsled through the
winter snows covering the steep hills. The horses also worked tirelessly in
the spring and summer months.

In December 1954 a fire destroyed the barn. All of the cows (but one), all
the calves, the team of horses, the tractor, the oats crop and hay stored in
the barn were burned, along with tools, harnesses, etc. Marjorie's sister,
Delores, sent the story of the fire to the radio program "Strike it Rich."
Teresa Brewer (popular singer of the early 1950's), won $100 for them to
buy a new team of horses. Neighbors, friends and relatives built a barn in
48 hours so the couple again could make a new beginning. Women served meals
and lunches to the crew.

Herbert worked hard to get a telephone line through Modena Township, and
served as secretary-treasurer of Modena Telephone Company for all its years
of service.

Marjorie attended Northern State College and taught school in the Alamo
School northeast of Java, in the Wakpala, Java, Hosmer and Eureka schools.
In 1964 she began substitute teaching at the Bowdle School and attended
extension classes at Northern State College. In 1965 she accepted a
position as Title I reading teacher and the first kindergarten teacher at
Bowdle School. In 1970 she received her B. S. degree in education and
continued teaching in Bowdle.

Herbert was a veteran of World War II, having served in the Quartermaster
Corp of the Army in Alaska. He was a member of the Bowdle American Legion.

On March 4, 1980 Herbert died of cardiac arrest. Stanley, who had been
farming with his father, continued with the dairy farming.

        Marjorie and Herbert Buechler

Three children blessed the Herbert Buechler family: Stanley (July 4, 1951)
received a degree in data processing from National College of Business in
Rapid City and is presently farming. He is married to Becky Lunders of
Hoven and they have two children: Jason and Sara.

Jeffrey (Jan. 9, 1955) received an M.A. degree in anthropology from the
University of Nebraska in Lincoln and at present is owner of Dakota Research
Service in Rapid City where he, his wife Jeanie McCallister and son Matthew
live.

Marjean (July 23, 1960), only daughter of Herb and Marjorie, received her
B.S. degree, majoring in biology from SDSU in Brookings. She and her
husband Barry Irons reside in Vermillion where Barry is attending medical
school and Marjean is continuing her education at USD. They have a son
Benjamin, born May 11, 1985.

IDA BUECHLER

The following letter was received from Miss Ida Buechler of 16-1/2 8th
Avenue S.W., Aberdeen. She recounts some of her experiences in Bowdle, as
well as memories.

"I was introduced to working with the public at Gross Brothers Department
Store in 1924. I still have a 1924 dime so I won't forget the year. We did
all the work. We wrote the customer's order down and filled it. We candled
the eggs they brought to see if they were fresh. Some were in pails of oats.
We had to dig them out. Our fingers sometimes went into soft shells. What a
mess!

In the duststorm years there was no end to the dusting of all the glass
showcases in the store. No time and a half. We worked every day. The stores
were open evenings in the summer and Saturday night, usually till midnight.
We earned a week of vacation each year.

        Ida Buechler

"On Sunday I was the organist at St. Paul's Lutheran Church. Sometimes this
didn't go well because I was tired.

Everyone walked to work, winter and summer. I made my second trip out of
South Dakota when I repeated a trip to California. At that time I had been
employed at Gross Brothers 23 years.

I worked nine years at Feinstein's in Aberdeen. Besides selling, we did a
lot of hard work such as shifting clothes. But the hours were not so long.

After my retirement I visited in seven states, besides our own beautiful
South Dakota. Now I do arm chair traveling on Public TV around the world.
My desire is to have peace."

JACOB B. and MARY [BOSSERT] BUECHLER

Jacob B. Buechler was born June 1, 1887 in Glueckstahl, South Russia. His
parents Jacob and Katherina (Rott) Buechler were among the Germans from
Russia who left for the United States because of the political unrest in
Russia. They came to South Dakota in 1890 where they established their home
by homesteading land west of Bowdle.

Here Jacob B. grew up much as he would have in South Russia. There were
many Germans from Russia who settled in the Bowdle area. They brought with
them their language, their traditions and their methods of building,
homemaking and farming. They were excellent farmers. Their farms in South
Russia had prospered and were examples of what hard work and good
management could do. Jacob B. also became a good farmer and good carpenter
as well.

As the oldest in the family, Jacob B. worked with his father and brothers.
Together they accumulated more land and better equipment. When he was a
young man he and his father hired a "coupler" to help him find a wife. The
young woman who consented to marry him was Mary Bossert (born Dec. 27,
1889.) She was the daughter of Christian and Magdelina (Bieber) Bossert from
Artas. Jacob B. and Mary were married Nov. 18, 1909 in her home church
located west of Eureka.

        Jacob B. and Mary Buechler

For the first year of their marriage they lived with his parents. Then they
moved to an abandoned farm nine miles north of Bowdle. Here their three
sons were born: Arthur Christian, June 7, 1911; Albert Jacob, Feb. 3, 1913
and Richard, 1914, died in infancy.

The buildings on the farm were all less than adequate and gradually Jacob
B. replaced them, starting with the house. This house was his first
building project. He had only the simplest tools and his memory of houses
he had seen to work with. The resulting house was a strong, well-built,
roomy house. It had two full stories--a large house indeed for those times.
Having never lived in a house with a basement, he saw no need to put one
under the house. Later as the advantages of a basement became apparent, he
added one. He also had a hot air furnace installed with a register in every
room.

Other buildings that Jacob built were a granary and a hip-roofed barn. By
the time he was done with these he was a pretty good carpenter. There were
other improvements as well.

Jacob B. kept up with the improved methods of farming. He and Christoph
Perman were among the first in their area to own a tractor and threshing
machine. For some years they owned it together until Jacob bought
Christoph's share.

Neither Jacob or Mary had had much opportunity to go to school as children.
They felt quite handicapped by their lack of formal education. They
therefore were very happy to give their sons the chance to learn. The boys
graduated from the Northeast Lake Public School. Their education also

included Confirmation instructions at St. John Lutheran Church in Hosmer.
If either of the boys had wanted to become a minister, he would have been
sent on to school. Since both wanted to be farmers they stayed at home.

Jacob B. and Mary had always been good managers. Now with the help of their
able bodied and intelligent sons they were able to expand their operation.
Later Jacob began to suffer from rheumatism and found the boys' help
essential. It affected all of his joints, making all movement slow and
painful. Eventually his condition improved. By that time the sons had
become full partners. They all worked very hard, not only on the farm, but
also in the community. For many years Jacob was the Modena Township
Treasurer. When his illness made it hard for him to drive, his son, Art,
had to go with him everywhere. Through this Art gradually was able to
handle more and more of the business and also eventually took over as
Modena Township Treasurer.

Jacob had a good wife and children. Because of the family's faithfulness
and hard work improvements were made in every aspect. There was better
machinery, more land was purchased and living conditions became more
comfortable. The house was equipped with a 32-volt charger and batteries.
That meant that they enjoyed electric lights in the house, as well as, Mary
could use an electric Maytag washing machine and an electric iron. Jacob
had some luxuries as well. Although never a good driver (he let his sons do
most of the driving) he owned a new Buick.

Everyone felt their home was a warm and pleasant place to visit. It was not
only because it was comfortable and there was always plenty to eat (even if
you came right at mealtime), it was more because of Mary's generous
hospitality. She knew how to make people feel at home without fussing. She
was intelligent and witty, yet very much down to earth. When you combine
her warm personality with good German cooking, and some of Jacob's
excellent sausages, it meant a good time.

Jacob and Mary were always active in church. Jacob took his turn reading
the sermon if there was no minister present and held all the church offices
at one time or the other. After he had retired from farming he volunteered
his services as the janitor of the church for many years. Mary had a
beautiful soprano voice and was always asked to lead the singing before
there was an organ in church.

Mary wanted Art to learn to play the organ so he could lead the singing in
church, but he was reluctant to do so. However, when she (with Jacob's
approval) told Art that he could get that 12 gauge shotgun he had always
wanted if he learned to play, he took a few lessons and practiced with a
will. Soon he could play most of the hymns and was the owner of a shiny new
Remington.

Then came the depression and the "Dirty Thirties." Some years the rust got
the crops. Other years it was the drought. Then if something did grow,
there was no market for it and it was worthless. There were years of dust
storms and grasshoppers. But through it all they worked together and not
only held on to what they had, but added to the family as well.

In 1935 Art married Edna Walth and in 1938 there was a grandson. Albert
married Helen Kosel in 1939. As the family grew there were changes in
living arrangements. After sharing their house first with Albert and Helen
and then with Art and Edna for a while, they decided to retire and move to
Bowdle. With a note that Mary had inherited from her dad, they bought a
house in town, but still continued to come to the farm frequently to
help with the never ending work.

Times got better again and they could relax a little more. They enjoyed
their six grandchildren when they came to visit or stayed at their house
during "Summer School." Some of the older grandchildren even stayed with
them while attending high school.

Life was full, but gradually things changed again. Mary developed cancer
and died in 1956. As the grandchildren graduated from high school they
moved away. In 1963 Albert and his family sold their farm and moved away.
In 1965 Art was killed in a power take-off accident and Edna moved away.
Art's farm, the old homeplace was also sold. Soon there were only Jacob and
one married granddaughter, Mardella (Mrs. Dale Bieber) who remained in
South Dakota.

His later years found Jacob going uptown every day for the mail for
himself, for his sister, sister-in-law, brother and for anyone else in the
neighborhood who couldn't get out to do it. If the weather was too cold to
start the car, he walked. Sometimes you could see him walking with a
handful of Christmas cactus blossoms from his own prolific plant on his way
to visit someone who was ill.

Although he was beginning to slow down Jacob always had an interest in
life. At the age of 85 he had his first airplane ride when he attended his
grandson, Allan's wedding in Phoenix, AZ. After a brief illness he died May
18, 1973.

JACOB M. and KATHERINE [JACOBER] BUECHLER

Jacob M. Buechler was born Sept. 18, 1881 in the Russian-Terman Territory
known as Neuglueckstahl. When Jacob was nine years old, he arrived in
America with his father Michael Jr. and his mother Katherina. Not satisfied
with the East Coast, the family boarded the train and settled a brief time
in the Eureka settlement. Shortly thereafter, Jacob's family homesteaded
northwest of Bowdle.

Jacob had a great interest in books and music. His only source of education
was his mother, who daily read the Bible and the German ABC Book. Singing
provided many hours of entertainment for this family. Many of the hymns
they sang in their home were sung in their nearby country church,
Neuglueckstahl Lutheran Church. Not only did Jacob love to sing, but also
learned to play the accordion and organ.

Jan. 24, 1905 Jacob married Katherine (Jakober) who was born Nov. 29, 1883.
They homesteaded on the farm four miles northwest of Bowdle. Here they
raised a family of three sons and one daughter. Although they experienced
the "Dirty 30's," they survived and progressed.

After 1941 Jacob and Katherine retired to Bowdle. They lived in the white
stucco house, north of the Seventh-day Adventist Church. Having a love for
nature, Jacob and Katherine raised a huge garden accented with beautiful
flowers. Those beautiful peonies were admired by the community for years
and some are still blooming there today. In the backyard they grew a
beautiful orchard of fruit trees and grape vines. Together Jacob and
Katherine could be heard singing while pulling weeds.

        Jacob M. and Katherine Buechler

After Katherine's death Mar. 21, 1948, Jacob continued living in his home
until his later years, when he returned to the farm and lived with his
youngest son Otto and wife Gertrude. Here he died at the age 91, Sept. 7,
1972. He will always be remembered by his family and friends, wearing that
special smile and singing:

        Was Kan es Schoner's geben,
        Und was kann Selger Sein,
        Alls wenn wir unser leben;
        Dem Herrn im, Glauben weih'n.

Together Jacob and Katherine had four children as follows:

August married Rose Schumacher, has four children and is retired, living in
Bowdle.

Herman married Althea Hieb and had five children. Herman died at the age of
42.

Freida married John F. Schilling. They had one child and live on the farm.

Otto married Gertrude Bentz. They have one child and are retired, living in
Bowdle.

JACOB SR. and KATHERINE [ROTT] BUECHLER

Jacob was born in Glueckstahl, South Russia May 14, 1858. In 1890 he and
his family arrived in the United States. They came to this new land with
Jacob's father Michael Buechler Sr. and brothers. The family traveled to
Eureka after their arrival in the U.S. Later they moved and settled on a
homestead six miles northwest of Bowdle. This homestead site was later
occupied by the Fred B. Buechler family (currently owned by Harold Nies.)

Jacob and his wife, Katherine Rott, had 14 children. Only seven grew to
adulthood: Jacob B., John B., Fred B., Rosina Doerr, Barbara Bieber, Mary
Bieber and Ida Buechler.

        Jacob Buechler Sr. Family Back: Jacob B., Fred B., John B. Front:
        Rosina, Jacob Sr., Mary, Katherine, Barbara

In 1910 Jacob's wife Katherine died. He later married Mrs. Christine
(Stoecker) Reib. After farming several more years, in 1919 they retired to
Bowdle. Then Sept. 19, 1924 Jacob died.

JOHN B. and MARY [EISENBEISZ] BUECHLER

John B. Buechler came to the United States in 1890 from Neuglueckstahl,
South Russia at the age of 1-1/2 with his parents and brother to homestead
northwest of Bowdle. His wife Mary Eisenbeisz arrived from the same area in
South Russia in 1898 with her parents at age 7. They homesteaded north of
Bowdle.

John and Mary were united in marriage Nov. 28, 1911 and blessed with 68
years of married life. They settled on a farm northwest of Bowdle where they
farmed until 1943 when they moved to Bowdle to make their home.

The couple had six children: Milbert (deceased,) Anna Weiszhaar, Hilda
Trefz, Alvin, Herbert (deceased) and Roland. They had 24 grandchildren and
31 great-grandchildren.

Their later years of life were spent at Bowdle Nursing Home. Mary died Jan.
21, 1980 and John died June 13 1980.

        John B. Buechler Family Back: Milbert, Herbert, Alvin, Roland.
        Front: Anna, John B., Mary, Hilda

JOHN J. and MAGDALENA [BOSSERT] BUECHLER

John J. Buechler was born Jan. 18, 1890 in Russia. In March 1890 his family
came to the United States and settled northwest of Bowdle where he grew up.
He was the son of John and Magdelena (Kirschman) Buechler.

John J. married Magdalena Bossert Nov. 24, 1912 in Artas. They made their
home four miles west of Bowdle until 1943 when they moved to town and
semi-retired. Magdalena Bossert was born Feb. 27, 1892 in Artas to
Christian and Magdelena (Bieber) Bossert.

        John J. and Magdalena Buechler

The couple had two daughters. Bertha Buechler is now Mrs. Albert Leidholt
and Edna Buechler married Arthur Aldinger. They also had two granddaughters
and a grandson. John J. worked for the Reede Produce many years grading
eggs every Wednesday and Saturday evening. John died May 12, 1978 and
Magdalena died Nov. 9, 1968.

JOHN M. and CHRISTINE [EISENBEISZ] BUECHLER

John M. came from Russia when he was 4 years old with his parents Michael
and Magdaline Buechler. He was united in marriage with Christine Eisenbeisz
Jan. 28, 1908. Christine was the daughter of Jacob and Katherine Eisenbeisz
who also came from South Russia in 1898. Both families lived on farms north
of Bowdle.

        John M. Buechler Family Back: Martha and Edna. Front: Christina and
        John

John and Christine farmed nine miles north of Bowdle at Buechler Lake for
nine years. In 1917 they sold their farm and moved to Bowdle. Unlike his
relatives who were farmers, John decided his priority was being a merchant.
So he and his brother-in-law, John G. Eisenbeisz, operated Bowdle Hardware.
Later John built the first filling station which is now the site of Bowdle
Cenex.

This couple was blessed with eight children, but only two survived. Martha
(Mrs Ray L. Keck) lives in Lodi, CA and Edna (Mrs. Alois Herman) of
Westport.

John M. Buechler died May 28, 1946 and Christine died Jan. 5. 1965.

JOHN SR. and MAGDALENA [KIRSCHMAN] BUECHLER

John Sr. was the son of Michael Sr. and Katherine Buechler. He married
Magdalena Kirschman. They homesteaded northwest of Bowdle on the farm
currently occupied by Elmer Buechler.

LEROY and ESTHER [ROESCH] BUECHLER

MICHAEL JR. and MAGDALENA [HERMAN] BUECHLER

Michael Jr., born Dec. 24, 1855 in Glueckstahl, Russia, was the first child
of Michael Sr. and Katherina (Strobel) Buechler. During his youth his
father moved to Neuglueckstahl, Russia. There Michael Jr. and his wife
Magdalena Herman, born Dec. 13, 1855, married and raised a family. Later
with their small family joined Michael's father's family and came to
America in 1890.

        Michael Jr., Magdalena, Jacob M., John M., Katherine, Magdalena

At the insistence of an uncle, they first went to Virginia, but believed a
better future lay ahead of them in the Dakota Territory, went to Eureka
where they lived a short while until they could locate land on which they
wished to settle. The entire group of Buechler families decided on
territory northwest of Bowdle in what was known as the Lucky Valley
District.

There they built their first home, a sod house and later replaced it with a
large wood framed house. In 1919 they retired to the town of Bowdle. After
they moved off their homestead, their son Henry lived on the farm home
until he decided to retire to Bowdle in 1941 and the John F. Schilling
family purchased the homestead. Mrs. Schilling is a granddaughter of
Michael Buechler Jr.

Michael Jr. died March 23, 1941 at the age of 85 and Magdalena died June 8,
1940 at the age of 84. The couple celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary
with their five children and 29 grandchildren.

Their children include: Jacob M. married Katherine Jacober, John M. married
Christine Eisenbeis, Henry M. married Elizabeth Opp (deceased) and then
married Margaret Opp, Katherine married Jacob Himmerich and Magdalena
married Jacob Gross.

MICHAEL SR. and KATHERINA [STROBEL] BUECHLER

Michael Buechler was born Aug. 4, 1828 and his wife, Katherina (Strobel)
was born Jan. 17, 1834 in Glueckstahl, Russia.

This couple is the source of all the Buechler relatives living here. When
Michael Sr. was about 60 years old in Russia, he had a dream to come with
his family to that promised land, America! During the year of 1890,
Michael's dream finally came true. He and his wife, Katherina with all
their beloved children and grandchildren left Neuglueckstahl, Russia to
sail the wide seas to that new land of the free.

        Katherina and Michael Buechler Sr.

They settled in Eureka with Katherina's sister and family, who helped them
locate their homestead, six miles northwest of Bowdle (now John Schilling's
farm.) Separately, the Buechler families, closely together, homesteaded
their acres, building their sod homes.

To gather to worship was no problem for the Michael Sr. families, who used
their home as a place of worship until their church Neuglueckstahl Lutheran
was built in 1902. Michael Sr. selected the high hill (the site in Harold
Nies's pasture) as the Neuglueckstahl Cemetery for their loved ones to
rest. Together with a strong faith in God and hard work they overcame many
hardships and continued to prosper.

This union was blessed with four sons and two daughters with most of them
married in Russia. Michael Jr. married Magdalena (Herman); Jacob Sr.
married Katherine (Rott); John Sr. married Magdalena (Kirschman); Frederich
married Magdalena (Oster) died, later married Elizabeth (Stotz) Katherina
married Christian Himmerich and Rosina married Fredrich Merkel.

Together they had 41 grandchildren. Four of their grandchildren are living
at the present time in Bowdle: David and Edward Buechler, Rosina Doerr and
Magdalena Schlecht.

Michael Sr. had two brothers who lived in this country: Christ Buechler in
Freeman and Joseph Buechler in Seneca.

Michael Sr. died a sudden death at the age of 76, Dec. 21, 1904 at his farm
home. His wife Katherina died Feb. 28, 1905. Both were buried in the
Neuglueckstahl Cemetery.

OTTO and GERTRUDE [BENTZ] BUECHLER

Otto is the youngest of three sons born to Jacob M. and Katherina (Jacober)
Buechler north of Bowdle Jan. 18, 1915. He attended rural school and as a
youth enjoyed hunting. Otto married Gertrude Bentz Sept. 23, 1940, daughter
of Mrs. Henry Jung and the late Edward Bentz.

Since Otto was such a dedicated farmer he and his family continued to farm
the homestead place of his parents, who retired to Bowdle in 1942.

        Gertrude and Otto Buechler

Otto and Gertrude were blessed with their only child, a daughter, Connie
Lee June 26, 1942.

In 1949 REA (electricity) was being put into farm homes in the surrounding
area. As the old farm home needed a lot of remodeling to accommodate the
electricity, Otto and Gert decided to build a new home on the farm. After
1950 most of the farms had electricity.

During 1977 the Buechlers decided to move to town to help care for Gert's
parents. The farming operation was continued by their daughter, Connie and
husband Gaylon Goetz. Again Otto and Gert built another new home in Bowdle,
their retirement home. But the two have not learned how to retire!

Otto still continues to go to the farm to help his son-in-law with the
farming and Gert is still sewing for her family and other people and does
charity work of all kinds besides. Although they are busy, they have time
to enjoy their two grandchildren, Selena and Jarrod.

representatives. All the children are Bowdle graduates and played in the
high school band. The boys were active in school sports and were altar boys
and lectors at St. Augustine's Catholic Church in Bowdle. Susan was a
teacher in religion and organist. Upon the graduations of Timothy in 1985
and Dennis in 1986, all the Carlson children will have four-year college
degrees. Bernard, Stephen and Dennis from St. John's University and John,
Susan, Richard and Timothy from the University of South Dakota. Stephan
will receive his graduate degree in 1985. Bernard and Susan are working
part-time on MBA degrees.

Bernard A. has been a volunteer fireman for the Bowdle Fire Department the
last 35 years. He is past president of the Commercial Club and Commander of
the American Legion. He is also a past member of the church council, city
council, hospital board, school board, Veterans of Foreign Wars and
Disabled Veterans, Knights of Columbus and active in Boys Scouts.

Margaret has also been active in church, teaching CCD classes for 14 years,
and community affairs, a member of the legion auxiliary, altar society,
bridge club, hospital auxiliary and past member of the Mothers' Club. She
has worked at the Bowdle Hospital for 16 years, where she is currently
Social Service and Activity Director for the Swing Bed Program at the
hospital.

HANS P. and CATHERINE [JOHNSON] CHRISTIANSON

Hans P. Christianson was born at Schleswig-Holstein, Germany in 1849. He
married Catherine Johnson, who was also born there in 1852. When Hans
completed his military service in Germany he was unable to find work to
provide for his family, so he, his wife and four children undertook the long
voyage to New York City. There they gathered a few resources and he
renounced his allegiance to the Kaiser.

They brought their family by train to Ipswich in 1886. At that time their
sixth child was 2 years old. They loaded their belongings on a cart drawn by
oxen and set out for Bowdle where the family settled south of town.

        Hans P. Christianson

The family managed a livestock and grain operation. The girls herded cattle
on the open prairie while the others planted and cultivated the fields. The
children attended Bowdle School and the youngest Harry, who was a good
athlete, went on to college. Katherine became a teacher and drove by horse
and buggy to Ipswich to attend teacher institutes.

Their children were Nick, Jens, Hans, Andrew, Katharane Rife, Ella Lemke
and Harry. All are deceased.

Hans Christianson died in 1931 and Catherine died in 1909. Both were buried
in St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Cemetery at Bowdle.

CHARLES and MARION [MERRIMAN] COMMET

Charles A. Commet, the eldest son of Suppree and Jennie McGlenn Commet, was
born Feb. 19, 1885 in Whiteford, MI and came to South Dakota with his
parents in April 1886. South Dakota has been his home ever since.

In the spring of 1906 he went to Perkins County and filed on land near
Lemmon. He sold his holding in Perkins County and returned to the Bowdle
area in 1910. Charley, his sister Maud and her husband Alfred Davidson
rented a farm and they farmed together until about 1912 when the Davidsons
rented another farm for themselves. Charley continued to farm the land
which his grandfather, George McGlenn, had homesteaded. Mr. McGlenn had
filed on the land in 1884.

Charles and Marion Merriman were married Dec. 3, 1919 and continued to live
on the farm. Their three daughters, Rachel, Doris and Carol were born
there. In 1932 they moved to Bowdle and acquired the property in the
northern part, which had belonged to Marion's parents George and Marion
Merriman. Their daughters graduated from the Bowdle High School and Charles
and Marion made their home there many years.

        Charles and Marion Commet

They farmed and also were in the dairy business and later he bought produce
and resold it and sold veterinary supplies and rendered valuable assistance
to farmers in the care of their livestock. They always had a big garden and
raised evergreen trees which he sold.

Charles continued to make his home there after the death of his wife Jan.
26, 1970 until he was in his 90's when he spent the winters with his
daughter and son-in-law Doris and Ron Campbell in Ravensdale, WA. He would
return every spring to plant and care for his garden during the growing
season. Even at age 99 years, he came back in the spring of 1984 to plant
what he was able to, but the work was too hard and the weather
uncooperative, so the garden was not the usual productive plot which
provided good vegetables for so many of the town's people.

In the summer of 1984 he sold his home and in September went to make his
home permanently with Doris and Ron in Washington.

Charles has three children, four grandchildren and nine
great-grandchildren. He celebrated his 100th birthday Feb. 19, 1985.

DWIGHT and PHYLLIS [MUELLER] COMMET

Dwight Commet and Phyllis Mueller were married Dec. 26, 1941 and made
their home on a farm they rented for six years. Dwight is the son of
Suppree Commet and Phyllis is the daughter of Joseph Mueller, a pioneer
businessman and hotel owner. In 1947 they bought a farm four miles south of
Bowdle. They continued to live there until 1954 when they moved into town,
but continued farming until 1980.

During her high school years Phyllis worked at the Gross Brothers store,
and she laughs as she recalls that the 50 cents a day she earned on the job
would purchase a good many items. Later her pay scale was increased to 75
cents a day and a pair of ladies silk stockings (yes everyone wore silk
hose in those days) was 79 cents -- so the store had to charge the
additional four cents until the next pay day.

Then she spent 20 years working at the Red Owl Store and for 24 years has
been employed at the Bowdle Sales Barn. She also does part-time nurse's
aide work at Bowdle Hospital.

Dwight also found employment in town, laying linoleum and carpeting and he
served on the Bowdle City Council. In 1966 they started the Bowdle Bait
Shop, which is still open for business. Their recreation is fishing.

They have two children. Dwight Jr. is married to Jo Anne Jeschke and lives
in Aberdeen. James married Kelly Brenneise and lives in Rapid City.

Mr. and Mrs. Commet have the pleasure of three grandchildren.

SUPPREE and JENNIE [McGLENN] COMMET

Suppree and Jennie McGlenn Commet came to South Dakota in April 1886 and
filed on a homestead southwest of Bowdle, in what is now the eastern part
of Walworth County. Mr. Commet died in Seattle, WA in 1949 at the age of
85. Mrs. Commet also saw her last days in Seattle, WA and died there in
1958 at the age of 92. They had five sons and seven daughters, all of whom
grew to adulthood on the homestead and seven are still living.

        Jennie and Suppree Commet

Charlie, the eldest, lives in Seattle, WA and celebrated his 100th
anniversary in February 1985. He had made his home in Bowdle until September
1984 when he went to live with his daughters in Seattle.

Ethel died at the age of 16 in 1903. George left South Dakota in 1910 and
was living in Spokane, WA at the time of his death in October 1969 at the
age of 80. His wife died in Spokane in 1953. They had one daughter who
lives in California.

Maud and her husband Alfred Davidson lived in the Bowdle area until 1926
when they moved to Mobridge. They had three children: Althea of Seattle,
Lloyd of Mobridge and Wilfred of California. These children all have
celebrated their Golden Wedding Anniversaries and are still living in their
own homes. Maud left South Dakota for Seattle in the 30's and lived there
until her death in 1966 at the age of 76. Alfred died in Mobridge in 1946.

Edna left South Dakota in 1941 and is now retired and living in her own
home in Everett, WA. Ralph and his wife Adele and their son and daughter
went to Mt. Vernon, WA in 1941, where he managed a ranch until his death in
1946 at the age of 50. Adele lives with her son Raymond and wife Adeline in
the Seattle area. Their daughter Laurice lives in Oklahoma City, where she
has been Sister Immaculate of the Carmelite Sisters of St. Therese since
January 1954.

Will, Dwight and their mother continued to live on the farm. The two men
farmed together until 1941 when Dwight and Phyllis Mueller were married and
bought a farm, where they lived several years before moving into Bowdle.
They had two sons Dwight Jr. who lives in Aberdeen and James who lives in
Rapid City.

Will and his mother continued to live and farm the home place until it was
sold in 1950. Pioneer families who came in the 1880's organized the
Walworth County Pioneer Club (WCPC) and on the roster was enrolled the
families of Suppree Commet, Sam Boyd, Bill Boyd, Morris Baker, Charles
Dorwin, Ed McGlenn and George Baumgartner, among others. All of these
families had settled in this area of Dakota Territory, coming from
Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota, when the land here was opened for
settlement. Their families socialized through this club until in the late
1940's when too few were left to carry on the tradition.

Mrs. Commet left South Dakota in 1950 after 64 years on the old homestead,
and went to Seattle, where she made her home with her daughters until the
time of her death in 1958. Will moved to Selby, where he served as Walworth
County Sheriff and has lived alone since the death of his wife Pauline in
1979.

Esther left South Dakota in 1937, going to Seattle and from there to
Juneau, AK where she worked for the government until she retired. She
continued to live in Alaska until she died in 1978 at the age of 77.

Margaret left South Dakota in 1926, going to Montana and then to Seattle,
where she is now retired and living in her own home. Dorothea and Claire
both left South Dakota in the 30's for Seattle, where they lived until
their husbands retired and they moved to Arizona, where both are still
living in their own homes.

The descendants of Mr. and Mrs. Suppree Commet as of September 1984 are: 12
children (seven still living), 11 grandchildren, 23 great-grandchildren, 37
great-great-grandchildren and 10 great-great-great-grandchildren. Five
generations including 95 persons.

DONALD and BETTY [KRAUSE] CORNISH

Donald Cornish married a former young Java lady, Elizabeth Krause and they
were both teachers. They taught in rural schools for seven years in the
Bowdle, Java and Eureka areas.

Their daughter Beverly was born at Bowdle Hospital Feb. 1, 1935. Dr. Jones
bill for a 10-day stay was only $50. It seems like a small amount, but for
a teacher whose salary was only $440 a year it wasn't a minor matter by no
means.

While Donald lived in Bowdle he refereed many of the Bowdle High School
basketball games. Being active in sports he played first base for the town
baseball team in 1935 as well as managed it in 1936. He recalls collecting
$60 from individual merchants for the purchase of bats and balls with which
to start the season. This was no trivial matter in those  days.

After teaching he served two years as Public Welfare Director at Mobridge
and two years at Pierre. Then Don and Betty were employed with the American
Red Cross for 31 years stationed in Texas, Panama Canal Zone, South Dakota,
Washington, D.C.; Virginia and Connecticut and now they live in a
retirement home in Sioux Falls.

ADDISON [PETE] and MARIE [WEISS] COYER

Pete was born July 27, 1892 in Wisconsin. He was the son of Michael and
Minerva Coyer. He lived in Huron and attended school there. Pete married
Marie Weiss, daughter of Joe and Amelia Weiss. Marie was born Sept. 29,
1900 in Watertown, but grew to adulthood and attended school in Hoven.

        Pete Coyer              Marie Coyer

Pete and Marie operated a pool hall in Pierpont and a cafe in Groton before
coming to Bowdle. In 1948 they moved to Bowdle and purchased the hardware
store on the north side of Main Street from Henry B. Baer, a pioneer
merchant of this city.

They had one daughter Eunice, who married Jerome Gjerde, a bus driver in
Seattle, WA now retired. They have four children: Brian, Brice, Barry and
Brett.

Pete died March 23, 1973.

ANTON and DOROTHEA [THOMAS] DEWALD

Anton Dewald was the eldest son of Michael and Magdalena (Sautner) Dewald,
born in Crimea, Russia in 1879. When he was 13 years old he came to the
United States with his parents in 1892. They settled in the Hoven area for
a short time before moving to a farm east of Bowdle.

In 1906 Anton married Dorothea Thomas, daughter of Franz and Elizabeth
Thomas, who had come to America from Odessa, Russia, where she had been
born in 1887. After their marriage they homesteaded on a farm 6 miles east
and 1/2 north of Bowdle where they lived until they retired and moved to
Bowdle in 1945. Anton and Dorothea had seven children.

Johanna was born in 1907. She married Joe Reis and they had six children.
They live in Mobridge.

Clara was born in 1909. She married Valentine Krumm. They had five children
and live in Hosmer.

George was born in 1911 and died one month after birth.

Mary was born in 1912. She married Maynard Lickfelt. They have three
children and live in Aberdeen.

Kate was born in 1915. She married Julius Buechler and they had two
children. They live in Hermiston, OR.

Joe A. Dewald's history is listed separately in this book.

Dorothy was born in 1922. She married Ben Schoch and had five children.
After Ben's death she married Eugene Corsi and lives in Pueblo, CO.

Anton Dewald died in 1965 and Dorothea died in 1970. They were buried in
Bowdle Cemetery.

EDMUND and FRIEDA [STUCKEL] DEWALD

Edmunds and Frieda Stuckel Dewald have made their home in Bowdle since
their marriage at St. Augustine's Catholic Church June 9, 1952. Edmund is
the son of Mr. and Mrs. Joe G. Dewald and was born on their farm Oct. 27,
1922. His father was born in the Hoven Territory July 9, 1897 and his
mother, the former Genevieve (Jenny) Hoerner, was born on a farm near
Bowdle Jan. 6, 1903.

Frieda's parents, Adolph and Martha (Schumacher) Stuckel are both deceased.
Her mother was born in the United States and her father was an Austrian by
birth. He died May 5, 1960. Her mother died Nov. 13, 1938.

Edmund has been farming since completing his education at Bowdle High
School. He has been on the Farmers Union Oil Company board of directors for
30 years. Frieda worked nearly 20 years at the Bowdle Meat Market until ill
health forced her retirement.

Frieda was the bride of Eddie Stappler. The wedding took place in 1947 and
ended in tragedy when he was killed in a car-train collision at the Gretna
Grain Elevator in 1948. They had a daughter Bernadette (Mrs. Dennis
Burger), who is employed at the 3M Company in Aberdeen. She has two sons
and two daughters.

        Back: Mary, Paulette, Bernadette Front: Edmund and Frieda Dewald

JOHN and BARBARA [BACHMAN] DEWALD

Barbara Dewald married John Dewald, son of Michael and Magdalena Sautner
Dewald in April 1923. They made their home on the farm in Cottonwood Lake
Township which had been a wedding gift to Barbara and her first husband
Raphael Dewald. John came to this country at the age of eight with his
parents from Crimea, Russia. He became a citizen of the United States April
15, 1957 in Aberdeen. Raphael and Barbara had a daughter Frances. John and
Barbara raised their family on the farm where they remained until 1947 when
they moved into Bowdle and their sons Joe and George assumed the operation
of the farm. They were members of St. Augustine's Catholic Church.

Barbara was an active member of the Altar Society, holding several offices.
She was a talented seamstress and used this talent by taking care of the
church linens, sewing for many people and making infants clothing and coats
and dresses for other people. John spent many hours taking care of the
church clock and tending the furnace. He died Sept. 24, 1964. After living
at the Bowdle Nursing Home for 12 Years, Barbara died April 15, 1985.

        Back: Kathleen, George, Frances, Joseph, Irene Front: Barbara,
        John, Gerald Dewald

Their family included: Frances, married Val Senn and lives in Missoula, MT.

Joseph B. married Patty (Patricia) Senn and lives on the farm in Cottonwood
Lake Township. They had seven children. Richard died in a tractor accident
in 1964, Karen, Rosemary, Marcia, Jane, David and Steven.

Irene married Herman Schreter (he died May 1983) and lives in Apple Valley,
CA. Children: Gregory, Rhoda Schreter Gomes, Brian, Lance and Scott.

Raymond died in infancy.

George married Novell Bieber and lives in Auburn, WA. Children: Jennifer
and Paul.

Kathleen married Alvin Eisenbeisz. They live on a farm southeast of Bowdle.
Their children are Cynthia Eisenbeisz Odenbach, Sandra, Clyde and Wade.

Gerald and Harold were twins. Harold died at birth. Gerald married Janice
Geffree and lives in Portland, OR. Their children are Gayle, Glenn and Guy.

JOSEPH B. and PATTY [SENN] DEWALD

JOSEPH G. and GENEVIEVE [HOERNER] DEWALD

The year, 1894, is an important date in the Dewald family as that is when
their great-grandparents, Michael and Magdalena Dewald, came to the United
States, making the trip aboard a cattle boat. The Dewald children and their
families grew up in the Bowdle area and longevity helped everyone in the
community to get to know them.

Joseph G. Dewald was born to Michael and Magdalena (Sautner) Dewald July 9,
1897 at rural Hoven, the sixth of 10 children. In 1899 the Dewald family
moved to the homestead 6 miles east of Bowdle.

Genevieve Hoerner was born to Balthasar and Elizabeth (Kiest) Hoerner Jan.
6, 1903 at rural Bowdle, the eighth of 13 children.

Joe and Jennie attended the rural school east of Bowdle and worked on their
parents' farms following their limited elementary education.

On May 23, 1922 Joe and Jennie were married at St. Augustine's Catholic
Church in Bowdle by Jennie's brother, the late Msgr. Henry Hoerner. They
made their home on the Dewald homestead which they farmed for 42 years and
moved into Bowdle in 1965.

Joe held various positions on the Cottonwood Lake Township and School
Boards, besides being busy on the farm. He was assessor for 8 years;
supervisor, 4 years and clerk of the school board for 12 years. He was also
ASC Township Committeeman a number of years; WPA foreman and later
timekeeper.

Jennie was kept busy with a houseful of children besides milking cows,
baking, washing, ironing, raising huge gardens and frequently was on call to
help in the fields.

About 1965 they retired from the farm and moved into Bowdle to live. Mrs.
Dewald kept busy making numerous afghans for her children, grandchildren
and great-grandchildren.

They were the parents of 12 children, one of whom, Bernadine, died in
infancy. Those remaining are:

Edmund: resides in Bowdle, was born Oct. 27, 1922. He married Frieda
Stuckel Stappler June 9, 1952. They have 3 children and 7 grandchildren.

Ralph: of Bowdle, was born Sept. 17, 1923. His wife is the former Bernice
Stuckel. Their marriage took place Oct. 9, 1951. They had five children, one
of whom, Terry, died in a vehicle accident Nov. 23, 1980. They have 3
grandchildren.

Edward: of Cudahy, WI was born July 16, 1925. He married Florence Maurer
Nov. 12, 1955. They have 5 children

Geraldine: of Aberdeen was born Sept. 8, 1929. She married Robert Senn July
5, 1952. They have 2 children and 5 grandchildren.

Jeanette: of Cudahy, WI was born July 6, 1932. She married Jerome Gosh July
11, 1953. They have 2 children and 1 grandchild.

Delphia: of Ipswich was born Aug. 5, 1934. She was married to Vernon Heinz
in May 1955. They had 3 children. Vernon died Dec. 28, 1960. She married
Carl Sanborn June 25, 1962 and they have 2 children and 4 grandchildren.

Betty: of Brookings was born Dec. 20, 1936. She married Marvin Hochstetter
Aug. 25, 1956. They have 2 children and 1 grandchild.

Carlotta: of Iron River, MI was born Nov. 7, 1939. She married Jerry
Williams Oct. 22, 1966. They had 2 children. Jerry died Sept. 21, 1970. She
married James Serena Dec. 23, 1972 and 2 children were born to this union.

Charles: of Burbank, CA was born Nov. 15, 1941. He married Judy La Beau June
26, 1965. They have 3 children.

Carol: of Aberdeen was born May 17, 1944. She married Harlin Knecht Oct.
16, 1965. They have 3 children.

James: of Cudahy, WI was born Sept. 12, 1946. He married Karen Zimmer Nov.
25, 1967. They have one child.

The Joe G. Dewalds had 33 grandchildren and 18 great grandchildren.

Mrs. Dewald died Sept. 15, 1984 and Mr. Dewald died March 25, 1985.
Survivors include five sons, six daughters, two brothers and one sister.

MICHAEL and MAGDALENA [SAUTNER] DEWALD

Michael Dewald and Magdalena Sautner were born in 1858 in Crimea, Russia.
In 1894 they came to the United States aboard a cattle ship. They lived
near Hoven, in Walworth County near Swan Lake, when they first arrived. But
since there was no longer any land available in that area, they came to
Bowdle in 1899 and homesteaded 6 miles east of town.

They had 10 children, two of whom died en route to the United States. Their
children were Rose (Mrs. Sebastian Wentz,) Anton, John, Raphael, Mary (Mrs.
Matt Bachman,) Joe G., Frances (Mrs. Tony Weindl) and Sr. M. Mechtild. All
are deceased but Frances of Rosalia, WA and Sister M. Mechtild of Mankato,
MN.

Mr. and Mrs. Dewald retired from the farm after more than 35 years of
farming and moved to Bowdle where they made their home. When unable to care
for themselves they lived out the remaining years with their daughter,
Frances (Mrs. Tony Weindl) who lived on a farm near Roscoe. Both Michael
and Elizabeth died in 1939.

RALPH P. and BERNICE [STUCKEL] DEWALD

Ralph Dewald was born Sept. 12, 1923 at Bowdle, the son of Joseph G. Dewald
and his wife Genevieve, nee Hoerner. He attended the Bowdle Schools and
served in the U.S. Army during World War II. On his discharge he returned
home to assist his father with the farm work and Oct. 9, 1951 he married
Bernice Stuckel, daughter of Adolph and Martha Stuckel, both of whom are
now deceased.

        Janet and Terrance Dewald

Nancy Dewald was born March 8, 1954 and lives in Glendale, CA where she

RAPHAEL and BARBARA [BACHMAN] DEWALD

Barbara, daughter of Leonard and Magdalena Heilman Bachman was born July
13, 1896 in Russia. She came to this country with her parents at an early
age, coming by ship from Odessa.

Raphael Dewald came to the United States with his parents Michael and

        Raphael and Barbara Dewald

Barbara and Raphael were married in 1915 and lived on a quarter section of

JACOB and KATHERINA [TREICHEL] DIEDTRICH

Mr. Jacob Diedtrich was born Feb. 1, 1898 in South Russia. At the age of 15
years he came to the United States with his parents Jacob and Anna Maria
Diedtrich May 18, 1913. He worked as hired help for Jacob Gross and Christ
Schumacher in the Bowdle area.

He married Katherina Treichel in October 1919. She was also born in South
Russia, but came to America when she was three years old with her parents

the West River country near Glencross in Dewey County for 14 years.

In the autumn 1936 they moved to the Tolstoy area until the autumn 1967
when they sold their farm and moved to Bowdle to retire. They purchased the

GLENN E. and LUCILLE [HUFF] DIPPERT

Glenn E. and Lucille Dippert were Bowdle residents from 1967 to 1982,
during which time Glenn served as Chief of Police.

Glenn Dippert was born March 26, 1926 in Arlington. His mother was also
born in Arlington and his father in Fort Robertson, NE. Both are now
deceased.

Glenn's parents moved to a farm or ranch near Faith, where Glenn lived from
age 11 to 30, working for his father and neighboring ranchers. Glenn, who
completed the eight grades at the district school, then decided to go into
law enforcement. His first instructor was the Faith Chief of Police. He then
served in that capacity in the following South Dakota towns: Midland, a
year at Highmore, two months at McLaughlin, a year at Timber Lake and at
Bowdle beginning Sept. 9, 1967 at the time R.J. Herman was city mayor. He
served as law officer at Bristol for six months, returning to Bowdle at the
time Albert Berg was elected mayor. He also served on the city ambulance
crew. In September 1982 Bowdle decided to go Contract Law with Edmunds
County.

        Glenn E. Dippert

Glenn married Lucille Huff in December 1965. She was the daughter of Mr.
and Mrs. George Huff, born June 6, 1926 in Highmore. Her mother died Jan.
11, 1949 and her father died Jan. 13, 1965. Glenn and Lucy were married
Dec. 19, 1965 in Highmore.

The Dipperts moved from Bowdle to Highmore in February 1983 where both are
employed as maintenance engineers at the Highmore Livestock Exchange. They
return to Bowdle frequently as they say, "We enjoyed working with the
Bowdle City Council and mayors and think a lot of the people here.

ARNOLD and PEARL [WEFEL] DOERR

Arnold Doerr was born at Bowdle to Jacob F. and Rosina Doerr. His father
was born at Freeman and died Oct. 31, 1967. His mother was born at Bowdle
and makes her home there.

Arnold graduated from Bowdle High School and served in the U.S. Armed
Forces during World War II. He married Pearl Wefel of Jeffers, MN June 11,
1944. Her parents were Mr. and Mrs. George Wefel. Pearl graduated from
Jeffers High School and Hollywood Beauty School in Minneapolis. Pearl Doerr
died Oct. 7, 1978.

After his discharge and marriage Arnold farmed from 1954 to 1982. He is
presently working as a surveyor for the WEB Water Pipeline.

Arnold and Pearl had five children. James lives in Minneapolis, MN; Thomas
lives in Aberdeen; Harvey, his wife Ardilla and son Mathew live in
Mitchell; Judy and her husband Wayne Koester live at Mansfield and Ronald
is a student at South Dakota State University in Brookings.

GEORGE and ELIZABETH [MERKEL] DOERR

George was born April 7, 1895 at Java. He was the son of Jacob and
Katherine (Bauder) Doerr. Jacob Doerr was born in Kassel, South Russia
March 15, 1868 and died June 30, 1930. Katherine was born in Neuglueckstahl
April 17, 1867 and died Oct. 10, 1940.

George married Elizabeth Merkel, daughter of Jacob and Elizabeth (Hinger)
Merkel. She was born in Sophienthal, South Russia. Her father was born in
Bergdorf, South Russia Dec. 25, 1865 and died Jan. 3, 1940. Her mother was
born April 27, 1867 in Glueckstahl, South Russia and died in May 1940.

George and Elizabeth farmed in Walworth County until he had a bad accident
with a horse. After trying to farm another year he sold out and moved to
Bowdle. Their home was then the second house south of the school. Since
then it has changed to the third house when they built a house beside their
house. Many happy moments were spent at that home and some sad ones too,
when their son died in 1931 at the age of 7.

When all the children had married or moved away from home George and
Elizabeth sold out and moved to Tacoma, WA. They bought a house and lived
there until 1961 when George died and Elizabeth moved in with her daughter
Tina. She lived with them several years until she moved in with Tillie and
lived there until 1970. Then she moved into a garage apartment on her
daughter Elanor's property and lived there until 1981 when she went to live
with her daughter Wilhelmine in Georgia. She lived there until April 12,
1982 when she died. Elizabeth and George are buried in Mountain View
Cemetery at Tacoma, WA.

The children of George and Elizabeth are as follows:

Wilhelmine, born Jan. 3, 1922, married James E. Lary. They live in Tucker,
GA. Wilhelmine worked in electronics many years while James was with the
U.S. Postal Service until 1982 when he retired. They have five sons: David,
Todd, George, James and Gene.

Elanor was born Sept. 24, 1923, married Wilfred Ryan and lives at Tacoma,
WA. She was a cashier at Safeway for 25 years and her husband retired from
Boeing. Their children are Linda, William, Joseph and Mary.

Rueben was born Oct. 11, 1924 and died in October 1931.

Albertina, born April 6, 1926, was married to Dess L. Ferguson. She is a
cashier at Safeway and lives at Tacoma, WA. Their children are Sandra and
Dess.

Ottilia, born May 19, 1927, was married to Frank DeLuca. Tillie lives at
Auburn, WA and works for Boeing. They have four children: Steven, Timothy,
Renee and Denise.

Raymond, born Dec. 30, 1928, married Elizabeth Watterson. They live in Las
Vegas, NV where Raymond is employed with the hospital. Their children are
Douglas, Robert and Brenda.

Norman was born Oct. 18, 1934. He and his wife live at Roseville, MN and
Norman is vice-president of material management for BN Railroad. Their
children are Rodney and Clinton.

Lloyd, born Oct. 2, 1938, married Mary Lou Coss and lives at Buena Park,
CA. Lloyd is employed with the BN Railroad. They have two children: Don and
Lisa.

PHILLIP and BARBARA [ROTT] DOLLINGER

The Dollinger family traces their ancestors back to Christian Dollinger,
born about 1759 at Birkenfeld Claw, Wuerttembergia, South Germany. His wife
was named Katharina. They had a son Gottlieb who was born Jan. 27, 1805 in
Germany and immigrated to Glueckstahl, South Russia. His wife was the
former Christina Gehring, who was born in Germany. They had seven children.
Gottlieb died Dec. 14, 1859. His wife also died in Russia. Gottlieb was
known as the biggest man in the German Colony. He was very strong and at
the time of his sudden death the neighbors said, "Death should have been
afraid of him."

        Back: Gottlieb, Jake, John, Magdalene Hagele, Christ. Middle:
        Christine Binder, Elizabeth Dollinger, Rose Nies, Rika Nies, Katie
        Hagele Maier. Front: Phillip Dollinger, Barbara Rott Dollinger, Fred
        Dollinger.

Their children included a son Gottlieb Jr. who came to the U.S. in 1905. He
married Rasena Karner. Fredrick married Elizabeth Opp. Elizabeth married
Adam Haas. Christianna married George Gross. Johann, born July 17, 1840 and
died March 15, 1915, married Elizabeth Reiger. She was born April 25, 1840
and died May 15, 1919. Phillip was born Oct. 3, 1842 and died Sept. 17,
1917. He married Barbara Rott in Russia. Kathrina Dollinger was born April
1845 and married Fredrick Rott.

Phillip was the first of the Dollinger family to come to the United States,
arriving in Eureka April 27, 1889. He and Barbara brought their family of 11
children with them including Fred, Gottlieb, Fredricka, Rosina, John,
Kathrina, Jacob, Christian, Elizabeth, Christina and Magdalina.

Phillip and Barbara Dollinger were the grandparents of Emma Binder, Dena
Holweger, Maggie Voegele, Sam Binder, Helen Holweger, John Binder, Leon
Binder, Lydia Heinrich, Matilda Johnson, Ellen Holweger and Milton Hagele.

Phillip Dollinger became the patriarch of the Dollingers in this area. He
homesteaded 12 miles south of Bowdle. The house was sold and moved to town
and is now the dwelling of Walter Jungs at 1012 7th Avenue.

ROBERT A. and PAMELA [WIECHMANN] DRAKE

        Pam, Kendra, Kim, Bob, Ryan Drake

After graduation in 1981 Robert became the animal nutritionist at McFleeg
Inc. in Bowdle. In the future he will return to school and work on his
doctorate. Bob's statement about Bowdle, "We had several reservations about
Bowdle at first, but the friendly people made it home."

JOHN J. and KATHERINE [BUECHLER] EISENBEISS

John J. Eisenbeiss, son of Jakob and Barbara Buechler Eisenbeisz was the
9th child born to them on Dec. 1, 1873. John died at Compton, CA Sept. 21,
1964. He was married to Katherine Buechler Dec. 6, 1898, who died June 9,
1927 at Bowdle.

The spelling of his name from Eisenbeisz to Eisenbeiss was due to a mistake
on the immigration papers and he added an extra J. to his name to
distinguish him from another John Eisenbeisz who was in business in Bowdle.

After World War I he bought the Ford dealership and sold the Model "T." In
1920 he sold out and bought the Anderson Hotel, converted it into a garage
and held the dealership for Buick, Oakland, Hudson, Essex, Durant, Star and
Overland cars. This is now the Alvin Reuer Garage.

All of John J.'s children were born at Bowdle or Java and after the death
of his wife, he moved to Compton, CA. The children are: John F., married to
Helen Riede, is deceased; Henry married Eva Bronkow, now deceased; Mathew
and Bertha died in infancy; David "Monk" married Anna Weddle and died Aug.
3, 1976; Theodore married Peggy Sherman in May 1930 and died in October
1930. Albert married Margie Orr; Otto married Helen Sippert; Hildegarde
married Frances Doebler; Herman married Mary Lou Madden; Harold married
Lucille Mirch (he is deceased) and Herbert married Lucille Stuck. The five
surviving children live in California.

ALVIN A. and KATHY [DEWALD] EISENBEISZ

Alvin A. Eisenbeisz was born March 24, 1929 at Bowdle to Fred and Anna
Eisenbeisz. Alvin graduated from Bowdle High School and attended Northern
State College in Aberdeen. He married Kathleen (Kathy) Dewald June 17,
1954. Kathy, daughter of John and Barbara Dewald, was born Oct. 22, 1933.

Kathy attended Northern State College after graduating from Bowdle and was
a school teacher. Alvin and Kathy made their home on the old Dorwin farm
southeast of Bowdle, the farm originally homesteaded by a Mr. Stockson.

The couple are the parents of four children.

Cynthia, born Nov. 25, 1957, is a registered nurse and the wife of Michael

ARTHUR JR. and ELOISE [LICKFELT] EISENBEISZ

Eloise (Lickfelt) Eisenbeisz was born Sept. 25, 1935 to Edwin and Irene
Lickfelt at Bowdle. She was educated at Bowdle and after graduation in 1953
she moved to Aberdeen with her father, two sisters and brother. In the fall
of 1953 she began her nursing career at Presentation College of Nursing.
During her three years of college she spent the summer between her junior
and senior years working at Bowdle Hospital.

In August 1956 she graduated from Presentation School of Nursing, took her
exams and while vacationing in the Black Hills word reached her she had
passed and was now a registered nurse. In September 1956 she began her
full-time work at Bowdle Hospital, along with a friend, alternating days,
nights and weekends. Her friend left in March 1957, leaving Bowdle Hospital
with only one RN and when the supervisor Mrs. McMahon left, Eloise took the
job of supervisor too.

While working at the hospital she met Arthur Eisenbeisz Jr. and after a
whirlwind courtship, married him Sept. 1, 1967. Arthur is the son of Arthur
and Martha (Trefz) Eisenbeisz Sr. of Hosmer. He received his education at
rural school and Hosmer High School. After graduation he returned to the
farm to help his father. Eloise continued working at Bowdle Hospital.

They were blessed with their first son Oct. 24, 1958, whom they named
Randall Scott. Working part-time at the hospital kept Eloise busy, but not
so busy they could not help but be joyful when their second son Edwin Jay
was born Aug. 20, 1961. Needing more help with the farming Art and Eloise
were more than happy to welcome a third son Derek Arthur born Sept. 16,
1963. By this time Bowdle had built a new hospital and Eloise found it an
exciting place to work. Their joy was short-lived when a baby girl born
July 15, 1965, whom they named Racheal Marie died July 18, 1965.

        Back: Randall, Derek, Eloise, Edwin Stephanie, Andrea, Arthur
        Eisenbeisz Jr.

Bowdle Hospital closed for a short time and then Eloise went to work at
Eureka Hospital, returning to Bowdle in 1968. In January 1972 Eloise
retired from her career of nursing due to the approaching arrival of a
daughter Stephanie Ann Sept. 12, 1972. The family was happy when Andrea
Lynn was born Jan. 19, 1975 and so were her Grandpa and Grandma Eisenbeisz,
as it was their 39th anniversary.

In August 1980 Eloise decided to go back to her career of nursing and again
worked at Bowdle Hospital and the Hosmer Senior Citizens Home. She has
since limited her work to Bowdle Hospital. Arthur still farms on the home
place, along with the help from their children.

Randall Scott entered the ministry and graduated from Luther Northwestern
Seminary in May 1984. He attended four years at Augustana College, three
years at Luther Seminary, one year of internship at Grand Junction, CO and
at the present time is with the North Dakota District serving three
parishes. He lives at Lemmon and is not married.

Edwin Jay graduated from Bowdle High School, attended Lake Area Vo-Tech
Institute at Watertown and graduated with honors. He began working as a
diesel mechanic and in March 1982 moved to Aberdeen to work for Brown
County Implement and was made shop foreman. Prior to that he worked a short
time at Huron. He married Shelly Jensen of Oldham May 25, 1985 and they
live in Aberdeen.

Derek graduated from Bowdle High School. He attended Lake Area Vo-Tech
Institute in Watertown and also has a degree in diesel mechanics, but
decided he liked farm life better and is farming with his parents.

Stephanie and Andrea attend school at Bowdle and keep their parents busy
attending all the activities in which they participate.

BLAKE and GLENDA [GILL] EISENBEISZ
