MRS. BASFORD [Nina] JARVIS

This pioneer day recollection by Mrs. Basford Jarvis was written in 1961
and is being reprinted as written then.

"I was born May 8, 1886 the spring that the town of Bowdle was platted.
Until I was six years old I lived north of Bowdle in Bowdle Township, known
in those days as the Basford farm. My mother, who was a widow, later bought
a house in town so that I could go to school. As I recall it is the second
house south from the Legion Hall, now belonging to the Krum family. She had
an addition from the farm house which belonged to my grandfather, moved in
and put onto the house she purchased.

The street at that time was the last one on the west side of town. The
house on the north of us was occupied by the Chris Laweins and to the south
lived the Shermans, the J. Jewetts, Strobels and Ole Knudsons. The last
house on the east side of town and on the south end of Milan Street (school)
and the highway was the Arthur Bickert home. It was considered out of town
in that day.

To the west of our house was a big race track. Big stacks of hay were cut
from the track area and stacked there. Sometimes they caught fire--a lot of
excitement for everyone. On the east side of Fuller Street where I lived
and back of the present Bitz Plumbing Shop, was a large warehouse which
later burned down. A family by the name of Pitts or Pitz lived south of the
warehouse and their girls used to stay with my brother Carl and me when my
mother went out. The last I knew, some of the family lived in Hoven.

A scarlet fever epidemic brought tragedy to the town when I was seven years
old. Several children died of it, including my three-year-old sister Vera, a
Hudson boy and the two Givens girls. Scarlet fever illness cost me my
hearing. The Clark Hudson's home at that time was on north Newcomer Street,
about where Kurle's have their shop now.

Other names that come to my mind are the Deckers, Prof. Schelleger, Harry
Gidley, Clayton Musser (who owned the harness shop east of the Aurand and
Amerpohl Store. They lived in the east part of town. I used to deliver milk
to the Amerpohls.

Mrs. Aurand's mother Mrs. Cooley was my Sunday School teacher when I was 12
years old. We attended the Methodist Church. The Aurand's daughter Vera
later became Mrs. Harry Slyder. Other oldtimers whose names I recall were
the hotel keeper Hub Meyers, John Meakins and the Rhodes family. Folks by
the name of Zimmer had a large house on the first farm just west of Bowdle.

There was a business section on the northeast side of Main Street as I
recall (site of the present post office) which included the Yaukey Drug
Store, Merrits Store, Givens Cafe, all of which were wiped out by a fire.
Another fire casualty was the Furset Cafe located back of the Hardware
Store. A livery stable was also consumed by flames.

When my widowed mother Mrs. Etoile Basford married my step-father Enoch
Rose in 1893 the band gave them a shivaree. Bowdle always had a band. My
mother used to talk about Spring Lake and I can remember her telling that
when she came here in 1885 the lake was full of water and the waves could
be seen from the old Bangor road (now U.S. 12.) Near the Painter home (now
just northeast of the Standard Service) there was always a big pond in the
early spring and we children used to skate and slide there.

Other Main Street recollections are the Henry Maas Drug Store and H.E.
Mason store. When Mason's store burned he set up in a store in the old
opera house until he could rebuild the building which now houses Erv
Gross's store and the bank. The old opera house was later converted into a
garage, after serving for school purposes when the first school house was
torn down. High school classes were held in the Masonic Hall. The old opera
house (Schaible Garage) burned down in 1956.

Bill Boyd built the hall which took the place of the opera house where the
Legion Hall is today. I also recall four saloons on Main Street competing
for the patronage of the thirsty, a pool hall and a Mr. Kresh who had the
barber shop about 1902.

The O'Neills (Bill, Fred and Charles,) W.J. Jarvis, Suppree Commet, Bill
Boyd, Morris Baker, Tom Murray and my stepfather Enoch Rose batched
together in the early days when land west of Bowdle was first filed for
settlement.

Other oldtimers in and out of town whom I recall were Charles Dorwin,
George Baumgarten, Henry Erbe, John Erbe, Gus Erbe, George Erbe, George
Sebert, the Stangls, the McGlenns, two families of Jergusons who lived near
Spring Lake, two families of Herrwalds of southwest of town and many others.
North of town were the Ketterlings whose daughters later became Mrs. Jacob
Hoffman and Mrs. Otto Helmer.

About 1910 or later The Chatauqua was the main entertainment of the summer.
They were nice clean shows and would last about six days with two billings
daily. They were held in a large tent.

Dr. Edwards was the town's beloved physician and I remember his daughter
Mary (now Mrs. Alex Searle) as a little girl with long curls.

Lawyer Ham's house was considered the real fancy place of the town--it was
the John Hoven home for many years and now belongs to Adolph Treichel.

The only oldtimers I know of from those early days who are now left are
Mary Searle, Charles Commet, Tillie Baumgarten of Selby, Carl Haupt, Pete
Murray and myself."

Since this recollection was written in 1961 it was noted that Bill Jarvis
died in 1960 and Nina Jarvis died in 1971.

JOHN and ELIZABETH [BOLLINGER] JENNER

John Jenner was born Oct. 31, 1885 in Odessa, Russia. He moved to America
with his family in 1887 when he was just two years old. His family
eventually settled near Fairfax where they farmed and ranched near the
Missouri River.

Elizabeth (Lizzie) Bollinger was born Nov. 29, 1885 at Tyndall. Her family
later moved across the Nebraska border near Anoka. John and Lizzie were
married in 1892 when both were 16 years old.

In 1919 John sold the farm at Fairfax and purchased the land on which the
Emil Mertz farm now stands. That year the Jenners, with their daughter
Katherine, moved to Bowdle. There were no buildings on the farm site. So
they stayed at the Emil Bollinger farm until a house could be built.

Their daughter Katherine Haupt remembers that their 1919 arrival took place
in a snowstorm so severe that sleighs were used to travel to the Bollinger
farm. Their horses, machinery and furniture, which were being sent by
train, were held up in Sioux City for a week due to the storm.

With the help of relatives and others John soon built the house, some small
outbuildings and in 1920 the large barn. In 1946 John and Lizzie retired to
Bowdle where they lived for a short time in their son-in-law's (Ernest
Haupt) house. Ernest then took over the farm. In 1947 the Jenners moved to
Aberdeen where they remained until their deaths. John died in 1949 and
Lizzie died in 1959.

        Elizabeth and John Jenner

They had two daughters. One lived only 11 days. The other, Katherine Haupt,
lives in Thornton, CO.

LEONARD and FRANCES [WOLF] JOACHIM

Leonard Joachim was born Oct. 18, 1918 in Danzig, ND to Mr. and Mrs.
Gottlieb Joachim. While he was a young lad the family moved to Eureka. At
age 18 he went to Aberdeen where he worked four years for Forkel Moving and
then for Culbert Ice Company.

Frances Joachim, nee Wolf was born Jan. 7, 1925 in Java to Mr. and Mrs. Wm.
Wolf. She graduated from Java High School in 1943 and worked for Schlepp
Drug Store until the fall, when she went to work at Cozy Cafe in Aberdeen
and later at White Way Cafe. Here is where she met Leonard Joachim and they
were married June 13, 1944 at Zion Lutheran Church in Aberdeen.

They moved to Bowdle Oct. 8, 1944 where Leonard and his father-in-law Bill
Wolf were in partnership in the City Dray Line, operating this business
7-1/2 years. They sold the business in 1952 and Leonard worked some months
on a farm in the Bowdle area. He went to work at Bowdle Creamery April 14,
1952 and remained for 31 years until March 11, 1983. Now he keeps busy with
his yard work, helps Frances with the housework and taking care of her
father Wm. Wolf. Frances has been working in different cafes in Bowdle and
at present works part-time at the Gold Nugget.

They have one daughter Judy Ann, who married Kenneth Horst of Java May 4,
1963. They have five children: Monica, Michelle, Melissa, Bradley and
Brian. Monica was married to Tim Sandmeier Nov. 20, 1982 and they have a
daughter Sarah.

EVON and EILEEN [HUFT] JOB

Evon Job was born Feb. 1, 1944 in Hoven, the son of Elmer and Violet Job.
He graduated from Gettysburg High School.

Evon married Eileen Huft of Bowdle Oct. 16, 1966. She is the daughter of
Jacob and Edna Huft and was born in Eureka. Eileen attended the district
school near her father's farm for the first year. Jake and Edna moved to
her grandfather's farm five miles north of Bowdle and Eileen attended that
district school. When in the fifth grade she went to school in Bowdle and
graduated from Bowdle High School.

        Back: Wesley, Eileen, Evon Front: Kerry, Jaci, Jodi Job

Evon and Eileen are the parents of four children. Jacquelin was born Nov.
6, 1966 and attends Watertown Vo-Tech. Wesley was born Jan. 20, 1970, Jodi
was born Dec. 21, 1970 and Kerry was born March 5, 1972. The younger
children attend Bowdle schools.

Evon and Eileen spent the first seven years of their marriage in Gettysburg
where he worked for a rancher. In 1973 they moved to Bowdle where Evon
worked for Bowdle Creamery and in 1979 he began his present job at Bowdle
Cenex. Eileen was employed at Our Closet clothing store until it closed in
June 1985.

FRED C. and ELIZABETH [MILLER] JOHNLE

Fred C. Johnle came to the United States in 1893 at the age of 10 with his
parents John and Johanna Johnle. John was born April 15, 1858 and died
March 12, 1915. Johanna was born April 26, 1850 and died Feb. 2, 1910. They
were natives of South Russia. They settled on a farm north of Hoven and
Fred attended the rural school.

Nov. 28, 1907 Fred C. married Elizabeth Miller who came to the United
States with her parents when she was three. They were married at the
Theodore Church southwest of Bowdle and made their home in the Baer
District. Elizabeth was the daughter of Jacob and Maria Miller, who had
grown up in South Russia. Elizabeth was born June 24, 1885. Jacob Miller
was born Aug. 3, 1852 and died Jan. 24, 1915. Maria Miller was born July 3,
1856 and died Nov. 21, 1918. Elizabeth received her education at the rural
farm school.

        Fred and Elizabeth Johnle

Fred C. and Elizabeth Johnle had four children. Sam was born Nov. 25, 1908.
He married Bertha Baer and they farm near Roscoe. Olga was born June 15,
1911. When her parents retired to live in Bowdle in 1946 she purchased and
operated the Cinderella Dress Shop eight years and then worked in the
Bowdle Nursing Home seven years. She is the wife of Mike Senger. Fred Jr.
married Evelyn Haux of Java. He was born March 12, 1917. They live in
Aberdeen where Fred works at the employment office and Evelyn is employed
at Dr. Rodine's office. Gertrude was born April 25, 1922 and is the wife of
Gilbert Quast of Menno. They have a daughter Susan. Gertrude is employed at
the Federal Land Bank Association in Menno.

Elizabeth Johnle died Feb. 27, 1966. Fred C. Johnle died Dec. 14, 1971.

FRANK and LILLIAN [GIBSON] JOHNSON

Frank J. Johnson was born June 29, 1872 in Urbana, IL, the son of James and
Lavina Johnson. He came to McPherson County in 1888 where he filed on a
homestead northwest of Bowdle. He married Lillian B. Gibson of Tyndall May
2, 1906 and in 1910 they moved to Bowdle where they spent the remainder of
their lives.

        Back: Ruth, Russell, Ramona Front: Frank and Lillian Johnson

Frank and Lillian Johnson had four children, one of whom died in infancy.
The other children were Russell, who married Vera Rockwood of Wisconsin
Rapids, WI; Ruth, who married Peter Goldade of Bowdle and Ramona who
married Earl Werner of Herreid. The Goldades had two children: James of
Grandview, WA and Holy of Mound City. Ramona and Earl Werner have one
daughter Judy Kay Fjeldheim of Herreid.

The Frank Johnsons continued to farm and he and his bride made their home
in Bowdle where he also operated a livery stable for which there was a
great demand. It was located on lots just north of the present Bowdle
Museum and could accommodate 26 horses. Most of the time the barn was full
of horses as people came to town from a long distance so they stabled the
horses and stayed overnight. Some brought blankets and bedded down for the
night in the hayloft. The cost of a horse's keep overnight including the
grain and hay was 50 cents a head. Many brought in a load of wheat to
exchange for their winter's supply of flour. Travelers who did not sleep in
the hayloft usually were patrons of the Mueller Hotel across the street
west from the stable or spent the night with friends or relatives. To those
who slept in the hayloft there was no charge.

Storms, blizzards and drought were among the hardships endured by the
pioneers. A few years later when automobiles were available Frank Johnson
was the owner of one of the first cars in Bowdle which was a Ford touring
car with side curtains to be used in inclement or extremely cold weather.
Part of the service of the stable was to drive the doctors to answer calls
in the country and the Ford was in great demand when he needed to take
doctors on calls when babies were born or people were ill and could not
come to him for care or to take the different ministers to serve in the
country churches.

The demand for this service was so great that he sold the Ford and
purchased a 9-passenger Studebaker. It had the usual front and back seats
plus two seats that raised up from the floor of the back seat. With this
additional seating capacity he could easily accommodate the pastors and
doctors. He also used it to take the baseball team to other towns to play
games.

The life span of this Johnson family, who were members of the Methodist
Church, is as follows: Frank Johnson died April 14, 1959; Mrs. Johnson died
Sept. 2, 1966; their son Russell died May 4, 1983 and Ruth Goldade died
July 5, 1979.

The History Committee especially thanks Mrs. Werner for the interesting
family history submitted and joins in her comment, "Bowdle was a great
place to live and my wish is that I may be able to be there and celebrate
with all the wonderful people in 1986."

WALTER and TILLIE [HAGELE] JOHNSON

Tillie Hagele and Walter Johnson were married in the Seventh-day Adventist
Church south of Bowdle July 3, 1929. Tillie was born in Odessa Township,
Edmunds County and received her elementary education there. She attended the
Plainview Academy in Redfield and Northern State College in Aberdeen. She
taught school near Leola a year and then taught four years in the Odessa
Township School. Teaching gave her much pleasure and satisfaction and some
of her best memories are the teaching years.

Walter L. Johnson was born in Grundy County, Iowa and lived with his
parents in Iowa, Minnesota and Colorado. In 1919 Walter's father Dan Johnson
bought a farm at Hutchinson, MN and the family moved there in the spring
1920. He received his secondary education at the Danish-Norwegian Seminary
in Hutchinson and Maple Wood Academy operated by the Seventh-day Adventist
Church.

Mr. and Mrs. Johnson established their first home in Odessa Township on
land homesteaded by Tillie's grandfather Philip Dollinger. The Johnsons
bought the farm from Eva Blumhardt who had inherited the property from her
family. Walter comments, "This farm has the shortest abstract I have ever
seen, one mortgage was made to the Federal Land Bank when we bought it."

The Johnsons have two children Dr. Lloyd Johnson and Carol Allen.

Dr. Lloyd Johnson is a dentist in Pierre and also comes to the farm and
sows the crops and comments, "It is a cheaper pasttime than many other
forms of relaxation." He and his wife Gayle have three children. Craig and
his wife Cynthia work at public relations jobs in Toronto, Canada but are
moving to Boise, ID soon. Rhonda is married to Scott Garensson. They live
in Mesquite which is north of Dallas, TX. Marlin works in Huron and attends
school.

        Back: Dale, Carol Allen, Gayle, Lloyd Front: Walter and Tillie
        Johnson

Carol Johnson married Dr. Dale R. Allen, an orthopedic surgeon practicing
in the Arlington, TX area and Walter says, "A wonderful place to live if
you like crowds, being close to the Rangers and Texas Cowboys--also six
flags flying over Texas. We do enjoy the mild weather when we visit." Carol
has a degree in science and specializes in nursing. She helps her husband
at the office and is also the Health Officer at a private college.

The Allens have four children. Randy and his wife Jennie live at College
Place, TX where Randy is working on his doctorate as a research scientist
with a biology major. They have a son Eric and to his great-grandfather,
"The most wonderful child in the world." Lori Allen married Curt Simmons, a
salesman. She runs the office for her father and is working on her
education at Arlington University and helps run things at home. Shari is a
junior in high school. Walter says, "We have seven wonderful grandchildren."

Then the "Prairie Sage" explains: "My wife and I have a built-in-love for
the land and we still live in Odessa Township in the house which Tillie's
uncle built in 1910. The native prairie will always be something great to
me. There is something about a spot that has never been grazed or mowed or
plowed. Living creatures, large and small, make their home there along with
insects and birds. Tillie loves to walk through the ripening wheat fields.
She has little pans in which she keeps a check on the crop progress from
the time the kernels begin to form. South Dakota has been good to us. We
have riches in many things other places do not have.

"Some of the public services we have enjoyed helping with are the township
board, township assessor, member of Federal Land Bank Board of Directors,
Farm Home Administration Board, Cenex Board as chairman for many years and
AAA Committee. I have received the Soil Stewardship Award from Production
Credit Association. We remember the "Dirty Thirties" and pushed a wheel
over a lot of miles measuring the grain fields in accordance with
government regulations to cut production.

"I would like to say thank you to the people of the Bowdle community. I am
glad you took me in as one of you. It has been a pleasant lot of years."

Then Walter added, "Now for some wisdom: If your wife does not love farming
at least half the time and you most of the time, you should try something
else. You might like it even less! Parenthood is not without pain. Farming
is not without frustration but when your children are successful and behave
themselves and when the wheat waves in golden glory and the cattle graze in
ample pastures, it is worth every minute.

"At one time we were known as the Baldheaded Board and at least one person
even referred to us as the Bull Headed Board. I am quite sure Walter
Fischer sometimes felt that way. We made our mistakes and good decisions
and we know you young folks will have to live with them and we hope profit
from them."

DR. and MRS. THOMAS D. JONES

Dr. Thomas D. Jones, the son of Thomas and Sue Jones, was born Dec. 23,
1890 at Plana, SD. He married Dorothy Edith Smith, who was born Dec. 2,
1896 in Chicago, IL and received her dietetics degree from the University
of Toronto, Canada. Dr. Jones received his medical degree from Rush Medical
College in Chicago. They established their first home in Bowdle where the
doctor served the community as physician and surgeon 20 years.

They had two children. Warren Leslie was born July 28, 1921 and Marjorie
Helen was born Dec. 10, 1922. Both children were born in Aberdeen. Dr.
Warren Jones received his medical degrees from the University of South
Dakota, Vermillion and Temple University at Philadelphia, PA. He is a
practicing internist in Sioux Falls. His wife is the former Alverna Blair.
They were married Aug. 14, 1943 and have eight children: Barbara, Thomas,
Kathleen, Susan, Laura, Frank, Ruth and Anne.

Marjorie Jones received her degree in nursing from the University of
Minnesota. She married John P. Howard Sept. 7, 1945. They live at 7502 W.
Meinecks Ave., Wauwatosa, WI. Their children are James, Judith, Steven and
Sandra.

Dr. Jones followed in the footsteps of Bowdle's Pioneer Physician, the
beloved Dr. Edwards, right into the hearts of the Bowdle people. The
building on 3rd Avenue which housed the hospital in 1918 is now the Bowdle
Clinic and also houses Bowdle City Hall. His concern for others is
recounted in the reports of his hazardous winter trips by sleigh or horse
and buggy as that was in the days before anti-freeze and cars had no
heaters. A cowhide robe was the means of conserving some heat during the
sleigh rides and it was not unusual to have the Doctor return home with
frost-bitten hands, feet and ears. Often these trips followed busy days of
surgery at the hospital. His surgical record at the Bowdle Hospital is
unsurpassed. Dr. Jones used to tell of doing surgery on the kitchen table
in the farm homes and of the privation that caring for the sick in farm
homes entailed.

A prairie fire started southwest of town in October 1922, fanned by a
strong wind that threatened the town. The men went out to fight the fire
and some were trapped and badly burned when the wind changed. Marjorie
Howard recalls, "Mother laid sheets on the floor in our home and the burned
men were laid on the sheets to be cared for. It was a time of great
distress and suffering.

"Those were the pre-health insurance days and when cash was scarce, the
Doctor would often receive payment for his services in chickens and home
canned goods. That did not discourage his compassionate care to others."

In 1940 the Doctor moved to Chamberlain and then to Aberdeen where he
practiced medicine until his death April 7, 1950.

Dr. Tom's widow married Bert Fuller, who was the local depot agent for the
Milwaukee Road in 1954. They lived in Aberdeen where Bert had been advanced
to dispatcher by the railroad. After his death Mrs. Fuller continued to
make her home in Aberdeen until 1981 when she spent time with her daughter
Marjorie and family. In October 1983 she moved to Sioux Falls and at
present lives in the Luther Manor, a retirement home at 2900 S. Lake Ave.
near her son Warren and family.

EARL E. and LOUISE [HARING] JULSON

Earl E. Julson, born Feb. 4, 1910 in Wisconsin, lived in Bowdle. He
received his PHD from Cornell University. Earl is remembered by Bowdlelites
as an instructor in the Bowdle School System.

Earl married Louise Haring July 1, 1937. Their son Jerome married Donna
Lyons. They have no children and live in Grand Lake, CO.

Janice Louise Kitchell lives in Aurora, CO. Her children are Drew and Julie.

Earl Julson lives at Estes Park, CO.

HENRY and KATHERINE [RIEGER, BENTZ] JUNG

Henry J. Jung was born in rural Hosmer April 4, 1894 to Jacob and Dora
(Hottman) Jung. His family consisted of seven brothers and one sister
including a grandmother, a blind aunt and a deaf aunt. At least this
household had enough cooks.

In 1917 Henry was called by Uncle Sam to serve in the U.S. Army in World
War I. He fought several wars in Europe, mostly in France. After the war he
was honorably discharged from the Armed Forces.

        Back: Anna, Edward, Gertrude Front: Henry and Katie Jung

Henry came home to marry a young Hosmer lady, Katherina (Dewald) daughter
of John and Katherina (Huft) Dewald. Henry and Katherina had a daughter
Anna, born June 27, 1922 near Bowdle. After Anna was three years old, a son
Aaron was born. Aaron was three days old when his mother died which left
the family in a sad situation. Henry's kind brother John and his wife Rose,
who had no children, came to the rescue and said, "We will take care of
Aaron for you as long as need be." They raised Aaron until he got married
and left home.

In the meantime Henry found another Katherine, a widow with two small
children who had lost her husband in a hunting accident.

This widow was Katherine (Rieger) Bentz, daughter of Adam and Barbara
(Stro) Rieger, born near Hillsview Nov. 28, 1900. She was married to Edward
Bentz, son of Jacob and Eva Bentz of Eureka. To this union a daughter
Gertrude was born Oct. 9, 1919. The family lived about 13 miles east of
Eureka. In the winter 1921 Edward died in an accident before his second
child was born. Aug. 28, 1921 Edward Jr. was born at his grandparents home,
Adam Riegers, near Hillsview where the small family made its home.

Since Henry and Katie had so much in common they married for the second
time Sept. 1, 1925 in the Hosmer Congregational Church. Then with their
three small children they lived on a rented farm owned by Alex Searle nine
miles north of Bowdle.

        For 17 years this family happily lived;
        In a pioneer home built of rocks and sod,
        This couple, their children raised with thrift,
        And trained them to work and worship God.

In 1942 the farm was sold and the Jungs moved to Bowdle. Henry continued to
work as a farm laborer and a carpenter for many years. He died at the age
of 84 June 20, 1979. At the present time Katie is living in the Bowdle
Nursing Home.

Henry and Katie's children are as follows:

Aaron Jung married Clara Hirsch of Eureka. They have five children and
seven grandchildren and live in Minneapolis, MN.

Anna Jung married Harold Baer of Hoven. They have three children and four
grandchildren and live in Billings, MT.

Gertrude Bentz married Otto Buechler of Bowdle. They have one child and two
grandchildren and live in Bowdle.

Edward Bentz married Agnes Kelsch of McLaughlin. They have three children
and two grandchildren and live in Redfield.

WALTER and CHRISTINA [HOTTMAN] JUNG

Walter Jung was born Nov. 6, 1900 east of Hosmer to Jacob and Dora
(Hottman) Jung. He attended the nearby rural school and grew up as an
ambitious young farmer. In November 1924 he married Christina Hottman, who
was born April 19, 1903 to David and Christina (Opp) Hottman. They lived
nine miles west of Hosmer.

        Back: Lloyd and Milton Front: Walter and Christina Jung

Walter and Christina had four children, two of whom died in infancy. Milton
and Lloyd grew up and learned to help their parents on the farm. The Jung
family operated three different farms north of Bowdle until 1963 when they
retired to live in Bowdle.

Besides being farmers Walter and Christina were very good butchers and for
many years would help neighbors butcher hogs and beef. They would make the
best sausage and head cheese and at the end of the day for their hard
labors (there was no hourly pay) they were lucky if they got a sausage or
two to take home.

Now in their mid-eighties Mr. and Mrs. Jung are still of sound mind and
able to take care of each other in their own home. Mrs. Jung can no longer
see, but by the faith in their Lord, they make out pretty well.

Milton Jung married Lucille Gab of Hosmer. They live in St. Paul, MN. Lloyd
Jung married Carol Mettler of Eureka and they live in Rapid City with their
children Candy, Todd and Lora.

JACOB and EMELIA [WALTER] JURIEF

Jacob Jurief was born Aug. 2, 1890 in Simferopol, Crimea Russia to
Constantine and Maria (Mohl) Jurief. Jacob grew up in the village going to
school and helping his father. When he was 14 he was sent away to school.

Jacob's father owned a saddle and harness shop and during the winter months
he made saddles, bridles, whips, harnesses and other items, as well as all
kinds of repairs for the villagers. During the spring and summer he farmed.
Everyone raised their own feed and grain for animal and family use. Each
villager had an area large enough to keep cattle, horses, chickens and a
garden to grow vegetables. When Jacob returned from school the farming
became his work.

In 1908 his father died during harvesting season. In the fall his mother
sold the shop and moved to Toksaba to be near her family. Jacob leased land
from the village landlord and farmed to provide for himself and his mother.

Jacob married Emelia Walter Sept. 23, 1912. She was born Dec. 20, 1891 at
Kloestiz, Bessarabia Russia to Michael and Magdalena (Diedtrich) Walter.
The following spring Jacob and Emelia, accompanied by his mother, came to
the United States, arriving at Baltimore, MD April 4, 1913. Traveling by
train, three days later they were in Crookston, NE where they met Maria's
brother-in-law Daniel Heinert. They stayed at the hotel that night and left
early the next morning by wagon across country to Parmelee on the Rosebud
Indian Reservation. It took three days, stopping at farm homes on the way
to spend the night. It was cold and rained at times. At dusk on the third
day they arrived at the farm home of her sister.

They stayed at the farm seeing and learning about life in America. Times
were hard. The Heinerts were a large family and to make extra money they
started a bakery in their home making and baking bread around the clock,
taking it to town and selling to the Indians every morning.

The last week in May they left for Butte, NE to the farm home of Peter
Mohl, Maria's brother. After a short time Jacob found work on a cattle
ranch. The women stayed at the farm helping with the work during the
summer. In the fall Jacob, Emelia and his mother Maria moved to Onoka, NE.
They bought two cows and 12 chickens and set up housekeeping. He then went
to work for the railroad on a section crew. After two years he wanted to try
farming. Wages were a dollar a day. Two more joined the family circle,
Martha and Stella.

The fall of 1915 they moved to a farm near Burke. With the help of good
neighbors he got started. The crops were good and they could buy things
they needed. They were again packing in January 1920 and moved to the
northeastern part of the state, bringing horses, cows, farm machinery,
wagon, a new buggy and furniture. It was all loaded in a boxcar and Jacob
came with the freight train feeding the animals on the way. Emelia and
children came on the passenger train arriving in Bowdle in mid-January.
They stayed with her sister at the George Bieber farm until their farm was
vacant which was west of Bowdle. The first year all that grew was wild
oats, which was cut green for feed.

Jacob bought his first automobile, a used Maxwell, in July 1923. Learning
to drive was an experience. He soon found out it was quite different than
handling a team of horses. The family had some real bumpy, jumpy rides over
the rough country roads. He would get excited and pull on the steering
wheel and yell, "Whoa! Whoa!" but the car didn't stop. Eventually he
learned how to operate the vehicle.

The fall of 1924 brought an epidemic of scarlet fever. The children all had
the fever and were quarantined for three months and the schools were closed.

        Back: Stella, Hilbert, Martha Front: Jacob and Emelia Jurief

Jacob bought his first new car, an Essex at Christmas 1925. It was black
with glass windows and when you rode in it the wind didn't whistle past
your ears. The neighbors also bought a new car. Each family claimed there's
was better. Sunday mornings there would be a race on the way to church.
First to the highway, then on to Bowdle and the one getting there first had
the better car. The Juriefs lived a mile further down the road. The
Buechler family would sit in their car waiting. When they saw the Jurief
car coming they would start down their driveway. After both cars were on
the highway the race was on. The Buechler's driveway was several hundred
yards up the road, which always gave them the advantage of getting ahead.
When both families went to town in the evening Jacob would drive without
lights until just before he turned on to the highway. It was the only
chance he had to get ahead.

The years had slipped by, the children were older and could help with more
of the work. In March 1928 the family moved to the Java area where Jacob
managed to get a place with more land to farm. His mother died that
October. Jacob and Emelia sold everything they owned at auction in January
1946. During the summer months they traveled and visited friends and
relatives in the Midwest. In September they went to Oregon and both worked
at a Marachino Cherry processing plant until they retired. In 1965 they
moved to Stockton, CA to be near their son and family. Emelia died Jan. 9,
1974 and Jacob died Aug. 7, 1975. They had four children.

Herbert died Sept. 20, 1918 at age 11 months.

Martha lives in Stockton, CA.

Stella married Oscar Goetz and they live on a farm northeast of Java. They
have four sons. Gaylon married Connie Goetz, they live on a farm at Bowdle
and their children are Selena and Jarrod. Dwight married Betty Berreth and
they live on a farm northeast of Java with their daughter Angela. Keith
married Mary Kraft and lives at Aberdeen and Gordon married Sharon Krause.
They live at Sioux Falls with their sons Justin and Travis.

Hilbert Jurief married Otillia Hoffman. He lives at Klamath Falls, OR. They
have four children. Sylvia married Claude Chambers and lives at Castro
Valley, CA with their children David and Susan. Terrance married Peggy
Leppert and lives at Klamath Falls, OR with their children Scott and
Kathryn. David married Catherine Bessone. They live at Castro Valley, CA
with their daughters Sara and Amie. Diane married Tim Delaney. They live at
Stockton, CA and have two sons Jess and Jon.

DAVID and KAREN [DEWALD] KARST

David Karst was born April 27, 1948 at Hoven, the son of Vincent and
Eleanor Karst. He graduated from Bowdle High School and Northern State
College with a bachelor's degree in business administration. He married
Karen Dewald, daughter of Joseph B. and Patricia Senn Dewald March 8, 1969.
She was born May 26, 1949 at Ipswich. Karen is a graduate of Bowdle High
School and attended Northern State College.

David and Karen have two children. Timothy was born July 12, 1969 and
Denise was born July 18, 1975. Both are students at Bowdle.

David served in the U.S. Army 1970-1972, completing his education upon his
discharge. Since 1972 he has been manager of the Edmunds County
Conservation District. Karen was employed as secretary for the Edmunds
County Health Department 1975-1982 and since has been employed at Bowdle
Hospital as director of Medical Records and X-ray Technician.

David was very active in high school and college athletics. The entire
family is involved in city activities, whether it be athletic or community
development.

VINCENT and ELEANOR [BAUS] KARST

Vincent was born Oct. 10, 1917 to Joe and Elizabeth Karst at Hoven. He was
raised on the farm and in 1941 married Eleanor Baus. She is the daughter of
Wm. and Gertrude (Flock) Baus, born Dec. 3, 1917.

Vincent and Eleanor farmed in the Wilmot and Peever area three years and
then moved to a farm south of Bowdle until they retired to Hoven. They have
four children.

        Vincent and Eleanor Karst and Families Back: David, Bill, Bob, Don.
        Front: Karen, Elaine, Vincent, Eleanor, Helen and Betty.

Bill, born in 1942, married Elaine Haar of Bowdle and they live in

ADOLPH and MARTHA [SANDMEIER] KELLER

Adolph "Jeff" was born Aug. 29, 1910 to Edward and Magdalena Wolff Keller
near Bison. Martha was born Dec. 15, 1915 to John and Barbara Wahl
Sandmeier north of Bowdle.

Adolph and Martha were married Dec. 29, 1936. The first two months they
lived with her brother Rudolf. Then they moved to the Mat Wolff farm,
Jeff's grandparents home. Here they herded sheep for Ben Stiegelmeier for
$20 a month. They owned two horses and four milk cows.

April 26, 1938 the stork brought them their first child Irene at a bargain
price for $6. Two years later they moved to the Adam Mertz farm where their
daughter Shirley was born May 8, 1939.

        Adolph and Martha Keller and Families Back: Wayne, Irene, Shirley,
        Arliss Front: Tom, Darlene, Martha, Jeff, Duke, Echo

This little family knew how to get along on a shoestring budget. They often
went to town and church with a team of horses to save gas. During the
winter they often moved into one room of their house to help save fuel.
Dec. 18, 1940 their last daughter Darlene was born.

Jeff bought a threshing machine and did custom threshing in the Bowdle and
Java area. Finally economic conditions improved for this family. They
bought a small farm five miles east of Java (240 acres at $7 per acre on a
five-year term.) Sometimes it was difficult for the Kellers to make the
payment. But they were lucky to have a golden-hearted friend, George
Sebert, who offered to lend them the cash for their land payments. They
paid him back whenever they had enough cash. Now they finally owned a farm
of their own.

Misfortune struck in 1959. Their house burned destroying many of their
daughter's wedding gifts also. With the help of good neighbors, relatives
and friends they again had a new house. Another tragedy struck when their
3-year-old granddaughter Doreen Holder died in 1965.

After living on the farm 30 years, Jeff and Martha sold their farm to Paul
and Sandy Jacobs. They now live in Selby. Since then a grandson Dean
Holder, age 9, was killed in a car accident.

Jeff and Martha had three daughters. Irene married Wayne Holder. They have
two children and live in Selby. Shirley married Arliss Opheim. They have
two children and live in Selby. Darlene is married to Tom Tefertiller. They
have two children and live in Bozeman, MT.

The Kellers also have two great-grandchildren.

Martha is still a busy homemaker and loves her needlework. Jeff often lends
a helping hand to the elderly and during his pasttime loves to fish.

REVEREND GREG KESTERSON

Bowdle welcomed a new citizen March 20, 1983. Reverend Greg Kesterson
arrived to take up residence in his chosen city. As a student and member of
Immanuel Lutheran Tour Choir of Eau Claire, WI Gregg had found this small
town an enjoyable experience. His thoughts had often returned to Bowdle
since that time, so it is not surprising that after his brother Reverend
Terrel Kesterson accepted a call to Redeemer Lutheran Church, Greg decided
to locate there.

Greg had been planning to further his life experiences by living
independently; so he left his parental home in San Jose, CA and boarded a
plane that would carry him to the prairies. His living quarters are located
in the lower level of Erma Maier's home.

Greg Kesterson was born July 17, 1952 at Oakland, CA to Robert and
Jacqueline Kesterson of San Jose. He was a premature infant and his life was
saved by the use of an oxygen incubator. It is now known excessive oxygen
causes Retrolental Fibroplasia, which caused many infants like Greg to be
completely blinded.

Greg was ordained into the ministry Dec. 9, 1979 at St. Stephen's Lutheran
Church in Sunnyvale, CA. He has served as Radio-Evangelist of that
congregation. His work, at that time, was concentrated in the Bay area.
Pastor Greg is often called upon to fill in for various CLC ministers. His
most recent vacancy pastor position was at Hecla in 1983. He prepares tapes
to be used for radio broadcast. Each broadcast is identified with the
Church of Lutheran Confession. Area residents may have heard his messages
being broadcast from Pierre on Sunday evenings in 1984.

REVEREND TERREL and PEGGY [REIM] KESTERSON

Terrel Kesterson, son of Robert and Jackie Kesterson, was born in Chico, CA
March 20, 1955. He was raised primarily in the San Francisco Bay area with
two older brothers Kirk and Greg.

        Terrel and Peggy. Heather and Jeffrey Kesterson

Terrel attended high school, college and seminary at Immanuel Lutheran
College in Eau Claire, WI. He met his wife Peggy there. Terrel graduated
from Immanuel Lutheran Seminary in May 1981. He received and accepted the
call to serve as pastor of Redeemer Lutheran Church (CLC) in Bowdle.

to Seattle, WA and in 1973 they moved to Phoenix, AZ.

Peggy also attended high school and college in Eau Claire, WI. She

Terrel and Peggy were married July 18, 1981 in California. Shortly

JACOB J. and KATHERINE [SIEWERT] KESZLER

Jacob J. Keszler was born July 4, 1897 in Glueckstahl, South Russia to
Jacob and Rosina (Schilling) Keszler. He married Katherine Siewert Oct. 16,
1919. She was born Oct. 22, 1899 in Kulm, ND to William and Christina
(Aldinger) Siewert. Her parents were born in Russia.

        Jacob and Katherine Keszler

Jacob and Katherine received eighth grade educations. In 1935 they moved to
Bowdle and purchased the service station and home Mr. Pietzke had
established on old Highway 12. Jake and Katie shared in the duties of
servicing cars. Katie remembers pumping gas by hand before the new modern
pumps were available.

Rheinie Eisemann worked for the Keszlers and his forte was playing
practical jokes. Norman Gross drove up one day to have his tires filled
with air and took advantage to play his own joke on Rheinie by blowing up
and popping a balloon as Rheinie was filling the tire. Rheinie thought he
had overfilled the tire and his reaction gave Norman the laugh he had been
wanting. Later they were both able to appreciate their crazy stunts.

Jacob and Katherine sold the property to Oscar Metzger in 1947 and moved to
Mobridge where they made their home. Mrs. Keszler continues to live there.

VERNA KIESZ

The "little" girl in the wheelchair ... Oh yes, she may have a child-sized
body, but that is not what attracts you. It is her smile, the hearty
laughter, the sense of humor, intense interest in what goes on around her
and willingness to help others. Multiple fractures of the bone have not
dulled her love of life.

        Verna and Rosina Kiesz

Verna Kiesz says that life is good and she shares her happiness with
everyone. This, the third child of Rosina and Alexander Kiesz, was born
April 5, 1925 at Hoven Hospital. She recalls the first fracture occurred in
the right thigh bone at the age of six weeks. Her mother thought the older
children had harmed her, until the cause of the pain was found. Then as the
medical team at St. Luke's Hospital in Aberdeen were removing the cast from
the right leg, they broke the thigh bone in the left leg. She was ill with
brittle bones, due to a vital nutrition deficiency before she was born
medically termed osteogenesis imperfecta.

She still wanted to do all the things the older children did ... playing
outside, making mud pies, etc. Her continual slide crawling to keep up, kept
her mother busy providing clean clothes. One time she followed her siblings
a half mile to the neighbors. She said her brother and sister were real
good. They did not walk faster than she could crawl. Discipline ended long
distant crawls for all of them. Another time she insisted on going to the
chicken coop with her sister, another no-no, because she was wearing a cast
on her leg. Then she begged and begged for the cast to be removed that day
instead of waiting. Her folks knew why when the chicken lice crawled out of
the cast.

During her 11th year another tragedy in the family caused Alex to take
Verna and his son Arnold to Mayo. On the 4th of July someone put a lighted
firecracker into a bottle they tossed. Arnold was watching and the glass
shards when the bottle exploded hit him just above the eye severing the
optic nerve. The trip was in the hope of saving his sight and also to
consult specialists about Verna's condition. There they learned that 11
years of taking cod liver oil did not benefit her and her body was
rejecting the oil. Doctors told them that anything taken by mouth would not
correct the bone condition she suffered.

In 1946 she acquired a three-wheeled cart. Real mobility came in 1956 when
friends bought her the first wheelchair. Before that she had gotten around
with a little wagon pulled by family or friends.

Though she could not go to school, Verna did learn from homework given her
brothers and sisters. When Lenora (Eisenbeisz) Berg was teaching in the
Bowdle Grade School, she coached Verna, thus giving her the pleasure of
being able to enjoy reading, spelling and math.

During her lifetime Verna has recuperated from 85 fractures in 58 years and
one year wore nine casts due to broken bones. She recalls the great
financial burden this put upon her parents and how they hauled grain to
town to pay the medical bills.

Verna Kiesz with the new "three-wheeler" cart she received just in time for
the 75th Anniversary Jubilee in Bowdle in 1961. The young man riding on her
first cart, which was hand-powered, is Verna's nephew, Douglas Kiesz.

Handicapped? No, that does not apply. It may slow her down, but does not
stop Verna. She has taken car trips to the Black Hills and other cities in
the state, plane trips to California and when weather permits, is out and
about town and to church faithfully.

Verna and her mother lived together at Prairie View Housing five years
until Rosina's health began to fail. Not until Verna could no longer take
care of her was Rosina placed in the Bowdle Nursing Home in March 1984.

Verna has done a lot of sewing, makes all her own clothes including coats
and shoes, sewed for her mother and others, has helped with laying out and
stitching quilt tops and because of her love of children, has managed to
babysit and does her own cooking. A new four-wheeler, battery-operated
Stevena motor chair which she purchased in 1978, allows her to be very
independent and gives a much wider range of adventure.

DR. WALTER and MARTHA KITZLER

Dr. Walter Anton Kitzler became resident physician of the Bowdle Community
in 1968. Under his auspices, the residents of Bowdle once again had access
to full medical care. The Bowdle Hospital again opened its doors.

Dr. Kitzler's closeness with this community was based on his ability to
communicate with those of all ages in whatever language was required;
English, Polish, his native German or at times even Spanish. His love of
the land and farming brought a kinship with many a Bowdle farmer. Dr.
Kitzler could often be seen feeding his cattle, himself, before he and his
wife Martha would begin the day at the clinic.

Clinic hours began following hospital surgeries and rounds which were three
times a day. Forty plus patients were not uncommon to this office with
interruptions for accidents and new babies a frequent occurrence.

Dr. Kitzler retired from active practice in 1973 but kept his ties with the
community through the land which he loved dearly. He died at age 61 in
March 1974.

He had graduated from School of Medicine of the University of Munich,
Germany. He emigrated from Germany in 1956, arriving in South Dakota in
1959 after a short interim in Canada. After receiving his basic sciences in
1962 he practiced in the north central region of South Dakota. At the time
of his death he had been temporarily called from retirement to act as
medical superintendent for the South Dakota Mental Health facility in
Yankton until a permanent replacement could be found.

Dr. Kitzler and Martha had three sons: Dr. Werner of Vermillion, Wolfgang
of Eureka and Walter of Chicago, IL and a daughter, Theodora K. Schroeder
of Denver, CO.

the rank of Corporal. In June 1932 he married Christine Doerr of Bowdle.

Christine was born April 28, 1904 at Java to Jacob and Katherina (Bauder)
Doerr. She was the sixth of a family of nine children. She attended Bowdle
Schools. Her father had many acres of land under cultivation and she and
her sister did much of the field work and milking.

Lloyd and Christine moved to Lantry in 1932 where they farmed extensively
in that region until 1970. Lloyd became ill and died in 1973.

Christine had major surgery in Sioux Falls in 1972 which left her in a
wheelchair. Now after 10 years of effort and determination, she walks in her
apartment unaided and outside with a light walker. She has lived in Bowdle
the past 10 years.

LEVI and IRENE [FIECHTNER] KRAUSE

Levi Krause was born Feb. 18, 1909 to I.R. Krause and his wife Mary in

two years to learn watch making.

In 1933 Levi purchased the O. Larsen Jewelry Store located next to Ozzie's
Super Valu (now the Dental Clinic) and operated this business until 1937
when he was appointed Welfare Director of Edmunds County in Ipswich. He
enlisted in the U.S. Navy Dec. 9, 1943 and was attached to a special repair
unit ship where his work was to repair ship clocks, watches and gun control
instruments.

Active in community affairs while in Bowdle, Levi was a member of the
Bowdle Band and had charge of the boxing contest held during the 50th
anniversary at Bowdle in 1936. After his discharge from the Navy Levi
located in Mobridge where he engaged in watch repair until his retirement in
1974. He continues to make his home there.

Mr. and Mrs. Levi Krause had four children. Russell was born July 9, 1936
in Bowdle. He is an engineer at Charlotte, NC. Judith, born June 28, 1937

Mobridge, is a mining engineer at Edmund, OK. Lorna, born Sept. 24, 1950 in
Mobridge, is a teacher and farmer in St. Lawrence.

ALBERT and KATHERINE [STADEL] KUNDERT

The place was Neuglueckstahl, Germany, the year was 1895, the event was the
arrival of two infants. Their lives ran parallel, for at the age of five
(in 1900) they came with their parents on the same boat to the United
States. Both families settled in the Eureka area. It was many years later
before they became acquainted.

The baby boy born in 1895 was Albert Kundert. The little girl born the same
year was Katherine Stadel. They were married at Eureka March 14, 1916 and
made their first home on a farm near there. After several years they moved
to the Blumhardt farm northwest of Bowdle, then to the Edwards farm
southeast of town and for a short time, farmed land owned by Peter
Stahlecker. In 1935 they moved to Bowdle and bought a house from John Koch,
located across the street from the Henry Baer home.

        Albert and Katherine Kundert

Albert Kundert did carpenter work for Federal Land Bank, fixing farms that
the bank had foreclosed on and were offering for sale. Then he operated the
Shoe Repair Shop, succeeding John Ulrich. When George Sautner was no longer
able to do custodian work at Bowdle School, Albert accepted the job and
recalls how much he enjoyed it, saying it was the one he really enjoyed
most of all the work he had done. A few years later Albert and Katherine
joined their daughter Mrs. Clara Bauer and family in Lodi, CA. Katherine
died there July 1982. Albert continues to live in their home alone.

They had four children. Tillie married Rudy Geist and in 1940 they moved to
Lodi, CA where she worked as a nurse. Ella married Erwin Wolf and worked in
Lodi as a waitress. Clara Kundert married Edwin Bauer, whose folks farmed
west of Bowdle. She had been a secretary for Federal Land Bank before they
moved to Lodi, where she assisted Edwin in the appliance business. Alvin
Kundert married Bev Christensen. He lives in Pierre where he has been
manager of a super large Red Owl Store many years.

Albert and Katherine Kundert have eight grandchildren, eight great-
grandchildren and one great-great-grandchild. Among their descendants are two
ministers of the Gospel, nurses, a doctor, secretaries and teachers.

JAKE and ROSE [GROSS] KURLE

Jake Kurle, well-known businessman in Bowdle, was born Sept. 9, 1888 in
Odessa, Russia to John and Rosie (Schealetter) Kurle. At age 17, Jake came
to the United States in May 1905. He worked for an uncle Dave Kurle near
Java a few months and then came to Bowdle in 1906 where he worked for
another uncle, Jake Kurle, who was in the Blacksmith and Implement Business.

In 1912 he bought an interest in his uncle's business, later becoming the
sole proprietor. He married Rose Kurle May 1, 1912. She was born in Odessa,
Russia Sept. 8, 1887 to Christian and Catherine Gross. Her family
immigrated to this area April 27, 1889, landing in Eureka and settling 12
miles north of Bowdle.

        Jake and Rose Kurle

Jake was active in many community projects including president of Bowdle
State Bank 19321943, school board member 10 years, mayor of Bowdle
1946-1948 and many church offices.

Rose was busy caring for their five children. Alice married Alfred
Heckenlaible and they had a daughter Mary who married Keith Jansen. They
live in Hibbing, MN and have two children.

Raymond Kurle married Lorraine Bader. He retired from the family business
and they live at Bowdle. They have three sons. Jack married Myra Ellingson,
lives in Tulsa, OK and they have two children. Donald married Louella
Roebke and lives in Charleston, WV. Charles married Vickie Kempf. They live
at Hastings, MN and have two children.

Lenora Kurle married David Hansen. They live at Groveland, CA.

Alvin Kurle married Donna Schumacher and continues to operate the business
with his brother Morris. Alvin and Donna have a daughter Yolonda who
married Kim Jahraus. They live in Rapid City and have one child.

Morris married Patricia Venoy Schumacher. They have two children. Connie
married Anthony Geier. They live in Aberdeen and have two children. John
Patrick Kurle lives in Minneapolis.

Jake Kurle died from an accidental fall at his business in March 1951. Rose
Kurle continues to reside with her daughter Alice in Bowdle. Rose Kurle is
considered one of the oldest living pioneers of Bowdle.

MORRIS and PATRICIA [SCHUMACHER] KURLE

Morris John Kurle was born Oct. 23, 1926 in Bowdle where he has lived all
his life. He is the third son of Jacob and Rose Kurle, both of whom were
born in Russia.

Morris graduated from Bowdle in 1944 and attended South Dakota State
University until he was called to serve in the U.S. Army. Upon his
discharge in 1947 he went into the J. Kurle and Sons Implement and Lumber
business with his father and brothers. He became the International Harvester
parts man.

Morris married Patricia Venoy Schumacher in 1951. Venoy is the daughter of
Ernest and Barbara Schumacher, both of whom were born in Bowdle. Barbara
died in 1978 and Ernest now lives in Mobridge.

Patricia Venoy was born May 2, 1929. She graduated from Bowdle in 1947 and
received her bachelor of science and master of science degrees from
Northern State College at Aberdeen. She began teaching in 1949. Her first
position was in the Selby School System where she was a member of the
faculty through 1951. In 1967 Bowdle added kindergarten to the curriculum.
Venoy accepted the position as instructor and has been serving in that
capacity almost 20 years.

Morris and Venoy have two children. Connie Barbara was born April 19, 1952.
After completing the Bowdle Schools Connie attended Northern State College
and graduated with a bachelor's degree in secondary education, majoring in
English and science. Connie married Anthony Geier in 1974. They have two
daughters. Jami Erin was born Feb. 27, 1976 and Laurie Leigh May 6, 1979.
They presently live in Aberdeen.

John Patrick Kurle was born Jan. 13, 1956. He completed the Bowdle Schools
and attended South Dakota State University, graduating with a bachelor of
science degree in microbiology. He is employed as a research laboratory
supervisor at the University of Minnesota.

A person who gives of himself with reserve and shyness, Morris Kurle has
devoted many hours to an extensive water project which will provide high
quality treated drinking water from the Missouri River for an estimated
30,000 residents of North Central South Dakota. The WEB Rural Water
Development Project, commonly called WEB Pipeline Project, was first
conceived in 1975.

Morris was appointed then as a representative to the project and in 1976
became chairman. He gave many hours of his time for the furthering of the
project and went to Washington, D.C. to help secure financing for the
project and other aspects of the work.

RAYMOND and LORRAINE [BADER] KURLE

Raymond H. Kurle was born June 2, 1917 at Bowdle, the son of Jacob and Rose
Kurle, who were born in Russia. Raymond married Lorraine Bader Oct. 26,
1941. She was born July 24, 1918 at Java to Christ and Minnie Bader. Christ
Bader was born March 7, 1892 at Ashley, ND and died May 6, 1971. Minnie
Bader was born Feb. 14, 1897 at Java and died July 6, 1976.

Ray Kurle grew up in his father's implement business. He graduated from
Bowdle High School, attended SDSU in Brookings and Dunwoody Institute in
Minneapolis, MN and went into business with his father. Ray's job seemed to
be doing whatever came to hand, for it included machinist's work, salesman,
mechanic, welding or making farm calls. It was work well done and the firm
was honored with a 60 year recognition plaque from the International
Harvester Company, among other honors. Through his work Ray has friends
within a large radius of Bowdle.

Ray served as a volunteer fireman 40 years, was a member of the city
council, school board, hospital board and always willing to do whatever
needed to be done. His rich baritone voice was in demand for many church
and civic functions. His favorite accompanist was Mrs. Fred (Theo) Grosz,
Bowdle's music teacher.

Lorraine worked as a store clerk before her marriage and has been active in
all phases of volunteer community and church work. Home life and hand work
are her favorite hobbies. Ray was designated "Man of the Year" by the
Jaycees in 1961 in recognition of his volunteer work with Bowdle's 75th
Jubilee. At that time Lorraine was co-chairman for the All-School Reunion.

Ray retired from business in 1981, but is not without something to do as he
has a well-equipped woodworking shop at his home and with retirement, he
has plenty of time for gardening and yard work.

Ray and Lorraine have three sons. Jack, Donald and Charles all attended the
School of Mines in Rapid City and graduated with bachelor of science
degrees in engineering and took ROTC work and were commissioned second
lieutenants. After they were on engineering jobs the three boys each took
post graduate work and are listed on the roster of the American Society of
Professional Engineers.

Jack Kurle was born May 15, 1947. He married Myrna Ellingson and is a
consulting engineer in Tulsa, OK. Their children are Betsy Rose and Michael
Duane.

Donald Kurle was born Aug. 17, 1950 and married Louella Roebke. Don is
senior engineer in the Plastics Division at St. Albans, WV.

Charles Kurle was born Aug. 29, 1952. His wife was Vickie Kempf. Charles is
a production engineer in Hastings, MN. Their children are Charles and
Joseph.

Lorraine comments: "We live in the house that was built by Ray's
great-uncle Jacob Kurle, which has been known as the "Kurle House" for
years. It is a large 2-1/2 story structure and we hope to continue living
there for many more years. The grandchildren enjoy coming home to roam
through every room.

SISTER KAREN LAFOLLETTE

Sister Karen LaFollette is the daughter of Zelda Kellen LaFollette of Sioux
Falls and Lee LaFollette also of Sioux Falls. Sister Karen was born and
educated through her high school years in Sioux Falls. In 1967 she joined
the Presentation Sisters of Aberdeen and began a course of study in theology
and pastoral counseling. She did her undergraduate work at St. John's
University in Collegeville, MN and her graduate work at Boston College in
Massachusetts.

        Sister Karen LaFollette

Sister Karen has two brothers and two sisters. Greg, a certified public
accountant, lives in Sioux Falls with his wife and daughter. Marsha, a

printer, lives in Sioux Falls with his wife and two daughters. Lisa, a

After graduation from college, Sister Karen was the Director of Religion
Education and Pastoral Associate at Sacred Heart Parish in Aberdeen from
1971-1978. From 1978-1984 she was the Pastoral Associate at St. Lambert's
Catholic Church in Sioux Falls. In 1984 she accepted an appointment to the
newly formed Pastoral Team that is serving the Catholic Church in Bowdle as
well as five other area churches.

Sister Karen lives in the Catholic Rectory in Bowdle with Sister Darlene
Gutenkauf, who is also a member of the Pastoral Team. The other members of

ANDREAS and LOUISE [HINTZ, HOFFMAN] LAIB By Hilda [Hoffman] Green

Andreas Laib was my paternal step-grandfather. He married my paternal
grandmother Louise (Hintz) Hoffman April 27, 1899 in Hosmer. My grandmother
was born Jan. 7, 1851 in Kulm, Bessarabia, South Russia. She married my
grandfather Johann Hoffman in Kulm, Bessarabia, South Russia. I have no
dates of his birth or when they were married.

There were several children born to this union, all in Russia, but only
four survived. My grandmother brought the three youngest children to the
United States after the death of my grandfather. He died in the fire that
destroyed his flour mill. I have no date except that it happened after 1892
and before 1898.

        Andreas and Louise Laib

The children included Maria (Hoffman) born April 16, 1886. She married
Jacob Laib Jan. 14, 1905 in Java. They had seven children. Maria died June
1, 1974.

Matilda (Hoffman) was born Oct. 15, 1888. She married Frederick Buechler
Nov. 23, 1909 in Bowdle. They had nine children. Matilda died July 13, 1975.

My father Gottfred Hoffman was born Jan. 15, 1890. He married my mother
Elizabeth Buechler Nov. 7, 1910 in Java. They had nine children. After the
death of Elizabeth Aug. 30, 1925, Gottfred married Rosina Sandmeier Jan.
10, 1927 in Bowdle. They had five children.

Nathaniel Hoffman, the oldest. had come to the United States several years
earlier. He was born Dec. 30, 1877. He married Christina Giese of Liepzig,
ND. They had seven children. Nathaniel died April 14, 1950.

MR. and MRS. LLOYD LANE

Lloyd Lane and his family came to Bowdle from Gallop, NM in 1925 where he
had been teaching. Lloyd, his wife and son Forrest had been camping in the
Black Hills that summer when he learned of the vacancy in Bowdle. Mr. Lane
was superintendent of Bowdle School eight years along with teaching math,
manual training and coaching basketball. He also helped out playing with
the school band that was organized then.

In his spare time he wired houses, weatherstripped windows and also built
his home in 1929 with the help of LeRoy Rouse, another teacher. This home
was just south of the John Hoven residence. After they left the house was
sold and moved to the Fred Bieber farm near Java. Lloyd Lane died in Los
Angeles, CA in 1949 from heart failure and his wife died in 1963.

Their son Forrest was born Sept. 29, 1915 at Beresford. He recalls the
memories of Bowdle. "I was 10 years old when we moved to Bowdle. I remember
coming into town and parking at the bank on the corner and going to Jones
Drug Store to purchase an ice cream cone. Our first days were spent in a
tent which we pitched on the southwest corner of the school grounds while
looking for a house.

        Mr. and Mrs. Lloyd Lane and son Forrest

"I have always felt my roots were planted in this community as it was where
I spent most of my school days. I remember spending many hours in the summer 
helping my father build the booths in Jones Drug and all the fixtures in the 
Carlson Restaurant. My Saturdays were always taken up going to Aberdeen to 
take violin lessons. I used to envy all my friends who could spend the day
playing. I still play the violin on occasions.

"After graduating in 1933 we left Bowdle. I attended University of
Minnesota, Junior College in Compton, CA; Henager Business College in Salt
Lake City, UT; UCLA in Los Angeles, CA and SCCO now located in Fullerton,
CA and received my O.D. degree at Fullerton. I entered the service Dec. 7,
1942 as an Aviation Cadet and graduated from Mather Field in June 1943. I
completed phase training in B-24 bombers at Lowry Field, CO with 446th Bomb
Group and flew with the 446th to Bumgay, England. I received 5 medals after
completing 30 missions over Europe, including the Distinguished Flying
Cross. Then I served as an intelligence officer with the 458th Bomb Group
at Norwich, England. After these missions I returned to the states and
attended University of California at Berkeley and married Faunice Wilson
Jan. 13, 1945. We have one son Forrest Warne of Bend, OR and a daughter
Julie Wilson Lane of Clovis, CA.

"In 1947 I established my practice in Antioch, CA as an optometrist and
retired June 28, 1984. Now we live at Arnold, CA in the Sierras."

JACOB C. and CLARA [BREKKE] LASSLE

Jacob C. Lasslie was born Sept. 6, 1899 in Glueckstahl, South Russia to
John and Rosina Lassle. In 1905 they immigrated to the United States and
lived south of Bowdle until 1912 when they moved to a farm northwest of
Tolstoy. Jacob grew up on the family homestead. John was born July 7, 1867
and died July 13, 1941. Rosina was born Sept. 18, 1871 and died July 1,
1960. Jacob went to work at St. Luke's Hospital and the Country Club in
Aberdeen as a cook.

He married Clara Brekke in 1923 in Watertown. Clara was born in Primrose,
WI Feb. 10, 1899, the daughter of Nels and Mary Brekke. Her parents were
natives of Norway. Nels was born Sept. 9, 1859 and died January 1940. Mary
was born May 9, 1862 and died Feb. 6, 1953.

Clara grew up on a dairy farm and in 1920 moved with her parents to
Bradley. She worked for the Bell Telephone Co. in Aberdeen as a telephone
operator three years before her marriage.

Jacob and Clara Lassle made their first home in Ashley, ND where he
operated a cream station. In 1924 they moved to a farm seven miles
southwest of Bowdle, which remained the family home 40 years. Six sons and
four daughters joined the family. Jacob and his sons enjoyed hunting,
fishing and trapping. Among the family fun memories are the happy hours
spent at a gravel pit a half mile east of the farm where many of the
neighborhood children and some youngsters from Bowdle spent Sundays
swimming.

        Jacob C. and Clara Lassle

        Back: Richard, Donald, Robert, Clarence Front: Bea, Erliss,
        Delores, Mary Lassle

Clara died July 27, 1940 when their son Jacob Carl was two weeks old. He
was adopted by Clara's sister and husband of Bradley and moved with them to
New York where he grew to maturity. He graduated from the University of
Missouri and lives with his wife Kit and two children in Tonawanda, NY where
he is employed at the Social Service Department.

In August 1945 tragedy struck again when Arthur was killed in a gun
accident at the age of 16.

Jacob C. Lassle moved to Bowdle in the early 1960's and worked for the city
of Bowdle until he retired in 1975. He died Oct. 29, 1981.

Eight children survive their parents: Mrs. Joe (Erliss) Heilman of Java.
They are farmers and live near Java. They have eight children. Robert Lassle
lives in Nisland and married Rauonna Nelson. He operates a gas station and
has three children. Richard Lassle lives in Aberdeen and works for
McLaughlin Electric. He married the former Adelida Voegele. Delores (Mrs.
George) Bichler lives in Longmont, CO where she works in a factory. They
have three children.

Mrs. Rollie (Mary) Mertz lives in Mobridge with her family of two children
and is employed at Mobridge Community Hospital. Clarence Lassle lives in
Bowdle and works at Gus's Bar & Bottle Shop. Donald Lassle married Jan
Sandland. Their home is in Rapid City where he works for Barber
Transportation and Beatrice (Mrs. Terry) Pitson makes her home in Rapid
City and works for the school lunch program. She has two children.

JOHN and ROSINA [BIEBER] LASSLE

John and Rosina Lassle were born in Russia. They were married Feb. 12,

south of Bowdle. In 1912 they moved to a farm northwest of Tolstoy which

John Lassle died July 13, 1941. Rosina loved to grow flowers and enjoyed

Rosina and John Lassle

JOHN F. and MARTHA [BRANDNER] LASSLE JR.

Glueckstahl, Russia was the birthplace of John F. Lassle Jr. He was born
Nov. 25, 1891 to John and Rosina (Bieber) Lassle, who immigrated to the
United States in 1905. They arrived in New York Dec. 3, with their five
children: John Jr., David, Jacob, Gottlieb and Teresa. Four sisters and one
brother were born in the United States.

In March 1906 the family joined an uncle Fred Roesch at Roscoe. This was
their home until they moved to a farm north of Bowdle. In 1912 the family
moved again--into a sod house on a farm north of Tolstoy.

Martha Brandner (born September 1894, died June 28, 1962) married John F.
Lassle Jr. Nov. 11, 1920. John and his bride from Zeeland, ND made their
first home on a farm northwest of Bowdle. In 1925 they moved to their
permanent farm home southwest of Bowdle. Seven children were born to this
couple: Bertha (Mrs. Herbert Schlafmann;) Hilda; Esther (Mrs. Ruben
Aldinger;) Otto (deceased;) Lydia (Mrs. Edwin Wolf;) Anna (Mrs. Bill
White;) and Helmuth Lassle.

        Martha and John F. Lassle

John F. Lassle Sr. was born July 28, 1867 and died July 31, 1941. Rosina
Lassle was born Sept. 18, 1871 and died July 1, 1960.

When Martha died in 1962 John was left alone and continued to pursue the
family hobby of reading. He also enjoys his grandchildren Larry, Carol,
Brenda and Mavis Schlafmann; Terry Lassle Marsha, Rhonda, Lynette,
Kimberly, Burtene, Chardene and Chad Wolf and Lyndon White.

DWAYNE and CAROLINE [MERTZ] LEE

        Vern, Carolyn, Caroline, Dwayne, Janet
