Larry and Alexzine have three sons. Marc was born in December 1976, Todd in
March 1982 and Eric in December 1984.

EDWARD J. and PAULINE [NAASZ] MILLER

Edward J. Miller (1899-1960) and Pauline (Naasz) Miller (1899-1963) were
born and lived their lifetimes in the Java-Bowdle area. They made their
home on the farm in Walworth County which had been homesteaded by his

        Back: Gladys, Marvin, Doris Front: Pauline and Edward Schlepp

FLOYD and HELEN MILLER

Since they left Bowdle in 1973 the years have been very busy ones for the
Miller family. Floyd and Helen became immediately immersed in the operation
of Huebl Funeral Chapel in Aberdeen and the combining of that operation
with the Miller Funeral Home in Bowdle and Chapel in Selby. Floyd's work
was not only intensified by keeping up with both operations, but Helen's
role in the business changed from the backup position in the Bowdle
operation to a very active role in the Aberdeen business.

By 1979 they had outgrown the downtown location of the old Huebl Funeral
Chapel and it was necessary to purchase property and build in the 1100
block of South Main. They moved there in June 1980 and became Miller-Huebl
Funeral Home. They are presently doing in the area of 300 funerals a year
in all locations and have seven employees in addition to themselves in
Aberdeen, as well as Ed Ackerson, the manager in Bowdle.

The demands of the business have been such that Floyd has had a more
limited public role than he had in Bowdle, but has a very big job the past
few years as secretary of the State Board of Funeral Service and is still
serving in that capacity. He also had a very active role with the
Metropolitan Dinner Club and is on the Board of the Dakota Midland
Foundation.

Once Helen got away from minding the phone, she began doing a lot of things
such as YWCA Board, United Way, Bethlehem Church Council NSC Alumni
Association, Aberdeen Chamber of Commerce, South Dakota Chamber of Commerce,
ALC District Council, etc.

        Pat, Mary, Helen, Floyd Miller

Pat Miller graduated from USD in Vermillion, attended two years of medical
school there and earned his M.D. degree from the University of Chicago. He
has spent the last six years in Nashville, TN completing a residency at
Vanderbilt University in general surgery. He is now a lieutenant commander
in the U.S. Navy and serving as a doctor at the military hospital in
Charleston, SC.

Mary Miller attended USD, Northwestern University, worked for the Aberdeen
American News for a while and then finished her bachelor's degree at NSC.
Since then she has worked at television stations in Sioux Falls and
Seattle, WA and presently works as an administrative assistant and in
production at KOMO-TV, the ABC affiliate in Seattle.

All of the Millers have wonderful memories of the 12 years spent in Bowdle
and are happy to still have a connection there which maintains a tie with
those people who are still very dear to them.

DR. FRED and RUTH [DOERING] MILLER

Forty years of service was the contribution which Dr. Fred A. Miller made
to the community of Bowdle. He gave not only through the practice of his
profession of dentistry, but also served in public offices and through
community service.

Fred A. Miller was born on his father's homestead in Walworth County
southwest of Bowdle April 2, 1907. His parents retired from the farm in
1919 to live in Bowdle and Fred graduated from Bowdle High School with the
Class of 1927. He attended dental college at the University of Minnesota,
graduating in 1933. Dr. Miller's parents Christ and Karolina (Bauder)
Miller were of German-Russian descent. His father was born in 1873 and came
to the United States with his parents in 1889. When 21 years old Christ
homesteaded land in Walworth County which is still in the family. Fred's
parents were married in 1897.

Dr. Fred Miller opened his first office in Zeeland, ND in 1933 and it was
there, in 1934, he met his future bride Ruth Doering. They were married May
5, 1935 and that fall they established their home in Hague, ND. In 1937
they moved to Bowdle where Dr. Fred began his long years of service, which
came to an end in November 1977 due to health reasons.

During World War II Dr. Miller was called to serve in the medical corp. and
his office was closed for two years. With the close of the war, the Bowdle
American Legion Post was re-activated and Dr. Miller was elected its first
commander.

Ruth Doering Miller, a registered nurse, had taken her training at St.
Luke's School of Nursing in Fargo, ND, graduating in 1934. Her healing skill
was greatly appreciated by the community. She assisted in the hospital and
in other ways caring for the sick from 1939 to 1955, when the illness of
their son Robert necessitated her full attention.

        Fred, Robert, Ruth, Janet Miller

During the years Bowdle was without a doctor in the late 40's and early
50's, it was Mrs. Miller and Mrs. A.C. (Wally) Merkel whom everyone
depended on for assistance in the time of a health crisis and many times
Mrs. Miller called Eureka Aberdeen or Ipswich doctors for advice on a
problem. It was Ruth people depended on to give prescribed shots and to
check on other illnesses. She was really kept busy. More than one heart
patient depended on her for help. In emergencies the people turned to her.

In 1978 there was a shortage of nurses again and Mrs. Miller gave of her
time and talent to help until her retirement in 1983. In those days there
was no designated director of nurses so the registered nurse on duty was
the charge nurse, which meant greater responsibility during their work
hours.

Dr. Miller served on the Bowdle School Board 12 years and was also a member
of the County Board of Education. He served on the City Council as alderman
and was mayor three terms. He was active in the Commercial Club and
instrumental in the erection of the new hospital structure and nursing
home. He was a volunteer fireman for many years, helped organize and coach
the junior baseball teams, managed the baseball teams for many years, was
president of the Central State League Amateur Baseball Association, coached
and managed the independent amateur basketball team for many years.

Dr. and Mrs. Miller have two children. Robert and his wife Joan (Swanson)
live at 87 Shan Drive, Churchville, PA, where he is an auditor for M.A.
Burdett Gas Products Co. They have a son and a daughter. Janet A. Miller,
born Feb. 7, 1941, is a registered nurse supervisor at St. Luke's Hospital
in Aberdeen.

Dr. Fred Miller died March 16, 1985. Ruth Miller continues to make her home
in Bowdle

JACOB and EMELIA [HILES] MILLER

Jacob Miller was born in 1888 in Hoffnungstal, South Russia. When he was 19
years old he came to America with his parents and they settled near Lowry.
Jacob married Clara Liebelt at Herreid in 1925. She was born at Garutina,
Bessarabia Aug. 24, 1900. They made their home near Isabel where their
three children (Milton, Eleanor and Loretta) were born. Clara Miller died
at Isabel May 19, 1934.

Jacob married Emelia (Martin) Hiles July 15, 1935. Emelia was married to
Albert Hiles Jan. 20, 1931 and two daughters (Gladys and Barbara) were born
to this union. In 1933 Albert lost his life in a farm accident near
Newcastle, WY. Emelia and her daughters returned to Streeter, ND to live
with her parents.

Jacob and Emelia were married in Jamestown, ND and they farmed near Isabel
until the fall of 1936 when they moved to the Bowdle-Tolstoy area. Four
children were born to this union: Harold, Eugene, Eldena and Arlyn.

        Back: Arlen and Harold Miller, Ray Hanchett, Ervin Wolff, Ronald
        Hanson, Milton and Eugene Miller and Loretta Wolff. Front: Errol
        Wolff, Gladys Hanchette, Emelia and Jacob Miller, Eldena Hanson and
        Ervin Wolff Jr.

Jacob and Emelia raised their eight children during one of the worst
economic times this country has seen but their family never went hungry.
For a time they lived on a farm east of Bowdle along U.S. Highway 12
(Yellowstone Trail.) During those times a lot of transits would come along
the road and invariably stop for a handout. There was always something for
them to eat. Emelia would feed them through the window ... probably the
beginning of the fast food service.

To supplement the income Jacob went into the trucking business which meant
long hours on the road and being away from the family, but Emelia kept the
home fires burning. Their love for each other and their family and working
together they made it through the depression. After several years of
struggling they bought their own farm in 1945 near Tolstoy and farmed there
until 1959 when they retired and moved to Roscoe. Jacob died in 1967 and
Emelia returned to Bowdle in February 1975. She died in 1983.

The children of Jacob and Emelia are as follows:

Milton, born July 17, 1926, resides in Bowdle and is engaged in farming. He
also considers him self a hobby trucker. He served in the U.S. Army
1950-1952.

Eleanor was born Sept. 30, 1927 at Isabel and died in October 1928.

Loretta, born Sept. 20, 1930, married Ervin Wolff. They farm near
Cleveland, ND, but live in Gackle where they moved in December 1983. Their
children are Ervin, Errol, Linda and Elon.

Gladys, born Feb. 1, 1932, married Ray Hanchett. She is an elementary
teacher in Lapeer, MI and their children are Gregory, Renee and Darrin.

Barbara, born May 15, 1933, married Donald Metzger. Donald died Nov. 3,
1973. They had two children Debra and Diane and lived in Marlette, MI.

Harold was born June 18, 1936. He married Mary Duenwald and they have a son
James. They farm near Tolstoy.

Eugene, born Nov. 12, 1937, married Betty Felix. They farm near Tolstoy and
have a child Tiffany.

Eldena was born Nov. 28, 1938 and married Ronald Hanson. She is a training
specialist at Redfield School for the mentally retarded. She was chosen "
South Dakota Woman of the Year" in 1984. She is co-author of a curriculum
entitled "Sexual Human Awareness." They live in Redfield and have two
children Lauri and Randall.

Arlyn was born Jan. 27, 1941. He married Sharon Haux and they farm near
Java. Their children are Victoria, Jan, Roger and Sarah.

JOHANNES and MARIE [BAER] MILLER

Johannes and Marie Miller came to this country in 1889. They had six
children: Nettie Miller Herman, Christ, Jacob, Elizabeth Miller Johnle,
Katherine Miller Baer and Emmanuel. Johannes and Marie came from South
Russia the same time Marie's parents and 13 children and they all settled
in this area which was known as the Baer Settlement. The Barnhardt Baers
settled one mile west of the Miller farm. Marie's brother Jake settled west
across the road and brother Benhart settled 1/2 mile west of the Miller
farm.

The first house which was called the claim shanty blew down from a storm.
They then built a house made of mortar stone, grain chaff and wood. They
had a garden and fruit trees beside the house and a well dug by hand about
15 feet deep all lined inside with wood and a top built to hinge a roller
and rope to draw water.

During these years the father and brothers built the church called the Baer
Church. This was served by the same pastor of St. John's Lutheran Church in
Bowdle. During this time the oldest daughter Nettie and her aunt Christine
Baer Nusz cooked meals for the family and pastor, who lived in Bowdle on the
plot where Miller Funeral Home stands.

All the family business was done in Bowdle where Marie had two brothers
Herman and Henry who had Baer Hardware and the Implement Shop and were
grain buyers. Johannes died in 1912 and Marie continued to remain on the
farm. Marie died in 1918.

Marie's daughter Elizabeth and her husband Fred Johnle moved to Bowdle a
few years later.

The two grandsons of this family are Reinie J. Herman of Bowdle and Harold
Baer of Billings, MT.

KIM and CYNTHIA [DOHN] MILLER

Kim M. Miller was born Aug. 9, 1952 in Hoven to Mr. and Mrs. Marvin E.
Miller. He graduated from Bowdle High School and attended two years at
National College of Business in Rapid City.

Kim married Cynthia Dohn Nov. 26, 1977. She was born April 29, 1957 in
Eureka to Walter and Martha Dohn of Eureka. Walter was born Aug. 11, 1931
in Eureka. Martha was born Sept. 25, 1932 in rural McPherson County.
Cynthia graduated from Eureka High School and attended Lake Area Vocational
Technical Institute in Watertown.

They farmed on the land that Kim's great-grandfather Christ Miller had
homesteaded in Walworth County in 1895. Kim and Cynthia continue to make
their home there. Kim was employed by Bowdle Cenex in 1984 and in 1985
became maintenance engineer for Bowdle Hospital and Bowdle Nursing Home.
Cynthia is employed as X-ray and lab technician for Bowdle Hospital.

They have two daughters. Sara Michelle was born Nov. 3, 1981 and Elizabeth
Margaret was born April 25, 1983.

MARVIN and ELSIE [REEDE] MILLER

Marvin Miller chose as his life's companion Elsie Reede, daughter of Mr.
and Mrs. Gottlob Reede, who was born on a farm in Edmunds County April 9,
1926. They were married June 27, 1947 at St. John's Evangelical Lutheran
Church in Bowdle with the Rev. P.G. Albrecht officiating. They made their
home on a farm in Walworth County.

Marvin, the son of Mr. and Mrs. Ed Miller was born on a farm Sept. 20, 1923
and attended the district school. The young couple were Bowdle High School
graduates.

Their daughter Melanie is a registered nurse and the wife of Delbert
Kilber, a mail carrier in Pierre. They have three children: Eric, 15,
Nicolle 12 and Robin 8. Their son Kim Miller is a farmer and his wife is
the former Cynthia Dohn of Eureka. She is a Lab and X-ray Technician at
Bowdle Hospital. They have two children: Sarah age 4 and Elizabeth age 2.

Marvin served in World War II and returned to the Java area to farm after
his discharge. He was a member of the Farmers Union Oil Co. Board of
Directors and a member of St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church Council.
Tragedy struck this family Oct. 22, 1977 when a tractor fire claimed
Marvin's life. Kim took over the management of the farm and Elsie moved to
Bowdle and lives in the Prairie View Apartments.

        Marvin Miller

        Melanie, Delbert, Kim, Cindy, Elizabeth Front: Robin, Eric, Elsie,
        Nicolle, Sara

The Miller farm has been in the family four generations. Marvin's
grandfather Christ Miller came to the United States in 1889 with his parents
and a group of relatives from Crimea, Russia. Christ was 15 years old at
the time. They spent a year at Freeman and then a delegation of men
traveled through the North and South Dakota looking for good land. His
father bought land from a Mr. Kuhle or Coolee in Cloyd Valley Township in
Edmunds County and in 1895 Christ homesteaded on land in Walworth County
where his family grew up.

When Christ and his wife, the former Karolina Bauder, retired to live in
town in 1919 their son Ed operated the farm, followed by Marvin, who was
succeeded by his son Kim.

WILLIAM C. and ADELINE [SCHUMACHER] MILLER

William C. Miller was born to Christ and Karolina Miller Oct. 24, 1910.
Adeline (Schumacher) Miller was born to Christoph and Lena Schumacher March
25, 1911.

William "Bill" and Adeline were born and raised in Walworth County and
lived in the same rural area about 13 miles southwest of Bowdle with their
parents. They attended rural school until their parents moved to Bowdle in
1918 and 1919. They continued their education in the Bowdle School with
Adeline graduating in 1929 and William in 1930.

Bill attended South Dakota State University in Brookings studying
dentistry, but later decided to be a teacher and finished at Northern State
College in Aberdeen with a B.S. degree in education and science. After
college he taught one year (1933-1934) at Veblen. In 1935 he took a
coaching and teaching position at Selby. Adeline continued her education
(1932-1933) at Aberdeen Business College.

July 27, 1936 they were united in marriage and lived in Selby for six
years. In 1942 they left Selby and moved to Miller where Bill taught school
including Wessington Springs and Iroquois as principal and superintendent.
These were called the bad years in the teaching profession with low
salaries and the war. Salaries were tops when you reached the
superintendent's job and were paid $2,400 a year. Every time you moved 10%
of your salary went to a Teacher's Replacement Association for the first
year you taught there. You were just content to have a job even though you
taught five classes, coached and were the administrator of the school.
There were no fringe benefits for what you did. The only rewarding part of
teaching then was when students came back to you time and time again
telling how much you had helped them in their education.

Their first son Creighton was born in Miller Feb. 29, 1944, when they lived
in Wessington. Their second son Terry was born in Aberdeen Dec. 18, 1946
after they had moved back to Bowdle in August 1946.

Bill decided there was no future in teaching and thought a business venture
would be better. They bought the Morris Jones home where Bill sold
insurance and did some income tax returns. Later he went into business with
Bill Schilling as a Kaiser Fraser dealer for one year.

In 1948 they bought Les Olson's drug business located in the Bowdle Theater
where Montana-Dakota Utilities is located now. In 1950 they decided to
expand and bought the lot across the street and built a brick and tile
building. Now the building houses Turner Drug and a drug store is operating
again in Bowdle. The Millers named their store the A & B Shop (Adeline and
Bill) which they operated together 33 years until Bill died very suddenly
Jan. 26, 1981.

Adeline says, "Our years in Bowdle seemed to be a most busy time of our
lives as we both tried to be active citizens by contributing our time toward
the betterment of our community in various organizations. Bill served as
mayor, councilman, member of the Board of Education, Bowdle Hospital
Building Committee, a charter member and president of the P.T.A. and
charter member of the Bowdle Sportsmen's Club, a member of the fire
department, active member of the Bowdle Commercial Club many years, played
baseball on the Bowdle team in its earlier years and was an active member
of St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church holding various offices. Before
retiring Bill went back to teaching at Roscoe 1967-1973. He felt this was
the most rewarding years of his teaching profession as he could devote all
his time on classes and students."

Adeline was busy as a housewife and helping out at the business. She was a
charter member of the Bowdle Mothers' Club, P.T.A., as well as a member of
St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church and Ladies Aid, taught Sunday School
and is still a member of the Hospital Auxiliary and Hi-Low Bridge Club.

        Creighton, Adeline, Bill, Terry Miller

She says, "We always seemed too busy for long vacations but found
recreation in the surrounding area. Bill enjoyed the fishing and hunting and
playing in the city band the first years. He read extensively collecting
history from many sources of historical records and also enjoyed playing the
piano."

Adeline's hobbies were cooking, gardening, sewing, knitting and traveling a
little in her later years.

After graduating from Bowdle High School their son Creighton attended four
years at Northern State College in Aberdeen, graduating with a degree in
business and administration. He married Judith Ham in September 1964. They
live in Pierre where Creighton is employed with the State Highway Public
Safety as a program manager since 1966. Judith is employed as an elementary
teacher in the Pierre Schools. They have three children: Noel, Trent and
Joy.

Terry Miller graduated from Bowdle High School and served three years in
the U.S. Army. When he returned he went to Southern State College in
Springfield and graduated with an associate's degree in industrial
carpentry. In July 1974 he married Virginia Christenson of Revillo, where
they now live and he is self-employed in carpentry. Their four children are
David, Daniel, Thomas and Nancy.

Adeline continued operating the A & B Shop until the business was sold to
Lloyd Jones of Aberdeen Feb. 18, 1982. He operated it once again with a
full-time pharmacist, repeating his father's service to the community until
he sold Jones Drug to Doug Turner in June 1985.

GIDEON and LAVERN [GEORGE] MITTLEIDER

Gideon Mittleider was a New Year's Day child born to John and Fredricka
Mittleider in Streeter, ND. His mother was a native of Russia and his
father was born in North Dakota.

Gideon married LaVern Christina George, daughter of Gottlieb and Tillie
George of Lehr, ND April 23, 1944. LaVern's mother was born in Braddock, ND
and died in 1947 at the age of 42. Her father was born in Lehr, ND and died
in 1955 at the age of 58.

Gideon and LaVern lived on a farm south of Bowdle until 1959 when they
moved to the Ervin Beitelspacher farm. When her health failed they moved to
Jamestown, ND and in 1978 to Denver, CO. Gideon is the head janitor at
Heritage High School in Littleton. LaVern is a vocalist in their church at
Wheatridge.

Sadness filled their home shortly after they moved to the Beitelspacher
farm in 1959 when their son Curtiss Dale died Nov. 12, 1959.

Gideon and LaVern's daughter Gloria married Barry Settle, who is a pastor
at Loveland, CO. They have three children: Kara Jean, Ron and Shaun. Linda
Mittleider married Ron Brieting and they live at Carbondale, CO where Ron
is a salesman and Linda works in the City Market at Glenwood Springs.
Ronnie Mittleider married Cindy Arbach. Their home is in New Castle, CO and
their son Jared works as a technician in Glenwood Springs. Their daughters
Coleen Ann and Melody Joy are at home with their parents and are active in
special work for the church.

        LaVern, Melody Joy, Gideon Mittleider

The terrible blizzard of 1952 stands out in their minds because of the
hardships when ice coated the power lines, causing them to break and they
had no electricity. Their story continues, "There were all the dairy cows
to milk and no power, but we got the job done by using the power through
the exhaust of the tractor. There was no electricity to keep the furnace
going in the house so Gideon drove to town on the icy roads and got a gas
heater we could use, but we could only heat the living room. We had no way
to cook a hot meal. The food supply ran low, finally we were down to
oranges, summer sausage and milk.

"We were surprised and maybe a little alarmed when we heard a knocking at
the door--who could that be in this stormy weather? We opened the door and
there stood our police dog Husky with a pheasant in his mouth. The live
pheasant he carried had not been harmed. He had dug it out of a snowbank
and when he had given us the bird, he went back to dig out some more
pheasants."

After that experience the Mittleiders fortified themselves against another
power outage. They acquired a kerosene stove, lanterns and candles. As Mr.
Mittleider says, "You name it, we had it and we were ready."

JOSEPH and CHRISTINA [KETTERLING] MUELLER

Joseph Mueller, a prominent pioneer of this area, came to Bowdle in 1895.
He was born in Crimea, Russia Jan. 10, 1867 and immigrated to the United
States when he was 8 years old.

        Joseph and Christina Mueller

They made their first home on a farm in Yankton County. He studied for the
ministry at Wartburg College in Waverly, IA for a time and then attended
University of South Dakota in Vermillion. He was the hammer thrower
champion and played on the football team. No protective equipment was worn
in those days and the flying wedge was popular in football.

Joseph was a land and cattle buyer in the early days and at one time was
the owner of over 1,000 acres of land which he rented to farmers in this
area and used it for grazing his cattle. During his lifetime he also owned
a saloon, department store, livery stable, bowling alley, restaurant and
hotel. At one time or another he owned many of the buildings on main street
of Bowdle.

He married Christina Ketterling in 1898, daughter of Valentine and
Elizabeth Ketterling, early settlers who came to Bowdle in 1890.

Nine children were born to this union. Two died in infancy. Lydia, Ovella,
Ella and Joseph are now deceased; Esther Johnston of Mesa, AZ; Phyllis
Commet of Bowdle and Joel Mueller of Lodi, CA are still living.

Throughout his life Joseph Mueller was interested in civic and charitable
activities, donating generously. He was outspoken; but wise, gracious, kind
and upright. Joseph died April 14, 1935 and Christina died May 19, 1965.

ANTON and ELIZABETH [SPODEN] NEHL

Anton was the son of Henry and Elizabeth (Beck) Nehl. He came from
Minnesota and homesteaded 7 miles northeast of Bowdle. Anton lived here
before the railroad was built to Bowdle. It was said that he often walked
to Ipswich to get a bag of flour for his family.

Anton married Elizabeth Spoden and they had 11 children: Monica, Minnie,
Frank P., Anna, Robert E., Paul, Edward, Alex N., Lucy, Elizabeth and
Henry. All are deceased.

KARL and DANIEL NICKISCH

Karl Nickisch was born May 1, 1889 and his brother Daniel was born Sept. 1,
1893 at Marion. They came to Bowdle with their parents in 1902. They
attended Bowdle schools and then both went one year to Barns University of
St. Louis, MO. On their return Karl went to Harding County where he
homesteaded land near the town of Buffalo. Dan entered the U.S. Army in
1916 and served in France during World War I.

        Karl and Daniel Nickisch

When Dan was discharged he and Karl took up farming, living on the old
Nickisch homestead one mile northwest of Bowdle and continued to make their
home there after retiring from heavy labor. Dan suffered a massive heart
attack and died Feb. 28, 1975. Karl then made his home at Bowdle Nursing
Home until he died March 26, 1983 after many years of suffering from
cancer. Both were buried in Bowdle City Cemetery.

HAROLD and HELEN [WITLOCK] NIES

For over a century members of the Nies family have referred to Bowdle as
home. Harold and his family continue this tradition. Harold's maternal
grandfather George W. Ryan homesteaded in eastern Walworth County in 1883,
coming from Erie, PA and making the last 60 miles by ox team. George Ryan
was the first teacher in that school district and in his honor, Ryan
Township was named for him. Harold's mother, aunt and wife taught in the
same school and the schoolhouse still stands, a remembrance of earlier days.

Harold's mother Ethel Ryan Nies was born in Walworth County, Dakota
Territory in 1886. She died in 1974. Peter Nies was born in Wayne, NE in
1892 and died in 1973.

Harold E. Nies was born in 1922 in Draper. He has lived in the Bowdle area
most of his life and grew up in Ryan Township. He completed one year of
college. Harold married Helen M. Witlock in 1949. She was born in Selby in
1925 and is the daughter of John and Louise Schuh Witlock. She received one
year of college. John Witlock was born in Holland in 1884 and died in 1971.
Louise Witlock was born in Russia in 1899 and died in 1949.

Harold and Helen Nies moved to their farm northwest of Bowdle in Spring
Lake Township in 1958 where they still make their home. This farm was
formerly owned by Fred B. Buechler.

They have three daughters. Patricia, born in 1951 is the wife of Brian
Hoffmeier and lives in Arvada, CO. Roberta, born in 1955, lives with her
husband Dan Viedt and daughter Sarah in Winner. Cynthia was born in 1956
and lives in Sioux City, IA. These young ladies are all teachers, another
family tradition.

OSCAR and GERTRUDE [GOETTLING] OLSON

Oscar P. Olson was born July 18, 1892 at Vienna. His parents were Paul and
Helene (Hanson) Olson. Paul was born June 24, 1853 in Wisconsin and died
Oct. 14, 1952. Helene was born April 14, 1865 in Oslo, Norway and died Oct.
14, 1952 at Veblen.

Oscar received an eighth grade education. He married Gertrude Goettling
Jan. 23, 1926. She was the daughter of Gottlob and Christina (Lange)
Goettling. Gottlob was born June 8, 1865 in Beinstein, Wurttenberg, Germany
and died Oct. 15, 1958. Christina was born Dec. 6, 1895 in Odessa, Russia
and died Dec. 15, 1932. Gertrude was born Sept. 20, 1898 in Odessa
Township. She attended Odessa Township School and Northern State Teachers
College in Aberdeen, earning a bachelor of science and special education
degree.

Oscar Olson served in the U.S. Army during World War I, serving nine months
in France. After his discharge he worked as a contractor and builder in the
Aberdeen and Bowdle areas until his retirement. His present hobbies are
gardening, fishing and hunting.

During his early childhood his parents moved from Vienna to Sisseton and
Oscar recalls they loaded their belongings onto a hayrack and the four-day
trip to the new home 11 miles northwest of Sisseton began. It was slow
because the livestock had to be driven by someone on foot.

Oscar was a very civic-minded person, serving as commander of the Bowdle
American Legion Post 1957-1958, alderman on the city council and was
instrumental in getting the hospital and nursing home started. He was a
member of the Bowdle Volunteer Fire Department and helped renovate the
building that houses the Bowdle Senior Citizens Center, serving on the
Executive Board and Building Committee.

Gertrude grew up in Odessa Township about six miles south of Bowdle. The
only girl in a family that included six brothers, Gertrude says it is only
natural she was a tomboy in her earlier years. She enjoyed learning and
school was a pleasure. She received her eighth grade education and upon its
completion she and a friend Katherine Gruber taught a six-months term of
school in McPherson County. They received $45 a month and paid $10 a month
room and board. They made their first trip on the Milwaukee train to Roscoe
where they stayed at a hotel and took a morning train to Eureka.

The County Superintendent of Schools, Mr. Hickman, assigned the teachers
their schools. Gertrude was given the Kassel Township School. At the end of
the six-months term her father came with a team and wagon to take her home.
The next two years she taught in North Odessa School, but decided teaching
was not her forte. She went to Aberdeen Business College and after
graduating was offered a job in the Pierpont Bank. In 1918 the disastrous
flu epidemic hit the nation and Gertrude was called home to take care of
her ill mother and brothers.

In January 1919 there was a vacancy in South Odessa School, so Gertrude
completed that school year and the next five years she taught in Odessa
Township. At that time teachers were required to take state examinations
given by the County Superintendent of Schools at the county seat. Gertrude
went to Ipswich where the tests were given for two days. Certificates were
given according to results of the test. A third grade certificate was good
for one year of teaching, a second grade certificate was good for two years
and a first grade certificate entitled the holder to teach three years.

After her marriage Gertrude remained at home with her family and parents
helping with home and farm duties. In 1950 there was a teacher shortage and
Gertrude went back to teaching and attended school at Northern State
Teachers College where she obtained her bachelor's degree in 1968.
Altogether she taught 29 years, 10 of which were at Roscoe with special
education classes, which she says were the most rewarding of her career.

Gertrude was president of No. 457 Northeast S.D. Chapter for the Council
for Exceptional Children of the National Education Association 1967-1968.
Community service has always been an important part of her life. She served
three years as president of the American Legion Auxiliary unit, president
of the Bowdle Area Senior Citizens Center three years, a member of the
Order of Eastern Star, Methodist Ladies Aid, 4-H Clubs and Homemakers Clubs
and held other offices at the Senior Center.

        Oscar, Gertrude, Viola, Gaylord, Vangie Olson

Oscar and Gertrude's children include Vangie, born Sept. 12, 1926. She did
secretarial work and married Julius Schilling of Eureka who farms in that
area. Their son Mark is in the U.S. Air Force stationed in Phoenix, AZ. The
Schilling daughters are Laurie Faunce and Gena Schlueter.

Viola (Olson) Schumacher was born Sept. 5, 1927. She is employed by a car
rental service in Santa Monica, CA. Her daughter Sheryl is a research
chemist and Viola's son Bruce is a certified public accountant.

Gaylord Olson was born Jan. 20, 1940. He married Eileen Brustman and lives
in Princeton Junction, NJ where he is an electronics consultant.

GERHART and DOROTHY [SCHMIDTGALL] OSTER

JACOB and KATHARINA [BUECHLER] OSTER

In 1747 in the Black Forest of Germany, a man by the name of Theobald Oster
heeded the call from Catherine the Great to come and settle in the southern
part of Russia. Thus was founded the Oster family in Russia.

Jacob is a fifth generation descendent of this man. He came to this country
with his uncle Adam and aunt Eva Oster when he was 6 years old. His mother
had turned him over to Adam and Eva because she thought she could never be
able to give him the life he deserved.

In 1901 Adam, Eva, Jacob and three non-family young people immigrated to
this country. The young adults were able to make their own way after
arrival. Being a child Jacob stayed with Adam and Eva. He learned to farm
from Adam as he had homesteaded 160 acres northwest of Bowdle in Walworth
County.

Jacob married Katharina Buechler Jan. 15, 1915. She was the daughter of
John and Magdalena Kirschenmann Buechler. The young couple continued to
farm on the homestead. Adam and Eva purchased a farm two miles north of the
homestead near Horseshoe Lake and continued farming there.

Tragedy struck in January 1934 when Adam died of a cerebral hemorrhage. In
March 1934 Jacob, Katharina and children moved to the Horseshoe Lake farm
because it was too much for Eva to operate. For many years they farmed the
tillable land and used the pasture lands on both farms. As the operation
expanded, there were more hands to help with the work.

Jacob and Katharina were members of the Neuglueckstahl Church. Their
marriage and the baptism of their 12 children took place in that church.
Five children: Theodor, Elanora, Loretta, Edgar and Alvin died in
childhood. They are all buried at Neuglueckstahl Cemetery.

After 32 years of farming Jacob and Katharina decided to retire and turned
the farm over to the two oldest sons. At that point in their lives they
purchased the Erbe house in Bowdle. Jacob was a deacon at St. Paul's
American Lutheran Church and Katharina was a member of the Ladies Aid
Society. They spent their leisure time gardening, remodeling the house and
enjoying their grandchildren.

Jacob died in March 1957. Katharina continued to live in the home until
1960, at which time it was sold and she moved to the Thommen house where
she resided until her death in February 1963. Eva had lived with the Oster
family up to this time. When Katharina died she moved to the Eureka
retirement home where she resided until her death in January 1967.

        Back: Erna, Gerhardt, Theophil, Helmuth, Alma Front: Waldemar,
        Jacob, Katherine, Renata Oster

The surviving children are: Theophil (Ted) of Aberdeen, who married Irene
Goetz; Helmuth of Billings, MT who married Isabella Kurle; Gerhart of
Bowdle married Dorothy Schmidtgall, Waldemar of Albany, OR married Alberta
Senn; Erna Sonnenfeld of Sioux Falls married Emil Sonnenfeld; Alma of Java
and Mesa, AZ married Erwin Sonnenfeld and Renata of Auburn, WA married
Elroy Jung.

There are 18 grandchildren and 23 great-grandchildren as of this writing.

JOHN and MATILDA [SCHLEPP] OSTER

John Oster was born April 13, 1895 in South Russia and immigrated with his
parents to the Buechler District northwest of Bowdle where he grew up on a
farm. He served in the U.S. Army during World War I as a Sergeant
Horseshoer and was discharged in 1919. He purchased a blacksmith shop in
Bowdle and in 1921 married Matilda (Tillie) Schlepp at the Glueckstahl
Lutheran Church. His bride was the daughter of Jacob and Katherine Schlepp,
who with their children Adam, Maggie and Emanuel had come to the United
States from South Russia in 1898. Katie, Lydia and Matilda were born at the
family farm in Edmunds County.

For 29 years John continued in the blacksmith business and five children
came to share their home. Robert was born March 2, 1923, Irene Feb. 18,
1926, Doris April 9, 1929, Dale Dec. 14, 1932 and Ward Oct. 4, 1940.

John sold the blacksmith shop to Aaron Aldinger in 1948 and built an
electric shop to the east of what is now the Bowdle State Bank. It was
destroyed by fire in 1950 and he built the electric shop on the south side
of Main Street where he serviced and sold small appliances, did electric
wiring, plumbing and installed heating systems. Robert Oster took over the
business in 1965, continuing with the electrical and plumbing work with his
father helping him part-time until his death in 1976.

Robert married Lila Buechler, a beautician. Irene married Milton Hoffman
and went to live in Grand Island, NE. Doris married Wilmer Bieber and they
live in Grand Island, NE. Dale married Jean Pfaff and lives in Rapid City
where he is a carpenter and cabinet maker. Ward married Arliss Brown and is
in the electrical and plumbing business in Bowdle with Rocky Gisi.

Mrs. Tillie Oster has made her home in the Prairie View Housing since 1978.

ROBERT and LILA [BUECHLER] OSTER

Robert Oster was born at Bowdle March 2, 1923 to John and Tillie (Schlepp)
Oster. John was born in Russia in 1895 and came to the United States with
his parents when he was 3 years old. He died in 1976. Tillie Oster was born
in Edmunds County in 1902 and makes her home in Bowdle.

        Lila, Marsha, Marshall, Robert Oster

31, 1985.

Lila graduated from Bowdle High School and Watertown Cosmetology Academy

Robert and Lila had two children. Marsha married Gene Johnson and they live

WALDEMAR and ALBERTA [SENN] OSTER

Waldemar (Wally) Oster was born March 16, 1936 to Mr. and Mrs. Jacob Oster
on the family farm in Walworth County. He says the midwife who was first to
greet him was Grandmother Buechler, so he always had an extra warm spot in
his heart for her. He lived his early years on the farm northwest of Bowdle
and began attending Bowdle in the sixth grade when his parents moved into
Bowdle and bought the John Erbe house. During his school years he worked
for Adolph Braufman and Ervin Gross at their stores. After graduation he was
stationed in Hawaii during two years of service in the Armed Forces. After
his discharge he attended Northern State College in Aberdeen.

        Carter, Waldemar, Alberta, Tamara Oster

In August 1957 he married Alberta Senn, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Albert
Senn. She was born Nov. 30, 1936. Alberta and Wally both graduated from
Bowdle High School in 1954. Alberta is a graduate of St. Luke's
Presentation School of Nursing and after their marriage was employed as a
registered nurse at St. Luke's Hospital in Aberdeen. Wally worked as an
electrician's assistant.

In 1958 they moved to Kent, WA where Wally worked for Boeing Corp. and
later was employed as shoe department manager for J.C. Penney Co. They were
transferred to Forest Grove and Albany, OR where they presently live. Since
1981 Wally has been accounts executive with the Albany Democrat Herald.

Alberta, while employed at Albany General Hospital, at the request of the
staff doctors, was sent to Sacred Heart Hospital in Eugene for a course in
coronary and intensive care nursing, and thus was instrumental in the
opening of the ICC and CCU unit in that hospital. In 1973 she accepted the
position of director of nursing at the Lebanon (OR) Nursing Home and since
1977 has been a Linn County Home Health Care Nurse.

They have two children. Tamara served in the U.S. Army and is the wife of
SFC Paul Clemons. They have three children and live in Marina, CA. Carter
Oster is a tune up technician for the Goodyear Co. in Sacramento, CA.

CYRIL and FRIEDA [WEBB] PAEPKE

        Cyril and Frieda Paepke

MERRIAM and HULDA [HABERER, SCHUMACHER] PAULSON

Hulda (Haberer, Schumacher) Paulson was born and grew up on a farm in

        Hulda and Merriam Paulson

ALBERT and EMMA [VOGELE] PERMAN

Albert Perman was the son of Christ Perman. Christ was born in
Neuglueckstahl, Russia Dec. 8, 1868, where he married Friedericka Diegel,
also of Neugleuckstahl and born March 17, 1871. They arrived in Bowdle
April 6, 1900 and made their first home with her brother Fred Diegel and
family at Java.

They were the parents of 17 children. Albert and his twin sister Carrie
were born Sept. 28, 1906 in Potter County. They attended the rural school.
After Albert completed the sixth grade he worked for his brothers Jake and
Fred until his marriage to Emma Vogele Nov. 24, 1927. Carrie Perman married
August Stotz.

        Emma and Albert Perman

Emma Vogele was the daughter of Christian and Fredericka (Schumacher)
Vogele. Christian was born Jan. 4, 1872 and came to the United States in
1892. Fredericka was born July 30, 1877 and came to New York in 1884. Both
were natives of Neuglueckstahl, Russia. They were married March 3, 1896.
Emma completed the eighth grade and helped her parents at home until her
marriage to Albert.

Albert and Emma farmed in the Lowry flats for half a year and then moved to
the land where LeRoy Perman now farms. They built a new house on the farm
in 1939. In 1962 they moved to Bowdle. Albert did farm and carpenter work
after his semi-retirement. They had three sons.

Clayton was born Dec. 16, 1928. He married Shirley Lake Jan. 11, 1951.
Their children are Douglas, Sonya and Sarita.

children: Valynn, Lyle, Valette, Valerie, Valessa and Lowell. Dennis was
born June 4, 1938 and died Nov. 24, 1938.

Albert and Emma are great-grandparents to Natasha and Tania Schmierer, Luke
and Kajsa Perman and Joshua and Jeremiah Horst.

JACOB F. and KATHERINE [THURN] PERMAN

I, Katherine Thurn, was born Nov. 15, 1893, the fifth child, but the first
child of the family to be born in America. I was born on the homestead of
Karl Schick which was east of the land my father chose to homestead in
Edmunds County. My ancestors on my father's side came from Alsace Lorraine.
My ancestors on my mother's side, Georg Jacob Ackermann was born in
Eulenhof/Unterweissach, West Germany. He and his family went to
Hoffnungstahl, South Russia in 1831 by the invitation of Czar Alexander I,
who opened the land for colonization.

My grandfather Georg Thurn on my father's side was a farmer in Neudorf,
Russia. He paid the way for all of the family to come to America in 1893,
except two married daughters who chose to remain in Neudorf with their
husbands.

My father, Friedrich Thurn was good-hearted and happy. He worked in his
orderly farmyard and well-cultivated fields. At first he farmed with oxen
and then horses. He was always up early and worked until late at night.

My mother, Margaretha Magdaline nee Ackermann, was a small, quiet, reserved
woman. She had a sharp, clear mind and was respected and loved by everyone.
Her foster parents were Pastor and Mrs. Gustav Becker of Hoffnungstal
Evangelical Church in Russia. Her mother was bedridden and unable to care
for her.

My parents left their homes in Neudorf and Hoffnungstal to come to America
to obtain free homestead land. Of my early childhood I remember our sod
house. We lived in the sod house for about seven years. At night when it
was quiet you could hear the coyote's howl. They were troublesome to the
homesteaders. At first we went to a one-room country school on the Gottlieb
Wolff place. My first teacher was Mary Hudson and there were only the
Wolff, Moser and us Thurn children. The next year the school was one mile
south and our teacher was Helen Michaelson. I remember the desks because
they were so big and long. We little ones would stand on the seat to write.
Later Adolph, Bill, Henry and I went by buggy into Bowdle to city school.
Gust, who was the oldest, worked in the Amerpol Lumber Store and Tillie
stayed home to help mother.

There was always plenty of work for everyone. I had one sister Mathilda, we
called her Tillie and four brothers: Gustav (who we later called George,)
Adolph, Bill and Henry. We all shared the work.

Christmas was a family time and always special. We went to church programs
and loved to sing. There were no fir trees to be cut and brought into our
house so Adolph made our first Christmas tree. He made it out of pieces of
wood bound together and mother decorated it with homemade cookies
(Lebkuchen) and walnuts. Later we had a tree with candles. Electric
Christmas lights came much later.

Feb. 3, 1918 during a blizzard that lasted several days, I married Jacob
Perman on the Fredrick Perman farm which was on a hill on the Bowdle-Hoven
road. The buildings are gone now. Later that fall we moved to Portland, OR
where Eugene was born Aug. 5, 1919.

We came back and tried to homestead land across the Missouri River. For
awhile we lived in a cook-shanty. It was a house built of wood on metal
rimmed wheels, sort of a forerunner to the RV's you see now. I often hunted
prairie chickens with a little handgun Jake had. There were many prairie
chickens and you could hear them for miles around. They had good meat to
eat. We only lived here a short time because the land did not suit Jake.
Then we farmed for a time with Jake's father Fredrick who came to America
from Neuglueckstahl, Russia in 1894. We lived on this farm three years.
Harvey was born Nov. 10, 1920 and Adeline April 4, 1922.

In the fall of 1922 we moved to Lowry where Jake sold farm machinery, cars
and grain. Another son Palmer was born Dec. 15, 1924 and died the following
spring April 21, 1925. This was a very sad time for us.

        Jacob J. and Katherine Perman

We moved to Java in 1925 when we bought the building a block off main
street from the Farmers Equity Exchange. Then later we moved to main street
where Jake had the International Harvester business and auto dealership.

Our house with the square nails was moved from Lowry to Java and ultimately
to Selby. This house in Java is where Jenny (Genevieve) was born Oct. 29
1928. Another baby girl was born and died in November 1932.

In the winter of 1934 there was no snow or moisture of any kind and the
wind blew almost every day. You could see dust clouds for miles around. It
was very hot that summer, no rain and the hot wind whistled through the
windows and doors. It was impossible to keep the dust out of the house.
When you went outside grasshoppers were everywhere and ate everything.

Vacations were unheard of but on one special event the whole family went on
a trip to Chicago to see the World's Fair in 1936. What a grand occasion
that was!

We were members of St. Paul Lutheran Church. Rev. George Kirchdoerfer
married us and confirmed all the children except Jenny who was confirmed in
Eureka. We lived in Moorhead, MN 1937-1940 when Jake went into business
selling parts and machinery in Eureka. In 1946 we sold the business and
retired in Sacramento, CA. Later my mother, who was an early pioneer of
Bowdle, came to live with us until she died Dec. 14, 1956.

Jake and I were active in church affairs. He was on the building and
finance committee to build the new St. Luke's American Lutheran Church in
Sacramento. I am still a member of the church and the American Lutheran
Church Women. After a long illness Jake died Jan. 6, 1982 in Sacramento. Our
children are:

Eugene (Gene) F. married Irene Pudwill, retired from the U.S. Navy and Air
Force Civil Service and lives in Sacramento. They have three daughters:
Joan Luton who has two sons: George R. and Nicholas B.; Nancy Oates has two
children: Michele Ruth and Brian Philip and Carol married Donald Gilman
Ostrander.

Harvey H. married Lois Rosenow and he is an orthopedic surgeon and lives in
Sacramento. Their children are: Guy Michael; William married Gayle Green
and their children are Emilie Ann and twins William Harvey and Michael
Gerhart; Barbara married Charles Protteau and they have a daughter Marcy
and James married Elizabeth Pickar.

Adeline M. married Harry Weston. She is retired from Bank of America where
she was a financial services officer. They live in Sacramento and have two
sons: Bradley Charles and Craig Douglas. Bradley has one son Jeremiah Ross
Weston. Two children died in infancy.

Genevieve (Jenny) married Duane Euren. He died in 1972. She is employed as
an employee relations assistant at McClellan AFB and lives in Sacramento.
She has two sons. Barry A. married Diana Hollingsworth. Their children are
Eric Brandon and Amber Dawn Euren. Richard married Susan Berte and they
have a son Jason Duane.

BERNADINE PESICKA

Bernadine was born in Belle Fourche to Peter and Helen Wilson. She joined an
older sister Caroline who was 3. When Bernadine was about 16 months old her
mother and an unborn child died from a ruptured appendix. This left her
father Pete in charge of her and Caroline. Unable to care for them properly
the Welfare Department placed the girls in an orphanage where they lived
several years.

In the meantime the Reinholdt Fiechtner family of Mobridge lost their only
child a 10-year-old son in a bicycle/truck accident. They went to an
orphanage to adopt a child and met two darling little girls who never
wanted to be parted. The Fiechtners decided to adopt Caroline and
Bernadine. Living with these loving parents the girls attended school in
Mobridge through high school.

Time came for the girls to find mates and establish their own homes.
Caroline married Jim Johnson and lived in Colorado. They had two children.
Tragedy struck this family when Caroline, age 27 and her four-year-old son
were killed in a car/train accident.

Bernadine was married to Joe Pesicka Jr. of Bowdle. They had no children.

Mr. Fiechtner died in 1959. Emma Fiechtner is a resident of the Bowdle
Nursing Home.

The following poem was written by Bernadine in honor of her mother.

        Bernadine Pesicka and her mother Emma Fiechtner

                MOTHER
A loving word, a cheerful smile
I would walk for that one whole mile,
Just to see that happy smile
And just to know that in a while
I would see her sitting there
In her little rocking chair.

To know she would do a thoughtful deed
For anyone who was in need.
She is so kind and good
Thank God mother always understood.
She is a mother with a patient heart
And we knew that from the start.

When as children we were at times bad
We couldn't understand what made her mad.
I thank God for giving us a good mother
Who loved us both one like the other.
In our youth taught us to pray
And often asked God to lead us day by day.

JOE and ANNA [WENTZ] PESICKA

Europe was the homeland of Joe's parents, Joe Sr. born in Bohemia, Austria
and Barbara (Gleich) born in Germany. In 1864 Joe Sr. boarded a ship and
came to America landing in Baltimore, later moving to Chicago and then
settling in Tabor, SD, where he married Barbara. In 1886 they moved to
Bangor and homesteaded their land in 1888 in Walworth County. Later they
moved to the Bowdle area 3-1/2 miles south of Bowdle where Joe Jr. was born
Feb. 4, 1905. Nine more brothers and sisters joined this family.

Joe Sr. worked several years on the railroad. During these years he met
Anna (Wentz) born in 1903 to Salvestin and Roselia (Dewald) Wentz. They
married and lived for a short time with his parents, later moving to the
Aldinger farm. After a few years they purchased the Barney Riede farm and
farmed until 1966.

Joe and Anna retired moving to town, establishing a home on east Main
Street. Anna died June 20, 1978. Joe and Anna had three children.

        Anna and Joe Pesicka

Joe Jr. lives in Bowdle. He farmed with his father and now works for D & D
Oil Company. Rosann lives in Sacramento, CA. She married Wm. Farrar and has
five children. Jim lives with his family in Sacramento, CA.

FREDERICK CARL SR. and SOPHIA [GRAMSER] PIETZKE

Frederick Carl Pietzke Sr. was born in Poland where he grew to manhood and
married. After the death of his first wife he immigrated to Russia, taking
his three daughters with him. There he met and married Sophia Gramser, who
was born in Richenfeld, Russia May 27, 1853. In 1886 Frederick brought his
family to the United States and settled in Freeman, where his sister
Justina Hein lived.

        Frederick Pietzke Sr.

In 1895 Frederick brought his family to Walworth County homesteading land
at the western corner of Edmunds County near Bowdle. They knew homesteading
at its most desperate needs. They built a wooden granary which they used as
a house for a while. Then they built a house and barn of sod attaching the
granary to make one long building. The sod mud was produced by horse power
using a grind mill with the horse traveling in a circle at the end of a
beam. The walls were more than a foot thick. A brick stove was built into
the house. All the work was done by the family. No one was hired to help.

Children were taught to respect all adults and all neighbors were called
"uncle" and "aunt" as a matter of respect. When going to church all the
ladies carried a flower or scented leaf and it was the custom for everyone
to greet and talk to every other church-going family.

Their children were Sophia who married John Baer. Margaret married Jake
Leidholdt. Mollie married Fred Trekofski and Christine married John
Trekofski. The Trekofski families live in Canada. Emelia married Christ
Knittel. Frederick Carl Pietzke Jr. married Elizabeth Lutz. Albert died in
his teens as a result of an accident. Pauline married Edward Koenig and
Emma married Adolph Schoenfelder.

Frederick Carl Pietzke Sr. died in 1908 and the family continued to live on
the farm several years. Fred Jr. took over the responsibility of the farm
which was sold to John J. Hoven after several years and is now operated by
his son Vincent Hoven.

After the sale of the farm Sophia Pietzke and daughters Pauline and Emma
made their home in Bowdle where Emma worked hand sticking type (each letter
had to be picked up separately and put into the "stick" at The Bowdle
Pioneer. The Schoenfelder family later moved to Minnesota where Adolph and
Emma died.

FREDERICK CARL JR. and ELIZABETH [LUTZ] PIETZKE

Frederick Carl Pietzke, Jr. was born in Odessa, Russia in May 1885, coming
to the United States with his parents the following year. In 1895 the
family came to Walworth County where Frederick Jr. married Elizabeth Lutz
in 1910. She was the daughter of John and Rosina Lutz, natives of Germany.
Frederick Carl Pietzke Jr. died in November 1973 and Elizabeth died in
September 1965.

        Frederick and Elizabeth Pietzke Jr.

Their children were Elinora Pietzke Meyer, who was born in 1911, lives in
Huntington Beach, CA and has one daughter. Edgar Pietzke was born in 1915,
was a trucker and has retired to live in Lodi CA. He had three children.
Hildegard Pietzke Gilbert was born in 1921, lived in Huntington Park, CA
and died. Aaron Pietzke was born in 1924, had four children and died in
Tacoma, WA.

Frederick and Elizabeth Pietzke brought their family to Java in 1916 where
he owned a cream station for 18 months. They moved to Bowdle and he
operated a pool hall, then a grain elevator and went into the auto gas and
service station on the old U.S. Highway 12 which he operated many years.
While living in Bowdle he built two houses.

In 1938 they moved to Lodi, CA where they lived until 1942 when they
returned to Bowdle to live on a farm. The following year he sold the farm
and returned to Lodi. He worked at many jobs there. His last job was with
the J.C. Penney Co. as custodian. He died in November 1973 at the age of
88. Elizabeth died at the age of 75 in September 1965.

EDGAR FRED and GERTRUDE [FIECHTNER] PIETZKE

Edgar Fred Pietzke, son of Frederick Carl and Elizabeth Pietzke Jr., was
born on his grandfather's farm southwest of Bowdle July 18, 1915. He
married Gertrude V. Fiechtner of Java July 18, 1940. She is the daughter of
Emelia and John Fiechtner, who were born in South Dakota. Emelia was born
in 1894 and died in 1983. John was born in 1890 and died in 1948.

        Gertrude and Edgar Pietzke

Edgar and Gertrude Pietzke's children were all born in Stockton, CA. These
fourth generation Pietzkes are: Brian, born Jan. 3, 1943, is an accountant.
Marilyn, born Aug. 27, 1946, is an auditor, the wife of David Phillips and
the mother of two children. Jerry was born Dec. 24, 1949 and is a trucker.
He and his wife Susan have two children.

Edgar states he lived in the Bowdle area for 21 years, part of the time was
on the farm north of Bowdle. In 1937 he moved to Lodi, CA and came back
later to help his father on the farm.

In 1943 when his father sold the farm he also took his family back to Lodi.
He worked as a second cook in a restaurant the first year and also did grape
and dairy farming. In 1945 he went into the trucking business and though he
retired from the business in 1979, he still occasionally drives truck.

ALFRED and IRENE [BUECHLER] RADER

"I was the second youngest daughter of Fred B. and Katherine Buechler. The
first 19 years of my life were spent on the farm my grandfather
homesteaded. I attended the Buechler School for the first eight grades. I
graduated from Bowdle High School in 1948. I attended Capital University in
Columbus, OH for two years and later attended and graduated from Northern
State Teachers College in Aberdeen with a bachelor's degree in elementary
education.

"My first teaching assignment was at the Spring Lake School on Highway 12
(also known as the Erbe School. ) Later I taught elementary grades in
Redfield, Clark and Bristol.

"I married Alfred H. Rader of Hoven Feb. 14 1955 in Aberdeen. We lived in
Aberdeen, Bristol and Mitchell before moving to California in 1963. Since
then we have been teaching in the Gilroy Public Schools. Presently I am
teaching kindergarten. We lived in Gilroy for 12 years where our three
children Tom, John Scott and Joan attended school and graduated from high
school. Joan is married and we have one granddaughter.

        Standing: Jose' Soenz, Tom, John Seated: Irene, Alfred, Joan, Audrey

"Among the recollections of the early years of my life on the farm is the
memory of living where the tallest windmill in the entire community was
located. We also had a large lake just east of our farm that provided many
hours of fun in winter when we ice skated on it after school and weekends.
During the thirties this lake was dry, but it was the only place where a
hay crop for the cattle could be cut. During the late forties and fifties
the lake teemed with wildlife. There were wild ducks and geese, muskrats
and even wild mink.

"I think everyone that ever attended Buechler School remembers the
Christmas programs we used to put on, with pie and ice cream being sold
after the program to raise money for our Young Citizens League fund.

"One of the saddest times during my school years was when our teacher Mrs.
Lemburg of Selby was killed in an automobile accident. We were all in
school and wondered where our teacher was, only to be informed that morning
that she had died in the accident the night before.

"The games we played brought many hours of enjoyment. Some of our favorites
were: Andy-I-Over, Red Light and Cricket. We may all have forgotten the
rules by now, but we still cherish the memories of good times. In winter we
played Fox and Goose in the snow. One winter we spent most of our time
twisting binder twine into ropes on a small homemade device and later we
knotted the ropes into a volleyball net. It was so strong and heavy it took
two people to carry it out and put it up on the court. After that we had
years of playing volleyball during, before and after school.

"Springtime usually found us playing baseball or hunting gophers. Once a
year we'd make a walking field trip to the gravel pit by the railroad line
about two miles away. Every spring there was a Rally Day in Selby with all
the rural schools competing for ribbons and a trophy in relays and races and
other track and field events. During my eighth grade year our school won
the trophy. We were especially proud since there were only 11 students in
our school by that time."

STANLEY and VIRGINIA [SCHUMACHER] RALL

GOTTLOB and LYDIA [KILBER] REEDE

Gottlob was born July 24, 1889 near Freeman to John and Carolyn (Haar)
Reede and attended school there. His parents moved to Bowdle when he was 14
and he attended the Cloyd Valley School and later farmed with his father a
number of years. He married Lydia Kilber Feb. 6, 1913 and the couple had
six children. Rev. Roy Reede is an institutional Chaplain for hospitals in
Madison, WI. Leonard was in partnership with his father and died April 1,
1970. Lorraine married George Trudeau, Lillian married Tillman Severson,
Agnes married Borden Mayer and Elsie married Marvin Miller.

        Lydia and Gottlob Reede

Gottlob and Lydia also raised a grandson Billy to maturity. He now lives in
Bloomington, NE where he has a small farm and also works as a caretaker of
a state park there. He is married and has three children.

The family farmed in the Roscoe and Bowdle areas until 1938 when Gottlob
purchased the Al Engelhard Produce in Bowdle and continued to operate it
until 1960 when he retired and his son Leonard succeeded him.

Gottlob and Lydia became residents of Bowdle Nursing Home in 1966 and
celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary in 1973. Lydia died in 1974 and
Gottlob died in 1978.

ALVIN and ERNA [GROSS] REUER

Alvin Reuer, son of George and Rosina Bitzer Reuer, was born on a farm 11
miles northeast of Tolstoy. He was the oldest of seven children and helped
his father farm when all the work was done with horses.

In 1927 Alvin attended auto mechanics school in Aberdeen and then worked
for Arnold Manke in Selby until 1929 when he went to Tolstoy to set up his
own garage business. In 1932 he moved to Bowdle and worked as a mechanic in
rooms at the back of the John Oster Blacksmith Shop two years. He then went
into business for himself in a building located on the site of the present
Bieber Library.

        Alfred and Erna Reuer and Families Back: Janene, Dennis, Connie,
        Dr. Duane, baby Eric, Kenneth, Sandra. Front: Joelle, Jonathan,
        Jason, Erna, Alvin, Jeffrey, Chad.

Alvin again progressed in his business and in 1943 bought the garage on
Main Street which had been operated by John Hennecke located in the old
Dumont Hotel building. He still operates this business which handles farm
machinery and he is also busy with farming.

In 1934 Alvin Reuer and Erna Gross, daughter of Jacob and Magdalena
Buechler Gross, were married. Erna was born on a farm eight miles southwest
of Bowdle and moved to Bowdle in 1919 with her parents.

The Reuers had three sons. Kenneth lives with his wife Sandra in Enumclaw,

GEORGE and ROSINA [BITZER] REUER

        Rosina and George Reuer holding a grandson

JACOB and MATILDA [KURLE] RIEGER

Jacob and Matilda (Tillie) Kurle Rieger moved to a farm on the north edge
of Bowdle in 1944 where they farmed and operated the Rieger Dairy. Milk was
bottled in glass bottles and distributed to homes and retail stores in the
area. Those were the days when milking was done by hand, but Riegers also
had a small milking machine.

        Jacob Rieger

Five years later the Rieger family moved to Aberdeen where Jake purchased a
shoe repair shop and learned that trade. In 1952 they returned to Bowdle and
opened Rieger Shoe and Canvas Repair Shop, which they operated until 1977
when Jake moved to Eureka.

Tillie Rieger had been active in helping her husband with the farm and
dairy business and also assisted in the shoe repair business until she died
July 8, 1973. She was very active in the Congregational Church of Bowdle.

Jake went into semi-retirement after moving to Eureka doing shoe repair and
canvas work in the basement of his home. He is now 82 years old and still
plying his trade.

The Riegers have five children and 14 grandchildren. Harry Rieger married
Ronita Stem of Bowdle. They own a motel in Brush, CO and have four children.

Darlene Rieger Hahler lives at Chelsea where her husband Melvin and their

JACOB and ROSINA [OTT] RIEGER

Jacob Rieger was born in Germany; his was one of many German families that
immigrated to Russia. Jacob married Rosina Ott in Russia and nine children
were born to them. Their second son Christof was born in 1869. He married
Carolina Willt of Neudorf, Russia. Three of their children were born at
Glueckstahl: Jacob in 1896, Friederich (Fred) in 1899 and Katherine in
1902. Christof and his family sailed from Hamburg, Germany in June 1903 on
the North Star line to New York. The following year he filed his petitions
for naturalization in Edmunds County, South Dakota. June 6, 1910 Christof
Rieger finalized his homestead in Edmunds County on Section 7, Township 123
North, Range 73 East (Bowdle Township) including 109.89 acres. Six more
children were born at Bowdle: Marie in 1903, John in 1906, Reinhold in 1908,
Mathilda in 1913, Edwin in 1914 and Alvina in 1917.

FRED and FRIEDA [LEMKE] RIEGER

Jan. 20, 1920 Fred Rieger, son of Christof, married Frieda Lemke. She was
the daughter of Hanna Froemming and William Lemke. She was the grandchild
of Fanne and Carl Froemming and the youngest of 10 children. She was born
in 1893 and died in 1972. Frieda's parents, with their four children
Bertha, Richard, Elizabeth and Theodore, immigrated to America in 1884 and
lived in Milwaukee, WI. Clara, Hanna, William, Carl, Helena and Frieda were
born there. In 1894 the Lemke family moved to South Dakota and homesteaded on
a farm north of Bowdle. After their marriage Fred and Frieda Rieger lived
on a farm in Walworth County. Later they built their own farm 1-1/2 miles
north of Bowdle.

        Fred and Frieda Rieger

In 1924 they built their first home. The lower part was constructed of mud
and stone. In 1935 they built a new house of wood. They farmed until 1941
when they moved into Bowdle and built a home. Frieda devoted much time to
her life long avocation-the cultivation of many house plants and an enormous
yard and garden filled with flowers, shrubs and trees. Fred's large garage
housed his woodworking shop and many tools. A gifted carpenter, his hobby
was a lifetime interest. Many Bowdle homes contain furniture, cabinets or
woodwork that he repaired or built. After Frieda's death Fred continued to
live in Bowdle. He married Frieda Johnson of Glenham in 1976 and lived in
Bowdle until his death in 1981.

        Mud-Stone-Wood Home on Fred Rieger Farm

GEORGE and LYDIA [DELKER] ROBINSON

Lydia and George Robinson came into the Bowdle community the spring of 1929.

Lydia was born Dec. 18, 1892 in the Sutley community northeast of Java in
Campbell County to Jacob and Regina (Blum) Delker. Her parents came to
America in 1888 by boat and then took the train from New York to Menno
where Regina's father Michael Blum lived. In 1889 they came to Campbell
County where they started their homestead May 21. They lived there 17 miles
south of Eureka for 24 years. This is where Lydia grew up and attended
school, which was part of their home. In 1913 they moved to Eureka where
Lydia worked in a store.

George Robinson was born in Green Bay, WI Feb. 23, 1896 to James and Laura
Robinson. His father was born in Denmark. He came to America and was a
foreman for the railroad which was built from Green Bay to Sturgeon Bay.
Laura Schley Robinson was born in 1880 in Germany.

        George and Lydia Robinson

When George was very young his parents died, leaving him, his sister Martha
and Julius to be cared for by relatives or in orphanages. George helped his
uncle deliver milk before going to school. Later he worked in the forests
of Northern Wisconsin, cooked on an iron ore ship and did whatever was
available to support himself.

In 1915 he worked in the harvest fields at Coleharbor, ND. Lydia was
working on the same ranch at the time. They met and were married Nov. 22,
1917 at the Congregational Parsonage in Bowdle by Rev. L. Brakenmirer.

They made their home on a farm 16 miles northeast of Java, living there
until 1929 when they moved to Bowdle where George worked for several years.
Times were hard. In 1936 George moved his family north of Bowdle to the
Fred Pietzke farm and he also managed a dairy. He never missed a day in
delivering milk. Raw milk was six cents a quart and every day 50-150
bottles were washed in preparation for the next day's delivery.

In 1940 he bought his own farm northeast of Bowdle, known as the Valentine
Wentz farm. He continued to farm and raise cattle until 1959 when they sold
the farm and moved to Denver, CO to be near their three sons. Big cities
were really not dear to their hearts and in 1964 they moved back to South
Dakota to live near their daughter in a trailer home they purchased at
Glenham. They celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary in 1967. Lydia died
Dec. 1, 1969 and George died Aug. 5, 1976. They are buried in Greenwood
Cemetery at Mobridge.

While in Bowdle George and Lydia were members of the Evangelical United
Brethren Church. In Glenham they belonged to Grace Congregational Church of
Mobridge.

        George Robinson Family LeRoy, George, Herbert, Lydia, Albert, Laura

They were blessed with six children. Edgar George was born March 4, 1921
and died at the age of 16, March 25, 1937.

Laura Regina was born July 9, 1922. She married Herbert Bohlander of
Glenham. They have two adopted daughters: Gail (Mrs. Larry Johnson) who has
two step-children and Marjorie (Mrs. Al Defender) who has three children.
Bert worked for Glenham Equity Exchange 29 years. They have been foster
parents since 1972. Laura and Bert are retired and live in Glenham.

Albert Harold was born Feb. 10, 1924. He married Irma Johnson of Underwood,
ND. Their three children are married: William James to Doris Lund and they
have three daughters; LouAnn Faye to Major Edward Huston and Richard Paul to
Georgine Ballard and they have a daughter. Albert served in the Pacific
Theater during World War II in the SeaBee Division of the Navy. He did
carpenter work before entering the Civil Service as a missile inspector for
the U.S. Air Force. Al and Irma are retired and live in Minot, ND.

Mildred Ruth was born Oct. 12, 1925 and died Nov. 15, 1925.

Herbert Norman was born Feb. 7, 1932. He moved to Denver, CO in 1952 and
married Elfriede Goehring in April 1957. They have two children, Ruth
Robinson and Linda Rankin and one grandchild, April Marie Rankin. Herbert
works for Rockwell International the last 31 years as a senior chemical
engineer.

LeRoy Walter was born Aug. 20, 1934. He joined the Navy in the fall of 1952
after graduation. He spent the next four years on the East Coast and
southern section of the country. After leaving the Navy he was employed by
Sperry Corp. in Minneapolis. He lived there two years, then traveled one
year for the Sperry Corp. before settling in Boulder, CO. He married Betty
Harris in Nov. 21, 1959. They have a 22-year-old daughter, Susan who is
attending UNC at Greeley and a 20-year-old son, Curtis who is attending CU
at Boulder. They live in Boulder and LeRoy does most of his work in Denver
for Sperry Corp.

WILLIAM and LEA [BERRETH] ROEBUCK

William (Bill) Roebuck was born Sept. 18, 1894 in Canistota, the child of

when they moved to Bowdle where they farmed south of town. After several

        Lea and William Roebuck

While a young man William Roebuck worked for Jake Schaffer at Glenham. In

They were blessed with five children: Nelvin of Flandreau, Lee of Selby,

REVEREND EUGENE and NANCY [PITTS] ROESLER

Eugene W. Roesler was born near Bellevue, IA in 1924. Later his parents

ADOLPH and ESTHER [FISCHER] SANDMEIER

Adolph Sandmeier was born on the family homestead six miles northwest of
Bowdle Nov. 17, 1919 to Joseph and Elizabeth (Voegele) Sandmeier. He
attended rural school near his home and helped with farm work until he

Company C, 205th Infantry Battalion in the Aleutian Islands in the North
Pacific, going there in June 1943 and returning January 1945. He was
discharged at Camp Polk, Louisiana Oct. 27, 1945.

        Back: Mary holding Jason, Gene, Georgia, Calvin. Front: Jerry,
        Esther, Adolph holding Amber and Cathy holding Erik.

Adolph was employed at area sale barns 1938-1982, with the exception of

CALVIN and JOSEPHINE [GRENZ] SANDMEIER

Calvin, son of Theodore and Mildred Sandmeier, was born Dec. 3, 1946. He

After college Calvin served a short term in the Armed Services as a second

CHRIST and MARIA [SCHICK] SANDMEIER

Christ Sandmeier was born in Neuglueckstahl, South Russia to Frederich and
Margaret (Oster) Sandmeier. At age 1 Christ was adopted by his aunt Rosina
Capp, who had lost her husband and had no children.

When Christ was 17 years old he decided to come to the United States to
join his parents, brothers and sisters who had already established a home
here. Two brothers remained behind because they were in the Russian Army.

Christ went to the courthouse to get a pass for America, but to his
surprise he did not get any because he was nearing the Army age of 19.
Afraid of being caught, he decided to escape by traveling at night and
hiding during the day. Getting close to the boundary line he met a man,
living on the German side, putting up hay. He helped the man load hay in
the wagon and that evening he hid there. This was his escape method to
cross the border into Germany. He went to Hamburg and boarded a freighter
ship, the S.S. Fredericka, which also carried about 400 passengers. The
trip took 11 days before Christ landed at Halifax, Canada. He traveled by
train to Minneapolis and then to Aberdeen.

With no more money Christ had to ride in the caboose of a freight train to
Roscoe. Since the railroad ended there he walked to Bowdle. At that time
Bowdle was just a new location and only had a few buildings and several
tents. He stayed overnight with a man in a tent and the next day walked out
to his father's place about five miles northwest of Bowdle, later known as
Jacob Huft place. Christ worked wherever he could find a job, mostly with
the steam engines.

Thereafter many events took place. In 1910 Christ married Maria Schick. In
1914 his father was killed in a horse runaway accident. A year later Christ
and Maria adopted a son Theodore.

Christ and his family homesteaded 80 acres of land in Modena Township in
1918 and a year later he bought another 120 acres just bordering it. In
1919 the family moved their farm buildings to a new location in the
Horseshoe Lake area. This is the same place their son Ted lives now.

In 1941 Christ and Maria moved to Bowdle to retire. Christ died April 26,
1946 and Maria died Sept. 20, 1962.

GARY and ROSEMARY [GRISMER] SANDMEIER

Gary, son of Theodore and Mildred Sandmeier, was born March 3, 1948. He
attended country school north of Bowdle and graduated in 1966 from Bowdle.
Gary's father died in the fall of 1967, leaving Gary and his mother to
operate the farm.

Gary's brother Calvin returned from the service and joined the farming
operation. Presently Gary and Calvin operate the farm northwest of Bowdle
raising registered Charolais cattle, dairy cattle and small grains.

The bachelor days came to an end when Gary married Rosemary, daughter of
Baldaser and Grace Grismer of Bowdle in June 1984. They have a little
daughter Kimberly.

JOHN and BARBARA [WAHL] SANDMEIER

        Barbara and John Sandmeier

Theodore and Mildred Sandmeier, who had lived on a farm north of Java until
