JOSEPH and ELIZABETH [VOEGELE] SANDMEIER

Joseph (Joe) Sandmeier was born April 9, 1891 in Russia. He came to the
United States in 1901 with his parents Fred and Margarette Sandmeier. They
settled on a farm six miles northwest of Bowdle. April 8, 1906 he was
confirmed in the Lutheran Church in Java by Rev. George Kirchdoerfer. He
married Elizabeth Voegele in Bowdle Jan. 23, 1917.

Elizabeth was born in South Russia Jan. 19, 1895 to Bernard and Elizabeth
Heupel Voegele. She and her family moved to the United States in 1911 and
settled in the Tolstoy area. In 1912 the family moved to the Hosmer area
where she attended rural school.

        Elizabeth and Joseph Sandmeier

Joe and Elizabeth established their home on a farm southwest of Hosmer. A
few years later they moved to a farm nine miles northwest of Bowdle where
they lived until 1955 when they retired to live in town.

Nine children were born to this marriage. Two died in infancy. The
remaining are Adolph of Bowdle, Edna Huft of Bowdle, Ruben of Bowdle,
Adeline of Mobridge, Emma Mittleider of Bowdle Raymond and Arthur, both of
Mobridge.

Joseph Sandmeier died Dec. 9, 1957 after a lengthy illness due to a heart
ailment at the home of his daughter Emma Mittleider. He was buried in the
Neuglueckstahl Cemetery in Walworth County. Elizabeth continued to live at
their home in Bowdle until she moved to the Bowdle Nursing Home. She died
Jan. 26, 1985 at the age of 90.

RUBEN and ALICE [SCHAIBLE] SANDMEIER

Ruben Sandmeier was born Dec. 5, 1921 in rural Bowdle to Joe and Elizabeth
(Voegele) Sandmeier. He grew up in the Bowdle area and attended rural
school.

Alice Schaible was born Oct. 17, 1926 in rural Mound City to John and Emma
(Kunz) Schaible. The family lived in the Eureka area and then moved near
Java where Alice grew up and was educated.

        Alice, Aldeen, Ruben Sandmeier

Ruben and Alice were married Nov. 8, 1949 in Java. Their son Aldeen Kenneth
was born Nov. 8, 1962. They farmed northwest of Bowdle until they moved
into the city in 1963 and Ruben began work at the Bowdle Sales Barn where
he is still employed.

THEODORE and MILDRED [SEMMLER] SANDMEIER

Theodore and Mildred Sandmeier began farming January 1946 on the family
farm eight miles northwest of Bowdle, living with his parents Rudy and Cora
Sandmeier. During that year their son Calvin was born. Ted then moved his
family to a farm northeast of Java in Walworth County, known as the Samuel
Oster farm. While living there Gary and John joined the family. Their
farmhouse was destroyed by fire Dec. 7, 1950 and Ted moved his family back
to the family farm northwest of Bowdle Dec. 23. Later they bought the farm
from his parents.

Their children attended the country schools, but after six years lapsed,
all the country schools closed and the children went to town school. The
first year they spent the winter months with their grandparents and the
second with Althea Buechler. When bus service was instituted the children
rode the bus to classes until they graduated from Bowdle High School.

Calvin attended South Dakota State University in Brookings and during his
second year his father died in October 1967. Gary stayed on the farm
working hard to keep his brother in the university and the farm operating
successfully. John graduated from Bowdle High School in 1968 and that fall
went to diesel mechanics school in Denver, CO, graduating with a doctorate
in mechanics.

Calvin bought the family farm in 1972 and Mildred and Gary moved to Bowdle.
Calvin married Joey Grenz of Eureka. They have two daughters Melissa and
Jessica. Gary married Rosemary Grismer and their daughter is Kimberly Marie.
John married Dorothy Lewis of Sioux Falls. They have three children
Jennifer, Joseph and Joshua. They live in Ralston, NE where John pursues his
mechanics trade.

Mildred Sandmeier has been employed at Ozzie's Super Valu in Bowdle since
1972.

THEODORE C. and MARY [HUFT] SANDMEIER

Theodore, born May 18, 1916, was adopted by Christ and Maria (Schick)
Sandmeier. Ted lived with his parents on a farm located in the Horseshoe
Lake area. He was 4 years old when his parents moved to this farm. After
drilling a well, they moved their buildings from their old homestead. Ted
remembers those long 2-3/4 mile walks to the country school southeast of
the farm. After his 8th grade he continued to farm with his parents. In his
memory are those horrible "black" storms in the 30's and the good crop in
1932.

Ted married Mary Huft Oct. 28, 1937, daughter of Jacob and Johanna (Wald)
Huft. They continued to farm on Ted's homeplace and his parents retired to
Bowdle in 1941.

Ted and Mary raised six children who also attended country school until
1949 when they had to attend school in Bowdle, but poor roads during bad
weather made it impossible. Knowing how important their education was, Ted
purchased a small Piper Cub plane and flew the children to school in three
minutes.

        Ted and Mary Sandmeier

When Mary's folks retired to Bowdle the children often stayed with them
during bad weather. A few years later the roads were improved and graveled
making it possible for the school bus to provide transportation. With
better roads all continued attending school and completed high school.

Emil Sandmeier was born Dec. 15, 1938. He married Gladys Schmidtgall and
they live in Bismarck. Their children are Mrs. Terry (Debbie) Lewis and
Bryan married Nancy Welch.

Roland, born Aug. 21, 1941, married Sharon Ehresmann. They farm east of
Hosmer and have four children: Mrs. Mark (Sherry) Perrion, Shirley, Sheila
and Rebecca.

LeRoy was born June 29, 1944. He married Betty Schneider and they farm
north of Java. Their children are Jeffrey and Traci.

Kathleen was born July 11, 1952. She married Ted Nipp and she is a
registered nurse at Dakota Midland Hospital in Aberdeen. Their children are
Michelle and Cody.

Arlene and Darlene were twins born April 9, 1955. Arlene married Rocky
Schmitt. They live at Redfield with their four children Amanda, Robert,
Robin and Angie. Darlene married Joe Duhon. They live at Shreveport, LA and
she is a hairstylist. Their children are Destiny and Serena.

Ted and Mary are semi-retired but continue living on the farm, enjoying
country life and they hope to continue staying on the farm.

PASTOR SAM and PENNY [ANDERSON] SAYLOR

Pastor Sam Saylor, his wife Penny and sons Brian and Barry moved to Bowdle
in November 1983, at the call of the Bowdle Church of God.

Pastor Saylor was born to Jesse and Beatrice Saylor in Miami, OK. He moved
to Wichita, KS when he was two and lived there until moving to North Dakota
to attend college. He is a graduate of Wichita West High School and
received his bachelor of arts in Bible from Northwest Bible College at

Pastor Saylor is currently working on his master of arts in Christian
counseling degree and plans to pursue a doctor of ministry in Christian
counseling degree. He is an ordained minister in the Church of God and
serves as a member of the Dakota State Council. In 1979 he was named an
Outstanding Young Man of America. While serving as president of the Hot
Springs Ministerial Association he drafted an effective minors pornography
law. He currently serves as secretary to the Bowdle Ministerial Association
and secretary to the Nutrition Site Council.

Penny was born in Mobridge. Her parents Lloyd and Evelyn Anderson farmed
west of Selby. The family left the farm when Penny was five to move to
Rapid City. She graduated from Rapid City High School and attended
Northwest Bible College two years. Penny has been very active in children's
ministries a number of years. She has traveled in the Dakotas and Colorado
doing Kids Krusades. Penny also operated a day care center in her home and
served as a substitute teacher in Hot Springs. She is presently enrolled as
a student at Northern State College pursuing a bachelor of science in
education degree. Penny's grandmother lives in the Good Samaritan Home at
Selby and her aunt lives on a farm in Glenham.

Brian was born in Hot Springs and is attending Bowdle Grade School. His
interests include piano, singing and bicycle riding. He is the delivery boy
for the Comet.

Barry was also born in Hot Springs and attends Bowdle Elementary School. He
enjoys bicycling and games of all sorts including chess and checkers.

ALTON V. and DELORES [BUECHLER] SCHAIBLE

On a cold January, South Dakota wintery night,
From the Buechler's farmhouse, came a bright cheery light.
Pa was shaking brothers Emil, Milton, Rueben and Leroy,
Irma, Eleonore, Renata and Irene were aroused once more.
It's time to go over to Uncle John's and Aunt Mary's,
That only meant; another baby for the old carriage.
Another mouth to feed, would the Buechler's be able?
Move over on the bench, Delores is now at the table.
The depression, the dust bowl, the thistles, were in full swing,
The only solution, the chickens would have to grow another wing.
Four days later, in nearby Hosmer town
Ma Schaible was pacing the floor, up and down.
Wilmer, Ramona, Delbert and Viola were not quite sure,
If Alton was the brother they could adore.
Cause it meant they must move over in their bed,
At night the sheets would once again be wet.
Pa was more than busy with his oil and gas fleet,
With the addition of Aaron, Delpha and Ronnie, the family was now complete.
The move from Hosmer to Bowdle, the children felt forlorn,
But several years later, "Schaible Chevrolet" was born.
The garage kept the energetic Schaible boys off the streets,
But each individual child's musical talent was the town's rare treat.
At the Buechler farm the hearts were all saddened,
For at the age of 47, God took their mother to her eternal home in heaven.
Delores began her education at the one-room Buechler School,
Hosmer and Bowdle Grade School were Alton's Learning tool,
Not in grade school, but at "Good Old Bowdle Hi" did our paths cross,
In band Alton's trumpet blared, but Delores's clarinet was usually at a loss.
Not until our senior homecoming dance,
Did Alton give Delores a second glance.

        Laura, Brian, Mark, Kathryn, Alton, Delores, Meg, Tim, Lynn,
        Richard, Kathy, Curtis

Delores and Alton were married Jan. 6, 1954. They each continued with their
education graduating with several degrees. Alton is an electrical engineer
at McDonnell in St. Louis, MO and Delores is a kindergarten teacher at a
Lutheran Church. They have four children.

Kathy married Mark Sylvester and is a senior at UMSL in computer science.
Their children are Laura and Brian.

Lynn married Richard Leslie and has a degree in school counseling.

Curtis is married to Kathy McCreight and is a senior computer science
programmer.

Tim married Meg Murphy and is a senior at University of Missouri (KS)
Dental School.

All the children live in the state of Missouri.

The section of poem was written by Alton and Delores about themselves.

CHRISTIAN and CHRISTINA [LIMLE] SCHERBENSKI

Christian Scherbenski was born Jan. 29, 1871 in Hoffnungsthal, South
Russia. In 1886 at the age of 15 he immigrated to America and settled in the
Bowdle area. Until 1900 he lived in Walworth County and until 1920
southwest of Bowdle. In 1892 he married Christina Limle. Seven children were
born to them. Gottlieb died in infancy. Christina died in 1913 leaving
Christian with six young children. He married Paulina Hockmeister in 1917
and she died six years later.

Christian took up a claim of land southwest of Bowdle and lived there until
his retirement. He then moved into Bowdle and died Dec. 18, 1937 at the age
of 66.

The remaining six children grew to adulthood in the area. John married
Lydia Hoffman and settled in the Jamestown, ND area. Magdalena married John
Schuh and farmed near Firesteel. Daniel is in the Bowdle Nursing Home and
never married. Anna married Fred M. Eisenbeisz and they farmed south of
Bowdle. Katherine married Henry Giedt and they farmed south of Bowdle.
William died from effects of being frozen in a snowstorm southeast of Bowdle
in the winter 1921 when he was 29. He never married.

Twenty grandchildren completed this family.

AUGUST and LYDIA [WOLFF] SCHICK

August Schick is the son of Wilhelm and Margaret Schick who were born and
married in South Russia. After the arrival of their first child Ludvig
(Louie) they came to the United States in 1888. They homesteaded on land
five miles northwest of Bowdle. August was born here June 2 1901, joining
five brothers and three sisters.

August married Lydia Wolff Nov. 30, 1922 at St. John's Evangelical Lutheran
Church in Bowdle. She was the daughter of Mathew and Magdalena Wolff,
natives of Marienberg, Russia. They came to the United States in 1898 to
make their first home in the Lowry area southwest of Bowdle. Lydia had six
sisters and five brothers. When she was four years old her parents moved to
a Herrwald farm 2-1/2 miles east of Java near the Alamo substation of the
Milwaukee Railroad.

        August's Parents                Lydia's Parents
        Wilhelm and Margaret            Mathew and Magdalena

        Lydia, Ida, Elnora, August Schick

After their marriage August and Lydia made their home on this farm and Mrs.
Schick recalls that they would often flag down the local passenger train to
go to Java in the morning and return in the evening. In those days the
Milwaukee ran two local trains and two flyer non-stop trains through
Bowdle. Farm work was strenuous and as threshing required many hands and
horses the women of the neighborhood got together to prepare the meals to
feed the crew of 14 or more men. Refrigeration was unheard of in those
days, so to keep the milk and meat out of the summer heat it was lowered
into the well by means of a pail and rope. If the weather turned wet and
cold the threshing had to stop. All the bread that had been baked and
supplies bought at the store would mold before the men could resume
threshing.

Mr. and Mrs. Schick had two daughters. Ida (Mrs. Elmer) Aman lives on a
farm south of Eureka. Elenora and husband Harold Haupt live in Bowdle and
have twin sons. Harold is a school bus driver and carpenter and Elenora
works at Bowdle Nursing Home.

Fifty-eight years of hard work on the farm and ill health forced them to
retire in October 1980. They now make their home in Bowdle where August
receives many visitors in his wheel chair.

JACOB and LYDIA [MARTEL] SCHILLING

Jacob Schilling's parents came to the United States in the spring 1898 from
Glueckstahl, South Russia. The spent the first summer with a sister and
brother-in-law Joseph and Christena Gab. That fall they moved to a
homestead in McIntosh County, North Dakota. Sept. 8, 1901 they welcomed
their first child Jacob into the family and in the fall 1903 brought him to
Edmunds County to make their home on a farm nine miles north and two west of
Bowdle. He attended the country school and grew to manhood on the farm.

Lydia Martel of Bowdle married Jacob Schilling Sept. 4, 1927 at St. Paul's
Lutheran Church in Bowdle. She was the daughter of Karl and Sophie (Wahl)
Martel. They migrated from Kassel in South Russia and for a while after
their arrival in the USA made their home with Karl's sister and husband
John and Barbara (Wahl) Sandmeier. They moved to a farm in Logan County,
North Dakota where Sophie Martel died in the spring 1916 when Lydia was
five years old. The next year she was adopted by Mr. and Mrs. Jacob H.
Eisenbeisz and given an eighth grade education.

Jacob and Lydia lived on the old Schilling farm for 16 years and in the
fall 1943 moved to Bowdle to their present home in the southwest part of
town.

        Back: Cornelius, Roland, Arnold Front: Jacob and Lydia Schilling

They are the parents of three sons. Cornelius was born Oct. 21, 1928 in
rural Bowdle. He attended country school and graduated from Bowdle High
School in 1947. He served in the U.S. Army during the Korean War, returning
in 1952. Cornelius established a new business in Bowdle going into the
concrete and cement and construction work. Later he worked for the U.S.
Corps of Engineers. He married Pauline Erck April 23, 1959 in Mobridge. They
have three children Thomas Kenneth and Sandra and now live in Santa Rosa,
New Mexico.

Roland was born Oct. 11, 1931 in rural Bowdle. He suffered a severe illness
at 2 years and 10 months of age from which he never fully recovered and
died Oct. 10, 1974 as he approached his 43rd birthday.

Arnold was born May 3, 1941. He graduated from Bowdle High School in 1959
and attended University of South Dakota in Vermillion and is now an
instructor for the Armstrong School System in Iowa. Arnold married
Jacqueline Gustophson June 6, 1961 in Alton, IA. They have a daughter
Vickilynn and two sons Matthew and Steven.

JOHN F. and FRIEDA [BUECHLER] SCHILLING

John F. was born near Hosmer to Fred and Marie (Keszler) Schilling Oct. 26,
1905. He was educated and grew up in that area.

John married Frieda Buechler Oct. 18, 1936. She is the daughter of Jacob M.
and Katherina (Jakober) Buechler. She was born north of Bowdle June 15,
1911.

John and Frieda have a son Ervin, who was born Aug. 8, 1937 at Eureka.
Ervin was also educated in a rural school and is a farmer at heart.

The Schilling family lives on her grandfather's (Michael Buechler)
homestead place. This farm will be 100 years old in 1999.

        Frieda, Ervin, John F. Schilling

The Schillings recall an early spring blizzard in 1942 which really packed
their yard with soft deep snowbanks. To feed their cattle John and Frieda
packed wheat sacks with hay and carried them over the snowbanks to the
cattle. This was a slow process without fear of overfeeding the cattle. John
was sure his 30 acres of wheat he had seeded were destroyed, but to his
amazement it turned out to be a bumper crop.

At present the Schillings are semi-retired, but continue to farm with their
son Ervin.

CHRISTIAN and MARTHA SCHLAHT

Rodney Ray, born Dec. 21, 1960, has followed in his father's footsteps and
farms in Walworth County.

FRED and BERNICE [SCHMIDTGALL] SCHLECHT

Fred Schlehct was born March 13, 1926 in Java, the child of John and Mary
Schlecht. His parents were born in Walworth County, John Aug. 27, 1890 and
Mary June 6, 1907. Fred received an eighth grade education. He married
Bernice Schmidtgall Jan. 10, 1954. Bernice was the daughter of William and
Katie Schmidtgall and was born in Selby April 22, 1935. William was born
July 12, 1900 and Katie Feb. 28, 1907, both in Walworth County.

Bernice was the daughter of William and Kathy Schmidtgall and was born in
Selby April 22, 1955. William was born July 12, 1900 and Katie Feb. 28,
1907, both in Walworth County.

After six years on the farm Fred and Bernice brought their family to Bowdle
in July 1960. Fred worked with George Seurer doing carpenter work and when
the new hospital opened he was employed as maintenance engineer. During the
times the hospital was closed he again worked for George Seurer or Ipswich
Lumber Co. Fred died Jan. 17, 1980 and Bernice has since supported her
family working in maintenance at Bowdle School.

Fred and Bernice had six children.

Sheila, born Oct. 25, 1954, lives at 720 N. 3rd Street in Aberdeen. She is
married to Peter Hesla of Webster, who is employed at Aberdeen Waste Water
Treatment Plant. They have a daughter Kristen Marie. Sheila is employed as
histology assistant at Dakota Midland Hospital.

Administration Office and lives at 209 S. Jackson Street in Aberdeen.

Randy was born Nov. 28, 1960 and is employed at Ell's Sheet Metal Co. in
Aberdeen. His wife is the former Julie Giese, a native of Minnesota and
teaches in the Ipswich School System.

Jim was born Aug. 14, 1962 in Bowdle and works for Perry Hoffman Combine &
Trucking firm.

Lisa was born Feb. 26, 1967 and is presently a senior (1985) at Bowdle High
School and works part-time at Bowdle Nursing Home.

Mark was born Jan. 26, 1969 in Bowdle and is presently a sophomore (1985)
at Bowdle.

GOTTFRIED and WILHELMENIA [BAER] SCHLECHT

Gottfried Schlecht was born Oct. 18, 1894 near Java in Walworth County to
Adam and Christina (Bauder) Schlecht, both now deceased. Gottfried was
married April 7, 1918 to Wilhelmina (Minnie) Baer at the Theodore Lutheran
Church southwest of Bowdle. Wilhelmina was born June 9, 1900 to Christian
and Ida (Edenbush) Baer near Hoven.

        Back: John, Hulda, Alvina, Arthur Front: Irene, Gottfried, Minnie,
        Esther Schlecht

Gottfried was called to serve in the U.S. Army during World War I July 23,
1918 and was discharged Jan. 17, 1919. They moved to a farm north of Hoven
until 1920 when they and their daughter moved to Dewey County near Trail
City. In October 1929 they brought their five children to Walworth County
near Bowdle and in March 1937 moved their family of six children to
Mobridge. Gottfried has been a member of the Browder Parker Post of the
American Legion in Mobridge since 1927.

Gottfried worked as a bellhop at the Brown Palace Hotel, at the Milwaukee
Railroad roundhouse and for the city of Mobridge until he retired in 1959.
He became a resident of the Mobridge Care Center in July 1980 and attained
90 years of age Oct. 18, 1984.

Minnie spent her married years as a busy housewife taking care of her
family and helping in the fields when they farmed. She died June 6, 1973 in
Mobridge.

The six children who blessed their home are. Hulda W. married Henry Huber
and lives in Mobridge. John married Marge Fulton. His second wife was
Letitia Dogg. John died Dec. 23, 1977. Arthur G. married Bette Mason and
lives in Vandalia, OH. Alvina married Bud Springer and lives in Seattle,
WA. Esther married Marvin Berg and lives in Mobridge. Irene married
Christie M. Goetz and they live near Selby.

HENRY and MAGDALENA [BUECHLER] SCHLECHT

Henry Schlecht was born March 30, 1897 in Walworth County to Adam and
Christina Schlecht. Adam was born June 20, 1870 and Christina Nov. 20, 1870
in Neuglueckstahl, Russia. Christina died Jan. 12, 1952 and Adam Feb. 22,
1959.

Henry Schlecht married Magdalena Buechler March 11, 1920. She was the
daughter of John and Magdalena Buechler, natives of Neuglueckstahl, Russia.
John was born Oct. 4, 1860 and died April 21, 1917 and his wife was born
Jan. 30, 1862 and died Jan. 1, 1945.

        Back: Eleanora, Arthur, Hulda Front: Lydia, Henry, Magdalena
        Schlecht

Henry and Magdalena Schlecht lived in the Java area on his parents farm a
short time. Their daughters Hulda and Eleanora were born here. In the fall
1922 they acquired land 3-1/2 miles west of Bowdle, bought a house in
Bowdle which they moved to the farm and made their home there over a
quarter century. Two more children were born, a daughter Lydia and a son
Arthur.

They farmed the land, milked cows, raised chickens, pigs and did whatever
else they could to make a living. They used horse power to put in the crop
until they could buy a tractor and it was a great day in the family when
they bought their first Model "T" Ford car. There were good years and bad.
The bad included the early 1930's when there was a drought and nothing that
was planted grew, only thistles and weeds were green and the grasshoppers
ate that and the carefully tended gardens. Those were the times when
duststorms darkened the sky and the daylight was hazy. All the livestock
had to be sold except four cows and six horses. These animals were herded
or pastured wherever they could find something to eat.

The Schlecht family were members of the Neuglueckstahl Church five miles
north of the farm and when that building was sold they joined St. Paul
American Lutheran Church in Bowdle.

The four children born to Henry and Magdalena include Hulda, who was born
March 5, 1921. She married William Erlenbusch April 20, 1945 and they made
their home in Tolstoy. He died Aug. 18, 1979. Their children are Kenneth,
Donald, Maryann and Larry.

Eleanora Schlecht was born June 12, 1922 and married Herbert Erlenbusch
June 3, 1947. They live in Bowdle and had four children: Donna and Dale,
both deceased; Diana and Debra. Eleanora is janitor for Bowdle State Bank,
as well as a homemaker.

Lydia Schlecht was born May 14, 1924 at Bowdle and has been employed as a
clerk at A & B Shop, Jones Drug and now Turner Drug.

Arthur Schlecht was born July 15, 1928 and married Irene Schmidtgall March
17, 1952. They live on the home farm 3-1/2 miles west of Bowdle. Their
children are Lexie Vetch, Marcia Beukelman and Rodney. Rodney is at home
with his parents on the farm.

Henry and Magdalena Schlecht retired from the farm in September 1959,
bought a home in Bowdle where Magdalena and Lydia still live. Henry died
April 29, 1963.

JOHN and MARY [FLECK] SCHLECHT

John Schlecht was born Aug. 27, 1899 to Adam and Christina (Bieber)
Schlecht in Walworth County on a farm southeast of Java. He attended rural

was born May 8, 1865 and his wife Maria (Portschy) Fleck was born Dec. 1,
1867. Mary Fleck went to a country school and completed the eighth grade.

        John Schlecht Family Back: Doris, Fred, Irene, Evelyn Front: John,

ADAM and EUGENIA [DUBS] SCHLEPP

Adam Schlepp was born Feb. 16, 1889 in Hoffnungstahl, South Russia to Jacob
and Katharina Bollinger Schlepp and was the oldest surviving son. In 1898
the family came to America and homesteaded northeast of Bowdle. He grew to
manhood in this area and married Magdalena Reiner in Hosmer April 13, 1913.

They moved to New Leipzig, ND where he operated a dray line until 1920. A
daughter Olivia Leona Hildegarth was born Nov. 24, 1914 and a son Roland
Gardner was born Sept. 11, 1916.

Tragedy struck the young family Nov. 3, 1918 when Magdalena was stricken
with the flu that plagued the country and she died. Two of Adam's sisters
Mathilda and Lydia came to help take care of the children.

        Eugenia and Adam Schlepp

May 12, 1919 he married Eugenia Dubs in New Leipzig and later moved his
family to a farm northeast of Bowdle, next to the farm where his father was
living. Seven children were born to them while living there. They were
Elsie March 14, 1920; Elmer June 15, 1921; Victor June 18, 1924; Oswald
Feb. 7, 1926; Dorothea May 22, 1928; Ramona June 27, 1930 and LaVaughn Dec.
21, 1932.

In 1933 the family moved to a farm southwest of Bowdle owned by Charles
Commet, who later sold the property to the Ottenbacher Brothers of Ipswich.
As with all farmers in the area, the 30's began and the drought moved in
along with the infestation of grasshoppers, dry summers and extremely cold
winters. Two more daughters were born into the family, Arliss Nov. 16, 1935
and Karen June 14, 1938.

With the aid of their sons Adam and Eugenia farmed southeast of Bowdle and
saw their children through grade school at a farm school called the O'Neil
School District. With the exceptions of Elmer and Ramona, all the children
attended and graduated from Bowdle High School.

In 1952 the Ottenbacher Brothers sold the farm to Jacob Mertz. Adam then
rented the land until 1955. Social Security then became known to farmers
and Adam needed two more crop years to become eligible, so he moved his
family to a farm seven miles west and two south of Bowdle, which was owned
by Jacob Klein of Mobridge. With the help of son Elmer, Adam put in the two
necessary crops.

In 1957 Adam, Eugenia and Ramona had a farm sale and retired to the city of
Bowdle. They bought a house at 4088 3rd Avenue. Ramona, who was a polio
victim the first year of her life, resided with them until she was in her
late thirties and then moved into the Bowdle Nursing Home when she became
an invalid.

Adam was active in baseball, served on the school board, church board, was
a staunch Democrat, avid fisherman and loved to spend evenings playing
cards with his family or friends. He died April 16, 1972 and was buried in
St. Paul American Lutheran Church cemetery in Bowdle. Eugenia lived in
their home until 1977 when she sold her home and moved into the Prairie View
Housing in Bowdle where she resided until her death Jan. 30, 1981. Eugenia
was active in church, American Legion Auxiliary, Senior Citizens and ALCW.

The eldest son Roland married Jeanette Heathman and they had one son.
Roland died May 9, 1979 in Spokane, WA. All other children are still
surviving. Hildegarth married Conrad Fix and has three children. Elmer
married Erna Fiechtner and had two children. Elsie is married to John Weil
and has two children. Victor married Doris Miller and had four children.
Oswald is married to LaVaughn Gross and they have four children. Dorothea
married Harlan Imbery and has three children. Ramona never married and
currently resides at the Clark Nursing Home. LaVaughn married Gordon Stotz
and had four children. Arliss is married to Clinton Blumhardt and has five
children. Karen wed DeWayne Weiszhaar and had four children.

To this date there are now 32 grandchildren and 44 great-grandchildren of
Adam and Eugenia Schlepp.

ELMER and ERNA [FEICHTNER] SCHLEPP

Elmer William Schlepp was born to Adam and Eugenia Dubs Schlepp June 15,
1921 in Bowdle. He attended eight years of school. He never attended high
school because of the need to help his father on the farm. He was inducted
into the service and served during World War II.

He married Erna Feichtner of Java Sept. 11, 1942. When he returned from
the service he farmed southwest of Bowdle. June 18, 1957 a daughter named
Marlys was born. She attended her first years of grade school at Bowdle. In
1952 a son Douglas was born on his dad's birthdate June 15.

After farming in the Bowdle area several more years they bought a cafe
business in Java from his uncle Emmanuel, known as Schlepp's Cafe. They
operated the cafe until 1983 when they sold the business and retired.

        Erna and Elmer Schlepp

They still reside in Java spending their winter months with their children.
Marlys lives in Greeley, CO and Douglas lives in Redwood City, CA. The
Elmer Schlepps have four grandchildren.

JACOB and KATHARINE [BOLLINGER] SCHLEPP

Jacob Schlepp was born in Hoffnungstal, South Russia Sept. 21, 1860 and
baptized Sept. 25. He married Katharine Bollinger Nov. 25, 1882 in
Kloestitz, South Russia. Twelve children were born to them, six survived.

In 1898 Jacob took his wife and four children (Katharine, Adam, Magdalena,
Emmanuel) and came to America where they homesteaded northeast of Bowdle.
Two more daughters were born, Mathilda and Lydia.

        Jacob and Katharine Schlepp

Katharine Bollinger Schlepp was a midwife and helped in the delivery of many
babies in this area. She was born Nov. 3, 1859 in Hoffnungstal, South
Russia. She was baptized and confirmed there. Since her conversion she was
a member of the Congregational Church.

There were many hard times in the family of Jacob and Katharine as were in
many other families. The loss of six children was their greatest hardship.
Happy times were found in their six surviving children. They lived to see
each marry and have children.

Adam married Magdalena Reiner in Hosmer. However in 1918 she died of the
flu that plagued the country. Adam later married Eugenia Dubs in New
Leipzig, ND.

Katharine married Archie Buckingham, Magdalena married Gottlieb Reiner,
Mathilda married John Oster, Emmanuel married Lydia Schuh and Lydia married
Henry Leidholt.

Jacob and Katharine farmed many years before retiring and moving into
Bowdle. Jacob suffered a fatal heart attack at 11 p.m. Dec. 15, 1929. The
funeral was at Congregational Church with Prof. Diede of Redfield College
officiating.

Katharine was in good health until after her husband's death. She suffered
from sugar diabetes and died just three months later March 12 1930.

JOHN W. and LENA [HOCHSTETTER] SCHLEPP

Lena Schlepp was born to John and Katherine Hochstetter in Java June 18,
1903. She married John W. Schlepp Sept. 7, 1920 and five children were born
to them. A heart ailment caused her husband's death Oct. 4, 1938 at the age
of 39.

        Lena Schlepp

Lena and the children continued to live in Java until 1949 when she moved
to Selby for a year and in 1950 came to Bowdle where she has resided and
worked a number of years as a nurse's aide at the Bowdle Hospital until ill
health forced her retirement. She now lives at Prairie View Housing
apartments.

The children are Lillian, who married Ellsworth Randall and lives in Selby;
Deloris is the wife of Alvin R. Bauer and resides on a farm west of Bowdle;
Arelene is the wife of Mahlon Gross of Bowdle; Verton is employed at the
Alvin Bauer farm and Mary Lou married Melvin Roebuck and died Jan. 9, 1980
in Flandreau.

RAMONA SCHLEPP

Ramona Ruth Schlepp was born to Adam and Eugenia Dubs Schlepp June 27, 1930
at Bowdle Hospital. She attended grade school at O'Neil School District
southeast of Bowdle. She was stricken with polio at the age of 10 months
and later with epilepsy. She never attended high school because of ill
health.

Ramona lived with her parents until 1970 when she became a resident of
Bowdle Nursing Home. She was a victim of the dreaded disease MS and was
confined to a wheel chair. She spent several years at Bowdle Nursing Home,
but because of the need for skilled care was transferred to Shirk Memorial
Home in Faulkton.

Ramona spent about a year in Faulkton and was again transferred to Clark
Nursing Home which is a Medicare/Medicaid nursing home where she now
resides. She enjoys reading, playing bingo, visiting with her family and
friends and watching television.

EDWARD H. and LYDIA [BERG] SCHMIDTGALL

        Edward and Lydia Schmidtgall

REV. JOHN and MARIE [BIEBER] SCHMIERER

She is married to Walter E. Pilgrim and lives in Seattle, WA with their
three daughters Kathryn, Kristen and Karyn.

The Rev. John Schmierer attended Wartburg Seminary in Dubuque, IA,
graduating in 1930. He was ordained into the Holy Ministry in the American
Lutheran Church July 6, 1930 and was assigned his first parish at the
Lutheran Church in Halliday, ND. He preached in Delmont and Leola 1946-1958.
He served the church 28 years in North Dakota and 12 years in South Dakota.
He also served as Chaplain and Administrator of the Beulah (ND) Nursing
Home after he retired from the ministry. He still frequently occupies the
pulpit in nearby Lutheran churches when the residing pastor cannot be
present.

        Marie and Rev. John Schmierer

In semi-retirement Rev. John took care of the Zeeland parish north of
Zeeland, ND. In 1972 John and Marie returned to Bowdle where they had many
friends and relatives. Marie's health failed and was a resident of the
Bowdle Nursing Home from November 1976 until she died Jan. 24. 1985.

MICHAEL and KATHARINA [KIRSCHENMANN] SCHMIERER

Michael Schmierer brought his family from South Russia to the United States
in 1892. They made a brief visit with an uncle John Schmierer and family in
Scotland, SD and then went to Naper, NE where they lived until 1896 when
they returned to Dakota Territory. They homesteaded land 10 miles northeast
of Bowdle.

Pictured in the back row are Elizabeth, Gustav and Emma. Seated are Michael
Schmierer and Katharina. The three little ones are Emil, Michael Jr. and
baby John on his mother's lap.

Now the Reverend John Schmierer, he is the only surviving member of the
family and makes his home in Bowdle in retirement.

OTTO A. and VIRA [ADAMS] SCHMIERER

Otto A. Schmierer was born Aug. 26, 1917 to Gustav and Mary (Sandmeier)
Schmierer in Java. Gustav was born in Naper, NE and his wife Mary at
Glueckstahl, South Russia. They were married Dec. 14, 1915 in Java. Gustav
and his family lived on a farm northwest of Bowdle where their seven sons
and four daughters were born.

Otto helped on the farm until he was drafted into the U.S. Army in
September 1942 during World War II. While stationed in the United States he
met Vira J. Adams of Aberdeen, WA. They were married May 16, 1944 at Chula
Vista, CA. Her parents are Emmett and Mary Gail Adams.

        Chester, Vira, Virginia, Otto, Wade

When Otto was sent overseas to the Philippines and Japan his bride returned
to Java where their first child Virginia was born June 19, 1945 in Hoven.
After his discharge in 1946 Otto moved his family to a farm northwest of
Bowdle where their son Chester was born July 8, 1947 and Wade joined the
family Jan. 25, 1951. Another son was born May 26, 1960, but died in
infancy.

Otto bought the farm in 1964 and the family lived there until 1971 when
Otto and Vira retired and moved to town. She has worked at the Bowdle
Hospital for eight years.

Virginia and her husband Tim Spiry live on the farm. Their daughters are
Michelle and Sherri. Chester Schmierer lives in Bowdle and Wade is in the
U.S. Army, stationed at Ft. Leavenworth, KY. His wife is the former Valynn
Perman. They have two daughters Natasha and Tania.

WADE and VALYNN [PERMAN] SCHMIERER

Wade Schmierer was born Jan. 25, 1951 to Otto and Vira Schmierer. He
graduated from Bowdle High School and has been associated with the Military
Police since he was drafted in March 1971. His tours of duty have included
Fort Ord, CA; Aberdeen, Yankton, Fort Benning, GA and he is currently
stationed at Fort Leavenworth, KS.

Valynn was born Nov. 25, 1953 to LeRoy and Vivian Perman of rural Lowry.
She attended SDSU in Brookings and is presently employed with Armed Forces
Insurance as an insurance counselor.

Wade and Valynn were married Aug. 10, 1973 at Lowry. They have two
daughters. Natasha Nicole was born Feb. 11, 1974 at Brookings and Tania
Courtney was born April 23, 1976 at Fort Ord, CA.

EMIL and JUSTINA [MILLER] SCHNAIBLE

Emil Schnaible was born Oct. 31, 1908 south of Bowdle. His parents were
John and Mary (Weber) Schnaible. The year after he was born they moved to
the Lowry area. Emil has three brothers and three sisters. In order in the
family are Mary, John, Oscar, Emil, Lily, Olga and Fred. Emil went to
country school and finished the eighth grade.

Emil's mother loved to sing and songs were sung often in their home.
Christmas was celebrated for two days. The 25th was Christmas and the 26th
was called the second day of Christmas. They got little toys only when they
were small, but always a sack of goodies. Ephipany was held as a holiday
with church services. They always attended church whenever possible.

Emil met Justina Helen Miller at a baseball game and soon there were dates
to her home, car when possible, but a six-mile ride by horse more often.
They got married Dec. 12, 1933 at the minister's house in Selby.

Justina Miller was born to Jacob and Louisa (Baer) Miller April 20, 1910
near Hoven. She had a twin sister Helen, another sister Hulda and two
brothers Johney and Julius. They lived on the farm and drove to school with
a horse and buggy and sometimes walked. The family moved to Bowdle after
her father accidentally died when a hay sling broke as they were unloading
hay. Justina went to school in Bowdle from the second through fourth
grades. She recalls when Bowdle built a new brick schoolhouse in 1918.

Her mother married Christ Walz in 1921 and they again moved to the farm.
Christ had a family of five children: Ella, Frieda, Althea, Metha and Gary.
Two boys later joined the family, Ervin and Roman.

Justina remembers going across the river at Mobridge with a ferry. She
said, "The ferry was filled with cars. Each family sat in their car until
the ferry took them across the river, then they drove off and visited
friends and relatives and returned by ferry again." On wash day the girls
all washed on the scrub boards and one girl took a turn to cook, otherwise
there was a fight. All washing had to be done by noon.

During harvest Justina worked in the header box. A header was something
like a swather of today, but it was pulled by 4 to 6 horses and had an
elevator that took all cut grain into a header box. Two people worked in a
header box, one drove the teams and the other would stack the grain. When it
was full they drove the team with their load to the end of the field or the
future threshing site. They unloaded the header box and her mother stacked
the cut grain, making large stacks all in a straight row. As they unloaded
the wagon another was being filled as the header cut without stopping.
Large stacks of cut grain remained in their location until threshing time,
which was busy and happy. There was much cooking, baking and cleaning plus
the regular chores.

When Justina was 14 she went to Montana and worked for Mr. and Mrs. George
Lenz and family. They raised 300 turkeys. She returned home again when she
was needed. She met Emil Schnaible and they planned marriage. She sewed her
own wedding dress and fashioned her veil. After their marriage they farmed
with the Schnaibles for a year, then rented the Searle's farm near Hoven for
one season.

The duststorm in 1934 was bad. Some people who plowed that year saw the
wind take away all the top soil the depth of the plowing. You couldn't see
the woven wire fences because the dust was piled up so high you could walk
over them at places. There was also no feed. Only a few thistles grew and
they were fed to cattle. To reduce, cattle were killed at a government land
fill near Lowry because the cost of shipping them to market was more than
they were worth. The government paid each farmer about $10 for a cow and $6
for a calf. They bought a farm five miles southwest of Bowdle. Grasshoppers
were bad in 1936 and 1937. They were the worst in 1937 when they chewed all
the heads off the grain.

Shirley Ann was born at home April 22, 1936, Mary Lou was born at Bowdle
Hospital Jan. 4, 1939 and Duane Donald was born at Hoven Hospital Aug. 23,
1945. The children all attended Northern State Teachers College. Shirley
taught the farm school they all attended. She married Ben Keller and moved
to Oregon, then later to Washington. Their children are Bernadette, Mary
Jane and Jonathan.

Mary Lou taught schools in Artas, Pollock and Greenway areas. She married
Leo Gruebele and lives on a farm north of Eureka. Their three children are
Jeanne Lou, Mark John and David Lee. After college Duane spent his time in
the service during the Vietnam War. He married Roxanne Johnson and they
live in Minneapolis, MN where he works for I.D.S.

Emil and Justina have four great-grandchildren. Mary Keller married John
Allen and their children are Joleen and Justin. Bernadette married Marshall
Ells and their children are Jamison and Mitchell.

On the farm they raised wheat, oats, corn, hay, alfalfa and always a big
garden. They had cattle, chickens, geese and a few hogs. Justina's pride and
joy were her chickens and geese. She had a special way with them and spent
a great deal of time tending them. Emil was treasurer of the Odessa School
for many years.

In 1965 they took their first real vacation. The went to Oregon to see
their daughter Shirley and family for Christmas. In 1977 Emil and Justina
retired and had a farm sale. They bought the Tony Hoven house on the south
side of Bowdle and moved to town in 1978. They are members of St. Paul
American Lutheran Church and Justina is a member of the Ladies Aid. In 1983
they celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary with family and friends at
an open house. Justina loves to crochet and together they put out a big
garden and tend their yard.

BALTASSER and BERTHA [SCHMIDT, SCHUH] SCHUH

JACOB and MATILDA [SCHMIDT] SCHUH

Jacob Schuh was born in Hoffnungstal, Russia Jan. 16, 1897 to Mr. and Mrs.
Jacob Schuh Sr. When he was 15 years old he came with his parents and their
children to the United States and settled on a farm northwest of Bowdle.

Matilda was born in Artas to Mr. and Mrs. Jacob Schmidt Sept. 11, 1904. She
attended the rural school near Artas where her parents were farming.

Due to a crop failure in 1913, Jacob and his brother John went to North
Dakota to work with a threshing crew. They traveled as far as Artas by
horse and buggy to wait to catch a train to North Dakota. Since there was
no hotel or public lodging in Artas they were overnight guests in the Jacob
Schmidt home and there Jacob saw his future bride for the first time.

Returning from North Dakota Jacob farmed with his father until 1917 when he
was inducted into the U.S. Army to serve during World War I. He was
discharged in November 1918. He bought two quarters of land north of Isabel
in 1923 and there he again met Matilda Schmidt at a social event. They were
married Oct. 26, 1924 at Hoffnungstal Country Church near Artas. The Rev.
Theo P. Peter officiated. John Schmidt and Henry Schuh, brothers of the
couple, were attendants.

Jacob and Matilda Schuh established their first home on a 320-acre farm 20
miles north of Isabel where they farmed with horses. Their four children
were born while they lived on that West River country farm. Florence was
born Aug. 12, 1925; Gideon May 25, 1927; Alvin Aug. 24, 1930 and Harold
Oct. 13, 1932.

Discouraged by the drought of 1936, when nothing grew and the dust blew,
they sold the land and moved to Artas where they farmed three years on the
Jacob Schmidt land. In 1939 they moved to the Jacob Schuh Sr. farm and in
1940 bought land southwest of Bowdle where they farmed until 1950 when they
retired and built a home in Bowdle. Gideon and Alvin took over the home
farm.

        Harold, Gideon, Alvin, Florence, Jacob, Matilda

After retiring Jacob and Tillie enjoyed fishing trips with friends and took
numerous trips to western states and Canada. Jacob died suddenly May 16,
1979 of a heart attack. Kept busy with many hobbies, Tillie resides in her
home with Gideon.

CHRISTIAN C. and MATHILDA [THURN] SCHUMACHER

The Schumacher family had its beginning in Bremen, Germany later migrating
to Glueckstahl, South Russia at the invitation of the present Russian
ruler. Like hundreds of other Germans they were looking for a better life.
Many promises were made to them and were also encouraged to institute their
own little colonies with their own government, churches and schools, but
with the coming of a new Czar they had to abandon all hopes.

They were taxed, could no longer speak their own language and were forced
to send their boys into the army. With resentment toward the Russians many
of the Germans left for North America settling mostly in the Dakotas.
Christoph and Katherine Schumacher were among those who came to the United
States in 1883.

They came to the Yankton area where Christian C. Schumacher was born in
1884. After a few years land became available near Eureka so Christ brought
his family here. Katherine died a few years later leaving eight children
motherless. The next move Christoph and his family made was to a farm south
of Java, a place he homesteaded. He died about 1910 and his land was
subdivided among his children. Much of the land is still being farmed by
grandchildren or great-grandchildren.

In 1908 Chris C. Schumacher met and married Mathilda Thurn in Bowdle. Her
parents, Frederick and Margaret Thurn also immigrated to America from the
South Russia area in 1902. They homesteaded south of Bowdle. The newlyweds
made their first home on a small farm south of Java. Trips were made to
Hoven for supplies mostly by wagon or horseback, depending on the weather.
Laundry was done on a scrub board until they saved enough money for a
hand-powered washing machine. A traveling salesman by buggy would come by
once or twice a year to sell his wares. Many a bolt of cotton material was
bought to make aprons, dresses, shirts and quilts. They spent about 10
years on this farm and five children were born here, namely Arthur,
Raymond, Bernice, Herbert and Alma.

        Christian and Mathilda Schumacher

In 1918 they sold the little farm and moved to a larger one four miles
southwest of Bowdle. The house was a big improvement for a growing family.
There were five bedrooms, a bathroom, electricity, hot water heat and a
full basement. As time went on more beds were added to the bedrooms as Paul,
Palmer, Vernada, Warren, Arvis and Virginia came into the family. Arthur,
Raymond and Arvis have since died. All attended the Bowdle Schools.
Transportation was by horse and buggy until one of the children was old
enough to drive the Model T. Church was an important part of the family
life. Everyone dressed up on Sunday morning and in two cars went to Sunday
School and worship. Sunday afternoon was spent with neighbors and if there
were enough interested players a game of softball was the entertainment for
the afternoon.

Good and bad times were experienced on the farm. Since the U.S. was
involved in World War I in 1917, the purchase of the farm had an immediate
crippling effect on their lives. With the high cost of cattle, feed and
grain there was a slow recovery. The twenties were good and prosperity was
ahead until 1929 when the stock market took a sudden plunge and a deep
depression set in. The depression years were difficult for everyone. Many
left their farms and went west seeking a better life.

Their daughter Bernice says, "Dad was a very sensitive man and a good and
kind father. When there was a need for punishment the razor strap would
come off the hook and after a few whacks we would both be crying. He loved
the prairies, the rustling corn and golden grain. He often said that the
farm is an island of dreams. Mother was quiet and reserved but was an
excellent cook and baked the best homemade bread with flour from the Bowdle
Flour Mill for miles around. She assigned the daily chores, girls in the
house and boys outdoors.

"In 1947 plans were being made to give up farming and move to town. They
bought Grandma Thurn's house and began remodeling. In May mother died very
suddenly--her dream of living in town never fulfilled. In September Dad
made the move into town with Virginia who was the only one left at home.
Now he dreamed of the past ... the chance his parents had in America
regardless of their birth; the golden opportunity to live, work and worship
with freedom. He died in September 1969."

CHRISTOPH H. and HELENA [RATHKE] SCHUMACHER

Christoph H. Schumacher was born Sept. 30, 1879 at Neuglueckstal, Russia.
This family had its beginning in Bremen, Germany in 1805 when the
grandfather John Schumacher was born. When he was nine years old he and his
father walked to Glueckstahl, South Russia, very likely with other
immigrants.

John learned the trade of chimney sweep. He married Barbara Schafer and in
December 1840 Christoph Sr. was born. Christoph learned the cabinet maker's
trade traveling from village to village to find work. In 1867 he married
Barbara Lang. A son Fredrick was born and the mother died soon after.

Christoph Sr. later married Katherine Steinbach. From this marriage eight
more children were born. In 1883 the family came to America settling in
Yankton. No more land was available for preemption or homesteading. They
then moved northward by train to Ipswich, the last station west. Here
Christoph's father purchased horses and a wagon, moving five miles
northeast of Eureka where he bought land.

Fredrick, a half-brother, went into the hardware business at Turtle Lake,
ND. The rest resided in Walworth County and are as follows: Mrs. John
(Elizabeth) Bieber, Mrs. Christian (Fredericka) Vogele, Mrs. Christ
(Katherine) Haidle who later moved to Spokane, WA; Mrs. Emanuel (Marie)
Sayler who moved to New Underwood, ND; Mrs. John (Rosinia) Eisenbeisz,
Christian Schumacher and Mrs. John (Christine) Beitelspacher.

Christoph was about 5 years old when he came to America with his parents
and lived with them until he was 21. He settled on a farm 14 miles
southwest of Bowdle. June 15, 1904 he married Helena Rathke whom he met in
Yankton while visiting relatives. They lived 14 years on this farm where
four children were born: Clarence, Ernest, Norman and Adeline.

In 1905 he bought his first threshing machine, Buffalo Pitts grain
separator powered by a Northwestern steamer which burned straw or coal.
Later rigs included Hart Parr and Aultman Taylor. This threshing caravan
included a cook car and sleeping car on wheels moving from farm to farm to
complete the harvest--sometimes until the snow came. These huge engines
were also used to break the prairie.

Most of these early years were blessed with good crops from the fertile
land. A large barn was built in 1913 to improve the farmstead. Lack of
medical care for the rural area caused much hardship when the flu struck in
the fall 1918. Many were ill and died. Winters were quite confining with
travel limited to horses and sled. Farmers stocked up with a good supply of
food as trips to Java or Bowdle were few.

More visiting was done during the summer. Fourth of July celebrations,
whether at Java or Spring Lake, were long anticipated events consisting of
baseball, races, band concerts and dancing until dawn on a newly-built
bowery platform. Leading citizens gave patriotic speeches. Just visiting
with friends and neighbors was enjoyable.

        Christoph H. and Helena Schumacher

Christoph held a sale in November 1918 and moved to Bowdle. He purchased
the Mickelson house directly south of the school with the aim of having
improved education for his family. He and his sons continued the threshing
business. He bought land near Wakpala which had to be broken.

While en route to California with a brother-in-law Sam Rathke, Christoph
died in Denver Nov. 27, 1928 following surgery. His wife Lena continued
living in Bowdle caring for her family. She later purchased the Henry
Bauder house where she lived until her death Feb. 6, 1976. Her later years
were spent quilting, knitting, sewing and baking favorite food for her
family. Christoph and Lena are buried in St. John's Evangelical Lutheran
Cemetery in Bowdle.

CLARENCE S. and MARIE [GIEB] SCHUMACHER

Clarence Schumacher was the first son born to Christoph and Lena Schumacher
Sept. 11, 1905 on a farm about 14 miles southwest of Bowdle in Walworth
County. He attended rural school until his parents moved to Bowdle in 1918,
where he continued his education. Later he returned to farming three miles
west of Bowdle. Clarence worked with his father with a custom threshing
business and later continued with his own enterprise.

He married Marie L. Gieb Dec. 30, 1935. Marie was born Feb. 16, 1913 in the
Henderson, MN area to John and Stella Gieb. As a child she moved with her
family to Bowdle. Marie helped her father with bookkeeping in the elevator
business he owned in Bowdle. After graduating from Bowdle School she
attended Northern Normal in Aberdeen. She taught in rural schools in the
Bowdle area until 1939.

Clarence was active in community affairs, serving on the board of directors
of the Bowdle Farmers Union, Agricultural Soil Conservation Service, Bowdle
School Board and many other community service organizations. Marie was
active as a member of the ABC Extension Club, Historical Society, Senior
Citizens and was one of the charter members of the Bowdle Mothers' Club.
Clarence and Marie were very active in the church and dedicated their time
and efforts to the young people of the church. They served as Sunday School
teachers, helping with the religious training of the youth. Marie was
active in Ladies Aid, holding various offices in the organization.

        Clarence and Marie Schumacher

Clarence continued to be active in farming and community affairs until his
health failed in 1963. He died July 21, 1968. After his death Marie returned
to Northern State College and renewed her teaching certificate. She resumed
teaching in the fall 1968. Much pride was taken in the profession she loved
and the fruits of her labor shall long be remembered in Potter County and
the rural Bowdle area. She retired in 1981 and joined the Retired Teachers
Association. After a short illness Marie died June 8, 1984 at a Bismarck
Hospital. Clarence and Marie are buried in the Bowdle City Cemetery.

The couple had two sons. Stephen was born Dec. 11, 1944 in Hoven. He
attended rural school until the eighth grade and graduated from Bowdle High
School. He attended Northern State College in the summer 1962, then
transferred to South Dakota State University where he studied agriculture
and engineering. He returned during his father's illness and helped manage
the farm. He moved to Ipswich in 1976 and operated a machine and welding
shop, specializing in repairs and manufacturing. In 1978 Steve was involved
in a near-fatal car accident and was no longer able to continue his
business. In the fall 1979 Steve continued his education graduating from
Northern State College with a double major in industrial education and
mathematics. He is active in education, computer programming and the
business world. He is currently continuing his education working towards his
master's in vocational education. He married Rosalie Haux Oct. 6, 1979. She
has a degree in interior decorating and devotes her time to community
affairs and being a housewife. They have two children Sarah and Kassandra.

Christopher was born Nov. 26, 1952 in Aberdeen. After graduating from
Bowdle he attended Northern State College and Presentation College,
graduating with a degree in nursing home administration. He moved to Volga
and is presently employed by Surge Central Supply. He married Linda Remmele
of Echo, MN Aug. 6, 1977. Linda is administrative assistant to the
president of South Dakota State University. Chris and Linda are active in
the church and community affairs. Chris currently serves as chairman of the
church council and Linda is church office secretary. They have a son Nathan
and a daughter Rachel.

ERNEST F. and BARBARA [KNAPP] SCHUMACHER

Ernest F. Schumacher was born April 12, 1907 to Christoph and Helena
(Rathke) Schumacher on a farm 13-1/2 miles southwest of Bowdle. In 1918 at
age 11 the family which included four sons and a daughter, moved into
Bowdle. Ernest attended school in Bowdle.

Ernest, his brother Clarence and their father "broke up" 280 acres of
virgin land west of the Missouri River near Mahto. The following year, in
the spring of 1927, Ernest's father allowed him to "break up" 50 acres of
land two miles west of Bowdle for a first crop. From that crop Ernest made
enough money to purchase a new McCormick Deering 15-30 tractor, a drill,
plow and a Model "T" Ford Coupe.

        Ernest and Barbara Schumacher

Ernest married Barbara Knapp Nov. 6, 1928 and lived on the home farm 13-1/2
miles southwest of Bowdle. Three daughters blessed their home. Patricia
Venoy Kurle, Donna Berdell Kurle and Lois Yvonne Jackson.

Ernest purchased a combine in the fall of 1929. It was the first combine in
this part of the country and was watched by skeptical and doubtful
neighbors. In 1932 farming was difficult. Prices were low.

Ernest remembers selling a hog, weighing 780 pounds, for 1-1/2 cents a
pound. It was docked 80 pounds, therefore his total receipt for the hog was
$10.50. His other hogs brought approximately 3 cents a pound. Wheat sold
for 25 cents a bushel in 1932. Along with this type of low prices, dry years
followed.

In 1934 there was not a crop of any kind. A small crop of wheat was
harvested in 1935. This small crop was sufficient for Ernest to feed 10
head of cattle. Each year that followed seemed to be somewhat better.
Beginning in 1945 Ernest fed large numbers of cattle, sometimes having as
many as 750 in the feedlot at one time.

He continued to do so until his retirement in 1972 when he sold the family
farm and he and Barbara moved to Bowdle into a lovely new home they built.
Barbara died Sept. 28, 1978.

Ernest married Ruth Fischer June 30, 1979 and then moved to Mobridge where
they presently reside.

FRED and MAGDALENA SCHUMACHER

Fred and Magdalena Schumacher were born in Russia and came to the United
States during their childhood. Fred was born in 1891 and his wife in 1890.
They were married Dec. 12, 1912 and made their home on a farm near Roscoe
until 1929 when Fred went into partnership in the gas and oil business in
Bowdle with John M. Buechler. They had five children: Hilda, Richard,
Elsie, Rueben and Milton.

The Schumachers moved to Bowdle in September 1929 and he soon sold his
share of the oil business, worked for the city of Bowdle and did carpenter
work. In the 1930's he began assisting his son-in-law Wm. Schilling,
driving the gas truck for deliveries until health problems necessitated
their moving to Aberdeen. Fred worked part-time for the Nordling
Construction Co. until a heart condition ended his labors and they returned
to Bowdle where he died in 1955.

Magdalena spent several years in Bowdle until she married Christ Leicht of
Long Lake where they lived for 10 years until he died. She then moved to
Eureka for 10 years and returned to Bowdle where she continues to make her
home.

Magdalena worked in the County Sewing Room during the WPA days and has done
considerable sewing and crocheting since the 1940's. She is active in the
Esther Circle of her church, the Senior Citizens Center and enjoys baking
and cooking.

Hilda Schumacher married Wm. Schilling and managed Our Closet until June
1985. Richard married Thelma Roundy and lives in Aberdeen. Rueben lives in
Northfield, MN and is married to Cylvia Abrams. Elsie died in 1937. Milton
lives in Vancouver, WA and is married to Vivian Schliebe.

NORMAN C. and BEULAH [ERBE] SCHUMACHER

Norman Christopher Schumacher, born Jan. 19, 1909 on the family farm 14
miles southwest of Bowdle, was the third son of Christoph and Lena
Schumacher. He had two older brothers Clarence and Ernest and a sister
Adeline.

Norman decided to farm when he reached maturity and purchased land just
south of Spring Lake. Norman married Beulah Erbe Oct. 6, 1945. She was born
Sept. 4, 1919 to Alvin and Ruth Mildred (Lee) Erbe.

Norman and Beulah attended school in the same rural area and graduated from
Bowdle High School, as did their children. Beulah graduated from Northern
State College in Aberdeen and taught in a rural Walworth County School and
in Dupree, Bryant and Miller.

Following the traditional honeymoon to Niagara Falls they established their
home on the former George Jurgenson farm near their homeplaces. For five
years they lived in the famous" Half-Way House" where immigrants stopped
en route from Bowdle, then the end of the railroad, to Bangor and points
east. Remnants of the stagecoach road have been erased by modern machinery.

In that day large tents provided hotel space for the flood of pioneers who
settled our great state. Frigid and drafty then, the Half-Way House did not
improve with age. Winter winds lifted the linoleum causing chilblains, an
inflammatory swelling or itching sores caused by exposure of feet to the
cold.

Their light came from kerosene lamps, no running water, no bathroom, etc.
Electricity through the REA changed their lives and was greatly
appreciated. Then in 1950 came the new home built by Oscar Olson's crew.
These experiences give understanding of the courage, tenacity, endurance
and self-reliance of the early settlers and faith in the future.

        Back: Owen, Cloris, Craig, Dean Front: Beulah and Norman Schumacher

The Half-Way House was moved to Gettysburg and the Schumachers continue to
live on the same farm. Their children include:

Dean Norman (5-8-50) became interested in animal science through 4-H
projects, graduating from SDSU. Aug. 29, 1984 Dean married Carol Bauer
(2-2-52) of McIntosh who graduated from NSC and teaches in Hosmer. Loni
Lynn (11-7-84) arrived to brighten the home on their grain and livestock
farm northwest of Eureka.

Tragedy struck when Lance Orrin (5-4-52) drowned in Lake Oahe July 4, 1970.
He had recently graduated from BHS excelling in academics and football.

Craig Alan (3-8-54) enlisted for four years in the Air Force following
graduation from BHS. Attracted to the Alaskan lifestyle and opportunities,
he now works for Bureau of Land Management in Fairbanks.

Owen Gene (4-2-55) graduated from SDSU with a degree in agricultural
engineering. He was employed by John Deere of Waterloo, IA and now works
for Kubota Tractor Co. traveling extensively including Japan. He is a
member of the professional engineers and lives in Seal Beach, CA.

Cloris Kay (10-13-58) has a home economics degree from SDSU. She taught at
Philip one year and presently is extension home economist at Scott City,
KS. She was named 1984 Rookie of the Year by the Kansas Extension Service.

The Schumacher family is proud of its rural heritage. Membership in the
Spring Lake Lads and Lassies 4-H Club has proved helpful in later life.

ALBERT and JULIA [HANSON] SENN

Albert Senn, publisher of The Bowdle Pioneer 1932-1959, was born Nov. 11,
1894 near the now extinct town of Edgerton in Charles Mix County, the son
of Edward L. and Christa Senn. Al's father had extensive land holdings in
the southern part of the state and had gone into the newspaper business in
1903 in Iona. Eventually he owned 35 newspapers in South Dakota towns--also
known as Final Proof Sheets. World War I interrupted Al's education as an
electrical engineer at South Dakota State in Brookings, but in 1919
President Willis E. Johnson called him back to the college to help organize
the School of Printing. He installed the first printing machine in the old
north building on campus and became the first instructor of printing there.

It was at the college he met his life's co-worker Julia Hanson, who was
employed as secretary to the college president. She was a graduate of
Northern State College in Aberdeen and a high school business teacher. They
were married in Deadwood in 1922. Their son Robert was born in Wessington
Springs in 1925 and Patricia was born in Deadwood in 1926. Alberta arrived
in Bowdle in 1936, completing the family.

Al had succeeded his father when he was made State Prohibition Director as
publisher of the Deadwood Telegram, but was competing with a daily paper
and sold the Telegram in 1929. Albert volunteered for service in World War
I in the 7th Balloon Co. of the Air Force and his son Robert, a volunteer
in the U.S. Navy in World War II, earned the rank of Gunners Mate and the
Good Conduct medal when Japan sued for peace in 1945. Father and son are
charter members of the Bowdle American Legion Post.

Al was also a member of the Sportsmen's Club, Bowdle Golf Club, Hiddenwood
Lodge A.F. & A.M., Volunteer Fire Department, Commercial Club, official
U.S. Weather Observer for 10 years, county chairman of the Red Cross,
served on the Bowdle Board of Education and superintendent of the Methodist
Sunday School.

Rubber guns were a favorite pastime when Bob was a youngster and drew a lot
of the young kids to our yard. They were called rubber guns because the
boys made them and ammunition was the bands cut from tire inner tubes and
fastened on with clothes pins. My spring-type clothes pins disappeared into
the new guns the boys made for their imaginary battles. "Kick the can" was
an evening game for both boys and girls in summer and winter sledding was
possible because of the ramp to the back of the Chevrolet garage for a few
years.

Printing was done the hard way, with "hot metal" type until in the late
1960's when offset printing and the compuwriter replaced the linotype and
recollections of 26 years of publishing include long hours of work getting
the Pioneer to bed. Most of the news was gotten only by walking the town
over, calling at the homes to learn of events of interest. Later telephones
became more popular and then phone visits saved time and energy.

The 1930's were drought and dust storm years and bugs of entirely new
varieties destroyed gardens and everything green when the government
established the soil bank to try and help farmers during the low price era
when many farmers were losing their farms due to taxes because wheat sold
for less than $1 a bushel.

Bowdle youngsters who learned the printing trade from Al included Arnold
Bauder who used to sing "Hold that Tiger" all the time he fed press;
Albert, Gary and Ruben Schlaht, Roger Wiederhold, Allen Loebs, Emma Schlaht
Rumbaugh and Kenneth Mayer. Clarence Weishar contributed his talents as
sports reporter. Emma Rumbaugh and Allen Loebs continued in the trade.
Allen retired from the business in 1982 and Emma has an offset printing
establishment in Compton, CA.

Lines of type had a way of getting into the wrong place on occasion and in
one issue caused us to advertise a plow for sale 3000 miles east of the
Hawaiian Islands. Bob purchased the Hoven Review in 1953 and the two shops
worked together and in 1956 when Schaible's Garage caught fire the printing
office was also damaged. The Review printed the Pioneer for us. The fire
caused one subscriber to remark, "Isn't it terrible, when something
exciting happens, the Pioneer is always late!"

Al was in the chair at Danny Schlecht's Barber Shop sometime before World
War II and Bowdle's photographer N.A. Brothers (recently of Aberdeen) took
a second look and said, "Al, let's fix your hair and put a mustache on you,
because you'd look like Adolph Hitler." The men had their fun, the picture
was taken and Al posted it in the Pioneer Office. We had a lot of laughs
fooling people with it. But there was someone who didn't think it was funny.

        Albert Senn

One day a visitor from Washington, D.C. arrived ostensibly to visit his
sister Mrs. Frank Pachernigg. Mr. Keene spent a lot of time at the Pioneer
and stayed about a month. Before he left he told Al he was from the F.B.I.
and spent time here and in Eureka because of the German people and also that
Al was suspected as a Hitler-lover. This devoted Legionnaire who served his
country in peace and war never dreamed the picture would cause him to be
considered a Nazi.

        Patricia, Robert, Julia, Albert, Alberta Senn

Our family grew. Patricia and Joe B. Dewald were married in 1947 and the
first grandchild, a son, arrived to be enjoyed. They had seven children to
love. Richard was with us only a short time. His life was taken in a
tractor accident in 1964. Other members of the family were Mrs. David
(Karen) Karst of Bowdle, Mrs. Paul (Rosemary) Mertz of Watertown; Mrs. Gary
(Marcia) Hawley of Prescott, AZ; Mrs. Douglas (Jane) Ramsell of Huron, David
and his wife the former Sara Boyd of Geddes and Steven. They have eight
grandchildren.

Robert and his wife, the former Geraldine Dewald, were married in 1952.
They have two daughters: Mrs. Francis (Joan) Minnaert of Huron and Mrs.
Dale (Laurie) DeRouchey of Hoven. They have five grandchildren.

Alberta graduated from Presentation School of Nursing in 1957 and that year
married Waldemar Oster. They have two children: Mrs. Paul (Tamara) Clemons
of Munich, Germany and Carter of Sacramento, CA. Alberta is a public health
nurse in Albany, OR and Wally is a salesman for the Democrat Herald. They
have three grandchildren.

Bob is presently with the Kirby Co. as salesman and repairman and has won
many award trips for his work. Gerry is a compuwriter operator for the
Comet in Aberdeen where they have lived since selling the Hoven Review in
1973. That sale ended 70 years of the Senn Dynasty in the Fourth Estate.

Patty and Joe Dewald have spent their married life on their farm six miles
east of Bowdle and are now operating in partnership with their son David.

A lengthy illness ended Al's life in 1961 and Julia was employed by Federal
Land Bank Association in Bowdle as assistant manager, working with Art
Merkel. In 1965 she went to Albany to be homemaker for the Oster family,
returning in 1978. She is a member of the Methodist Church and served as
Sunday School Superintendent eight years, a member of the Order of the
Eastern Star and presiding officer of the Bowdle Senior Center three years.

ROBERT and GERRY [DEWALD] SENN

GEORGE and CHRISTINE [MILLER] SEURER

Mr. and Mrs. George Seurer claim the distinction of having lived the
longest in the same house in Bowdle. The house was purchased by her father
in 1919 and Christine has lived there since.

Christine is one of five children born to Christian and Karolina (Bauder)
Miller. Christian was born Nov. 9, 1873 in South Russia. He immigrated to
America in June 1889 and settled on the homestead (where the Kim Miller
family now lives) in 1896. He married Karolina Bauder May 29, 1897, who came
to America in 1894. The Millers lived on the homestead until 1919 when they
moved into Bowdle and resided in the home where the George Seurers now
live. Christian Miller died May 22, 1944. Karolina continued to live in the
house until she moved into the Bowdle Nursing Home in 1969. She died Jan.
24, 1971.

Christine Miller was born Sept. 23, 1903 and lived with her parents until
her marriage to George Seurer Sept. 22, 1945. Christine and George took up
residence in the Miller home where Christine worked with her mother and
tended to her needs as she grew older. In her spare time Christine did
fancywork and quilting.

Work never seemed to bother Christine as her duties included outdoor
farmwork while the family was living on the farm and when her father became
to ill to continue farming, she became his nursemaid until his death. The
rigorous schedule forced the young lady to end her formal education after
the sixth grade. She attended a country school located near their farm.

Christine is a member of St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church and the
Ladies Aid. Her hobbies include playing cards and she was once a member of
a bridge club in Bowdle. She was an active member of the church choir for
15 years.

George was born Jan. 6, 1910 to Charles and Eva (Kaiser) Seurer at Hoven.
His father was born Nov. 13, 1882 and died Jan. 8, 1936. Charles moved to
Hoven in 1906 where he was a storekeeper to supplement his main income as a
farmer. Eva (Kaiser) Seurer was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Michael Kaiser
of Hoven. She was born Dec. 8 1889 and died April 14, 1976.

        Christine and George Seurer

Education was important to George's parents. They made sure all their
children received an elementary education and George finished the eighth
grade in 1924. He worked on the family farm for 10 years after his
schooling. In 1934 he moved west to Montana in search of the elusive job
which was so scarce during the depth of the Great Depression. The following
year George went further west to Washington. Finding little work there he
went to California where he was located when he received word of his
father's death.

George came back to South Dakota and took over the family farm until his
marriage to Christine. To supplement his income George worked with the
Triple A, measuring land for the government from 1936 to 1941. After his
marriage he began working for J. Kurle during the winter months and after
spring's farm work was completed. In 1946 he was the first man hired by
Farmers Union Oil Co. in Bowdle. He first job was digging trenches for the
present building. As George states, "I didn't have any other tool but a
hand shovel." He worked there until 1947 in between planting and harvesting
seasons.

In 1947 he began his six-year association with Oscar Olson from whom he
learned the carpentry trade and struck out on his own in 1954. "I've been
on my own ever since," George says proudly. George has built many houses
from the ground up. The last home he built was for Emil Sandmeier in 1972.
Although George is officially retired, he still manages to keep active with
shop work in his backyard and garden.

George still keeps his carpentry skills sharp by doing small jobs for
various people in Bowdle and has done extensive work on the St. Augustine's
Catholic Church and rectory in recent years. He is a member of St.
Augustine's Catholic Church and a lifetime member of St. Joseph's Society
in Hoven. He is a past member of the Bowdle Sportsmen's Club.

The couple has no children.
