GOTTLIEB and SOPHIA [WEISS] SIPPERT

The line of the Sippert family has been traced back to 1817 in the region
of Wartburg, Germany at which time 1,500 German families migrated to
Russia. The Sippert family found their new home in the Province of
Bessarabia. The German people came at the invitation of Catherine the
Great, a Prussian princess who became the wife of the Czar, Peter III. By
1880 there was a great increase in the German population and the immigrants
began looking elsewhere for land and that year Wilhelm Sippert brought his
wife and four sons Daniel, Mathias, John and 3-year-old Gottlieb to the
United States.

The little family departed from a seaport in Odessa on the Black Sea and
Wilhelm earned their steamship passage by caring for the animals. The
family settled near Tripp until 1885 when Wilhelm moved his family to a
farm nine miles southwest of Eureka near a large lake.

        Gottlieb Sippert

In 1899 Gottlieb, then 22 years old, took as his bride 14-year-old Sophia
Weiss who had been orphaned by the death of her father in 1899 and her
mother married Wilhelm, but she also died when Sophia was 6 years old and
she continued to live with her stepfather and family. The summer before the
nuptials Gottlieb and his brothers prepared a sod house and other sod
buildings for their new home near the large lake.

Gottlieb and Sophia Sippert faced the hardships of pioneer life with great
ingenuity. Their cash crop came from gathering bones of buffalo and other
wild animals found on the prairie. These were hauled by the wagonload to
Ipswich and shipped to sugar factories in the east to be used to bleach the
sugar. They received $6 to $8 for a load of old bleached bones. The years
income netted Gottlieb $900 and in two years he had saved $1,800 with which
he bought a half section of land 31/~ miles north of Bowdle and the lumber
for the roof of the sod house and other outbuildings for the livestock and
machinery.

Earlier Gottlieb spent the winter 1897-1898 with a prospecting mining
metallurgist seeking gold or silver and from him learned the art of
draftsmanship and the science of separating metals by chemical action. He
built a weir of brush at the lake to catch (or pen) fish and his blunderbus
gun supplied the family with ducks, geese, prairie chickens, rabbits and
antelope. Son Albert, in his family history writes, "One could live the
Life of Riley on the open South Dakota prairie with the aid of 50 pounds of
flour purchased for $1.50, 25 pounds of sugar costing $1, 20 pounds of
coffee for $2 and $2 for rifle shells saving $8 for clothes."

The death of 6-month-old baby Josephine in 1906 was a terrible blow to the
family, which now included Gustav, Caroline and Samuel. That year Gottlieb
and Sophia sold their farm goods at auction, stored some of the beds in the
new frame house which had been built on the farm and went by train to
Goodland, KS near the Colorado border to farm. Rattlesnakes were a constant
worry to them and the flax crop on the newly broken land was wiped out by
hail. Discouraged, they decided to return to their South Dakota farm and
traveled by covered wagon this trip.

They encountered Indians on this trip and Sophia and the children were
afraid of them until Gottlieb gave them tobacco, cigarette papers and
matches. The Indians danced for the travelers and shared some of the meat
from their cows they had butchered during their trip through the Rosebud
Agency. They found their household goods and home on the farm near Bowdle
just as they had left it and resumed life there.

        Back: Albert, Gus, Sam, Helen Emma, Julius, Sophia holding Alice,
        Carrie, Elenora

In 1908, due to ill health, Gottlieb sold the farm and moved his family to
Bowdle where five more children were born. He bought a pool hall and
bowling alley which he operated until 1912 when fire destroyed it and the
Artz Photo Gallery. Gottlieb then took up photography, but sold the
business to Joe Schlaht in 1921. Gottlieb received a U.S.A. patent in 1908
for a compression well water pump and a patent for windmill regulators from
Canada in 1915 and the U.S.A. in 1916.

Gottlieb was ill with tuberculosis for several years and died in 1922.
Sophia married Charles Krause in 1928. Charles died in 1958 and Sophia went
to California where she made her home with her daughter Elenora Edstrom
until her death in 1961. She was buried in the Bowdle Cemetery.

Surviving children were: Gustave of Dennison, TX; Caroline Eisenbeisz of
Buena Park, CA; Samuel who died in 1979; Albert of North Mankato, MN; Helen
Eisenbeiss of Lakeport, CA; Emma of Lakeport, CA and Elenora Edstrom of
Lakewood, CA.

ALBERT and EVELYN [BLUMHARDT] SIPPERT

Albert Sippert remained longer in Bowdle than other members of his family,
attending 10 years of school in Bowdle and then graduated from Dr. Martin
Luther High School in 1927. He attended Northwestern College in Watertown,
WI where he received his B.A. degree and the Lutheran Theological
Seminary at Theinsville, WI. He was ordained into the Wisconsin Synod
Church in 1934 and pastored the Lutheran Church in Estelline. Evelyn,
daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Philip Blumhardt became his bride June 4, 1935.

Albert pastored churches in Carrington, ND; Kaukauna, WI; Pueblo, CO; Clear
Lake and Hidewood Township before retiring from the ministry in 1959,
having served his God and the church 25 years.

Their lives took a different turn. Albert went into the brokerage and
securities business and owned his own business in Sioux Falls, was an
accountant for the Nicollett Co-op, invented a bead breaker for rusty truck
tires and then went into income tax preparation business. He worked for H &
R Block in Mankato and owned the H & R franchise in Owatonna, MN where he
also taught in the tax school, teaching Evelyn the business and she became
his office manager. He also served as auditor for the Lutheran churches and
Lutheran College in Wisconsin. He made a great contribution to his family
when he compiled an extensive family history tracing the ancestry back to
the 1800's.

Albert is present contemplating writing four books relative to the
Christian religion. Albert and Evelyn have four children. Paul of
Lakeville, MN is a pilot for Northwest Airlines. Ruth Sibbett is an
accountant and teacher in Visalia, CA. Nancy Abel is a horticulturist in
Winter Haven, FL and Carol Jackson of Eugene, OR is a computer system
analyst.

Albert and Evelyn have 10 grandchildren and live at 330 Wheeler Ave. N.,
Mankato, MN.

"And oh, how those pioneer women could cook from a few basic ingredients:
flour, sugar, meat, potatoes, salt, pepper and vegetables. I know that when
my mother had enough of these, she was set to provide the tasty meals for a
family of 10 children. Some of the tasty dishes are still in demand today
such as halupsie, fleischkueckla, strudels, knepfla, blatchinda,
hassenpfeffer, borscht from fresh garden vegetables, headcheese and
bratwurst and above all, homemade dill pickles. During the threshing season
the women were especially busy. Besides milking the cows and taking care of
the little children they did extra baking, cooked and served three heavy
meals for large crews of hungry men, women and children from 20-30 and more
people. They also had to prepare forenoon and afternoon lunches. The
afternoon lunch often included schnapps made of pure alcohol mixed with
water and a touch of anise.

"The Sears Roebuck and Montgomery Ward catalogs also played a big role in
those early days. These catalogs, next to the Bible, were the most
important publication in many homes. The descriptions in the English
language had an educational value. During the long winter evenings under the
dim kerosene lamp on the kitchen table members of the family were
entertained by all the interesting pages and pictures. When the catalog
became outdated, the non-glossy pages served an extra purpose in the
outhouse.

"Among the many hardships and threats to life and property of the pioneers
were droughts, hailstorms, blizzards and prairie fires. The high thick
grass was a real threat after the heavy frost of early fall. Once on fire
and fanned by a strong wind the flames swept along burning thousands of
acres, which even narrow roads could not stop. The fastest horses would
sometimes be unable to keep ahead of it, depending on how strong the wind
blew. The only way fire could be checked would be to backfire from wider
roads or with firebreaks plowed in the sod. While in the eighth grade I
went to a farmyard with two other boys and a Syrian storekeeper to backfire
a prairie fire that raced 20 miles northeast from Hoven in about an hour.
One of my friends died in the fire when the wind switched. The other was
badly scarred on his face and body. I was fortunate to catch the car of the
storekeeper as he rushed out of the farmyard."

TIMOTHY and VIRGINIA [SCHMIERER] SPIRY

Timothy W. Spiry was born Nov. 16, 1945 to Samuel and Hertha Spiry in
Mobridge. He lived in Java and attended school there. After graduation he
worked at Mobridge until he joined the Air Force in March 1965. He was
stationed at Guam and Thailand during the Vietnam War. Tim has a brother
Wallace, who lives in Rapid City and a sister Betty Pfitzer, who lives in
Sun City West, Arizona.

        Michelle, Virginia, Tim, Sherri Spiry

Virginia L. Spiry was born June 19, 1946 to Otto and Vira Schmierer in
Hoven. She grew up on a farm with her two brothers Chester and Wade. She
attended two years of school at Horseshoe Lake and then her family moved
1-1/2 miles east of Java, where she attended school. After graduation her
parents and brothers moved to Bowdle and Virginia moved to Aberdeen and

Mobridge at Penny Saver.

Tim and Virginia were married Oct. 2, 1966 in Java. Then Tim went overseas

family moved to Bowdle in February 1972 on Virginia's parents farm. Sherri

JACOB and GRETCHEN [LEMKE, HUFT] SPRENGER

Jacob was born in 1916 at Wishek, ND and farmed in the Dupree area. He was
also a mechanic for Rabenberg's in Selby. He married Gretchen (Lemke, Huft)
in 1965 and farmed south of Bowdle.

Jacob made medical history when he was one of eleven patients who received
a homograph valve at the University Hospital in December 1965. In November
1967 his body rejected the valve and he was flown by air ambulance to
Seattle University Hospital and the valve was replaced with a plastic one.

Jacob was able to operate his farm and cattle ranch near Bowdle. In October
1969 he toured the Holy Land. In 1971 calcium and infection developed in
the plastic valve and he was flown back to Seattle University Hospital and
died August 1971.

        Back: Darrel, Gretchen, Carolee, Richard Front: Joy, Cara, Matthew,
        Wilma, Shani, Darby

Jacob Sprenger had four children. David lives in California. Richard, a
driver improved-hearing officer, married Carolee Huft, an RN and
psychologist and they live in Sioux Falls with their children Shani and
Darby. Joan married Don Bennett, a forest ranger and they live in Montana.
Steven lives in Liberty, MO.

Gretchen's son Darrel Huft, manager of Glass Co., married Joy Hieb and they
live in Billings, MT with their children Matthew and Cara.

Wilma Lemke (pictured in front row) graduated from Commercial College in
Aberdeen. She lives in Washington, D.C. where she works as a fiscal analyst.

ALVIN and ALVINA [SCHLECHT] SPRINGER

Alvin Springer was born Nov. 29, 1922 at Murdo to Charles and Nora

        Back: Gerrie, Rick, Penny Front: Alvin and Alvina Springer

ANTON and WILHELMINE [BRANDT] STANGL

Anton Stangl came to the Bowdle area in the spring 1888. He celebrated his
21st birthday in December 1887. He joined his brother Joe in Spring Lake
Township north of Spring Lake and just north of the Bowdle to Bangor Road.
He filed on a homestead and tree claim--320 acres.

The Stangls came to this country from Austria. Joe came to the Bowdle area
and homesteaded in 1886. He had come to the United States in 1881, living
and working in Minnesota before coming to Dakota Territory. Anton came to
America in March 1884 and worked in Minnesota on a farm for his uncle and
acted as a lumberjack. He had to be 21 years old before he could be
eligible to file on land in Dakota Territory. A younger brother Adolph came
to visit his brother in 1898 and stayed, filing on an adjoining homestead.
A sister Elizabeth (Mrs. Charles Meyers) settled in Spring Lake Township in
1907 with her husband and children. Their youngest daughter Marie (Mrs. Joe
Herman) and her husband still live on that farm. Three brothers and one
sister remain in Austria.

Anton married Wilhelmine (Minnie) Brandt in early March 1897 and to this
union nine children were born. Two sons died in infancy. Anton and Minnie
farmed the original homestead and additional acres purchased later, until
they retired in the fall 1926. They bought a house in Java and moved to
town with their three youngest children. Just a few weeks after moving to
Java Minnie became ill and died in October 1926. Anton and his children
returned to the farm to live with sons Donal and Albert, who were now
operating the farm. Anton remained active on the farm in his retirement
caring for an orchard, garden, poultry and helping his sons with the work
from time to time. He died in June 1946.

The seven children of Anton and Minnie Stangl were as follows:

Frances, born in 1897, married Raymond Lee in 1919. They farmed next door
for a year, then moved to Isabel where they operated a ranch and farmed
until 1959. Their son Arnold purchased another farm south of Selby and they
moved there in the spring 1959. Arnold still operates this farm and his
mother lives with him. Raymond died in July 1983 at the age of 91. Their
daughter Vronna (Mrs. Lowell Endahl) lives in Alexandria, VA. They have
twin sons John and Jay, married and a son Mark. The youngest Lee daughter
Florine (Mrs. John Glaus) lives near Chamberlain on a ranch. They have a
son Jim and twin daughters June (Mrs. Arden Shields) and Janet (Mrs. Roger
Wehde) who live in Sioux Falls. Their youngest daughter Barbara lives in
Sturgis.

Vina was born in 1899 and married Ralph Sawinsky in 1930. She attended
Northern Normal in Aberdeen and taught rural school in the Java area. Ralph
and Vina farmed south of Selby near the old Bangor townsite until Ralph
died in 1957. She moved to Selby and died in February 1976. They had no
children, but showed enthusiastic interest in young people. Since 1977 a
scholarship was established in their memory at NSC in Aberdeen, to be given
to a freshman student from this area each year.

Donal, born in 1901, spent his lifetime on the home farm. He married Ella
Tronson in 1930. They have a daughter Lois (Mrs. Marvin Wolf) of Java, who
has two daughters Laurel and Eleanor. Another daughter Elaine (Mrs. Richard
Osterday) of Sidney, NE has two children Renee and Rick. Donal was active
in community services including being a member of the Masonic Lodges. He
retired in 1967, but continued to live on the farm and died in July 1974.
Ella moved to Java in 1976 and continues to live there in retirement.

Albert, born in 1903, also lived all his life on the home farm. Donal and
Albert formed the Stangl Bros. partnership in 1925. Albert married Gladys
Tyner in 1932. Gladys was a rural school teacher in the Spring Lake area,
coming to South Dakota from Shenandoah, IA. They have four children. Mary Jane
(Mrs. Charles Dunham) lives in Pocatello, ID and has two children Gary and
Lisa. Thomas married Janice Huber of Bowdle and lives in Sterling, VA. They
have three children Janell (Mrs. Rich Leach), Janeen and Tom. Jean (Mrs.
Frank Moore) lives near Phoenix, AZ. They have four children Nathan, Ben,
Melissa and Valerie. Gerald and his wife Linda live near Perry, OK.

Gladys died in 1955. Albert retired from farming in 1971, but continued to
live with his youngest brother Orville. Albert died in December 1975. He
was active in community service including the 4-H program and Masonic
Lodge. His biggest pride was his garden and orchard. The children
established a scholarship at SDSU in Brookings honoring the memory of their
parents Albert and Gladys.

Emma Stangl was born in 1909, taught rural and town schools for many years
and married J. Herman Fiedler in 1944. He farmed north of Java and was
office manager of the ASCS office in Walworth County many years. They have
three daughters Dr. Marion married Dr. Roger Ehrich and lives in
Blacksburg, VA. Carolyn (Mrs. Roger Lind) lives in Jackson, MN with two
daughters Carin and Dena. Diane (Mrs. Mike Smith) lives in Laramie, WY and
has a daughter Emily. Emma and Herman live in retirement in Java. They have
done extensive traveling throughout this country and foreign countries.

Irving, born in 1912, left the home farm and worked on various farms in the
area. He moved to Oregon but returned to this area in 1949. He died in
August 1969. Irving had an interesting hobby working with agate stones.

Orville, born in 1921, attended the rural Spring Lake School near the Earl
Erbe farm, as did all his older brothers and sisters. He graduated from Java
High School in 1939. He attended SDSU in Brookings and received a degree in
agricultural education in 1943. June 1, 1942 he enlisted in the Army
Reserve. Orville was commissioned a Lt. Infantry Reserve in August 1943. He
served overseas in Europe 1944 and 1945 as a combat infantry officer. He
was wounded three times. He returned to South Dakota in December 1945 and
joined Donal and Albert in farming. His farming career was interrupted by
the Korean War as he was called back to active duty Oct. 1, 1950. He served
at Ft. Riley, KS as an instructor in basic training several months. In the
spring 1951 he was transferred to Japan and Korea and served as a combat
infantry officer in Korea July 1951 to January 1952.

He returned to the farm in February 1952, arriving home between snowstorms.
This was one of the most severe winters ever to hit this area. Orville
became very active in community and agricultural related organizations. He
served as a 4-H leader several years. He was a member, director and
president of many organizations too numerous to mention. Some included were
Masonic Lodge, American Legion and many crop and livestock organizations.
He was the director of Java Equity Exchange for 15 years and secretary for
13 years.

In 1981 he received a special honor by the American Shorthorn Association
being named Builder of the Breed and that same year the South Dakota Beef
Cattle Improvement Association named him Seed Stock Producer of the Year.
Breeding and raising registered Shorthorn cattle has been Orville's main
interest on the farm. He has seen his cattle sold in many states as well as
in Canada.

Orville continues to operate the home farm, but has reduced his breeding
herd of cattle. Rick Osterday, Donal's grandson, has been assisting with the
farm work several summers. Hopefully Rick will assume full responsibility
of the farming operation when Orville retires in a few years.

THOMAS and JANICE [HUBER] STANGL

Thomas Anton Stangl was the second of four children born to Albert and
Gladys (Tyner) Stangl. They lived on a farm in the Spring Lake area west of
Bowdle. Thomas attended Java and Bowdle High Schools, graduating in 1953.
He then graduated from South Dakota State University with a degree in
animal husbandry in 1957. The Interior Department Bureau of Indian Affairs
employed Tom and sent him to Gordon, NE to work as range conservationist.

        Thomas holding Jordan, Richard, Janell, Thomas, Janice, Janeen

Thomas Stangl married Janice Huber June 15, 1958. She is the daughter of
Edward and Lydia (Haberer) Huber of Bowdle. Janice graduated from Bowdle
High School and attended Northern State Teachers College in Aberdeen on a
Ruritan Vocal Music Scholarship. She taught elementary music and fourth
grade at Selby two years. While attending college she gave piano lessons to
16 pupils in Bowdle.

Tom and Janice made their first home in Gordon, NE where Janice again
taught elementary music and piano. In 1959 Tom was transferred to Durango,
CO where their two daughters were born, Janell July 15, 1961 and Janeen
Nov. 7, 1962. Tom was transferred again, this time to Eagle Butte. Janice
taught music part-time at Dupree. Their son Thomas Allan was born Sept. 2,
1966 at Rapid City. The family moved to Cortez, CO in January 1967 where
they lived 3- 1/2 years until Tom was transferred to the BIA office in
Washington, D.C.

In 1969 Tom was selected to attend the Department of Interior management
and development program and the family went to the U.S. Capitol. In 1970 he
was transferred to the Bureau of Indian Affairs central office where he
became a program analyst in the program planning division. He attended
University of Virginia under a civil service commission sponsored education
for public management programs in 1974. In 1981 Tom Stangl became chief
budget officer of the BIA and is presently acting assistant director of
financial management, BIA central office in Washington.

Janice's musical talent has always found work either teaching elementary
music or piano where they have lived and in their home at Sterling, VA. She
is also an organist for the Presbyterian Church, soloist and piano
instructor.

The couple's daughter Janell and husband Richard Leach have given them the
pleasure of a grandson Jordan Thomas Leach.

KENNETH and PAT [KRULL] STEPHAN

Kenneth Stephan farms in the Tolstoy area and is a graduate from Bowdle. He

Kenneth is a very sportsminded person. His interest began when he attended

Kenneth was on the 880 yard relay and sprint medley teams which held
records unbroken for 30 years 1955-1985. Stephan's love for baseball
continued over 25 years. He has the record of playing in seven amateur
baseball tournaments and has been a player/manager of the Bowdle softball
team which has won many trophies. He played in the "Over 40" softball
league with Aberdeen teams and participated in two national tournaments. He
served as a South Dakota Amateur Baseball Association Commissioner and has
promoted, played and managed independent basketball several years.

The family's original farm home burned down May 3, 1983 and a new
doublewide trailer home with a basement replaced it.

WALTER and PANSY [COOPER] STEPHAN

Walter was born March 13, 1896 to John and Caroline (Schleuner) Stephan.
Walter's father was born at Warsaw, NY Oct. 22, 1857. Three years later
John moved with his parents to Sheboygan County, WI where he grew to
manhood and he married Caroline Schleuner. The couple settled on a farm
near Kiel, WI where their seven children were born: Meta, Amanda, Frank,
Hilda, Walter, Oscar and Clarence. All are deceased but Oscar, who at this
writing is living at the Hosmer Senior Citizens Home.

In 1904 John sold the Wisconsin farm and loaded an emigrant car billed to
Bowdle. They arrived by train Nov. 10, in Bowdle. The family was met by Ed
F. Schuler who had them live with his family until they found a home. John
Stephan purchased the Jacob Miller farm six miles north of Tolstoy.

Only three years after settling on this farm John became ill and died Nov.
28, 1907 leaving his wife and seven children to operate the farm.

Their son Walter married Doris Nylander of Lebanon who died in 1936. Walter
remarried in 1940 to Pansy Cooper, daughter of Cleve and Emma Cooper of
Lebanon. Walter and Pansy lived on the farm until the fall of 1961 when
they moved into their new home at Bowdle. Their only son Kenneth married
Pat Krull and they continue to operate the home farm.

In 1970 Walter died. Pansy continues to live in Bowdle. She had been
librarian at Martin Bieber Library 10 years and served as a volunteer worker
for the first grade at Bowdle school seven years. Pansy continues to enjoy
her five grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.

MARK and MARY [JORDON] STEVENS

Mark D. Stevens was born May 30, 1864 to Mr. and Mrs. A.J. Stevens at White
Oak, MI. When he was a young lad he moved to South Dakota where he filed on
160 acres of land nine miles northeast of Bowdle in Edmunds County.

Mark built a sod house and pigpen sided with rock on his homesteaded land.
The pigpen remained many years, long after the sod house was gone. The land
was legally his in 1896. In 1884 Mark married Mary Pulling. She died soon
after their marriage and there were no children.

Several years later Mark married Mary Jordon. She was born May 27, 1877 at
Casco, WI to Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Jordan. Mary's mother died when she was 4
years old and it was then her father decided to come to South Dakota.

        Back: Emmaline and Ada Front: Everette, Mark, Lee, Mary Stevens

Mark and Mary were married at Bowdle in 1891. Seven children were born to
this union: Emmaline (Mrs. Dallas Jones) born Dec. 26, 1893, died Sept. 21,
1913; twins Elsie and Elsto died shortly after birth; Ada (Mrs. Walter
Goodwin) born March 26, 1897, died Oct. 21, 1984; Everette, born March 12,
1900, died July 28, 1933; Lee, born March 22, 1903, died Nov. 7, 1980 and
Esther (Mrs. Edwin Blumhardt) born April 9, 1906. Esther is still living at
Bowdle.

Mark and Mary lived in the sod house Mark built until he built a house and
barn of lumber on the southeast corner of the land. The farming was done
with horses. Working behind the plow gave him plenty of exercise! The grain
was hauled by team and wagon to Bowdle to market. A few years before he
retired Mark purchased a tractor. In 1915 he bought a Ford Touring Car with
side curtains and a top that could be put down if it didn't rain!

Mary died in 1910 at age 33, leaving five children for Mark to raise. They
attended school in the home district and Mark was on the school board many
years. In 1919 he retired and moved to Bowdle. He bought the Hart house and
his two sons Lee and Everette remained on the farm. Mark enlarged the house
and lived there until he died in 1929.

EUGENE and ALMA [McINTOSH] STOEBNER

attended Northern State College. He taught over 25 years at schools in

        Alma and Eugene Stoebner

Aberdeen one year before she resigned to move to Eureka where she became
director of nursing at the Eureka Community Hospital. She held that
position over 30 years until December 1980. She kept her "hand in" by
working part-time through May 1984.

Eugene and Alma have three sons. James is an electrical engineer with Texas
Instruments in Houston, TX; John is a science and computer instructor at
Cresbard and Joseph is a registered pharmacist at Kessler's Pharmacy in
Aberdeen.

The Stoebners also enjoy four grandchildren.

FRED and CHRISTINE [REMPHER] STOTZ

        Back: Shirley, Gordon, LuVurne Front: Fred and Christine Stotz

JOHN and ALBINA [RUFER] STROUCKEL ANTON and ELSIE [SCHUBERT] STROUCKEL

Mr. and Mrs. John Strouckel, with their 1-1/2-year-old daughter Mary, came
to America from Austria in 1886. They settled on a tract of land about 14
miles southeast of Bowdle. It was here in Cloyd Valley Township that they
built their first buildings.

The house was built by John Strouckel. He had dug a big trench with a team
of horses, into which he hauled dirt, straw and water. He then used the
horses to mix it. When the dirt was thoroughly mixed, it was used as
cement. Wooden boxes were made, into which the mud and straw mixture was
placed to form blocks. When the blocks were dry, they were used as cement
blocks to build the house. The outer walls, being 15 inches thick, provided
good insulation, keeping the house warm in the winter and cool in the
summer. There are eight windows in the house and being deep, they make
appropriate places for house plants.

In the winter a hard coal heater and cast iron stove were used to heat the
rooms. In later years an entry and bathroom, electricity and water system
were added. The outside walls have siding and the inside walls were
plastered and papered. The house has four rooms and an attic. It is one of
a few of its kind and is still occupied.

To John and Albina (Rufer) Strouckel four sons Joseph, Adolph, Anton and
William and four daughters Mary, Antonia, Tillie and Anna were born on the
farm.

After the death of their father and the married members of the family moved
away, Anton and his mother farmed the homestead. In 1931 Anton married
Elsie Schubert and they continued living on the home place. Three sons
Lloyd, Allen and Ronald and two daughters Elaine and Sharon were born. They
grew up on the home place and later married.

Lloyd married Bonnie Myrann of Tolstoy. Their children are Jerry and Karyl.
Allen married Diane Bieber of Java. They are the parents of Teresa, Denise,
Cindy and Karin. Ronald married Rhonda Hieb of Hosmer. They are the parents
of a son Jesse and a daughter Lindsey. Elaine married Lloyd Hettich of
Tolstoy. Their children are Robert, Michael, Loni and Laurie. Sharon
married Gerald Guthmiller of Roscoe. Their daughters are Gina, Suzanne and
Lana.

Anton Strouckel died in 1963, but his wife Elsie and two sons Allen and
Ronnie continued to operate the farm. In the summer of 1937 Emil Aldinger
came to help Anton with farming as the hired man. He lived with the family
and completed his school years there. He became as one of the Strouckel
family. He is still living on the home place, running the farm with Allen
and Ron, has his own cattle and acreage and his hobby is fishing.

Also on the Strouckel Ranch, to the east of the farmyard, is a spring
called "Silver Spring" so named by an early pioneer because of the silvery
deposits found on the nearby rocks in early spring. Many neighbors in those
early years and others from miles around came with barrels and tanks to
get spring water. They even drove their stock to it, as wells were scarce
in those days.

It has been told by early pioneers that Lewis and Clark stopped to water
their horses at the Silver Springs during their journey to the West Coast.
Relics such as a double barrel muzzle loading shotgun and an old-time
musket were found around the place in 1885 and 1886, which indicates the
Springs must have been known to trappers and hunters. From the condition of
the relics they must have lain there many years prior to 1884. One journal
of an officer with Lewis and Clark tells that they were near this area in
1805. This Spring is located on farm ground and pasture about two miles
east of the Strouckel farm. The last ones living on the Silver Springs
ranch were the Emery Clark family.

REV. ROGER and ARLUE [NIX] THOMAS

The Rev. Roger John Thomas was assigned the pastorate of United Methodist
Churches in Bowdle and Tolstoy, taking up residence in Bowdle June 23,
1983. His dependable assistant in his calling is his wife Arlue.

Roger Thomas was born in Jones County to Ernest A. and Bertha (Green)
Thomas May 16, 1919. His father had been a school teacher in Iowa before
coming to Murdo in 1905 to work for the Milwaukee Railroad. The next year
when he returned from Iowa he brought along his bride to live on a ranch
east of Murdo. They moved to the river in 1921 where they farmed and
ranched.

After graduating from Murdo High School in 1938 Roger spent a year on the
ranch and then attended Black Hills Teachers College at Spearfish, working
on a dairy farm so he could eat. He taught in a rural school 1941-1942 and
in August 1942 was drafted into the U.S. Army Air Force where he was
assigned the duty of Link Trainer Instructor to teach pilot instrument
maneuvers.

The World War II years also brought Roger his bride, Arlue L. Nix, who was
born in Jones County in 1921, daughter of Walter Nix, a local farmer. Her
mother worked for Murdo State Bank 40 years. Arlue graduated from Murdo
High School and attended Free Methodist Junior College at Wessington
Springs. She taught five years in rural schools in Jones County. They were
married Nov. 1, 1943 making their first home in California where their first
child Edward Kent was born.

After his discharge in December 1946 Roger tried ranching again, but that
life was too strenuous for his injured leg and that fall he enrolled at
University of South Dakota in Vermillion, graduating with a B.A. Degree in
1948 and in 1949 received a master of arts in history degree. He taught a
year at Springfield and then took work toward an advanced degree at
University of Wisconsin.

The family moved back on the farm near Murdo in 1952 while Roger worked as
business manager for the REA two years. During this time he began speaking
in the churches, filling in when pastors were absent.

Though it meant additional summer months of college work he responded
affirmatively when urged to make the ministry his life's work, beginning in
1953.

        Arlue and Rev. Roger Thomas

He has served as treasurer of the United Methodist Homes seven years. The
past four years he has also been chairman of the Archives and History
Commission for the Annual Conference. During this time the Commission had
been planning for the 1984 Bicentennial Celebration of 200 years of
Methodist Church Service in America.

Rev. and Mrs. Thomas have seven children. Edward is a physician/surgeon in
Shawnee, OK. John is public relations officer for Augustana College at
Sioux Falls. Melvin is a medical doctor on staff at the Veterans
Administration Hospital in Sioux Falls. David, also in the medical
profession, is a teacher at Fitz Simmons Army Hospital in Denver, CO. Roger
Jr. is an attorney for the Department of Interior in Billings, MT. Mary
lives in Greeley, CO and Gary is assistant coach at Augustana College in
Sioux Falls.
