ADOLPH and AGNES [BRAKEMEYER] THURN

Adolph Thurn was born Jan. 10, 1888 in Neudorf, Russia to Friedrich and
Margaretha Thurn. His earliest memories were of being aboard ship with his
family sailing from Europe to Halifax, Nova Scotia. Young Adolph and his
brother Gus raced on deck to the consternation of their seasick parents.

After growing up in Bowdle Adolph and his brother Gus and several other
young men went to Harding County and homesteaded eight miles from Buffalo.
Although the others soon departed, Adolph stayed on the homestead and soon
owned adjacent land. He built a sod house and from that shanty he built
himself a sheep ranch.

He returned to Bowdle to marry Agnes Brakemeyer in the Congregational
Church where her father was pastor. The nuptials took place in November
1917. Less than a year later Adolph was in World War I, returning home in
January 1919, ten days after the birth of his daughter Vivian at the Rev.
Brakemeyer home.

        Adolph and Agnes Thurn

The young Mrs. Thurn was a teacher and when they returned to Buffalo was a
member of the first faculty of Buffalo Public School. Adolph and Agnes were
charter members of the Congregational Church, the first church in Buffalo.

In those days a trip back to visit the family at Bowdle entailed
negotiating a steep hill and a ferry crossing at Mobridge. Agnes went back
to Ipswich in January 1923 to stay with her sister Edna (Mrs. Harry
Woodworth) where their son Wayne was born.

Agnes Thurn taught school many years and was teaching at age 60 when a fatal
stroke caused her death in the classroom June 29, 1953. After her death
Adolph stayed in Buffalo until 1959 when he moved to Sturgis. At this
writing he is living there at age 96. He remarried twice, Eda Thurn and Mary
Thurn are deceased. Adolph, Eda and Mary spent thousands of hours
volunteering at the Veterans Hospital in Sturgis.

Adolph and Agnes Thurn had two children. Vivian was born at Bowdle Jan. 15,
1919. She married Thomas Frame, now deceased. They had four children
Elaine, Mark, Lynn and Jan and lived at Oakton, VA. Wayne Thurn was born
Jan. 28, 1923 at Ipswich. He married Evelyn Stido, is a retired major and
pilot of the Strategic Air Command. They have two children, Terry and
Laurie and live at Grants Pass, OR.

FRIEDRICH and MARGARETHA [ACKERMANN] THURN

In the early 1800's the Thurns left their homes in Alsace Lorraine and
Wurttemberg when Czar Alexander I invited the Germans to settle on the
steppes or prairie land in South Russia. They were people who loved the
land and made their living from it. After 60 or so years in Russia, there
was a population explosion. Most families had many sons that were without
land. It became necessary to buy land from the Russians who sold at high
prices. In the meantime, the people heard about free homestead land that
was available in America. This, plus political unrest motivated them to
leave the land of the Czars.

Then, in the late 19th Century we fine our future Bowdle pioneer settlers
preparing to leave their homes near the Black Sea in search of free
homestead land in the Dakotas.

In the winter 1892-1893 plans to obtain passports were made by the Russian
German colonists. The passports were in three languages French, German and
Russian. This passport would allow the immigrants to go to America freely
without interference while traveling. They left their home in the colony of
Neudorf, which was located approximately 40 miles north of Odessa on the
Black Sea.

There were other families leaving at the same time and they agreed to meet
in a small village of Goshirko in the Ukraine. From here the families went
by wagons to Tiraspol, where they boarded the train for Rotterdam, Holland
via Warsaw, Poland. While in Rotterdam Grossvater Thurn had his money
stolen. Can you imagine the catastrophe this caused? But there was no
turning back so from Rotterdam they took a cattle boat to Hull, which is on
the east coast of England. No doubt the North Sea was lively and only added
to their discomfort. The boat had double deck bunks which were filled with
straw and no sanitation facilities were available between Rotterdam and
Hull. From Hull they crossed the British Isles by train to Liverpool. Here
they boarded the S.S. Vancouver (Dominion Line) which arrived April 9, 1893
in Halifax, Nova Scotia. According to the passenger list aboard were
Friedrich Thurn, age 30; his wife Margaretha, 28 and their four children:
Gustav 5, Adolph 3, Mathilda 2 and Wilhelm an infant. Friedrich's parents:
Georg Thurn 58 and Katherine 57, his brother Jacob 28, Jacob's wife
Christine 25 and their two children Katherine 4 and Ludwig an infant.

After arriving in Nova Scotia they went by train to Winnipeg, Manitoba
where the immigrants were quarantined for six weeks before entering the
United States. They finally arrived at Roscoe and then made their way to
Eureka where they were met by his brothers Ludwig 27 and August 18, who had
made the trip the year before.

Friedrich Thurn, a native of Neudorf, Government of Cherson, District of
Tiraspol, South Russia, was born Jan. 3, 1861. He was the firstborn child of
Georg and Katherine (nee Raile) Thurn. He married Margaretha Ackermann April
16, 1885. She was the daughter of Daniel and Rosina (nee Eisemann)
Ackermann who lived in the nearby colony of Hoffnungstal. Her birthdate was
Aug. 13, 1863. They lived and farmed with his parents in Neudorf where
their first four children were born. They were Gustav July 7, 1886, Adolph
Jan. 10, 1888, Mathilda Nov. 26, 1889 and William Oct. 12, 1891. This young
family then arrived at Eureka to find land. By the time they arrived
however, the homestead land around there was taken, but they located some
land in Edmunds County about 14 miles south of Bowdle.

The Homestead Application #10912 shows this description of the 160 acres:
E 1/2 of the SW 1/4 and W 1/2 of the SE 1/4 of Section 31 in Township 122
N., in Range 73 W. 5th P.M. Ultimately it was proved up Oct. 9, 1901. There
was a sod house 18 by 28, a barn 16 by 48, a summer house, a well (hand dug)
and 80 acres plowed land. Valued at $480.

For the summer they stayed with the Kline family and then were invited to
spend the winter with the Carl Schick family who lived east of their land.
After locating his homestead Friedrich found employment with a rancher
named Windling who loaned him a horse so he could go home for Christmas.
Mrs. Schick also was expecting a baby so the two women were midwives to
each other and the babies slept in the same cradle.

As soon as the ground could be broken in the spring of 1894, they built
their sod house and barn, even before the land was surveyed, so they had
squatters rights. The walls of the house were built of sod laid in
horizontal layers. The sod was prairie covered with grass and weeds baked
hard by the sun. The prairie was plowed by oxen and then cut into pieces 12
by 18 inches wide, two or three feet long and 4-6 inches thick. These
pieces were stacked one on the other to form the walls of the house. The
end walls were built to a point so poles could be placed from end to end,
then covered with branches and over this sod was placed. The floor was so
hardpacked that it could be swept clean. Window frames and doors were made
from wood purchased in town. The home was warm in winter and cool in
summer. It had two rooms. The smaller one was the bedroom of the parents
and girls, while the other was where the family lived. It was kitchen,
living room and bedroom all rolled into one. The room had a double bed
shared by the four boys, two at each end. The rest of the furniture was a
kitchen table discarded by a saloon in Bowdle and some chairs. The house
was heated by a bake-oven which was built at the end of the dividing wall
facing the storm shed entrance. It was built on a special foundation about
8 inches high. The base was filled with sandstone and then flat stones. Over
this a red, sticky clay, from a nearby pit, was smothered over the entire
inside of the oven. A square, the size of the oven door, was cut out of the
sod to form the mold into which the red, sticky clay was poured for the
oven door. The door handle was also made of clay. The house was heated by
buffalo chips and flax straw which gave high heat, also from kindling wood
which they bought from the Indians near the Missouri River.

To the front of the house which faced south, was an opening about 10-15
feet long and about 8 feet wide. This was called the storm shed or entrance
to the house. There was plenty of rain so they had a nice garden and the
land was outstanding in grass for hay. There was always a fear of prairie
fires since the time they had one that was started by lightning. It was
necessary to have firebreaks around the buildings and haystacks. In those
days it seemed there were more thunderstorms and blizzards. During the
winter the shovel was always taken into the house at night so they could
shovel their way out in the morning. Sometimes the snow was so high that
they had to shovel the snow off the chimney on the roof before they could
start a fire. One year it rained early in the fall and got real cold and
then snowed so that the wild geese and ducks that flew over the fields to
go south, had their wings frozen together so that they were unable to fly.
Great numbers of birds were caught and butchered. A big barrel with the
ends open was put over the chimney and the meat was hung inside to be
smoked. The geese and ducks provided the family with meat for the winter
and feathers for their pillows and featherbeds.

        Adolph, Gust [George], Bill, Christ or Jake Gross, Katherine,
        Margaret, Frederich, Henry [sitting]

Christ Gross, their neighbor, came to visit and brought a cow for them to
use for a year so the children would have milk and butter. There were no
churches so brothers Christ and Jacob Gross took turns having church
services in their homes. Friedrich could read well so he would read the
scriptures. Sundays when they went to church meetings they rode a stoneboat
which was hitched to an ox. One very hot Sunday in June they were late
getting away from home for the church meeting at Grosses which was about
2-1/2 or 3 miles away so Friedrich walked along side of the ox urging it to
go faster when all of a sudden the ox smelled a puddle of water in the
field and ran right into the middle of it. Stoneboat and all, everyone was
wet and muddy. It was many hours later before the stubborn ox was ready to
leave his cool sanctuary.

While living on the homestead they had another son Henry Sept. 20, 1895.
They lived on this homestead until about 1901 when they sold it to a
neighbor for $8 an acre and bought two claims for the same price an acre
eight miles from there and four miles from Bowdle. This was much better
since they would be closer to town. They built up this farm and in a couple
years bought another claim, paying $12 a acre, totaling 480 acres
altogether. The dream of owning land had finally come true.

The parents retired in Bowdle and Bill stayed on the farm. Friedrich made
one trip to his old homeland in Russia in 1910 to visit his sisters and some
of his wife's family who did not come to America. Later they moved to a
warmer climate to Lodi, CA but after a few years returned to their friends
and family in Bowdle. Friedrich died in Bowdle Aug. 8, 1934 and Margaretha
went to live with her daughter in Sacramento, CA where she died Dec. 14,
1956.

Gustav (George) married Sophie Sannes in 1914 and she died in 1929. They
had two children. Robert died in November 1975 and Lorraine Brown-Davy
lives in Auburn, CA. Later he married Hazel Halvorson and they had three
sons: George who lives in Cocoa Beach, FL; Richard in El Macero, CA and
Thomas in Auburn, CA. Gustav died in 1947.

Adolph married Agnes Brakemayer in 1917 and she died in 1953. He is living
at the age of 96 in Sturgis. They have two children: Vivian Frame who lives
in Oakton, VA and Wayne in Grants Pass, OR.

Mathilda married Christian Schumacher in 1908 and she died in Bowdle in
1947. Their children were Arthur who died in October 1958, Raymond who died
in May 1941, Bernice Weishaar, Herbert and Virginia Rall live in Lodi, CA;
Alma Leno in Bowdle; twins Paul in Pierre and Palmer in Bath; Vernada Poile
in Clarendon Hills, IL; Warren in Aberdeen and Arvis who died in October
1942.

William married Katherine Hochstatter in 1918. She is living in Bowdle.
Bill died at age 93, Nov. 16, 1984. Their children are Violet Cowden who
lives in Huntington Beach, CA; Lillian Riede who lives in Gardina, CA;
Donald who died Aug. 10, 1984 at Fairfield, CA and Betty Nies who lives in
Palm Springs, CA.

Katherine married Jacob F. Perman in 1918 and she is living in Sacramento,
CA at the age of 90. Their children were Eugene F., Harvey H., Adeline
Weston and Genevieve Euren, all of Sacramento, CA. Two children died in
infancy.

Henry married Beth Keen in 1936. He died in Bowdle in 1965. Their children
were James who lives in San Gabriel, CA and Peter who lives in Lodi, CA.

GUSTAV [GEORGE H.] THURN

Gustav was born July 7, 1886 in the colony of Neudorf near the Black Sea in
Russia. He was the oldest child of Friedrich and Margaretha (Ackermann)
Thurn and was named after his mother's foster father Pastor Gustav Becker,
who was the pastor in Hoffnungstal. Since he was the eldest son he often
went by wagon with his father to Odessa to purchase supplies. His family
came to America in the spring of 1893 and located a homestead in Edmunds
County about 14 miles south of Bowdle.

Gus first worked in the Amerpohl Lumber Yard in Bowdle. The store was later
consolidated with Aurands to become the Aurand-Amerpohl Store. He went to
night school to take a business course from Mr. Aurand's son-in-law who
was the instructor. Gus clerked in the yardage department and his brother
Adolph worked in the produce.

While growing up in Bowdle Gus and Adolph played the clarinet in the Bowdle
City Band. There were many dances at that time and Gus took first prize as
the best dancer. A neighbor taught him to play the violin and he played and
sang the popular tunes of the times.

        Gustav [George] Thurn

Around 1908 a group of about 6-8 young men from Bowdle went to Buffalo,
Harding County to homestead. Each one found his own 160 acres and proved it
up. Among them were Gus and Adolph. At that time he owned a pair of horses,
a buggy and the one-room shack on the homestead. He lived there about 21
months until he was able to obtain the final proof and then he sold it. For
a few years he worked in Doland, Webster and Gettysburg where he obtained
valuable merchandising experience. His goal was to own his own men's
clothing store. His nephew, former Vice-president Hubert H. Humphrey wrote
in his book, "The Doland Opera House was on the second floor above a
clothing store run by Uncle Gus and Aunt Sophie Thurn." He had married
Sophie Sannes in May 1914 and they were living in Webster when Robert was
born and in Gettysburg when Lorraine was born. In the meantime his parents
moved west to Lodi, CA and they also moved west. They had been engaged in
business in Idaho and after a tour of the west selected Yuba City as a
location for a department store. They were living in Yuba City, CA when
Sophie and baby died as a result of an accident Nov. 14, 1929. They had two
other children.

Robert was born in September 1915 and married Barbara Wilder. He died Nov.
9, 1975 and she died June 3, 1976. Their children were Lisa and Megan.

Lorraine was born Sept. 11, 1921. She married Horace Brown and later David
J. Davy. She has three children Carol, Kenneth and Robert.

On Jan. 21. 1931 George (Gus) married a nurse Hazel Halvorson. They lived
in Grass Valley, CA and had three sons:

George H. was born Feb. 8, 1933 and married Dorothy Knappon. Their children
are Andrea, Mark and Julie.

Richard was born Feb. 25, 1934 and married Sharel Geer. Their children are
Jeffrey, Richard, Michele and Scott.

Thomas was born Oct. 28, 1945 and married Gail Collins. Their children are
Jason and Allison.

George (Gus) Thurn died in January 1947.

HENRY and BETH [KEEN] THURN

Henry Thurn was born Sept. 29, 1895 at his parents homestead, 14 miles
south of Bowdle. His parents were Friedrich and Margaretha Thurn.

        Henry Thurn

Henry married Beth Keen Jan. 13, 1937 at Bowdle. Henry served in the U.S.
Army during World War I and after his discharge worked as a flagman for the
Milwaukee Railroad out of Minneapolis until his retirement when he returned
to Bowdle. He died July 22, 1965.

Henry and Beth had two children. James is a manufacturer's representative.
He and his wife Jean live in San Gabriel, CA and have two daughters Julie
and Jill. Fred P. Thurn is a truck driver. He and his wife Marge have a
daughter Shawee and live in Santa Ana, CA.

WILLIAM and KATHERINE [HOCHSTETTER] THURN

William (Bill) and Katherine Thurn mark a special notch in Bowdle's
history. They were one of the oldest couples living in town.

William was born in Odessa, Russia in 1891. His parents were Friedrich and
Margaretha Thurn. They brought their family to America and the Bowdle area
when William was 2 years old. He had three brothers Gustav, Adolph and
Henry and two sisters Mathilda (Thurn) Schumacher and Katherine (Thurn)
Perman. The family homesteaded 14 miles south of Bowdle and later moved and
homesteaded four miles south of Bowdle where William later raised his own
family.

Katherine was born in Java in 1897 to John and Katherine (Biel)
Hochstetter. Her parents were born in Russia. Her father was born in 1807
and died in 1943. Her mother was born in 1807 and died in 1948. She had
four brothers John, Fred, Fred J. and Christ and four sisters Sophia (Mrs.
Wells Tyler), Barbara (Mrs. Oscar Mortenson), Magdelina and Lena (Mrs. John
Schlepp.)

William and Katherine were united in marriage in 1915 in the Java Reformed
Church. This building was moved to Bowdle several years ago and was located
where Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. has a sub-station now. To celebrate
their golden anniversary Bill and Katherine renewed their wedding vows
again in the same church. The ceremony was witnessed by their grandson Rev.
James Riede and Rev. Izler.

        William and Katherine Thurn Family Back: Donald, Darlene, Kathy,
        Robert, Buster, Lillian, James, Violet, Scott, Betty, George.
        Front: Karen, Donna, Kristie, Katherine, William T., William N.,
        Kim, Peter, Peggy.

The couple had a humble beginning and weathered many hardships. Their first
home was a sod house on the Thurn homestead where their first child Violet
was born. They lived here 2-1/2 years. Then about 1922 a tragedy struck. A
big prairie fire burned all their hay and granary feed. It burned everything
except their home. To add to the event, the fire burned to death Jacob
Bollinger and A. Kundert and severely burned Ted Artz and Arlo Stroup. It
was a frightening experience with cattle running loose and everything being
destroyed in its path.

Soon after the fire they moved to another farm five miles away so their
cattle would have feed. Neighbors and relatives helped provide feed for the
animals and Bill did a lot of fur trapping for subsistence for family
survival. After five years living on this farm they purchased the Thurn
homestead and moved back home.

Now they were blessed with several profitable years followed by the Great
Depression. Drought and grasshoppers entered the picture of farming. Many
cattle had to be destroyed by the government due to lack of feed and
disease. Bill struggled hard to keep their farm, but like many others,
found it impossible. After many hard years of labor they were able to
purchase back their land. Despite all this Depression, Bill's strong faith
helped him and his family conquer these problems.

Katherine did her part during this trial time earning money for the family
by teaching neighborhood women to sew and manage limited resources. Through
these efforts she was paid $20 a month from the government.

Besides her jobs, Katherine became very active in the following community
activities: Extension Club for over 60 years, Ladies Aid for 67 years,
member of American Legion Auxiliary (Gold Star Member), Bowdle Hospital
Auxiliary, Committee Woman in political elections for 30 years, Chairman
for Red Cross and March of Dimes, 4-H Leader and Sunshine Lady (visiting
hospitals and writing letters to servicemen during World War II,) well-known
coffee lady for many weddings and funerals in the community. For all these
accomplishments she received the Honorary Woman of the Year award in 1965.

Bill farmed about 320 acres of land mainly with horses. He owned three
tractors, the first one a 1925 Fordson. In 1968 he received the Outstanding
Senior Farmer of the Year award.

Bill and Katherine retired from the farm in 1963, moving to Bowdle in the
house north of the Bowdle E.U. Methodist Church, which is one of the oldest
homes in Bowdle. In 1980 they moved to the Prairie View Housing apartments
in Bowdle. Bill died Nov. 16, 1984.

Bill and Katherine had four children.

Violet was born Oct. 1, 1916 and served as a WASP in World War II. She
married Warren Cowden and they live in Huntington Beach, CA. They have a
daughter Kim.

Lillian was born Dec. 19, 1919. She is a bookkeeper and married Leo Riede.
They live in Gardena, CA and have two sons Rev. James and Robert.

Donald was born Oct. 25, 1926 and died Aug. 10, 1984. He was a teacher and
World War II veteran. He married Darlene Ronfeldt and they had four
daughters: Katherine, Karen, Kristie and Donna. Darlene lives in Fairfield,
CA.

Betty was born April 24, 1930. She married George Nies and they live in
Palm Springs, CA. Their children are William, Tom and Peggy.

ANGELO and LILLIAN [WIEPKING] TOCCOLINI

Lillian Wiepking was born on a farm southeast of Bowdle Dec. 28, 1915. She
attended country school in Cloyd Valley. Her most remembered teacher was
Art Hagele. She attended two years of high school at Bowdle, but graduated
from Loyalton in 1935.

Lillian stayed home a couple of years after graduation to help on the farm.
In 1937 she went to Litchfield, MN and got a job in a produce company for
two years. Then she moved to Lockeford, CA and worked at Stockton Ordnance
Training in data processing. During World War II she worked long hours to
keep supplies on hand.

In 1942 she moved to San Francisco to work for the U.S. Treasury Department
in data processing. Later she rented an apartment with her sister Esther
and worked for the Veterans Administration.

In 1948 Lillian married Angelo Toccolini. He had been in the Marine Corp.
and served in the Pacific. After his discharge he went to work in
construction. They moved to Santa Clara, CA (known as Silicon Valley) where
they have lived 33 years.

        Back: Linda, Raymond, Lillian, Angelo Front: Hyde and Renita

Their children are Renita who lives in Santa Rosa, CA and works in
radiology in a clinic. She married Hyde Gillespie. Linda married Bill
Thompson, a teacher and they live in Santa Clara, CA. They have a daughter.
Raymond operates his own business (Crown Bolt Co. Inc.) and lives in San
Clemente, CA.

ADOLPH and ESTHER [HOLWEGER] TREICHEL

Adolph Treichel, a farmer and salesman, was born Aug. 23, 1907 in Hudson
Township south of Bowdle. His parents were Gottlieb and Margaret Dumdei
Treichel. Gottlieb was born in 1866 in Germany and died in 1947. Margaret
was born in 1868 in Russia and died in 1917.

Adolph received a grade school education and in 1946 married Esther
Holweger. She was the daughter of Henry and Christine Holweger. Henry was
born in Glueckstahl, Russia in 1881 and Christine was born in 1887 in
McPherson County. Both are deceased. Esther was born Dec. 13, 1913 in Grand
Forks County, ND.

After their marriage Adolph and Esther Treichel farmed in Hudson Township
20 years, then moved into Bowdle and purchased the house built by pioneer
Judge Ham, which was owned by John J. Hoven. Adolph became a salesman for
the Newton Company. After 30 years ill health forced his retirement. He
died Nov. 6, 1984.

The couple had three children. Marla Kay was born in May 1941. She is a
public school teacher at Hull, IA and married Donald Hungerford.

        Back: Leland, Merlin, Adolph Front: Esther and Marla Treichel

Merlin Gale was born in May 1944, is a salesman living at Mina and his wife
is Donna.

Leland Niel was born March 17, 1951. He lives with his wife Tracy in Roscoe
where he has served as mayor. He is an insurance salesman.

LAWRENCE P. and MILDA [ALDINGER] VETCH

Lawrence Peter was born at Roscoe Dec. 14, 1920 to John and Elizabeth
(Bernbum) Vetch. He farmed with his father near Roscoe and later served in
the U.S. Army during World War II. He married Milda Aldinger Aug. 23, 1947.
She was born Sept. 23, 1924 at Bowdle to Robert and Minnie (Haar) Aldinger.

After Lawrence and Milda were married they lived on different farms near
Bowdle. Later they moved to Bowdle where Lawrence worked for Harton
Construction of Aberdeen. For several years he was employed by Bowdle
Hardware where he was self-employed as a digger. Then the family again
moved to a farm east of Bowdle, but Lawrence joined Henry Leidholdt and
they did carpenter work.

Milda worked for about 15 years in various restaurants and still works
part-time, along with her flower shop operation. The Vetches were blessed
with six children.

Their first child LeRoy died in infancy.

Molly Ann was born July 1, 1951. She married Dave Wurtz and they live on a
farm east of Bowdle. Dave farms and works at the creamery while Molly works
part-time at a restaurant. They have a daughter Mindy.

Lonnie Lynn was born July 1, 1952. He married Lexie Schlecht and they live
in Watertown where Lexie manages B.P.I. Lumber Co. Their children are
Glenda and Misty.

Ronnie Larry was born Dec. 5, 1954. He married Marsha Judd. They live in
Graham, WA with their children Dana, Kylee and Bradley.

Jean Kay was born Aug. 6, 1955 and married Alan Sandquist. They live in
Aberdeen where Alan owns a body shop. Their children are Randy, Kirsten and
David.

Marla Kay was born July 31, 1965. She married David Langley and they live
in Maryland. They have a son Joshua.

CHRIST C. and ROSE [ROESCH] VOGELE

Christ C. Vogele was born on a farm in McIntosh County near Venturia, ND
Jan. 19, 1897. In 1898 he moved with his parents to a homestead five miles
east of Lowry. May 11, 1919 he married Rose Roesch, who was born in South
Russia and came to America when six months old. She and her parents settled
on a farm near Tolstoy.

        Christ and Rose Vogele

Rose and Christ Vogele farmed nine miles east of Lowry until 1945 when they
retired and moved to Bowdle. Christ was active in church and civic affairs.
In June 1969 he died at the age of 69. Rose is still alive at age 86 and
lives in the Mobridge Care Center.

Their children all attended Bowdle High School. They were Ida (Mrs. Hugo
Goehring) of Mobridge; Dr. Alvin C. Vogele of Aberdeen and Velda (Mrs. Ray
Nelson) of Fargo, ND.

HAROLD and VIRGINIA [HAUX] VOLLER

Harold, the eldest son of Jacob and Esther Linden Voller, was born Oct. 31,
1924 in Ipswich. He attended grade school in Modena Township where his
father was farming land. He completed two years of high school in Bowdle
and then farmed with his parents until February 1945 when he was inducted
into the U.S. Army. He served in the German Theatre of Operations November
1945 until October 1946, receiving his honorable discharge. He returned to
Bowdle and resumed farm operations with his father.

Virginia and Harold Voller

Oct. 1, 1950 he was united in marriage to Virginia Haux, daughter of the
late Henry and Emma Pleinis Haux of Java. Virginia is a graduate of Selby
High School. Harold and Virginia made their home on the farm until 1976
when they built a home in Bowdle on the site of the original Phillips 66
Station along old Highway 12.

Harold still helps farmers in the spring and summer, but is semi-retired.
He is an active member of the Bowdle American Legion Post. Virginia is an
officer of the Bowdle American Legion Auxiliary Unit, having served as
treasurer the past 15 years. She is also active in the work of her church
and is president of the St. Paul's American Lutheran Church Women.

JACOB and ESTHER [LINDEN] VOLLER

Jacob Voller and Esther Linden were married Dec. 5, 1922. In 1923 they
built a home in Modena Township and farmed there until October 1950 when
they moved to Bowdle.

Two of their four sons, Harold and Herbert, continued farming. Robert was
employed as a telegrapher and station agent by the Chicago, Milwaukee and
St. Paul Railroad in Montana and was freight agent at Billings, his present
home. George attended a school for mechanics in Fargo and is now employed
by the International Harvester dealer in Powell, WY.

        Esther and Jacob Voller

Jacob Voller was a veteran of World War I and was in France when the war
ended. His Army duties included shoeing horses and mules and other
blacksmith work. He enjoyed working with tools and had a blacksmith shop on
the farm. After moving to town he operated a blacksmith shop east of
Highway 47, where he was busy until health problems developed and he died
Nov. 21, 1974.

Esther Voller taught rural schools near Ipswich and in Modena Township.
After marriage she found plenty to do as a farmer's wife and mother of four.
She raised turkeys, geese, ducks and chickens; milked cows, fed calves and
pigs; tended a big garden and generally had extra help to cook for and
boarded teachers.

After moving to town she became active in community
organizations--extension club, PTA, American Legion Auxiliary, St.
Augustine's Catholic Church and Altar Society and Senior Citizens. She
served several years as city magistrate and was a reporter and columnist
for The Bowdle Pioneer several years. Writing is one of her hobbies. She
also enjoys crafts and music.

In 1983 Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Eisenbeisz Jr. bought the Voller farm home,
which had been farmed by Herbert Voller.

JOE and ADELINE [AMAN] VOLLER

Joe, the seventh son of John and Katherine Voller, was born Jan. 29, 1902
in Bowdle. His parents were born in Russia. John lived 1857-1940 and
Katherine 1861-1927.

Joe took as his bride Adeline Aman, daughter of Rochus and Margaret Aman of
Java. She was born Jan. 31, 1912 and was a graduate of Java High School.
Rochus was born in Russia Dec. 9, 1870 and died in Java June 25, 1952.
Margaret was also born in Russia June 25. 1872 and died March 25, 1956.

        Back: Virginia and Lloyd. Front: Adeline and Joe

Joe and Adeline were married Oct. 21, 1931 and their first home was
established on a farm eight miles northeast of Bowdle in Modena Township. In
1943 they moved to Bowdle where Joe opened his own garage and began a
modest auto repair business.

The year 1952 was a bad one. Their home was gutted by fire and they lost
most of their possessions. After moving several times they built a home
just east of the city limits on land Joe owned and where he had established
his repair and salvage business. He is still engaged in some farming.

They had two children. Lloyd, born Jan. 21, 1933, is a veterinary assistant
and Virginia, born Dec. 28, 1939, is the wife of Harry Bieber and lives in
Bismarck, ND.

Lloyd and his wife Renata (Buechler) have a son Terron. They make their
home near the repair and salvage business east of the city. Virginia and
Harry Bieber have two children Debra (Bieber) Ely and Todd. Debra Bieber
Ely has a daughter Allison.

Many friends and relatives gathered at the Bowdle Senior Center in October
1981 to help Joe and Adeline celebrate 50 years of married life.

JOHN and KATHERINE VOLLER

In 1882 John and Katherine Voller and their two children Dennis and
Margaret left Odessa, Russia and with a trunkful of clothing and household
supplies, crossed the Atlantic to make a new home in a prairie state which
welcomed homesteaders. They first homesteaded near Faulkton. John worked
for a farmer in that area who kept the Voller family supplied with food and
also allowed them to use a small piece of farmland to raise grain and
vegetables.

In that community there were few who spoke German and they moved to another
homestead in Modena Township. Here they felt more satisfied in their sod
house with a sister and brother of Katherine living nearby. John continued
working for farmers and sometimes was absent for several weeks. When he
returned to his family he carried supplies on his back that he had bought,
even 50 pounds of flour. He was a man of great strength and with thrift he
finally became the owner of a team of horses and machinery for farming.

Near the sod house an outdoor oven was built where Katherine baked large
loaves of bread. Fuel for the oven was straw and its wall was a warm spot
where the children kept warm. Seven more boys and two girls were born after
the Vollers settled in South Dakota and to make room for them a house was
built of lumber. Margaret, the eldest girl, often told of sitting at the
sewing machine sewing for the family and keeping a watchful eye on her
younger sisters and brothers. In addition there was always worn and torn
clothing to be mended.

Katherine had a spinning wheel and carded wool that was clipped from their
flock. When the ducks and geese began moulting feathers, she plucked the
loose feathers which later filled pillows or feather beds. Nothing was
wasted. When a goose was dressed the last joint of the wing, with all the
feathers in tact, was cut off and saved to be used in cleaning out ashes
and soot that accumulated inside the cook stove between the oven and stove
top.

John did his own blacksmith work and his sons learned the trade, assisting
or watching him. All became skilled mechanics. Before combines were made
grain was cut by headers or binders drawn by horses. Headed grain was
stacked and often twine-tied bundles were too. Threshers were scarce and
snow could fall before a farmer got his grain into bins. John and Dennis
bought a thresher separator and huge tractor and threshed their crop, as
well as their neighbors. With home-raised work horses and machinery farming
was profitable and John increased his acreage, buying another farm in the
eastern part of Modena Township. Here the Dennis Vollers farmed before
building on land close to Highway 47.

About 1918 John and Katherine Voller moved to Ipswich. They later built a
house in Hillsview where they resided until their deaths, Katherine in 1927
and John in 1940. They were preceded in death by two sons Valentine and
Peter. Since then Dennis, Anton, Jacob, Steve, Margaret, Madelena and
Libbie have died with Andrew and Joe surviving.

In 1983 the land that John and Katherine homesteaded was bought by a
neighbor Arthur Eisenbeisz Jr.

Mr. and Mrs. John Voller and sons Valentine, Peter, Anton and Jacob are
buried in St. Augustine's Catholic Cemetery in Bowdle. Margaret is buried
in Eureka, Libbie in Aberdeen, Madelena in Bakersfield, CA, Steve in
Yakima, WA and Dennis in Baldwin Park. CA.

LLOYD and RENATA [BUECHLER] VOLLER

Lloyd was born to Joe and Adeline (Aman) Voller Jan. 21, 1933 at Bowdle. He
was educated at the Bowdle School and then served two years in the Armed
Services. Lloyd married Renata Buechler, daughter of August and Rose
Buechler. Renata was born March 1, 1935 at Bowdle.

        Lloyd, Terron, Renata Voller

After their marriage Lloyd worked about a year for a construction crew.
Later he worked for Arlyn Erbe as a farm laborer. In 1963 Lloyd and Renata
built a home on the east end of main street near his parents.

Lloyd worked with his father as a mechanic and farmer. At present he is
employed with the veterinarian Jacob Sieck and Renata works at Turner Drug.

They are the parents of a son Terron who was born July 13, 1971.

NELS and REGINA [WENTZ] WALTMAN

Nels Waltman, a businessman of Bowdle 35 years, was born in Aberdeen in
1905 and moved with his parents to a farm near Onaka about 1920. He also
became a farmer and in 1929 took as his bride Regina Wentz, daughter of
Valentine and Johanna (Thomas) Wentz of Bowdle.

They established their home on a farm near Onaka. Harold was born in Bowdle
in 1930, James arrived in 1932, Alice was born in 1938 and Shirley
completed the family arriving in 1940.

In 1942 Nels and Regina brought their family to Bowdle and opened Waltman
Confectionery in a building that at one time housed Bryon Painter Shoe Shop
and Pressler Dress Shop. Waltman's Confectionery was very popular with the
young and old of the community. After 20 years in business, in 1962 Nels
sold the business to Harvey Bonen and put up the building south of the city
where they opened a butchering and meat market service. Their German
sausage was soon in demand over the whole countryside.

The work was hard and hours long and in 1967 Nels sold this business to
Everet and Angie Lemke and retired. They purchased the Aurand house which
had been the home of Regina's parents in 1970 where Regina now lives
keeping busy with handiwork such as tatted or crocheted tableclothes,
bedspreads and afghans for her family. Nels Waltman died in 1972.

        Harold, Alice, Regina, Nels, James, Shirley

Their children were educated in Bowdle Schools. Harold, a civil service
employee, married Esther Anderson at Hot Springs. They live in Security, CO
and have four children: Marcy, Monty, Lonny and Brian.

James earned his masters from Northern State College at Aberdeen. He and
his wife Rosella (Krier) of Presho live in Rapid City where Jim is a
principal in an elementary school. Their children are Kelly and Scott.

Alice received her R.N. Degree from St. Luke's Presentation School of
Nursing. She married Kenneth Schulte of Hoven, who is a pressman for the
Chicago Sun Times. They live in Midlothian, IL and have three sons: Tim,
Jeff and Keven.

Shirley married Eugene G. Larson, who is a mill wright by trade. They live
in Richland, WA and have three children: Debbie, Peggy and Wesley.

CHRIST and PAULINE [MUELLER] WALZ

Christ Walz was born on a farm near Freeman Sept. 24, 1889 to Friedrick and
Marguretha (Becker) Walz. When Christ was still a child his parents
homesteaded a farm southeast of Java.

Christ married Pauline Mueller and they farmed in the Java area. Christ
also worked as a custom thresher. Five children were born to this couple:
Ella Hochhalter, Frieda Schott, Althea Hochhalter Scott, Metha Hochhalter
and Gerhardt. During the flu epidemic of 1918 Pauline Walz died Oct. 25, and
Christ moved his family to a farm near Hoven called the Bonen farm.

Christ then married Louisa Baer Mueller in 1921 and they established their
home eight miles north of Hoven. Two sons were born to this union, Erwin
and Roman. Roman died May 4, 1948.

Christ loved music. He formed a band with his family and brother Fred. The
violin was his instrument and he coaxed its melodies forth with his left
hand. The family band played at barn dances and other events in the area.
Christ was the organist at Baer Church 30 years and was active in the
affairs of the Country Lutheran Church.

        Back: Metha and Ella Front: Frieda, Pauline, Althea, Christ, Gary

Christ was stricken with a stroke in 1944. Unable to get around much after
that he and his wife moved into town and he lived in the Eureka Nursing
Home until Aug. 22, 1954 when he died.

FERDINAND and EMILIE [BIEBER] WALZ

Ferdinand Walz was born in 1897 in Freeman. His future bride Emilie Bieber
was born in Eureka in 1903. They both grew up in Walworth County south of
Java and were married in November 1921.

        Back: Ferdinand and Emilie Front: Norwin, Orville, Leota

Their first home was northwest of Hoven on the Herman Bonen farm where they
lived one year. Then they moved to what is now the Herbert Bieber farm
south of Java. It was on this farm their three children were born: Leota.
Norwin and Orville.

Feb. 16, 1926 they bought the Alex Borg farm and two years later built a
home and moved to the new farm.

Their children are now mature and established. Leota married Robert Elkins.
They live in Richardton, ND. Norwin Walz married Darlene Albrecht and lives
on the home farm. They have five sons. Orville Walz married Delores Schuh.
They live on the Edwin Jurgenson homestead and have three daughters.

Ferdinand and his brother Christ owned a threshing rig and did a great deal
of threshing every fall. Ferdinand was active in church and community
affairs. He was a member of the Ryan District School Board many years and a
director of Java Equity Exchange.

Ferdinand and Emilie lived on the farm until the fall 1953 when they
retired and built a home in Bowdle where they enjoyed the fruits of their
labors. Ferdinand died March 19, 1975. Emilie continues to live in Bowdle.

FREDRICH and MARGARETHA [BECKER] WALZ

Fredrich J. Walz was born in South Russia in 1865 and came to the United
States in 1870 where his parents established their home on a farm. Here he
met and married Margaretha Becker, who was born in South Russia in 1867,
who also came to the States in 1870.

Their first home was on a farm near Freeman in 1897. In 1900 Fredrich J.
loaded all their belongings into a boxcar and shipped them to Bowdle, the
end of the railroad, and then to a farm three miles south and nine west in
what is now eastern Walworth County. The area was then known as the Baer
District.

The Walz family became members of Trinity Lutheran Church. The church had
been built on a hill and when lightning struck it and it burned to the
ground, the members got together and soon had another edifice erected for
worship services. This building was sold to the Faulkton Lutheran Church in
1946 and the members transferred to St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church
in Bowdle.

The Walz family now included Fredrich J., his wife Margaretha and their
children: Paulina (Baer), Christ, Ferdinand, Elsie (Gorne), Edward, Fred and
Theodore. Three died in early childhood.

Besides farming Fredrich J. was in the threshing business with Mr. Baer and
Mr. Miller. In 1911 he bought his own gas Mogul engine and threshing
machine and with the aid of his sons Christ and Ferdinand, they were in
business threshing for all the farmers in a 15-mile radius.

Fredrich J. died Oct. 24, 1918 during the terrible flu epidemic that
followed World War I. With the aid of her children Margaretha kept the farm
going until the Dirty Thirties. Those were the years when there was no rain
and strong wind. If a rain cloud floated in a strong wind swept up all the
dirt until the buildings were splattered with mud. The lilacs had no
fragrance that year and only smelled of dust.

In 1933 Fredrich Jr. took over the farming operations, along with the debts
and the feed and seed loans which had to be paid. Fred comments that the
farm was so far in debt that he thought he would never see the day when it
was free of incumbrances, but he continued to work and worry until the
1940's brought good harvests, good prices and life was brighter. Farmers
were able to buy much needed machinery, combines and tractors that made
their work a bit lighter.

        Christ, Fredrich, Paulina, Ferdinand, Margaretha

The Fifties the Walz family and a lot of others remember because of the
deep snow when drifts piled 15 feet high and there was no mail and no way
to get to town for weeks. The County Red Cross chairman Albert Senn secured
help from the U.S. Army with track snow vehicles and later the Commercial
Club brought in an airplane to reach the stranded people. Fred recalls not
only the hardship of no mail or groceries, but also of no cigarettes and
when the list of needed supplies was given, there was also the caution,
"don't forget the cigarettes."

        Fred Walz

This family enjoyed music in their home and Christ also played for barn
dances and Fred still plays the church organ on invitation.

Fred Walz Jr. sold the family farm to Orville Walz and Ernest Schumacher in
1969 and moved to Bowdle where he has made his home. He operates a Fix-It
Shop, doing radio and television repair and has served the public in this
capacity many years.

Second generation of the Fredrich J. and Margaretha Walz family who survive
are Elsie Gorne of Roscoe, Fred of Bowdle and Theo of Minneapolis.

GERHARD and QUENTIN WALZ FAMILIES

Gerhard (Gary) Walz was born on a farm southwest of Bowdle Nov. 24, 1916.
His parents were Christ and Pauline (Miller) Walz. In his youth Gary helped
his father with the farming and threshing. Although they were busy, the
family took time to play baseball Sunday afternoons, usually at the John
Bieber farm.

Being a musician Gary played for many barn dances. This is where he met
Lillian Schreter. She was the daughter of Henry and Marie (Baer) Schreter
of Lowry. Gary and Lillian were married Sept. 18, 1938.

They established their first home eight miles north of Hoven for two years
and then moved to a farm now occupied by Norman Schumacher. Here is where
their only child Quentin was born in 1940. After farming this area until
1956 they decided to purchase a close townsite farm, which is located just
north of the railroad tracks in Bowdle. Here they continued to milk cows
and raise small grain.

        Ron, Cheryl, Jordon, Derrick, Quentin, Marcella Gerhard, Annette,
        Lillian

        Darvin Walz

Their son Quentin attended Bowdle Schools. Being musically inclined like
his father, Quentin joined him and they played for many dances. In 1960
Quentin married Marcella Haar, daughter of Raymond and Helen Haar.

Marcella also attended Bowdle Schools. They live on the same farmsite as
his parents. Quentin operates a body repair shop, specializing in restoring
old automobiles. Marcella, a homemaker and part-time Watkins dealer, is
also a Sunday School teacher at Redeemer Lutheran Church. They had four
children.

Cheryl was born in 1960 and married attorney Ron Ottenbacher. They live in
Louisville, KY and have a son Jordon. Darvin, born in 1967, was tragically
killed in an automobile accident in 1981. Derrick, born in 1969 and
Annette, born in 1973, are students at Bowdle School.

NORWIN and DARLENE [ALBRECHT] WALZ

Norwin Walz, son of Mr. and Mrs. Ferdinand Walz, was born near Java March
9, 1925. He attended rural school and graduated from Java High School.

Darlene Albrecht, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Alex Albrecht, was born in
Bowdle March 21, 1931. She attended rural school and graduated from Bowdle
High School in 1949.

Their lives began together June 2, 1953 when they were united in marriage
at St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church in Bowdle. They moved to a farm
eight miles south of Java and still live there. It is a grain and livestock
operation.

        Back: Sheilan, Gavin, Bryan, Nolan Middle: Shawn, Darlene, Norwin,
        Cathy Front: Brandon, Shawna, Dustin

They were blessed with five boys. Shawn, born March 7, 1954, married Cathy
Bynum in Spring, TX June 4, 1977. Their children are Shawna, Dustin and
Brandon and they live in Rapid City.

Sheilan was born May 25, 1956 and is the right-hand man on the farm. Gavin
was born Nov. 21 1960 and graduated from SDSU in Brookings with an
agricultural engineer degree. Bryan was born June 14, 1963 and is attending
S.D. School of Mines in Rapid City. Nolan was born Oct. 9, 1967 and is a
senior at Bowdle High School.

Darlene writes, "There never was a dull moment on the farm. When we looked
out the window we never knew what to expect. Maybe one was on the silo,
windmill or walking across the top of the barn. One incident most people
won't forget was in 1958 when Norwin bought a new combine. He parked it in
the yard and had to run an errand in town. Sheilan, age two, climbed in the
combine which he started, backed up and wrecked the gas pump, garage and
combine. One day we got a horse. Bryan wanted to go for a ride. The horse
ran too fast for him so he decided to jump off. It took a few stitches to
repair the injuries. Gavin was bitten by our dog, which died the next day.
Gavin had to get rabies shots. At times we felt we were at the doctor more
than at home, either for stitches, broken bones or just plain illness.

Gavin and Bryan attended All-State Chorus. Gavin was also a boy stater. We
took each day at a time and have some very good memories of our family.

"Everyone in this area remembers the severe blizzard of 1966. We were very
fortunate. We and the cattle got through it fine. We still had the old coal
furnace that did not need electricity to run and kerosene stove, so we kept
warm and well fed. Another bad winter was 1977 and 1978. This was the first
time I was every called for jury duty. One morning they called that I
should come to Selby for court. I told them it was impossible because the
roads were blocked. That didn't stop things. The snowplow started for our
farm, followed by the County Sheriff. Norwin and I got in the tractor and
started from the farm when we met down the road, where I got an escort with
the Sheriff. This was a fun ride in a police car.

"The fall 1970 we moved our house to a new basement, added a kitchen and
entrance and completely remodeled the rest of the house.

"Norwin has been active in church affairs, served on the Java Equity Board
several years, as a member of the Crop Improvement he received the 1968
State Tree Farm Award, a member of Walworth County Extension Board and
Selby's Men Chorus. They organized in early 1975 and sang for Java and
Selby's 75th anniversary. The group performed at the lighting ceremony at
Mt. Rushmore in 1976 -- America's Bicentennial Year, at Governor Janklow's
inauguration in January 1979 and at the National Association of Wheat
Growers Convention in Phoenix, AZ. The program was presented in many South
Dakota cities."

Darlene is active in church and ladies aid, Java Band Mothers, Walco
Extension Club and Walworth County Extension where she is county
vice-president at present. She enjoys sewing, fancy work and crafts.

ORVILLE and DELORES [SCHUH] WALZ

Orville Walz was born in 1926 at Java to Ferdinand Walz. Delores Schuh was
born to Bertha and Baltaser Schuh in 1935 at Java. They grew up on farms in
Walworth County.

Orville graduated from Java High School and shortly thereafter entered the
U.S. Army serving in the Pacific Theatre during World War II. After his
discharge he farmed with his father and brother south of Java.

Delores completed her high school at Bowdle before their marriage in June
1954. They now live 13 miles southwest of Bowdle on what was known as the
Edwin Jurgenson homestead. The farm consists of 1200 acres with small grain
and livestock as the main source of income.

Orville enjoys flying and did crop spraying and aerial predator hunting for
many years in his Piper Cub.

Since their marriage Delores has received her degree in elementary
education at Northern State College and her master's in administration. She
is presently employed by the Selby School District as a sixth grade teacher.

        Back: Colleen, Laura, Wayne, Jeanne, Terry, Connie, Levi. Front:
        Delores, Orville, Jesse.

The family includes three daughters. Colleen is married to Wayne Winter, a
park ranger. Their home is in Custer State Park. Colleen is employed as
Custer County Health Nurse. They have a daughter Laura.

Connie married Terry Kary. They live in Selby. Terry is employed at Ken's
Western Lumber. Connie is a bookkeeper for Selby Equity Exchange. Their
sons are Jesse and Levi.

Jeanne graduated from South Dakota State University in May 1984 with a
degree in pharmacy and is employed as a pharmacist in Flagstaff, AZ.

JOHN and ELSIE [SCHLEPP] WEIL

Elsie Schlepp was born to Adam and Eugenia Dubs Schlepp March 14, 1920 in
New Leipzig, ND. She attended country grade schools near Bowdle and
graduated from Bowdle High School in 1936.

She attended business college in Minot, ND 1937-1938, went to work for the
Western Auto Parts Company for two years and Ward Mercantile Company for
three years in Minot until 1943. She joined the WAVES in March 1943 and
served as Chief Yoeman until May 1946. She was stationed at Hunter College,
NY; Stillwater, OK; Washington, DC and San Francisco with the Bureau of
Yards and Docks. She attended University of California in Berkeley August
1946 to June 1950, graduating with a bachelor of science degree in health
sciences and administration.

Elsie married John Philip Weil of Rodeo, CA in August 1949. They have two
children. Stephen Randall was born May 1951 and Jean Cheryl in October
1952. Elsie was a homemaker until 1973. In March of that year she went to
work as a health insurance clerk in a three-doctor office, Memorial Medica
Group, Inc. She became the business administrator of this group as it grew
to 12 physicians and 21 employees. She retired in October 1984.

John Weil is an education major, also a graduate of the University of
California in Berkeley where they met and married. He taught for two years,
then went into school business administration and served in that capacity
at various school districts located in Richmond, Pleasant Hill, Simi Valley
and Long Beach, all in California. He retired in July 1985.

        John and Elsie Weil

Plans for retirement are to make a nuisance of themselves visiting
relatives and friends who have been long neglected. The rest of the time
will be spent lying in hammocks, looking up at the clouds going by, sitting
in rocking chairs (and sometimes exercising by rocking slowly back and
forth!), walking quietly and stopping to smell the flowers, occasionally
to follow the wind and our dreams to some exciting part of the world.

MARVIN and BERNICE [SCHUMACHER] WEISHAAR

Marvin, son of Mr. and Mrs. R.J. Weishaar and Bernice, daughter of Mr. and
Mrs. C.C. Schumacher, grew up in Bowdle and graduated from Bowdle High
School. In 1936 they were married and left Bowdle for their home in
Chicago, IL where Marvin attended college the next seven years.

With the great discern and challenges facing the church he enrolled at
North Central College in Naperville, IL, a denominational college and
graduated with a bachelor of arts degree in history and psychology. In the
fall of 1939 he enrolled at the Theological Seminary, also in Naperville
and graduated three years later with a bachelor of divinity degree.

The road was not always easy for them in those seven years. Money was
scarce and very few good paying jobs were available. To stay afloat he
worked after school hours doing such things as washing windows, washing
down walls, scrubbing floors and manicuring lawns at a rate of 35 cents an
hour. While in the seminary he was elected to manage the school book store
which paid enough he no longer had to scrub floors.

Bernice also went to work to help out on the ever increasing expenses. She
worked for an independent grocer as a telephone girl seven years, starting
at $12 a week and at the end of seven years, her top salary was $18 a week.
She worked six days a week 7:30 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Over the years they have moved from Nebraska to Oklahoma, Kansas, Illinois
and lastly California. By then they were parents of three children: Sheldon,
Sharilyn and Brent. Bernice had resigned herself to the home
diaper-child business for a few years. She was often called upon to
entertain church officials or take an active part in the women's
organizations. She taught Sunday School, sang in the choir, played the
organ on occasion and did secretarial duties for the church when needed.

        Back: Marvin, Sharilyn, Sheldon Front: Bernice and Brent

In 1959 a call came from California to minister the Presbyterian Church in
Granada Hills. Marvin accepted the call and made the move in December. But
in 1971, with a new vision, Marvin resigned and set his sights on a
master's degree. This aim was fulfilled after one year of study with a
degree in family counseling. He then went to work for the Clergy Counseling
Center in Los Angeles, which position he held until retirement. Bernice
worked for a large insurance company 18 years, at which time she also
retired.

Retirement for both came in 1980 and after much thought they sold their
home in Granada Hills and moved to loveable, liveable Lodi. "Age is a gift
to enjoy ... the best is yet to come," Marvin says.

WILLIAM and ALTHEA [HIEB, BUECHLER] WEISHAAR

Althea's first husband Herman was born near Bowdle to Jacob and Katherina
(Jacober) Buechler Feb. 3, 1909. He received his education in a rural
school. He married Althea M. Hieb Oct. 24, 1935. She is the daughter of Mr.
and Mrs. Rudolph Hieb of Hosmer. Althea was born Sept. 22, 1913.

This young couple farmed in Walworth County four miles northwest of Bowdle.
They had five children, but not all of them learned to know their dad. He
was only 40 years old when he died unexpectedly Jan. 21, 1950. The oldest
child was only 13 and the youngest 4 months old.

It was a difficult winter for this young family with lots of snow. That
following spring the young widow auctioned the farm machinery and livestock
and moved to town.

To aid with the income she purchased a large home close to school and
rented the upstairs to tenants. She also did sewing, ironing and
housekeeping for people to help supplement the income.

        Herman and Althea Buechler

        Back: Janet, Robert, Marian, Marvin, Arlene Front: Althea and
        William Weishaar

In 1969 Althea moved to Aberdeen and continued to work at different jobs to
help support her family and give them an education. Later in Aberdeen she
married William Weishaar, also from Hosmer. He was a widower and they were
united in marriage April 16, 1979. He had no children, but through the
marriage gained a family which consisted of the following:

Arlene, born Oct. 10, 1936, married Wayne L. Pfitzer and lives in Las
Vegas, NV. Their children are Perry, Penny and Kelly. Arlene is a secretary.

Marvin was born Sept. 10, 1938. He married Janice Willmott and lives in
Kokomo, IN. He works for General Motors and they have a child Debborah.

Robert was born Nov. 30, 1944. He married Linda Johansen and lives in
Aberdeen where he works for 3M Company. Their children are Amy and Brian.

Marian was born Nov. 25, 1947 and lives in Minneapolis where she works at
Orthopedic Consultants. She has a son Tavyer.

Janet, born Oct. 4, 1949, is a captain in the U.S. Air Force stationed in
Illinois, but has been stationed in many European countries.

HENRY and ELLA [BLUMHARDT] WEISZ

Henry Weisz was born May 10, 1911 in Castor, Canada where his parents Gust
and Katie Riddel Weisz lived seven years. Gust was born in Crimea, Russia
Jan. 7, 1887 and died July 1959. Katie Riddel Weisz was born April 14, 1890
in Odessa, Russia and died Nov. 19, 1973.

Gust Weisz brought his family to the United States in 1918 and farmed in
the Akaska-Glenham area. Later they moved to Mobridge. After his death his
widow Katie moved to Bowdle.

Henry Weisz married Ella Blumhardt Nov. 18, 1934. She was the daughter of
Frank and Karolina Walth Blumhardt. Frank was born in Crimea, Russia March
18, 1885. Karolina was born Nov. 20, 1888 near Glueckstahl, Russia.

Frank and Karolina Blumhardt farmed 10 miles northeast of Bowdle until 1922
when they sold their equipment and moved to Bowdle. Frank was a cream buyer
until 1925 when they moved back to the farm where they lived until he died
July 9, 1939. Karolina then married Herman Bonen, the school custodian. She
died Nov. 25, 1976.

Henry and Ella Weisz farmed west of Roscoe three years, then moved to the
Peterson farm, then the Schick farm and then bought a farm 10 miles north
and one west of Bowdle where they farmed 37 years before moving into
Bowdle. Henry worked for A.G. Reuer until his death Oct. 22, 1984.

        Carol, Henry, Allen, Ella, Judy, Connie Weisz

The couple had five children. Judith was born May 18, 1933 and married
Robert Jarvis. They had two children: Janell and Brian. They lived in

They farm at Long Lake.

Dean was born Aug. 30, 1940 and died Dec. 18, 1940.

Allen was born June 8, 1942 and married Janice Junkert of Roscoe. Their
children are Sandra, Lyle and Michael. They live in New Iberia, LA where
Allen is a diesel mechanic.

Carol was born May 12, 1948. She married Lester Aman and they farm five
miles northeast of Hosmer. Their children are Victoria, Cheryl and Shelly.

Connie was born Nov. 24, 1957. She married Les Helm, who served in the
Armed Forces five years and is now a police officer in Redfield. Their
children are Jason, Matthew and Melissa.

ALEX J. and ANNA [BUECHLER] WEISZHAAR

Alex J. was born May 16, 1915 to Christ and Lydia (Walther) Weiszhaar. Both
parents were born in Campbell County. Christ was born July 26, 1893 and
died Aug. 23, 1950. Lydia was born Oct. 19, 1890 and died Jan. 9, 1973.

Anna's parents were John B. and Mary (Eisenbeisz) Buechler, both born in
Neugluecksthal, South Russia. (Their history is included in this book.)

        Anna and Alex Weiszhaar

Alex and Anna were married on a hot sultry day June 7, 1936. The wedding
ceremony was at 4 p.m. in Neuglueckstahl (Buechler) Church. The reception
was held at the Buechler farm. After the wedding they established their
first home three miles north of her folks for six years. When they started
farming everything was done with horses. Horse power changed to tractor
power within a few years. In 1943 they moved to Anna's parents farm and
lived there for 34 years. In 1975 they retired and sold the farm to Gary
Sandmeier, but Weiszhaars continued to live on the farm until they built a
home in 1977 in Bowdle. Alex continued to work for Sandmeiers during the
summer months until he had a fatal truck accident and died Sept. 21, 1979.

They were blessed with two sons and two daughters. Orville was born June 4,
1937 and is married to Barb Dorset. They live in Minneapolis where he has
his own psychology clinic and teaches.

DeWayne was born May 20, 1938. He married Karen Schlepp and he owns and
operates Haberer's Implement Inc. in Bowdle. Their children are Scott,
Becky, Mike and Curtis.

Marilyn was born Nov. 29, 1939. She married Robert Fischer. They have two
sons Bryan and Bradley. Marilyn is manager of the First Bank branch at
Rushmore Plaza in Rapid City.

Marsha was born March 28, 1952. She married Jerry Mertes and they have a
daughter Kristan. Marsha teaches at St. Anthony's School in Hoven and also
teaches piano.

CHRIST and LYDIA [WALTHER] WEISZHAAR

Christ Weiszhaar was born in Campbell County July 26, 1893. He was the son
of Jacob and Elizabeth (Bossert) Weiszhaar of Lowry.

Lydia Walther was born Oct. 19, 1890 in Campbell County to Alex and
Katherine (Wagner) Walther. Her family moved to the Linton, ND area.

The romance began when Christ was working in the Linton area with a
threshing crew. Christ and Lydia were married March 15, 1913. He worked as a
meat cutter at Ernie Merkel's meat market. He opened several filling
stations, the latest of which was the Phillips 66 where the Harold Voller
home is now. They also owned the home now belonging to Oscar Metzger.
Christ and Lydia owned and operated a meat market at Linton many years.
Their retirement years were spent in Selby. Christ died Aug. 23, 1950 and
Lydia died Jan. 9, 1973. They had seven children.

        Back: Freida, Oscar, Alex, Henry, Christ Jr. and Ernestine. Front:
        Christ Sr., Elsie, Lydia.

Ernestine married Theo Bollinger Jan. 11, 1934. She lives in Ashley, ND,
has a daughter and two granddaughters.

Alex married Anna Buechler June 7, 1936. They had two sons and two
daughters and lived on a farm seven miles northwest of Bowdle.

Christ Jr. married Viola Seiler and lives at Lodi, CA. They have four sons
and two daughters.

Frieda married Emil D. Buechler Dec. 3, 1939. They have a son and daughter
and live in Mobridge.

Oscar married Arlowice Strom. They have a son and daughter and live in
